en: In the *Mahābhāṣyadīpikā*, the first lesson [1.1]: The separate mention of Vedic words is for the purpose of making their preeminence known (*prādhānyakhyāpanārtham*). For even that which is included within a general category is seen to be taught separately when its preeminence is intended, as in: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived; Vasiṣṭha has also arrived. Alternatively, if only "of worldly words" were said, one might fail to understand that the word "worldly" (*laukika*), though a general term, refers here to a specific subset. This is an instruction solely regarding the words of common speech (*bhāṣāśabda*), not regarding Vedic words.

Because they are restricted to specific usages and have their own fixed Prātiśākhyas—since they follow what is observed in those texts—therefore both are included: namely, both the worldly (*laukika*) and the Vedic (*vaidika*). Now, one might object:

"If this is its nature, then this instruction does not apply to the Vedic words that appear in the Prātiśākhyas themselves. For there are persons who, due to negligence or incapacity, speak incorrectly even regarding those words for which this instruction exists; for example, the Taittirīyas pronounce the word *agni* with a cerebral *ṇ*. Furthermore," [the text continues].

And those words which, though not explicitly prescribed (*anāmnāta*), function toward the manifestation of the unprecedented (*apūrva*)—for example, in the injunction "having counted the potsherds, set them aside"—one sets them aside by means of the numbers conveyed by the word "counting," such as one, two, or three, in accordance with what is taught in the scripture. Similarly, regarding this [injunction] in the Agnihotra, "Do this like a human being," there too the words of application (*viniyoga-śabda*) are explained in the scripture as being to be employed; their functions reside in those [words]. And there is also a function in other [words] that have acquired a specific sequential order (*anupūrvī*).
How so? Prosperity results from practice preceded by the treatise; for those who employ [the means] having understood their true nature through the treatise, it is dharma.

[1.3] First, the worldly [words]: "cow," "horse," "man," "elephant," "brahmin. The particle *iti* here has the sense of "in this manner" (*ity-evaṃ-prakāra*), because the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) is undertaken with respect to such types of words. Furthermore, since in common usage it is precisely the words—which are the primary bearers of meaning within sentences and whose sequence is not fixed—that are subjected to grammatical analysis, only those that constitute words (*pada*) are indicated as "worldly. As for the non-human Vedic [words], since terms such as *śam* and so forth are never used in isolation, it is the sentences themselves that are indicated.

The instruction concerns only those words that reside within sentences, not the sentences themselves. Furthermore, all of this is merely the author of the Bhāṣya’s introduction to stating his purposes; it is stated before the explanation of the purposes for the sake of encouraging the students.

[2.1] Now, this word *go* (cow) is a term whose constituent parts refer to many meanings, such as "denotation" (*abhidhā*) and so forth; and all of that has been pointed out by the author of the Bhāṣya. Just as the word *saṃskāra* has multiple meanings in other treatises, so too is this the case here. If, in the phrase *śabdānuśāsanam*, the word *śabda* is assumed to function in its conventional sense, then the instruction (*anuśāsana*) would be entirely redundant; for worldly words are already established through common usage, and Vedic words are established in the Veda itself.

In this regard, just as someone might say "Now, therefore, we shall explain inhalation and exhalation" and speak thus in vain, so too is the expression "instruction of words" (śabdānuśāsanam). Therefore, in this context, the word *śabda* cannot apply to its conventional meaning. This is likewise true for the phrase "of which words? and for examples such as "cow," "horse," and "man. Thus, if the word *śabda* is employed here in its actual sense, there is a purpose in providing an instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding that very thing.

Now, if there exists some other technical term (*pāribhāṣika-śabda*) for this [word], whose instruction is being given, and that [term] does not itself fall under the category of a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), then [one must ask]: "In the word *gauh*, what is the word? Alternatively, the word has two parts: the part consisting of its own form (*svarūpa-bhāga*) and the part consisting of its meaning (*artha-bhāga*). Since an explanatory analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of the formal part would be useless, the second part is resorted to; because of the analysis of that [meaning-part], it is said "by means of the word" (*śabdena*). This is just as when, having begun with the statement "we shall explain Dharma," the instruction on substances and so forth follows precisely for the sake of understanding that [Dharma].
Moreover, in this case, substances and so forth are expressed by the word "cow" through association.

[2.2] In this regard, he sets forth those [features] residing in the word "cow": Is that which consists of the dewlap, tail, hooves, hump, and horns the actual form of the object? For one who holds that the substance (*dravya*) is the referent of the word, the horns and so forth—which are in contact with the substance—are the differentiators of the object for a substance that is otherwise indefinable and untouched by any other attribute when the word "cow" is uttered; but they are not so for that which is expressed by the word "non-cow. Just as the sweetness of molasses differentiates it from other substances in the dark, such that one knows, "This is molasses, not another substance."

The meaning is that the "mass of cow" (*gopiṇḍa*) has the form of an object (*artha*). He says: "No; it is called a substance (*dravya*). He says: "No; it is not well-known here as the word 'cow' (*gośabda*) itself. What then? It is well-known by means of another property (*dharmāntara*). And he demonstrates this other property: "It is called a substance. Just as in the case of number, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is produced from two [words] because the meaning of the number is not understood [otherwise] and because it is the referent of another word (*anyapadārthatva*), so too is there a multiple remainder (*anekaśeṣa*).

Why would there be a designation by means of another convention, abandoning the well-known convention of "substance" (*dravya*)? If the instruction on substance were intended, he would have simply said, "the instruction on substance. What then [is meant by] "gestures," "movements," and "winking"? A "gesture" (*iṅgita*) is a certain modification of the body that indicates an intention. "Movement" (*ceṣṭita*) is the vibration of the body. "Winking" (*nimiṣita*) refers to the actions pertaining to the eyes.

How could one consider these [actions] to be "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*)? Because these actions are possible; for these actions are indeed possible for the sake of the cow. Alternatively, it is the universal (*jāti*) of cowness itself that possesses the nature of action, just as there is the expression of the action "existence" (*sattā*). Just as "gone" refers to cowness, so too, by implication, "gestures" (*iṅgita*) and so forth are observed in buffaloes and other animals.

Even if one resorts to etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) for the object [of the word], then like the word *gama* (going), it would require an improper qualifier, such as "the cow goes," "the cow roars," or "the cow speaks. In this way, even blinking and so forth are designated by the term "sound" (*śabda*). To this, he states that there is indeed a well-known distinction based on another property: "No," he says, "for that is called action (*kriyā*). But what about [words] such as "white" or "blue"? These too possess the capacity to exist, and because they abide specifically, like gestures and the like.

The properties belonging to the domain of a cow, such as whiteness and so forth, are distinct from those belonging to the domain of a horse. And because they are distinct, when the horse is called "white," "red," or "golden," and the cow is called "white," "red," or "blue," [the distinction is evident]. Likewise, even if the word *varṇa* is understood as an instrument (*sādhana*), meaning "that by which one goes" (*gamyate 'nena*), it can still be conceived thus: by means of "whiteness" and so forth, it is understood that "this [cow] is a different entity from that [horse]. [To this] he says: "No; that is what is called a quality (*guṇa*)."

To this, he says that it is not the case [that this is a separate meaning] because it is stated by means of another cognition, namely: "That which is called a quality (*guṇa*) is not [the universal]," because [the universal] is designated as a substance (*dravya*). This is not a fault, because there is a twofold statement. White and so forth were previously presented as being like substances; now, however, the designation refers to qualities. As for the statement, "What remains undivided when [the object] is divided," this expresses the oneness [of the universal]; "what remains uncut when [the object] is cut" expresses the permanence of the genus (*jāti*); and "it is the common nature (*sāmānyabhūtam*)"—here the word *bhūta* expresses a comparison.

In this regard, for those [theorists] for whom *jāti* (universal) is a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhūta*), the "cowness" (*gotva*) that persists through specific individual cows (*gopiṇḍa*) is the commonality (*sāmānya*) among them, and not among all things such as horses; thus, the connection with comparison (*upamā*) depends upon that [distinction]. For those [theorists] for whom it [the universal] is identical with the substances themselves, it has been stated that even though non-difference from certain things is not possible, there is the status of being a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇatva*) because of the exclusion of those [things] from which non-difference is impossible, and because of the inclusion of that from which the cognition of non-difference is possible. To this, he says: "No, that is called *ākṛti* (form)."

"Form" (*ākṛti*) is not that configuration (*saṃsthāna*); what then? It is simply the universal (*jāti*). As Vājapyāyana says, "it is by means of the form that [the universal] is manifested. It is called *ākṛti* because "by it things are formed" (*ākriyate ’nayā*). It is called *ākṛti* because "things are differentiated from other categories" (*ākriyante... bhidyante padārthāntarebhyaḥ*). It is called *ākṛti* because "cognition and the word are established therein" (*ākriyete buddhi-śabdau*). Now, since substance and the other categories have been refuted, only two possibilities remain: either a collection (*samudāya*) or some technical designation (*pāribhāṣika*).

In this context, even a collection (*samudāya*) is well-known as a "collection," just like a substance (*dravya*) and so forth; nor does there exist any other technical term for it. Furthermore, since employing what is already well-known would be redundant, he asks: "What, then, is a word (*śabda*)," [answering] with the words, "that which, when uttered... Here, there are several views. Some think: "That which is uttered is sequential and perishable; however, another non-sequential essence of speech (*śabdātman*), residing in the intellect, penetrates [the mind], and from that, the comprehension of meaning arises. Why? [Because...]

Others think: "Just as a part of a letter, being dependent on another [letter], does not cause another [letter] to be understood, so too that which is dependent on its own form (svarūpa) is not capable of causing [the universal] to be understood. Just as the fourth parts of letters manifest the letter-universal (*varṇajāti*), so too those letters which arise in sequence and are not simultaneous within different sentences manifest that letter-universal residing in the word (*padasthā*); for example, the word 'vṛkṣa' [manifests] 'treeness' (*vṛkṣatva*). From this universal, the meaning is apprehended."

And this very nature of the object is this *sphoṭa* itself, which is the eternal essence of speech (*śabdātmā*). However, those [entities] which arise in succession, occurring at non-simultaneous times, are the manifestations (*vyaktayaḥ*) whose essence is sound (*dhvani*). Others think thus: "Speech possesses two powers; it is capable of manifesting both itself and the object, just as a lamp, while illuminating itself, illuminates hidden objects. But that internal illumination called the sense-organ (*indriya*), while not illuminating itself, illuminates the external object.

Therefore, the phrase "by which [word] is uttered" is explained in two ways: either as "by which, when uttered and manifested," or simply as "by which is uttered. Alternatively, it means "that whose referent is well-known. In the case of the word *śabda*, its well-known referent is *dhvani* (sound). *Dhvani* is its denotable meaning. Through sound, this [word] acquires its own form independently of context, purpose, and other words. He explains this very point by using the term *pada* (word).

The meaning of this word is that the meaning [of a term] is not something to be understood from a sentence; this is the literal sense (*śabda*). For what purpose, then, is this stated? Because the engagement with a topic is seen to proceed through either the determination (*nirṇaya*) or the rejection (*apākaraṇa*) [of alternatives]. For example, when asked, "How many sons do you have?", the question has already issued forth by presupposing a number. The determination of that number occurs either through affirmation or through negation. Someone might say, "One," or "Two," or "Many."

Even if one were to say, "I do not have even one," this person would simply be rejecting the question, implying that it is not at all a question that ought to be asked. Likewise, here too, in the case of the word "cow" (*gauh*), the question "What is the word? is not at all to be asked, because it would contradict what is already well-established. Whatever is already established as a word is precisely what is grasped by the term "word. Furthermore, he explains that its referent is already understood: one says, "Make a sound" (*śabdaṃ kuru*), "Do not make a sound" (*mā śabdaṃ kārṣīḥ*), or "This boy is making a sound" (*śabdakāry ayaṃ māṇavakaḥ*); thus, one who is producing a noise is called "one who makes a sound."

In that context, the phrase "making a sound" (*dhvaniṃ kurvan*) is employed as being related to the expression "this is the effect of sound" (*śabdakāryam*). However, in the two preceding cases, something else must be understood [as the object]. Alternatively, he who makes a sound is impelled [with the command], "Make a sound. And thus, one whose action has already commenced is prohibited; that is, one who is just beginning to produce a sound is prohibited with the words, "Do not make a sound. But is it not the case that sound (*dhvani*) is a quality of the word (*śabda*)? For it has been stated thus: "The *sphoṭa* is the word; *dhvani* arises from its manifestation through the air."

It is said: words such as *dravya* (substance) and so forth do not exist [as ultimate entities]. Since there is no purpose for distinguishing between "sound" (*dhvani*) and "word" (*śabda*) in an inquiry directed toward such [ultimate] ends, they are designated as one. As for the other [view]: if there is no contradiction with established usage, that very word which is common in the world is what is relied upon; and this treatise is the instruction concerning that [word].

[3] Furthermore, engagement with this treatise regarding study occurs only when there is a purpose; and a purpose exists only when there are actual objectives. This [treatise], however, is not an obligatory duty (*nityakarman*) that must necessarily be performed. In the case of an obligatory duty, non-engagement constitutes demerit (*adharma*); in the case of non-obligatory duties, one may act according to one's desire. If there were no purposes for this, one would not engage in it; therefore, he asks: "What, then, are the purposes of this instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*)? The purposes are:
preservation (*rakṣā*), addition (*āgama*), brevity (*laghu*), and the removal of doubt (*asaṃdeha*).

[3.1] Protection (*rakṣā*) is defined as the avoidance of the loss of an existing meaning. For one who knows elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and the modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*) will correctly preserve the Vedas. An example of elision: in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is the elision of *pīvaḥ*, *upa*, and *vasana* in the compounds *pīvopavasanānām* and *payopavasanānām*. An example of augmentation: in the Vedic language, the suffix *duk* is added after *nīca* to form *nīcāduccā*. Likewise, there is the substitution of *yaK* for the absolutive suffix *ktvā*: "Having bestowed good fortune upon her, go back home" (*saubhāgyam asyai dattvāyāthāstaṃ viparetana*). An example of modification: in the Vedic language, the root *hṛ* and *grah* undergo the change to *bh* (e.g., *hṛgrahorbhaḥ*).

Therefore, O fair maiden, why do you desire me—an aged man, worthless, quivering, and having the form of a *kṛtyā*? Thus, the gods increased the *brahman* as both elevation and depression. He takes [the portion] of honey. In some places there is no modification. He says: "There may be a transposition of [suffixes] such as *-syat-*; therefore, by the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the word is correct according to the *kṛt* suffixes. For example: *triṣṭubh aujaḥ śubhitam ugravīram*. One would expect *suhitam*."

[Objection: But surely, here [in this world], elisions, augmentations, and modifications of phonemes are already known through the recitation of the entire Vedic corpus exactly as it exists. [Reply: It is said: because the performance [of recitation] depends upon the performer; and the performer might pronounce it otherwise due to negligence, a defect of the ear, or forgetfulness, or he might be in doubt. Furthermore, those who know that [Veda] are not present, while there are others who know other treatises. If one were to pronounce something other than the Veda, one would pronounce it indistinctly (*mliṣṭam*). Therefore, such a state of affairs existing, no one at all would be able to correctly apply [the Veda].
Furthermore, grammar should be studied for the sake of refining oneself; therefore, the term "correctly" is included. For one who has refined himself is capable of correctly preserving the Vedas.

[3.2.1] Furthermore, there is *ūha* (modification). There is a lack of capacity in modified forms (*vikāra*) for those [words] that possess capacity in the original form (*prakṛti*). When the original form is required for the purpose of taking up [a meaning], it is modified by means of another word, gender, or number. For example: in the original form, the word *agni* is seen to be capable in the phrase *agnayaḥ*. In the modified forms, there is *ūha*. When a partial extraction occurs and the application [of the original] is set aside, there arises the necessity of either deviating from the primary function or taking up a different meaning.

The employment [of a word] occurs when one meaning functions in place of another meaning. In that case, if the modification (*vikāra*) were performed silently or in a whisper while the original form (*prakṛti*) possessed sound, the modification would become soundless. Alternatively, if the word "fire" (*agni*) itself were employed, its primary function (*mukhyā vṛttiḥ*) would not convey the sense of the sun. Furthermore, if its application to the sun—another meaning based on a quality (*guṇa*)—were resorted to by bypassing its primary function, one would be relying on a mode of linguistic operation that is contrary to the nature of the original form.
Therefore, in this instance, a different sentence with this specific inflection is employed.

[3.2.2] There occurs modification (*ūha*) due to differences in gender, number, and case. For example: "O divine waters, you are pure" (*devīrāpaḥ śuddhā yūyam*); "O divine clarified butter, you are pure" (*deva ājya śuddhaṃ tvam*). This word *śuddham*, ending in the nominative case and having its nominal stem meaning not separated [from the attribute], is used when it is in the vocative case. Similarly, for other case endings as well: *āyurāśāste* becomes *āyurāśāsāte* and *āyurāśāsate*.

However, for those [mantras] which lack the capacity for the primary meaning due to the injunction—for example, in the archetype (*prakṛti*) where the injunction "O Vāyus, stand! O Upāyus, stand! prescribes the calf (*vatsa*) in the plural—it is because of that incapacity that there is no modification (*ūha*) in the modified form (*vikṛti*). Likewise, even when only a single tether (*pāśa*) is present in the archetype, the plural ending is heard in the mantra, "May Aditi release the tethers" (*aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu*). In that case as well, there is no modification in the modified form. But among the Vājasaneyins, it is recited with the singular ending: "Aditi [releases] the tether" (*aditiḥ pāśam*).

Modification (*ūha*) applies to them if Aditi is present there; or else, by the rule "there is no modification regarding the fetters" (*pāśeṣu nohaḥ*), this is a Vedic option (*naigama-vibhāṣā*). When the plural number occurs, the usage may be as desired. Thus, in the Veda, it is recited in the feminine gender: "Thou art swift, held by the mind, beloved by Viṣṇu; of thee, who hast true impulse... (*jūrasi dhṛtā manasā juṣṭā viṣṇave tasyāste satyasavasaḥ*).

Therefore, when in the *sādyaskra* sacrifices a three-year-old bull with testicles (*sāṇḍa*) serves as the purchase-price for Soma (*somakrayaṇa*), then, without regard for the function of the words directed toward a female, they substitute an unseen masculine word in the Veda that denotes a male object: "Thou art swift, held by the mind, beloved of Viṣṇu; of thee, whose impulse is true... (*jūrasi dhṛto manasā juṣṭo viṣṇave tasya te satyasavasa*).

Likewise, in the praise of the *rājakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchase at the royal sacrifice), it is recited in the feminine gender: "Thou art thought (*cit*), thou art mind (*manas*), thou art intellect (*dhī*), thou art the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), thou art worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyā*), thou art the ruling power (*kṣatriyā*), thou art Aditi, double-headed; as such, be favorable to us from the front and from behind; O Goddess, come hither to the God. In the *Sādyaskra* sacrifices, however, it is modified into the masculine gender: "Thou art thought, thou art mind, thou art intellect, thou art the sacrificial fee, thou art worthy of sacrifice, thou art the ruling power, thou art double-headed; as such, be favorable to us from the front and from behind; O God, come hither to the God."

In the same way, they carry him [the fire] for one who desires strength (*vājameyin*). Likewise, in the mantra for leading the Soma-purchase cow (*somakrayaṇī*), there are feminine gender words such as: "Thou art a Vasu; thou art a Rudra; thou art Aditi; thou art an Ādityā; thou art Candrā. In the *Sādyaskra* sacrifices, there is a modification (*ūha*) of these: "Thou art a Vasu; thou art a Rudra; thou art Aditi; thou art an Āditya; thou art Candras. In the *Sādyaskra* sacrifices, there is a modification of these: "Thou art a Vasu; thou art a Rudra; thou art Aditi; thou art an Āditya; thou art Candras. In the *Sādyaskra* sacrifices, there is a modification of these: "Thou art a Vasu; thou art a Rudra; thou art Aditi; thou art an Āditya; thou art Candras."

Likewise, when a mantra is recited in the masculine gender for an animal victim, one applies a wooden splinter to it; in that case, when the omentum of a female animal is seized, they modify the feminine suffix, saying, "Announce these to her. Similarly, regarding the animal itself, when the offering is made, the text says, "Go by the paths traveled by the gods," which is modified to, "Having been offered, go by the paths traveled by the gods."

[3.2.3] Some maintain that because modified [portions of a mantra] are not themselves mantras, expressions such as *ghasat* and *hvaret* do not occur within them. How then is it that we find *aghastām*? There is no fault, because it has been recited exactly in that form: "May Indra and Agni eat [it] with the goat; may they cook it from the marrow; may they accept it through the sacrificial cake; may they cause it to increase. Therefore, some hold that there should be no modification (*ūha*) of the word *akṣan* because of its non-human origin. Others hold that these are simply different mantras intended for the scope of modification.

In the section on modification (*ūha*), it is recited: "aghāsad aghasatām aghasan," and likewise "agrabhīṣur akṣan. Similarly, in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) itself, while the original text says "gharmasya tapasā tapyadhvam" ("heat yourselves with the heat of the *gharma*"), in certain instances a modification is indicated as "tapyasva tapyethām. Furthermore, in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*), many things requiring modification are envisioned. Thus, when the rule has been established as to what is to be modified and what is not to be modified, the function of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) consists in the correct application of gender, number, and case-endings.
The limbs, names of kinsmen, similes, and the sense organs—these are the bases for modification.
These do not go with the *adhrigu* formula, for that would be improper.

The *adhrigu* formula is used elsewhere [than at the Soma sacrifice]. "The two arms are the praise; the two forelegs are the *śalā*; the two shoulders are like the *kaśyapa*; the two hips are the *acchidra*; the two thighs are the *kavaṣa*; the two knee-caps are the *srekaparṇa*. This *avyaya* formula is repeated twice when there is more than one animal. [Then follow] the limbs: "If the animal has made a cry, or if it has struck with its feet against the chest—may Agni release me from that sin, from all distress. [When there are two animals: "If the two animals have made a cry, or if they have both struck with their feet against the chest... [When there are many: "If the animals have made a cry, or if they have struck with their feet against the chest... [Then follow] the names of kin.

"May the mother approve of him, may the father approve, may the brother born of the same womb approve, may his companion of the same herd approve. [This is] the comparison. "Make his shoulders like those of Kaśyapa, his hips faultless, his thighs like the *kavaṣa* reed; make his chest like that of a hawk"—this refers to the vital powers (*indriyāṇi*). "Let him lead the eye to the sun, let him release the breath after the wind, the life-force to the atmosphere, the hearing to the quarters, and the body to the earth. Let him flay his skin in one piece; before reaching the navel, let him extract the omentum with its fat; ward off the heat within. [Thus it is said.]

In that very context of the *ūha* (modification), it is recited that for these [animals], terms such as "mother," "father," "brother," and "kinsman" (*sanābhi-saṃsargin*) are not to be modified; likewise, some have enumerated the limbs as well, such as "hands and feet," "head and neck," and "the seven vital breaths" (*sapta prāṇāḥ*). Now, the *aghrigu* [priest] [recites]: "O divine slaughterers and also you humans, take hold! Bring forward the sacrificial animal from the altar-ground. Desiring the sacrifice for the two lords of the sacrifice, bring the fire toward it; spread the sacrificial grass."

May his mother approve him; may his father, his brother born of the same womb, and his friend of the same herd approve him. Place his feet toward the north. Make his eye go to the sun; release his breath to the wind; [place] his life-force in the intermediate space; his hearing in the quarters; his body on the earth. Strip off his skin in one piece. Before reaching the navel, cut out the omentum from the fleshless part. Ward off the heat within. Make his breast like a hawk; fashion his arms with the carving-knife.

The shoulder-blades are the two arms; the two shoulders are like those of Kaśyapa; the two hips are without holes; the two thighs are hollow; the two knee-caps are like the leaves of the *sreka* plant. There are twenty-six ribs in him; pull them out one by one. Make every limb of his complete. Dig a pit in the earth for the receptacle of the undigested food. Bind the *rakṣas* with the fat. Do not crack the rectum, thinking it to be a mere piece of wood. Let it not crack for our children and grandchildren, O slaughterers. O Adhrigu, perform the sacrifice well! O Śamibhṛt, perform the sacrifice well!
Perform the sacrifice well, O Adhrigu! Both Adhrigu and Vipāpa are the two slaughterers of the gods.
Therefore, you two, being knowledgeable, cook him in such a manner that his cooking is performed correctly.

Thus they perform the modification (*ūha*): "O wide-expanding one, expand widely; may the lord of the sacrifice expand widely. Because this is intended for the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), even when there are seventeen sacrificers, the modification does not become "may the lords of the sacrifice expand. In that regard, the application of grammar does not occur in the modification of ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) nor in the modification of chanting (*gīti*). These two are established through common usage and other characteristics found in the *Prātiśākhya*s and similar works.

Regarding the subject of phonetic modification (*ūha*), only a mere illustration has been provided concerning the extent of grammar's operation therein. Furthermore, the scope of *ūha* is restricted to those cases where the relationship between an original form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is well-established; it does not constitute *ūha* merely by the assertion of something that is difficult for the dull-witted to abandon. Consequently, [the formula] "I perform what is dear to both gods and men" [is an example]. If this were not recited in some instance within the performance of the archetype (*prakṛti-kṛti*), it would certainly not be a subject of *ūha*.

Regarding the subject of sacrifice, some rituals are *prakṛtis* (archetypes), some are *vikṛtis* (modifications), some are both *prakṛtis* and *vikṛtis*, and some are neither *prakṛtis* nor *vikṛtis*. The Agniṣṭoma is the archetype for all *soma* sacrifices; and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices possess the status of being the archetype for all *iṣṭi* sacrifices.

[3.3] Furthermore, there is scripture (*āgama*). Scripture is instruction handed down through an unbroken lineage; it is characterized by revelation (*śruti*) and characterized by tradition (*smṛti*). What, then, is this scripture? "The Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is to be studied by a Brahmin as a duty without motive (*niṣkāraṇa*). "Without motive" means without aiming at any specific reward, just as obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) must be performed because there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform them.

However, regarding those rites which are non-obligatory (*anitya*), such as those performed for specific desires—for instance, "one desiring a son should sacrifice" or "one desiring food should sacrifice"—there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform them, because one engages in them only when there is a desire for the result. This study of grammar, by contrast, is an obligatory rite (*nitya-karma*) that must necessarily be performed, like the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth; this is what is being demonstrated here.

[3.4] Words must be known by a Brahmin. Teaching is the livelihood of a Brahmin. Furthermore, one who knows incorrect words (*apaśabda*) is not accepted as a teacher if his speech is disjointed due to his failure to grasp correct sentences; therefore, words must be known. And for the knowledge of those words, there is no means (*upāya*) other than grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) that is more efficient. A "means" is defined as a particular arrangement of causes toward the accomplishment of an effect. Therefore, grammar is the efficient means for the knowledge of words; no other means is even possible.
Therefore, grammar should be studied. Alternatively, "facility" (lāghava) refers to the quick attainment of correct understanding; and grammar is the means for that.

[3.5] The ritualists recite: "One should sacrifice a speckled cow (sthūlapṛṣatī) to Agni and Varuṇa. It is stated in the Veda: "A speckled cow (pṛṣatī) is one with small spots; a sthūlapṛṣatī is one [with large spots], and she belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa. In that context, the word *sthūla* ("large") occurring in proximity to *pṛṣatī* is not understood as a qualifier of the spotted cows themselves. For if it were a qualifier of the spots (*pṛṣat*), it would clearly function as a compound whose referent is something else (*anyapadārtha*). Grammarians maintain that a difference in meaning follows from a difference in accent.

And regarding that grammatical operation, since its gross traces are perceived there, the grammarians have undoubtedly determined that in this case it is certainly a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
[4] And furthermore, these are the purposes of the instruction on grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*). The word "furthermore" (*bhūyas*) has the sense of "again. The meaning is: "and these others again."

[4.1] Those Asuras were defeated while crying out, "Helayo! Helaya! [4.1.1] This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) employed for the purpose of preventing barbarian speech. An explanatory passage may be either inciting or prohibitive; in this case, it is an inciting statement: "By means of the animal sacrifice, he conquers all these quarters, all worlds; indeed, all these quarters and all worlds become conquered by him. The prohibitive [passage]: "One should not cause [the victim] to go with its teeth [bared]; if one were to cause it to go with its teeth bared, serpents would be intent on killing him; rather, he pacifies the serpents themselves for the sake of non-injury."

Since they were defeated while acting in this manner, therefore a Brāhmaṇa "must not speak like a Mleccha" (*na mlecchitavai*); here *tavai* is used in the sense of the gerundive (*kṛtya*). What, then, is speaking like a Mleccha? To this he says: "he must not speak corruptly" (*nāpabhāṣitavai*). Corrupt speech is Mleccha-speech. But what was spoken corruptly by the Asuras in that instance? Regarding this, some say: [in the phrase] "O Hai! O He! (*hai-he-prayoge*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed for the two words *hai* and *he* was not employed.

Others say: "The *pluta* [protracted vowel] has been applied, but the *svarasandhi* (euphonic combination) was applied rather than *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form). Another says: "'He 'layo he 'laya'—the reduplication has been performed. Others say: "This does not begin with the letter *la*; because they have not been employed by destiny (*diṣṭa*), the substitution of *la* (*latva*) there is a denial [of its existence]. Now, for what purpose does he conclude thus: "Lest we become barbarians (*mleccha*)" and not "lest we be defeated"? It is said: This has already been stated; this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and it prescribes non-barbarism.

[4.1.2] Others explain that because of a certain cause their defeat occurred, it is said that by abandoning that cause one avoids defeat. But what is the defeat of the Asuras? It is the connection with transgression (*pratyavāya*), due to which they do not rise even today. Even those sons and grandsons of the Asuras who did not employ [the science] were likewise defeated. Therefore, just like the Asuras, we too must study grammar so that we do not suffer defeat.

[4.2] A word is "corrupt" (*duṣṭa*) by reason of its accent (*svara*) or its phoneme (*varṇa*). The suffix *tasi* is used here because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*. Thus, it is corrupt by means of both accent and phoneme. That which is corrupt by these two is called "misapplied" (*mithyāprayukta*). Being such, it does not express that intended meaning. Not expressing that intended meaning, the "thunderbolt of speech" (*vāgvajra*) destroys the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). "Speech-thunderbolt" (*vāgvajra*) means speech that is a thunderbolt. Because of his connection with this sin (*enas*), and being joined with that sin, he becomes destroyed through the transgression in the next world. For the sacrificer is the primary element in the sacrifice.

Alternatively, this [grammar] is also for the sake of avoiding injury to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), just as in the case of Indra’s enemy (*indraśatru*). Just as this *indraśatru* injured the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), so too might another [incorrectly applied word] cause injury; therefore, grammar must be studied so that such things do not happen. It is heard in scripture regarding the use of corrupt words: "The mantra *svāhendrashatru vardhasva* (O Indra’s enemy, may you prosper) was to be performed with the accent on the first syllable. But it was performed with the accent on the first syllable [of *indra*], and consequently, Indra himself became his destroyer. To this, an objection is raised:

Even though the final syllable of the compound is udātta, this meaning is not thereby excluded: "Indra is his enemy" (*indraḥ śatrur asya*), just as in the cases of *somasakhaḥ* ("friend of Soma") and *rājasakhaḥ* ("friend of the king"). Furthermore, this must be addressed here: regarding the phrase *indraśatro vardhasva* ("O Indra-śatru, prosper"), why does the first case ending (*prathamā*) not occur in the vocative? As for what was said—that even with the final udātta, there is no cessation of that meaning—this is not a fault.

This word *śatru*, which is employed in the mantra, is indeed a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*), yet it is used here depending on its etymological basis (*nimitta*)—namely, the established meaning determined by the context. Therefore, one does not rely solely on the sense that "Indra’s enemy" (*indrasyāmitraḥ*) or "Indra is his enemy" (*indro vāmitro 'sya*). How then? It is used by taking the very action as the basis, in the sense that a "śatru" is one who "shatters" (*śātayitṛ*) or "pacifies" (*śamayitṛ*). In this context, while "O Indra, be the shatterer" (*indra śātayitā bhava*) was intended to be said, the form "Indra is your shatterer" (*indraḥ śātayitā asya*) was used. And as for what...

What is it that ought to be expressed by the vocative case? The vocative case occurs when an object, already established by its own nature, is directed toward a connection with another property; for example, one directs Devadatta toward a connection with another property by saying, "Devadatta, listen! Eat! But for one whose very nature is already being enjoined, how could there be a vocative case?

For example, in the case of "O King, become! Fight! O man, become!"—where kingship itself is being enjoined and manhood [is also enjoined]—there is no vocative case-ending. Likewise here too, since it is *indraśatru-tva* (the state of having Indra as an enemy) that is being enjoined, there is no fault. In that regard, the fault concerning the phoneme (*varṇa*) was previously demonstrated in the examples "he 'layo" and "he 'laya"; now, the fault concerning the accent (*svara*) is being shown.

[4.3] “That which has been studied but not understood is merely recited as sound (*nigada*); by this it is explained that even the mere verbal expression (*saṃśabdana*) of that very Veda when followed by grammar leads to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). In that regard, the author of the *Nirukta* explains it as “that whose meaning is not understood. Here, however, “not understood” is taken to mean that the accentuation (*svara*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) are not understood. And that which is of such a nature is “merely recited as sound”; the meaning is that it is done solely through the instruction of the teacher (*ācārya*).

Like dry fuel in the absence of fire: just as wood, though capable of burning, is not capable of burning and is useless when not assisted by fire, so too a scripture, even if studied, is incapable of producing its fruit when not assisted by grammar. Therefore, "let us not study what is useless" means "let us not study what is purposeless."

[4.4] “But he who employs [it]” (yastu prayuṅkte): by means of grammar, this is explained as the connection with demerit for improper usage and with the desired fruit for proper usage. “He employs” (prayuṅkte) means he impels [the word]. “The skilled scholar” (kuśalo vidvān). “In a specific [sense]” (viśeṣe): it is explained that that very same word is correct (sādhu) in one particular meaning and incorrect (asādhu) in another. For example, the word *goṇī* is incorrect when applied to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth; likewise, the word *aśva* is correct when applied to that which possesses a mane and so forth, but not when applied to a pauper (*niḥsva*).

The word *aśva* is correct when used for one who lacks wealth, but not for that which possesses the characteristics of a single-hoofed animal and so forth. However, if the word *goṇī* were also employed for a cow on account of another cause—such as its dewlap and so on—as in "like a *goṇī*, a *goṇī*," it would indeed be correct. Or, if one were to employ the word *aśva* for a horse by way of its lack of wealth, that too would be correct. Alternatively, regarding the rule "one who is skilled [is used] without distinction": even though the scripture does not specify, forms such as *tata āgataḥ* ("come from there") and *tena khanati* ("digs with that") are indeed correct; yet they are employed only in specific instances, not everywhere.

"He has come from the foot of a tree; he digs with his finger"—this is the reading of others. "Skilled in the particulars" (viśeṣaiḥ) means by means of the particulars set forth in the treatises (śāstra), according to the rule: "one who studies that [treatise] knows it. "Conduct" (vyavahāra) refers to livelihood; it is the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa), specifically the ritual procedure for officiating at sacrifices. Who is this? Only one who knows the application of speech (vāgyogavit). Since no other person is mentioned, he asks: "Who? and answers: "Only one who knows the application of speech. He thinks thus: in whatever matter [speech] is practiced, that constitutes Dharma.

Therefore, that which is contrary [to this] must result in a contrary fruit when practiced; just as for a Brahmin, performing what is pleasant is *dharma* (merit) and performing what is painful is *adharma* (demerit). Likewise, because one who knows the science of word-usage (*vāgyoga*) understands words from their correct forms, that constitutes *dharma*. Furthermore, the knowledge of words is necessarily accompanied by the knowledge of incorrect words (*apaśabda*). Thus it is said: "For he who knows words... This objection is raised based on the logical derivation of meaning, not on the functional operation of the word itself. For incorrect words are more numerous, while correct words are fewer.

How is the suffix of excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*) to be understood? It is said: it is to be conceived in relation to the highest degree (*paramatā*), based on the assumption of a commonality of quality. How so? You might think as follows: "Even though one who knows the application of speech (*vāgyoga*) knows both, nevertheless, words are many; because they are numerous, corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are few. Because they are few, the transgression is slight. But this too is not correct. That words are "fewer" is not so, for those which are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) are also non-expressive (*apratyāyaka*).

This very position—that these [words] do not convey meaning—is a refuge for ignorance. Granted, such a person might not be joined with merit (*dharma*), but he would certainly be joined with transgression (*pratyavāya*). Likewise, animals and others who act out of ignorance are not joined with transgression. All this has been set forth thus: "Dharma resides in knowledge; the application, however, is the inference of that very knowledge. Ignorance cannot serve as a refuge in the ultimate sense.

For it is not the case that an object consumed through ignorance does not lead to death. Ignorance serves as a refuge only for animals and the like; it is no refuge for Mlecchas and others who proceed to commit acts such as the killing of a Brahmin. "In that case, then"—this is what he explains. Because proximity [to the subject] makes its capacity more powerful, the term *avāgyogavid* (one who knows the application of speech) is connected [to the preceding context]. Therein, one who knows the application of speech—that is, one who knows correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*)—will employ correct words and not corrupt words.

He says: "Prosperity or transgression results from ritual performance (*prayoga*), not from knowledge"—this [point] is neither established in the *Śruti* nor in the *Smṛti*. Therefore he asks: "Where, then, is this recited? [The answer is: "In the verses known as the *Bhrāja-ślokas*. This is his intention: whatever matter is traditionally handed down (*āmnāta*) in the *Smṛti*, that ought to be considered authoritative (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, he does not categorically declare that even verses (*ślokas*) lack authority; rather, he maintains that verses are indeed authoritative.

For verses composed in the Smṛtis are authoritative when they are of such a nature; however, those that are not so are not authoritative. If only such [verses] were authoritative, then any verse whatsoever would deserve to be considered authoritative—for instance, the one beginning "those who are the color of udumbara fruit. This verse indeed declares the incapacity for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Therefore, having abandoned the Sautrāmaṇī, wine should be drunk only in a tavern. This is a song sung by one who is intoxicated; the meaning is that it was uttered by one whose mind was not composed.

How is this known? Because it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti. However, this [verse] was sung by one who is not negligent; for there is a Smṛti: "A single word, correctly understood, well-employed, and in accordance with the scriptures, becomes a cow of plenty that grants all desires in the heavenly world."

[4.5] By the statement "the ignorant [should not respond]," this is what is being said: without grammar, women are set apart from the cultured (*śiṣṭa*), and they are unable to bestow favor upon the one who greets them. For by means of a formal response (*pratyabhivāda*), that woman becomes refined, becomes a partaker of the Dharma, and herself becomes endowed with prosperity.

[4.6] "The *prayājas* are accompanied by case-endings (*savibhaktika*). This means the *mantras* of the *prayājas*. It is not on account of those case-endings that occur word-for-word within the words *prayāja* that they are said to be "accompanied by case-endings," for those [endings] are always present [by virtue of being part of the word-form]. Therefore, a different verbal form from what is traditionally recited (*āmnāta*) is employed in the *prayājas*. And since a bare case-ending is never used, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is understood as the base (*prakṛti*) by implication of the meaning.

In that case as well, because of the observation that "O Agni, you are before the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s" and "you are behind," another scriptural passage (*śruti*) with a different meaning is not adopted. Furthermore, although the use of all case-endings would otherwise be applicable, the form *agnināgninā* is not employed due to the statement: "Those [names] which consist of two syllables or four syllables [are used]. Likewise, one should not create a verbal redundancy (*śabdajāmi*); for that which ends in the fifth case (the ablative) constitutes such redundancy.

Therefore, the form *agner agneḥ* is employed with the genitive ending. In the *punarādheya* (re-consecration) rite, one should apply the case-endings either before or after the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; for both ways are observed, as in *narāśaṃso agnim agnim*. The sandhi *samidhaḥ samidho agne agne* is observed, and the hiatus (*vivṛtti*) *il̥o agninā agne* is observed, according to the *Bahvṛca-sūtra-bhāṣya*.

In the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, the case endings for the four *prayāja* offerings are stated as: "ye yajāmahe samidhaḥ samidho agnim agna ājyasya haviṣo vetu / iḷo 'gnināgna ājyasya haviṣo vyantu / barhiragniragna ājyasya haviṣo vetu. In the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, the case endings for the four *prayājas* are given as: "agnāgne," "agnāv agne," "agnināgne," and "agnim agne. The final *prayāja* is recited exactly as it is traditionally chanted, namely "agnā"; no case ending is applied after that.

Even when a modification is made, the case endings are not omitted; for example: *ye yajāmahe svāhāgnim svāhā somam / agnihotram svāhā agnīṣomau svāhā devā ājyapā juṣāṇā agne ājyasya haviṣo vyantu*. Since these *prayāja* offerings must be performed with their case endings intact, a grammarian should correctly pronounce the words ending in those case endings. Therefore, grammar should be studied for this purpose as well.

[4.7] Regarding the term *ārtvijīna*: both he who is worthy of being a priest (*ṛtvij*) and the priestly office itself (*ṛtvikkarma*) are called *ārtvijīna*. Only one who is learned performs the sacrifice; it is not for the unlearned, because they lack the qualification. Thus, it is encouraged that for a Brāhmaṇa, neither the status of a patron (*yajamāna*) nor the status of a sacrificer (*yājaka*) is possible without grammar.

[4.8.1] There are four classes of words (*padajātāni*), which are like its horns. Since *karmapravacanīyas* are included within the *nipātas*, they are said to be four. For others, there are two classes of words: noun (*nāman*) and verb (*ākhyāta*). There are three times regarding the application of a word for denotation: it has been applied (*prayuktah*), it will be applied (*prayokṣyate*), or it was applied (*prāyojīt*). Or, regarding the act of denoting itself: it has come into being (*abhūt*), it will come into being (*bhaviṣyati*), or it exists (*bhavati*). There are two natures of the word: the eternal (*nitya*) and the produced (*kārya*).

By some it is seen as eternal, by others as non-eternal; or else as genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*); or else as *sphoṭa* and sound (*dhvani*). The seven case-endings are those beginning with *su*. Alternatively, together with the remainder (*śeṣa*), there are the seven case-endings corresponding to the grammatical relations (*kārakas*); however, an eighth relation, even including the remainder, is not possible.

“They do not stir,” “they do not move,” “they do not blink,” and “they do not exert themselves”—these are mentioned through the distinctions of *sāyujya* (union) and so forth. “May we attain equality with those who are wise (*manīṣiṇaḥ*)”: for they too have reached this ultimate state solely through the sacred teaching (*śāstra*).
[4.9] Even while seeing, one does not see; even while hearing, one does not hear. They exercise mastery over the words of those who study grammar; that is, sovereignty resides in their speech.

[4.10] "Like flour through a sieve": *saktu* (flour) is used as an illustration for that substance which is difficult to purify; in this way, corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are purified by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) through its power. Here, [the word] is *sakhāyāḥ*. According to the rule *ṛci tunudhamakṣu*, there is a long vowel. Here, *sakhāyaḥ* means those who have the same name, those whose knowledge is equal.

[4.11] "The one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) employs an incorrect word"—this is what he demonstrates. Just as one who establishes the sacred fire necessarily brings home a wife, because the establishment of the fire cannot proceed without her, so too must one who establishes the fire necessarily study grammar; thus, he establishes that it is indeed an obligatory duty (nityakarman).
[4.12] "On the tenth day, one should give a name to the son"—this is what is meant: that the *vyākaraṇa* (prognostication) is employed starting from the rite of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*).

[4.13] "You are a good god, O Varuṇa"—this hymn in praise of Varuṇa belongs to the *Bārhaspatya* *sūkta* and *pragātha*. This is a praise of Varuṇa, specifically the verse beginning with "You are a true god" (*tvaṃ satyadeva*). Because of this knowledge of grammar, it should be recited.

[5] As for the question "What, then, is this?": here, one should not assume the roles of student, teacher, or one who resembles a teacher. It is the author alone who analyzes this treatise, and nothing else whatsoever. For if the purpose were stated, one would proceed with the thought: "I shall be encouraged by this means. But these are not purposes. Alternatively, if it were explained [that there is no purpose], one might think, "Why should I study something useless that causes only fatigue? and thus would not study at all. Having said "Om," [the author proceeds].

It should not be understood that [the word] *oṃ* is uttered; what then? The meaning is that, having accepted [the text] as "thus" (*evam*), they recite it without regard for any purpose. Regarding the term *vṛttāntataḥ*: *vṛttāntas* refers to chapters (*prapāṭhakas*). Here, the suffix *-tas* is used according to the rule beginning with *ādyādi*. Thus, they recite by means of *vṛttāntas*, that is, by means of chapters. For others, there is the reading *vṛttāntaśaḥ*; they recite in this manner. Reciting chapter by chapter is what is meant by "reciting by sections" (*vṛttāntaśaḥ*). In ancient times, this was so.

This explains the following: at the stage when one is being taught grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), one is simply incapable of asking questions; how then could one state the purposes? Regarding the phrase "to those who know the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of production (*karaṇa*), and the secondary efforts (*anupradāna*"): in former times, one learned the places of articulation and so forth from grammar itself, and thereafter the Vedic words were taught. In that context, there might be a question regarding the purpose of studying the Veda.

The purpose of that [grammar] is also explained: "Grammar, as a limb of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), must necessarily be studied. But nowadays it is not so. "Nowadays" (*adyatve*) is a nipāta meaning "in this time"; for nowadays, even children who have not mastered grammar are taught the Veda. The Veda is recited with the points of articulation (*sthāna*), the places of production (*karaṇa*), and the modes of emission (*anupradāna*) uncomprehended. Having studied the Veda, they become speakers in haste. "In haste" (*tvaritāḥ*) means: [they speak] hurriedly.

They are in haste either for the acquisition of wealth or for the enjoyment of pleasures; or else, as stated in another section of the *Adhyāya*, they say this while simultaneously studying the Veda so that there may be no "appointment" (*niyoga*) that would cause dependence on others.

[6.1] Sound has been defined; its essential nature (*svabhāva*) has also been explained as "sound is phonation" (*dhvaniḥ śabdaḥ*). The purposes, such as protection (*rakṣā*) and so forth, have also been stated. Now, the instruction of sound (*śabdānuśāsana*) must be performed—meaning it must be explained, introduced, and commenced. How is it to be performed? To explain how it is to be performed, he shows what must be explained: by one who teaches, how should it be done? Is it the teaching of correct words (*śabda*), the teaching of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), or the teaching of both?

When something is explained by means of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) through the absence of any other characteristic (*paralakṣaṇa*), it becomes much clearer; thus, there is the adoption of both types of instruction. Even though it becomes clearer, because the treatise would otherwise become excessively cumbersome (*atigaurava*), he adopts instruction by means of the own-characteristic alone. The meaning is that one is accomplished in [distinguishing] correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) by the adoption of either one. For if even the instruction of both were adopted, he would have done so by means of the instruction of either one alone. For example: [The verse: *Śabdapūrvako hy artho nityaṃ yasmāt prayujyate | tasmāc chabdārthayor aikyaṃ manyante bahavo janāḥ ||* [The commentary: Since the object is always employed preceded by the word, many people consider the word and the object to be identical. However, this is not so, because they are distinct. For instance, the word "cow" (*go*) is not the animal itself, nor is the animal the word; yet, due to the connection between them, the word is used to denote the object. Furthermore, since the object is perceived as having a form, while the word is perceived as having the nature of sound, they are distinct. Moreover, the word is produced by effort (*prayatna*), whereas the object is not. Therefore, they are distinct. However, because the word is the cause for the cognition of the object, and because the object is expressed by the word, some maintain that they are identical. But this is not tenable, because they are perceived as different. For example, when one says "the cow is white," the two are perceived as distinct. Furthermore, the word is a means of expression (*vācaka*), while the object is the thing to be expressed (*vācya*). Since the relationship between the signifier and the signified is established based on convention (*saṃketa*), they are distinct. Thus, the identity of word and object is not established. Therefore, one should understand that the distinction between correct and corrupt words is established by means of their own characteristics alone. This concludes the section on the definition of words. Now follows the section on the definition of corrupt words. Therein, first, the definition of corrupt words is stated: [The verse: *Yasminn arthe prayukto yaḥ śabdo 'nyatrāpi dṛśyate | sa tatraivārthe vaktavyaḥ sa cāpaśabda ucyate ||* [The commentary: A word which is employed in a certain sense, but is seen used elsewhere as well, should be spoken only in that specific sense; otherwise, it is called a corrupt word. For example, the word *gāvī* is used in the sense of a cow, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of a cow; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *goṇī*, *gotā*, *gopotalikā*, and *gopottikā* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of a cow. Furthermore, the word *ajñāna* is used in the sense of ignorance, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of ignorance; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *ajñāni*, *ajñānin*, *ajñānatā*, and *ajñānatva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of ignorance. Furthermore, the word *mleccha* is used in the sense of a barbarian, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of a barbarian; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *mlecchaka*, *mlecchika*, *mlecchimat*, and *mlecchitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of a barbarian. Furthermore, the word *pāka* is used in the sense of cooking, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of cooking; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pācaka*, *pācanaka*, *pācanika*, *pācanimat*, *pācanitva*, *pācanatva*, *pācanatā*, *pācanī*, *pācanikā*, *pācanīmat*, and *pācanitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of cooking. Furthermore, the word *pāṭha* is used in the sense of recitation, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of recitation; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhaka*, *pāṭhanaka*, *pāṭhanika*, *pāṭhanimat*, *pāṭhanitva*, *pāṭhanatva*, *pāṭhanatā*, *pāṭhanī*, *pāṭhanikā*, *pāṭhanīmat*, and *pāṭhanitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of recitation. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīna* is used in the sense of a fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of a fish; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhīnaka*, *pāṭhīnika*, *pāṭhīnimat*, and *pāṭhīnitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of a fish. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīnī* is used in the sense of a female fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of a female fish; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhīnikā*, *pāṭhīnimat*, and *pāṭhīnitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of a female fish. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīnīmat* is used in the sense of possessing a female fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of possessing a female fish; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhīnīmitra*, *pāṭhīnīmitratva*, *pāṭhīnīmitratā*, *pāṭhīnīmitraka*, *pāṭhīnīmitrikā*, *pāṭhīnīmitrimat*, and *pāṭhīnīmitritva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of possessing a female fish. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīnitva* is used in the sense of the state of being a female fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of the state of being a female fish; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhīnitvatā*, *pāṭhīnitvatva*, *pāṭhīnitvatā*, *pāṭhīnitvatka*, *pāṭhīnitvatikā*, *pāṭhīnitvatimat*, and *pāṭhīnitvitva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of the state of being a female fish. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīnīmat* is used in the sense of possessing a female fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of possessing a female fish; otherwise, it is a corrupt word. Similarly, the words *pāṭhīnīmitra*, *pāṭhīnīmitratva*, *pāṭhīnīmitratā*, *pāṭhīnīmitraka*, *pāṭhīnīmitrikā*, *pāṭhīnīmitrimat*, and *pāṭhīnīmitritva* are also corrupt words when used in the sense of possessing a female fish. Furthermore, the word *pāṭhīnitva* is used in the sense of the state of being a female fish, but it is also seen used in other senses. Therefore, it should be used only in the sense of the state of being

By the rule regarding what is fit to be eaten (*bhakṣya*), the prohibition of what is unfit to be eaten (*abhakṣya*) is understood. In the section concerning what is fit and unfit to be eaten, this is heard: "Five five-toed animals are fit to be eaten. From the context, there follows the exclusion of other five-toed animals. Alternatively, because of human desire, eating prompted by hunger proceeds toward all objects without being based on scriptural injunction; it is in that regard that this statement occurs: "Five five-toed animals are fit to be eaten."

In that case, if by this [injunction] it were intended to establish that "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," then on the very day one does not eat them, one would incur sin due to the non-performance of what has been prescribed. Furthermore, as for those five-nailed animals other than the *śalyaka* and so forth, their eating would remain unrestricted, being prompted by no specific occasion. Therefore, it is precisely that same eating which was previously undertaken out of desire that is here taught in reference to the five five-nailed animals.

"The warding off of hunger must be accomplished by these [five] alone and not by others. Within this extent of verbal operation, there is the exclusion of other five-nailed animals; this [exclusion] is not expressed by words. What then? It is characterized by implication (*sāmarthya*).

This being the case, regarding what is stated in this sūtra on the vow (*vrata*) concerning the term "one who eats at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī*)—namely, that if one eats at a funeral feast he is an *aśrāddhabhojī*, and on the very day he does not eat at a funeral feast there is a lapse of his vow (*vratalopa*)—here too, eating at a funeral feast is implied by the sense [of the context]. Therefore, this is said: "One should not eat at a funeral feast. Thus, the cessation of the very act of eating at a funeral feast, which was implied by the sense [of the previous rule], is now explicitly enjoined.

When one is already eating, the injunction "Do not eat the *śrāddha*" functions by precluding that very act of eating the *śrāddha* meal through the force of its specific prescription; thus, how could there be a violation of the vow? In this way, since both the correct word (*śabda*) and the corrupt word (*apaśabda*) function toward conveying the same meaning, it is clear that the exclusion of the corrupt word occurs through the instruction of the correct word. Alternatively, the restriction regarding what may be eaten is established by the prohibition of what is not to be eaten; for instance, when it is said "The village cock is not to be eaten," the primary purpose of the prohibition is the stated meaning itself.

For here there is no sublation by means of the inference of acquisition; rather, this is indeed a sublation. Likewise here, through the instruction of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), one understands that "cow" (*go*) is a word other than *gāvī* and the like. What, then, is superior in this case? Because both are taught, and because the lighter [form] is experienced as more excellent due to its brevity, it becomes connected with the suffix denoting excellence (*prakarṣa*) in their mutual rivalry. Furthermore, it is indeed the correct grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of what is desired. How is the instruction of words the correct analysis of what is desired? It is said:

Just as the words [of the Veda] possess that very quality (dharma) according to tradition, so too these [words] are said to have this [quality] because they serve the purpose of dharma; thus, this is called "the exposition of desired forms. Alternatively, if corrupt words (*apaśabda*) were being taught, the understanding would be inferential—[thinking], "this word is yours"—and since there is an infinity of such mental constructs in inferential understanding, it would be impossible to discern whether the word *gaur* is different from *gāvī* and so on, or not; consequently, this [system of] exposition would not even exist.

[6.2] Now, when this instruction of words exists, at this time people consider the word-by-word recitation (*pratipadapāṭha*) alone to be easy. For here there is no grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) to be remembered; one need only utter the words themselves. For if there were an instruction on bases (*prakṛti*) and so forth, comprehension would take a long time. Regarding "word-by-word recitation": that which is uttered in its own form is the word-by-word recitation. A "word" (*pada*) is that by which a meaning is delimited. Regarding "not a means" (*anabhyupāya*): [it is not a means to the goal].

This term *abhyupāya* is a synonym for the word *upāya*. For it is heard [in tradition] that Bṛhaspati [taught] for Indra. This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) employed to discourage the literal recitation of every single word: "Such a speaker and such a listener did not reach the end even in such a length of time; how much less so today? The expression "the mastery of words" (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) is a conventional term denoting a particular treatise, just as one says, "a headache afflicts the stomach."

The term *śiroroga* (head disease) is a conventional designation for a specific ailment of the abdomen; it is said that "it afflicts both the head and the entire abdomen. Similarly, there is a treatise named *Śabdapārāyaṇa*, which means "it has taught [the study] of words. Furthermore, knowledge becomes utilized in four ways. Even if it is only half-utilized, it is considered not utilized at all because it is fruitless. Alternatively, in common usage, something is understood as "utilized" even from a partial application, just as one says, "the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) has been utilized."

Thus, this [Veda] is not "utilized" merely by its partial application; rather, it is said to be "utilized" through its application as a whole. The time of transmission (*āgamakāla*) is the time of initial acquisition (*grahaṇakāla*). The time of recitation (*svādhyāyakāla*) is the time for practice (*abhyāsakāla*). The time of exposition (*pravacanakāla*) is when it is to be imparted to disciples. The time of ritual application (*vyavahārakāla*) is its employment in sacrificial rites or the definitive determination made among the learned (*śiṣṭa*). A certain definition (*lakṣaṇa*) characterized by both general and specific features must be formulated.

That which possesses both a general rule and a specific exception is "possessing general and particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). For example, in the rule *karmaṇy aṇ* ("the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when [the object] is in the objective case"), the phrase "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) constitutes the general rule in this definition; whereas in the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* ("the suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in *ā* when no prefix is present"), the condition "ending in *ā*" (*ātaḥ*) constitutes the particular rule. By means of this slight effort, one masters vast masses of linguistic forms, such as *kumbhakāraḥ* ("potter") and *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("reaper of stalks"), and likewise *pārṣṇitraḥ* ("shoe-maker") and *godaḥ* ("cow-herder"). This principle is to be applied everywhere—in cases of substitution (*sthānyādeśabhāva*), as well as in positive injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*).

[7] Furthermore, is the word-meaning (padārtha) the form (ākṛti) or the substance (dravya)? There is doubt because of the disagreement among the teachers: for Vājapyāyana it is the form; for Vyāḍi, however, it is the substance. On this point, some explain: although this was stated specifically, it is nevertheless asked regarding those words in which both are possible—namely, both substance and form—such as "cow" (go) and "horse" (aśva), but not in cases such as "Ḍittha. Others, however, say:

By the term *ākṛti* (form/structure), everything up to the specific qualification (*paraviśeṣaṇa*) is expressed as being possessed of existence (*sattvavat*). It is so called because it is "fashioned" (*ākriyate*) by it, or "delimited" (*paricchidyate*) by it; thus, different actions are delimited. Others say: "Form (*ākṛti*) is possible everywhere; it is that which is designated as the universal (*jāti*). In this regard, according to Vājapyāyana, the word denotes only the form and not the substance (*dravya*) and so forth. For example, the word "blue," independent of other referents, acquires its form through the commonality of the quality (*guṇasāmānya*).

When that [universal], having attained its own essential nature and being supported by it, becomes expressive of a quality—such as "blue"—it undergoes an immersion into blueness through association with the blue substance; it experiences the state of being its property and attains a single commonality of destiny (*ekayogakṣema*) because there is no separation. Thus, while remaining entirely overwhelmed by the configuration (*ākṛti*), it brings about the cognition of the quality.

Just as a crystal is perceived as possessing the quality [of another object] by virtue of its proximity to that object, so too this word "blue," while denoting the substance, produces a cognition directed toward the very substance which is the substratum of the quality blue—the substratum of the universal blueness (nīlatva) that is the primary referent of the word—despite being separated from it by the quality itself, due to the relation of inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya). This is likewise the case when a cloth is dyed with another substance.

It is precisely through the relation of inherence in that which is conjoined with that which is inherent (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*)—in this indirect sequence—that the white cloth and its quality are perceived even between two red cloths. Likewise, this word "cow" (*gaura*), having acquired its own form in the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), functions only with respect to the substance that is the substrate of that universal.

Thus, in the word "pacati" (he cooks), there are actions such as placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth; those general properties (*sāmānya*) which are restricted to each respective object, such as the act of placing on the fire, manifest a universal that encompasses all objects by virtue of its inherence in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāyin*). That [universal] is what is denoted by the word "pacati. Just as the property of rotating (*bhramaṇatva*), which pertains to many individual actions, is called "rotation," so too, in the case of a person named Ḍittha, from birth until death, that [universal] exists such that one says, "This is Ḍittha, this is Ḍittha."

The cognition that "this is that very same person," which remains undifferentiated across childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, is the *ākṛti* (form) denoted by the word. Furthermore, such a cognition occurs even with respect to a mere infant: "This is Ḍittha; he is being drawn. Therefore, a universal (*sāmānya*) exists here as well. Alternatively, that specific configuration (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*), which is a specific conjunction [of parts], is indeed the *ākṛti*, just as in the case of elephants and other animals. However, this is a designation of a substance (*dravyābhidhāna*) through the conceptualization of a quality (*guṇakalpanā*), because it is designated by that word after having been brought to the status of a universal (*jātitva*).

For one who holds that the substance (*dravya*) is the referent (*padārtha*), however, "substance" is what is expressed; whereas universals (*jāti*) and so forth are mentioned in order to express the existence (*sattva*) of the substance as its differentiators. These are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the word. In this regard, according to some, sweetness and other qualities—which are not directly denoted by words such as "molasses"—are nevertheless apprehended through those objects. Universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are treated in the same way. For this view as well, the denotation of the universal is figurative (*gauṇa*); it is the universal, having been brought to the state of a substance, that is denoted by that word. In this matter, the view of Vājapyāyana is as follows.

For Pāṇini, since the form (*ākṛti*) exists everywhere, it is not tenable that there would be a single application [of a rule], nor that there would be sublation by a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*), nor that there would be the application of a different word (*śabdāntaraprāpti*). Now, if the individual substance (*dravya*) alone were the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), even so, because all individuals would be accepted by all injunctions, the distinction between general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*) could not be established; furthermore, fixed optional alternatives (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) could not be established. He says: "Both. Both the individual and the form are employed by worldly people who take the meaning of a word as their basis.

Among those words of instruction (*upadeśa*) found in the treatise (*śāstra*), some denote a genus (*jāti*) and some denote a substance (*dravya*). This being the case, no word-meaning of this [treatise] is secondary (*gauṇa*). For that which is a genus-word has the genus alone as its meaning, and that which is a substance-word has the substance alone as its meaning. Even among the words of instruction, when one adopts a word-meaning according to one's preference based on the requirements of the linguistic object (*lakṣya*), all the various grammatical operations (*prakriyābheda*) and philosophical perspectives (*darśanabheda*) presented in the treatise become logically consistent. Thus it is said by the Teacher: "In both ways. Here, an objection is raised:

[Objection: But surely, when the referent consists of both [the genus and the individual], the plural number is established for the category of substance (*dravya*) when there are many; whereas the expression of many by one [word] occurs when the category (*jāti*) is the referent. [Response: This is indeed true according to that view. However, when a genus is employed as the word’s referent—either in the teaching or the prohibition of a certain action, or because it is the subject under discussion—then, since that [genus] is singular, the plural number, which would otherwise not apply to many, is introduced [as a rule].

Thus, when there is an intention to express a substance (*dravya*) and that constitutes the context, then—just as in the case of a sentence—where a plurality of words might occur, such as "plakṣa, nyagrodha, dhava, khadira, palāśa," an effort is made to achieve the state of a single word, namely "tree, tree, tree" (*vṛkṣa-vṛkṣa-vṛkṣa*). Another method will be stated here: in the case of the expression "let one dressed in white be made," it is the state of being dressed in white itself that is being made, while the substance [is not being made].

In the case of the injunction "Bring the one wearing white clothes" (*śuklavāsasam ānaya*), the substance [the person] is being acted upon, whereas at that time the connection [with the attribute] is not being acted upon. Here, however, in the phrase "Bring the one wearing white clothes," even the qualifying attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*) is included within the action; for it is the person who possesses that attribute who is engaged in the action because he is characterized by it. But here, in the sense "Let him who is seen wearing white clothes be brought," the two garments are merely the differentiators of the person who possesses them; there is no inclusion of those two garments within the action itself.

Likewise here too, the view of Vājapyāyana is that by the word "cow" (*gaur*), only "cowness" (*gotva*) is denoted, not the substance (*dravya*). Similarly, the opinion of Vyāḍi is that the substance is also denoted, while cowness and so forth serve as its indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). However, this venerable Pāṇini maintains that both are expressed by the word; this is what is being stated here. And this [point] is brought forward in connection with the relationship [between word and meaning], for the Teacher has indeed taught it in both ways.

In this context, when it is said, "What is this lion? It is a dog," if what is intended is the quality of courage (*śaurya*), then the dog is transformed into a lion; if what is intended is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then the lion is transformed into a dog. Likewise, regarding the word *vrīhi* (rice), when both [the universal and the substance] are relied upon, if the universal (*jāti*) is brought to the state of a substance (*dravyatva*), then the plural number is established; and when the substance is brought to the state of a universal, the singular form is established.
