However, regarding the performance of contrary purposes, he recites two [logical] rules so that the state of having multiple words might not result from what is expressed in the singular. This should be applied similarly to the words of instruction as well. For this very reason, it has been said: "some [words] are primary (pradhāna), while others are secondary (guṇa)."

[8.1] Furthermore, is sound eternal (*nitya*) or is it a product (*kārya*)? Regarding this, there is also a disagreement: for those who know the Vedas, it is eternal; for others, it is non-eternal. Alternatively, the meaning is this: those words such as *gaurī* and so forth are indeed eternal. However, for those for whom the characteristic is the form (*ākṛti*), this very thing is a produced entity. This convention has been adopted by the Grammarians (*vācika*). Some think thus: "Those very words which are *prākṛta* (original) are themselves eternal. They are called *prākṛta* because they exist in the *prakṛti* (the primordial source).

Others think: "This is the divine speech; however, it has become disordered due to human incapacity or laziness, just as a child learning to say 'svasti' might pronounce it incorrectly. Or else, just as here an object exists in two ways through the distinction between its substance (*dravya*) and its form (*ākṛti*), so too is the word. Are these words the forms of words (*śabdākṛti*) or the individual manifestations of words (*śabdavyakti*)?

In this regard, when words such as "tree" arise in succession and do not exist simultaneously, the comprehension of the meaning occurs through the word-ness (*vṛkṣaśabdatva*) of the word "tree," and that [comprehension] is eternal. Furthermore, through repeated practice, the form (*sākṛti*) is grasped by a person by means of only a few individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*). Just as in a painting where a person understands through mere lines that "this person is being depicted" and "this is not an elephant," according to this view, the word is eternal.

And in this regard, it has been stated that "the sound *ra* is indicated by the sound *la*" refers only to the *sphoṭa* from both sides. Even for one who holds that the manifestation of the word (*śabdavyakti*) is the word itself, the word is nonetheless eternal; however, it is manifested by *nāda* (articulatory sound). The *nāda* is restricted to each individual word (*padaniyata*). Just as the eyes and other sense organs are fixed manifestors with respect to the objects to be manifested, such as form and so forth, and they conform to the increase and decrease of the forms [they reveal].

Or rather, just as reflections seen in a mirror-disk and the like are observed to be long, circular, large, or otherwise different; so too are sounds differentiated by the differentiation of the *nāda* (articulatory sound). Just as a single moon is perceived as many due to the differentiation of waves upon water, and shadows are differentiated by the differentiation of lamps, and reflections are differentiated by the differentiation of mirrors; therefore, the individual sounds (*vyaktiśabda*), though manifested by specific *nādas* and following the increase and decrease of the *nāda*, are nonetheless eternal.

And that resonance (*nāda*) functions as a benefit to the auditory organ; the auditory organ, thus benefited, becomes capable of perceiving sound. Some say it is like collyrium for the eyes; others say it belongs to the sound itself, just as sprinkling benefits the earth alone and not the sense of smell; still others say it belongs to both, just as one who has mastered his senses first benefits the visual rays and the jar. This being the case, phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*) are all eternal.

However, this is the distinction regarding Vedic sentences: there, no use of a word occurs with its meaning reversed; but in common worldly usage, such usage does exist. For example, there is the usage "Bring the vessel," "The vessel, bring it," "You cook," "You cook," and "For food thee, for strength thee"; but not "For thee food," "For thee strength. Such is the distinction between the worldly and the Vedic: the constancy of usage belongs to the Vedic, while the variability belongs to the worldly.

Eternality is also twofold: that which is based on conventional usage (*vyavahārāśrayā*) and that which is based on ultimate reality (*paramārthāśrayā*). In the Vaiśeṣika system, atoms and space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are based on ultimate reality. That which is based on conventional usage is, for example, the statement in the *Caraka-saṃhitā*: "A decoction of *nāgara*, *viṣā*, and *mustaka* may serve as a digestive of undigested matter (*āmapācana*). It is not from the words of Caraka that these possess the quality of being a digestive of undigested matter; rather, it is by their own nature (*svabhāvāt*). Likewise here, since words—whether composed by Pāṇini or by another—are merely remembered (*smṛta*) as being inherently expressive of meaning, it is precisely this eternality based on conventional usage that is of service in this context.

In this *Saṃgraha*, it has been examined primarily whether [the treatise] is eternal (*nitya*) or a product (*kārya*). There are fourteen thousand topics in this compendium. Regarding the statement that "prosperity (*abhyudaya*) results from practice preceded by the scripture," the conclusion in the *Saṃgraha* is that the definition must be applied in both ways. But how is this [treatise] of the Blessed One either a product or eternal? Furthermore, on the basis of what philosophical view did this teacher proceed? Is he one who follows the knowers of the Vedas, or others?

He asks this, or rather: "But how is this so? Even if for Pāṇini there is either permanence or impermanence [of linguistic usage], how has this treatise been introduced? What, first of all, do we understand? Is it that "I alone am the creator of the relationships between words and their meanings," just as a Brahmin might act out of pride regarding procreation? Or is this the view: "These relationships between words and their meanings are indeed already established;
however, because of my knowledge of the *vṛttis* and my great learning, I shall be the one who remembers them"?

[8.2] Once the relationship between word and meaning is established, there arises the question of whether the application of the term "eternal" to a word refers to ultimate eternity or conventional eternity. The application of the term "eternal" may be eternal or non-eternal; it is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Sound (*dhvani*), which is produced by the conjunction of the vocal organs and is specifically restricted to objects such as phonemes (*varṇa*), acts as the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). Consequently, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is effected either upon the form (*ākṛti*) or the individual instance (*vyakti*). Either the form or the individual instance conveys the meaning. However, the refinement of the form—like the act of touching and so forth—is mediated through the individual instance.

In that regard, for those who maintain that words are eternal, the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is easily avoided. When words are restricted to specific regions—as in "the word *hammati* is used among the Surāṣṭras"—so too do names such as *Ṭittha*, which are taught without qualification, come to reside in specific meanings. For these [words] have been employed in this way; Pāṇini merely records what was already known. This applies to the meaning as well: for those for whom the form (*ākṛti*) is the denotation, that [form] is eternal; even when the substance (*dravya*) is the referent, there is eternality in terms of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Whenever there are jars and other such objects, they always possess this very configuration; thus, their relationship is also one of fitness (*yogyatā*), just as it is understood that the eye is fit for the perception of form, whereas the ear is not. Alternatively, since the object is prompted by the word, the relationship between word and object is characterized as that of cause and effect.

In that regard, because the meaning (*artha*) is eternal, meanings such as distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the *kṛtvasuc* suffix, and so forth, as well as [compounds] like *upasikta* and others, become subordinate members (*aṅga*) even when not explicitly stated—as in the cases of *saptaparṇa*, *tridaśa*, and *dadhyodana*. And thus it has been said: "The grammatical description (*anvākhyāna*) of those [words] which exist by their own nature (*svabhāva*) in relation to meanings is made by way of a formal cause (*nimitta*). For example: *kūpe hastadakṣiṇaḥ* ("one who puts his hand into the well"). Furthermore, the eternality of the relationship (*saṃbandha*) was stated in the *Sarūpa-sūtra*; therefore, it must be stated that [the word] has two meanings or many meanings.
One might say it, but it would not be understood; for if someone were to say "cow" when meaning "horse," there would never be any comprehension.

[8.3] Now, what is the referent (*padārtha*) of the word *siddha*? It is not the meaning of its individual parts that is being asked about. What then? It is the conventional collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*). By implication, it is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*). The word *siddha* is a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*); it expresses the meaning of "eternal" by way of a synonym. For sometimes the word *nitya* expresses that meaning, and sometimes the word *siddha*.

When the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is relied upon, the word *siddha* is a synonym for the word *nitya*, which expresses that very nature; and since the word *siddha* is a synonym for the word *nitya*, he says "the word *siddha*" to refer to that.

In that regard, just as the designation "self" (ātman) is applied to the omnipresent [space] with respect to the self because of the commonality of pervasion (*prāptisāmānya*), even though space is inactive; in exactly the same way, the word "established" (*siddha*) is applied to those things not being established because of the commonality of the locus where their perfection is achieved. How is this known? It is through intention. A synonymous term (*paryāyaśabda*) expresses that meaning independently of other words, just as "Indra," "Śakra," and "Puraṃdara" do.

Furthermore, words such as *śakra* and others do not denote objects other than their primary referent, Indra; however, this established word *siddha*, when joined with another word, expresses the meaning "eternal. It is observed in the case of effects such as jars and the like. As for the word *kūṭastha*, it applies to entities that are immovable and unchanging. This word does not undergo expenditure (*vyaya*) where it functions. For example: "Make a *kūṭastha* heap; no expenditure should be made from it."

The term "unchanging" (*avicāliṣu*) expresses both the non-attainment of another location and the absence of transformation. For his intention is this: that which has its measure diminished or is transformed is not eternal. Furthermore, even in the case of synonymous words, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed when there exists a relationship between a general term and a specific term. The word *varāha* applies to a mountain and applies to a boar; however, it is more commonly established in the sense of a boar. Nevertheless, it experiences coreferentiality with the word "mountain."

[The examples are: "Varāha is Himavat," "Varāha is Pāriyātra. In these cases, since the word *varāha* is used as a synonym conjoined with another word for the sake of conveying a specific meaning, so too the mention of earth and the other elements for the sake of conveying their eternal distinctions does not contradict their status as synonyms. However, the word "white" functions as a synonym [only] when it occurs in such expressions as "white cloth. [Examples of this are: "the sky is established," "the earth is established," and "space is established."

For the Arhats and the Mīmāṃsakas, there is no destruction whatsoever of these [sounds]. Or, even if there were destruction, because these [sounds] transcend the linguistic usage of their users, they are said to be eternal; for they are not observed to be produced or destroyed by the mere difference of the users. But surely, sir, this is also seen in the case of effects? We admit that there is a material cause (*upādāna*) for the sake of perceiving a specific distinction, even though the term is used synonymously.

In this regard, what is that form of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) based upon which the word *siddha* is applied to eternal things? If it were based on the form of accomplishment, then since the form of accomplishment exists even in produced effects (*kārya*), there would be no definitive distinction made by the word *siddha*. If you first think that it is based on that [form of accomplishment] even though such a form exists, what then? It is simply conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). For example, although the Ganges is based on its physical form, it gives rise to the name *Gāṅga* for things belonging to it.

When it is accepted as having the form of a deity or the like, one says, "The son of Gaṅgā is Ḍhaka," or likewise, "Vāsudeva. When it is expressed as being a descendant—that is, "the descendant of Vasudeva"—then it is called a *kṣatriya* name. But when it is said, "The gods dwell in him (*vasanti asmin devāḥ*)," thus "Vāsudeva," then this is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) for the Blessed One there. As for "Duryodhana," since he is fought with difficulty (*kṛcchreṇa yodhyate*), then in the state of being a Kaurava, it is not called "Dauryodhani"; rather, it is "Kaurava" or "Duryodhana."

Just as [the word] is established among eternal things (*nitya*), so too is it in the case of produced things (*kārya*). Whether it depends on a cause (*nimitta*) or is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*), the conclusion is that there is no such thing as a synonym for the eternal. This is because, in the *Saṃgraha*, it stands in opposition to the produced. Here, the general property (*sāmānya*) has multiple causes for the recollection of its own object, such as association (*sāhacarya*) and so forth; just as the general property of the word "stone" (*śilā*) is differentiated by those things with which it is associated.

When it is said, "Bring the iron staff and the stone," there is no apprehension of physical exercise [as the primary meaning], because the stone is a subordinate element; this is the case with the subordinate element in the act of grinding. Similarly, "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa" refers to the son of Daśaratha; "Rāma and Keśava" refers to Baladeva. Even through opposition, there is some degree of association, as in "Rāma and Arjuna," which brings about the understanding of Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni) and Kārtavīrya respectively. Thus, in the *Saṃgraha*, this was introduced: "Is the word something to be produced (*kārya*), or is it already established (*siddha*)?"

Because it is used in proximity to the word *kārya* (that which is to be produced), the word *siddha* (established) functions as a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*). It is not so; what then? [The meaning is] "it is established (*siddha*), not something to be produced (*kārya*). Because its state of being produced is negated while its state of being established is not negated, it is certain that in the *Saṃgraha*, this is a synonym for "eternal. Here too, it is exactly the same. Why? Because the *Saṃgraha* is also a part of this very treatise, and since they follow the same system and because Vyāḍi is an authority, the word *siddha* is employed here in that very same sense.

[8.4] Alternatively, there are also single-word emphatic particles (*avadhāraṇa*). Without depending on other texts, it is now explained: here, a certain two-word phrase constitutes an emphasis where the particle *eva* is heard, such as "he eats only water" or "he eats only air. The emphasis, which is not explicitly indicated for the object being emphasized when that object is expressed by another word, is indeed made manifest by the word *eva*.

However, when that meaning is manifested through context, purpose, and so forth, the word *eva* is not heard; thus, the restriction is said to be expressed by a single word (*ekapada*). In that regard, in the case of "no one eats water" (*abbhakṣaḥ*), the hearing of the word *abbhakṣa*—by virtue of its capacity—is intent upon the exclusion of others. It means: "Let him who eats only water be brought here. Likewise, when it is said, "He has now become one who eats only water," the waters are restricted for the purpose of excluding other things, even though he was previously engaged with them.

Furthermore, what is the functional implication (*sāmarthya*) here in the word *siddha*? What is that implication? It is said: by the employment of the word *siddha*, it is understood that this object is not of both kinds; namely, it is either permanent or impermanent. There is nothing else that is both permanent and impermanent.

In that regard, just as when it is said "a maiden should be given to one who is handsome," the application [of the term] occurs toward excellence of handsomeness and not merely toward handsomeness in general; likewise, the word *siddha* alone refers only to that which is accompanied by an unvarying state of being established (*siddhatva*). Since the state of being established belongs to permanent (*dhruva*) and unvarying things, whereas for produced effects (*kārya*) it is variable, the word functions in relation to effects only when conjoined with another word.

And even when [a word] is employed there, it functions by relying on a portion that has an eternal object; therefore, this is said: "That which is already established is not something to be accomplished. And this is appropriate when the application of a word relies on a form consisting of actual production (*niṣpatti*), but not when it relies on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). This being the case, expressions such as "water-eater" (*abbhakṣa*) or "air-eater" (*vāyubhakṣa*) are appropriate. However, when "water-eater" and "air-eater" are conventional names for a specific vow (*vrata*), then they denote a genus (*jāti*). In that case, since the word is entirely conventional, there is no restriction regarding its application to the action.

[8.5] Alternatively, one should understand that there is here an elision of the preceding and following words (*pūrvottarapadalopa*). But what is this method of eliding the preceding and following words? For neither Pāṇini nor anyone else is capable of effecting the elision of a word like *Devadatta* when it has not been uttered. Regarding this, some think: "When a single word is perceived, there is a recollection of the whole; from that alone comes the comprehension of the meaning. This is incorrect, for there is no communication of meaning from something merely being cognized, nor is there a grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) for that which is inferential.

And its permanence is stated in grammar, because this view holds that at the time of the formation of a name, [the constituent parts] are produced as a corollary (*anuniṣpādita*) due to their inseparability (*nāntarīyakatva*), like the whey (*vājina*). For example, for one who takes up milk seeking the curd (*āmikṣā*), the whey—which is accomplished by the same means—is produced simultaneously with the curd. In the same way, the word *satya* and the word *bhāmā* are produced together with the word *Satyabhāmā*.

And Pāṇini declares the correctness (*sādhutva*) of such [words] as *jyeṣṭhā* and others precisely by way of their elision (*lopa*), and not by stating that for *jyeṣṭhā* and so forth, the form *jye* is used, nor that *viśākhā* becomes *khā*. Thus, in this context, the word "established" (*siddha*) refers to that which is produced in accordance with words that are absolutely established (*atyanta-siddha*). As for the phrase "but there, according to the sense and context," however, any disagreement arises only in the absence of such [context].

When one calls for an inheritance that has been given, or when there is such a purpose as "this is what must be done by Devadatta," then Devadatta is understood through the word *tat* (that). It is the same here as well. How so? It is said: if here too recourse were made to the form of the completed [result], then since this would be a grammatical description (*anvākhyāna*) of that which is being produced and that which is already produced, the defining rule (*lakṣaṇa*) would have no further scope.

Therefore, that which has been accomplished, that which is being accomplished, and that which will be accomplished—all these are established. And thus, in space, there exists the state of being accomplished, the state of being about to be accomplished, and the state of having been accomplished. Since these are absolutely established, by virtue of this capacity, this [unconditioned nature] is designated as "that which follows in the wake of what is absolutely established."

[8.6] Alternatively, it is said that "the specific meaning is understood from the commentary" (*vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattiḥ*). This demonstrates that something is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) simply because there is doubt; for it is not the case that the speaker and so forth, or the hands and so forth, fail to be the defining characteristics of a post or a person when the object is being doubted. Therefore, just as in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* and others, where these [terms] are understood through such an interpretation despite being mentioned in a general way, so too here one understands the word *siddha*—which is a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*)—from that very statement.

[8.7] For the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The accomplishment of a desired object that is free from blemish is "auspiciousness. And whatever is undertaken for that purpose is also designated as "auspicious" because it serves that purpose. In this context, "for the sake of auspiciousness" means for the sake of accomplishing the intended object. One who is "auspicious-seeking" (*māṅgalika*) employs auspicious rites; just as one who seeks rain employs the rites of Indra (*aindra-mahika*) as a means to accomplish the intended object. Thus, the difficulty of crossing the vast flood of this great treatise is made known.

They spread; and first, there is non-overpowering. Another [reason] is that there is no interruption of the study; thus he says: "belonging to heroic men" and "belonging to long-lived men. And the students have their purpose accomplished. The accomplishment of their task is either the completion of the treatise without obstruction or its prosperity, which is preceded by that [completion]. Even when the word *nitya* (eternal) is employed, this very same situation applies as with the word *siddha* (accomplished); this he expresses by saying "in the sense of frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇye*).

It might be argued that because of the employment of a word denoting action (*kriyā-śabda*), repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is appropriate. Even so, when it is stated that "the relationship between word and meaning is eternal" (*nityaḥ śabdārtha-sambandhaḥ*), it is understood that this grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) applies only to those words which are used repeatedly even among commoners such as cowherds, and not to others. Furthermore, in the phrase "it is a wonder that it is non-eternal" (*āścaryam anityaḥ*), that which does not occur repeatedly is called "non-eternal"; thus, there exists the expression of repetition even without a verbal form (*kriyāpada*).

[9.1] But with what meaning of "referent" (padārtha) in mind is this analysis performed—namely, "when the word, the referent, and the relation are established"? Regarding the word, the referent is that which is denoted; it is precisely with respect to that that the question is asked: "With what denoted object of the word in mind is this analysis performed? The answer is: "The generic form (ākṛti). For a word, without depending on a connection to another referent, acquires its own essential nature (svarūpa) in the generic class alone among words for genus, quality, action, and proper names.

However, substances and the like are denoted by being brought to that very form (*tādrūpya*); for example, as the word "cow" denotes a *bāhīka*, or as a proper name denotes a substance. In that regard, when a substance undergoes an action, it is denoted by another's form, as in "bring the cow. Likewise, in the expression "white cow," the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is indicated through whiteness by means of inherence-in-the-inherent (*ekārthasamavetasamavāya*). In the expression "one Brāhmaṇa," Brāhmaṇahood is indicated through oneness; thus, every word expresses the generic form (*ākṛti*).

Furthermore, it is impossible for the simultaneous production of the appearances of identity and difference to occur with respect to a single object—just as one cannot say, "He is that very Yajñadatta who is different from Yajñadatta. In this case, however, having seen a child who was weak and brown in Mathurā, and later perceiving [the same person] as dark and stout in Pāṭaliputra, one determines his existence through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), thinking: "This is that very same object endowed with qualities such as blueness, which was previously seen by me as endowed with qualities such as childhood."

Furthermore, there can be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of what has not been previously seen; therefore, it must be that the object was seen before, since it is now being recognized. For all those who maintain that the universal (*jāti*) is distinct [from the individual], there is no disagreement regarding its eternity; thus it is said: "The form (*ākṛti*) is indeed eternal. However, it is manifested by impermanent substances and so forth; such is the function of substances and the rest.

[9.2] Now, if the *padārtha* (referent) is taken as a substance (*dravya*), the analysis (*vigraha*) should be performed as follows: it is the substance itself that is denoted by the word; whereas *gotva* (cowness) and so forth, though not themselves denoted, serve as qualifiers (*upādhi*) and are the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word. This is just as the svastika and other such symbols, while not denoting Devadatta’s house, serve as its distinguishing marks (*upalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, because the destruction of a substance is observed, [the word must denote the substance]. Alternatively, the analysis should be made in this way: "when the word and its connection with the meaning are established."

"Arthasaṃbandhaḥ" means connection with the meaning. In the phrase "it is eternal in that [connection]," the mention of "meaning" (artha) in the sentence is not for its own sake; rather, it is for the purpose of indicating the connection. Just as the mention of *num* is for the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra*, so too, when it is stated that [the relation] is eternal in both word and connection, this would also be understood: "that which is the connection of a word by way of its own form, in that [connection] it is eternal. However, when the term "meaning" (*artha*) is included, there is the comprehension of the denotable object.

Now, how could the relation be eternal if its object is impermanent? It is said: like inherence (*samavāya*). Just as inherence—whether its objects are eternal, both eternal and impermanent, or impermanent—is itself eternal, so too would this [relation] be.

Alternatively, with reference to that fitness (*yogyatā*) whose object is the fact that the word "jar" is never devoid of its referent—that is, the form of the word is always permeated by the form of the referent—he states this as a property of the word: "For the connection of things possessing meaning with their meanings is eternal. And he will state this very same view at the end [of the work]. Or rather, what is the use of this distinction between "this is eternal" and "this is non-eternal"? This analysis is more appropriate when the referent is the substance (*dravya*) itself; for the substance is eternal.

The earth-element is eternal. What is real in the earth-element? Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). What is real in conceptual construction? Knowledge (*jñāna*). What is real in knowledge? *Oṃ*. That, then, is Brahman. This is what is being said: beyond this, the conventional usage of words and meanings ceases; this reality is beyond conventional usage. In that regard, however many designations there may be—whether "impermanent" or "eternal"—they all depend upon states, and those states are not other than it. Therefore [it is eternal].

And just as a dream or another cognition—whether it be of the three worlds or of a house—is without form and undivided by distinctions such as mountains and so forth, even though it appears in the regions of mountains and the like; in this same way, that object, such as the *puruṣa*, is postulated as eternal and transcending all linguistic conventions. And since it is eternal, its analysis [into constituent parts] is logically untenable.

[9.3] This analysis is also logical even when the referent is a generic form (*ākṛti*). The word "also" (*api*) is intended to show that such a case is likewise possible for a substance (*dravya*). Since it does not cease anywhere, it follows that it has ceased everywhere. As for the claim that "another generic form arises," that is incorrect; for while one [form] disappears, another appears. In the view held by the ancients, existence and non-existence do not belong to the genus (*jāti*); rather, they consist of appearance and disappearance.

And since both [word and meaning] are not perceived apart from the Blessed One Pāṇini, the rememberer, this is his established doctrine (*siddhānta*): that both constitute the referent of a word (*padārtha*). In that regard, even though both constitute the referent, the permanence of the meaning does not cease; thus, one cannot postulate its presence or absence. In this way, that which resides in the nature of *pradhāna* is unperceivable and does not deviate from non-existence; yet, when situated in another substance, it is perceived, and when situated in another substance, it is manifested.

In that regard, because identity and difference—when both are fully manifest—are contradictory within a single substratum, it is logically untenable for there to be both the oneness and the indestructibility of the configuration (*ākṛti*). Furthermore, even according to the view you have presented, since it is non-different from the substance, you yourself have stated that the "configuration" is nothing other than the substance itself. This is not so; for if the substance is eternal, then the configuration must also be eternal. Or, if this [view] is accepted: at least everything would be one yet diverse in form.

Within the collection of powers (*śakti*), however, a certain power sometimes becomes latent and sometimes becomes manifest; it is in this manner that the word functions. Alternatively, this is not the only definition of permanence—namely, as being constant, immutable, and unchanging. By this passage, he speaks of three kinds of impermanence (*anityatā*). For impermanence is indeed threefold: the impermanence of association (*saṃsarga-anityatā*), the impermanence of transformation (*vipariṇāma-anityatā*), and the impermanence of the destruction of the entity (*vastuvināśa-anityatā*). Permanence, conversely, is defined by the absence of these.

Impermanence through association (*saṃsargānityatā*) is, for example, like a crystal whose own nature is not perceived when it is obscured by various other substances acting as associates, even though that [nature] exists inherently. Likewise, impermanence through transformation (*vipariṇāmānityatā*) is, for example, like the disappearance of the blackness of a jujube fruit and the manifestation of its redness. Impermanence through the destruction of the entity (*vastuvināśānityatā*) is that which is the total annihilation of everything into the indefinable (*nirupākhya*). In that case, one should not understand that "that which is permanent" refers to the time when these phenomena do not exist.

For if it were conceived in this way, then according to the Sāṃkhya, the self (*ātman*) would be unchanging and eternal, whereas the primary matter (*pradhāna*), being subject to transformation, would entail the consequence of impermanence. Therefore, this too is the definition of the eternal: that in which the reality (*tattva*) is not destroyed is eternal. "This is that very same [thing]" refers to the cause of the cognition of identity; "this is that very same self. Or, the substantial entity (*vastu*) that has not perished is the entity of the self, such as the nature of a jar and so forth. Alternatively, "this is that very same" is said by way of its particular state. Or rather, what is the use of this?

This treatise is not the exclusive companion of any single school, but is common to all. Just as for the Sāṃkhyas and others, the cognition [of an object] arises from the substance itself—whether it be the pot as an inherence of color and so forth, or as a distinct entity—such that whoever has a pot applies the word "pot" to it; likewise, this analysis of the meaning is performed by relying upon whatever kind of permanence is intended by each [school]. In that regard, for the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), that which is a continuous flow without interruption is what constitutes permanence.

The permanence of other things is established by observing their primary arrangement. Now, regarding this [word], what does it signify? Is it that "this is permanent" and "that is impermanent"? What is the use of our investigation into the nature of things? This analysis is performed by considering that object which we regard as permanent; and for us, the object is that which is denoted by the word.

In that regard, whether the object (*vastu*) is eternal or non-eternal, the word itself is never such that it is both denotative and non-eternal; nor does a word ever fail to have previously applied to its meaning. Since, at all times, [words] are pervaded by their own forms, every word—whether it be the word "jar" or the word "rabbit's horn"—is at all times not empty of its objects, but is indeed permeated by the form of the object. When things are of such a nature, this analysis (*vigraha*) is entirely appropriate: "when the word, the object, and the relation are established."

[10.1] How, then, is this introduced? He asks about the origin [of the term]. It is established from worldly convention that "this is permanent" and "this is impermanent. The way things proceed regarding worldly objects is not the same as it is regarding words. Those worldly matters which require prior training cannot be accomplished without such training. For example:

One who desires a jar, though untrained in the making of jars, approaches a skilled potter [saying], "Make a jar; I shall perform the task with this. In this same way, if words such as "cow" and so forth had been produced by Pāṇini and others merely for the sake of worldly transaction—like a game of dice—then a person untrained in that matter would have to approach grammarians to employ them correctly. Yet he does not do so; rather, he employs words while taking up each respective meaning for itself.
Having examined the meaning through the intellect, one indeed employs it; therefore, this must be understood: these relations between words and their meanings are indeed eternally established.

Others describe it thus: they are produced like the game of Soma and Saura. Just as one asks about words, so too does one ask about meanings: "What is the meaning of this word? In this way, one also establishes the relationship [between them]. For one does not establish the word and the meaning separately and then join the two together; therefore, this must be understood: these relationships between word and meaning are already established, since they are examined by the intellect at one and the same time.

Others describe it thus: that which was stated [in the sūtra]—"because perception is for the sake of another" (parārthatvāt) and "because it functions diversely" (viprapravṛttatvāt)—is precisely what has been expressed by this commentary (bhāṣya). Even because of the application (viniyoga) of effects alone, there is another perception regarding their origination. However, whatever perception, apprehension, or accomplishment belongs to this [perception], it is exclusively of the nature of being for the sake of another. For there is no time whatsoever that is devoid of being for the sake of another. Therefore, this must be understood.

"It is precisely that [word] which, being already existent, is manifested through the conjunction of the speaker, the instrument, and so forth. In this conception, two things do not cohere: namely, the claim that "the world is the authority regarding words," and the statement that "when the use of words is prompted by meaning according to worldly usage, there is a restriction of dharma by means of the scientific treatise (*śāstra*). "From the world" (*lokataḥ*) means from the world (*lokāt*). "Prompted by meaning" (*arthaprayukte*) means impelled by purpose (*arthena*). Since the world is that from which one learns this, that world is at fault; it teaches both the correct and the incorrect.

That which serves to communicate meaning is the instigator (*prerayitṛ*). Just as one employs the word *go*, so too does one employ *gāvī* and other such forms. Therefore, the application of the treatise has this purpose: "How might the incorrect forms be excluded? Now, regarding the phrase "the employment of words" (*śabdaprayoga*), what is the purpose of including the term "employment"? One could simply say, "words are employed for the sake of meaning according to common usage. It is replied: "Communicating meaning" (*arthapratyāyana*) is cognition (*bodha*). In that context, the meaning is the object to be communicated (*pratyāyya*), and the communication itself is the result (*phala*).

The word is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Since there can be no connection between the word and its meaning—acting as the object (*karman*) and the instrument—respectively, in the absence of an action (*kriyā*), an action must be admitted. Just as in the case of threshing grain such as rice, where the connection occurs through the mediation of the raising and lowering of the pestle, and the result—the removal of the husk and the separation of the chaff—is thereby accomplished; so too here, the word, being a substance, is the instrument, the meaning is the object to be conveyed, and the comprehension of that [meaning] is the result.

That is the fruit of the action. But what is that action? It is said: it is the *praṇidhi* (volition) of the agent who impels the sounds, having them as its object. *Praṇidhi* is a mental activity [in the form]: "This person is capable of producing this sound for this purpose. That is the action. For it has been said: "The self, having empowered the objects through the intellect (*buddhi*), joins the mind (*manas*) with the desire to speak."

Just as, even when the eye exists and a visible form is present, the eye is not capable of perceiving the object without being directed and presided over by the mind, so too a word, even when its meaning is established, is incapable of conveying that meaning without the speaker’s intention (*praṇidhāna*). This is what he expresses by the inclusion of the term "application" (*prayoga*). According to the view of others, however, a word possesses many properties.

When this [term] *yatheṇ gatau* is understood to be meaningful through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then, by virtue of its meaningfulness, it attains the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). However, when this very same term—having abandoned its meaning—is resorted to as a mere phoneme (*varṇa*) in the rule *ekāco dve*, then, for that which possesses both a meaning and a word-meaning, this [term] is brought into a relationship with the word *ekaḥ* (singular) in the sense of "this is one *ac*" (*ajiti vyatireke asyeti*).

Similarly, words such as "brāhmaṇa" are meaningless at the time of practice (*abhyāsakāla*), when they signify their own phonetic form (*svarūpa*) in the instruction of others, as in "recite thus," "recite thus. At the time of application (*viniyogakāla*), however, they possess meaning. In that context, the engagement with objects that possesses a grasped meaning at the time of application is the "relation" (*saṃbandha*). And that dependence which is observed is the inherent property (*dharma*) of the word; it is the eternal essence of the word (*śabdātman*). This is what is subsumed by the term "usage" (*prayoga*). It is only a word of this nature that is impelled by its object, not every word.

Others describe it thus: "that which is employed" is *prayoga*; this is both a word (*śabda*) and an employment (*prayoga*), hence "word-employment" (*śabdaprayoga*). The restriction of the property does not apply to the mere word; rather, the word exists for the sake of its employment.

Others describe it thus: some sounds are employed and some are not employed. "The three hidden in the cave do not stir; they do not move"—these [sounds] are not employed. "The fourth part of speech humans speak"—thus the fourth portion is employed. Regarding those that are employed, there is a restriction (*niyama*). Therefore, from that which is the preeminent *dharma*, there arises knowledge of those three. *Dharmaniyama* means a restriction for the sake of *dharma*. *Dharmaniyama* is a certain conventional term.

However, its status as being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is necessarily indicated by the analysis using the dative case. For this is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), just as the name "horse-food" (*aśvaghāsa*) is conventionally established for certain types of grass such as *iṣīkā* and so on. Because its status as being for that purpose is fixed, it is analyzed with the dative as "food for horses" (*aśvebhyo ghāsaḥ*). It is strictly a genitive compound; and thus it has been said: "Words such as *aśvaghāsa* are genitive compounds."

Alternatively, "dharmaniyama" means a restriction for the sake of *dharma*; the elision of the middle term [in *dharmārtha-niyama*] occurs because it belongs to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*. Because this very restriction has *dharma* as its purpose, it is designated as *dharma* itself, being closely related to *dharma* as its cause. Or, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, it is that which has *dharma* as its motive (*dharmaprayojana*). *Dharma* is eternally established; however, it is manifested by the *agnihotra* and other rites, and when impelled by them, it becomes the bestower of results.
Just as a master is impelled by his servants toward service for the sake of a reward, so too this rule of dharma is the motivator for the production of its fruit.

[10.2] Just as among those belonging to the worldly and Vedic traditions, the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyāḥ*) are fond of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). Now, should it be understood that this word is a corruption (*apaśabda*) because of its fondness for secondary derivatives? No, he says. For in this case, those constituent parts which exist in the world or in the Veda can be subsumed by a collective term—such as "the world" or "the Veda"—even without a secondary derivative. But this Teacher, having separated those parts which do not constitute a whole, indicates their status as the substrata within both the world and the Veda.

In this regard, what else could it be, since [the term] is fond of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*)? Just as someone might speak of "forest-lords" (*vanaspati*) by way of distinction, while another speaks of "the forest-tree-kingdom" (*vānaspatyam*) as a collective form; or rather, the meaning of the secondary derivative here is indeed appropriate. There is no relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) here. What then? By both worldly usage and the Veda, the intended meaning is a portion of a sentence itself. But what is that? It is the established conclusion (*kṛtānta*), the settled doctrine (*siddhānta*), the composition of a treatise on convention (*samaya*). This is what is meant:

Just as other textual compositions are for the purpose of restricting the nature of things (*dharmaniyamārtha*), why is this one also accepted as being for the purpose of restricting the nature of things? First, in common worldly usage, the statement "the village cock is not to be eaten" is not an example by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*). What then? It is an example by way of exclusion (*pakṣe*). In that case, the restriction of the nature of things is: "that which is not edible [is not to be eaten]. Because eating was applicable here due to a general desire for food, it was thus [erroneously] assumed based on instruction; therefore, a restriction is made therein: "hunger is to be countered by this [meat] and not by anything else. Regarding this, there is the view of some:

If that statement [is the basis], then because the rule "the domestic cock is not to be eaten" has not been explicitly mentioned [as a source], it would follow that this is *dharma*. Others think: just as poison is not consumed because death from consuming poison is certain, so too [the domestic cock] is a minor offense (*upapātaka*) by its very nature; therefore, *dharma* consists in its avoidance. Thus, for one who seeks to understand the meaning, every object is expressed through both correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*). In that regard, a restriction is established that the object is to be conveyed by the correct word and not by the other.

But surely, since the *kṛtya* suffix is not prescribed for the word *kṣudh* (hunger) when it is the second member [of a compound], and the *kṛtya* arises with respect to the object (*karman*), it ought to be so in that case as well: "and this can be done by him" (*śakyā cānena*). This is not a fault. The introduction is made generally, but the expression is specific. Here, the *kṛtya* suffix after the root *śak* is applied to the sense of an object with respect to a general substance. That very form, having already acquired its gender, is differentiated by the specific quality of not abandoning its original gender (*ajahalliṅgatā*). In that specific instance, the state of being the object has already been utilized by the *kṛtya* suffix; therefore, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used.

As it has been said: "His speech is through the mouth and nose," rather than saying "he whose speech is to be uttered by the mouth and nose. Likewise, due to exhaustion (*kheda*). Exhaustion is the incapacity of a faculty to restrain itself when operating upon its own object. Alternatively, exhaustion means that which causes weariness; thus, passion (*rāga*) itself is called exhaustion, for indeed, from passion arises the engagement with women. Or else, exhaustion is dejection (*dainya*).

Thus, having first shown that the Smṛti treatise accepted as human-authored was composed based on the Veda, he now demonstrates that very point within the Veda itself: "In the Veda, indeed, it is said, 'A Brāhmaṇa is one who observes the milk-vow'. Now, is this state of observing the milk-vow for the sake of the sacrifice? He says: No. If it were for the sake of the sacrifice, then just as there is necessarily engagement in other cases such as the cutting and eating of portions, so too would it be here. But the initiated person does not necessarily consume only milk; rather, it is when there is a [specific] need.

Just as in the case of the statement "he scratches with a black antelope horn," the scratching which is already established is performed with the black antelope horn when itching arises; and if it were admitted that [the act] is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), then the eating which is prohibited in another context would apply here when there is a desire for it. For example, in the injunction "he looks at the clarified butter," since the looking is for the sake of the ritual, the looking at other substances is not thereby prohibited. Likewise, [the rule] "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should be made of *bailva* or *khadira* wood" [does not prohibit other woods].

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is employed for the purpose of rendering the animal dependent; for in that case, the visible result produced is the act of making [the animal] dependent, provided that the animal is tied to a wooden post which has been fashioned with a *caṣāla* and possesses eight corners. Just as in the case of "the potsherds on the fire," where the visible result is the cooking of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), we do not perceive any specific kind of cooking by means of this mantra. Therefore, it establishes that there is an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) result here.

Even if this position were held—that corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are expressive just like correct words (*sādhuvada*)—the visible result would be the same, namely, the comprehension of meaning. However, in this case, there is also an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*), which is spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Therefore, he says: "In this case as well, since the comprehension of meaning is the same through both [types of] words. By stating that it "brings about prosperity," he accepts this: that demerit (*adharma*) perishes through the abandonment of what is not prescribed. Others, however, think otherwise.

By abandoning that [practice], demerit (*adharma*) does not arise at all; indeed, this itself is prosperity (*abhyudaya*), namely, that one is not joined with sin in this regard. [Objection: There is the charge of being "unemployed" (*aprayukta*). This is accepted as an explanation for those who employ [words] here. But are these words beginning with *uṣ* employed in common usage, or are they written in grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*)? In which treatise is such a rule established? Wishing to demonstrate this by way of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states: this state of being "unemployed" regarding words does not stand merely on the authority of just anyone's statement.

"That it is from the word of those alone who are learned, refined, esteemed in linguistic usage, and independent—this is contradictory. This is the intended meaning: this mode of expression is appropriate for those things that are established even without their own causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as a jar, which is established and proven even without its own causal efficiency, like the fetching of water and so forth. But this word is never established or proven without its own causal efficiency; for it is only through its actual application that it attains the form of "being" (*asti*).

In this regard, just as someone might say, "Because of non-application," so too is this of that same nature. Indeed, while you yourself are actually applying [the word], you say it is "not applied" only because the operation of the vocal organs has not yet ceased; thus you are describing an application that has just recently occurred, for you mean that "this has only just now been applied. It is just as if someone were to say, "I maintain silence for as long as I live, therefore I do not speak"—so too is this [your statement] by you.

In this regard, if you consider that because [the word] is not employed by me, it must therefore be unemployable; or if you think, "I employ it, but others do not," and thus conclude that these [words] are non-existent because they are not employed by anyone else—this too is incorrect. For even if these words were not uttered by others, they would not thereby cease to exist. Indeed, many words are not uttered by women. Now, if this is your thought—"Am I an unreliable person when I utter them?"—then he says this for the sake of encouragement.
"Do not despise yourself, thinking, 'I am a trusted friend. For who else now is of your kind? Who else is wiser than you?"

"This is not contradictory," he says. He explains that existence (sattā) is twofold: perceptual and inferential. Among these, the perceptual [existence] is exemplified by forms such as *dādharti* and *dardharti*. The inferential [existence] must be established through the instruction of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), because there is an instruction of roots and suffixes such as *uṣ* and others. As for the root *dhṛ*, its *ślu* replacement and the absence of the *śap* suffix have not been explicitly stated because they belong to restricted domains; however, since they are recorded in the grammatical treatises, it is established that these [forms] exist.

If you say that [these words] are not used in the world, we reply that they are "unemployed. To the question, "How can I, who am speaking, say they are unemployed? he says: "We do not say they are unemployed by us; rather, I am an insider to the world, but I am not the world itself. This is what is meant: I do not employ these words beginning with *ūṣ* in the same manner as the world employs them.

[11.2] It is not [the case that the word exists] because of the application of the word to the object; for objects such as time, persons, and so forth, do exist. Furthermore, since a word functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to various objects, the word must be present together with its primary referent. Alternatively, the perception of an object is an inference for the existence of the word; for there is no object whatsoever that is without a word.

In this regard, just as the words "heaven," "unseen force" (*apūrva*), and "deity," when perceived, serve as an inference for the existence of objects that are absolutely imperceptible, why is it not accepted that an object, when perceived, serves as an inference for the existence of the word?

[11.3] Non-application [of the reason], because it is different from application. As for this reason taught for the existence of sound—that an object exists "because of its form, even though it is without sound"—to this we say: if these objects did not have expressers [i.e., words], we might understand their existence; but since they do have them, this is no reason. Now, one might object that the word *ucita* does not have the same meaning as *uṣita*, because it expresses the invisibility (*parokṣatā*) of a person. This is not a fault. A sentence must be employed in such a way that the manifestation of all its meanings occurs.

[11.4] As in the case of long-term sacrifices (*dīrghasattra*). By the first principle, one establishes existence: just as long-term sacrifices performed in former times—even though they are not being performed now—still establish their status as objects such as ritual actions (in the sense that curds, honey, and so forth are *dharmas*), so too it is logical that there is conformity with things performed by others at all times, even if they are not being performed now.

However, for those who hold that curds, honey, and so forth are *dharmas*, this meaning is not possible in the context of grammatical analysis (*vyākaraṇa*); for in this system, something is a *dharma* merely because of the utterance of a word.

[11.5] All [words] are used in other regions. Furthermore, even today, those who perform sacrifices say "hari" and "ari. We maintain that all these words are employed in other regions. *Vākovākya* is a work consisting of dialogues, such as "What is the great sowing-ground? and so forth. *Itihāsa* is the narration of past events. Among these, a particular word is employed in a particular context.

For example, the word *puruṣī*, which is feminine in gender, though not used elsewhere, is employed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the Maitrāvaruṇīyas: "Having given a draught-ox and a *puruṣī* cow as sacrificial fees, they should go toward Kārapacava to perform the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) in the Yamunā. The root *śav-* signifies motion; it is spoken with all case-endings only among the Kambojas, while the Āryas speak of its derivative form as *śava*. It is a modification (*vikāra*) of the living being (*prakṛti*); "dead" means it has gone to destruction.

Alternatively, it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the root *gati* (to go), meaning the cessation of motion. Regarding this, they say that one who has ceased activity is a "corpse" (*śava*). However, in the *Nirukta*, it is recited thus: "They speak of its modification among the Āryas. The meaning there is this: they speak only of that modification which is a single part of the root *śavati* ending in the suffix *ac*, and not of the entire verbal base (*prakṛti*) *śavati* ending in all possible suffixes.

[12.1] Furthermore, is the *dharma* (the property) of a word located in its cognition or in its usage? This much is stated by the treatise: "The restriction of *dharma*. Is that restriction of *dharma* due to cognition or due to usage? It is Abhijñā herself who asks, "What is the recollection (*smṛti*) in this matter? Or rather, it is Smṛtijña who asks. But that recollection is sometimes contradicted by direct revelation (*śruti*), such as: "The student of the Veda (*brahmacārin*) must practice the vow for forty-eight years."

This Smṛti contradicts the Śruti; for it is stated in the Śruti: "While his hair is still black, the father shall unite the son [with the sacrificial fires]. In that regard, the Smṛti is a constant authority only in the case of inference. Furthermore, a Smṛti whose purpose is unperceived (adṛṣṭārtha) is not authoritative. For example, some have accepted that the swan (*haṃsa*) is edible, and some have accepted the marriage of those born from the same mother’s womb. In these cases, the Veda has been set in motion by greed or passion. Regarding this, the learned (śiṣṭas), having previously considered it to be Dharma, practice it even today.

"The single word *smṛti*, when correctly understood, consistent with the scriptures, and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world. What does this mean? Is it that only when it is employed does it become correctly understood? If it is employed correctly, then merit (*dharma*) arises precisely from knowledge. Or is it that when it is employed in this way, it becomes correctly understood? But correct employment occurs only when there is correct understanding. Regarding this, we ask: what is the logical basis for this *smṛti*? Of which revealed scripture (*śruti*) is it a restatement?

[12.2] If it is argued that *dharma* resides in the knowledge [of correct words], then by that same logic, *adharma* would reside in the knowledge [of incorrect words]. This is stated as a separate point: if *dharma* exists in the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*), then in that case, *adharma* would result from the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*). This [consequence] might hold true in this sense: that *adharma* results from the killing of a Brahmin, whereas *dharma* results from living [by other means]. However, one cannot say that while *adharma* results from the killing of a Brahmin, *dharma* results from the killing of a Śūdra.

For in this case, it would be logical [to argue] that if dharma results from the knowledge of correct words, then adharma would result from the ignorance of those very words. To this it is replied: he states that this tradition (smṛti) is equal to traditions whose objects are perceptible. For in a tradition concerning perceptible objects, such as medicine, that which aggravates phlegm is the opposite of what is dry, which [aggravates] wind. Thus, others maintain that from the knowledge of correct words there is neither dharma nor adharma, but from the knowledge of corrupt words (apaśabda) there is adharma.

"Dharma arises from the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*), but not unrighteousness (*adharma*) from the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*)," as he will state later: "We have the Word (*śabda*) as our authority. Some believe that dharma and adharma proceed from the knowledge of correct and corrupt words respectively, and that adharma is overcome by dharma, just as one might employ a well-digger. In that context, he demonstrates that [the claim] "unrighteousness results from the knowledge of corrupt words" is incorrect; for no harm follows from the study of grammar. Furthermore, it is not the case that words cannot be known without grammar.

Now, it might be argued that "dharma is greater and adharma is smaller. But this is incorrect; since corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are more numerous, their result must also be more abundant, and thus it follows that adharma itself would be greater.

[12.3] There is a restriction regarding conduct (*ācāra*). Thus, this *smṛti* is first of all contradicted by what has been stated [in the Veda]. Furthermore, the *śruti* does not corroborate it; for this reason as well, it is not authoritative. Regarding the application in conduct, the *ṛṣi-mantra*—"Those were the Asuras"—demonstrates this very conduct. And [the Veda says]: "One should not speak like a barbarian (*mleccha*), nor should one use corrupt speech. This *smṛti* states that one must not engage in barbarism or corrupt speech; it does not, however, state that barbarism or corrupt speech is not to be known.

But is it not the case that here it is merely stated, "This corrupt word must not be used," and thus there is no merit (*dharma*) from the use of words? This is not a fault. When the speaking of corrupt speech is prohibited, does one simply have to remain silent? In that context, it is understood that even if speech is generally discouraged, that which is beneficial should nevertheless be performed as a means of accomplishment.

[12.4] The intention is that the undertaking of a treatise on linguistic usage (*prayoga*) is useless for all the world, because usage is observed even without grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). To this, an objection is raised: Even if usage exists without a treatise, nevertheless, the effort [toward it] is not purposeless. Just as some people, despite being naturally healthy, proceed by rejecting the instruction of physicians, yet medical science is still composed because certain sick people must indeed be treated by it; so too, grammar must be set forth and studied.
Because one who desires to employ words is taught [them], and for that purpose, [the treatise] must be composed—this is said.
It is true that this is so; however, it has already been stated regarding them in that very place:
"Those with blazing digestive fires, those who eat coarse food, those devoted to ritual action, and those with large bellies."
For those men who oppose them, one must necessarily consider the relative gravity or lightness of the offense.
Thus [it is said]. But here, nothing of that kind exists. This much is said: "Without grammar, words cannot be known."

[12.5] Prosperity results from usage preceded by the treatise (*śāstra*). When there is knowledge based on the *śāstra*, the usage that follows from it leads to prosperity. He who, having understood [the rules] according to the *śāstra*, employs words, is endowed with prosperity. Therefore, this traditional rule (*smṛti*)—that "one word is correctly known"—is equal to the Vedic word (*vedaśabda*). It is equal to the meaning expressed by the Vedic word. This is like the Vedic statement: "He who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma, and he who knows it thus."

The word "Veda" expresses this meaning: he who, being learned, performs the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is joined with prosperity, because only the learned have the right to perform ritual acts. Another says: now, the Vedic sentences themselves are the examples; just as they, when studied according to the rules such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and others, are the means for accomplishing *dharma*, so too, since the performance [of the rite] is a means for accomplishing *dharma*, it is established that prosperity results from a distinguished performance characterized by knowledge preceded by the scriptures.

Alternatively, let it be that [the cause] is indeed knowledge. This memory is not equivalent to the perception of an object; rather, in that case, this is remembered through an unbroken tradition as "dharma arises from knowledge. Thus, whatever is enjoined or prohibited based on the authority of scripture (āgama) is precisely what is performed or avoided. But is it not the case that this statement [from scripture] implies that there is either non-dharma or dharma resulting from the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), and not [dharma or non-dharma] from the corrupt words themselves?

And that which is neither prescribed nor prohibited involves neither merit nor fault in its performance or avoidance. Alternatively, the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is itself a means (*abhyupāya*) to the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*). Since that which is a means for something else cannot function without it, that [knowledge of *apaśabda*] is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it. For example, someone might think: "Whiteness residing in the earth is a property because it is seen there. But this [earth] is black; seeing it, one is unable to perceive whiteness therein.

Therefore, this [knowledge of corrupt forms] is indeed a means for the perception of the correct word; just as in the case of the horse-sacrifice and other rites, violence is merely a means to dharma. Likewise, the knowledge of the correct word is necessarily accompanied by the knowledge of corrupt forms. Thus, there is no connection between this [knowledge of corrupt forms] and adharma. In this way, the Smṛti is justified; thus, the Smṛti does not become purposeless.

Alternatively, there is the analogy of the well-digger; this is the logical justification. Even if demerit (*adharma*) were to arise from the knowledge of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), it would still be very slight; whereas from the knowledge of correct words (*śabda*) alone, there arises superior and abundant merit. Thus, one indeed engages in study even though a fault exists. That [superiority] is understood precisely through the force of the composition of the *Smṛti* texts, namely that merit is more excellent from the knowledge of correct words. An example of this is the well-digger.

Just as one who considers himself to be endowed with great prosperity proceeds even to a faulty undertaking, such as digging a well, thinking, "I am able to remove this defect as well," so too is the praise of verbal knowledge (śabdajñāna) effected by this [statement]. As it has been said: "One should not build the Śyena-altar facing downwards; the sacrificer would die. This is not a censure of the downward-facing altar; rather, by means of this, the praise of the upward-facing one is effected. Know that women are dead!

And having acted thus, Yājñavalkya will speak these words: "These two grey arms—where indeed has the word of a Brahmin gone? For had he killed the sacrificer while lying face-down, he would have known: "I myself, having understood [the truth], would not have come to this. Therefore, this action too is seen [as a consequence]. This is the view of others; it is merely a censure of one who lies face-down.

The restriction applies specifically to the sacrificial rite (*yajña-karman*). This is what is meant: that scriptural injunction (*śruti*) does not refer to the general case; rather, it refers to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*). And the purpose of the context is such even for other [acts]: for instance, approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā-gamana*) occurs in the *gosava* sacrifice; drinking liquor (*surā-pāna*) in the *sautrāmaṇī*; and the killing of a Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇa-vadha*) in the *sarvamedha*. Just as in the absence of a tortoise, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is restricted to a specific object—namely, if one cannot find a tortoise, one should place a *karka* (a type of turtle)... [etc.]...

"At the conclusion of the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, one should offer an oblation upon the head with the mantra, 'To Jumbaka, svāhā!'—[offering it] to Piṅgala, the bald, the moist, the descendant of Atri, who is submerged in water. This establishes that such a rule applies only to sacrificial rites and not elsewhere; for thus it is heard in the *purākalpa*: "Those whose dharma was perceptible to them were the worldly dharmas that are imperceptible to the world, yet were perceptible to them. They were knowers of the higher and the lower; they were knowers of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate."

Furthermore, according to scripture, they may indeed possess direct knowledge of dharma, yet they are not necessarily knowers of what is logical or illogical, nor have they realized all that is to be known; even if they are worthy of sacrifice and speak incorrectly regarding rituals other than those of the sacrifice, they are not defeated.

[13.1] Now, regarding the term "explanation" (*vyākaraṇa*), what is its referent (*padārtha*)? By asking "what is expressed by this? and "in what sense is it established?", he asks this by means of the term *padārtha*. For some words, while having an identical form, function with different meanings and different causes, operating in mutual dependence; for example, the word "horse" (*aśva*) when ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) and when ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). However, some [words] function because their cause is identical.

Just as the word "water" (ap) applies to both the ocean and a drop by virtue of a generic property (*jāti*), so too does a certain term apply to a specific object through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) because its action is identical, even when there is a difference in genus; for example, "eye" (*akṣa*) from the root *aś* (to reach), "foot" (*pāda*) from *pad* (to go), and "māṣa" from *mā* (to measure). In those cases, it is established by the commonality of action. Alternatively, some [words] function by bringing about that state or by superimposition (*adhyāropa*), such as the word "cow" (*go*) applied to a Vāhīka person, or the word "snake" (*sarpa*) applied to a rope. In this context, which of these types of words is to be understood by the term "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*)?

Desiring to explain the ground for the application of the term [grammar] by means of this gateway, he makes the following presentation: "Furthermore, it has been stated repeatedly that one cannot understand those [words] without grammar; therefore, let your honor explain the meaning of the word *vaiyākaraṇa*. [The opponent asks: "Is it the *sūtra*? Or is it the collection of *sūtras* in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*? The meaning of this [term] is not established. [The opponent further objects: "But surely even the use of the word *sūtra* itself is untenable. It is said in reply: When the expression begins with a general reference, it is called a *sūtra*.

The distinction that "what is the *sūtra*? and "it is the *vyākaraṇa*," is appropriate, just as in the case of "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*. However, the expression of the meaning of the words [as distinct entities] is not employed because there is no difference [between them]. But when the word *vyākaraṇa* functions as a term for the whole (*samudāyavṛtti*) and the word *sūtra* is applied to a particular part (*avayava*), such as in "vṛddhir ādaic" and so forth, then the sense of the genitive case is also justified. When, however, both are terms for the whole, then it is objected that there is an absence of the sense of the genitive.

[13.2] There is no comprehension of the word itself. For we do not comprehend the meaning from the mere word *vṛddhir ādaij*; what then? From the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). From the example, we comprehend words belonging to the same class. But is it not the case that the very sūtra, when analyzed, constitutes the commentary? Commentary is the means for manifesting the meaning of the sūtra. Just as the meaning of "the tusked one situated in the *vaṭa* tree" is manifested by saying, "the tusked one is situated in the *vaṭa* tree."

It is not merely the words of the discussion; for the meaning is not understood from a sūtra when it is analyzed in the same way that it is understood from the words of a discussion, such as "the tree is at the banyan."

[13.3] In the word *śabda*, the sense of the suffix *-lyuṭ* [is intended]. When there is a distinction [between the two], the sense of the genitive case is understood. For the *sūtra* is related to the word as its expounder; however, the sense of *-lyuṭ* is not tenable here. For a word being refined (*saṃskriyamāṇa*) is primary because it is for the sake of another [the meaning]; and it is not logical for that which is primary to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Just as, in the cases of production, refinement, and communication, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) possesses primacy precisely because it is what is to be produced, what is to be refined, and what is to be communicated;
whereas it has a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) in the communication of the word.

[13.4] And regarding the word *bhava*: would these not be called *bhava* because they are explained (*anvākhyāpaka*) within that [context]? This being the case, every grammatical rule (*yoga*) whatsoever would result in the designation "grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇa*). Therefore, what is intended here is the relationship between part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*).

[13.5] Even terms such as *prokta* (pronounced) are not tenable, for words are not themselves "pronounced. This has been stated previously. Since the *bhāṣya* and the *sūtras* do not rely on brevity (*laghu*) versus prolixity (*guru*), and since both definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) and elaborations (*prapañca*) are resorted to in the root *sūtras*, here too the operation proceeds by means of both definition and elaboration. For example: *praskandanaṃ* and *prapatanaṃ*. But surely these are recited among the *bhīmādi* group? It is said: this very point is expressed by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; that is, the *bhīmādi* group is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that rule.

Alternatively, words are also analyzed by means of words. For a word, when uttered, prompts [the listener] toward its own essential form and manifests its exclusion from what is contrary to it; it serves as the indicator of other words belonging to the same class. Furthermore, there is an absolute cessation of anything belonging to a different class, even if it be correct. In that regard, it is stated in a portion of the Bhāṣya: "It is not a horse, nor is it a donkey."

[13.6] If that is so, then grammar consists of the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa). This should not be understood as being like the case where one calls the *vanaspati* "bilva" and another "śarada," as if they were different things; nor is it a case of a single word (*ekaśabdattva*) like "water" (*ap-śarad*), because there is a single cause; nor is it like "eye" (*akṣa*), because of a common action; nor is it based on the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one of several identical words). For if it were conceived in such a way, every word would simply conform to the *bhāṣya*.

If that which is about to be stated is the object of definition (*lakṣya*) and the other is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and yet another is the collection (*samudāya*), why is it said that "the word functions with respect to collections"? Therefore, just as these words—*saṃgha*, *maṇḍala*, *senā*, and *vana*—denote the collection and do not denote the individual parts, so too the word *vyākaraṇa* denotes the collection and does not denote the individual parts. Even so, this fault remains:
just as these [words] such as *vana* do not apply to a single part, so too this [word *vyākaraṇa*] does not apply to a single part.

Regarding the expression "the Eastern Pañcālas": when a collection has been brought to the state of being a whole, it is designated by a word denoting that whole. This is just as a Bāhīka, when brought to the state of being a cow, is designated by the word "cow. For it is not possible for a word to abandon the whole and apply to a single part. Therefore, when the whole completely deposits its own self within a part, then the word denoting the whole functions. Likewise, in the case of the word "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) as well, when its application to the whole is deposited upon a single part, namely a *sūtra*, by whom should the application of that word be effected?

"Oil has been eaten," "ghee has been eaten"—in such cases, having conceptually attributed the word to either the harmful or the beneficial ghee or oil, the term for the whole (samudāya) functions by applying to its parts (avayava). Likewise, in the case of "white" and so forth, because a certain part alone is made white, one says that this whole called a "cloth" has been made to have another color; thus, the word for the whole applies to a single part.

Just as one does not perceive a jar in its entirety, yet the cognition "jar" arises in him with respect to only some of its parts, even so, while understanding a collection [of rules] from merely a single sūtra, one employs the word "grammar" (vyākaraṇa) with reference to that alone. For example, when someone uses the expression "he cooks" upon seeing only the act of placing [the pot] on the fire, it is said in reply to him: "He is not cooking; he is merely placing [the pot] on the fire; rather, he is preparing water."

[13.7] It will be by way of the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). And this treatment as if possessing a designation occurs in some cases in a certain manner. Here, in the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, there is indeed the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose meaning is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and there is also the status of being a phoneme (*varṇa*). In that regard, for that which is based on one form, there is a designation associated with another form.

Alternatively, in the conceptualization of a whole and its parts, that which is the whole inherent in the usage [of the word]—namely, "that which goes" (*eti*) or "the act of going" (*ayanam*)—is the root *eti* as a constituent part thereof. Just as this "stone-child" (*śilāputraka*) is seen to be the object of various actions, such that one says "this is his body," so too here, in the case of "Rāhu has a thick head" (*sthūlaśirā rāhuḥ*), even though there is no actual relation of whole and part, the designation occurs merely through the operation of words, despite the absence of any real distinction.

For a word functions by determining only a certain portion of an object, regardless of whether the knowledge of the whole object exists or not. For example, although a mountain exists, the word "finger" does not speak of it; likewise, although Rāhu possesses only a head, the word "Rāhu" does not speak of that mere-headedness. Indeed, only as much as is denotable by the word "Rāhu" is expressed; its designation is connected with the head.

Just as, even though a thing is a single entity, a notion of excellence arises from expressing its particular state—as in, "Last year you were clever, but this year you are more clever"—so too here, grammar possesses both the nature of a continuous textual composition (*grantha-saṃdarbha*) and the nature of constituent parts (*avayava*).
