Therefore, the designation [of it as "sūtra"] is justified either by the distinction of states or by the relationship of general and particular. Here, it is understood that the word "sūtra" expresses the general form.

Regarding the question "of what?"—even for one who maintains non-difference (*ananyatva*), the term "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) is applied when there is a specific distinction; and when the word "grammar" functions as a collective designation and the word "sūtra" refers to a particular sūtra, then there is non-difference as if it were primary. In that case, it is either the specific itself or the universal itself.

Therefore, there is no such thing as "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (vyapadeśivadbhāva) in cases such as "the scent of sandalwood" or "the color and so forth of color and so forth. However, even for one who maintains the doctrine of non-difference (*ananyatva*), a designation occurs when there is a relationship between a universal and its particular, as in "the fragrance of sandalwood. This happens to one who does not understand; what is meant is this: someone may not comprehend [the meaning] even through an explanation. How then? Through winking the eyes and other such gestures. In that case, what can be said? That the comprehension of the word arises from mimetic representation (*abhinaya*).

In this regard, it should be understood as follows: these are not the actual methods; rather, their manifestation comes from the Sūtra. For it is precisely from the Sūtra, whose meaning has been manifested, that the application of words occurs. This employment of examples and so forth is intended so that one might understand a different word [not previously known], and not so that one might state something contrary to the system (tantra) or the Bhāṣya. What, then, is its purpose? It is to manifest that which was unmanifested in the Sūtra. And he supports this very point.

For if someone were to speak contrary to the sūtras (*utsūtra*), their statement would not be accepted; that [statement] is not accepted. But why is what is contrary to the sūtras not accepted? It is said: this is a treatise on traditional law (*smṛti-śāstra*). In that regard, if someone were to say, "This is the word," he must necessarily be asked, "How are we to understand this? If he cites a sūtra from the *Smṛti*, it is consistent; then his utterance is accepted. For example: "This is a Pāṇinian sūtra: there is no prohibition regarding the [suffixes] *ny* and *aṅ*."

In this regard, there is a misconception: [some hold] that it ought to be *naiyaṅkava*. However, if someone were to employ the form *nyāṅkava*, we do not consider it to be an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). But if he were to cite another traditional authority (*smṛti*), then indeed there is a prohibition of it in that other tradition. Just as here, because of the rule "and of the solitary *nyagrodha*," we understand without doubt that this is a correct word.
Therefore, this alone must be accepted: from the Sūtra itself, through examples and so forth, the application of words is understood from their established meaning.

[14.1] For what purpose is the instruction of phonemes (*varṇa*)? When the employment of words is prompted by meaning, there is a restriction regarding *dharma*. In that regard, these [phonemes] do not possess meaning; therefore, their instruction would be purposeless. Nor is instruction possible for the sake of the meaning of a composite whole. Since the instruction applies to roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and suffixes (*pratyaya*), it follows that the phonemes occupying those positions are also being instructed. Instruction is for the purpose of establishing their occurrence in grammatical operations (*vṛtti-samavāya*); for the instruction of these is certainly not for the purpose of determining their own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*). What then is its purpose?

The meaning is "for the sake of sequence. This means that by this sequence, they should perform certain tasks in the treatise (*śāstra*). Alternatively, he explains this for the purpose of summarizing the components of the treatise. [Regarding the term] *vṛttisamavāya*: it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the inherence of occurrence" (*vṛtteḥ samavāyaḥ*). The distinction is shown by way of its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), as in the case of "horse fodder" (*aśvaghāsa*). Or, it means "inherence for the sake of occurrence" (*vṛttyarthaḥ samavāyaḥ*); thus, the state of being the cause (*nimittabhāva*) of occurrence with respect to the inherence for the sake of occurrence is explained.

For [the term] *pravṹttisamavāya* functions based on mere sequential arrangement (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). It is a *samavāya* (inherence) for the purpose of application; thus, it is "inherence as application. This is like the compound *śākapārthiva* ("vegetable-king"). Alternatively, it means "having application as its purpose. By this, an indirect causal status is indicated: the application of the treatise (*śāstra*) is indirectly prompted by inherence (*samavāya*). This application of the treatise, characterized by the [technical] markers (*anubandha*), such as in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, has inherence as its indirect cause.

And this will indeed be seen in the Bhāṣya as well. What, then, is *vṛtti*? It is the operation (*pravṛtti*) of the treatise. Why so? Because *vṛtti* is an action (*kriyā*), and an action requires an instrument (*sādhana*). In that context, the topical treatise of grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana-śāstra*) is understood as the instrument. The instruction of the phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*) has as its purpose that which is the inherent connection (*samavāya*) in the operation of the treatise. [Objection: Is it not called "instruction" (*upadeśa*) because something is taught (*upadiśyate*) by means of it? [Reply: No; for nothing at all is taught by these [phonemes].

The other [author] explains that it is a derivation based on the action (*bhāvasādhana*): it is "utterance" (*uccāraṇa*). Why is this so? Because the root *diś* signifies the act of uttering; for having uttered the phonemes, one says, "the phonemes have been taught by me. In this context, when an action has ceased, whatever subsequent word is employed, its purpose is understood to be directed toward that [action]. For example, when Brahmins have finished eating and have entered [the house], one says, "the Brahmins have eaten" or "the Brahmins have entered. It is understood from this that the meaning of the roots *bhuj* and *praviś* is indeed [the completion of those actions].
Similarly here too, when the phonemes have been uttered, one immediately asks: "For what purpose is this instruction? We understand that the root *diś* signifies the act of utterance.

[14.2] And for the purpose of establishing the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters). The establishment of *anubandhas* is necessarily required as a constituent element (*aṅga*) for the operation of the treatise (*śāstra*). And that [establishment] does not occur without instruction. In this regard, the *anubandhas* consist of consonants (*hal*) alone. However, this one [letter], *laṇ*, is without an *anubandha*; here, the vowel *a* is attached to the letter *l*. Furthermore, in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, it serves the purpose of making the *ṛ*-vowel and the *l*-vowel followed by *r* and *l* respectively. It also serves the purpose of forming *pratyāhāras* (abbreviated designations). A *pratyāhāra* is a concise abbreviation of something extensive.

In this regard, it is stated that the abbreviation (pratyāhāra) "the first [letter] together with the last" does not exist without the arrangement [of the alphabet] and the markers (anubandha). Therefore, the collection [of letters] and the application of markers are for the sake of abbreviation; abbreviation is for the sake of the grammatical operations (vṛtti), such as "a long vowel replaces a homogeneous vowel following *ak*" and "ay, av, āy, and āv replace *ec*."

[14.3] Furthermore, the instruction of phonemes (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of correct cognition. For when there is instruction, those [phonemes] are pronounced exactly as they are; thus, those that are such are correct (*sādhū*), while those that are otherwise are incorrect (*asādhū*). Therefore, instruction must be performed even for the sake of understanding correctness. The instruction of the accents (*udātta*, etc. must also be performed. For these phonemes are recited in a single tone (*ekaśruti*) in the *ac* alphabet; consequently, it would follow that only those [phonemes] distinct from the accents and distinct in duration would possess correctness. Therefore, all [phonemes] must be taught.

But surely all these [sounds], such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and the rest, are already explained by the treatise? It is replied: since their specific nature is not taught when they are not being explicitly instructed—as in the question "What kind of acute accents and so forth are to be understood?"—it would be impossible to comprehend them.

[14.4] It is established through the instruction of the form (*ākṛti*). In the instruction of the form, the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is necessarily concomitant; however, at that time, it is not yet dependent upon it. Thus, they will understand that the form exists even among those things differentiated by time and qualities. This very phoneme (*varṇa*) which was taught in the traditional recitation of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) is precisely this one. Just as when there is an instruction regarding a single form, one understands "this is that very same one" even with respect to particular forms that are distinct.

In this regard, just as the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those [sounds] distinguished by time and quality follows from the existence of their *ākṛti* (general form), so too would the correctness of those distinguished by quality and accent follow from the existence of their *ākṛti*. Therefore, an effort must be made to exclude that; thus he says: "A prohibition must be stated for the *saṃvṛta* and others. That which is called *saṃvṛta* is the external effort (*prayatna*). For the internal effort is what produces the vowel *a*; the *kala* is not like that. That which is blown is predominantly breath; that which is made like a gazelle (*eṇīkṛta*) is indistinct.

These are the conceptualizations of defects in pronunciation; these are the classes of defects in pronunciation. For it is understood that the defects in pronunciation of speakers arise from negligence or incapacity. Through the recitation of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups [in Pāṇini’s grammar], there will be the exclusion of [defects such as] *saṃvṛta* (closed) and so forth. This is what is intended: nowhere are individual phonemes (*varṇa*) actually uttered. What then? It is only collections of sounds (*samudāya*) that are recited. And a collection consists of phonemes; furthermore, a collection is recited as having its constituent parts (*kalā*) already excluded.

In this regard, it is established that the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of *kalā* and so forth applies to [names] beginning with *garga* and those beginning with *bid*. There is another purpose for the recitation (*pāṭha*) of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups. This is what is meant: the recitation of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups serves this specific purpose. How so? By means of this particular arrangement, there shall be grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), and not by any other. For example, in the case of "Garga": what must be done? The exclusion of *kalā* and so forth must be effected for those forms established in the recitation. However, as for those word-forms which are not recited, *kalā* and so forth remain unexcluded in them.

In that case, I shall demonstrate by way of illustration that which is the eighteenfold classification of *pratyāpatti* (recovery from a lapse) at the end of the treatise. Why, then, is it said "one who has ceased [the study of] *kalā* and so forth," and not "one who has ceased [the study of] *saṃvṛta* and so forth"? Because it is *saṃvṛta* (conventional). For the sake of a specific purpose, *kalā* and the others are accepted. [One might say: "I will study the *śīṅ*, *māsiṃ*, and the blown *kala*; I will not study the *ṅkāra* and the *akāra*. And I shall speak thus: 'The *ātmanepada* occurs after a root beginning with *kala* when it is blown.'"

But here, it is impossible to understand [the rule] *iko yaṇ aci*; for if the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) does not exist, there is neither the technical definition of *it* nor this rule stating that "that which is first [in a series] is [designated] by the last [along with the intervening letters]. Therefore, in all operations characterized by *pratyāhāra*s, all [the letters] must be explicitly mentioned.

[14.5] In that case, both are accomplished by this [single effort]: the *samavāya* (the composite whole) is established as correct, and it is indicated that the [individual] phonemes such as *a*, *kāra*, and so forth are indeed of such a nature; whereas *kalā* and the like are incorrect (*asādhūni*) in all instances. But how can both be obtained by a single effort? Here, in the case of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), the instruction is intended for the whole (*samudāya*); thus, the two constituent parts do not undergo the grammatical operations (*varṇakārya*) pertaining to individual phonemes.

Just as the instruction of phonemes (*varṇa*) is for the purpose of discerning their constituent parts, so that in the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional list of phonemes) only the parts are relied upon and not the whole; in the same way, in the recitation of the *garga*- and *bidādi*-classes, it would be the parts alone that are intended to be discerned, and the mention of the whole is made only in accordance with those parts. Alternatively, [one might argue] that it is indeed the wholes [that are intended]. If they were wholes, then for those parts belonging to such domains, there would be an absence of *kalā* and so forth; elsewhere, however, [the rule] would simply be set aside. Or rather, [the term refers to] the parts.

This being the case, it would be impossible to understand the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the collective form; consequently, words such as *gargāḥ* would not be excluded [from the application of the rule]. To this he says: "It is obtainable. How so? Causes (*hetu*) can have two applications. "Two-fold" (*dvigata*) means having gone to two meanings. Causes are capable of accomplishing an effect. In this world, a single cause is seen to be the accomplisher of two purposes. For example, water.

The action directed toward that [water], characterized by its relinquishment, has a single common cause when performed at the foot of a mango tree for both the libation to the ancestors and the watering of the tree. However, in other cases, that same water does not serve two purposes; for instance, when Devadatta and Yajñadatta are both to be satiated, or when mango trees located in distant places are to be watered.

In this regard, just as the act of pouring water, having been undertaken with the understanding that it is capable of accomplishing both a visible and an invisible purpose, brings about both results; so too the recitation of the *garga* and *bidādi* groups is capable of performing both functions, operating upon both the individual parts (*avayava*) and the whole (*samudāya*) for the sake of the grammatical operation. Alternatively, there is the establishment of the meaning through the definition of *prasaṅga*. If something not directly motivated by a specific purpose leads to the comprehension of a purpose by means of another, that is called *prasaṅga*.

Just as one who desires food is the instigator of the act of cooking, yet one who eats the remnants (*vighasa*) is not the instigator; for he who would cook again even when the food is already finished is of such a nature [as not to be the primary agent]. When much food has been prepared for that purpose, a prohibition is enjoined against those who eat from the covered [remnants] and so forth. In that case, if the parts were to convey their own specific forms everywhere by means of a word intended to denote the whole, what fault would there be?
Thus, the mango trees are the actual instigators of the watering, while the ancestors are not; in that case, the water offered is experienced by them only as a secondary consequence.

[14.6] Likewise, sentences that possess a dual status are also observed. This explains that this is not merely a property of meaning (*arthadharma*), but rather a property of the word itself (*śabdadharma*). Here, a certain single word is endowed with multiple capacities (*śakti*); of it, only the delimitation of its potential meanings is performed. For example, the single word *purā* and the word *ārāt* denote both "ancient" (*purāṇa*) and "near," as well as "distant. In the same way, the word *śveta* is endowed with many capacities.

In that case, only a delimitation of its power (*śakti*) is performed. [For example,] the speaker employs the expressions "the white cow" (*śveto gauḥ*) or "that dog has come" (*śvā sa itaḥ*). The hearers understand the object according to the delimitation of its power. These two words are uttered with distinct meanings; just as a lamp, functioning through a single mechanism (*tantra*), accomplishes the desired purpose for those who seek it, or just as a single [lamp] simultaneously fulfills the needs of one seeking knowledge and another desiring to see.

Thus, regarding words, such an action is brought about through the movement of the articulatory organs that two words are uttered by means of a single effort (*tantra*). And there are two methods for the use of words in the world: either sequential usage or simultaneity. Sometimes one employs words in a sequence, as in: "Let the die be cast; let the die be played. Sometimes, having set aside the sequence, one utters them simultaneously: "Let the dice be cast; let them be played. These two methods are established for the employment of words.
"Whether in sequence or simultaneously, those two ways which the world does not transcend.
Therefore, in this case as well, the recitation of the *Garga* and *Bida* groups serves as a means for the tantra to convey both the whole and its parts.

[14.7] "Alternatively, this person should first be questioned regarding the Veda"—this is the intended meaning. For all these [words] are taught as existing within a collection [of phonemes]; thus, the exclusion of parts (*kalādi*) is already established therein. Furthermore, the verbal roots (*dhātu*) are recited in their pure form, and words such as *culumpa* are also pronounced in the Bhāṣya itself—this is the intention. As for those [names] that are not included [in the grammatical lists], such as *ḍittha* and so forth, instruction must necessarily be provided for them as well, for the sake of knowing the sequence of their vowels and consonants.

Alternatively, the instruction of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups must be provided for the sake of their specific sequence of vowels and consonants; thus it is recorded in tradition: "Whatever is the pronunciation of these here is for the purpose of formulating grammatical suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*). Or rather, by one who speaks in this manner, it is implied that all these [words] are derived [from roots]; what then is the status of those which are not so derived? It is said: he explains this point—namely, that even these *gargādi* words which have been recited were not produced by Pāṇini either.

Rather, they are remembered as being of such a nature; just as those very [words] are remembered as being of such a nature, so too other words are established in a general sense by the rule "uṇādayo bahulam" (Uṇādi suffixes are manifold). It should be inferred from both the suffix and the base: having observed the usage of the learned, the base and the suffix must be inferred. And this must necessarily be understood in this way; for instance: [The following verse is provided: "The suffix *man* is seen after the root *kṛ*, preceded by *pra*; likewise, *man* is seen after *vṛ* with *ni*. The suffix *kan* is seen after *pṛ* with *vi*; the suffix *kan* is seen after *mṛj* with *vi*. In this regard, the suffix *man* is observed after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *pra*, as in *prakramaṇa*. Likewise, *man* is observed after *vṛ* with *ni*, as in *nivaraṇa*. The suffix *kan* is observed after *pṛ* with *vi*, as in *viprakarṣaṇa*. The suffix *kan* is observed after *mṛj* with *vi*, as in *vimārjana*. Thus, through the observation of the usage of the learned, the base and the suffix are to be inferred. Therefore, it is established that the Uṇādi suffixes are manifold. This is the meaning.

Even when there is instruction regarding [the accents] such as the udātta, once the removal of the *kalā* and other elements has been effected, this form "ḍittha" is correct and not "ḍuttha. This very fact must be accepted as the understanding of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, without the usage of the learned, it does not follow that the removal of the *kalā* and so forth is established in all cases.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya in the commentary of Bhartṛhari.

In the *Mahābhāṣyadīpikā*, the second *āhnika*: [1] The teaching of the vowel *a* as *vivṛta*. The four internal efforts (*ābhyantara-prayatna*), beginning with *spṛṣṭatā* (contact), operate both for the application and the cessation of the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous). Among these, since the vowel *a* is *saṃvṛta* (contracted) while *ā* is *vivṛta* (expanded), there is an absence of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity); consequently, in the absence of its inclusion [by the rule], *ā* would not undergo the grammatical operation. Therefore, the teaching of *a* as *vivṛta* is adopted.

But surely, because phonemes have fixed efforts (*prayatna*), just as there is a restriction of their places of articulation (*sthāna*), it is impossible—given that their places are fixed—for the vowel *i* to be articulated by the lips, or for the vowel *a* to be articulated with the teeth; likewise, how could the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowel *a* possibly be articulated as the open (*vivṛta*) one? It is replied: a certain effort cannot be performed by the speaker due to inadvertence (*apramāda*). But this [open articulation] can be performed without inadvertence, just like the "clenched" (*saṃdaṣṭa*) articulation and so forth. And because it is possible, the instruction regarding the open [articulation] is enjoined.

[1.1] In this context, the word *ākāra* contains the suffix *kāra*. According to the rule "The suffix *kāra* [is added] after a phoneme" (*Pāṇini* 3.3.108, Vārttika 3), the suffix *kāra* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after a word denoting a phoneme, when that phoneme is to be expressed. Thus, by means of the *akāra* situated in the sentence, the *akāra* situated in the sūtra—namely the *akāra* in "aiuṇ"—is designated. Now, how is the suffix *kāra* applied in the case of *kakāra*, since this is not a single phoneme? What is it then? It is a collection of phonemes. This is not a fault.

It is for this very purpose that this has been introduced: "This suffix denotes the phoneme (*varṇa*). Since a consonant (*vyañjana*) cannot be pronounced without a vowel (*anacka*), the suffix *kāra* is applied to a phoneme accompanied by a vowel (*sāckāt varṇāt*) to denote that phoneme. However, what is being explained is understood as being indeed without a vowel (*anacka*). For example, when the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* are present, the *khakāra* and *phakāra* are pronounced; yet, when they are actually apprehended, they are understood as pure [consonants] alone.

[1.2] But surely, because the suffix *kāra* is eternal (*nitya*), the grammatical formulation "asya cvau" (Pāṇini 7.4.32) would be untenable; for it ought to be "akārasya cvau. It is replied: when the distinction between the signified and the signifier is not intended to be expressed, there is an apprehension of identity in the form "this is that very same thing," and thus, since there is no denotation of a specific phoneme (*varṇa*), the suffix does not occur. Alternatively, one should understand from this very formulation that the suffix is non-eternal (*anitya*).

[1.3] Regarding the statement "the teaching of *a* as *vivṛta*": since the word *vivṛta* is dependent, there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), and thus the formation of a compound with the word *upadeśa* would be untenable. It is replied: because *vivṛta* is a quality (*guṇa*), its dependence on a substratum (*guṇin*) is unavoidable; thus, being dependent, it functions [in the compound]. Or, being a qualifier of the whole (*samudāya*), it will also touch upon the part (*avayava*) that has occurred [within it].

Furthermore, the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*) has been stated in that context: "In this case, because it conveys meaning, the application [of the rule] will occur" (MBh 2.19.11). Alternatively, it is an instruction given with explicit expansion (*vivṛta*); thus, when the compound "sādhanaṃ kṛtā... (P 2.1.33, vt. 2) is formed, that explicit expansion belongs to the vowel *a*, and therefore there is no fault.

[1.4] Now, for what purpose is this stated: “the teaching of the vowel *a* as open (*vivṛta*)”? For one might ask: since it is already understood from the mere pronunciation of the sūtra that this vowel *a* is open, what specific quality residing in the sound is to be grasped through practice alone? Just as the [intonations] such as the acute (*udātta*) and others are well-known only to those who study the Vedas, and likewise terms such as *ṛṣabha* and *gāndhāra* are known only to musicians (*gāndharva*), so too is this [vowel] open and difficult to perceive except through practice. Therefore, he says: “this has been taught as open.”

[1.5] Others think: This [anusvāra] is also taught as having already undergone *pratyāpatti* (restoration to its original form) within the *pratyāhāra*. However, for the purpose of making the vowel *a* audible when it is pronounced, it is understood as being closed (*saṃvṛta*). Just as in the case of the root *sthā* in the sense of "cessation of movement" (DhP 1.175) and the rule "after *dh*, *ṣṭran* is added in the sense of an object" (P 3.2.181), when the form with *ṣṭu*-substitution has been pronounced, it conveys the forms *sthā*, *nn*, and *ṣṭran* as they are perceived within the scope of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

And in that very form which is the object of the grammatical operation (*prayoga-viṣaya*), because the status of being *ṣṭu* is not yet established, the modification of the root-initial and so forth takes place. In that regard, when restoration (*pratyāpatti*) has been effected—as in the case of *aśva*, *arka*, and others—this occurs only for those [words] that are imitations (*anukaraṇa*) in the view that the individual instance (*vyakti*) is the referent. However, in the view that the generic form (*ākṛti*) is the referent, the universal is what is imitated. In that case, since all [words] have their restoration effected once the member belonging to the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the alphabet) has been restored, they do not seek to apply restoration at all for the establishment of the form of words such as *ādi*.

[1.6] Others think: "This is neither an imitation nor does it indicate anything for which a restoration has been made. What then? It is simply meaningless, uttered as something revealed without having undergone restoration.
[1.7] "What is the purpose? "It is for the sake of grasping the form (*ākāra*). "But in that case, it should be stated as 'grasping the form' (*ākāragrahaṇam*). It is said: . . .

[It is said: Sometimes the substratum (*dharmin*) is designated by means of its attribute (*dharma*). For example: "horned," "humped," "having a tail-tip," or "possessing a dewlap. When that very possessor of the attribute is designated as such, it acquires a specific qualification, such as "short," or likewise "long," or likewise "three or four morae" (*mātrā*). In that state, when another sound (*dhvani*) is initiated from the vocal apparatus (*karaṇa-saṃnipāta*), the operation of the former has indeed ceased; thus it is rightly said: "Furthermore, time is external to the mouth."

Furthermore, even if the very first effort is undertaken—just as in the act of exhaling by emerging from a pebble—the activity proceeds precisely from that specific external impulse; thus, when applied for this purpose, the effort regarding the mode of the wind is initiated at the region of the navel itself, and therefore the externality of this time indeed exists. (p. 3)

[1.8.1] But does this not contradict the rule *tapas tatkālasya* (P 1.1.70)? For it is stated there: "The sphoṭa remains exactly the same; there is merely a difference in its mode of manifestation (*vṛttibheda*). Consequently, since the duration of time is the same across all modes of manifestation, here too—because the duration of the short and long vowels is equal—one would have to apply the substitution *ais* in the form *khaṭvābhiḥ*. It is replied: This is not a fault, because of the acceptance [of the permanence of the word]. Since the permanence [of the word] is accepted, there is no contradiction.

Thus, it is precisely for this purpose that the eternity of words is accepted. Furthermore, regarding that eternal [word], those which are its manifestors are of two kinds: some are primary (*prākṛta*), and some are secondary (*vaikṛta*). That which arises from the conjunction of the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*) and that which arises from it—these two are primary, because a specific distinction is perceived through them. However, the sound (*dhvani*) that arises from the [primary] sound is secondary, because there is no further distinction beyond it; it merely serves as the means for its perception in such a manner.

This is the distinction: if, in the case of long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, there is a difference in duration because no other sound intervenes, then there would likewise be a difference in duration in the quick (*druta*), medium (*madhyama*), and slow (*vilambita*) tempos. Now, if in the case of long and protracted vowels there is a repeated striking of the articulatory organs (*karaṇābhighāta*), then—this being the case for the quick tempo and so forth—it would be difficult to establish that time is external (*bāhyatva*), because the striking of the articulatory organs does not cease. [1.9] What, then, is this? Is this something unprecedented by Pāṇini?

Is the state of being open (*vivṛtatva*) something not previously established that is now added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), or is it a restatement (*anvākhyāna*) of what has already been established? This is because [the author] teaches a restoration (*pratyāpatti*) in the rule *a a* (P 8.4.68).

If the form *akāra* were intended here as being closed (*saṃvṛta*), what would be the purpose of its restoration (*pratyāpatti*)? From the mention of its restoration in that context, it is determined that the *akāra* is open (*vivṛta*). This applies both to the *pratyāhāra* [of vowels], and to the references in subsequent rules such as "asya cvau" (P 7.4.32) and "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (P 6.1.101), as well as in words used in actual usage such as *aśva*, *arka*, *artha*, and so forth. Indeed, there is another purpose for stating this; such is the intention.

The phonetic modification (*saṃskāra*) expressed by "a a" occurs only in the case of words used in actual linguistic usage (*prayogaśabda*), and not in the case of meaningless words that serve as illustrative examples (*pratipādakaśabda*). Furthermore, this is indeed a defect arising from the speaker's negligence, namely the state of being wide-open (*vitatatva* or *vivṛtatva*). Moreover, since this was established by Pāṇini, one should pronounce the state of being wide-open in such words used in actual usage as *atikhaṭvā* and so forth. Therefore, the restoration of the original form (*pratyāpatti*) is stated.

And yet, it would not have been taught as open (*vivṛta*). To this, an objection is raised: if the vowel *a* is not open in the *pratyāhāra*, in the subsequent references (*anuvṛtti*), or in the specific instructions (*nirdeśa*), then because of the difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*), the vowel *ā* is neither a homogeneous sound (*savarṇa*) nor a substitute (*ādeśa*) for it. Since it is not grasped due to non-homogeneity, there is an absence of the status of being a vowel (*actva*) for both the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute. [The original element] is not a vowel, nor is the substitute; so of what is there restoration (*pratyāpatti*)? It is said in reply:

This is determined from an indicative mark (*liṅga*): that the vowel *ā* becomes the vowel *a*, because [the author] says in the rule for the substitution of *it*: “...in place of *āt* preceded by *ya* or *ka*” (P 7.3.46). There is no vowel *ā* without the shortening [prescribed] by “*ke ‘ṇaḥ*” (P 7.4.13); for on account of this indicative mark, a paribhāṣā with a deficient member would not apply. And [this is also shown] by the rule “*ūkālo ‘j jhrasva...*” (P 1.2.27), where *ā* is preceded by *ya*.

If this is so, why is it not postulated that there is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) on the basis of an indicative mark (*liṅga*)? And if there were homogeneity, what would be the need for the rule for the opening of the mouth (*vivṛta*) or for the restoration (*pratyāpatti*)? It is said in reply: An indicative mark belongs to the category of inference (*anumāna*). We understand that inference has a specific scope, as comprehension does not arise from inference in every case. Thus, homogeneity does not exist on the basis of an indicative mark. What then? It is merely a substitute (*ādeśa*). Alternatively, the mention of "cow" (*go*) and "female" (*strī*) was made there;
since the mention of "female" there is without occasion (*anavakāśa*), the substitute would apply, but not homogeneity.

Regarding the phrase "therein there is no interval" (*tatrāntarya*): the intention is that for the speaker, there exists an extreme proximity (*antaratama*) arising from negligence. As for the statement "neither in the world nor in the Veda," this is what is meant: the faults mentioned by you exist as arising from the speaker's negligence; however, a counter-exception (*pratyāpatti*) need not be stated for the sake of their removal. There are indeed faults such as *kala* and so forth, yet there is no counter-exception directed toward them, for they are already excluded simply by the recitation of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups.

Therefore, Pāṇini himself asserts that [the suffix] is manifest; thus, *pratyāpatti* (reversion) is the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this. But what is the distinction here? He asks regarding the operation residing in the sentence. For since the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is to be inferred within the sentence, there is no distinction whatsoever between whether it is "to be done" (*kartavya*) or "done" (*kṛta*). Indeed, there is nothing [of substance]; it is merely a matter of self-aggrandizement (*āhopuruṣikā*). One who speaks with such self-importance is called an *ahaṃpuruṣa*.

[Ahōpuruṣaḥ]: one who esteems himself; one who considers himself superior to others, that is, one possessed of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). The abstract state of such a person is called *āhopuruṣikā*, derived with the suffix *-vuñ* according to the rule beginning with *manojña*. Thus, *āhopuruṣikā* denotes the state of being self-conceited. You have said: "What you have stated is not correct; rather, only what I have said is logical, because it is a statement of rectification."

[1.10] Therefore, because of this explicit instruction (*vivṛtopadeśa*), that which belongs to the traditional collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*)—which is open (*vivṛta*), meaningless, and restored to its original form—is what is established by this very treatise in the rule *aiuṇ*. Just as in the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123), the designation *it* does not apply to the sound as it is being uttered; rather, it applies to that which exists in the mind as an object of phonetic modification. That [phoneme] is indeed established by this [treatise].

Furthermore, since this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of sounds situated in a collection, there might be an imitation of only some [sounds] as if they were individual entities (*dravya*). Therefore, this is stated: "The open articulation (*vivṛta*) must be prescribed even for those situated at the beginning of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth. Otherwise, due to the difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*), [the sound *i*] would not be included by the traditional phonetic inventory (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*); consequently, since the property of being a vowel (*actva*) would be absent, it would lack the status of a substitute base (*asthānitva*), and thus in the case of *śāmyati*, the long vowel [substitution] would not occur. Furthermore, the rule "the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is udātta" would not apply to words such as *dṛṣad*.

Furthermore, in the case of *pratyaye cāyakaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* (*āyādeśaḥ*) would not occur; nor would the accentuation in *avagataḥ* be correct, because of this rule: "A long vowel replaces [two] homogeneous vowels of the *ak*-class" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*). This is known by the mark of the *anubandha*: that very [vowel] is one belonging to the traditional list of phonemes (*ākṣarasamāmnāyika*). If [the vowel] standing at the beginning of a root were not included, he would have simply said, "A long vowel replaces [two] *ik*-vowels in a homogeneous vowel" (*ikaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*); for there are no two [vowels] in the traditional list of phonemes that begin with *r*.

Even though there is not even one [single phoneme], this is stated regarding the long vowel because it has two objects [of articulation]. This may be for the sake of its form (*ākāra*), for that [long vowel] becomes homogeneous (*savarṇa*) due to being open (*vivṛta*). What kind of effort is this being urged, namely, the so-called "instruction as open"? He says this very thing: what regard is there here, since the verbal roots (*dhātu*) are simply recited? And those being recited do not produce any heaviness or lightness by virtue of being either closed (*saṃvāra*) or open (*vivāra*).

Regarding those nominal stems (*prātipadika*) which are not explicitly mentioned, such as *raṅka* and others used in common worldly usage—in these, the vowel *a* is employed in its closed (*saṃvṛta*) form. Furthermore, there is no recitation of these in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), and it is impossible to assert their "open" (*vivṛta*) nature without such recitation. Moreover, if there were an explicit instruction (*upadeśa*), the treatise would become overly cumbersome. Therefore, this must be stated: "and that which stands at the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is open."

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the *dhātus*, since the *dhātus* are already recited [in the *Dhātupāṭha*]? It is said in reply: if this [rule] is undertaken for the sake of the meaning of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), it will also apply to the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Consequently, they will be pronounced with the vocal organs closed (*saṃvṛta*) during their utterance, but they will be understood as being open (*vivṛta*) when performing their grammatical function. And this being so, there is no need even to state the absence of the articulatory organ (*karaṇa*).

[1.11] And regarding the statement "long" and "protracted," it is for the purpose of excluding the closed [vowels]. Some explain as follows: when the phonemes listed in the *akṣarasamāmnāya* are taught as open, this second purpose is subsequently stated. Because they are [otherwise] closed, by virtue of being the closest [to the closed vowels], the long and protracted [vowels] would result in being closed. Others state that the purpose [of the open teaching] applies to those situated at the beginning of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth.

In this regard, the following objection is raised: because it is contracted (*saṃvṛta*), the long and protracted vowels lack the status of *ac* (vowels), and thus their status as substituends (*sthānin*) is untenable; they exist neither in common usage nor in the Veda. As a reason, he cites the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*): for the learned do not employ the long and protracted vowels in a contracted form. [The rule] "this [rule] would establish these two as substituends" means that some consider this grammatical definition to be productive (*nirvartaka*).

But here these venerable ones say: "Just as the learned pronounce the semivowels (*antasthā*) with nasality, so too here, by recourse to the paribhāṣā 'the most similar [substitute occurs]', there arises the understanding that nasality is permitted in this context. Thus, even if the long and protracted vowels were not closed (*saṃvṛta*) here, permission would still apply on the basis of similarity. This is an unequal presentation; it is appropriate that there be an established rule for what exists.

He says this—"because it is impossible"—as follows: in this world, some things are possible, such as being able to go by means of the two hands, but not by means of the head. Likewise, the long or protracted form of the vowel *a* cannot at all be uttered in its closed (*saṃvṛta*) state by any person in the world. Furthermore, defects of phonemes (*varṇa*) are fixed; for it has been said: "The cultivation of defects of vowels is thus described; other than these are the defects of consonants" (MBh 1.13.26–27).

As for the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), they can indeed be pronounced with nasality; however, even among them, the letter *r* cannot be so pronounced. Thus, two reasons have been specified: the lack of usage by the learned (*śiṣṭāprayoga*) and the impossibility of pronunciation (*aśakyatva*). Even so, from where is this [conclusion] derived? If it is argued that if the vowel *a* were closed (*saṃvṛta*), then because the vowels *ī* and *ū* are open (*vivṛta*), how could there be equality of effort (*tulyaprayatnatva*) between them? For it has been stated thus: "The articulation (*karaṇa*) of vowels and sibilants (*ūṣman*) is open."

Regarding this, they explain: "Those [vowels] are *vivṛta* (open), except for those of the *ārbhava-sāman*, which are *saṃvṛta* (closed)" (p. 6). But this is not so; it is merely the style of the author of the *Pārṣada*. For in this very recension (*śākhā*), with the exception of the *ārbhava-sāman*, there is no openness (*vivṛtatva*) in other *sāmans*; whereas for others, they are indeed open. Therefore, this is the meaning. Even so, from where does this [distinction] come? Even if [the vowels] were open, the status of the letter *a* would not be established. For the letter *a* is open, the letter *ā* is more open (*vivṛtatara*), while the letters *i* and *u* are even more open (*vivṛtatara*).

In that case, there ought to be an equal effort for both. If this were so, then even the perception [of the sound] would not occur. [Objection: The perception will occur because of an explicit statement. Or rather, this is said with reference to the teaching of the *vivṛta* [open] position; it means "the teaching of the more open (*vivṛtatara*) [position]. How then is one to understand the statement: "Among the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), that which contains the *avarṇa* [vowel] is more open than the other"? This too must be understood as being "most open" (*vivṛtatama*).

[2] In that regard, concerning the description of the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*), there is no inclusion of homogeneous letters (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) because they are not *aṇ* sounds (Vt. 4). One view holds that this applies to "aiuṇ"; another view holds that it applies to "akaḥ savarṇe... (P 6.1.101). As for the pure vowels themselves, they are governed by "asya cvau" (P 7.4.32) and "yasyeti ca" (P 6.4.148). In those cases, we understand them either by means of their indicatory marks (*anubandha*)—thinking "this is that"—or simply as they are. However, in the case of the pure vowels, the status of being an *aṇ* does not exist.

In that case, just as the vowel *a* is always only the object of cognition (*pratyāyya*) and not the means of cognition (*pratyāyaka*), so too this [augment] *a* is only the object of cognition. Consequently, it would only undergo grammatical operations (*kārya*); thus, forms such as *śuklībhavati* ("becomes white") and *mālībhavati* ("becomes garlanded") would not be possible. Likewise, [forms like] *auḍhiḥ* and *bālākiḥ* would not be established.
[This objection is answered: It is established because the vowel *a* is one and the same; for it persists through its recurrence (*anuvṛtta*).

[2.2] But there would be a confusion of subsequent applications (*anubandhasaṃkara*) because, in reality, there is no distinction between the letter *a* [in the rule for *aṇ*] and the letter *a* [in the rule for *ka*]. This applies to the rule "after a verbal root ending in *a*, *aṇ*" (P 3.2.1), and likewise to the rule "after a verbal root ending in *ā*, provided no preverb precedes, *ka*" (P 3.2.3). Just as when a theft is committed by a bald man, one who has long hair (*kuntalī*) does not fail to be apprehended as a thief; in that case, in the formation of *godah* ("milk-cow"), *ka* would apply because it is subsequent [to *aṇ*]. The inclusion of the *k*-marker (*kitkaraṇa*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule. Alternatively, because they lack any scope of application (*anavakāśatva*), they would apply alternatively (*paryāya*).

[2.3] Regarding the example *kiriṇā giriṇā*: the vowel *a* is not cited because it is prohibited by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa...* (P 6.1.182). In the case of *ghaṭena tarati*, there is merely a double utterance, for the object is one and the same. However, the suffix *ṭhan* has already served its purpose in words such as *bāhuka*. [2.4] "Metaphorical designations (*upacāra*) function like substances" (Vārttika 8). For a single jar does not simultaneously perform multiple functions, such as bringing butter and so forth. One utters the vowel *a* as residing within the sound *ka* following the word *aśva*.

[2.5] "But because the instrument is made manifold by means of the object" (Vt. 9). The author of the Vākya (*vākyakāra*) indicates the instrument as a generality (*sāmānya*); the author of the Bhāṣya (*bhāṣyakāra*), however, speaks of its distinction and its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇabhāva*) by means of two locative cases expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). He would say: "One should pronounce this single [word] possessing all its qualities. Or, he would state that when a verbal root has an object as its attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *kaṇ* (or *kaṭ*) occurs. Alternatively, one should pronounce as many [qualities] as one is able to pronounce.

"But he declares that others are indicated by elision. For if the designation *itsaṃjñā* were applied only to two [specific letters], then the designation *itsaṃjñā* itself would be restricted (*āyacchati*) with respect to the treatise, because it would be established as having a single agent. In that case, the *itsaṃjñā* would apply only to those two, and it would certainly not apply to those falling in between. However, it is established by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) through the employment of the object (*viṣaya*).

But surely this would be for the purpose of restriction—that [the udātta accent] occurs only when caused by that [suffix], and not when caused by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, such as in the case of words beginning with an udātta at the end (or beginning). Since a restriction is understood only when there is something to be enjoined, this very point will be known: namely, that elsewhere it is not caused by that. Otherwise, one should have stated it simply as "a [suffix] after *śiva* and so on. This is established by common usage. It is not stated in this way; rather, he pronounces this single [element] as possessing all qualities.

How, then, is it so? Just as with words (*śabda*), wherever a grammatical marker (*liṅga*) is relied upon for a specific operation (*kārya*), that operation occurs in common usage only for that particular marker. However, in the case of theft, those such as the shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*) are not "possessors of the word" (*aśabdavantaḥ*). In that context, just as one who has a topknot (*śikhin*) or matted hair (*jaṭī*) undergoes the prescribed action because the shaven-headed and others are excluded from what is to be done, so too here, for the sake of the operation, the suffixes (*anubandha*) are attached; therefore, in each respective domain, they will obtain their corresponding operation at the appropriate time.

Regarding the rule *a sāṃpratike* (P 4.3.9), why is the marker *ṇ* not applied there? For since there is no visible marker (*liṅga*) in this case, an absence of restriction would follow. It is said in reply: although the desired result is already established by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in *madhyānmo 'sāṃpratike* (P 4.3.8–9), the recourse to the unmarked (*niranubandha*) form is for this purpose: namely, so that the very absence of a marker may serve as the indicator (*liṅga*). In that regard, just as someone might be told, "Be naked here," one is likewise enjoined: "Be unmarked."

[2.6] Because of the enumeration of repetitions (vt. 10). In this world, where the primary number [seventeen] is established, it is stated regarding a repetition whose scope is not otherwise fixed: "He recites the first thrice; he recites the last thrice" (Tai.S. 2.5.7). Thus, the first and the last are the two instances of the enumerated repetitions. A function based on repetition would occur only where multiplicity is relied upon.

But where there is indeed oneness, the accent necessarily applies because its own substratum has not been removed, as in *kiriṇā giriṇā*. This too is established: number is completely superseded by another number, whether it be secondary (*gauṇa*) or primary (*mukhya*).

As it is said in the *Mahābhāṣya* (1.142.23): "Just as in the grammatical treatise, when there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*), the fact that this [word] consists of three syllables (*tryack*) subverts its having two syllables (*dvyack*); since the suffix *ḍhak* would then not apply, why is it stated that [the rule applies] 'in the case of a previously non-existent prescription' (*apūrvavidhau*)? For example: "A thousand sages [gave] a single brown cow each" (*ṛṣisahasram ekāṃ kapilām ekaikaśaḥ*). Here, in the state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed by "a thousand sages," the direct connection is with "each one" (*ekaikaśaḥ*).

Alternatively, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), there is a relationship characterized by semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), as in the case of "one who eats" (*bhujivat*). For they, having mutually accepted [the cows] through wealth, gave them a thousand times. And this giving is the relinquishment of an object already accepted. In that regard, even when one person gives, if it is said, "Let those with a thousand sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) be brought," then they are indeed brought; if it is said, "Let those with a single fee be brought," then they are not brought.
Just as in that case the number serves only to exclude the previous number, so too here; thus, there is no fault.

[3] But there is difference in nature because of the intervention of time and sound (Vt. 11). This reason is based on similarity and dissimilarity: similarity with those whose diversity is well-established, and dissimilarity with those whose unity is well-established. Here, the intervention of sound is observed among those whose diversity is established—for example, in the word *dṛti*, the letters *ṛ* and *i* are separated by the letter *t*. In this case as well, in the word *daṇḍa*, the vowel *a* following the letter *d* and the vowel *a* in the syllable *ḍa* are seen to be separated by the word *eḍ*.

Furthermore, this property does not belong to a single, unitary self (*ātman*). When this letter *a* is pronounced in its pure form as *a*, it is then not separated from the sound itself. Likewise, priority and posteriority, which are mediated by time, are observed only among distinct entities in the absence of phonetic combination (*asaṃhitā*), such as in the sequence *a-i-u*. However, no temporal distinction exists within the scope of the pronunciation of a single, pure *a*-self.

In this case, however, in the *asaṃhitā* (non-composition) form "daṇḍa-agram," there is a sequence [of sounds] separated by time; therefore, the *nānā-kāra* (the rule for distinct sounds) applies. But surely, even when there is an intervention by a word (*śabda-vyavāya*), there is also an intervention by time (*kāla-vyavāya*); in that case, the rule would be established simply as "intervention by time. It is replied: the intervention by time alone is shown in two ways—that which is devoid of words and that which possesses words.

[3.1] Because it is observed simultaneously in different locations (yugapad-deśapṛthaktva-darśanāt). There is a simultaneous observation of the form *akāra* in different locations. This is a property that contradicts oneness; for a single Devadatta is not perceived simultaneously in different locations, yet the form *akāra* is so perceived. Therefore, the *akāra* is not one. Thus, two reasons have been presented for its multiplicity.

He states the rebuttal to this one [objection]: regarding what you have said, "because of the intervention of time and sound," we reply: "If, however, these phonemes were like birds. What is meant by this is as follows: this intervention that you postulate between the phonemes by means of time and sound is not an intervention of the actual entities themselves. What then? These are merely the perception and non-perception resulting from the operation and cessation of the manifesting cause.

That which constitutes the manifesting cause (*abhivyañjaka-nimitta*) of the sound *a*—being inactive when another manifesting cause for a different phoneme is operating, it does not cause the perception of the *a*; yet, when it operates again, it causes its perception. Therefore, this [distinction] arises from the operation and cessation of perception and non-perception through their engagement and withdrawal, but not from a difference in the actual entity (*vastu*).

Is it as when a bird is distinct from another bird because it is separated by another object, such that one is "prior" and the other "subsequent"? This much can indeed be said: "What was previously unperceived is now perceived. And having made this assumption, he says: "In this way, this letter *a* is seen in the word *ad*, perceived in the word *da*, and is seen and perceived in the word *ṇḍa*. But this cannot be so; otherwise, there would be impermanence. There is, however, this resolution based on reasoning (*tarka*).

However, this is not the established tenet of the treatise (*śāstra*). For in the treatise, the eternity of a meaningful word—whether a *pada* or a *vākya*—is asserted; and that [word] is accepted in the treatise as a composite (*samudāya*). Furthermore, a composite consists precisely of phonemes (*varṇa*). In that regard, if one asserts its unity, there is a contradiction, for that composite of phonemes does not exist. One can indeed say that the composite characterized as "ka-ra" is such that the phoneme *ka* is perceived twice, the vowel *a* is perceived [once], and the *repha* (*r*) is perceived once.

In this way, the word *kāruka* is characterized by being simply *kāru*. Furthermore, because there is no application [of the suffix] here, it lacks meaningfulness altogether. Therefore, this must be accepted: these linguistic wholes (*samudāya*) exist as established entities within their meanings, followed by distinct phonemes (*varṇa*). If, however, these phonemes were like the sun, then the argument "because they are seen in different locations simultaneously" would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). For even a single sun is observed in various different locations.

In that regard, the argument that "the form exists in Devadatta, but not in the sun"—which is presented as a dissimilar reason—is an unequal comparison (*viṣama-upanyāsa*). This is what he explains: I have stated this; it is not the case that a single observer perceives Devadatta simultaneously in different locations (*deśapṛthaktveṣu*). Nor does one perceive the sun in this manner. For the observer who is in Sāketa is not the same as the one in Saurāṣṭra; nor is the one who perceives the sun above a tree the same as the one who perceives it elsewhere.

One perceives the letter *a*, and [furthermore] perceives it again. Even for one who does not possess a simultaneity of perceptions regarding momentary objects, there is a dissimilar perception of the letter *a* compared to the perception of the sun, because a simultaneity of perceptions whose object is a duration of a *muhūrta* is possible. Moreover, space is not a single entity; therefore, the letter *a* cannot logically have spatial extension (*deśatva*). Thus, one does not perceive even the letter *a*.

If there were distinctions within the letter *a*, then its plurality would be established. Likewise, the space (*ākāśa*) is the single locus for sound as well. Therefore, the argument "because of the observation of plurality in simultaneous locations" is not a valid reason. [Sound is] perceived by the ear, it is an object of cognition, it is to be grasped by the intellect (*buddhinirgrāhya*), and it is manifested through articulation (*prayoga*). For what purpose is this stated? It is said: for the purpose of demonstrating properties that are non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

The property of being perceived by the auditory organ is invariable; it is never seen by the eye. Likewise, because it is apprehended by the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not apprehended by any other sense. Being manifested by sound, it is not manifested by lamps and the like. Thus, space (*ākāśa*) is invariable; therefore, there is nothing else that can produce the letter *a*. As for the perception of it in different locations while it exists in one location, that is due to the power of instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).

Just as there are designations such as "distant" and "near"—for instance, "the sound is distant" or "the sound is near"—so too do the cognitions produced by the operation of the sense organs reveal both unity and multiplicity in a single object. For example, when a sound is uttered in a spacious place, another similar sound is perceived here; for cognitions indeed proceed with unstable forms.

"You have said this: 'Indeed, a single Devadatta cannot exist simultaneously in both Srughna and Mathurā. To this we reply: since the earth is one, why is it that the Devadatta who is here is not in Srughna, or why is he not in some place in Mathurā? In the same way, even though space is a single location, the conventional usage of "many locations" will proceed; for there are indeed many spatial locations."

But surely, since the earth is composed of its own parts, those parts are rightly considered its location; whereas space (*ākāśa*), however, is not so composed. True, this is so. Nevertheless, although those parts do not possess the nature of space itself, they are designated as such because they are its inherent constituents (*samavāyin*). Why then is it not accepted that space is designated as being "here" due to its conjunction with trees and other objects? This, however, is the distinction: the locations, being inherent constituents, are—as if brought into identity through inherence (*samavāya*), which causes a confusion of entities—treated as one with space.

Furthermore, since some have even accepted its impermanence, there is no distinction whatsoever in the conventional usage of space regarding parts and wholes. Therefore, because of the multiplicity of locations, the reason is established: "The letter *a* is subject to change (*anyabhāvya*) because it is seen to occupy distinct locations simultaneously."

[4] But it is established by the apprehension of the form (ākṛti). In the case of a pratyāhāra and in an instruction involving a reference back (anuvṛtti), it is only the genus (jāti) that is enjoined, not the individual (vyakti). However, the inclusion of the individual occurs as follows: for example, a resident of Nālikeradvīpa is instructed—"This very cow must not be touched by you with the foot. Having been so instructed regarding that black and thin [cow], he does not touch even an old, brindled, or fat one.

For that *ākṛti* (form), however, there is neither obstruction nor exclusion; rather, it is the state of being open (*vivṛtatva*), as well as whatever other properties there may be—all of these are mediated through the individual instances (*vyakti*). In this regard, the open form is taught in the *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive enumeration), and its very restoration occurs at the end of the treatise; thus, everything is established. However, where the mention of the class (*jāti*) results in the inclusion of the vowel *a* when the form is perceived, that inclusion does not actually occur because of the difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*). This is just as in the rule: "A Brahmin who is in his early youth should be saluted by rising."

But [if one were to argue that the rule] would apply to the *pluta* vowel, there too the following rebuttal is given: "The *pluta* is remembered as being within its scope" (*plutaś ca viṣaye smṛtaḥ*, P 6.1.87, Ślokavārttika 2). And likewise, the inclusion of *taḥ* after the *ṛ* (*taparakaraṇam*) [is the solution]. By this, it is meant that "and likewise the inclusion of *taḥ*" refers to the phrase "and like that" (*tadvac ca*). This is because [the inclusion of *taḥ*] was over-extended by the mention of the *grahaṇa* [of homogeneous vowels]. For even when the *yoga* is rejected, the inclusion of *taḥ* remains subject to doubt: does it serve to include the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) as the referent of the word, or does it exclude the generic form (*ākṛti*)?

Therefore, just as there was a rejection [of the objection] regarding the apprehension of the generic form (ākṛti), so too is there the apprehension of the generic form even in the case of those [sounds] followed by *t*.

[4.2] And regarding the mention of *hal* (the consonants) [Vt. 14]: there, the rule for the actual mention [of the consonants] (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) has no operation. The letter *t* mentioned in the *pratyāhāra* is cited as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that [consonant] occurring therein. It would belong to one—either the preceding or the following [letter]. In that case, by the rule "when *jh* follows *jhal*" (P 8.2.26), the elision (*lopa*) which depends on both the preceding and the following [letters] would not occur. Where, then, would it occur? It would occur where the two *jhal* sounds are of different forms, as in *abuddha* and *abuddhāḥ*.
However, when there is a mention based on the generic form (*ākṛti*), the elision is established because of the mention of the generic form of the letter *t*.

[4.3] Or, because of the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*). How is this a solution? Regarding this, some explain: even if there were no generic form (*ākṛti*) at all, there would still be no fault. For example, in the case of *kārṣāpaṇa* coins and the like, even though the universal (*jāti*) does not exist; nevertheless, for you, there exists a "sweet" *kārṣāpaṇa*. And yet, it is precisely the objective entity itself that becomes such as it is when there is non-deviation from its true nature (*tattva*). Thus, it is not the case that the word's form is [the object].

Now, however, they say: "It is established by the very form-generality (*ākṛti*) because of its commonality of form; thus, this [word] is applied [to the individual]. To that, one might say: "It is established because of the apprehension of that form-generality. But that is not so. It was already stated previously: "The form-generality is denoted by the word"; in that case, it was established because the form-generality was what was being enjoined. But now, regarding individuals... (p. [number])

11) Because it is subject to inquiry: even if individuals (*vyakti*) are taught and the form (*ākṛti*) is not taught, [the point] is nevertheless established. How so? First, this person should be asked: regarding this "otherness," does this otherness belong to the sound (*śabda*) itself as it is uttered—such that this *ikāra* is different from the *akāra*—or is some distinct entity (*padārtha*) understood through a certain specific property (*viśeṣa*)?

If this is so, for what reason do you maintain that the *ākṛti* (form/structure) is distinct from the particular (*viśeṣa*), and not rather identical to it as a universal (*sāmānya*)—such that one might think, "This is that very same thing"? It might be argued: "In common worldly usage, transactions proceed only through distinction, not through non-distinction. But this is not correct; for there is also usage in the world through non-distinction, such as: "We are covering ourselves with those very same cloths. Therefore, he explains this: even though the *ākṛti* is not explicitly denoted, it exists, and it is not the case that it serves as the cause for the cognition or recovery of that [true nature].

[1] Why is the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* specifically questioned? For the purpose [of its instruction] has already been stated without distinction in the case of the instruction of all the phonemes (*sarvavarṇopadeśa*). Therefore, that very same purpose must apply to this as well. Alternatively, "specifically" means by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*). For other phonemes are questioned in another manner: the vowel *a* by virtue of being "open" (*vivṛtatva*), the phonemes *r* and *h* by virtue of being taught before and after [their respective counterparts], and the semivowels (*antasthā*) by virtue of being taught among the *aṇ* sounds. But this one (*ḷ*) is stated specifically.

"And its scope of application is even smaller. This he explains: the instruction (*uddeśa*) of the phonemes is for the sake of the operation of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), and the treatise is for the sake of practical usage (*prayoga*). Yet that usage does not exist for the sound *ḷ*. "Even smaller" indicates a comparative degree regarding the scope of the vowel *a* (or *ṛ*, as the case may be). The scope of application for the sound *ṛ* is small; therefore, the scope of this [sound *ḷ*] is even smaller than that.

It might be argued as follows: even that which is the object of application (*prayoga-viṣaya*) belongs only to one who stands within the realm of *ḷ* (*ḷpastha*). Furthermore, the substitution of *ḷ* for *ṛ* (*latva*) is not established [at the time of the rule's application]. Therefore, those operations concerning vowels (*ackārya*), such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, are already obtained while the sound is still in the state of *ṛ* (*ṛkārāvasthāyām*); thus, there is no purpose in the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* (*ḷkāropadeśa*).

[1.1] "The purpose [of the treatise] is for the sake of arbitrary names, power, imitation, elision, and so forth" (Vt. 1). As it has been stated: "The treatise is for the sake of practical usage, yet in actual usage, the letter *ḷ* does not exist with its own form assigned. However, there is indeed the usage of the letter *ḷ* in the case of arbitrary names (*yadṛcchā*) and the like.

What is called "arbitrariness" (*yadṛcchā*) is that which functions or ceases to function without a cause for its application, without a basis in the object itself, and without a restrictive cause for its engagement or withdrawal; it proceeds or desists by chance. For instance, the word *ḍittha*, being based solely on its own form, is applied wherever one thinks, "I shall give this name to him," and it functions in those instances and is withdrawn from others.

Furthermore, since words whose basis is solely their own form (*svarūpa*) cannot convey that very form through another form, there is no other word capable of excluding it. In that case, when the word *ḷtaka* is employed as a proper name (*nāmadheya*), it does not depend on any external cause; and since there is no other word to exclude it, it is correct as being based solely on its own form.

Why, then, is it not employed [in its own place]? Therefore, the instruction [of the letter *ḷ*] must be performed for the sake of establishing the grammatical operations (*ackārya*) pertaining to a sound that possesses *ḷ*, provided that the rule "there is a prescription of homogeneity (*savarṇavidhi*) between *ṛ* and *ḷ*" (P 1.1.9, Vt. 5) does not exist. For if that [rule] were present, the letter *ḷ* itself would undergo the grammatical operations of a vowel (*ac*). Regarding the statement "the occurrence of words is fourfold," by this he conveys the following: some words have fixed meanings, and the synonyms of these words are also fixed.

They are not to be produced by a person, because no author is remembered in this regard. However, there exists that collection of words which, when being assigned as names to some object, is indeterminate and is then assigned through a human (pauruṣeya) operation.

[1.2] In that regard, when a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) functions with respect to a genus, because it possesses a required cause [or: because it does not possess a required cause], it can be said to be an arbitrary word (*yadṛcchāśabda*). There is another human application [of words]: for instance, according to the view that a genus exists, or to whatever extent [it may exist]. In that case, a person cannot exert effort to create [the connection]; this is the distinction.

But when it functions with respect to a substance by depending on a cause (nimitta), then it is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*). However, when its denotable object is a substance, it is a substance-word (*dravyaśabda*). The same applies to quality-words (*guṇaśabda*): a quality-word such as "white" is an arbitrary word (*yadṛcchāśabda*) with respect to the universal [the universal of quality]; it is a genus-word with respect to a substance by depending on the cause that is the quality; and it is a quality-word because it denotes a quality.

Thus, a word for action may be an arbitrary (yadṛcchā) word in reference to the general category of action, or it may be a generic (jāti) word or a specific word for action in reference to a particular action. Furthermore, as long as there is an association with action within a word, that word possesses the nature of a word for action—this applies to both words formed with *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛdanta*) and those with *tiṅ* suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Others hold the view that those objects acquire their designation through mere proximity to a generic property (*jāti*). Still others hold that these are simply arbitrary words, while the generic properties and so forth serve merely as differentiators.

Therefore, in the first three types of word-usage (or word-occurrences), there is both fixedness of the word and fixedness of the meaning. But in the fourth type of word-usage, there is human agency (*pauruṣeyatva*). [1.3] Regarding the phrase "for the sake of imitating what arises from incapacity": now, who is considered to be "so-and-so"? First of all, it is not an arbitrary word (*yadṛcchāśabda*), because its usage is fixed. Therefore, this is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*); when it is being imitated, it expresses the connection with whatever genus exists through that [imitation]. Just as the word "jar," by expressing an object qualified by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), is called a genus-word.
Furthermore, that sound *ḷ* (or *ḷtaka*) cannot be made intelligible by any other imitative word; thus, the imitation remains unaltered by another term, like the phoneme *ḷ* itself.

This serves the purpose of [the rules concerning] prolation (*pluti*) and so forth. Since the substitution of *ḷ* for *l* is established in the cases of prolation, the circumflex accent (*svarita*), and reduplication, the *ḷ* occurring in the root *kḷp* necessitates its formal instruction (*upadeśa*). (p. 13)

[2.1] The conceptualization [of words] such as *saṃjñā* is based on their being established by convention (*nyāyya*). The word *ṛtaka* is established by convention. But how is its status as established by convention [determined]? From the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Just as in the case of words for universals (*jāti*) and so forth, where there is an uninterrupted traditional instruction [regarding the words], such that it is said, "these words are exactly this many," so too is this [usage of *ṛtaka*] uninterrupted. Even arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) are of this very same nature.

In that regard, just as words are not produced by themselves in the case of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, so it is also with arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*). For it is not possible to create a name such as "I shall make this its name *kākavāsita* or *haṃsavāsita*," because such a name has not been practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). In the phrase "in names and so forth" (*saṃjñādiṣu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates a class (*prakāra*).

What, then, are the types of designations (*saṃjñā*)? Even those barbarian (*mleccha*) designations produced regarding the subject matter of social assemblies (*goṣṭhī*) should not be employed by creating words (*śabda*) on one's own authority. Alternatively, regarding "designations and so forth" (*saṃjñādiṣu*): among all these designations based on genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*), it is precisely *yadṛcchā*-words (proper names) that serve as their primary basis. For [these other types of designations] do not establish themselves upon objects without depending on some other underlying cause (*nimitta*).

Therefore, among the arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) that constitute the primary basis for designations, that which is logical must be postulated. Another says: by this he demonstrates that there is also a traditional authority (*smṛti*) with its underlying rationale regarding this matter. In this regard, we also understand it from the convention of the treatises: "such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). This is what is meant: where there is established renown, that is what is employed; however, comprehension is not properly achieved through mere existence alone.

Words such as *ḷtaka* and the like do not exist at all; therefore, they should be employed by him (the learned). Furthermore, the learned rely both upon established usage (*prasiddhi*) and upon the treatises (*śāstra*). You, however, reject both and are based solely on the mere existence [of the word]. And for this reason, when the learned imitate an indistinct sound with a distinct one—as in "paṭapaṭāyati"—they do not do so with a word that is itself of that same [indistinct] nature. In that case, this arbitrary word (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) is unavoidable.

As for what is said—"the word *ṛtaka* is accompanied by grammatical authority"—for this is derived from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *niṣṭhā* and the suffix *kvun*, or it is called *ṛtaka* from the root *ṛtīy*. But in the same way, *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa* have not been so derived. Therefore, these too exist, namely *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa*. To this, the reply is: for even this (*ṛphiḍa*) is indeed *ṛphiḍḍa*; for in common usage, the non-application of the [derivation] from the root *ṛ* is observed.

In the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), only the root *ṛ* (to go) and others are taught, not the phoneme *ḷ*. Furthermore, the suffixes *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* can be postulated, according to the principle: "That [suffix] is to be inferred from the suffix and the base" (*P* 3.3.1, *Ślokavārttika* 2). Alternatively, one may say "the occurrence of *arti*. And indeed, a modified or corrupted occurrence of the root *ṛ* is observed; in common usage, a restless *gandharva* is called *ḷphiḍḍa*. Thus they explain it at length. And this is so.

Alternatively, here too this objection may be raised: "The learned do not employ only *ṛtaka*; what then? They also employ *ḷtaka*. One must consider that *ḷphiḍḍa*—that which resembles *ḷphiḍḍa*—is the name for an *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt form). For this traditional rule (*smṛti*) has a visible purpose, like the cases of the swan and its eating [of lotus stalks]. Indeed, its conformity is observed: namely, that this [term] is considered edible because it is remembered as being made [from *ṛtaka*].

But the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) do not regard [corrupt forms] as synonymous with the name "barbarian" (*mleccha*), for they consider them to be linguistic deviations (*apabhraṃśa*). Having thus rejected [the view that words are] arbitrary (*yadṛcchā*), he also refutes the view that [words] serve the purpose of imitating what arises from incapacity—(p. 14)

[2.2] Imitation (*anukaraṇa*) applies to those things that are prescribed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and not prohibited. Whatever has been enjoined, or whatever is neither enjoined nor prohibited—that alone is imitated by the learned. However, that which is prohibited is not imitated even if it has been performed by another. But an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is defective; its imitation must not be performed. For indeed, whether one is imitated or not—if the meaning is Vedic, nevertheless, because words belong to common worldly usage (*laukika*), it is said to be "in the world" (*loke*).
This, however, is stated in the Veda as: "The Viśvajit [sacrifice]—they sit for the sacrificial sessions (*satra*). It is thus recited (*paṭhyate*).

This is an inappropriate comparison. What is meant is this: dharma or adharma does not arise from mere imitation; rather, it arises from renunciation or performance. And it can be said that this [act] is not even an imitation at all. For where an action is seen to be merely similar to what was imitated—only in its outward form—it does not constitute an imitation. This is shown by the examples: "He who indeed thinks, 'This is that,'" and "The one who has bathed and anointed himself."

This is an illustration of being in good health; for when the mind is unwell, one undertakes what ought not to be done by the mind. "With a garland around his neck" is an illustration of being manifest. For a Brahmin drinking liquor would drink it in secret, but this man has a garland around his neck. Even though there is no suspicion of drinking intoxicants, nevertheless, here there is the cutting of a plantain tree (*kadala-ccheda*). Furthermore, there is no fault here in imitating someone who resembles another.

For the learned indeed perform such imitation. If one were to employ the word *ḷtaka*—uttered by a Brāhmaṇī woman with the intention of conveying its actual meaning—as an imitation intended to convey that same meaning, there would be sin. But since he employs it as having the word itself as its object, this is not a fault, just like drinking milk.

Even the word *apaśabda* (“ungrammatical word”) would itself be ungrammatical.
