For all the incorrect forms such as *gāvī* and so forth are indeed its denotable meanings; therefore, because there is no difference in meaning, it lacks the status of being ungrammatical. Just as the word *goṇī* is correct when referring to a sack, but incorrect when referring to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth. This might be argued: the word *apaśabda* is correct because it has been formally explained [by grammatical rules], whereas this word *sādhu* ("correct") is explained by the rule *arthavat prātipadikam* (P 1.2.45).

Furthermore, this is indeed even more so... What is the distinction here? It is said: even this is not present here at all, because this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of what is incorrect (*asādhū*). If one were to say *kḷpisthasya*, this is what is meant: it has already been provided for at the very outset. That which exists in actual usage is this; and this is not found in actual usage. He says: "that which was previously established as not having taken effect" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*, P 8.2.1). There would be no purpose served by that meaning, but this is another case where the word *kḷpistha* functions as its own referent (*padārthaka*).

The rule that "an imitation follows the form of the original" (*prakṛtivad anukaraṇam*) does not apply in certain cases even when there is an explicit statement to that effect. However, when one imitates the phonetic form (*rūpa*) of a constituent part (*avayava*) rather than its semantic form (*artharūpa*), then—because it is based on the form of a verbal root (*dhātu*)—that property is lost within the original itself, and consequently the grammatical operation dependent upon it does not take place. For example, in the case of *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.19), the substitution of *iyaṅ* does not occur. But when one relies upon the semantic form, then... [the operation applies].

15) Regarding the phrase *dhātv-anukaraṇe* ("in the case of an imitation of a verbal root"), that which was observed in the original form undergoes the substitution of *iyaṅ*, as in the rule *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.18). For example: *dviḥ pacantu ity āha* ("He said, 'Let them cook twice'"). And this [form] is not a finite verb (*tiṅ*), because a finite verb denotes a grammatical factor (*sādhana*). Similarly, having stated *agnī jvālitau* ("The two fires have been kindled"), one imitates that and says *agnī ity ayam āha* ("He says 'Agni, Agni'"). In that case, there is either a dual or a singular for two meanings, or else a dual or a singular for a single manifesting entity; it is not otherwise.

In this regard, however, the following must be said: when these roots *gam*, *sṛp*, and *muc* are situated [in a grammatical rule] and are reproduced [as they are], as in "he studies the correct *ḷ*-sound," then this reproduction is not like the original form (*prakṛtivat*). Now, if you think that because this [sound] is attached to the beginning of the root *kḷp* (or *kḷpi*), it is likewise [attached] even in the case of *ṛtaka*, then the situation is equal. Regarding this, they say: "It should be stated that there is either a reproduction of a single sound or a combination [of sounds] in the case of *aṭ* and the others."
The expression *ṣṭad* (or *ḷti*, or *rṛti*) is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). By this, it will receive the designation *it*.

If an imitation is like its original form (*prakṛtivat*), then this is indeed a corrupt word (*apaśabda*). ... "He says *abrāhmaṇyḷtaka*. In this case, the original form of the imitation is that very corrupt word whose meaning is the referent. And since an imitative word acquires the properties of its original form, the status of being a corrupt word follows. Furthermore, it is the established practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) that a corrupt word must not be employed.

Therefore, according to the authoritative principle that "an imitation follows the model," whatever base (*prakṛti*) is taught is accepted as the model. Just as in the grammatical rule "the substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*...), that which is the original is what is relied upon; and in grammar, no such thing as an *apaśabda* (incorrect word) is ever taught as a base, because the purpose of grammar is to provide a descriptive account of correct words (*sādhūnām anvākhyānāt*).

Now, if it is explained that [the word] is a corrupt form (apaśabda) by means of inference, and it cannot be the case that a base-form (prakṛti) is grasped through semantic capacity; or alternatively, if it is argued that "as if it were the base-form" refers to an operation (kārya) preceded by the grammatical treatise (śāstra), yet no such operation preceded by the treatise exists for a corrupt form—for it is impossible to explain the state of being a corrupt form by means of grammar.

Furthermore, even in the case of a word-form that is connected with grammatical function (*kāryayogi*), it is impossible to extend the designation of "ungrammatical word" (*apaśabdatva*) to it. Therefore, because there is no such original form (*prakṛti*), because the specific property (*dharma*) pertaining to each such object is not relied upon by the treatise, and because it is impossible to extend [the designation] to an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), it is said: "Even an imitation of an ungrammatical word is not itself an ungrammatical word. Thus, the teaching of the phoneme *ḷ* is established for the purpose of imitating sounds produced through incapacity (*aśaktija*).

Others describe it as being simply rejected (*pratyākhyāta*). "This is indeed a corrupt word (*apaśabda*)," because "a corrupt word is its source-form (*prakṛti*). And a corrupt word cannot serve as a purposeful means; this is the remainder of the sentence. Why is this so? The other says: "Because corrupt words are not taught. Nor is there a source-form that has not been taught; the remainder of the sentence is: "such as *yaṇ-ādi-vanam*. (p. 16)

[2.3] "Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], [the rule applies to] *pluti* and so forth" (Vārttika 4). It should not be understood here that this refers only to substitutes (*ādeśa*), for if it were understood in that way, since this would be a rule concerning phonemes (*al-vidhi*), the *pluti* [vowel lengthening] would not occur. Therefore, the usage of common worldly practice (*loka-pravṛtti*) alone is relied upon. Now, in the world, there is a cognition of "dog" due to the association with the genus; here too, there is an association with the genus.

And when there is a rule for the inclusion of *ṛ* and *ḷ* as homogeneous (*savarṇa*), and the rule for the inclusion of sounds (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) is rejected on the grounds that the class-form (*ākṛti*) is what is grasped, then—even though there is a difference in phonetic manifestation (*śrutibheda*)—there is indeed a single class-form, just as in the case of short and long vowels. [In the example] *rājñakīyam* [from *rājñaḥ ka ca*; *rājakīyam*], the elision of *an* by the rule *allopo 'naḥ* applies. He thinks thus: because of the connection with the presence of some property (*dharma*), there is a connection with the traditional grammar (*smṛti*); therefore, he now begins the statement: "of that which is specified by the genitive."

When there is a mention by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) at the time of a grammatical modification—that is, at the time of prescribing a substitute—it indicates non-difference (*ananyatva*). In this context, at the time of prescribing the substitution of *k* for *n*, the word *rājñaḥ* is in the genitive; thus, the word would be *rāja-* and not *an-*. Consequently, in the example *kḷptaśikhaḥ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not apply, because here the *ṛ*-vowel is not indicated by the genitive. What, then, is indicated? It is the *repha* (the letter *r*). Therefore, there is no non-difference with respect to the protracted vowel. However, in this case, the *ṛ*-vowel is indeed indicated by the genitive.

This is a Vedic-style (sautra) formulation, according to *Pāṇini* 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk* etc.). Furthermore, the term *ur* is taken merely as a sign of connection. In that case, for one whose topknot (*śikhā*) has been arranged, the prohibition "not false" (*anṛtaḥ*) would apply, because the letter *ṛ* is considered to be modified in one part (*ekadeśavikṛta*). This explains as follows: (1) Just as there is an instruction (*upadeśa*) for other [sounds], yet their cessation (*nivṛtti*) is not heard through a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*), such as in the case of *yādi* followed by the suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap*; so too, since there is an instruction for the sound *t*, there is no rule that would cause it to cease. Therefore, this is stated: "The utterance of *t* after [the vowel] must be performed" (*taparoccāraṇaṃ kartavyam*). (2) Alternatively, instruction (*upadeśa*) is also the bringing about [of a form] by means of its qualities (*guṇa*).

If the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) were followed by *t* (i.e., *tapara*), they would not be obtained as *tapara* because they are pronounced without being followed by *t*. Alternatively, "the instruction regarding *tapara*" is a reference to the result of being *tapara*. If you consider that result of being *tapara* to be desired, then the pronunciation of the diphthongs as *tapara* must be performed.

[2.1.1] The term "diphthongs" (*saṃdhyakṣara*) is a technical designation used by former teachers. Its etymological meaning (*anvarthatva*) is due to their having parts that are joined together (*saṃdhīyamānāvayavatvāt*), for their constituent parts—the preceding and the following—are joined together.

[2.1.2] Regarding this treatise, there is a disagreement. Some maintain that all [vowels] must be followed by the marker *t* (*tapara*). Others maintain that only *e* and *ai* are *tapara*, whereas *o* and *au* attain the status of being *tapara* by virtue of the rule "that which follows even when *at* is elided is *tapara*" (MBh 1.23.20).

If all [sounds] here were followed by *t* (tapara), then the designation *it* would not apply to "ot" and "aut," because the letter *t* would not be final in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). But what is the purpose of the *it*-designation for the letter *t*, given that the *it*-designation would not apply to that which is followed by *t*? This is an optional rule: "In the case of the mention of a suffix, [the *it*-designation applies to the suffix itself]. Here, it should not apply to that which is explicitly uttered [in the sūtra], such as in "diva aut" (P 7.1.84); rather, the *it*-designation applies to that which is being taught.

In that context, that which is made known by the *ti* suffix undergoes that grammatical operation—it is the named entity (*saṃjñin*) that undergoes the operation. This is because, in that case, the addition of the *t* has no other purpose. But here, the *t* is for another purpose; it is employed to indicate that specific duration (*tatkāla*). How, then, could it be the cause for applying that designation to the named entity? There is no fault, because an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) can have multiple functions.

For a single suffixal element is observed to serve multiple purposes; for example, in suffixes such as *ṭhak* and others, the letter *k* serves both to indicate *vṛddhi* and to determine the accent. If it were a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it would have to be stated in every instance.

For in the case of the others, a *tapara* diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*), by indicating its own duration, indicates its own nature. But that which is indicated as having a duration exceeding that is not so indicated. Why? Because there is no pronunciation of those things to be indicated by it; there is no means for pronouncing it [in such a way]. Even so, the designation *it* must be stated for the *t* of the diphthongs.

Otherwise, the diphthong followed by *t* (tapara) would indicate those [vowels] of the same duration; thus, the form of the technical term (*saṃjñārūpa*) would include the letter *t*. And once the actual form has been indicated, the designation *it* does not apply, because there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*).

Now, why is it not the case here that there is a mention of the *svarūpa* (the word-form itself)? Some explain: "What, then, is the name (*saṃjñā*) here? He says: "The first (*ādi*). But the last (*anta*) is its indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). If this is so, then the first alone is meaningful for the purpose of being a name, while the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is like a scent remaining in time; thus there is an absence of case-endings, as in the forms *ikaḥ* and *aci*. Therefore, the aggregate is the name.

Although the aggregate (*samudāya*) consists of phonemes followed by *at* (the marker *a*), nevertheless, it is the final member that is assigned the designation *it*. In this case, however, because it is not final, the designation *it* does not apply, and thus the form is obtained with the letter *t* included. But the object to be signified (*pratyāyya*) is of that same measure and remains indeed followed by *at*. For example, in the command "bring one who is equal in size to a white-clad person," the white-clad person is not included within the scope of the other's characterization (*anyopalakṣaṇa-vyāpāre*); yet, in its own function, there is the cognition of its qualities.

In this way, the designation *tapara* (followed by *t*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other [sounds] as well; however, in its own function, the *tapara* rule includes the letter *t* itself. Alternatively, if it is argued that [the *tapara* rule] applies to the technical name (*saṃjñā*), there is no fault because of the distinction between the whole and its parts (*samudāyāvayavabheda*). For the letter *ṅ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory marker) of the whole [term] *e-o*, while the letter *t* is an *anubandha* of the sound *o* alone. Similarly, the letter *c* is an *anubandha* of the whole [term] *ai-au*, while the letter *t* is an *anubandha* of the sound *au* alone. This is just as the letter *ṣ* in *suṭ* belongs to the whole [augment], whereas the letter *ṅ* in *auṅ* belongs to only one part of it.

[2.2] The rule for *aj* applies even in cases such as the *pluta* vowel (Vārttika 2). Having accepted the *pluta* vowel, defects such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth are stated; just as, having accepted the shortening of vowels (*hrasva*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), the prohibition of the *tuka* augment is stated for verbal roots (*dhātu*).

[2.3] Now he raises an objection regarding the *pluta* vowel itself: "[... and the designation of *pluta*" (Vt. 3). For a vowel consisting of three morae (*trimātra*), because its duration is distinct, is not conveyed [by the term *dīrgha*]. Not apprehending it as such—failing to recognize its status as an *actva* vowel due to the non-inclusion of that [term]—it is impossible to designate it as a *pluta*. In that case, whatever *pluta* exists that is somehow proximate [to a long vowel], that would apply to the phonemes *i* and *u*.
This being so, while the doubling [of the consonant] in forms such as *gotrātā* would be established, an undesired three-moraic vowel would be heard.

[3] "ecaḥ" alone [is the rule] when there is the substitution of a short vowel (*hrasva*). However, if the *tapara* marker were present, then because the *ekāra* of the *ardhamātrā* would have a different duration, it would lack the status of being a vowel (*actva*), and consequently, the designation "short" (*hrasva-saṃjñā*) would not apply. But surely this applies even for one who holds that the *tapara* markers are [phonetically significant]? This is what is meant: there is equality regarding the initiation of the grammatical rule (*yogārambha*); however, this is the distinction—previously it was stated "ecaḥ," whereas now it must be stated "eca ig-hrasvādeśe."

[The objection: "Since *ai* and *au* consist of disjoined phonemes (*viśliṣṭāvarṇa*), they cannot be considered as having joined phonemes (*saṃśliṣṭāvarṇa*) such as half-*e* and half-*o*. [Reply: That is rejected by the statement: "And because of the greater quantity of the subsequent [element] in *ai* and *au*" (P. 1.1.48, Vt. 4). The division is as follows: one half-mora (*mātrā*) belongs to the *a*-phoneme, while one and a half moras belong to the *i*- and *u*-phonemes.

In this regard, just as the designation "Sālavana" for a village of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇagrāma*) is based on its preponderance, so it is here as well. This too is rejected by the statement: "'The rule is established because *eṅ* has a common place of articulation" (P 1.1.48, Vt. 3). How was this rejected there? By stating that the half-*e* and half-*o* sounds do not exist at all. If these two do not exist, then for a palatal sound, the palatal is the one with a common place of articulation, and for a labial, the labial.

Thus, those who follow the *Śikṣā* have practiced that [the sounds] are labio-palatal. Here, the objection that there is a discrepancy in the *Śikṣā* because the half-*e* (*ardha-e*) and half-*o* (*ardha-o*) are not observed is refuted. How can there be a difference in the audible quality (*śrutibheda*) of *e* and *ai* when they are palatal, and of *o* and *au* when they are labial, given that all their places of articulation (*sthāna*), efforts (*prayatna*), and so forth, are identical? There is no fault here due to the difference in traditional views (*darśanabheda*). Some hold this opinion.

The very same breath that produces the sound *varṇa*, when bringing about the realization of the vowel *e*, merely brings the throat into contact with its own vicinity; the actual place of articulation (*sthāna*) is the palate alone. Similarly, the lips alone are the place of articulation for the vowel *o*; however, the breath merely strikes the throat. Others, moreover, consider that even this [throat] is a place of articulation. The difference in auditory perception arises from the distinction between the tip, middle, and root of the tongue—just as in the case of the *c* and *ya* sounds.

[Objection: But surely it has been said that "the *eṅ* vowels [are] more similar (*sasthānatara*) [to their respective counterparts]. If you argue that this statement regarding their existence implies that these two possess similarity (*sasthānatva*), then those very [vowels] would be the more similar ones; however, they do not exist [as such]. For the sake of brevity, those very [vowels] which exist within the *pratyāhāra* should have been recited [there]. [Reply: But perhaps the instruction [of these vowels] is for the purpose of the technical names (*saṃjñā*) "guṇa" and "vṛddhi. [To this we reply: The mention of the long vowel will be made within the definition of the technical name itself. If that were the case, then in the rule "for *sah* and *vah*, the *o* replaces the vowel" (P. 6.3.112), both the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) and the explicit mention of the term "vowel" (*varṇagrahaṇa*) would have to be performed.

Now, indeed, there are the Sātyamugris and Rāṇāyanīyas among the Chandogas. For what purpose is the mention of "Chandogas"? Because the Sātyamugris and others are not well-known. In the passage, "O well-born one, O Aśvasūnṛtā," they prescribe the substitution of *e* for the vowel following an *m* within the foot (*antaḥpādam*), provided that *m* is followed by a non-*v* sound (*avyapara*). This is merely the style of their school's composition; they compose their own Prātiśākhya.

But is it not the case that this is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) intended to refer specifically to a single school? As in the rule: "In the *Yajus* of the *Kaṭha*, [the substitution of *su* for *sma* occurs] in the words *deva* and *sumna*" (Pāṇini 7.4.38). True; this is indeed so. What is meant by this is that they possess the character of a school (*pārṣada*). Their pronunciation belongs to a school, and this designation as a school applies to them in their own place, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, they have many such usages, such as the forms *kitakiṭa* and the musical interjections (*stobha*) and so forth. It is for this purpose that it was stated: "for the *Chandoga*s."

[3.1] Regarding the *āntarya* [proximity] of those [vowels] consisting of three or four *mātrās*: because there is nothing else [of that duration], this [distinction] also does not exist here, as it is stated: "The *pluta* [vowel] is prescribed for a specific object" (*P* 6.1.87, vt. 2). In this case, for example, in *paśum*, the result is established by the rule "[*ami*] *ekaḥ*" alone. Or rather, even this [rule] need not be formulated; for the long vowel is already established by the rule "In the first two [cases], [the substitute] is the same as the preceding" (*P* 6.1.102). True; this is so. (p.)

20) However, when this [sūtra] *ami* is being commenced, the rule *vā chandasi* (P 6.1.106) would continue to apply because of that commencement; therefore, for the purpose of ensuring that *amyekaḥ* applies instead, the mention of *pūrva* is made for the sake of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitution of the preceding form). [But surely the previous *pūrva* is already carried over by context? True. Nevertheless, *dvitva* (or rather, *dīrghatva*, "lengthening") would also continue to apply.

But surely, in that case, the purpose of the recurrence of the word "pūrva" (prior) is so that the prior [vowel] may be long; however, let the subsequent [vowel] not be the one most similar to both. This second mention of "pūrva" from the rule "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ" must also be carried over here. Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates this. But would it not rather be for the sake of restriction, so that it does not apply here in the case of *uta*?

In that case, this is the indicator (*jñāpaka*): *sau ca* (P 6.4.13) and *saṃprasāraṇasya* (P 6.3.139). This too would be for the purpose of excluding the short vowel, according to *iko hrasvo ’ṅyo . . .* (P 6.3.61). This very rule is the indicator that when there is the substitution of a semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*), two instances of the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) are to be understood as recurring. [The result] is established by [the rule] *ato guṇe paraḥ* alone. In that context, the *e*-vowels and *o*-vowels are indeed long; what, then, is the purpose of the mention of the form (*rūpa*)? It is understood to be for the sake of the letter *a*.

First, regarding the example *khaṭvarśya*: this is the intended meaning. When the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (P 6.1.87) applies and all [possible] substituends have presented themselves, the vowels *e* and *o* remain in place in forms such as *khaṭvendraḥ* and *khaṭvoḍhā*. Since the vowel *a* is heard [in the resulting form] with the technical designation *guṇa*, it would follow that the [original] separate elements would be heard [instead]. As it has been stated: "The phonemes *jha* and *bha* do not exist at the end of a word" (MBh 1.36.3).

The technical terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply when followed by *t* (*tapara*). Although the things designated (*saṃjñin*) are distinct from the designations (*saṃjñā*), nevertheless, when they are expressed in the form of the designation, they are expressed with the gender and number of that designation, as in "the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are called *gha*" (P 1.1.22). Alternatively, "when followed by *t*" refers to the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) accompanied by *t*. Or rather, "followed by *t*" (*tapara*) is a locative case; it means that within the domain of the thing designated (*saṃjñin*) which is followed by *t*, the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are applied.

For whom, then, is the *tapara* status (the status of being followed by *t*) stated? For the *saṃjñins*. Why? Because a technical name (*saṃjñā*) exists for the sake of another. In that case, since the *tapara* status belongs to the name, the gender attached even to the name is understood to belong to the *saṃjñins* themselves. If this is so, there is no determination of time for the *saṃjñins*, because they are not being uttered [they are not explicitly pronounced].

If it were not known for what duration this *tapara* status applies, then by the force of the employment of *tapara*, it would not include homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds; however, this is not the case, as it includes those of two morae (*dvimātra*), but not those of three morae (*trimātra*). Now, if you think that the designation itself is *tapara*, even so, the *ekāra* which is *tapara* would indicate its own homogeneous sound of that same duration, but it would not include the *okāra* and *aukāra*; thus, there would either be no inclusion at all, or else there would be an indication of every possible duration.

There is no fault in the *tapara* designation for the term *saṃjñā*. For where both *ec* and *aic* do not form a composite whole (*samudāya*), the paribhāṣā regarding defective members (*vikalāṅga*) does not apply there. In that case, the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (P 1.1.70) operates only to this extent: "that which has a mention [in the sūtra] applies to its own duration. And that mention occurs because of the *tapara* designation. Consequently, then, [the rule] *ādir antyena sahetā* (P 1.1.71)...

21) Regarding the rule *tanmadhyasya ca* (P 1.1.71, Vt. 2): when there is the inclusion of vowels with short *a*, *i*, and *u* (such as *aṇ* or *aṭ*), the vowels beginning with *i*—whether actually heard or unheard—are understood through the initial vowel *a* that has been indicated; the same applies to *o* and *au*. Even when the names (*saṃjñin*) themselves are followed by the marker *t* (*tapara*), that which is situated according to the rule *ādir antyena sahetā* is grasped, and subsequently it grasps those sounds of the same duration (*tatkāla*).
Furthermore, since *o* and *au* are present [within the *aṇ* group], their comprehension as being of the same duration is logical.

Regarding the statement "tād api ras [paras] tapara," the mention of these two is by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a pair), because when the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not explicitly mentioned, one relies on the mere form itself. This is indicated by the evidence in the rule "sahivahorodavarṇasya" (P 6.3.112), where two rules are uttered by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) due to conflicting interpretations, just as in the case of the specific mention of case endings in "ig yaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (P 1.1.45).

Or rather, it is because a single sound cannot simultaneously express two meanings. [Question: What is the purpose of the letter *da*? [And what is the purpose of the letter *ta*? [Answer: Since all vowels ending in *ṛ* are both udātta and nasalized (or non-nasalized), the addition of *t* as a *tapara* marker is neither applicable as an instigator (*pravartaka*) nor as a restrictor (*nivartaka*), because such a vowel is not an *aṇ*. Therefore, the letter *ta* is equivalent to the letter *da*.

[4] Those which are parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*) among the phonemes that have the same form as the phonemes themselves—namely, the *a*, *i*, and *u* vowels within the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), which are constituent parts having the same form as other phonemes; likewise, in the case of *ā* and so on, the prosodic measures (*mātrikā*) themselves are the constituent parts; similarly, the *r* sound in *ṛ* and the *l* sound in *ḷ*—are these included within the injunctions concerning *ag* and so forth? He states the reason for whether such a constituent part is grasped or not grasped: "For here, both wholes (*samudāya*) are taught, as well as parts (*avayava*)."

Furthermore, a part is included within a whole; for example, when a tree moves, it moves together with its parts. In this context, the former reason [for inclusion] pertains to the case of being grasped (*grahaṇa*), while the latter reason for not being grasped (*agrahaṇa*) is also indicated here in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the reason: when there is grasping, there is grasping; when there is non-grasping, there is non-grasping. In rules such as "a long vowel replaces a homogeneous vowel after *ak*" (P 6.1.101), the constituent parts (*avayava*) are grasped. Why? Because they are grasped here—in this *pratyāhāra*.

The groups (*samudāya*) are also taught, as in *eoṅ* and *aiauc*; the individual elements (*avayava*) are also taught, as in *aiuṇ*. Where the teaching refers to the individual elements, the group, even though it exists there, is not intended to be taught; for example, in *aiuṇ*, the group is not [meant]. Or rather, it is *aṅ* or *aḍ*; what then? Only the individual elements, as in *hayavaraḍ*. Because of the teaching of the vowel *a* here... since it is impossible to pronounce [the *a* otherwise], this is not a teaching of the vowel *a*; thus, in the case of consonants followed by *val* (semivowels and spirants), the consonants are designated as being without vowels (*anacka*).

Thus, when *eṅ* and *aij* are taught as technical terms (*upadeśa*), it is the entire aggregate itself that is taught according to the rule "the first [element], together with the last, [denotes the whole]" (P 1.1.71), not the individual components such as *a* and so forth, because those have been taught elsewhere. Although they are not explicitly taught here, the components of the aggregates *ay*, *āv*, and *āy*—which are substitutes for *ec* according to "for *ec*, *ay*, *āv*, and *āy*" (P 6.1.78)—are understood through inference; for these components are not directly denotable by the word [of the rule]. What then? They are the aggregates. Just as the word *vṛkṣa*... [is not the same as its parts].

22) Regarding the statement concerning the result (*phala*) and so forth: in this regard, the following [objection] arises—where both the function of the whole (*samudāya-kārya*) and the function of the parts (*avayava-kārya*) converge, what ought to prevail there? It is the function of the part. Why? Because it is the part that is enjoined (*codita*) in that context. For when the function of the whole is present, the part is brought under its dependence by that very whole; thus, out of conformity with the whole, the part ceases [its own independent operation]. As in the case of the mantra: *agna āyāhi* ("O Agni, come hither").

Just as when one says, "Let ghee be given to him," even though the vessel has reached the hand, it is not included [in the act of giving]; thus, although it has been given, it is as if not given, and although it has been received, it is as if not received—so too, a constituent part that is included is not truly included. Consequently, the collective grammatical operation prescribed by inference in the rule *agna indra* (Pāṇini 6.1.108) is not realized; rather, only that which is directly enjoined is realized, namely, the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*).

Since phonemes existing within wholes—such as *arka* and *aśva*—are understood even when not explicitly enjoined and thus participate in grammatical operations, just as those situated in word-constituent groups (*padādisamudāya*) undergo such operations, so too do those situated in phoneme-constituent groups (*varṇasamudāya*). Therefore, by virtue of being included in a *pratyāhāra*, they are grasped at the locations where grammatical operations apply.

Now the reason for not grasping [the individual parts] is stated: "and a part is within the whole. As for what you think—that in the instruction of the *pratyāhāra* only the wholes are taught—how is this so? Even though there is an instruction of the wholes, this must be considered.

Is it then that the constituent part (*avayava*) has not been included, for otherwise it would be impossible to produce the form of the whole (*samudāya*), and thus the teacher’s activity is directed toward the whole alone? Or is it that the parts have been internalized? We say: they have been internalized. In that case, just as one understands the substitution (*ādeśa*) because it is included within [the whole], so too is the *ectva* [included]; however, regarding the grammatical operations (*kārya*), the designation applies primarily to the [whole].

Just as in the case of the *praṣṭhī*, attachment to the action is secondary while the acquisition of the name is primary, so too this effect of the parts—that is, the acquisition of a designation—is something that the parts undergo. This is what it demonstrates: by virtue of acquiring the name of the whole (*samudāya*), the part proceeds having undergone dependence and having set aside its own [independent] operation.

Just as a composite (*samudāya*) also exists as a distinct color (*varṇāntara*) endowed with a different genus (*jātyantara*), so too the "man-lion" (*narasiṃha*) genus is a distinct composite from the genus "human. For in that case, if one says, "Let lion-meat be brought, or let human-meat be brought," it does not follow that either of those meats is actually brought. Therefore, how could parts that do not exist within composites be designated, or how could they be apprehended?

Another perspective is adopted: speaking while relying on the distinction between the whole (*samudāya*) and its constituent parts (*samudāyin*), it is said—"The parts are one thing, the whole is another; yet both are taught. In that regard, how could that part which exists within the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) not undergo grammatical operation? For the part is internal to the whole. Thus, there is identity between the whole and its constituent parts; the whole is not something other [than the parts], and the parts are likewise [not other than the whole].

If these two, being thus situated, receive a designation such that "this very movement is that of the parts," or alternatively, if here both the wholes (*samudāya*) and the parts (*avayava*) are taught, then it is said that they share the same object. This is the case in the teaching *eoṅ* and *aidauj*, where both are taught; the phrase "with intent" (*tātparyeṇa*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sense. Just as the recitation of the *garga-* and *bidādi-* groups is intended to establish the correctness of the wholes and to exclude [the application of rules] to parts such as *kalā*, and because a part is internal to the whole.

The instruction refers only to the collective meaning and not to the individual meanings, just as in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the recitation of the *gargādi* and *bidādi* groups [of surnames].

[4.1] Prohibition of the rule concerning identical vowels (Vt. 6): In the case of *agne indra*, two rules would apply, one based on the whole and one based on its parts. The scope for the substitution of *ay* (by Pāṇini 6.1.78) is seen in *agna ā yāhi*; the scope for lengthening (by Pāṇini 6.1.101) is seen in *dadhīndra*. Here, in *agne indra*, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), lengthening prevails. Alternatively, the substitution of *ay* is inferential (*ānumānika*), whereas lengthening is directly taught (*sākṣāt*); thus, that which is directly taught is stronger.

How is it in the case of the substitution of *yaṇ*? There too, the constituent part (*avayava*) is directly taught. True; this is so. Yet that [substitution] is superseded because it has no scope of its own, according to the principles "that which applies when [the other] does not yet apply" (*yenāprāpte*) and "intermediate exceptions supersede those preceding them" (*madhye 'pavādāḥ pūrvān*).

[4.1.1] Since this [sūtra] teaches *tug* after a long vowel (*dīrghāt*), *tug* occurs when there is a *ch* following a long vowel. Of what [is it taught]? According to the rule "when [something] is specified by the locative case, the operation applies to what precedes it" (P 1.1.66). But would this not apply for the sake of the vowels *e* and *o*? For in those cases, the subsequent portion consists of more than one mora (*mātrā*). Even there, it could be argued that by removing half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), the operation could be made to apply to the preceding portion. The analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is the indicator [that this is not so], showing that *tug* does not occur [there].

[4.1.2] It will not occur because of the force of the inclusion of *ta* (the long vowel marker). For in this case, the operation (*pravṛtti*) has already achieved its purpose in the word *vṛkṣaiḥ*; however, the cessation (*nivṛtti*) has not yet been accomplished. And since the inclusion of *ta* is the indicator (*liṅga*) for that cessation, the direct scriptural statement (*sākṣāc chruti*)—that it does not occur after a long vowel—is sublated by the inferential scriptural statement (*anumāna-śruti*).

[4.1.3] Regarding the rule *yad ayam āto ’nupasarga* ("when this [suffix] follows a verbal root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix"), here too, because the presence of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) *k* would otherwise be without scope, the removal of the long *ā* is prescribed. Here an objection is raised: if the addition of the indicatory *k* were not made, there would be a fault in the following case: *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.50).

If this [root] were stated as having the vowel *a* by the rule "āto ’nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), then, since this would fall under the domain of roots ending in *ej*, once the vowel *ā* is substituted for the roots beginning with *mī* (such as *mīnāti*), and when the suffix *ka* is added, there would be the fault of the non-application of the augment *yuk* to those roots ending in long *ā*. This is not a fault. First of all, because the root *dīṅ* is intransitive, it cannot have an object as its subordinate word (*upapada*). It would become transitive only when accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*). Even in that case, it is stated that it is "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*).

In the rule *mīnātiminotyor apy hvāvāmaś ca* (P 3.2.2), the term *ātaḥ* is a general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). This being the case, it is stated: "This [mention of *ātaḥ*] would be for the sake of the subsequent rule. If that is so, consider the rule *gāpoṣṭak*. There too, an objection is raised: in the form *chandogāya*, there would be elision [of the final vowel] by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (P 6.4.140). Furthermore, one cannot rely on a term as specifically prescribed (*pratipadokta*), for otherwise the form *papuṣaḥ* would not be possible. (p.)

24) Regarding the letter *y* characterized by conjunction (*saṃnipāta*), however, the [vowel] *kāra*—that is, the long vowel *ā*—would not occur at all. It is said in response: "By virtue of being an *āt* [vowel], there is no elision (*alopa*)," which means that there is indeed elision (*lopa*). This being the case, it follows that there must be elision in every respect.

[4.2] And like a single syllable (vt. 8). The word *saṃkhyā* (number) is a restrictor in all cases; thus, the word *vāk* is designated as "having two vowels" (*dvyaj*). In that regard, there is either an extended application (*atideśa*) of the status of having one vowel, meaning "let the original state of having two vowels remain," or else [the rule] "this [suffix] follows a monosyllabic root" (*asāv ekācaḥ*, P 6.1.168) would apply where? [It would apply] in cases such as *srucā* and *tvacā*. Alternatively, the mention of *go-naus* (cow and ship) serves as an inference regarding a general domain, which is then conceived as applying to all domains.

[4.3] "There is no application of that rule to a part of what is not separated" (Vt. 9). That in which separation (*vyapavṛkta*) does not exist is "not separated" (*avyapavṛkta*); it refers to a collection (*samudāya*). There is no application of that rule to a part of such a non-separated whole. Alternatively, whatever rule is observed to apply to a part that has become separate from a part of something that is not separated—that rule is not applied.

Regarding the statement, "There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," the word that is applied to the *ṛc* verses is used by extension for the sacrificial wood (*kāṣṭha*) due to their association. However, a piece of wood measuring only sixteen *aratnis* does not receive the designation "seventeen. For the number seventeen applies to distinct entities; it does not apply to that which is qualified by the number one. In this regard, just as the parts, being inseparable, are themselves undesignated, so too are the single phonemes (*varṇa*) and their portions.

For that ritual action is enjoined for each verse (*pratyṛcam*). In that case, if there is neither deficiency nor excess in the milking, there is no deficiency in the ritual (*karmavaiguṇyam*). Now, it might be argued: "Let him place the entire [fuel] on the fire and then recite the verses. Even so, this is impossible both with respect to the fire and the altar (*vedī*). For the altar measures three and a half cubits. Therefore, this point was raised for the following reason: because of the connection with the *ṛc* verses and because of their small size, the term *samit* (fuel-stick) would not be applicable here.

Regarding the phrase "here too, with each *praṇava*," it is exactly as before. As for the example "clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and oil (*taila*)," this is what is meant: comprehension based merely on the possibility [of a word's application] is not logical. Even though the possibility of clarified butter and oil exists, there is a sale of clarified butter because it is designated by the word "cow" (*go*), and there is a sale of oil because it is designated by the word "mustard seed" (*sarṣapa*). [Since they are not so designated, there is no sale of those two.]

For if it were merely by way of possibility, then even a seller of cows would be a seller of meat. But this contradicts the established rule that "māṣa beans are not to be eaten," for by this rule, māṣas are not consumed even when mixed with other things; likewise, by the rule "one who drinks liquor," even liquor that is mixed with other substances is not drunk.

"In that case, where is it observed that there is a separation (*vyapavarga*)? Separation is observed even in some instances characterized by the number one. Where? In places such as inner rooms (*apavarakādi*). For it is said: 'This is five beds,' or 'This is seven beds' (*sapta-khaṭva*). Thus, in the case of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), the distinctness [of their constituent elements] is indicated by the cessation and the undertaking of effort."

Regarding the statement "because of the openness (*vivṛtatva*) in the diphthongs" (Vt. 10), [the opponent argues that] it should be understood as "more open" (*vivṛtatara*) or rather "most open" (*vivṛtatama*). In that case, because there is a difference in the articulatory effort (*prayatna*), there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) at all; so how could there be any inclusion [of one by the other]? (p. 25)

[5] Alternatively, however, they are not perceived. This non-perception was stated in the rule "not of that which is not distinct" (*nāvyapavṛktasya*), referring to [sounds] such as *ā* and so forth. And where there is distinction, as in the case of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), there too there is a lack of homogeneity (*asāvarṇya*). Therefore, only the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* remain established. Regarding this, the view of Vākyakāra is as follows: "The constituent parts do not exist at all; rather, it is the composite whole itself that is endowed with a different genus (*jātyantara*), like Narasiṃha. With this view, he proceeds as follows:

[5.1] Regarding the rule *nuḍvidhilāḍeśavināmeṣu* (Vārttika 11): Now, if there are constituent parts (*avayava*) within that aggregate (*samudāya*), then when the operation pertains to the aggregate—as in the case of *ay* and so forth—the constituent part would not be subject to the grammatical effect. However, where it is the constituent part itself that is active, and not the aggregate, then the existing constituent part would not be subject to the effect. Since the aggregate is not what is enjoined in the case of *nuṭ* and the others, *nuṭ* and the rest will apply by depending on the constituent parts. Therefore, there is no purpose in the explicit mention of the phoneme *ṛ*.

If this were so, then since a short vowel is also dependent [on a consonant], a *tuk* augment would have to be applied after a short vowel as well, as in *ālūya* and *pralūya*. To this, it has been replied: either because there is no separation (*avyapavarga*), or because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) stating that "one teaches the *tuk* after a short vowel before *cha*," or by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Or rather, [the rule applies] only to the root *aś* when it has *a* as its penultimate letter (*avarṇopadha*). Thus an inference is formulated; it is not the case that one thinks: "How can it apply only to *aś*, and not to *aśnāti*?"

This is an undivided (avibhaktika) designation. Since this designation exists, the term *ur* is the one being designated; because that [term] has no other occasion for application, the substitution of *l* will occur for the *r* which is a constituent part of it. Only the *sphoṭa* is being designated. What is meant is that the *sphoṭa* is characterized by its phonetic manifestation (*adhvanika*). But is it not the case that there is no perception of the *sphoṭa* at all without the phonetic manifestation? If that is so, then only that initial phonetic manifestation which conveys the mere form is relied upon.

However, that which indicates a specific distinction—namely, "this one resides in a collection" or "this one is independent"—is not relied upon; for even when such a distinction exists there, it is merely a formless appearance (*ārūpamātra*), just as the perception of a cow occurs either through its specific characteristics or through its mere formless appearance. Therefore, the apprehension of the mere formless appearance belongs to both. Alternatively, this is stated by treating the cognition as if it were the effect.

In that regard, according to the view that the effect is produced (*kāryapakṣa*), the *sphoṭa* itself is produced from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), from disjunction (*vibhāga*), or from both conjunction and disjunction. As for the resonance (*anuraṇana*), however, that arises from sound alone. Therefore, one should rely only on that much—the activity of the hand (or the instrument) which is the producer of that *sphoṭa*. Alternatively, it is stated that the expression "merely the *sphoṭa*" (*asphoṭamātra*) is a reference to its generic form (*ākṛti*).

In that regard, since one cannot comprehend the form (ākṛti) without sound when the form is being indicated, the substance (dravya) must necessarily be comprehended; thus, when the substance is indicated, that which is heard [as a phoneme] lacks functional application [to the grammatical operation]. This is the purpose of resorting to the form: for the sake of the comprehension of the two *r*-sounds, whether they are included or not included [within the technical name].

That which follows the *bhakti* (vowel-portion) of the *repha*, or that which stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *repha*—that is, the *bhakti* is the *repha*, and [the rule refers to] what follows it; or else, it refers to what follows the *bhakti* of the letter *a* or the *bhakti* of the letter *i*. Thus, the condition "even when separated by an augment" (*aḍvyavāya*) will apply. He thinks as follows: just as the letter *a* includes the long and protracted vowels because it belongs to the class *aṇ*, so too it will include the *bhakti* as well. Or, since the class-form (*ākṛti*) is grasped, and because the class-form exists everywhere... (p.)

26) "There is this view here": by this view, it is meant that only those [phonemes] which are established [in a specific arrangement] can be grasped. This is what is being said: for those [phonemes] which possess *ātva* elsewhere, they are also found as distinct phonemes (*vyapavṛkta-varṇa*). This is to be connected with the phrase "this is what is being said. However, this fourth type of phoneme is not seen elsewhere anywhere; even its similarity (*sāvarṇya*) does not exist. For in this case, there is no effort of the parts distinct from the effort of the whole, nor is there a [distinct] place of articulation (*sthāna*).

And this small portion of phonetic description cannot serve to indicate the genus (*jāti*). By the phrase "by these very [sounds] belonging to the traditional list of phonemes" (*ākṣarasamāmnāyikaiḥ*), it should be understood that even the vowels *ā* and so forth, which belong to the traditional list of phonemes, are what are to be indicated. However, *bhakti* (the individual manifestation) is neither the indicator nor the indicated; for that purpose, there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

[5.2] "The *pluta* vowels *ai* and *au* are marked with the *u*-indicator" (Vt. 12). For there is indeed a separation (*vyapavarga*) here. Even though such a separation exists, when there is no inclusion [of the *u*-indicator], then this must be stated: "The *pluta* vowels *ai* and *au* are marked with the *u*-indicator. But when there is inclusion, the vowel *ai* is heavy; its final vowel is the beginning of that which is designated as *ṭi*, and thus it is established by the rule "after a heavy syllable, except for *ṛ*" (P 8.2.86). Furthermore, there is an absence of *ā* and the other vowels here because there is no separation. This is done precisely in the *Nyāsa*.

This demonstrates the following: even if they are perceived, this [status of being a vowel] is not established. For it has been stated: "Because of the openness (*vivṛtatva*) in the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*). In that case, even if there is an equal portion (*samabhāga*), because the effort (*prayatna*) is different, if there is no perception [of the second element], then the status of being a vowel (*actva*) does not exist at all; how then could there be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel? Even if there is a greater amount of the latter [element], even so, that which consists of one and a half morae (*adhyardhamātrika*) lacks the status of being a vowel. Furthermore, there is no distinct demarcation (*vyapavarga*) for that half-mora. Therefore, it is only logical to rely upon the alternative arrangement (*anyāsa*).

[5.3] When a conjunction consists of similar forms, the rule for two consonants applies (Vt. 13). A conjunction is said to consist of "similar forms" because its constituent parts are of similar form. For a conjunction cannot possess similarity of form simply by virtue of being a single unit. The intended meaning is as follows: just as there is no distinction [of individual letters] among vowels such as *a* and so forth, and thus no linguistic usage regarding their constituent parts exists, so too here, the lack of distinction (*avyapavarga*) is the same.

Since no distinction based on smallness or greatness is included by the mere indication of the form (*ākṛti*), the designation *saṃyoga*—which depends on two consonants—would not apply to the aggregate [of consonants] according to the rule "the [consonant] group is *hal*. This being the case, the designation *guru* would be absent, and consequently, there would be no protracted vowel (*pluta*) by the rule "after a heavy syllable (*guru*) that is not *ṛ*" (P 8.2.86). Here, the duration of one mora (*mātrā*) is understood, and a single-mora consonant does not exist. In this context, vowels such as *ā* and so forth are understood from their recitation in the *pāṭha*.

Since the *ākāra* and other vowels also exist, it is known through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*) that "the long vowel *ākāra* exists, just like the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*). For these [diphthongs] are indeed taught as having two morae (*dvimātra*). Furthermore, the *pluta* [vowel] is specifically mentioned [as distinct from the others] in the rule, "The short, long, and *pluta* vowels have the duration of *u*, *ū*, and *ū3*" (P 1.2.27). Its inclusion is established by the rule, "An *aṇ* vowel and an *udit* vowel include their homogeneous counterparts" (P 1.1.69). Therefore, because they are both taught (*upadeśa*) and prescribed (*vidhāna*), we consider that these [long vowels] have been taught and accepted by the learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*).

However, there is no instruction regarding consonants, nor their apprehension, nor is there any prescription for them anywhere. Therefore, how could those not taught by the learned be capable of being pointed out? And this is the reason for it: just as in the case of [vowels] such as *a* and so forth, the sound produced by the articulatory organs impelled by a single effort, while initiating another sound, displays a difference in time even while the operation of the organs has not ceased; this is not the case with consonants.

It is undisputed among the learned that after one phoneme has been articulated, another organ is exerted with a further effort for the sake of another phoneme; the distinction here is that in this case [of the vowel], one articulates it repeatedly. Just as when one articulates the sound *a* repeatedly, one exerts the organ again and again, so it is with the consonants.

But here, how is it that [the forms] *saṃvatsaraḥ* and *tal-lokaṃ yal-lokam* occur? One might assume their absence because they were not included in the previous [list]. However, the semivowels (*antasthā*) have been taught as being included within the vowels (*aṇ*). Therefore, they will be understood there as part of the whole, just like the vowel *a*; thus, these [semivowels] are established by the treatise as having the duration of a vowel. Here too, the duration of a mora (*mātrā*) is understood. Furthermore, this is also present here: one [of them] is nasal (*anunāsika*), and the other is non-nasal (*niranunāsika*).

In this regard, the claim that there will be both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) forms is difficult to establish. Therefore, having withdrawn the articulatory effort (*karaṇa*), the second [consonant] is uttered with a different effort; thus, a consonant does not occupy the duration of a mora (*mātrākāla*). If it were non-existent, how could it be perceived? For only what exists can be grasped by its homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇa*). Indeed, an *a*-vowel of one-mora duration is not capable of grasping an *a*-vowel of one mora [or half a mora]. Why? Because of its non-existence. [The consonants are: ha, ya, va, ra, ṭ. (Pāṇini 1.1.5)

This letter *ha* is taught twice: both as the preceding and as the following. This status of being preceding or following does not depend on other letters; for if it depended on other letters, then every letter except *a* would be both preceding and following.

[1.1] "The mention of *aṭ* [is] for the purpose of including *ha*" (Vt. 1). Here, some mention of *aṭ* is uttered that is without purpose, namely in the rule *'śaś cho 'ṭi'* (P 8.4.63). Furthermore, the mention of *aṭ* has been presented by the author of the Vārttika as having a specific purpose; for in the example *'mahāṃ hi saḥ'*, since the letter *ha* is not *aṭ*, the substitution of *ru* [for *s*] would not occur by the rule *'āto 'ṭi . . .*' (P 8.3.3).

[1.2] Furthermore, the non-inclusion of *aś* necessitates the rule "bho-bhago... (P 8.3.17). For in the example "bho hasati," because [the sound following *bho*] is not *aś*, the substitution of *y* (yatvam) by the rule "aśi" would not occur. This [mention of *aś*] is merely for the sake of illustration; one should not say that the mention of the letter *h* is for the purpose of [applying the rule to] *utva*.

[1.3] If it is asked whether there is some other instruction elsewhere, this is demonstrated: for here, the recitation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is not for the purpose of understanding their form; what then? It is for the purpose of the operation of the treatise (*śāstra*). And that treatise does not function with respect to the letter *ha* unless there is an instruction. [II] [1] This is the letter *ra*. The question is raised because there are purposes and faults in both cases.

[1.1] Regarding the form *svarṇayati*: the nasalized *ṇakāra* would result [by Pāṇini 8.4.58], for in this rule (*yoga*) there is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). In the case of *madrahradaḥ*, when doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the *repha* has been applied, since the doubling is not yet established, the elision by *na ro ri* (P 8.3.14) would not occur; thus, two *rephas* would be heard. As in *kuṇḍaṃ rathena*.

In this case, since no specific qualification has been provided that the *parasavarṇa* must necessarily be nasal, it follows that the *parasavarṇa* could be either a nasal or a non-nasal *repha*. Because the *parasavarṇa* is considered *asiddha*, the elision prescribed by the rule *ro ri* does not occur.

[2] Regarding the prohibition of the *kittva* designation when the teaching is prior (Vt. 5): If the teaching were prior, the letter *va* would also be included in the term *ral*. Furthermore, there is the statement regarding the elision of *v* (Vt. 5). Since the *repha* is not included within *val*, the statement concerning the elision of *v* was rejected as being for the sake of the letter *va* and not for the sake of the letter *ya*.

[2.1] There are no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds for the letter *repha* (ṛ) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*). But has it not been stated: "Since homogeneity is not prescribed in one instance, and because of the nasal [in another], there must be [doubling] by means of the letters *repha* and *ṇakāra*"? True; this is so. However, this speaker, while stating the resolution regarding doubling (*dvirvacana*), also provides a counter-argument for those two [letters]. These two, *ra* and *ha*, are not the objects of the operation (*kāryin*) of doubling. What then? These two, *ra* and *ha*, are the cause (*nimitta*) of the doubling. For in this sentence [of the rule], "after a vowel, due to *ra* and *ha*" (*aco rahābhyām*).

In this rule (Pāṇini 8.4.46), the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the *hakāra* (the sound *h*) are adopted as causes (*nimitta*) and are not able to attain the status of being the effect (*kāryitva*) from this sentence. Why? Because in this sentence, in the mention "after *ay* and *ar*" (*ayara*), the *repha* and *hakāra* are merely inferred; whereas in the expression "after *ra* and *ha*" (*rahābhyām*), they are directly enjoined as causes. It is just as in the case: "Let the Brāhmaṇas be fed; let Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya serve the food."

In this context, the act of eating, which is inferred from the sentence, is sublated by the act of serving, which is directly enjoined; therefore, on account of this sentence, those two do not experience the status of being agents with respect to the act of eating.

If this is so, there is a fault regarding *dadhi* and *udaka*. In the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (P 6.1.77), although the vowel (*ac*) is inferred as the cause (*nimitta-bhāva*), it is directly enjoined as being connected to the operation (*kārya-yogitva*) of the *ik* sounds; thus, the status of being the cause must be sublated by its connection to the operation.

Now, it might be thought: "In the case of a single [element], there is no connection with an effect because of its being a cause; but here, 'ikaḥ' and 'aci' are indeed distinct. Even here, in the rule *madrahṛde*, the letter *h* is one thing as the cause, and the *r* following it is another; why then is reduplication not understood in this way?"

[The objection is] not a fault because of the difference in philosophical views (*darśana-bheda*). According to the view that the word-meaning is the *ākṛti* (form), that a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) operates only once, that a rule applies to a collection [of sounds], and that a treatise (*śāstra*) is merely an auxiliary to knowledge—according to this view, it is stated that "there are no homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) for the sibilants and *ūṣman* sounds," and "these two, *r* and *h*, are not subject to grammatical operations. If one asks: "How then does the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (P 8.4.45) apply here? [the answer is: the treatise is not required for actual usage (*anapekṣita-prayoga*).

In actual usage (*prayoga*), there is no substitution of nasalized sounds for the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*). Furthermore, the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) does not apply where it would lead to such a realization; as it has been said: "The letters *jha* and *bha* do not exist at the end of a word" (MBh 1.36.1–2), meaning that the suffixes *jhuṭ* and *bhuṭ* will not occur. Likewise, the rule "for *anusvāra*, there is the *parasavarṇa* before a *yay* letter" (P 8.4.58) operates by determining both the collection of *anusvāra*s and the collection of *parasavarṇa*s.

In this context, by the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P 1.1.50), the criterion for "most similar" (*āntaratamya*) regarding the cause of nasality is established by the aggregate as a whole. For an aggregate can possess a quality insofar as some of its constituent parts possess that quality; as in the expressions "this city has cattle" (*gomad idaṃ nagaram*) or "staff-bearers are walking" (*daṇḍino gacchanti*). Thus, at the time of comprehension, it must be understood that the *parasavarṇa* (the following homogeneous sound) must be the most similar. Since no such *repha* (the letter *r*) exists in that state, the fault arises.

In the expression "a single operation of the defining characteristic" (*sakṛllakṣaṇavyāpāra*), there is no nasalized *r* (*repha*). Likewise, this rule of grammar as well—"after *ac*, [doubling occurs] after *ra* and *ha*" (*aco rahābhyām*)—does not depend upon actual usage. Is there a co-occurrence (*sāṃnidhya*) of *r* and *h* in actual usage? No, there is not. It operates only to this extent: "after *ra* and *ha*, a following *yar* (consonant) becomes doubled. In that case, just as the *yar* (here, the letter *h*) has been excluded, so too has the *repha* (*r*).
Since there would be no further application once this much has been understood, by what application could the letter *r* following the letter *h* undergo doubling?

Furthermore, in the case of curd, water, and so forth, the individual instance (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning, while the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is a subordinate factor in its application; thus, the rule (*lakṣaṇa*) operates repeatedly. According to this view, comprehension occurs through the understanding that "those various rules which would apply to each respective instance have not been uttered out of laziness. Consequently, under the alternative view expressed by the rule *na veti vibhāṣā* (P 1.1.44), there is acceptance in one case and rejection in another. Is this not a different way of explaining how a rule operates simultaneously upon its object?

The attainment of the *madrahṛada* and so forth is made known by that very [rule]. Since the operation of the treatise (*śāstra*) applies to each individual object of perception, the attainment regarding curd, water, and so on is innate (*prākṛtī*). Just as with yoga, therefore, this [attainment] is not something to be taught (*aśiṣya*).
[III]

[1] These *ayogavāha* sounds are not taught anywhere; they are not recited in the *pratyāhāra* [sūtras] as other [phonemes] are. Yet they are heard in actual usage and in the grammatical treatise at the time of rule-application, in such rules as "the *visarjanīya* occurs in place of [a final *r*] before a non-*khara* (vowel) or a pause" (*Pāṇini* 8.3.15) and "before *k* or *p*, [the *visarjanīya* becomes] *k* or *p*" (*Pāṇini* 8.3.37). Therefore, their instruction must be provided for the sake of their grammatical operation. Through this rule-application, their correctness (*sādhutva*) would be established, but that grammatical operation which is dependent upon the *pratyāhāra* would not otherwise occur.

Who, then, are those that carry [the grammatical operation] without being joined (*ayogavāha*)? This is a designation of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). He asks—"How, then?"—thinking that this "Great Army" (*mahatī camūḥ*) must surely be significant according to its literal meaning. [Those which] carry [the operation] without being joined, and which are heard even when not explicitly taught. Here, certain phonemes (*varṇa*) carry [the operation] while being joined; they accomplish the grammatical effect (*kārya*) by means of their technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) or their form (*ākṛti*), such as *k*, *ā*, and so forth. For these [others], however, [are governed by the rule]: "A vowel followed by *ṇ* or *u* denotes its homogeneous class... (*aṇudit savarṇasya...* P. 1.1.69).

"Or they carry [the sounds] joined by this [rule] (P 1.1.69), because of their connection with the form of the letter *a*. However, some [sounds] are heard as being taught, such as *ka* and so forth. Thus, these [consonant clusters] are neither joined by a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*), nor do they possess a [perceptible] form (*ākṛti*), nor are they taught (*upadiṣṭa*). Now, what role does the term *ayogavāha* play regarding the fact that they are not taught? This is the intended meaning: conjunction (*yoga*) is of two kinds—conjunction by way of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa-yoga*) or conjunction by way of instruction (*upadeśa-yoga*). Neither of these two types exists for them."

The text of others states: "They carry [the burden] improperly, and they are heard of even though they have not been taught. By the phrase "they are heard of even though they have not been taught," they demonstrate the very meaning of "they carry [the burden] improperly. For "teaching" (upadeśa) occurs in a treatise either by way of definition or by way of recitation; and that [teaching] does not exist for them.

[2] [Regarding the substitution of *jaś* for *śar* and the substitution of *ṣatva*: (Vt. 7)] It is stated that at the stage of *śar*, *jaś*-hood (*jaśtva*) applies in accordance with its being a *jhal* sound. And here, *jaś*-hood is also established by the original instruction (*upadeśa*), as in the case of the *upadhmānīya* and so forth. If "what is not established in the preceding" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) applies except for reduplication (*advirvacane*), or even if reduplication occurs first—in either case, the undesired form results. [It is] established precisely by the exceptional rule (*nipātana*). What is the status regarding reduplication? Here, this is the intention: for an exceptional rule (*nipātana*) is indeed an indicator (*liṅga*).

We shall not accept this [interpretation], namely that its *bha*-status arises by means of this [rule]. By what, then? By the rule "In the Vedic language, *bha* replaces the *h* of *hṛ* and *grah*" (P. 8.2.32, Vt.). One will infer a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) that it also applies to the *d* of *udj*. However, this is not the only originative rule (*prāpaka*) for it; rather, that [rule] is an originative rule in a domain where *kutva* does not apply. Thus, an inference is obtained that it pertains to a specific domain: that this [form] is derived from the root *gam* with two prefixes followed by the suffix *ḍa*.

Although at present the grammatical derivation (nipātana) alone is the means of proof, nevertheless, by the force of the instruction of the letter *da* (the force of the instruction of the letter *da*), it will be understood that the reduplication awaits that derivation.

[3] The inclusion of *num* must necessarily be made. In this context, *anusvāra* ought to occur in place of *num*. For that very purpose, *num* is included—so that it may apply only where *anusvāra* occurs, and not merely where there is an *anusvāra* resulting from the intervention of *śar* sounds, as in the case of *puṃsu*. Therefore, the inclusion of *num* remains established.

[4] Alternatively, the instruction should be given without distinction. By this it is not meant that [the letters] should be taught as being other than the *aṭ* and *śar* groups; what then? A specific purpose is cited. It need not be stated that "nasalization (*ṇatva*) is the purpose, and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated (*jaś*) and the sibilant (*ṣatva*) are the purposes. If they are taught among the *aṭ*s and the *śar*s, then all those purposes which do not require further specification are accomplished. Precisely because of their inclusion among the *śar*s, they possess the status of *hal*; from that, the designation of *saṃyoga* (conjunction) applies, as in [the word] *śvaḥstotā*. And among the *aṭ*s, they possess the status of *al*.
[5] There are substitutes for that which is being specified (*nirdiśyamāna*), as in the case of *vaiyāghrapadya*.
[6] Regarding reduplication—as in *uraḥkeṇa* (or *uraḥka*)—it is stated with reference to a distinction in phonetic form (*śrutibheda*).

[7] As in *vyūḍhoraskena*: in the specific instance of the augment *aṭ*, there is the generality of being an *al* (vowel, semi-vowel, or nasal). Furthermore, because it is taught (*upadeśāt*) that the *visarjanīya* is an *al*, the substitution of *ṇa* (as in *vyūḍhoraskaṇa*) would apply to the domain of *al*; however, in that case, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not exist.

[IV] [1] Furthermore, do these phonemes possess meaning? A question is asked only when there is a basis (*nimitta*) and a purpose (*prayojana*). In this regard, what is the basis or the purpose here? It is said: In this world, some things are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); some, though not being perceived, are established as existing through inference (*anumāna*); and some, though considered to be directly perceived, are understood through inference to be non-existent.

Furthermore, among collections such as trees and the like, no object consisting of [mere] colors is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In that case, its existence is established through inference (*anumāna*), just as the movement of the sun—which is not perceived—is established by its arrival at another location. And even that which is considered "directly perceived," like a firebrand-circle (*alātacakra*), is actually produced only through inference, because that form is seen even though it lacks actual motion. For example:

The wheel of a chariot, even when its activity has ceased, remains the cause for the cognition of a "wheel," whereas the fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) is not so. Therefore, this perception of a pervasive form is indeed an illusion. For in the case of the wheel-form, there is an absolute non-separation from the perception of touch; just as there is a continuous stream of perception of form in the wheel, so too is there a continuous stream of perception of touch. This is not the case with the fire-brand wheel, for the perception of touch occurs only at a specific location.

Furthermore, the meaningfulness of all linguistic elements in grammar is entirely inferential, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding roots (*dhātu*) and so forth. It is also possible to postulate a meaning for individual phonemes (*varṇa*), because they possess meaning when combined in a compound.

And the purpose is that, as with a meaningful word, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies to the word, and based on that, the derivation of case-endings (*svādi*) occurs. If, however, the meaningfulness of the phonemes is merely inferential, then their meaningfulness would be like that of the ingredients of wine (*surāṅga*), being connected to a meaning entirely unrelated to the meaning of the composite whole. Alternatively, just as meanings related to the composite whole come into being, so too are the meanings related to the composite whole distributed among the parts—namely, "the verbal root expresses the action" (*kriyā*) and "the suffix expresses the means" (*sādhana*).

Thus, the aggregate expresses the substance, while the phonemes express the constituent parts, such as the genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Alternatively, just as words that are mutually dependent express that very same meaning, so too the phonemes, through mutual dependence, express that very same meaning.

[2.1] “Because meaning is seen in those that consist of a single phoneme” (Vt. 9). For meaning is indeed perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). What is the reason for this perception here? If it were merely perception, then only those [phonemes] in which the meaning is actually perceived would possess meaning, and not others. Therefore, being a single unit (*ekatva*) and being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) are the reasons. In this world, the possession of meaning is observed in the case of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth, which are accompanied by both unity and phonemic nature; and these [phonemes under discussion] are likewise followed by both unity and phonemic nature.

Therefore, these [phonemes] must also possess meaningfulness by way of following [the usage]. This is the nature of phonemes (*varṇadharma*); however, this is its intended meaning: here, whatever entity is incapable of being associated with a certain property is absolutely incapable [of it]. For example, an atom, being incapable of perception, would be incapable in every respect. Therefore, a phoneme that is capable of being associated with the property being presented—namely, meaningfulness—is sometimes perceived as such when it is isolated and independent.

[2.2] "And because of the transition to another meaning upon the loss or the transposition of phonemes" (Vt. 10). Just as in the expression *rājavyatyaya* ("the change of king"), when one [king] departs and another arrives, so too here, when a certain phoneme is lost and another arrives, it is understood as a "transposition of phonemes. In this context, a transition to another meaning is observed through the arrival and departure of meaningful elements.

Just as when the word *loman* is established, the addition of the meaningful prefixes *anu-* and *prati-* results in a shift to a different meaning through the senses of "approach" (*upagama*) and "departure" (*apagama*)—namely, favorability and opposition—so too here, while the word *ūpa* remains, a shift to a different meaning occurs through the transposition of the letters *ka* and *sa*. Therefore, these two possess semantic significance.

The text of some is: "That which is the meaning of the well (*kūpa*) is [the meaning] of the letter *ka*. They explain it thus: "Even though it is dependent, nevertheless, this [meaning] exists. The text of others is: "[It is the meaning] of the letter *sa*. They say this: "Its meaningfulness is together with the letter *ka*," just as it is with the prefix *pra-* and the suffix *an*.

[2.3] And because meaning is not understood when a phoneme is not perceived (Vt. 11). Here, when that which possesses a meaning is not perceived, that meaning is not understood, as in the case of *pibati* and *vipibati*. In *vi* here, there is the sense of separation (*pṛthagbhāva*) and action; *vipibati* means "he separates. When the word *vi* is not perceived, the sense of separation in "he drinks" (*pibati*) is not understood. Likewise, in *pratiṣṭhate* and *tiṣṭhati*. And here, in the case of *ṛkṣa*, when the letter *v* is not perceived, the aggregate beginning with the root is not understood.

This is what is meant: all phonemes possess the capacity for all denotations; however, within them, according to each respective sequence, a certain capacity remains latent while another becomes manifest.

The term *anarthagateḥ* is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound), meaning "the non-arrival of the object" (*arthasyāgateḥ*). Its distinction from the previous case is this: in the former instance, there was both departure and arrival, whereas here there is only departure. Why, then, is it said "*anagateḥ*" (or "*anarthagate�:*)"? For you have stated that "that object is not understood. By speaking thus, you have effectively said that no other object is understood.

In this regard, what is meant by "because the meaning has not arrived"? It is not very sound; it is a worldly argument. For example, someone says to another: "What is the use of this person going? He will not do it. Another replies: "Let him go himself; he will certainly accomplish the task. That is the meaning of that [statement]; it is the meaning of the word "because the intended purpose has not been achieved" (or "because of the non-arrival of that which was intended").

Now, if you think: "In the phrase *tasya*, is the whole [word] being indicated, or is it the phoneme?"—this is incorrect because that very entity is what is to be proven. Therefore, he says: "That object is *tadartha*. Whatever object was introduced is accepted as the object; that very same [object] is not perceived when the letter *va* is removed. For example: in the case of *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"), since a face consisting of nothing but a camel is impossible, the word *iva* ("like") is excluded.

And since that collective term does not apply to anything other than its constituent part, the word "mouth" is excluded; furthermore, it is stated with this specific qualification that the collective term applies to nothing other than the part, namely the mouth itself. Likewise here too, by relying on the fact that it does not denote the subject matter at hand, it is understood through the force of the context that it functions by taking up its referent only in that specific instance.

[2.4] And because the aggregate possesses meaning (vt. 12). Both perception and non-perception are the cause. Just as there is a certain measure of oil in sesame seeds, so too there is a certain measure of the awakening to meaning within the phonemes. However, when multiple phonemes are uttered, the matured intellect comprehends the meaning.

[3] If, then, these phonemes (varṇas) possess meaning, it follows that they would undergo the grammatical operations prescribed for meaningful units. What is meant by this is: while there is no fault in their having meaning in actual usage, in the technical treatise (śāstra), however, nothing is lost. This thought might occur: "The technical designation (saṃjñā) does not cause a fault. To this he says: because the designation is for the sake of grammatical operation (kārthatvāt), the suffixes beginning with *su* (svādi) would arise; yet, since they are not heard [in the case of a compound], the suffixes (*svādi*) are not applied, and there must be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

But if meaningful aggregates are for the sake of restriction, then a sentence that possesses meaning would not receive the designation of a *prātipadika*. This is not a fault. The designation of *prātipadika* applies to the letters and their aggregate at one and the same time; thus, there is no state of being an aggregate of inflected words (*subanta*). Their meaning is unity. Alternatively, they arise without distinction, and once arisen, there is a restriction; thus, there is connection with case-endings (*vibhakti*).

But surely, the case ending arises from the whole (*samudāya*) and not from the parts (*avayava*), just as there is reduplication of the whole. True, this is so. However, the parts are intended to be separate words (*pṛthakpadatvena*).
