In that regard, if you think that when the whole is reduplicated, the parts are also reduplicated, then, since the whole possesses the status of a word (*padatva*), the parts likewise possess the status of a word; thus, the grammatical operation pertaining to a word (*padakārya*) certainly applies.

[4.1] "Because the aggregate has a single meaning, the absence of *sup* suffixes follows from the phoneme" (Vt. 13). Some explain: because the aggregate is a single entity, even if the meaning of the phonemes is thus [unified], universals (*jāti*) and so forth are not necessitated by that singularity. At the time of the operation [of grammar], regarding technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and metarules (*paribhāṣā*), there is the rule: "From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the dual and singular endings are used for two and one respectively" (P 1.4.22). How then can there be a case ending (*vibhakti*) for indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack singularity?
The statement that there is elision (*luk*) of *āp* and *sup* after an indeclinable is the indicator (*liṅga*) that case endings (*sub*) are produced [only after stems].

[4.2] Others explain as follows: Even though phonemes (*varṇa*) possess meaning, all that is understood from their mere conjunction is simply that "something" has been begun to be spoken, namely, a "thing" (*vastu*). However, the comprehension of the number of that thing arises only from the aggregate (*samudāya*). Therefore, the meaning of the aggregate is its oneness. (p. 34)

[4.3] Others describe it thus: this oneness is one and the same for both the phonemes and their collection (*samudāya*). In that regard, if the case-ending (*vibhakti*) arising from the collection were not capable [of expressing it], then a case-ending would arise to manifest a single oneness common to all; however, since it is indeed capable . . . just as many observers do not take up another lamp while performing their task with a single one.

[4.4] Here, however, the venerable ones say: the meaning is the oneness of the aggregate (*saṃghāta*). Just as a collection of vowels (*ekāc*) is not a single vowel even when accompanied by consonants, so too are its constituent parts. Furthermore, a case-ending (*vibhakti*) arising from the aggregate is able to touch upon the constituent parts through inference. But there is no designation of "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) for the parts. Why? Because the prescription of the designation "word" applies to that which possesses phonetic form (*śabdatva* / *śabdavattva*).

The designation of a "word" (*pada*) is prescribed for that which possesses sound (*śabdavat*), because the rules for suffixes (*sup*) and verbal endings (*tiṅ*) apply to it; just as the designation of a "base" (*aṅga*) applies to that which possesses sound. This inquiry—whether phonemes (*varṇa*) possess meaning or are meaningless—is like an examination of a crow’s teeth. Whether they possess meaning or are meaningless, there is no fault whatsoever.

[5.1] But the phonemes are meaningless, because no meaning is perceived for each individual phoneme (Vt. 14). Even through inference, their meaningfulness is not perceived. For no persisting meaning is observed for the phoneme *kṣa*, in the way that "existence" (*sattā*) persists in the case of [the words] *bhavati*, *bhavataḥ*, and *bhavantī*. Therefore, like the verse beginning with "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*), phonemes are meaningless according to both perception and inference. [The phrase] "for each phoneme" means...

Since the particle *prati* heard in the sentence functions as a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of indication (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, he asks: "What is this *prativarṇam*? The other shows the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) by means of reduplication: "with respect to each letter" (*varṇaṃ varṇaṃ prati*). And the distributive sense ceases in a compound because its meaning has already been expressed, as in the cases of *saptaparṇa* ("seven-leaved") and *aṣṭāpada* ("eight-footed").

[5.2] "And because meaning is observed despite changes in phonemes—such as transposition, elision, addition, and modification" (Vārttika 15). This reason does not establish the point that [phonemes] are meaningless. What then? This is a reason for the fallacy of the opponent's argument. Here, "transposition" refers to the fact that within a single established collection [of sounds], what was initial becomes final, and what was final becomes initial; it is a usage occurring through a change in temporal order. This inference is stated regarding the meaningfulness of other phonemes distinct from the initial phonemes of verbal roots such as *bhū* and so forth.

In this case, when there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇa-vyatyaya*), no transposition of meaning (*artha-vyatyaya*) is observed. Furthermore, if each phoneme were individually meaningful in relation to the others, then just as in the case of *ādyantau* and *antādī*, where the cognition differs according to the different usage of the initial and final elements, the same would occur here as well.

Now, if you think that the single meaning is fully present in each individual letter throughout all the phonemes—even so, there is a diversity of displacement (*vyatyaya*): in some cases, such as in the word *kūpa*, there is the comprehension of a different meaning; in others, such as in *tarku*, there is the comprehension of that very same meaning; and in others, there is indeed meaninglessness, as in *kākaḥ kakā*. Just as there is the disappearance (*apāya*) of the letter *va* and the comprehension of a different meaning, so too here in the case of *ghnantī* there is the disappearance of the letter *a*; yet, in that instance, there is no comprehension of a different meaning.

Therefore, there is no inference regarding meaningfulness in cases such as *lavitā* and *lavitum*. For it is observed that when a meaningful word is added, a corresponding meaning is also added, as in *datto* and *yajñadattaḥ*. And a word, proceeding by means of an inferred meaningfulness, either effects the imposition of a power—as in *aupagavaḥ*—or [functions otherwise]. But this is not the case with the Vedic tradition (*āgama*). Therefore, how can there be meaningfulness for a phoneme (*varṇa*)? As in the case of a modification (*vikāra*), which is similar to [the addition of] broth and so on, here too some phoneme departs and another arises, yet there is no comprehension of a different meaning.

[6] Both of these have been stated regarding phonemes (*varṇa*). This is what he asks: Is this to be understood from the fact that verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth possess meaning—that all [phonemes] are meaningful, and their non-perception is due to some cause? Or rather, because they are meaningless in some instances, are they meaningless everywhere, such that this [perception of meaning] regarding roots and so forth is an illusion, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*)? He says: "Both."

This demonstrates the following: the perception and non-perception of an object should be understood as having distinct objects. Where a conventional efficacy of an object is possible through inference, there it should be postulated. And it is observed that, with respect to an identical object, one person possesses a connection to that object while another does not; regarding this, he says: "among those striving for the same [goal]. These are indeed different aggregates; this is a statement of the actual reality.

For wherever there is a meaningfulness established through inference, it is observed that when a recurring word is possible, there is for the most part a conformity to the meaning (*arthānugama*); only some particularity, however, is caused by the variation of the suffix. For instance, in *paktiḥ*, *pacanam*, and *pākaḥ*, the distinction of gender alone is produced by the suffix. Likewise, here, despite the recurrence of the word-element *ūpa*, no conformity of meaning is observed.

Therefore, this should not be accepted: that when the word *ūpa* is established, there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*). Furthermore, as for what was stated by you—"this indeed [is the case]"—the following is demonstrated: if it is not admitted that [the word *ūpa*] is a distinct aggregate, then meaninglessness follows all the more, because it would entail admitting the meaninglessness of many words. For this is the logical principle: that which is established as the word *ūpa* must express its own specific meaning.

"If he does not say this, then you have admitted futility. Regarding the argument "because the aggregate possesses meaning," he will state the following rebuttal: "For it is observed that even by means of a quality that does not possess that [same] purpose, the possessor of the quality has purposefulness, as in the case of a beautiful chariot or the parts of a chariot.

[Question: How is it that the *anubandhas* of the *pratyāhāras* are not included when there is a mention of the letter *a*? [Answer: For these too are situated here and have been recited; they are indeed present. Furthermore, the letter *ha* has been taught more than once for the sake of grammatical operations (*kārya*). In the same way, these others too would have to be taught many times for the sake of grammatical operations.

[This is] from usage (*ācāra*). Activity is based on conventional usage (*upacāra-nimitta*). Thus the teachers have proceeded [in this way], in that they did not apply the grammatical operations (*akāryāṇi*) to these [words]. Regarding [the rule] *tṛṣimṛṣikṛṣeḥ...* (P 1.2.25), just as an exceptional formation (*nipātana*) sublates the general application of *ṇatva* [as in] *sarvanāmāni* (P 1.1.27), so too, even though there is the inclusion [of the word *sarva*], the exceptional formation sublates the substitution of *yaṇ* for vowels when followed by consonants (*halṣu*). This is one interpretation.

Alternatively, it is determined from usage that this instruction concerns those who are not *prajaka* (i.e., not the motivators) among those situated here; for in this context, only the vowels beginning with *a* are the *prajakas*, according to the rule "the first [element] together with the last [marker] denotes its class" (Pāṇini 1.1.71), and not these [consonants]. (p. 36)

[2.2] "Because of its non-primacy" (*aprādhānyāt*), as stated in the verse. By this, the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) is explained. A subordinate element is employed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the principal; it cannot be enumerated as if it were on an equal footing. This is because, while connection with the ritual action (*kāryayogitva*) is understood for the principal, there is no such connection with the action for the suffixes (*anubandha*) that have been employed as qualifiers.

In that regard, just as two reasons were stated for why *prakṛti* and the others do not receive the designation of *pratyaya*—whereby by the first it is shown that they are not the cause, because "the purpose of a cause is to serve as the basis for an effect" (P 3.1.1, vt. 2), and by the second there is the occurrence of a relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), because "an operation is understood to apply to the principal" (P 3.1.1, vt. 3)—so too here, due to the fact that the *anubandhas* are not the cause and are subordinate, there is no inclusion [of them]. Why is this so?

The intention is this: just as the recitation of the *garga* and *bidā* groups serves both purposes, so too this recitation of the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) would serve both its own purpose and the purpose of others. He sets aside this [objection] by means of the practice of the Teacher himself. Just as people in the world proceed—eating together with Brāhmaṇas among those of the same class who are Brāhmaṇas, and with Kṣatriyas among those of the same class who are Kṣatriyas—so too here, this very same method is observed. *Śailī* means that which exists in *śīla*; it is an activity preceded by a settled convention.

[2.3] And elision (*lopa*) is more powerful (*balavattara*). If the derivation were not accepted, you should understand from this very point that there is no apprehension [of the elided element]. In the *pratyāhāra* "aj," only the *anubandha* is apprehended; for according to "the first [letter] with the last [includes those in between]" (P 1.1.71), the designation "it" (*it*) was applied to something non-existent (*asan*), and it is understood that what is non-existent itself does not operate within grammatical operations. For it has been said: "Elision (*lopa*) is indeed a non-entity (*abhāva*) whose purpose is the accomplishment of an operation, and which serves no other purpose" (P 1.3.9, vārttika). Therefore, how can there be an apprehension of that which is non-existent? Thus [it is argued].

[2.4] Or rather, the rule *ūkālo ’j* (P 1.2.27) is a *yoga-vibhāga* (a splitting of the rule). Since it is already established by the rule *ādir antyena* (P 1.1.72) that vowels (*ac*) consist of those sounds delimited by time (*kāla*), this *yoga-vibhāga* is performed for the purpose of establishing the vowel-status (*actva*) of those sounds delimited by time. Just as when a preceding and following element are employed together, the designations of "verb prefix" (*upasarga*) and "path-verb" (*gati*) would otherwise apply, but they are restricted; in the view that these are restrictions on technical designations (*saṃjñā-niyamana-pakṣa*), the designation of "path-verb" and "prefix" would apply to those being employed before the verbal root, according to the rule *te prāg dhātoḥ* (P 1.4.80).

The point here is that there is no "occurrence at an improper time" (*ukālatva*) for those sounds consisting of half a *mātrā*. Even so, the word *kukkuṭaḥ* would still result [as an unintended application]. But how can this [sound], whether explicitly recited or not, be included within the *pratyāhāra*? The intention is that it is because of the grasping of the general form (*ākṛti*). The general form has been taught; sometimes it depends on half a *mātrā*, sometimes on a full *mātrā*; sometimes it is manifested by one consonant (*hal*), sometimes by two.
And in this case, the rule for inclusion (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), namely *aṇudit savarṇasya ca* (P 1.1.69), is rejected.

[2.4.1] This one says: Let the rule (yoga) remain only as far as that which precedes the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) and so forth; that is, let the rule remain as far as the verbal form *hrasvadīrghaplutaḥ* (P 1.2.27), prior to this point. How much is that? It is from *ūkālo ’j...* (P 1.2.27). This is explained here: "This is a reference to individual instances (*vyakti*). And there is this [rule]: *aṇudit*. (P 1.1.69)

And in the case of *pratyāhāra*, the property of having the duration of *ū* is relied upon, because that which has the duration of *ū* (*ūkāla*) is included within the *pratyāhāra* "aC" (as in the rule *ūkālo yaḥ so 'c*). This term "aC" is merely an illustration; even if it were true that [the vowels] are included in *pratyāhāras* such as "aC" or "aṆ," one must admit that they are indeed included therein. Therefore, since there is no designation as "aC" (or "aṆ") for the sounds beginning with *ṇ*, they lack the status of being *grāhaka* (designators). One should establish their reality, and thus the desired grammatical operation will follow. [VI]

Now, for what purpose [is it said] "of the semivowels"? This is what is being asked here: why is a *pratyāhāra* formed with the letter *ṇa* by the rule *aṇudit savarṇasya...* (P 1.1.69), in which the semivowels (*antasthā*) are also included, rather than a *pratyāhāra* being formed with the letter *ca*? For otherwise, if they were not recited here, the mentions of *iṇ* would exclude the semivowels; consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur in forms such as *gīrṣu* and *halṣu*.

But surely there is a distinction; one speaks having determined a distinction created by the *śruti*. This remains extremely doubtful for the Noble Ones (the Teachers). For they infer the continued application of the option (*vibhāṣā*) on the basis of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*); however, because those marks are inconclusive, the inference of them remains indeed doubtful. (Pāṇini 3.2.108) //6//

[1] Here, this letter *ṇ* is attached twice. In this context, six factors are proposed: proximity (*āsatti*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), capability (*sāmarthya*), established usage (*prasiddhi*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and lightness (*lāghava*). According to the principle of proximity (*āsatti*), it should belong to the preceding one; and because there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence, it would likewise belong to the preceding one. However, according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that it should be understood by the majority—it ought to belong to the subsequent one. Thus, depending on the specific instance to be characterized (*lakṣya*), a doubt arises as to whether it is proximity or pervasion that applies.
In that context, by the force of the two mentions of *aṇ* (in the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*), non-occurrence (*asatti*) is established and pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated.

Regarding the statement "of an *aṇ* that is not a *pragṛhya*," the author of the Bhāṣya himself cited the form *vṛkṣav karoti* in the eighth [chapter]. There, it is not known with what intention he said: "Final letters of words (*padānta*) cannot be *aṇ*s.
He gave the example *ajardhāḥ*, which is the form of the root *gṛdh* after *yaṅ*-luṅ, in the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *sip*; likewise, for the root *spṛdh*, he gave *apāspāḥ*.

He employs the mention of "dhātu" (root). It could be argued here that, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mention of *dhātu*, only the augment *mātrā* is produced, and not a relationship of substituendum and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*). However, this contradicts the fault [already pointed out] regarding forms such as *cikīrṣati*. In that case, it would not apply here either, in forms such as *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*. To this, it is objected: since the substitution of *rapara* is set aside by the mention of *dhātu*, is it not established that the *ittva* (substitution of *i*) occurs in *cikīrṣati*?

This is the intended meaning: by the mention of *dhātu*, the substitution of *ra* for the final vowel (*raparatva*) is excluded specifically for what is not a verbal root (*adhātu*), whereas for a verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution of *ra* would indeed occur. Consequently, because it is not at the end of a word (*anantyatvāt*), the rule [for *it*] would not apply. Alternatively, the mention of *dhātu* may serve this purpose: once the substitution of *ra* has been applied everywhere, since [the *ṛ*] is no longer at the end of a word, the substitution of *it* would not otherwise apply; therefore, the substitution of *it* occurs for the *ṛ* of a verbal root wherever it may be situated. [Objection: Let it not be so; it will apply to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) alone.

In that case, even here [in the word *mātṝṇām*], the rule would apply even without the mention of "root" (*dhātu*), because once *r* is substituted for the final vowel by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) no longer exists. Therefore, the mention of "root" must necessarily be made. Furthermore, as for the point raised in the commentary on the sūtra *uraṇ raparaḥ*—namely, that "the substitution of *r* for the final vowel applies to vowels such as the udātta"—that fault certainly remains when the subsequent [vowel] is included, as in forms such as *kṛtiḥ*. Thus, since the universal application is set aside by the force of the context, this established principle holds: the mention [of the vowel] is according to the preceding [rule].

Therefore, because of this established usage, he asks: "In that case, there is a doubt regarding the mention of *aṇ*—is it here [the mention of *aṇ*] based on established usage (*prasiddhi*), or is it based on pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Established usage is sublated by an indicative mark (*liṅga*). [The rule] "mention of *aṇ* applies to its homogeneous vowels" is an indicative mark. For this reason, in the rule *ur ṛt*, the addition of *ta* (in *ṛt*) is appropriate so that a one-mora vowel might occur in place of the vowel *ṛ* in *acīkṛtat*. [Objection: But surely it is a principle that "there is no inclusion by means of a vowel being in the process of being taught (*bhāvyamāna*). [Reply: True, this is so. However, there is indeed a possibility of inclusion that is warded off with effort. Therefore, in this instance, established usage is sublated by the indicative mark.

In that case, there is doubt regarding the inclusion of vowels (*iṇ-grahaṇa*). [And that becomes cumbersome. Here, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), there is pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus there is no lack of proximity (*āsatti*). Now, it might be argued that the time of a vowel (*ackāla*) is assigned to the time of a consonant (*vyañjanakāla*). In that regard, whatever is the time of a vowel is the same for the preceding consonants; this is the opinion of some (*ekīyamata*). For others, the time differs. Alternatively, pronouncing with difficulty is cumbersomeness (*gaurava*), while pronouncing with ease is parsimony (*lāghava*).

This is a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*): even if the listener does not understand that meaning, the teacher’s lack of capacity to express a specific meaning is not observed, even if [the expression is] concise. Therefore, the Teacher employs this; for from the commentary, the specific distinction is understood. *ña ma ṅa ṇa na m*; *jha bha ñ*. 7.8.

[1] For what purpose are these two? Because there would be heaviness due to the operation of the place (*sthāna*) and substance (*dravya*), as well as the destruction of the *karaṇa*, he asks this. Even so, there are five augments (*āgama*): *ṅ, ṇ, n, j, bh*. There are three augmenters (*āgamin*): *ṅ, ṇ, n*. Therefore, for each one, there would be five [augments]. Let it be so for those augments that have augmenters; however, in this system, the inclusion and exclusion [of rules] are bound to the *śāstra*.

In that regard, the traditional teachings (*āgama*) concerning the numerical order obtained from the treatise (*śāstra*) are understood independently of formal application (*prayoga*); they function at the time of application as they are individually distinguished according to their respective domains. Since the two sounds *jha* and *bha* do not exist there, they do not function. Furthermore, because there is no injunction (*codanā*), they do not function again among the *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *na* sounds. (It should be understood that nine sūtras have been omitted, as they are largely explained by this very commentary.)

[2] Now, what is this "syllable" (akṣara)? For some, a phoneme (varṇa) is the syllable; for others, it is a word (pada) or a sentence (vākya). And this has been stated: "He who [knows] this by its vowels and by its syllables... and so forth.

"One should know that the *akṣara* is not perishable" (*Ślokavārttika*). It is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*), like "cook" (*pācaka*). Because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*) and does not decay (*na kṣīyate*), it is called *akṣara*. The expression "it does not perish" is not well-known [in this specific sense]; therefore, he explains the well-known meaning in this context by saying "it does not decay. Just as "moment" (*kṣaṇaḥ*) is derived from the root *kṣaṇoti*: "time wears away" (*prakṣṇutaḥ kālo bhavati*). The root *kṣaṇoti* has the sense of the action of decaying (*kṣayatikarma*).

Or, according to the *Ślokavārttika*: "The syllable (*akṣara*) is so called because it is reached (*aśnote*). Because it reaches its meaning, or because it pervades the meaning, or because it is pervaded by the meaning, it is therefore called a syllable. And that [syllable] is either a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*).
Regarding the phoneme (*varṇa*), they spoke [of it] in the previous *sūtra*; now, however, this is called a "name" (*nāmadheya*). For thus it is recited by another: "Phonemes are syllables."

For what purpose is it taught? (*Ślokavārttika*) It is certainly not for the sake of establishing the correctness (*sādhutva*) of individual phonemes (*varṇa*). Of what, then? Of the aggregate (*samudāya*), because that is employed for the sake of meaning.

Or rather, the cognition of phonemes is the object of speech (*vāgviṣaya*). That by which phonemes are cognized is "the cognition of phonemes. What, then, is that? It is the treatise (*śāstra*). That is the object of speech; for in the treatise, speech is fixed (*viṣīyate*) or bound (*avabadhyate*).

And where Brahman exists (Ślokavārttika)—that is, where the Veda exists as Brahman. And where does it exist? In the *pada*. The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise (*śāstra*) is that phoneme (*varṇa*). This is what he says: "and of worldly words. For that purpose (Ślokavārttika): by the word "that" (*tat*), the knowledge of phonemes is connected [to the purpose]. Phonemes are taught for the sake of the operation of the treatise. This is exactly what was stated by the author of the *Vākya* [Kātyāyana]: "The instruction is for the sake of the application and the collection" (Paspaśā, Vt. 15); the author of the Ślokavārttika has also said the very same thing.
"For the sake of easy comprehension" (*iṣṭabuddhyartham*) [Ślokavārttika]; "those from whom the *kalā*s and so forth have ceased" (*nivṛttakalādikān*);

and "it is taught for the sake of brevity" (*laghvarthaṃ copadiśyate*) [Ślokavārttika]. By this, he demonstrates the connection with the *anubandhas*, in accordance with the statement: "And it is for the purpose of establishing the *anubandhas*" (*anubandhakaraṇārthaś ca*) [Paspaśā, Vārttika 16].

This very collection of syllables is the collection of speech. This much is the speech that has been handed down; this much is the linguistic usage. It is both flowering and fruiting, through the visible and invisible fruits of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). It is adorned like the moon and the stars. What is meant by this is as follows: just as these things such as the moon and the stars are unbroken [in their continuity], even so there is no creator whatsoever for this linguistic usage.

In this very way, this is remembered as being remembered through tradition: "the mass of Brahman" (*brahmarāśi*). Just as the mass of Brahman, with its sequence withdrawn, is established within each individual, so too can this withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) be described. It is accumulated by Brahman like the Brahman of consciousness (*vijñāna-brahman*). Upon knowing it, one obtains the fruit of the merit of all the Vedas; that is, one obtains whatever fruit results from the merit of having studied all the Vedas.

"And his parents"—even when they have died, study must not be abandoned, for the sake of attaining the desired fruit for them; or even while they are alive; for when they are about to die, one is further encouraged toward study by thinking, "Then [the merit] will go to heaven. Thus ends the second lesson of the first chapter in the *Śrīmahābhāṣyadīpikā* composed by the venerable Mahopādhyāya Bhartṛhari. The *pratyāhāras* are completed.
In the *Mahābhāṣyadīpikā*, the third daily lesson (*āhnika*):
[1] Since these have been largely explained by the preceding commentary itself, it should be understood that nine sūtras have been omitted.

[2] In some cases... however, because its own form (*svarūpa*) is present everywhere, it is not [explicitly] resorted to. For instance, this rule ‘diva aut’ (Pā. 7.1.84) is an injunction by means of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), whereas this vowel *au* is enjoined by its own form.

[3] The mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the present context continues. This would be established by the word *ikaḥ* alone, meaning "the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions occur in place of *ik*. Since this is already established, the explicit mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in the sūtra is for the purpose of indicating the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the word as it has been relied upon. However, this [sūtra] conveys this meaning through two mentions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, although it would be established even with one. The mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the present context continues; indeed, in every part of grammar, a statement of the subject matter (*grahaṇaka-vākya*) is uttered.

However, that [rule] does not itself establish the operation; rather, another sentence (*vākya*) which brings about that operation, being inherent in what is indicated (*lakṣya*), emerges—just as in the cases of *kartari* (Pā. 3.4.67), *paśau* (Pā. 3.2.25), and *kartror hastisūcakayoḥ* (Pā. 3.2.13 Vārttika). Thus, from both the inferred mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* and the directly heard [mention], we understand a distinct sentence: "In place of *ik*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [occur]. That is to say: those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which are associated with [the conditions for] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur in place of *ik*.

[4] If that [designation] were to follow [the rule], then the designation *vṛddhi* would also apply to *a*, *e*, and *o*, because the governing context (*adhikāra*) is present with every individual rule. But is it not the case that the word *vṛddhi* is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), and here it presents itself as referring to the items *ā*, *ai*, and *au*; therefore, the designation *guṇa* would necessarily apply only to *a*, *e*, and *o*? This is the intended meaning.

When a designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied to specific locations (*pradeśa*), because it has already been connected with another designation, it is understood as being merely a word; thus, even though the term *vṛddhi* is what is being inferred, it is inferred as being of such a nature. This is why it was stated that the designation *vṛddhi* would apply to the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o*. [5] It will follow the connection. What is this "following the connection" (*saṃbandhānuvṛtti*)? It is said: Just as subsequent rules (*anudeśa*), having obtained their respective correspondences (*yathāsaṃkhya*), cease to apply at the time of usage due to their absence—just as in the case of *ig yaṇaḥ* (Pā. 1.1.45)—[so too does this designation].

Thus, because of the connection with the *svarita* accent, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) is inferred; subsequently, realizing that *āt*, *aic*, and so forth are also present here, one understands that the recurrence of *āt-aij* serves this very purpose, thereby perceiving the absence of a connection [with the preceding rule], and through the connection with the *liṅga* (indicatory mark), perceives the connection with what follows.

[6] Alternatively, the "frog's gait" (*maṇḍūkagati*) refers to the manner of skipping over intervening topics. Having now left behind the vowels *ai* and *au*, only the word *vṛddhi* itself continues to apply. Just as frogs seeking water, without exhausting their energy, undertake such an action that they remain suspended in mid-air due to their weight yet nonetheless reach a single desired destination, so too it is with words regarding their meaning: one infers [the application of a term] precisely where its meaningfulness is intended. This is the similarity to the frog's gait.

[7] Or rather, a single application (*ekayoga*) will be made. Singleness of application arises from the application of separate actions; thus, the verb *bhavati* is supplied once in the utterance: “*vṛddhir ādaij*, *adeṅ guṇa*. Even though the verb *bhavati* is distinct at the time of comprehension, it is indeed a single time of comprehension. There is no such time at which the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would be devoid of the designation *vṛddhi*, or the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* would be devoid of the designation *guṇa*.

[8] Or rather, it is because of another statement and because of the non-application of the suffix *ka*. What is the distinction here between these two—the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*)? First, the distinction is that the relationship of general and particular exists between the general rule and the exception, as in the cases of “*karmaṇi...* (Pā. 3.2.1)” and “*āto ’nupasarge kaḥ* (Pā. 3.2.3). When there is the injunction “*dhātoḥ* (Pā. 3.1.91),” the inclusion of those ending in long *ā* is present; thus, there is a general application (*sāmānya*) among those ending in long *ā*. However, for other verbal roots (*dhātu*), their inclusion is restricted to those specifically ending in long *ā*; this is the distinction.

Thus, here in the rule "vṛddhir ādaij," there is no inclusion of *adeṅ* (the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o*), nor does the rule "adeṅ guṇaḥ" apply to *ādaic* (the diphthongs *āi* and *āu*). Now, what is the commonality? It is the state of being doubtful or not doubtful. Just as when a general injunction (*utsarga*) is subject to doubt, a non-doubtful particular (*viśeṣa*) applies, so too is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of "vṛddhir ādaij. Is this recurrence intended for subsequent purposes and thus required here by necessity, or is it intended for the purpose of this very rule as well? However, the rule "adeṅ guṇaḥ" is one whose purpose has not yet been fulfilled and which is not subject to doubt; this is the commonality.

Here an objection is raised: Just as the designation "suffix" (*pratyaya*), even while being subject to doubt, achieves its purpose regarding *san* and the others despite the possibility of its application to other [categories], yet it is combined with the designations *kṛt*, *kṛtya*, *taddhita*, and *tadrāja* which do not achieve their purpose [there] because they are not subject to doubt—why does such a combination not occur here as well? To this it is replied: Since the purpose of the designation "suffix" is the comprehension of the named element (*saṃjñin*), that comprehension occurs, but it will not assist in any operation at the place of application (*pradeśa*).

Because they occur at different times and because there is no contradiction, [the general term] is combined with specific designations. However, here, from the instruction "vṛddhir ādaij," this is understood: by means of this connection, having internalized the designata, this is the designation of the technical name (*saṃjñā*). And this is made clear by the application of the mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*); for, due to the association with the word *vṛddhi* as it occurs in the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī," some assistance will be rendered in the subsequent rules (*pradeśa*).

In this context, with respect to the rule *adeṅ guṇaḥ*, no operation (*vyāpāra*) that has been introduced there is being followed. Whether it be the operation of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) or the operation of the thing named (*saṃjñin*), its very status as a technical term is itself being doubted; thus, while the connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is beyond doubt, the status of the word *guṇa* in the rule *adeṅ guṇaḥ* as a technical term is not doubted. Therefore, it is rightly said that "the exception (*apavāda*) is of the same level as the original rule (*prakṛti*)," since it is not proper for an operation whose technical-term status is doubtful to be on equal footing with an operation whose technical-term status is not doubted.

Alternatively, he will say this: by this, he demonstrates that the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkagati) movement, though logically established, has also been set forth by the grammatical rule (*vyākaraṇa*). In that regard, even when there is no purpose for what has been carried over (*anuvṛtta*), the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) indicates a lack of connection; thus, by this, it follows that one should join [the rule] only where there is a need. However, in the intervening space, it is like returning to the base village while traveling to another village.

[10] Or rather, we shall rely on both when they have ceased. Is it not the case that here one must exist, for there is either a positive injunction or a prohibition regarding what follows immediately? For where both are explicitly stated, both are inferred; where only one is stated, there is an inference of the other. True, this is so. However, regarding that which is depended upon, the cognition of the one who depends is twofold: by way of distinction and by way of non-distinction.

First, by way of non-distinction: "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra"—this is [an example] of non-distinction (*abheda*). When one considers them with distinction (*bheda*), then there must be what follows immediately (*anantara*). But when one considers the aggregate (*samudāya*), then the aggregate itself is what follows immediately; thus, depending on the specific instance (*lakṣya*), this [term] sometimes depends upon something [else].

[11a] But is this a remainder (*śeṣa*) that includes everything except the final [element], or is it an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning the non-final? "Remainder" (*śeṣa*), "part" (*avayava*), and "portion" (*ekadeśa*) are synonyms. An "exception" (*apavāda*) is that which sets aside [the general rule]. He himself establishes both [possibilities]: because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), it is a remainder; because they form distinct syntactical units (*nānāvākyatva*), it is an exception. However, it has not been stated at all how that [status of] being a single syntactical unit or distinct syntactical units [is established].

And how could these two constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), given that they are heard at different times and are separated by numerous other connections? (2) Furthermore, since a multiple-sentence structure (*nānāvākya*) cannot exist when the condition for a single-sentence structure is present, and a single-sentence structure cannot exist when the condition for a multiple-sentence structure is present, a doubt is untenable. Moreover, it is impossible for both a multiple-sentence structure and a single-sentence structure to coexist within one and the same [text].

(3) For what reason have only these two—contradiction (*bādha*) and the relationship between part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—been presented here, and not also option (*vikalpa*) and combination (*samuccaya*)? (4) Likewise, it has been stated that here "separateness of sentences" (*nānāvākyatva*) is the cause of contradiction, whereas elsewhere it is the cause of co-occurrence (*samāveśa*), as in: "In that case, there is a prohibition of the suffix *khyun* and others because of the separateness of sentences" (Pā. 3.4.67 Vārttika 2). All of this must be explained.

[11ā] (1) As for what was said: "How can there be a connection between two things that are separated?"—proximity (*ānantarya*) is not the cause of connection. For it is said: "For those words that are semantically incapable [of connecting], proximity is no cause. For example: "O noble lady, did you see the water-carrier running away while carrying a jar on her head? Even though these words are arranged in immediate succession, they provide no assistance toward that action. Why? Because it is impossible.

"There is no carrying of a water-jar by the head of an ox," and "the running of a jar"—based on these [sentences], another sentence, which is the object of the intellect of the perceiver, arises in a different sequence. Just as one who is muttering prayers (*upāṃśu*) understands the meaning based on those [sounds], some think that by this means one understands the meaning itself, even though it is non-linguistic (*aśabdaka*).

Likewise, in grammar as well, the relationship is characterized by meaning rather than being produced by immediate sequence, as in the rules "the plural [suffix] is used for many" (Pā. 1.4.21) and "[suffixes are added] after a nominal stem ending in ṅī, āp, or prātipadika" (Pā. 4.1.1). However, this [latter rule] teaches the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ) as occurring in a different location [from the nominal stem]. Similarly here too, the meaning of "rājñaḥ ka ca" (Pā. 4.2.140) and so forth would constitute a separate teaching of the meaning.

(2) Furthermore, if there were a relationship based on meaning (*arthalakṣaṇa*) with respect to some object, then in that object where these two [rules]—each prompted by its own cause—meet, both [possibilities], namely the status of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) and sublation (*bādhā*), are possible; hence the doubt. However, where only one is possible, there the application belongs to that one alone, as in the injunction regarding the agent and the animal (*kartṛpaśucodanā*): [the rule] *kartari...* (Pā. 3.4.67) requires a substratum (*āśraya*) because [the suffix] possesses capacity (*śaktimattva*).

Because it conforms to the substance and its cause, that *paratantra* [suffix] necessarily depends on a second factor, since the word *paśau* (in the case of "an animal") denotes a substance (*dravya*) by means of the nominal stem. It cannot be assumed that the suffix *ñya*, arising from a verbal root (*dhātu*) which expresses an action, can function as a *sādhana* [kāraka], such that the suffix would apply to the bare animal or to one endowed with qualities such as being the object (*karman*). Why? Because the [specific] *kārakas* such as the object have not been enjoined.

Therefore, because these two have an absolute requirement for mutual assistance as benefactors, a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) regarding this subject is inferred, such that [the rule] "it occurs when *paśu* is the agent" applies. Thus, when the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* meet upon a single referent, since each one expresses this same meaning, the specifically prescribed [rule] subverts the general domain; thus, the requirement exists precisely by way of sublation. But here, in the case of "guṇa and vṛddhi occur for the *aṅga*," there is a genitive relation between the *aṅga* and the guṇa-vṛddhi.

In relation to the sixth [case], the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pā. 1.1.52) does not apply; however, in relation to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the rule *ikaḥ* (Pā. 1.1.3) does apply. Thus, in this case of the convergence upon a single domain, if this explicit mention (*śruti*) of "of the *aṅga*" operates with respect to other vowels (*al*), there is indeed no form of it other than the aggregate of its parts. For this very thing is the form of that *aṅga*. It is just as in the cases of *ruhaḥ paḥ* (Pā. 4.3.43) and *rājñaḥ ka ca* (Pā. 4.2.140).

This is what is meant: [the substitution applies] to the *ik* of *ruha* and to the *n* of *rājan*. In that context, when the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is restricted to the final phoneme (*al*), the word *ikaḥ* becomes a qualifier of this [stem]. Thus, this remains as a subordinate element (*taccheṣa*) by way of being a qualifier of the final phoneme. When the collective term *aṅgasya* is restricted to the final phoneme, the rule for "that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*)—which was applicable to the *ik*—is joined with the restriction, resulting in: "of a stem ending in an *ik*, [there is a substitution] of the final phoneme."

Even so, by virtue of being the qualified element (*viśeṣya*) in the rule "there is *guṇa* for a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *ik*," the principle "of the final letter" (*alontya*) would apply as a supplement. However, if this "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) in the rules prescribing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is not a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), but rather "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) is the genitive of locus and "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is its qualifier—just as in the rule "for the penultimate [vowel] of *guh*, there is *ūṭ*" (Pā. 6.4.89)—then the principle "of the final letter" would absolutely fail to apply in the domain of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; thus, it is understood that this [principle] is sublated.

And this very sublation is what is meant by "non-attainment. In that case, if one assumes it to be a supplement to that [rule], there is a primary remoteness from the principal element; for the verbal cognition and the conceptual understanding of the word "vidhinoktam" (stated by the injunction) would be sublated, as they would apply only to the quality of the subordinate member (*aṅga*). However, in the alternative view of an exception (*apavāda*), the quality belongs to the *ik* vowel, while the primary remoteness applies to the subordinate member.

(3) Why is conjunction (*samuccaya*) not proposed? Because it is impossible. Here, conjunction is observed among things that have a non-different purpose when they share a single action, as in: "Feed Devadatta with soup, salt, and ghee. In this case, the soup and so forth—which have a non-different purpose through their functions of sprinkling, flavoring, and lubricating—are conjoined in the act of eating. Likewise, here, the *aṅg* suffix and the *ik* suffix cannot be conjoined for the sake of the *guṇa* [vowel substitution].

For when a particular grammatical element (*aṅga*) has been reached and a specific quality (*guṇa*) is applied to it, that [element] must then be qualified by the other genitive case, namely the *viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*. Even in this way, there is no conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the form of a single operation. Rather, optionality (*vikalpa*) operates because when things are mutually exclusive and share a single function, the task is accomplished by one or the other—just as in the command, "Feed Devadatta in the palace, in the house, on a bronze plate, or on silverware," he is fed either in the house or in the palace. Likewise here, it occurs either for the *aṅga* or for the *ik*, and they do not operate simultaneously, because a single genitive case can only be connected to one operation at a time.

(4a) Now, if there is a plurality of sentences, what is the resolution of the contradiction? It is said: In this case, regarding the statement, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya," some maintain that it is indeed a single sentence because a single verb is heard. For there is but one act of giving (*dadāti*), even though it has different objects and different recipients.

Just as the act of eating (*bhuj*) involves multiple instruments, so too—even when the verb *bhuj* is used many times—there is indeed a single sentence, as in: "Feed Devadatta for a month; feed him with curd; feed him with vegetables. Yet here, you say that these are two sentences: one sentence is "Let curd be given to the Brahmins," and the second is "Buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"; however, the verbal action (*kriyāpada*) is not employed because its meaning is already understood.

In that case, there are indeed two acts of giving: one has curd (*dadhi*) as its object and the other has buttermilk (*takra*) as its object. Why, then, does this not constitute a single collective act in common usage? It is impossible to say. Why? Because it is never observed. Even by those who have not mastered the technical treatises, it is said: "Curd should not be given to him. Now, if a logical justification must necessarily be stated, this is the justification: for those for whom these are two distinct sentences, one action sublates the other.

The act of giving curd is sublated by the act of giving buttermilk. Although Kauṇḍinya is included within the category of "brāhmaṇa" in the Vedic revelation (*brāhmaṇa-śruti*), he is nevertheless not mentioned specifically in his individual form as Kauṇḍinya; rather, he is mentioned in a general sense. Furthermore, the fruit of the gift accrues to the giver because it was given to a brāhmaṇa. However, the gift of buttermilk specifically mentioned as being "for Kauṇḍinya" is heard as a particular instance. Moreover, the gift of curd can occur even without Kauṇḍinya, but the gift of buttermilk cannot.

Therefore, where an action is enjoined in a general form and is thus subject to doubt, and where it is enjoined in a specific form and is thus free from doubt, one does not effect a combination (*samuccaya*) of those two actions. For how can inference be made equal in status to perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of its sublation? Consequently, there is neither a combination nor an option (*vikalpa*) between perception and inference.

According to others, there is an inference here of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), and its indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the phrase "the buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya. This very point is introduced at the very beginning here: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas," [which] excludes Kauṇḍinya.

Others think as follows: the word "brāhmaṇa" has many [referents]. Among them, some have Kauṇḍinya excluded, some have Māṭhara excluded, some have Māṭhara included, and some have Kauṇḍinya included. In this regard, this word "brāhmaṇa" applies to others from whom Kauṇḍinya has been removed even without the inference of a supplementary sentence; thus, the cognizer understands from the expression "buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya" that it refers to those others.

If it is asked, "Whence is this?"—it is because one who is instructing others instructs in this manner; therefore, this [thought] occurs to him: "Just as I instruct others, so have I been instructed by him. In this view, Kauṇḍinya was not instructed in his form as a Brāhmaṇa regarding the gift of curds. For those for whom that is a single sentence, the curds exclude the *tarka* (sour gruel) which serves as an alternative means of accomplishment. Why? Because while the curds are being considered doubtful, the *tarka* is directly specified by the word "sour gruel" (*takram*).

(4ā) Furthermore, one understands the inclusion [of a suffix] in cases such as *khyun* and others due to a difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*). Just as, due to a difference in context, [the suffix] does not sublate the [suffixes] prescribed for offspring (*apatya*), nor are they exceptions (*apavāda*) to those prescribed by their respective governing rules (*adhikāra*), in exactly the same way, the suffix *kta* [sublates] the suffix *laṭ* prescribed for the present tense, but not that characterized by the past tense; likewise, it sublates the characteristic of the locus (*adhikaraṇika*) in the case of offspring, as in *pācchaveyāma*.

Thus, because the contexts are distinct, it has been established that by the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the suffix *khyun* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) in another context; yet, because it is a *kṛt* suffix, it would also apply to the agent (*kartari*), while its form suggests the instrument (*karaṇe*). Thus, a conflict is perceived. To this, the resolution is stated: just as when the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* coincide in a single meaning, the specific (*viśeṣavān*) sublates the general (*sāmānyavān*), so too here, in the single word *khyun*, two meanings coincide—the instrument and the agent.

In that regard, by relying on the form *khyun*, one understands the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas by relying on the state of being a *kṛt* suffix, one understands the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); thus, a specific scriptural statement (*viśiṣṭa-śruti*) sublates the meaning of a general scriptural statement (*sāmānya-śruti*). Likewise, within this word *laṭ*, the time dependent upon a specific accompanying word (*upapada*) sublates other times. Similarly, even in the case of the *kta* suffix, since it relies on a specific verbal root-form, the present time sublates that "state of having come to be" (*bhūtatā*) which is expressed by the term *niṣṭhā*.

Thus, in the case of *bāḍhaga*, the hearing of the word *vaḍavā*—which possesses a specific form like that of a bull (*vṛṣa*)—sublates the application of the suffix *yañ* by virtue of its connection with the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). Furthermore, the unexpressed word *ca* removes that very same scope [of application]. Or rather, another [meaning] is accepted even for a conventional term (*rūḍhi*); likewise, although they do not blink, the word *animiṣa* functions to denote fish (*matsya*).

But those who maintain that [the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*] is a single sentence have understood it thus: just as this is a single sentence, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," so too this is a single sentence: "The *kṛt* suffixes occur after a verb when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, and *khyun* occurs when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expressed. In that case, what is meant is this: "Other than *khyun*, [the *kṛt* suffixes] occur when the agent is expressed. But how is this to be understood here in the rules "There is elision (*luk*) of the case endings" (Pā. 2.4.71) and "There is no elision (*aluk*) when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)" (Pā. 6.3.1)?

In this case as well, there is this statement: "The *sup* suffix is elided (*luk*) except after the final member of a compound. Alternatively, the statement concerns different times; just as an instruction regarding location is given, so too does the suffix occur at a different time, just as Kauṇḍinya receives curds and buttermilk at different times. The resolution stated is that, by implication, they occur at the same time.

In all cases, non-attainment constitutes an invalidation (*bādhā*)—both in the case of direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and traditional law (*smṛti*). This very invalidation is seen, for example, in the rule: "The village cock is not to be eaten. For here, eating is not prompted by the word itself; rather, it is prompted by desire. That [eating], having become applicable, is thereby turned away. Furthermore, since grammar is a tradition (*smṛti*) based on words, in every instance where a specific term is present, non-attainment alone is inferred.

[12] "The term *ig* must be included in the rules for the *mid*-class roots and so forth. Because they do not end in *ig*, the term *ig* must be included in the rules for the *mid*-class roots and so forth; otherwise, due to their specific restriction (*upasaṃhāra*), the inclusion of *ig* would not apply to the stem. Therefore, the term *ig* must be included in the various specific rules (*pradeśa*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substitution would apply to the entire non-*ig*-ending stem. Thus, "the term *ig* must be included in the rules for the *mid*-class roots and so forth" is one fault. And this is another: in the cases of *yātā* and *vātā*, the *guṇa* substitution would result as a replacement for the whole stem.

He thinks as follows: because the condition (*nimitta*) "of a single [vowel]" (*ekah*) exists, there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*). That [restriction] operates when the condition is present. In that regard, just as there is a restriction once the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) has been determined, so too there must be a restriction when the state of having an *ik* vowel at the end (*igantatva*) is present. However, where the cause for restriction does not exist, the genitive remains unrestricted. This is also his view: by means of the term "of the member" (*aṅgasya*), he establishes the genitive with respect to all members without distinction.

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) established by [Pāṇini 1.1.49] *iko ’lontyasya* is restricted to those stems ending in an *ik* vowel; it does not apply to those ending in non-*ik* vowels, nor to those not ending in an *ik* vowel at all. However, in the case of *yātā* and others, there is indeed a genitive [in *aṅgasya*]. Therefore, since a guna substitute must occur as a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa), he says this: "For the genitive of the final letter (*alontya-ṣaṣṭhī*) has been transferred to the final *ik*, while [the genitive in] *aṅgasya* is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, that which is now the stem (*aṅga*) does not end in an *ik*."

Regarding the statement "of the *aṅga*," this very form [is understood] through the genitive case of the final vowel (*alo 'ntyasya*). And since that genitive "of the *aṅga*" resides only in the final *ik*, he says: "This is not a fault. Just as the genitive of the final vowel has been transferred to the final *ik*, what you said—that it effects modifications upon distinct *aṅgas*—is not so. This being the case, how could there be a genitive in forms like *yāta* which lack a final *ik*, and in its absence, how could there be a total replacement?"

And this *ca* is read here in the sense of *hi*; since the word *hi* signifies a reason (*hetu*), this [particle] should also be understood as having the sense of a reason. Because a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) would otherwise result, the mention of *ik* must be made in the rules concerning *mid* and so forth. Due to the statement "there is *guṇa* for *mid*" (*mider guṇa*), the substitution does not apply to the final letter, because there is no basis for such a restriction. Because of the rule stating "of the final" (*antyasya*), it does not apply to the *ik*. For if there were no restriction to the final letter, there would be no *ik* that is final in *mid*, yet *guṇa* is prescribed. That [guṇa] will occur by virtue of the explicit statement.

What is the purpose of the term "of the *aṅga*"? He says: no; it is "of *midi*. In that case, although the genitive "of the *aṅga*" does not occur in rules such as those for *vāta* and so on, here it does occur in "of *midi*"; and since this [genitive] is not included [in the aforementioned cases], it would result in the replacement of the whole (*sarvādeśa*). If it is argued that [the rule applies] to "merely *ik*," the word "merely" (*mātra*) signifies "entirety. Consequently, there would have to be a single [substitute] for the whole—whether it concerns the final or non-final [element]—by means of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Because "of the *aṅga*" functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and "of *ik*" is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply to "of the *aṅga*."

[Objection: "Since that which is known to exist in its proper place is then withdrawn (*upasaṃhriyate*), there is no application of the withdrawal to the domain of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* due to the absence of a cause; thus, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would apply to an *ik* in every state, and a prohibition must be stated for the case of what is followed by an *an* (long vowel), as in *agnicit*. [Reply: These examples are not possible. Why? Because by these injunctions regarding short vowels and so forth, the *aṅga* (stem) is qualified; thus, the rule "there is *guṇa* of an *aṅga* ending in a short vowel" is logically correct in cases such as *he buddhe* and *budhāḥ*.

The remaining examples, such as *duhitari*, *śuddhaye*, and *śucavya*, are to be adopted for the sake of clarity, not examples such as *agnicit* and so forth. This is not a fault; it is established that the genitive case in the word *aṅgasya* is not intended to apply to the grammatical operation (*kārya*) under the view that [the genitive] is a restrictive exception (*apavāda*). In that context, since the prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) is subordinate, how could it be qualified by injunctions regarding short vowels and so on? Rather, it is the *ik* vowel itself that is qualified, because it alone is connected to the grammatical operation.

And since that [substitution] is not possible in its literal sense for a short vowel, the connection is as follows: "The guṇa substitute occurs for that *ig* which is a short vowel belonging to the *aṅga*. Alternatively, because it is being prescribed, the guṇa is the primary element; and because they serve that purpose, both the *ik* and the *aṅga* are subordinate (*guṇa*) elements.

In that context, since the perception of short vowels and so forth is not possible in the primary element (*pradhāna*), when it is understood to apply to its subordinate member (*aṅga*), it is logical that it qualifies that which is proximate as the subordinate member—namely, the *iK*—and not the remote subordinate member which is the *guṇa*. For this reason as well, these [rules] alone are applicable. This is merely an illustration; here too, a prohibition regarding non-final vowels must be stated, as in Pāṇini 7.2.115: *aco ñṇiti*. In this case as well, it should be understood that the vowel of the subordinate member (*aṅga*) is intended, regardless of where it occurs.

In cases such as *daridrāyaka*, a *vṛddhi* substitution would apply to the non-final vowel. But surely, since [the rule] "guṇa and so forth" (*or guṇādiṣu*) specifies a particular locus, this paribhāṣā has no application here? True; that is so. However, it is said with this in mind: you have not determined that there is indeed an application to a non-final [vowel]. Since "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is a general term and "of the single [substitute]" (*iko*) is a specific term—and among specific terms—then here too, "of the *aṅga*" ought to be a general qualifier for the specific terms such as the short vowels (*hrasva*) and so on.

Consequently, there is no contingency of infinite regress (*anantyaprasaṅga*). This being so, it is also appropriate that what will be stated later—that "this [rule] does not apply when characterized by *ik*"—is valid, according to the statement: *“taddhitakāmyor iglakṣaṇāt”* (Pā. 1.1.5 Vārttika 4). Others explain: here, the operation of *ik* is relied upon; namely, "there is guna for the *ik* of the base (*aṅga*). Is it for all [instances]? No. What then? It is "for the *u*" (*or*). But for what purpose is this mentioned? For the sake of understanding it as applying to every state.
However, what is about to be stated is not tenable in this case, because this [suffix] is characterized by *ik*.

[14] The mention of *puganta-laghūpadha* is for the purpose of restricting [the application] to non-final [vowels]. For the *guṇa* substitution is already established for a non-final vowel; therefore, the repetition [of the rule] there will serve to restrict it. By this, the following is demonstrated: in the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pā. 7.3.84), the term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is that which is connected to the operation; it qualifies the *ik* [vowel] because it is that which is connected to the operation. But surely, since [the vowel] is something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), a restriction (*niyama*) is untenable?

Furthermore, what is to be prescribed? [The rule] "it causes shame" (*hrepayati*) is established for the non-final [vowel]. However, it would have to be prescribed for the final *pakāra* (the *p* in *bhettṛ*), as in the case of *dakāra* (the *d* in *bhettṛ*). It is said in reply: this restriction is explained by relying on the meaning of the sūtra itself, namely, that when there is a *puK* suffix, the penultimate vowel is light. But even so, would this not apply to the meaning of *dāpayati*? Let it be; let there be a *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ā*, and we shall apply *vṛddhi*. In the case of circular arguments (*cakraka*), the determination is made according to one's preference.

This other portion of the Sūtra will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): "the *upadhā* is light. This restriction applies specifically to what has been under discussion: that [guṇa substitution occurs] only for a stem ending in *puK* before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, and not for anything else. Since the light *upadhā* is the one connected with the operation [of guṇa] in the rule "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes," [the guṇa] would not occur here in the case of *īhita*. However, since the guṇa of short vowels and so forth is not restricted [to light *upadhās*], both [the genitives] in the expression "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) are indeed genitives of specification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Furthermore, suppose there were such a restriction—that [the rule] "guṇa occurs for a stem ending in *pu* or having a light penultimate vowel" applies only to *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. In that case, when the cause [of the suffix] is restricted, one would not obtain the *guṇa* in instances such as *hrasva*; for the cause is restricted by that rule. Consequently, *guṇa* would necessarily apply in cases such as *īhita*. Alternatively, suppose there were a restriction in both directions. But how can a restriction in both directions be obtained, given that a repetition of the statement constitutes a restriction?

In that case, once one [meaning] has been restricted, there is no further mention of another [rule] by which a second meaning could be restricted. It is said: True; this is stated for exactly this purpose, namely "even so" (*athāpi*). Even if it were explained in this way—that this sūtra serves to restrict both sides—even so, the *guṇa* substitution in the case of *jusi* would remain unrestricted, because it is included in both categories. Furthermore, this [root] has a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), and *jusa* is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

[15] If that is so, then this is neither a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that rule nor an exception (*apavāda*) to it. As for your thought—that these two technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) depend on each other because they apply to the same domain, either due to conflict or through the relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—that is not the case. This is because they function toward their respective effects independently of one another: one [the rule *iko yaṇ aci*] applies in cases such as *rājñaḥ ka ca* (Pā. 4.2.140), while the other [the rule *vṛddhir ād aic*] functions by establishing that the *ik* vowels are the substituenda (*sthānin*) for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

Even if, by some chance, there is a co-occurrence (*saṃnipāta*) of these two in one place, it cannot be assumed that they have a mutual dependence merely on that account. Just as length (*dīrghatva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), though independent of each other, are seen to co-occur in a single object as in the word *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, so it is with these two paribhāṣās. In that case, the paribhāṣā "of the final [element] of the base" (*alontya*) is occupied with establishing a part [of the base] through a genitive of the whole (*samudāya-ṣaṣṭhī*); this [present paribhāṣā] is likewise [occupied] with establishing that *ik* is the substitute in the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

[The rule regarding] *niyama* and so forth results in the increase of qualities (*guṇavṛddhi*) by way of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*). For if [the suffixes] were considered "remaining" (*śeṣa*), there would be a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the *ātmanepada*; what kind of mutual exclusion could there be then? Furthermore, when there is a contradiction, a mutual exclusion between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) is also untenable. The scope for the *niyama* is provided by the rule: *arājñaḥ ka ca* (Pā. 4.2.140).

Where the operation of the paribhāṣā "iko guṇavṛddhī" does not occur—its scope being, for example, *cayanaṃ*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanaṃ*, and *lāvakaḥ*—and where no specific distinction is perceived caused by the operation of the paribhāṣā "alo 'ntyasya," its application there would be purposeless.

If, by the rule *iko yaṇ aci* itself, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the final *ik* were already established, then the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would merely be prescribing that same thing; thus, nothing new would be accomplished. Therefore, we conclude that the restrictive rule is indifferent (neutral) regarding that matter. Here, however, both possibilities arise: *medyati* and *mārṣṭi*. By the restrictive rule, the substitution would apply to the consonant (*vyañjana*), and by this [general rule], it would apply to a non-final *ik*. This contradiction is not tenable.

First of all, he explains that they do not even understand the arrangement of the sūtra itself when he says, "This is a prior rule (yoga), this is a subsequent restriction (niyama). Even so, there is usage with the word *para* signifying "desired," but not with the sense of "established" (*vyavasthitatva*), because [the latter] would preclude what was previously obtained by stating "without beginning. Therefore, he says: "The word *para* signifies what is desired. Even so, this contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) is improper; for a contradiction consists in the application of two grammatical operations (*kārya*).

Where there is the conjunction of two operations (*kārya*) pertaining to a single locus (*sthānin*), that is "conjunction of two operations" (*dvikāryayoga*). That which resides therein [the locus] receives its designation (*tācchabdyam*) from this [conjunction] due to the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because it is the object of the conjunction of two operations. Alternatively, *yoga* means connection (*saṃbandha*). Conjunction with two operations is what constitutes the conflict; thus, conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is specifically a particular kind of connection. Just as the word "contradiction" (*virodha*) has a particular kind of connection as its meaning, so too does the word "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*).

A conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) does not necessarily consist only in the conjunction of two operations. What then? It is also impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). This conflict which you have accepted as being due to the conjunction of two operations—that which is the impossibility therein is the conflict. In that case of impossibility, there is no operation, nor is there a conjunction of two operations; and even where the conjunction of two operations is not possible, that too is a conflict. In that instance as well, it is simply impossibility.

And he demonstrates that the occurrence of two replacements for a single locus is indeed impossible: "In this case, first, in *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, there is one locus and two replacements; yet such a possibility does not exist. Now, one might object: "But surely two replacements can occur in place of one, just as in *ekapakṣe*, where there is one word *pac* and two words *pac*. Why, then, do the vowel *a* and the vowel *e* not both occur in place of [the final *a*] in *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*? It is replied: "We do not say that it is impossible in every instance."

What then? It is that such a thing as this which is under discussion does not occur. For in that case, there is lengthening immediately following *yaṇ*, and there is also the substitution of *e* before a *jhal* consonant; yet it is impossible for both [operations] to have immediate succession by means of their respective causes. Having considered this, it is stated: "It is not possible for one single substituendum (*sthānin*) to have two substitutes (*ādeśa*). Here now, in the form *medyati*, there are two substituenda and a single substitute.

"And there is no possibility"—even here, a possibility is observed, as in the rules *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pā. 6.1.84) and *bhrasjo ropadheyo ram anyatarasyām* (Pā. 6.4.47). It is replied: In this case, there is no possibility. Why? Because if *mideḥ* were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), it would have to be restricted by way of inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). And in such a restriction, since the single [phoneme *i*] is not understood, the non-singular (*ani*) is understood. However, if it is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*)—namely, of the "stem" (*aṅgasya*)—then a restriction is impossible.

In this case as well, a restriction (niyama) would apply; such is the intended meaning. [The rule] "it becomes a quality" (guṇaḥ bhavati) operates in cases such as *cayana* and so forth, whereas a restriction brings about indifference (*audāsīnya*). What is the reason for this? It might be argued that there is no distinction whatsoever. This very thing is the distinction: namely, that the rule concerning the final letter (*al-antyavidhi*) must be set aside. As long as this [rule] "ika" has not been commenced, what do you think—what would occur here? A restriction.

Since this [rule] is undertaken because such a restriction would otherwise apply everywhere, it functions as an exception (*apavāda*). Therefore, the view of the followers of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana (Kroṣṭrīyas)—that there is a mutual dependence between these two [rules] due to their opposition—is not incorrect; for this *paribhāṣā* is not unrelated to it. Even if, by some means, one were to assume this statement: even if the restriction might somehow produce indifference toward the *cayana* and other rites, nevertheless, a fault remains precisely when there is a prohibition.

[16] If that is so, then there is "vṛddhi" (increment) and there is "guṇa" (substitution); how is this established? This does not apply to everything; rather, in the technical designations of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, it is understood that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur in place of *ik*. What then? Wherever *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed by the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the genitive sense of "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) is also present there. Alternatively, the direct mention of "*ik*" (*ika iti*) is present [in the rule].

However, the application of the operation will occur precisely from the specific location; thus, as many sūtras as are subsumed under the technical names *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, so many are made to possess the sixth case-ending by means of this device, namely, the suffix *ika*. This is the very same principle: that a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), being subordinate because it exists for the sake of another, attains its operation from that primary location. We accept this as an *anārabhyavāda* (a statement not introduced in connection with a specific context), which, having been set aside due to the difference in the primary subject matter, is abandoned once the task is accomplished, even though nothing specific was initiated.

In all instances where a mere vowel (*ik*) is produced, the primary rule (*pradhānavākya*) results in the form: "The *guṇa* substitution occurs for the *ik* of the root *mid*. Since it does not depend on a specific operation as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), nor does it depend on the maxim regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*) due to contradiction, a human (authoritative) operation is resorted to.

A person acting according to his own will, because it is impossible for *ik* to be the final element in roots such as *mid*, understands *mid* and so on as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and *ik* as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), just as in the rule "ūṭh is substituted for the penultimate vowel of *guh*" (Pā. 6.4.89), where *guh* is understood as the qualifier of the penultimate vowel.

"But in the case of *jus* and so on, since it is possible for [the rule] *iko 'ntyasya* to apply, the *aṅga* is understood as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the *ik* vowels as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Why then is it not assumed that in *jus* and so on, the *ik* vowels belonging to the *aṅga* [are meant]—that is, by favoring the majority? It is said: "In such matters, there is freedom of choice. If this is so, and there is freedom of choice, then if a single *aṅga* is qualified, there is indeed no favoring of the majority. The logical justification (*upapatti*) is also described in this very way.

In this context, if *ika* were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the application of the term *aṅga* whose form is unrestricted, and *aṅgasya* were the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then the direct requirement of the word *aṅga* toward the *guṇa* substitution would be lost, because it would already be occupied by the qualifier. Furthermore, there would be no connection with the meaning, since the *guṇa* would be established in place of the *ik*. However, if *aṅgasya* is qualified by *ika*, then the primary connection of the word as it is actually employed is not abandoned.

Although *ik* may be separated from the principal element by the word [intervening], because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless, there is a close connection with the principal element through the sense that "the *ik* must be replaced by a *guṇa*. Therefore, one should adopt that interpretation in which the *ik* and the *guṇa* come into contact with the principal element. However, since this [interpretation based on logical sense] is seen to be fallible in certain instances within the technical treatise (*śāstra*), one must instead follow the actual application of the treatise itself.

[17] Alternatively, in this context, the substituend (*sthānin*) is indicated everywhere. Since the substituend has been indicated by depending on what remains of it, he explains that the mention of the letter *i* need not be repeated in the specific rules (*pradeśa*). This applies even to the cases of *kṣipra* and *kṣudra*.

Regarding what is said by relying on the meaning of the sūtra—"on account of the mention of *pūrva*, it will apply to *ik*": if, first of all, "yaṇādi" means that which begins with a *yaṇ* (i.e., *yaṇādiḥ*), and that which follows a *yaṇādi* is elided, while a *guṇa* is substituted for the preceding sound—meaning "for that which precedes a *yaṇādi*"—then forms such as *kṣepiṣṭhaḥ* and *kṣodiṣṭhaḥ* are established; for here, the *guṇa* substitution applies to the *pakāra* and *dakāra*, which are the beginning of the *yaṇ*. However, in the case of *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, the *guṇa* would undesirably apply to the *yakāra*.

Now, that which begins with a *yaṇ* is "yaṇ-ādi"; when a verbal form beginning with a *yaṇ* follows, it is elided and there is *guṇa* substitution for the preceding vowel. On this view, since the *van* suffix is elided in the word *yuva*, the form *yaviṣṭha* is established. However, in the case of *kṣepiṣṭha*, *guṇa* would apply to the letter *p*. If that is the case, then in the rule for *sthūla* and others, *guṇa* will simply be applied to the *o* sound. Furthermore, the principle that "what precedes *bhā* is not established" (*prāg bhād asiddhatvam*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). This prescription of *guṇa*, however, is intended solely for the meanings "swift" (*kṣipra*) and "small" (*kṣudra*).

In that case, the *guṇa* substitution will apply to the preceding element before the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) and so forth. But surely, for words such as *sthūla* ending in *-o*, once the *guṇa* has been applied to the *o*, an undesirable result would be produced by this [rule]. Therefore, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: first, "the [element] following the semi-vowel and so forth in *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra* is elided"; then, "there is *guṇa* of the preceding [element]. Only *kṣipra* and *kṣudra* are carried over because they are marked with the *svarita* accent; *sthūla* and the others are excluded. For these, there is only the *guṇa* of the *o*.

If this [substitution] is thus characterized by the absence of *i* (*aniglakṣaṇa*), because its place of occurrence has been specified, then [the rule] would apply here in the cases *bhinnaḥ* and *bhinnavān*. It is said in reply: Just as in this case, even though there is no *i*-characteristic, the rule does not apply due to intervention, and it is stated that "since the mention of *kṅit* in this rule is without scope, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] takes effect," so too here, even though there is no substitution for *i*, [the same logic applies]. [Objection: But then, regarding the rule *or guṇe* (Pā. 1.1.50), in the case of *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pā. 7.2.116) ...

And in this regard (under P. 7.2.116), since the mention of *kṅit* would be without scope, there would be a prohibition; therefore, one must ensure that the status of being characterized by an *ik* vowel applies to the light *upadhā*. Now, one might object: "Since there is nothing here to be excluded, the presence of the *ik*-paribhāṣā is useless. Furthermore, if the vowel *a* is not present, there is no distinction [between the two cases].
