[To this we reply: The inferential [application of the paribhāṣā] will take effect prior [to the application of the rule], just as in the case of *pugantalaghūpadha*.

[18] Why is the mention of *vṛddhi* specifically enjoined? Since the author of the Vārttika stated, "The mention of *vṛddhi* is for the sake of what follows," it is inferred that the mention of *vṛddhi* is indeed enjoined. Therefore, he is asked: "Why specifically? [The answer is: In the rules concerning *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, a *sthānin* (original element) is nowhere explicitly indicated. The negative particle (*nañ*) is employed here in the sense of exclusion (*vyavahita*). That is to say, in the rules concerning *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, a *sthānin* is not specified in any instance.

For that purpose, the mention of *i* (the vowel *i*) should have been placed first in order to exclude the final letter (*alontya*). However, since in the rule for *vṛddhi* the substituend (*sthānin*) is specified in every instance, there is no need for this [mention of *i*] for the sake of *vṛddhi*; for it is said: "In the case of an operation prescribed by means of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), there is a restriction."

The mention of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is for the sake of what follows. For previously, the prohibitive rule was rejected; furthermore, since that [other rule] does not cover all cases, this very point is now introduced: he will state the prohibition *kṅiti*, so that it may apply to *vṛddhi* as well. If *vṛddhi* is prescribed for vowels (*ac*), then in *nyamārṭ*, *vṛddhi* would also apply to the augment *aṭ*. This is because *aṭ* is included by the mention of *mṛj* under the rule *ād iṭ* [P. 7.2.35]. Thus, the *aṅga* becomes possessed of *j* (*jatam*).

But how can there be *aṭ*-vṛddhi here, given that because it is subsequent, the [vowel] vṛddhi ought to occur; yet, because its effect has already been realized, it will not occur again? It might be thought: "Since it is done for another sound, this is not tenable. [This refers to the rule: "In the case of a modification of a non-final element, [the substitute applies] to that which is in the same position as the final. For once the vṛddhi has been applied here, there is no longer the possibility of both [operations] occurring; rather, it is only for a non-final vowel. Even if one were to assume that *aṭ* occurs in the state of *l* (the intermediate stage before substitution), by what would the vṛddhi also be prohibited in the state of *l*? Therefore, this is stated having accepted the priority of *aṭ*.

In this regard, there are other grammarians. Here it is objected: must those forms that are explained in another grammar necessarily also be explained here? No, he says. What then? This too is a traditional rule (*smṛti*); where there is a conflict between two traditional rules, there is an option (*vikalpa*), provided that neither of them has a perceptible purpose. But here, there is no conflict.

In one instance, an increase (*vṛddhi*) is prescribed without distinction, while in another, regarding a specific subject, it is stated that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*); thus, according to this traditional rule (*smṛti*), *kṛtavṛddhi* is to be applied, and for that [other case], *akṛtavṛddhi* is also [prescribed]. Furthermore, in another traditional rule, a prohibition is initiated with the words "not after *nyaṅku*," as in the form *nyāṅkavam*. Here too, according to the view that [words] are not etymologically derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), since the form *nyāṅkavam* has been uttered by the assembly of the learned (*śiṣṭa-parṣad*), this [authoritative usage] establishes the correctness of the explanation.

For both traditional recollections (*smṛti*) and revealed scriptures (*śruti*) are held to be restricted by time, as in the cases of the immolation of cows and the drinking of intoxicants. It is because Śukra practiced them that performing them now leads to transgression. Indeed, a traditional recollection regarding the immolation of cows is seen to be restricted by time; it results in sin today. Words are remembered for the sake of prosperity, while others lead to harm. And this form of the word must be employed even today; therefore, this is what is to be established.

In that regard, let there be only this much: "vṛddhi [occurs] for *mṛj* before a vowel" (*aca*). Then, the author of the Bhāṣya is the one who remembers this rule: "it optionally occurs before a vowel marked with *k* or *ṅ*," and he considers this [vowel] to be "taught first" (*ādiśiṣṭa*).

He intended [this rule] to be so: "The elision (*lopa*) of this [augment *iṭ*] will be the sublater. For even before the application of Pāṇini 6.4.48 (*ato lopaḥ*), by virtue of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the elision of the *ā* must occur; and even after that [elision] has been applied, the elision of the *ā* must still take place. In the case of *uda[vo]ḍhām*, because the elision of *ḍh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), if the *vṛddhi* were applied first and then the elision of *ḍh* and other operations were performed, the substitution of *au* would not occur once it has already been effected, since its purpose would have been fulfilled. This prohibition applies to the *vṛddhi* in the *sic* affix as well.

How so? For that which is called a *lakṣaṇa* (grammatical rule) resounds and revolves; it does not remain fixed even for a moment. In this context, the term "resounding" (*dhvanati*) is employed by taking up an indistinct generality (*avyakta-sāmānya*). Just as in common worldly usage, one who speaks indistinctly is asked, "What are you mumbling? What are you grumbling?"—so here [in grammar], the indistinct proceeds in the form of "neṭi" (Pāṇini 7.2.4). Is there a negation of this [rule]? There is no such distinct entity as "the negation of another negation."

Alternatively, just as sound (*dhvani*) pertains to all words, yet upon the perception of its mere essence (*tanmātra*), one thinks only this much: "this word is sounding; someone is pronouncing it by means of this"—so too here, the prohibition has a universal scope. Because of the commonality of its universal scope—namely, that "there is no *vṛddhi* for that which ends in a consonant (*halanta*) when *sic* follows"—it is said to "sound" (*dhvanati*). It might be argued: "Even though it sounds, once it has accomplished its purpose with respect to a single object of prohibition, it would not operate elsewhere"; therefore, he says "it revolves" (*bhramati*).

A general injunction is intended solely for the sake of a particular; thus, just as it applies to one object, so too does it apply to another distinct particular. Now, if it is thought that—as long as it applies to another particular that is to be negated, so long has the injunction already applied elsewhere—and once it has applied, it cannot be negated even by a deluded person through a defining characteristic; therefore, he says: "it does not remain even for a moment. Speech is a universal whose form is external.

This very [sound], because of its rapid movement, is said to be non-abiding even for a moment; however, this is not the case with the word (*śabda*). What then? Those other negations are indeed distinct, characterized by the objects to be negated. Therefore, it is said that there is no object to be negated devoid of characteristics—that it does not abide even for a moment. Others explain: furthermore, it is called "sound" (*dhvani*) because of the commonality of its repeated occurrence.

Just as a bell is designated as "ringing" when its sound is produced again and again, so too these grammatical rules—such as *sici vṛddhiḥ*, *halantasyācaḥ*, and *neṭi*—are said to "resound" (*dhvananti*) as they continue to operate. It might be argued that there is only a single application [of each rule], but this is not the case; they revolve like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*). For even while revolving, they do not remain stationary for even a moment.

In that case, since there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition regarding this subject, the definition must simply not apply. Now, if there is no fixed rule regarding circular arguments (*cakraka*), even so, since a rule is established according to what is intended, the rule will be established through negation. Furthermore, does this occur elsewhere as well? It is asked whether a universal (*sāmānya*) is employed here because the definition does not apply; he replies, "It exists."

In the verse *sujāte aśvasūnṛte*, he introduces this [example] by relying on the reading *nāntaḥpādam* (Pā. 6.1.115), and not on *prakṛtyāntaḥpādam*. Here too, by employing a rule that is either unmanifest (*avyakta*) or refers to a general category (*sāmānyaviṣaya*), he implies that this [rule], namely *nāntaḥpādam*, applies to the sequence *eṅaḥ ati*. Alternatively, because the rules such as *ay-ādi* do not remain fixed, they simply do not apply. Now, how is it in the case of *vṛkāv*? In this instance, [the rule] *nād ici* (Pā. 6.1.103)...

By the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 6.1.104], the *vṛddhi* [substitution] prescribed by ‘*vṛddhir eci*’ (Pā. 6.1.88) must also be prohibited. Now, if you think that these two rules belong to different sections (*prakaraṇa*), then here too it is appropriate to regard ‘*aśvasūnṛte*’ as a separate section from the general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*). Or, if they belong to the same section by virtue of their meaning, then it is the same here as well. Therefore, in this case, one must rely on a specific distinction:
the prohibition applies only to the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* [substitution] for the first two cases, and not to the rule ‘*vṛddhir eci*’.

Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the substitution *uvaṅ* applies. ... Having relied upon the rule "vṛddhi [occurs] before *sic* in the Parasmaipada," the letter *v* is indicated as being elided. Some explain this here as "it is both indicated (*nirdiṣṭa*) and elided (*lupta*). However, this is not tenable, because that which is indicated cannot be connected with elision. For how can that which has been indicated be elided, as if it were a hair on the head? Therefore, just as in the case of "yasya... (Pā. 6.4.148)... [the rule applies].

From this form [by Pāṇini 6.4.148], we indeed understand the presence of the vowel *i*; likewise, at the time of understanding, we shall understand the presence of the consonant *v*, even though it has been elided. [To this, he replies: "I shall state that [the substitution does not apply] after *avi* and *mavya*. This might be the case, but since it would be cumbersome, he says: "Those two [suffixes] must be designated as having *ṇi* and *śvi* [as their markers]. This indicates the intention of the Teacher (Pāṇini). [The question is: "Is it not intended that I should employ the mention of *vṛddhi* [in the rule], thereby avoiding the status of being *antaraṅga* for the *sic* suffix? He says: "No."

This [rule] is not intended for the purpose of applying [the suffix *iṭ*] in cases such as *anayīt*, *acecāyīt*, *acirāyīt*, and *ajirāyīt*; for in the case of the roots *ci* and *jṛ*, as well as those ending in *yaṅ*-luṅ, once the *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* substitutions have been made, they would end in *yā*, and thus the prohibition [of *iṭ*] would apply.

[19] Because it is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), there is the exclusion of *iK*. In the rule "of *iK*" (*ikaḥ*), the genitive denotes locus. In that case, all *iK* sounds would have to be replaced by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, this should be understood as follows: this is not a genitive of locus. The repetition [of the word *iK*] is for the sake of one of the two [alternatives]. But would it not rather be for the sake of excluding those ending in *an*? Once the *guṇas* have been applied to those *iK* sounds [ending in *an*] within the governing context of the *aṅga*, the statement would be for the purpose of excluding those ending in *an*.

Why? Because between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the injunction is stronger; therefore, it would not be a non-restrictive (*anigara*) sense. In this regard, the intention is as follows: in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, the mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" is carried over (*anuvartate*). Having functioned there as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), this [mention] now undergoes the status of being subordinate (*parāṅgatva*). And wherever one says "guṇa" and "vṛddhi," it should be understood that the word "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) is present there. And [this applies] also in the case of *saṃprasāraṇa*.

Because the genitive case in *yaṇaḥ* functions as a *sthāneyoga* (indicating substitution), it would follow that all *yaṇ* sounds are replaced. [Examples: *yātā*, *vātā*. First, there is *prasāraṇa*. How so? [Question: How is the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa* established? [Answer: A separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is made: first, “*ig yaṇaḥ*”: an *ik* vowel occurs in place of a *yaṇ*. Then, “*saṃprasāraṇam*”: the *ik* vowel thus produced in place of a *yaṇ* here receives the designation *saṃprasāraṇa*. The repetition [of the rule] is for the sake of specifying its scope (*viṣaya*).

But surely, even this [interpretation], when understood for the sake of application (*ayaṇārtha*), might be conceived thus: that the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *vac* and so forth. In that case, the intention is that [the rule] *ig yaṇ* also applies there. In the rule *ur aṇ raparaś ca*, as in *kartṛ* and *hartṛ*, since there is no closest (*antara-tama*) [substitute] available, the *aṇ* substitutes would apply by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*). It is precisely for this purpose that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is introduced. Otherwise, there would be a restriction to verbal roots (*dhātu-niyama*)—as in the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100).

[This is] by [the rules] Pāṇini 7.1.100 and 7.1.102 (*ud oṣṭhyapūrvasya*). But it is established [that these rules apply] because of the statement within the governing context of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyadhikāra*). When there is the governing context of the genitive, rules such as *aṅgasya*, *vacyādīnām*, and *ṛta id dhātoḥ*—which are prompted by their own specific causes—accomplish their respective operations by depending on a genitive denoting the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not without a genitive. These two rules (*yoga*) as well will continue to follow the governing context of the genitive. These two rules are marked with an accent (*svarita*).

In that case, because of dependence on another, there is no application of the grammatical operation by means of these two [terms]. Alternatively, we shall refer to these two rules within the context of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*): the rule “The genitive [is used] in connection with *sthāna*” (Pā. 1.1.49) is divided into two separate rules: “The genitive” and “in connection with *sthāna*. That which has been introduced as “the genitive” is present wherever the genitive occurs; by virtue of this capacity, it is connected only to these two. Or rather, he should first be asked this:

However, you must necessarily establish a connection by justifying the repetition for the sake of one or the other [meaning], such that wherever it says "guṇa" or "vṛddhi," the term "ika" is understood to apply there. In this way, forms such as *yātā* and others can be excluded.

In that case, since there is a requirement for mutual dependence (*apekṣā*), why is this dependence established through a division of rules (*yogabheda*), rather than by connecting them into a single sentence? To this, [the author] says: "We shall establish the dependence in this way: 'The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions'—those which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—become *ik*s. This is what is stated by this commentary (*bhāṣya*). This is what is required there. ... Just as this is required there, so too shall we require that here as well.
Thus ends the third daily lesson (*āhnika*) in the *Śrī-Mahābhāṣya-Ṭīkā* composed by Bhartṛhari.
The Fourth Āhnika in the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā.
A 1.1.4: [The designation *aṅga*] does not apply when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

[1] A verbal root (dhātu) is the designation for a sound whose measure has been delimited; and since such a sound is elided, there is no possibility at all for guna or vṛddhi substitutions. Why, then, is a prohibition necessary? Therefore, the author of the Vṛtti explains: "The elision of a verbal root is 'dhātulopa'; [the rule applies] when an ārdhadhātuka suffix is the cause for the elision of a portion of a verbal root."

Another says this: "Dhātulopa" (the elision of a root) means the elision of a root and of a portion of a root; it is "caused by the elision of a root. He explains the usage of the term such that both the elision of an entire root and the elision of a portion of a root constitute "dhātulopa," yet in this context, only the elision of a portion is accepted as possible.

In this manner it is explained: the designation "root" (dhātu) is applied to the parts [of a verbal base] when they possess similarity [to a root], but not by virtue of the entire domain [of the root], because when the whole is elided, the two things to be prohibited would no longer exist; such is the view regarding the mention of "root."

The word *dhātu* [in the compound *dhātulopa*] refers to the whole (*samudāya*) itself, while *lopa* (elision) is simply the absence of a part. That which is the absence of a part is designated as belonging to the whole, because the action pertaining to a member is figuratively attributed to the whole—as in the examples: "the cloth is burnt," "Devadatta is adorned," or "Devadatta is wet. This very meaning has been demonstrated by the authors of the *vṛtti*s: "the elision of a portion of a verbal root is called *dhātulopa*."

[2] What is the purpose of mentioning the term *dhātu* (root)? Is it not the case that because [the root] is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*), the question is inappropriate? And thus some commentators read: "What is the purpose of saying *dhātulopa*? Even for those who maintain that the word denotes the whole (*samudāya*), it is the constituent part (*avayava*) alone that is questioned. Otherwise, it would be like the speech of a child, where a prohibition applies to the very same thing to which a rule applies. This is not a fault; for by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it indicates that which is expected as being already established.

*lūñ* [is the root]; *lavitā* [is the example]. Now, one might object that a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) is not possible here in this commentary (*vṛtti*), because there is a rule prohibiting [the substitution of *śn*] before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix when it is caused by the elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*). This is the intended meaning: when the mention of *dhātu* (verbal root) is present, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is possible; when a *bahuvrīhi* exists, it serves as a qualifier for both [members].

[2.1] But how is it that there is the disappearance of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) and not the disappearance of the verbal root (*dhātu*)? It is said: here, the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "verbal root" and the designation of "indicatory letter" (*itsaṃjñā*) operate simultaneously. And the accepted principle in the grammatical treatise is that whatever bears the designation of "indicatory letter" does not [then] exist. This being so, at the very stage where there is the designation of "verbal root," there is also the designation of "indicatory letter. And when the designation of "verbal root" has come into effect, the *anubandha* no longer exists; since it is non-existent, there can be no designation of "verbal root" for it.

Now, even if the designation *dhātu* applies to those [elements] whose meaning is "being" (*bhāva*), the meaning of the word used in actual application is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by postulating it for a specific portion [of the form]. Furthermore, there is neither positive nor negative concomitance for the *anubandha* (indicatory letter). To the extent that positive and negative concomitance exist, to that very extent the designation *dhātu* is applied, having postulated the status of expressing an action (*kriyāvacanatva*). Thus, this is not a fault.
Indeed, the status of expressing an action is observed even for forms containing the letter *s*, such as *tiṣṭhāsa-* and so forth.

[2.2] "The bull bellows. Since the term *ārdhadhātuka* is mentioned [in the rule], the author of the Bhāṣya also presents these counter-examples for this very purpose, thinking: "I shall subsequently reject the formulation of this sūtra, and I shall state that, in one view, the mention of the term *dhātu* is redundant."

[2.3] Four positions are possible here; two are presented: (1) the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* is a qualifier of the elision (*lopaviśeṣaṇa*), (2) it is a qualifier of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, (3) it is a qualifier of both without a *bahuvrīhi* compound due to repetition, as in the mention of *upadeśa* in the rule “*ekāca upadeśe ’nudāttāt*” (A 7.2.10), and (4) it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

[3] But what is the purpose of this mention of "ārthadhātuka"? Is the *ārthadhātuka* base being taken as the locus for the elision (*lopa*) intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, or is the elision—though not caused by them—being taken as an indicator for the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* that reside in the *ārthadhātuka* bases? What, then, is the correct view here? He says: both. How so? He asks because it is possible for the *dhātuka* element to be related to both.

[The rule] would also apply here in the cases of *uppeḍhaḥ* and *preḍḍhaḥ*. But surely, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution for *ad* should occur first, according to the principle that "the root is joined with the prefix first. Therefore, this example is *kaṣṭeddha*. And if the status of being a prefix (*upasargatva*) were not to be understood [in such cases], and if the suffix were produced before the prefix, how could there be forms like *uppeḍhaḥ* and *preḍḍhaḥ*? This is not a fault; for he will indeed explain the relationship between the internal and the external (*antaraṅga-bahiraṅga-bhāva*).

If the connection with the prefix (*upasarga*) is accepted first, then the *guṇa* substitution is internal (*antaraṅga*) and the prohibition is external (*bahiraṅga*). If, on the other hand, the production of the suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs first, even so, the *guṇa* is external and the prohibition is internal. However, this resolution has not been stated here because it does not possess the defining characteristic (*aniglakṣaṇatvāt*); I shall explain this further below.

But is it not the case that, according to the principle "there is no designation of externality when there is immediate succession of vowels," the discernment of correct and incorrect forms would not occur? This, however, is not tenable, because the application of correct and incorrect forms proceeds from the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Others say that it is the production of phonemes [that occurs]. In the word *hiraṇyadyūḥ*, there is the realization of the *yaṇ* [substitution]. This being so, the meaning is that even a prohibition is thereby produced.

Therefore, this is the meaning: in that grammatical system where there is recourse to the rule regarding the immediate succession of vowels (*acāmānantarya*) as a positive injunction (*vidhi*), [the rule] does not apply. But here, in the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there is no recourse to those two; thus there is no fault. [Objection: Even in the case of *knopayati*, [the substitution of *guṇa*] would result. [Reply: But surely, because the augment *puK* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the elision of *yaL* (*yalopa*) does not apply here. Or, if the elision occurs by virtue of the irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule "in *cela*, [it becomes] *knopa*" (A 3.4.33), then by that same irregularity, the *guṇa* will also occur.

If this is so, there is no need for the mention of the term *dhātu*. Even without a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* as qualifying both [the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] is possible; that is, when there is elision (*lopa*), those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which would otherwise apply before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix do not take place. Furthermore, in the case of the elision of an *anubandha*, the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is not the cause [of the operation].

[4] An enumeration must be made: this rule, "na yaṅy akkyavalope ārdhadhātuke," should be recited. When it is recited in this way, forms such as *knopayati* and others are established. Regarding the phrase "elision of *val*," a certain specific restriction must be applied; by that, the suffix is added after the root *jīv*, but not after *sriv*.

[4.1] This is for the purpose of preventing the prohibition [of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitution] when there is the elision of *num*, the elision of a suffix (*pratyaya*), or the elision of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). The term *num* is used here to denote the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal augment); this should be understood as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the ancient teachers. Otherwise, if it were not so, the mention of "desired" (*iṣṭa*) would not include the case of the elision of that which occupies the position of *num*. Because these cases are specifically enumerated here, there is no application of the prohibition; for if this enumeration did not exist, the prohibition "when there is the elision of a verbal root" (*dhātulopa*) would apply.

[4.2] Due to the context of the *ik*-pratyāhāra, there is *vṛddhi* when *num* is elided. Wherever this [rule] "when *num*" applies—specifically for the purpose of excluding other substituends—there this prohibition holds. In this case, the term "when *ik*" has no operational role. [4.3] It is established elsewhere because it depends on an affix (*pratyaya*). The intention is that "ārddhadhātuka" qualifies both [the base and the affix]. In the case of *jīradānuḥ*, the [vṛddhi] does not apply; for this elision does not depend on an affix. What then? It depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), because of the statement "elision of *val*."

[4.4] Regarding *rak-i-jyaḥ-prasāraṇam*: therein, the prohibition is established by the rule *kṅiti*; the *avagraha* is also established; and the accent is not defective because it is a *bahuvrīhi*. *Bahiḥ* is a separate root (*prakṛtyantara*); and they teach in the *khilapāṭha* that *ātaḥ* is also a separate root, distinguishing it without contradiction. For this is not like *ahi*, which has five parts as its domain.

In this case as well, [the rule] would apply to forms such as *bhedyate* and *chedyate*, because both of these occur in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain—since the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is caused by the *ārdhadhātuka* affix—and because *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would consequently apply to the *ṇi* when it is an *ārdhadhātuka*. However, this is untenable, because the *guṇa* substitution has already been effected in the *ṇi* itself, even prior to the introduction of the *sārvadhātuka* and *vikaraṇa* suffixes.

"It is not understood in this way" means that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. When it is a *bahuvrīhi*, there is the acceptance of a single cause for both the elision (*lopa*) and the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions. In the case of *bhedyate*, the elision occurs before one *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, while the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur before another; thus, there is no prohibition. Where there is a substitute for the *hal* and *ac*—in the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74)—the entire complex is designated as a suffix (*pratyaya*). And for that, non-appearance (*adarśana*) through elision (*luk*) is possible.

In this case as well, when the elision of the vowel *a* has been performed, the intention is as follows: the mere *yakāra* alone retains the designation of "affix" (*pratyaya*) even after the elision of the *a*. Just as in the form *apacad*, even though one part has completely departed, the remaining portion still possesses the designation of "affix. Nor is the entire complex intended to be expressed by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), just as in the teaching of the universal form (*ākṛti*) "cow," the color and other qualities are not intended to be expressed; thus, whether it possesses those qualities or lacks them, it remains simply "cow. Likewise here, whether the *a* is present or absent, it remains simply *yaṅ*.

When elision (*luk*) has been applied, [the rule for] elision (*lopa*) does not apply; the intention to be stated is that elision (*luk*) is obligatory (*nitya*). This must be considered here: the intention is that elision applies to what remains. The scope of *lopa* is, for example, *cikīrṣitā*; the scope of *luk* is the mere *yak* suffix. Both would apply to the whole form. However, because it is subsequent, there is *lopa* of the vowel *a* of the *yaṅ*. Elision (*luk*) is obligatory; its obligatoriness consists in the fact that the application of the grammatical rule is itself obligatory. But when everything has been removed by *luk*, there is no possibility for *lopa* to occur, and thus it is non-obligatory (*anitya*).

In that case, the elision (*luk*) would have no scope. How do you consider it to have no scope? Because *luk* is prescribed when the [general] elision (*lopa*) has not yet applied. For if *luk* were not stated, then the elision [of the suffix] would occur [by the general rule]. Alternatively, it is the elision of the suffix (*pratyaya-luk*) that is being stated. And the letter *y* alone is not a suffix. Why? Because it does not exist as such in actual usage (*prayoga*), and because the letter *y* alone is not taught (*upadeśa*) in the grammatical instruction. Therefore, its status as a suffix is determined neither from usage nor from the instruction.
Furthermore, in the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the entire complex [the suffix *yaṅ*] is indicated. Consequently, *luk* has no scope [for the individual *y*].

The *luk* elision has its scope (*sāvakāśa*). What is that scope? It is the remainder (*avaśiṣṭa*). He thinks as follows: the elision of *l* (*lopa*) and the elision of the suffix (*luk*) have different domains. Furthermore, there is the recognition of the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*) for the mere *yak* in forms such as *lolūyitṛ*, because of the determination of identity through the thought "this very [element] is that. Nor is the form of the rule "yaṅo 'ci ca" intended to be emphasized here. Therefore, the remainder is the scope. Even so, in some way—meaning, according to the aforementioned conceptualization—it is said that even then, the *al*-elision will be treated by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*), and this split in the rule is solely for the purpose of overriding the *luk* elision.

The elision (*luk*) which shares the same locus is superseded by elision (*lopa*), because they are simultaneous. However, the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (A 2.4.73) indeed applies, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and thus operates without regard for its specific cause. [Objection: But is not the elision of *ā* (*ato lopaḥ*) also prescribed for the general category of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes? [Response: Here, a specific *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended, as well as the governing context of the stem (*aṅga*). Alternatively, even though it is stated generally, it nevertheless relies upon a conceptual generality; however, in the case of *luk*, there is no reliance even conceptually.

[6] It is also stated in the *Nikucita*: "Is the rule characterized by *saṃnipāta*? Since elision (*lopa*) is prescribed in connection with *kit*-ness, that [elision] does not become the cause for this *akit*-ness [which is required] by the rule *udupadhāt* (A 1.2.21). Therefore, in this case, the prohibition [of guṇa] by the rule *kṅiti ca* (A 1.1.5) will apply. Thus it is said.

[7] If the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule is rejected, then in the case of *jaṅgama*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would apply; likewise, in *yāya*, the elision of the long *ā* [as prescribed by A 6.4.64] would apply; and in *dedya*, the augment *yuṭ* [would apply] according to A 6.4.63. Now, one might object that in the case of *jaṅgama*, there will be a prohibition [of the elision] by the rule A 6.4.98 (*anaṅi*).

But how can this [augment] *aṅ* be [substituted], given that *yaṅ* is taught here? Even if it were to occur upon the removal of the letter *y*, even so, this [augment] would be purposeless. Furthermore, how can there be a prohibition [of the augment] in the case of *agamad*? Because it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and because it possesses meaning. Moreover, an operation observed in the original element (*sthānin*) is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the substitute (*ādeśa*). And no operations are observed in the case of the vowel *ā*; how then could they apply when [the *ā*] has been elided? This being the case, in the word *yāyāvara*, the elision of *ā* (*ato lopaḥ*) is not applicable at all. What, then, is the use of the prohibition regarding "as if it were the original" (*sthānivat*)?

In this regard, Pāṇini’s intention is as follows: just as an objection is raised on the grounds of mere possibility—that an operation not seen in the *lakāra* would apply to the substitute (*ādeśa*)—so it is here as well. And just as when the vowel *a* is removed, the suffix remains as the mere letter *y*, so too here, while it is possible for the suffixhood to exist even if the *a* is replaced by *y* in an inappropriate place, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* is initiated in the case of *yāyāvara*. But how [does one account for] words such as *jaṅgama* according to the Vārttikakāra? For him as well, there is elision (*luk*).

Therefore, forms such as *yāyāyaḥ* or *dedīyaḥ* should not occur. However, in the case of suffixes like *loluva*, the status of being a suffix will be admitted merely on the basis of its possibility; and due to that, by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *uvaṅ* takes place.
(A 1.1.5) *kṅiti ca*.

In this context, both the prohibition and the [conditions for] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are inferred; however, the prohibition is primary because it is that which is being enjoined. Furthermore, from this form of the word (*śabdarūpa*), there is no manifestation [of the primary element]—namely, the primary [prohibition] qualified by the expression "when followed by *k* or *ṅ*. If there were a need [for such a qualification], it would not be proper to qualify the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* while bypassing the primary [prohibition]. Therefore, since the term "when followed by *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅiti*) is indicated in the locative case, the prohibition must apply to that which is immediately adjacent.

It might be argued that the term *guṇavṛddhi* is a qualifier of both [the preceding and following elements], just as the word *striyām* (A 4.1.3) is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) which is subordinate [to the feminine suffix]. That is indeed appropriate there because it benefits both; however, here it is not so, and thus it is proper that the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) be a qualifier. But surely, if *guṇavṛddhi* were a qualifier, the prohibition—applying to both separated and immediately contiguous instances—would be made to have a vast scope. This is not the case.

This would be like the Śunaskarṇa-stoma sacrifice. Just as when the principal [element] has perished, they do not perform the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), so too the primary element would have its purpose fulfilled by the very fact that the nature [of the rule] is restricted to a specific object; for this reason also, this position is untenable. But surely, even if there is a qualifier of the negation, it is indeed a qualifier of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; for in every case, when an action is being enjoined, it is simply whether *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur or do not occur.

Even if this is so, nevertheless, that which has attained similarity with *sattā* (existence) is apprehended, not its exclusion (*nivṛtti*). Thus, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are qualifiers of *sattā*, not of *nivṛtti*. Even so, since immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not possible in the case of a negation, it is improper for that [negation] to be a qualifier. This is likewise true even when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are the qualifiers; for there is no immediate succession between *kṅit* suffixes and *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. Therefore, the negation qualified by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* results in the production of an *āru* substitute for the original element (*sthānin*), and since *ik* is the specific grammatical operation (*saṃskāra*), and because *ik* can indeed possess immediate succession, this is stated as follows:

[1.1] Regarding the phrase "the apprehension of that cause" (*tannimittagrahaṇam*): this is not the actual reading. What then? This is an exposition of the meaning. In that regard, the commentators should adopt that wording in which this meaning is fully contained. For it should be read thus: "And when *kṅit* is the cause, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur. The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that the mention of "cause" (*nimittagrahaṇa*) must be added as something new; others, however, explain that the mention of "cause" is merely to be interpreted (*vyākhyeya*).

The mention of *kṅit* is a qualifier for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. And when it qualifies *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, this paribhāṣā—namely, “*tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya*” (A 1.1.66)—is simply not applicable. Because a paribhāṣā is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of a rule (*vidhi*), it applies only where that which is enjoined [by the rule] occurs; just as the rule “*iko guṇavṛddhī*” (A 1.1.3) applies only where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are being enjoined.

However, where *vṛddhi* is established and employed for another purpose—as in the rule “That [base] is called *vṛddha* whose initial vowel among its vowels is *vṛddhi*” (A 1.1.73)—the term “*ika*” does not apply there. If it were to apply, the designation *vṛddha* would not occur in words such as *śāliya*. Furthermore, the mention of the word “*sthāne*” in the rule “In place of *ā*, according to the Northern Grammarians... (A 7.3.46) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), so that when a genitive case is used, the prohibition based on non-substitution (*asthāneyoga*) shall not take effect. Likewise here as well, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not being prescribed.

For this [rule], namely *kṅiti*, is taken as referring to those [operations of] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* that have been prescribed elsewhere; thus, because of its presence, the prohibition is established both in the case of what is immediate and what is separated by the *anantaraparibhāṣā*. When *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed before *kṅit* suffixes, they do not occur. In the prohibition regarding *kṅit*, there is no grasping of a cause (*nimitta*). But this is not tenable, because the prohibition is the primary element.

Since this favor (*anugraha*) belongs only to that which is included within the meaning (*artha*), what is the insistence on a favor toward a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but not toward the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*? [The rule] "when [something] is specified as 'in that' (*tasmin*), [an operation applies] to the preceding" is a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*); therefore, the mention of a cause (*nimitta*) must be made. Furthermore, based on some indicative mark (*liṅga*), one must assume that [the word *tasmin*] qualifies *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

By this [statement], it is shown that due to the diversity of factors (*dharma*), the primary [agent] sometimes becomes attached to the qualities (*guṇa*) for the sake of performing those factors—and that non-attachment is solely for the purpose of accomplishing its own task—while at other times, having itself undertaken those factors, it proceeds toward the effects. Furthermore, as for the example [cited] therein, where the death of the sacrificer is heard to occur directly, whereas here [in the present case] it does not exist, it is therefore postulated that there is a multiplicity of objects, specifically regarding the direct increase of the qualities.

[2] It should be understood that the purpose [of the rule] is for the sake of the meaning separated by the *upadhā* vowel; otherwise, there would be no prohibition of the cause for *yaṅ*. This is stated for this very purpose: "In the case of a prohibition regarding that which undergoes *guṇa*, because there is an absence of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Wherever there is a state of being subject to *guṇa* immediately following a *kṅit* suffix, [the rule applies]. Thus, this is said: in the prohibition of that which undergoes *guṇa*, due to the absence of immediate succession.

Just as here in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (A 6.1.77), the immediate succession of an *ic* vowel to a vowel (*ac*) is possible through the substitution of a *yaṇ*, so too here [in the present context], there is neither a prohibition nor a *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* [substitution]; rather, it is only an *ik* vowel that follows immediately. Thus, he explains the occurrence of *guṇa*. Why is no example given for *vṛddhi*? It would indeed occur here in the form *mṛṣṭa*. The intention is this: in that case, the locus (*sthānin*) of the *vṛddhi* is specifically indicated by the rule *mṛjer vṛddhir acaḥ*.

[2.1] But surely, for that which has a *guṇa* prescribed [for it], how can one rely upon that which is neither explicitly mentioned (*asaṃśabdita*) nor under discussion (*aprakṛta*), namely, that which ends in *pu*, *ga*, or has a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*)? And if there is no objection to qualifying the *pu-ga-laghūpadha* that has become subject to *guṇa* by means of *kṅit*, why should there be any resentment toward qualifying [the same element] by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*? As for what was said—that it is neither under discussion nor explicitly mentioned—[we reply as follows].

To this we reply: proximity does not necessarily arise from word-order (*śabda*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) alone; for proximity also arises through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). And here, in the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi do not occur before *kṅit*," there is an expectancy as to "of what [do they not occur]? Alternatively, since *kṅit* refers to an affix (*pratyaya*), the stem (*aṅga*) is also proximate; thus, the proximity of that which has *puK* or a light penultimate vowel is obtained through semantic capacity. As for the statement, "What is the objection to [the suffix] being a qualifier of guṇa and vṛddhi?"—[that is answered as follows].

Even though *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are specified [as the conditions], they would not apply at all when there is an intervention. How so? Just as in the case of *iko yaṇ aci*, even though the *yaṇ* substitution has already taken place, the requirement of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is operative—namely, that "the *yaṇ* occurs for an *ik* followed immediately by an *ac*"—and thus the *yaṇ* proceeds; in the same way here, even though the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have already occurred, the condition of immediate sequence with respect to *kṅiti* would indeed still apply.

Therefore, where an *ik* vowel followed immediately by a cause for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* occurs, the prohibition would simply not apply; thus, the same fault remains that was pointed out regarding the qualification of the prohibition. Consequently, one must rely on the immediate succession (*anantarya*) of the element ending in *puk* or having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) with respect to the occurrence of *guṇa*, so that the technical rule concerning immediate succession (*anantaraparibhāṣā*) may be operative and supported. This is the meaning: in forms such as *saṃpannaḥ*, because there is an intervening *kṅit* suffix, *guṇa* does not occur for the element ending in *puk* or having a light penultimate vowel. Furthermore, the term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) was not stated [in the rule], because it is not merely the stem that undergoes *guṇa*.

What then? It is a specific member [of the word]: *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* and *pugantalaghūpadhasya*. It is not understood in this way [as referring to the whole]. Here, a composite (*samudāya*) is not being referred to; rather, a constituent part (*avayava*) is. And since that [part] is separated [by other elements], there is no applicability of the prohibition. Thus, by the rule *laghvā upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, [the prohibition] does not occur.

[2.2] There is a fault when the condition (*nimitta*) is included. When that condition is grasped, a guna substitution occurs even where it is not conditioned by that [condition], as in the case of *śeriyati*. But surely, if the inclusion of the condition is made, there is no fault at all; for the guna is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), while the prohibition is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), and "that which is extrinsic is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is intrinsic. Furthermore, he will state this other resolution regarding the form *roravīti*. Here, however, the condition is described in this way: as for what you think—that the position including the condition is faultless—even here there is a fault.

[2.3] *hataḥ*, *hathaḥ*. The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is intended here. He thinks as follows: just as in the case of the rules "after roots beginning with *adi*, the suffix *śap* is elided" (A 2.4.72) and "the suffixes *āya* and so forth are optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix" (A 3.1.31), which are established through distinct syntactical units (*vākyabheda*), so too this vowel *a* taught in the Dhātupāṭha is elided when followed by *k*, *ṅ*, or *s*. [The phrase refers to] that which was applicable but has not been realized.

For what purpose are two [terms] stated, rather than just one of them? To this it should be said: first, there are two types of that which has arisen—namely, the "engaged" (*prasakta*) and the "unengaged" (*anabhinirvṛtta*). If that is so, let it simply be "of the unengaged. But even that is of two types: the engaged and the unengaged. Therefore, because it must exist here as a property of the object (*dharmin*), it is "engaged"; and because the negation of the self proceeds with respect to that which is "unengaged," both are stated.

The intention here is as follows: in cases such as *hataḥ* and *hathaḥ*, a certain quality (*guṇa*) exists even though it has been "struck down" (suppressed). In cases such as *kartṛ* and others, a certain element is to be applied (*vidheya*), even without being explicitly recited, as in the rule regarding the suffix *tṛc*. When an *ik*-vowel is taught, *guṇa* is prescribed for it in forms such as *kartṛ*; however, that *guṇa* is subsequently nullified when a *kṅit* suffix follows. In that context, this prohibition—being prescribed precisely because the [quality] was about to occur—prevents that very [quality] from arising, but it does not affect what has already occurred.

But here, since there is neither any other substitute (*śap*) nor any *āya*-class suffixes, even though they exist [in other contexts], they are to be excluded. Therefore, he says: "of that which is applicable but not actually realized."

Regarding the example *upoyata*: the *guṇa* substitution, which depends on both members of the compound, is *bahiraṅga*. Even so, although it has presented itself, because it has not yet been fully realized (*anabhinirvṛtta*), it can be prohibited once it has ceased—that is, as in *auyata*. In *auyata*, the *vṛddhi* is also *bahiraṅga* because its cause is *bahiraṅga* (namely, the augment *āṭ*). In *lauyamānī*, the *vṛddhi* depends upon an external cause. In *anenija*, [the *vṛddhi* is prevented] because it is intervened by another form. How is this the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is like the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86).

That for which the *guṇa* is prescribed is qualified by its being followed by *k* or *ṅit*; this is the latter view—the *guṇa* belongs to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and that [syllable] is separated [from the following element].

[2.4] We shall qualify the *dhātu* by its being followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Because of the inclusion of the *svarita* accent, the *dhātu* is understood from the context. In that regard, either the meaning is inferred, or the word itself. When one employs a word whose meaning is not present, the meaning is inferred; or the word itself is inferred by which the meaning is determined. Thus, having been so designated, it introduces a distinct and separate sentence as a means of expression:
"When followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the internal vowel of the *dhātu*. This is the sentence that arises.

If the term *dhātu* (root) were qualified [by the prohibition], it would not apply to the *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix). This is the intended meaning: the mention of *dhātu* is not carried over for the purpose of preventing the prohibition from applying to the *vikaraṇa*. However, there is a purpose for its being carried over; by the force of its being carried over, it is possible to accept that which is subordinate as being qualified. Thus, the mention of *dhātu* qualifies that which is prescribed [by the rule]. Because the sūtra requires supplementation (*sopaskāratvāt*), the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is supplied.

That which is related to the root does not [apply] to that [which is not related]. And what is related to the root? That which is prescribed after it. The other [opponent], supplying the ellipsis "that which is prescribed after the root does not [apply]," says: "In that case, it would not apply to the root at all. The other [author] supports the fact that *kṅiti* has the same scope as this elliptical statement by saying: "It is not understood in that way."

Alternatively, there is the principle: "Technical definitions and governing rules [apply] at the time of their operation. How is this a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*)? It is said: the terms "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" are understood to carry over from the preceding context. Therefore, wherever guṇa and vṛddhi are prescribed by the very expression "guṇa-vṛddhī," this rule must present itself there. And here, in the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (A 7.3.86), a guṇa is prescribed; thus, this rule must present itself.

In that case, because of the rule stating that there is no [guṇa] for a root ending in a consonant (puG) or having a light penultimate vowel (laghūpadha) when followed by a suffix marked with K or Ṅ, the prohibition will apply even when there is an intervention, according to the principle: "That which cannot be separated [by anything else] applies even when there is an intervention, on the authority of the explicit statement."

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "in this rule" (*yoge*): even if this were not a *paribhāṣā*, nevertheless, when a prohibition is required, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not take effect; for otherwise, once they have already occurred, they would be impossible to prohibit. This very prohibition in the form of *kṅiti* also depends upon that which is to be prohibited in order to establish the required contiguity (*ānantarya*).

Therefore, there are as many prohibitive sūtras as there are things to be prohibited according to their actual state. Thus, when the *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by] *pugantalaghūpadha-guṇaḥ* is to be prohibited, this prohibition—being without scope elsewhere—applies even when separated [by other rules]. Others explain: it has been shown that technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) operate at the time the operation (*kāryakāla*). Now, the solution is stated regarding the place of enunciation (*yathoddeśa*). Principal elements, though distinct, undergo the location of the subordinate elements and thereby bring about a distinction among those subordinates. In this regard, we apply these rules to each principal element with respect to the rule *kṅiti*.

Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher indicates this: the mark [of the rule] shows that the immediately preceding technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply here; namely, that the qualifiers "vṛddhi" and "guṇa" do not qualify [the roots] as subordinate elements, but rather that the element for which "guṇa" is prescribed is qualified by its being followed by *k* or *ṅ*.

[3] "When there is elision (*lumat*), that [operation] does not take place in that [context]"—this is stated by adopting an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). Alternatively, even according to the established text (*yathānyāsa*), the instrumental case in *lumatā* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*). Thus, an operation does not apply to that which has its status as a stem (*aṅga*) marked by an elision. Furthermore, if the word *aṅgasya* is also pronounced with a high pitch (*svarita*), then—even so—since technical terms and interpretive rules (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the operation is to be applied, this [rule] belongs to that very same location [of the rule]. However, its teaching here is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).

Alternatively, in the preceding rule (*yoga*), the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* is without scope (*anavakāśa*). But is it not said that the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* does have scope because it serves to qualify both [the root and the suffix]? True; however, this is appropriate only if the *bahuvrīhi* compound exists even in the absence of the mention of *ārdhadhātuka*, as in the case of “*ekāco dve . . .*” (Pāṇini 6.1.1). For as far as the application of the prohibition regarding the elision of a verbal root (*dhātulopa*) extends, so far it does not apply when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows.

Even those who argue that the inclusion of the term *ārdhadhātuka* is for the sake of providing scope—lest there be [the form] *johortu*—should be questioned as follows: this is not the form derived from the root *hurch*, but rather it is the root *juhoti* with the augment *ruḍ*, just as in the case of *devā aduhra*.

[4] Why does this not occur here: *laigavāyanaḥ kāmayate*? On the view that it is an exception (*apavāda*), the *guṇa* substitution would also be characterized by the presence of an *ik* vowel (i.e., it would be an *iglakṣaṇa*). However, because the *taddhita* suffix and the suffix *kāmya* are characterized by an *ik*, that position of being an exception is abandoned. The emergence of the genitive case and its status as a remainder (*śeṣatva*) remain established. Therefore, it is not characterized by an *ik*. The terms "of an *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) and "guṇa and vṛddhi" (*guṇavṛddhī*) continue to apply. Consequently, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which are characterized by an *ik* do not occur in this case.

[5] Because the letter *l* (in *laṭ*) is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅittva*), the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies to the substitutes (*ādeśa*). Due to this *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitute undergoes the grammatical operation even without depending on the specific rule; that is to say, it simply follows that "as in the original, there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. Alternatively, "not depending on the rule" means not depending on the cause (*nimitta*). The rule stating "when *k* or *ṅ* follows" (*kṅiti*) applies to the substitute just as it does to the original, regardless of whether a cause exists or not. Or else, "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) is independent of the presence of the actual object; one need not consider whether the letter *ṅ* actually belongs to this [substitute].

Furthermore, substitution (*sthānivadbhāva*) in every respect is not applicable here, because it is not a rule conditioned by an *al* (vowel or consonant). For example, in *pradīvyet*, there is an absence of *utva* due to the presence of a *val* (consonant). If this were so, then *guṇa* would apply in the case of the suffix *lyap*. Therefore, the following is explained here: the prohibition applies when that which depends on the substituendum (*sthānin*) does not depend on an *al*. However, an *anubandha* does not exist at all in the substituendum; for it is a formal agreement (*pratijñā*) that whatever is designated as an *it* does not exist here. But a *val* is present in the substituendum, and therefore the prohibition takes effect.

Even so, there must be a grammatical quality (*guṇa*) here. For it is stated in the third chapter: "When *pi* is not present, *ṅit* does not become *pit*; and when *ṅit* is present, *pi* does not become *ṅit*. In that context, in the form *acinavam*, because of the *ṅit*-ness, the *pit*-ness does not occur; and because of the *pit*-ness, the *ṅit*-ness does not occur. Thus, once both *pit*-ness and *ṅit*-ness have been eliminated, the *guṇa* based on the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is indeed established. It is maintained that this is the interpretation of the author of the Bhāṣya, and not that of the author of the Vārttika.

[5.1] It is established by the statement that *yāsuṭ* is marked with the *ṅit* designation. Since the optative (*liṅ*) is *ṅit*, its substitutes are also necessarily *ṅit*; and since *yāsuṭ* is a part (*bhakta*) of those [substitutes], its *ṅit*-status is established. However, the Teacher perceives that there is no *ṅit*-status [for *yāsuṭ*] because of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original); therefore, he initiates the *ṅit*-designation for *yāsuṭ*. If this is what is being indicated, how is it that [the rules] "always [there is elision] of a *ṅit* [optative ending]" and "also after [a root ending in] *i*" (A 3.4.99, 100) apply? To this, it is objected: for it is not described there in that way—that there is elision of a *ṅit* substitute.

If this were understood in such a way, then in forms like *pacāvaḥ* and *pacanti*, there would be elision [of the augment]. How, then, [should it be understood]? It means "those which are the parasmaipada suffixes belonging to the lakāra that has an indicatory letter ṅ. In that case, how can it be said: "If this is being indicated, how is it that [the rules] ‘nityaṃ ṅitaḥ’ and ‘itaś ca’ apply"? This is the intended meaning: because the augment *yāsuṭ* has the indicatory letter ṅ, the ṅ-ness of the prohibition that applies [to it] is effectively negated, provided that the designation of ṅ-ness for the substituend itself is not abolished.

Surely, the letter *ṇ* alone does not receive the designation [of being *ṅit*]; rather, it is by means of that [designation] that the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* is stated. And for what purpose is this made *ṅit*? It is for the sake of understanding specific grammatical operations, namely: "The *sūyuṭ* [augment] follows the *liṅ*" (A 3.4.102) and "In the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*, the augment *aṭ* is acute" (A 6.4.71).

That which is an operation conditioned by *ṅ* does not occur; that which is an operation conditioned by *ṅit* does occur. Just as the meaning of the rule is that there is no substitution for a *ṅit* *l*-suffix, so too in that case there is no status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), yet the designation itself is not abolished. If it is asked why this is so—it is because of the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is *ṅit*. For one should not postulate what cannot be inferred.

And it cannot be assumed that because a certain type of grammatical operation occurs when a suffix is marked with *ṅ*, that same type of operation does not occur when *yāsuṭ* is present. But surely, once the substitute has taken effect, there is a reference to the *ik* vowel in the genitive case (*ikaḥ ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśaḥ*) when it is marked with *ṅ*; however, in that case where the designation "*ṅit*" applies, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvaḥ*) does not exist. This being so, both are accommodated: the *ṅittva* of *yāsuṭ*, as well as this [rule] "nityaṃ ṅitaḥ" and "itaś ca."

Otherwise, where would this [designation] exist? The entire designation of *ṅit* would be cut off due to its being a *liṅga* (indicative mark). Furthermore, what purpose would there be for *yāsuṭ* [being marked as *ṅit*]? [The purpose is] the prohibition [of guna and vṛddhi] by the rule *kṅiti*, and the occurrence of *saṃprasāraṇa*. Moreover, the mention of "that which causes it" (*tannimitta*) could be abandoned. Therefore, the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* is merely an inference; because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no actual *ṅit*-ness.

As for the designation that the *lakāra* is *ṅit*, its removal serves as the indicator (*liṅga*) for this [point], which he explains as follows: "Indeed, *yāsuṭ* is insufficient for the *ṅit*-ness of the whole. It is "insufficient," meaning incapable. If it is incapable when the *ṅit*-ness of the whole is to be effected, then by virtue of *yāsuṭ* being *ṅit*, the prohibition "before a *kṅit*" would not apply to the whole, and thus there would be no prohibition of *guṇa*. Furthermore, since the *ṅit*-ness of the whole exists through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* is redundant.

But surely, since a marker (*liṅga*) applied to a constituent becomes a qualifier for the whole, the *yāsuṭ* alone would be sufficient for the *ṅit*-status of the whole? It is replied: there is a view in the grammatical treatise that augments (*āgama*) are incapable [of affecting the status of the whole]. For instance, in the rule "ṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca" (A 4.3.23), although the *ṭit*-status of the affixes is already established by the *ṭit*-marking of the augment *tuṭ*, why are the two affixes themselves stated to be *ṭit*? Otherwise, there would indeed be a fault: [the undesired feminine form] *agnicit brāhmaṇī*.

Because *tuka* is marked with the *ugit* designation, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply to the entire complex (*samudāya*) as being *ugit*. This is not a fault. By the statement, “The rule ‘*ugit*’ is established for [stems] other than verbal roots (*adhātuḥ*) because of the inclusion of the root *añc-*” (A 4.1.6, Vārttika 3), the form ‘*ukhāsrad brāhmaṇī*’ will not even arise. However, in this case, ‘*paṭhitā vidyā*’, since the augment *iṭ* is marked with the *ṭi*-designation, *ṅīp* would result. And this is the correct principle: that when an augment (*āgama*) is a qualifier of the whole (*samudāya*) by virtue of having no other scope (*anavakāśa*), it serves its purpose only in the application of that specific rule, and nothing more.

It is stated that both the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the prohibition of *guṇa* can be accomplished; thus it is said: "And *yāsuṭ* is not sufficient for the *ṅit*-designation of the entire complex" (5.2). Others explain this as follows: the meaning of "always for a *ṅit*" (*nityaṃ ṅitaḥ*) is that this operation applies to those substitutes which are *ṅit*. Why then does it not occur in forms such as *pacāvaḥ* and *pacanti*? To this it is replied there: "A *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *P* is treated like a *ṅit*" (*sārvadhātukam apit ṅidvat*). Since the suffix *-vat* occurs in the sense of a locative (*saptamyarthe*), this mention of *yāsuṭ* being like a *ṅit* refers to that previous extension (*atideśa*) which treats what precedes as if it were *ṅit*.

In one case, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there exists the designation "having a *ṅ* marker" (*ṅit*); thus, there is a reference by the genitive case [in the rule *nityaṃ ṅitaḥ*]. However, in the case where the designation "when a *ṅit* [suffix follows]" (*ṅiti*) applies, there is no status of being a substitute. This being so, both are accommodated: the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* and this [rule] "always [the substitution occurs] when a *ṅit* [suffix follows]. Otherwise, where would this [prohibition] "not when a *ṅit*" (*akṅitaḥ*) apply? It is inferred that if every designation as *ṅit* were to be severed on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

[5.3] Another’s text: “For *yāsuṭ* is indeed not sufficient for the *ṅit*-ness of the whole. For *yāsuṭ* is thus not sufficient because it is a part (*bhakta*). Alternatively, it is sufficient for the *ṅit*-ness of the whole *yās-ṭ*. The word “*loṅ*” (the augment *luṅ*) is the ellipsis of the sentence. And he makes this [augment] *ṅit*. What is the indicative mark (*liṅga*)? In that case, he accepts this very thing: namely, that *yāsuṭ* is acute (*udātta*) in the *parasmaipada* endings and that the *liṅ* [suffix] is *ṅit*.

Others explain it as follows: by the rule *udātto ṅic ca*, this is extended [by analogy]—that is, operations occur in this [suffix] as if it were marked with the indicator *ṅ*. And if the designation "as if marked with *ṅ*" (*ṅit*) or the resulting operation were obtainable through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), then the act of marking it with *ṅ* would be purposeless.
[This is the context for the rule: *dīrghīvevīṭām* (P. 1.1.6).
[1] Because *dīrghīvevyaḥ* is restricted to the domain of Vedic meters (chandas). Vārttika: For these two, there is no usage in the spoken language (bhāṣā).

And because it follows what is observed. [Vārttika: But is it not the case that even in the spoken language (bhāṣā) one follows only what is observed, according to the principle: "The use of words is prompted by meaning based on common usage"? In that regard, this meaning is explained: "In Vedic literature (chandas), there is conformity with what is observed. Now, this is not an example found in Vedic literature, namely *ādīdhyānam* and *ādīdhyaka*. For the Vedas consist of fixed word-connections. Alternatively, [the reason is] "because it follows what is observed."

Just as compliance is observed on the grounds that "the *guṇa* is not seen," so too is the *guṇa* actually seen; for that reason, compliance must be performed. Now, if you think, "How is it known that the *guṇa* is seen?"—therefore, he demonstrates this by citing *adīdhet* or *adīdhayuḥ*. And since that *guṇa* is indeed seen, it is therefore said to be "on account of the observation of the *guṇa*."

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because of observing the [presence of the] *guṇa*," other such types of *chandasa* (Vedic) forms have also been observed, and compliance with them has been established; this [rule] should also be inserted among them. What, then, was that which was stated? It was the mention of the term *bahula*. For in forms such as *adīdhet* and *adīdhayuḥ*, the *guṇa* is also seen. And this would not be established without an explicit statement, even when the application of the rule (*yoga*) has begun. In *adīdhet*, the *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) from the *laṅ* tense. Similarly, in *adīdhayuḥ*, the *guṇa* is also observed.
"Whatever Prajāpati meditated upon with his mind, that he obtained by means of the *ādhītayajus* formulas; that is why the *ādhītayajus* formulas are called *ādhītayajus*. (Maitrāyaṇī-Saṃhitā, 3.6.4)

In this *Nirukta*, the root *dhyai* is described; for there is this explanatory passage: “Whatever Prajāpati meditated upon (*adhyāyat*) with his mind, he obtained that by means of these [mantras]. Likewise: “Chosen for the office of the *hotṛ*, he, being compassionate, shone forth” (*Ṛgveda* 10.98.7). This too belongs to the root *dhyai*, as it says: “Chosen for the office of the *hotṛ*, being compassionate, he meditated upon (*anvadhyāyat*)” (*Nirukta* 2.12). This being the case, what connection is there for the root *dīdhīṅ* such that it is said to be used because of the observation of its specific quality (*guṇa*)?

This is not a fault. This is indeed the form of the root *dīdhīṅ*, but its meaning is explained by means of another root that has the same sense. Just as the meaning of *kṣaṇoti* is described by *kṣṇauti*: “*Kṣaṇaḥ* [is derived] from *kṣaṇoti*; time becomes worn away (*prakṣṇutaḥ*)” (Nirukta 2.25). For *kṣṇauti* has the action of wasting away (*kṣaya*) as its meaning.

[2] This example would be appropriate for the rejection of *yogavibhāga* (the splitting of a rule). However, even when *yoga* is present, this form "adīdhayuḥ" is not at all defective. [One might object: "This guna substitution in the context of *jusi* falls within the scope of the prohibition. This is not a fault. It subverts that which is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And what is of the same class? That which is dependent on an affix (*pratyayāśraya*). For with that, it shares the same time-period (*tulyakālatā*).

But how is it that this negation—which does not depend on a suffix and relies solely on the *prakṛti*—having operated due to its being *antaraṅga*, is subsequently sublated by the *guṇa* substitution [of *u* for *v*] before the *jus* suffix? It might be thought: "The negation cannot occur without a suffix. Even if that were so, nevertheless, there is no mention of a suffix here as there is in the case of the word [in *śabdavat*].

Alternatively, [the phrase] "by which it has not been reached" means: by which [rule] it has not been reached (*nāptā*), by which it has not been occasioned (*nāprasakta*), or by which reason that [subsequent] rule sublates it. Why? Because with respect to that [earlier rule], it has no scope (*anavakāśatvāt*). However, that which applies both when [the other rule] has been reached and when it has not been reached possesses scope with respect to it; for that subject matter which has not been occupied is its domain. This, however, is possible only in consideration of the mutual operation of the grammatical rules (*śāstra*).

But when there is a simultaneous coordination of multiple treatises, then the application of those multiple treatises is required simultaneously; because there is no room for them all at once, everything is sublated. Even when there is the apprehension of a mere effect, since every object is occupied by that effect, it results in nothing but sublation.

[3] How is it that *dīdhyat* occurs? A single instance has been presented here by way of illustration. However, in some places, the form is used with the prefix *ni*: "The vital breath of Indra is established (*ni dhīdhyat*) in every limb" (*Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* 1.2.17). In the absence of such a grammatical connection (*yoga*), the *guṇa* substitution would apply, resulting in *dīdhayat*. The form *dīdhyat* occurs through the application of the *śyan* suffix by means of transposition (*vyatyaya*). (Vārttika 2).

Because *śyan* has the marker *n*, it is udātta on its first syllable; because it has the marker *ṅ*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa*; after the elision by *ayīvarṇayoḥ* (A 7.4.53), there is also the *nighāta* accent by *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (A 8.1.28). Similarly, in the case of *śe* as well, since *guṇa* is prohibited due to the *ṅ* marker, and after the *nighāta* and the substitution of *yaṇ*, the result is the same. And thus some read: *dīdhyad* [and] *śa* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). For those whose reading is *śap* by way of transposition, *guṇa* would also apply.

Now, how is it here [in the case of the word *dīdhyat*] in the passage: “He offers while meditating with the mind” (*manasā dīdhyaj juhoti*, Mai-Saṃ 3.6.4)? This is a form ending in the suffix *śatṛ*. Here, if the suffix *śyan* were applied, the augment *num* would have to occur by the rule “*ugidacām...*” (A 7.1.70), because that [suffix *śyan*] intervenes [between the root and the *num*]. But the accent is established by virtue of the *nit*-designation. Alternatively, if the suffix *śa* is applied, there is no fault; for since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed after a root taught with a short *a* vowel (*adupadeśāt*), it receives the grave accent (*nighāta*) according to A 6.1.186, and once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, the prohibition of *num* applies by the rule “*nābhyastāc chatuḥ*” (A 7.1.78).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of a transposition of the suffix" (*śabdavyatyayena*), even so, this "transposition" (*vyatyaya*) is described as follows: by the transposition—that is, by the displacement—of the *śap* suffix, according to the rule "the *śap* is elided after roots beginning with *ad*" (*adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ*, A 2.4.72), the form is established. For in that case, when there is displacement, there is immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) to the *śatṛ* suffix. While the term *iṭ* is still in force, the rule "there is no *iṭ* before a *kṛt* suffix ending in *vaś*" (*neḍ vaśi kṛti*, A 7.2.8) contains a repetition of the word *iṭ* for this purpose: that the *iṭ* remains as *iṭ* itself; it does not undergo any other form. It persists in its unaltered form.

That which is the operation pertaining to the *aṅga* is restricted. The term *aṅgasya* is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. Therefore, regarding that which is stated as "of the *aṅga*," the form *iṭ* is not excluded. How is it grasped? It occurs by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacanāt*). How is it that in *pipaṭhīṃṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "sāntamahataḥ" (A 6.4.10) does not apply? Because of the restriction "of the *aṅgas*," [the condition for that rule is not met].

But surely, *num* should not occur here by the rule "of a neuter [stem] ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or a vowel (*ac*)" (A 7.1.72). Once *num* has been applied, when the *lopa* of the *at* [augment] is performed by A 6.4.48, the status of ending in a *jhal* consonant no longer exists because of the *sthānivadbhāva* [principle]. If that is so, then it will apply as "ending in a vowel (*ajanta*). Even this, however, is a new injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) stating that *num* follows immediately after the final vowel (*midaco 'ntyāt parasya*).

Even so, because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the letter *i* does not become the final element; therefore, the rule "midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.47) does not apply. Consequently, the form must be "pipaṭhiṣi brahmaṇakulāni."

Alternatively, length (*dīrghatva*) is unestablished; because it is unestablished, there will be no restriction. Since length does not exist in this treatise, this [form] remains in its unmodified state, while the modified form occurs only in actual usage (*prayoga*). In that case, however, this fault is observed: forms such as *alāvīt* and *apāvīt* would not be obtained. It might be thought: "This is a substitute for both the vowel with *iṭ* and the vowel without *iṭ*. But that is not so. Here, when two things are indicated by the genitive case, that which occurs in place of them receives the designation of either one.
Therefore, this very point appears more authoritative: that which is to be performed is restricted by its own specific context.
"Consonants not separated by vowels constitute a *saṃyoga* (conjunct). (Pāṇini 1.1.7)

[1] How is this understood? From what does the question arise? First of all, the sense of "support" (*āśraya*) for sound is untenable, because the word *anantara* (immediate/without interval) has been heard [in the sūtra]. The question arises because the word *antara* has multiple meanings; for it is seen to be used in the senses of "interval," "space," "external connection," and "clothing. Since these [other meanings] are possible, [if one assumes it means] "interval," this is not a valid question.

Regarding the term *anantarā*: how is this to be understood? It refers to those for whom there is no *antara*. *Antara*, *vivara*, *chidra*, and *madhya* are synonyms. But what kind of gap (*vivara*) belongs to a word? It is the intervening time devoid of phonemes (*varṇa*). Or alternatively, it means "those for whom there is no *antara* in between. In this case, the second [interpretation] would apply; we shall explain its refutation later. According to some texts: "those for whom there is no *antara* existing"—in this view, the second [interpretation] simply does not occur at all.

But why should this phrase *vigrahapada* (the word for the analytical statement) be recited subsequently? He says: "No. What then? This is what he asks: there are these two words, *halo 'nantarāḥ*. One occurs with a referent (*anyapadārtha*) qualified by a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) that is not a real entity; the other occurs with a substratum that is not excluded and which does not require a superstratum (*ādheya*). Alternatively, this is a single word possessing multiple powers (*anekaśakti*). Depending on the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), one must determine which word is being relied upon and which power it possesses.

In the case of an *avagraha*, the designation of a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) would not apply. For example, in *apsu* [which is analyzed as] *ap-su*, there is indeed an interval here; for an *avagraha* is held to have the duration of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*). Having paused for the duration of half a mora, another phoneme is uttered. What, then, would be the fault? [The fault is that] the protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed by Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.86, *guror anṛto ’nantyasya*, would not occur. But surely, there is no connection between the word expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇavācin*) and the terms *anṛt* and so forth? If that were the case, then [the rule] would not apply in *apsavya*.

Let it be such that there is no fault; this treatise follows the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). In this regard, one should adhere to it in such a way that it does not contradict the activity of the learned. Thus, there is neither a fault nor a purpose [for the application of the term]. Alternatively, the designation of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) might be adopted for the sake of removing a fault, or for the sake of engaging in a specific purpose. However, since there is no fault when it is not applied here, nor any purpose when it is applied, the designation of "conjunction" does not apply at all in this case.

But was it not said: "In *avagraha*, there would be no protracted vowel (*pluta*), as in *apsavya*"? They do not accept an *avagraha* in this case. Even in grammar, there is no rule for an *avagraha* to be applied within a single word; for in grammar, there is only *saṃhitā* and *asaṃhitā*.

Others describe it thus: just as in the expression *paramavācā*, the term *vāk* receives the designation *bha* by virtue of the continued application of the rule *tadādi subantaṃ ca* (Mahābhāṣya 1.167.1–2), so too the word *ap* [should receive the designation *bha*] by the rule *yaci*. This is not correct, because of the intervention; for here the word *ap* is intervened upon, whereas the word *vāk* is immediate.

In that case, however, this would not be obtained in the forms *apsuyoniḥ* and *apsumatiḥ*, because the elision (*aluk*) has been applied by the rule *apo yoniyanmatiṣu* (A 6.3.1, vā. 7). Even here, there is no *avagraha*. For it is recited thus: "The end of compound words is subject to *avagraha*. And a compound word consists of a nominal stem together with a case-ending (*sup*), not the word *ap-* alone.

[2] Furthermore, in the technical treatise (*śāstra*), the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is connected with each [individual member], except where there is an expression of accompaniment (*sahavacana*). However, "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is for the purpose of indication; those indicated by immediacy should be understood as receiving the designation individually.
