[1.3] Here they raise an objection: If the letter *ś* is included under the term *ac* by virtue of being grasped by the vowel *i*, then just as it receives the prohibition of *ac*-operations, why is this [rule] not also understood? That is, [why does the rule] "when followed by a vowel (*aci*), a consonant (*śara*) does not become doubled" (A 8.4.49) not apply, while [the rule] "and when not followed by a vowel (*anaci*), it becomes doubled" (A 8.4.47) does? And would doubling not also fail to occur here because of that [prohibition]? To this, they offer the following resolution: This [rule] "and when not followed by a vowel" (*anaci ca*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), meaning "in something other than a vowel. And this [consonant *ś*] is indeed something other than a vowel.

This is incorrect; for it is not possible to establish this regarding technical designations (*saṃjñā*). Here, the letter *ś* is both a consonant (*hal*) and a vowel (*ac*). If it were stated that [a rule] must apply when there is something other than a vowel (*acaḥ*), one might ask whether the letter *ś* is excluded or not excluded. Without doubt, it would not be excluded, even in an injunction concerning a single meaning, because it is understood in whatever meaning it occurs.

Regarding the statement, "Let those who are not sitting in the palace be brought," should they be brought because they reside on the ground, or should they not be brought because they cannot be designated as "residents of the palace" since they are distinct from those who reside in the palace? Likewise, regarding the spotted goat: when it is said, "Should one sacrifice a non-black [animal], or should one sacrifice a pure white one?"—is it to be sacrificed or not to be sacrificed? It is not to be sacrificed.

In this way, however, the threefold nature of the *śakāra* is indeed established by logic here. How so? For it has been stated: "In the rule concerning prohibition (*pratiṣedhasūtra*), there is no prohibition because this prohibition itself is not yet fully established; but elsewhere in the *pratyāhāra*, the prohibition certainly exists. From what, then, does its status as a vowel (*actva*) follow in the prescription for doubling (*dvirvacana*)? Therefore, an effort must be made so that the *ikāra* here in the *pratyāhāra* does not include the *śakāra*.

For when there is a perception [of a sound], it is evident that the perception of the letter *ś* exists elsewhere; and this has been introduced on the grounds that this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). And having done so, the sentence is recited: "There is a prohibition regarding *ac* and *hal*. He says "prohibition" with reference to the *prasajya-pratiṣedha*.

If it were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then since there would be no rule whatsoever that either prescribes or prohibits *aj* and *hal* in the statements "those with equal place of articulation and effort are homogeneous" (*tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*) and "not *aj* and *hal*" (*nāj jhalau*), there would be no fault; for, by excluding *aj* and *hal* from one another, the designation of homogeneity (*savarṇasaṃjñā*) would apply between vowels (*ac*) and between consonants (*hal*).

[2] It is established that there is no [application of the rule] due to the absence of effort (*anactvāt*). Because of the difference in the articulatory effort (*prayatna*) residing within the mouth, there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*); since that [homogeneity] does not exist, what is the use of a prohibition? Thus, the resolution is stated by means of the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the sūtra. However, according to how it is recited by the followers of Pāṇini—either "the term *īṣat* is supplied in both cases" or "it is excluded in both cases"—he states the resolution accordingly:

[2.1] Or, because the sentence is not yet complete (*vākyāparisamāpteḥ*). [The statement] "there is no grasping" means that this sentence is said to be incomplete because its meaning is not fully established, just as the rule *aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (A 1.1.69) is said to be incomplete. But how is this sentence incomplete? Because its two constituent parts have not been determined. These two are the parts of the sentence: *aṇ* and *savarṇasya*. When these two are determined—such that one knows "this is *aṇ*" and "this is *savarṇaḥ*"—then there is grasping.

In this regard, it has no function with respect to the inclusion of these—namely, the *upadeśa*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), and the *pratyāhāra*. As long as the form *aṇ* is uttered, such as in the rule "aṇuditsavarṇasya," there is no inclusion [of the homogeneous sounds]. How much less so where these forms are merely expedient means? For at the time of their *upadeśa*, these are not homogeneous (*asavarṇa*).

The statement that "the designation *savarṇa* does not apply after the time of *pratyāhāra*" does not intend the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). What then? It refers to the order of operation (*pravṛttikrama*), namely the sequence in rule A 1.1.69 (*aṇuditsavarṇasya ca*) consisting of both "aṇ" and "of the *savarṇa*. Just as there is no grasping [of a phoneme] in the case of the *upadeśa* and so forth because its form has not yet been established, likewise, since the *savarṇa* is not yet determined, the operation of grasping cannot take place.

When the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneity) has been understood as being both inclusive (*sotsarga*) and restrictive (*sāpavāda*), then it will also serve as a grasper by virtue of *savarṇa*-status in other instances designated as *actva* (vowel-ness). Thus, there is neither an inclusion here nor a prohibition. In this case, neither the letter *i* nor the letter *ś* is grasped; therefore, the *savarṇa*-designation for the letter *ī* and the letter *ś* is not prohibited. Since the letter *ī* and the letter *ś* are identical, they possess *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity), and consequently, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from *savarṇya* would apply in the example "kumārī śete.
This is precluded by the governing context of *aj* (vowels).

[2.2] In that case, just as the letter *ś* does not include the letter *i*, it would likewise not include the letter *ī*. This is the view held: wherever there is a designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), there the circularity (*cakraka*) applies. There is no inclusion [of a sound] even in the original instruction (*upadeśa*) of the letters themselves; for those letters are employed for this very purpose.

Just as a jar does not exist at all in the state of being potsherds, how could there be any specific effect (*kāryaviśeṣa*) for it? As for those rules such as *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), they do not have that [jar] as their purpose; why then would this [jar] not be included as having that as its purpose? Therefore, by this means he explains that in this context there is inclusion, while in that context there is non-inclusion.

[2.3] Another says: All of this is the same; however, there is this much distinction: for the proof (*siddhi*), the absence of a reason (*ahetutva*) is the cause, while for the absence of a reason, the non-completion of the sentence is the cause. But here, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is different, he says that a variation of the reason (*hetuvikalpa*) is not tenable.

In this view, the [previous] position is rendered untenable; however, this [present position] is established. The intention is that the remainder of the sentence will be supplied for the sake of an alternative interpretation of the thesis. Alternatively, it is established because the sentence is not yet complete, or because the letter *ś* is grasped by the letter *i*. But surely there is a difference [between the two]? This is stated while conceding the difference produced by the audible sound (*śruti*).

"Vibhāṣā" means "optionally. The rule *A 8.4.45*, "yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā," is understood to apply here. How could this not be a distinction? The meaning is that there certainly is a distinction. The other says: If the elision were obligatory (*nitya*), then there would be a distinction.

However, that elision is optional (*vibhāṣā*). The rule *A 8.4.62*, "jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām," is understood to apply here. If this is so, then the treatise remains established in such a way that there is no distinction between us. According to the explanation of others: while the position remains at the point "How could this not be a distinction?", the other says:
It would be so if the elision were permanent; indeed, there would be a distinction if the elision were permanent. Thus ends the fourth lesson in the commentary of Bhartṛhari.
The Fifth Āhnika in the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā.
*īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* // Pāṇini 1.1.11 // Dual endings with *ī*, *ū*, and *e* are *pragṛhya*.

[1] Although in cases such as *īd* and so forth, specific individual instances (*vyakti*) are heard, and although in the case of a rule prescribing the word-form (*svarūpa-vidhi*), the very word being uttered causes the meaning to be understood and is itself grasped as the object to be conveyed because it possesses two powers (*dviśakti*), and although another word can be imitated through imitation due to its identical phonetic form—nevertheless, because they are inseparable, one relies upon the universal (*sāmānya*) while setting aside the specific features (*viśeṣa*) that have been presented; or else, the application of the term would be directed solely toward the specific features.

Both possibilities arise here: if there is an intention to express the generic form (*ākṛti*), then by abandoning the distinction [of individuals] and resorting to the universal, this inclusion of *t* (in *tapara*) would serve to delimit the generic form from other individuals that possess different times; or, if there is an intention to express the individual (*vyakti*), then even when other individuals possessing different times or endowed with other qualities are resorted to as the referents, this [inclusion of *t*] is also appropriate for the purpose of excluding them.

First, regarding the generic form (*ākṛti*), the exclusion of short vowels is established precisely because of the greater effort required [for their production], and the inclusion of protracted (*pluta*) vowels is desired. For if it were otherwise, the use of *t* as a marker (*tapara*) would result in an unintended consequence. Furthermore, regarding the individual phoneme (*vyakti*), since forms such as *anaṅ* are mentioned by their own words, it has been proven that even though they depend on pronunciation, accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and others do not cause differentiation. Therefore, he asks: "For what purpose is the designation *pragṛhya* stated for *it* and the others which have *t* as a marker?"

Relying on the intention to express individuality (*vyaktivivakṣā*), he states that the accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and others are indeed differentiators: *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70). This is so that there may be the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) having the same duration as the one followed by *t*. But how can the acute and other accents be differentiators, given that the author of the *Cūrṇi* has stated that the mention of the acute accent for [the vowels] beginning with *ā* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of their non-differentiating nature? This was stated by the author of the Vārttika: “The addition of *t* after the long *ā* is for the sake of including its homogeneous sounds, because the accent is a differentiator. (Vārttika on A 1.1.1)

Alternatively, for one who has stated [in Vārttika 1 on A 1.1.69], “The [term] *savarṇa* [is used] because of the differences in vowel quality (*svarabheda*), nasalization (*anunāsikyabheda*), and duration (*kālabheda*),” it is intended that [the vowels] are indeed differentiators (*bhedaka*). Furthermore, since the author of the Sūtras employs the term *aṇ* with respect to *savarṇa*, and because of the connection with their own respective vowels, it is inferred that they also possess the status of being differentiators. As for *anaṅ* and the others, if there is an intention to express the generic form (*ākṛti*) despite they being udātta, then it is possible to understand them as being without gender (*aliṅga*). Whose is this opinion?

For if *tapara* were applied, there would be no comprehension of other homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) associated with a different duration, because of the rule stating "that which has that [specific] duration. This refers to the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*) accents. Others also maintain that the mention of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel applies to others as well; however, vowels such as *ī*, *ū*, and *ṛ* cannot possibly be nasalized, because of the prohibition of nasality for those falling within the scope of the *pragṛhya* designation. This was mentioned incidentally.

[2] However, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply to protracted (*pluta*) vowels. This fault does not arise because of the inclusion of the marker *t* (in Pāṇini’s rule 1.1.70). Why then? Because of the acceptance of the individual entity (*vyakti*) as the referent of the word. The protracted vowel is not established; since it is unestablished, they retain only their original duration. But surely, because the protracted vowel is unestablished, its three-moraic nature (*trimātratā*) would not exist? And since its having that duration was already precluded, how can it come to be again when it is non-existent? This is not a fault, because of the understanding that it is unestablished only within the technical system (*śāstra*).

And since there is no cessation [of the application of rules], it is understood that they apply at that very time. The cognition regarding the application or non-application of words based on the technical treatise remains, in the absence of such a treatise for the instructor, solely in its natural form as the object to be conveyed.

Furthermore, prior to the statement of the rule [declaring non-application], since the doctrine of non-establishment (*asiddha*) has not yet taken effect, the original element (*sthānin*) has not ceased to exist and the substitute (*ādeśa*) has not yet arisen. Thus, even when a rule has been applied, if it subsequently attains the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by virtue of a specific injunction, then the cognition regarding the object of operation (*lakṣya*), which was previously proceeding in one way, now proceeds in the opposite manner: it again relies upon the original element as being present and the substitute as being absent.

And so he will say: "In the case of the designation *pragṛhya* before the vowel *m*, because that [substitute] is unestablished, the fault of the undesired application of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ay* does not arise."

Now, one might object: when the treatise is active for the sake of accomplishing its own purpose while its effect is not yet accomplished, then the treatise—being established in its nature as a communicator within the treatise itself—would be understood as unestablished. But once the activity of the treatise has ceased after the meaning of the treatise has been understood, the treatise has naturally withdrawn because its purpose has been fulfilled; how then could it be made known by verbal statement to be unestablished? At that time, since the effect exists, it is appropriate to rely on the "unestablishedness" of the effect.

And thus, because the original form (*sthānin*) no longer exists, its temporal status [as being "before" or "after"] does not exist. This is not a fault. Even when the grammatical treatise has ceased after having conveyed its own meaning, when that [meaning] is resorted to as something established (*siddha*), then it must necessarily be resorted to as having been taught by the treatise. For without following the treatise, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of even *ay* and other such forms would be indistinguishable; therefore, they are not resorted to [independently].

Thus, just as during the stage of the scripture's operation, when the non-establishment of the scripture is recognized, the cognition regarding the function of the scripture ceases due to the absence of its cause, so too, whenever an action is required to be followed according to the scripture, at that very time the scripture itself must be relied upon; therefore, it is logical to maintain its non-establishment [in that specific context].

Therefore, when the designation *pragṛhya* is to be prescribed upon the occurrence of a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, at that time the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) that establishes the protracted vowel is not yet established; consequently, even though the protracted vowel has not been formally prescribed, the form of the original element (*sthānin*) remains unaltered. Thus, because it possesses the same duration (*kālatva*), the *pragṛhya* designation is established.

[3] The protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established. . . . Since this [rule] teaches the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the protracted vowel, and since there would be no preservation of the original form if the protracted vowel were not established—given its non-established status—a vocalic sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*) would necessarily apply to it; therefore, the preservation of the original form must certainly be stated. We do not say that an effort must be made for the sake of the preservation of the original form; rather, because [the protracted vowel] is non-established, such a basis as “the protracted vowel is by its original form” would otherwise be untenable, yet it is indeed respected.
Therefore, it is inferred from proximity that the protracted vowel is indeed established.

But surely, one can necessarily infer the presence [of a rule] only in that domain where the prescription of an operation for a protracted vowel (*pluta*) would otherwise be untenable without its being established. By this, the protracted vowel would be established as having *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of its original form) alone, and not merely for the sake of vowel-sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*). And so he will say: “And establishment [is attained] through dependence, as in the case of *ru* before *utva*” (A 1.1.12 Vārttika 4).

This is true; thus, in this regard, three possibilities arise: either the inference of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) is established by the fact that it has been accomplished within the context of *pluta* [vowels], or it pertains to the section on vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*), or it should be understood that *prakṛtibhāva* applies only to those substituends (*sthānin*) for which there is no *pluta*. Even in the case of inference, when a sentence is being inferred, is the sentence inferred as pertaining to what is established by a single rule (*ekayoga*), or as pertaining to what is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*)?

There is indeed inference based on what is seen specifically (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) and that based on what is seen generally (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). In both cases, for one who has grasped the relationship, there is no deviation from the primary denotation. This is the distinction: when there is a single object of application, the meaning that is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) is itself inferred. However, in the case of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) within a specific context, although there is an inference of the general concomitant, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is nonetheless relied upon.

However, if it is understood as "plutabhūyiṣṭhāḥ," then even though the word *pluta* functions in a non-primary sense, nevertheless nothing unmentioned need be inferred anywhere. Thus, relying here on the mark (*liṅga*) of general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), a sentence pertaining to the context is inferred: "The *pluta* is established in vowel-sandhis (*svarasaṃdhiṣu*). Furthermore, he shows that there is brevity in this interpretation: the expression "from a non-*pluta*, [after] a non-*pluta*" need not be stated.

For once the *pluta* vowel is established, because it does not belong to that same time [of the preceding rule], it will not serve as the cause for the substitution of *ut*; thus, following the principle that "technical names and paribhāṣās function according to their enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*), he asks: "What follows from the fact that the *pluta* is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasaṃdhi*)? This is not a vowel-sandhi, for this designation of *pragṛhya* is prescribed in a different section.

[4] And it is established in the rule for assigning technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*). How so? Because "the rules for technical names and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is to be performed. This means that the application of technical names is prompted by a grammatical operation; without being subordinate to a grammatical operation, a technical name cannot attain its own purpose. In cases such as *bhavati* and *pacati*, if the technical names *ac* (vowel) and so forth were not applied to the sounds *a* and so on, nothing would be expressed. Furthermore, a grammatical treatise cannot function without a purpose; therefore, the technical names *ac* and so forth do not apply here [in the context of the word *bhavati*].

However, even for technical designations (*saṃjñā*) whose application is restricted to specific locations, there are cases where, in order to establish their status as subordinate members (*aṅga*) across many principal locations, they are prescribed as being "for all purposes" (*sarvārthā*) by being extracted from their context (*prakaraṇotkarṣa*) and not connected to any particular rule. But this [designation *pragṛhya*] acquires its very existence only within the scope of its specific location. Therefore, even when it is recited elsewhere, the designation *pragṛhya* is understood to be situated within the context of the section on vowel sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*).

In some cases, because there is no distinction [between the *pluta* vowel and other vowels], he asks: "But what is the purpose of stating that the *pluta* vowel receives the designation *pragṛhya*? With reference to where there is a distinction, he says: "So that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) dependent on being *pragṛhya* may occur. He shows the very same lack of distinction intended previously in some cases: "Let it not be thus—that 'the *pragṛhya* [vowel] remains in its original form'—but rather let it be 'the *pluta* [vowel] remains in its original form. There is no distinction whatsoever regarding the preservation of the original form."

Where the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prohibited, there the preservation of the original form based on a *pragṛhya* designation must necessarily be intended; thus he says: "It cannot be so, for a fault would arise when [the protracted vowel] is present. For example, in *agnī3iti*: when the preservation of the original form based on the protracted vowel is prohibited by the rule *aplutavad upasthite* (Pāṇini 6.1.129), if the *pragṛhya* designation were not applied, then even the preservation of the original form based on that *pragṛhya* status would not exist, and consequently, the rules for vowel sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*) would apply.

But when the designation *pragṛhya* is indeed present, once the [application of] *pluta* has been prohibited, the *prakṛtibhāva* based on the *pragṛhya* status occurs. In this regard, one might think that *prakṛtibhāva* is not intended here at all; for that reason, he says: "The teacher will indeed state: ‘The mention of *vat* is for the purpose of prohibiting the operation of *pluta*; for if there were a prohibition of *pluta*, it would follow that even the *pragṛhya-pluta* is prohibited, since it is prescribed by another rule’” (A 6.1.129 Vārttika 1, 2).

If only the *pluta* were prohibited, then even for that *pragṛhya* which is *pluta*, once its three-mora nature (*trimātratā*) has ceased, there would be the hearing of it as having two morae (*dvimātra*). However, when the *prakṛtibhāva* dependent on the *pluta* is prohibited, only that *pluta* which is not *pragṛhya* undergoes vowel-sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*), as in *devadattā3* becoming *devadatta*.

But as for that which is a *pragṛhya*, even though its treatment as a *pluta* is prohibited, once the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-modification) based on its *pragṛhya* status has been applied, the perception of it as having three morae (*trimātra*) becomes possible. Therefore, there is a purpose for assigning the *pragṛhya* designation to a *pluta*. And that [designation] does not apply [to a *pluta*] because of the acceptance of the individual entity (*vyakti*) as the referent of the word.

[5] But if, on the other hand, the designation *pragṛhya* were stated for long vowels followed by *t* (as in *ataparāṇām*), why then does this fault arise from the inclusion of *t* (*taparatva*), such that it is said: "But if, on the other hand, for the long [vowels]"? This fault arises because of the acceptance of the individual entity (*vyakti*) as the word-meaning. Regarding this, some say: he says exactly this; if, setting aside the individual entity, the [designation] were stated for the long vowel when the class-characteristic (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, then because of the greater effort [required], there would be no application to the short vowels.

There might be the status of *pragṛhya* for a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, and likewise, it might serve as a substitute for a short vowel; therefore, he says "of those not followed by *a*" (*ataparāṇām*). But the other [teacher] says that this was stated by the latter [Vārttikakāra] with reference to the manifest phoneme (*vyakti*) as the referent of the word: "Even so, only the phoneme *e* would include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), but the phonemes *ī* and *ū* would not include them, because they are not *aṇ*."

Alternatively, since for someone the word-meaning is indeed the individual (*vyakti*), there is the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) by virtue of the functional capacity [of the rule]; thus he says, "If, however... The other [opponent] says that even so, a certain fault does not cease; thus he says, "Even so... Another says: even for long vowels, vowel-operations (*ackārya*) such as those in "aṇo 'pragṛhyasya... (A 8.4.57) and so forth are observed.

Therefore, it has been stated that "if, however, [the rule] *aṇ* applies to long vowels followed by their own stops (*ataparāṇām*)," then in the rule *aṇ-savarṇasya* as well, it ought to be exactly the same. Elsewhere too, long vowels receive their operations by means of this [rule] *aṇ-savarṇasya*. In the science of technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*), there is no other definition-rule for the term *aṇ* than this one; and it is illogical for that very definition-rule of *aṇ* to operate upon itself.

Without the inclusion of *aṇ*, that which remains would be unable to effect the inclusion [of the sounds] because its meaning is incomplete; thus he says: “Even so, *e* is *eka*. But if [it were stated] as “of the short vowels...,” then by virtue of the *tapara* designation (*t* being the final element), the rule would not apply to forms such as *agnī* and *vāyū*. However, since it is not *tapara*, even when the referent is an individual phoneme (*vyakti*), the designation *pragṛhya* is established for the long and protracted vowels by the principle “*aṇ* includes its homogeneous counterparts” (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*). But it would also undesirably apply to the short vowel.

But how, then, is there a plural number here? Some say it is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an irregular residual formation), just as in the case of the rule *prathamayoḥ* (A 6.2.102; 7.1.28). Others, however, state that the distinction arises from the difference in the examples.

[6] If that is so, then what is the purpose of this effort [to establish] that "the *pluta* vowel is established in vowel-sandhis"? How is it that [this rule] was stated as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark)? The *jñāpaka* is explained otherwise: [it indicates that] one who is about to become a *pluta* (*plutabhāvī*) undergoes the *pluta* [vowel], or that for whom a *pluta* is about to occur (*pluto bhāvī asya*). Or, [it indicates that] one who is about to become a *pluta* undergoes the [operation], or that for whom a *pluta* occurs. [The term] "one who is about to become a *pluta*" (*plutabhāvinaḥ*) refers to the very substituend (*sthānin*) undergoing the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi). Under this interpretation, a sentence not explicitly heard need not be inferred.

By means of the *paribhāṣā* "asiddham" and by the assumption of a rule for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), both [the rule and its exception] are supported. Furthermore, this very fact—that he teaches the prohibition "not after a non-protracted vowel, not before a non-protracted vowel"—is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the assumption of the term "guṇa. Now, one might object: even in the case of a protracted substitute, there must first be a dependence upon the status of being produced from a protracted vowel (*plutabhāvitva*) in the original element (*sthānin*). And since that [status] is not established (*asiddha*), it is illogical for there to be a dependence on what is non-existent.

Regarding this, they say: here, in some cases, linguistic usage is carried out by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) with respect to words based on technical treatises (*śāstra*); in other cases, worldly perception (*laukika-darśana*) is relied upon. Thus, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya-doṣa*) is avoided in various instances, as in: "But [the usage] is established because words are eternal" (A 1.1.1, Vārttika 9).

For the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are not produced by the technical name "vṛddhi"; rather, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those existing *ā*, *ai*, and *au* is merely being described. Thus, even though there is no grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) that brings them into existence, their correctness is nevertheless accepted. This being the case, the principle "between that which is taught by a rule and that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ*) would apply. However, in some instances this principle is not resorted to; when words are employed independently of the science of grammar, nothing can be said to be either "taught by a rule" or "taught by its specific form."

But surely, since the relationship of substituendum (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*) does not exist in common worldly usage, the state of being produced as a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is untenable? This is not a fault. For even in the world, the distinction between the domain (*viṣaya*) and the non-domain is determined; that is, it is understood that "this [rule] applies within its own domain. And so it has been said: "Indeed, the application of *ij-ādi* and *yaj-ādi* is observed in the world," and so forth. Furthermore, he will state immediately thereafter: "[The forms] *mārtha*, etc., have the sense of *id-ādi*, etc."

But in this hypothesis, the cognition of a future state would be purposeless, for even the status of being present can be maintained according to worldly perception. Or rather, what is the distinction such that the existence of the *pluta* vowel, which is resorted to for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), is accepted, but not that of the actual subject (*kāryin*)? Regarding this, some say: "True, both the state of being present and the state of being future are possible; however, it is the state of being future that is resorted to here. That is not correct.

For in the absence of a present [application], the state of being future is everywhere respected; moreover, another alternative is possible: that "the technical terms and the paribhāṣās follow the order in which they are enunciated" should be adopted.

[7] Even so, that which is established as the grammatical operation (*kārya*) for the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to the *pluta* vowel, for both technical designations (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the operation is to take effect. Since the *pragṛhya* designation occurs in a location where the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is excluded, the *pluta* vowel is already established there. In that case, because it consists of three morae (*trimātra*), the *pragṛhya* designation would not apply; consequently, in the example *agnī3*, the exclusion of nasalization would not obtain. If this is so, then what is the point of saying "designations and interpretive rules are operative at the time of the operation"?

It will be exactly as stated. But how can this be established by mere assertion? Regarding this, some say: here, the primary elements enter into a relationship with one another even without a quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, due to the difference in the way they assist, two modes of activity are observed among the primary elements: sometimes the king resorts to a location such as a palace, and sometimes locations such as palaces are brought to the king's location.

In that regard, when the operations pertaining to the secondary element (*guṇa*) fall upon a primary element (*pradhāna*) situated in its own place, then the primary element also comes to reside in the location of the secondary element for the sake of accomplishing its own operation, just as the movement of water occurs toward the location of its cause. In that case, when the primary element resides in the location of the secondary element, there is a deviation from the original designation (*ayathoddeśatva*).

But when, for the sake of establishing the status of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) among distinct [rules], there occurs a state of being governed by various sentences—even though [the rule] is not connected with any particular primary [rule]—and when, for the sake of brevity, the distinction is abandoned and a non-distinction is assumed based on a commonality, and when that [non-distinction] is applied through the elevation of the context (*prakaraṇa*) during the instruction of this or that [rule], then for a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or a metarule (*paribhāṣā*) that is disconnected from a primary [rule], there is no function whatsoever to be performed in accordance with its own time, because at some stage...

When there is a dependence characterized by lack of independence due to the innate sequence of the word's operation upon its meaning, there is a tendency toward the principal element; [then], when non-distinction is reached through the principal sentence, there is the principle of "the time of the effect" (*kāryakālatva*).

[8] Others, however, justify this duality in another way: for it is observed that when there are qualities directed toward multiple principal objects—as in the case of garlands, ointments, and so forth—their activity occurs with distinction for each principal object, and yet without distinction when those qualities are presented as being non-distinct. In that context, if one assumes a distinction for each principal object, the state of occurring at the time of the effect is possible only through the assistance of the principals themselves, provided they have not fallen away from their own time.

However, in the case of non-distinct operation, it is impossible for a single quality (*guṇa*), even while established at its own time, to enter into a relationship with multiple primary elements (*pradhāna*). Since the qualities remain within their own selves, dependent upon specific self-refinements (*ātmasaṃskāra*), the primary elements would have to follow the time of the qualities simultaneously; yet this is not the case according to the nature of their respective designations. Thus, neither of these two positions is tenable.

For he will say this: "If, within the seven chapters [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] including the fourteenth (sapādāyāṃ saptādhyāyyāṃ), a chapter or a quarter thereof is not established, then those references in the fifth case and seventh case found here [in the Kātantra]—because of their non-establishment—the rule ‘when [the word] *tasmin* is mentioned, [an operation applies] to what precedes; when *tasmāt* is mentioned, [it applies] to what follows’ would not apply. "This is not a fault," [he replies]. "Even though this is not established there [in the Aṣṭādhyāyī], it is established here [in the Kātantra]. How so? For technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the operation is to be performed (*kāryakālam*)."

In that regard, just as when subordinate elements (*guṇa*) belonging to the time of the action form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhāva*), there is no such thing as "this is established in this" because the designations "prior" and "subsequent" are lost due to their lack of separate function; likewise, when principal elements (*pradhāna*) occupy the same location as the subordinate elements and form a single syntactical unit, the rule for the designation "prior" and "subsequent" is not recognized.

[9] Having thus imagined a fault in both cases, and anticipating the need to demonstrate another purpose for the fault, the question is asked: [a] If it is argued that "the forms beginning with *ī*, *u*, and *ṛ* are *pragṛhya* when they are duals," then this would be a rule applying only to the final [syllable] (*antyasya vidhiḥ*). For example, in *pacete*, the form beginning with *ī* is not a dual; nor indeed is there any single *e*-vowel that is a dual. Thinking thus, he says: "It will be so by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacanāt*). The intention is that the word "dual" (*dvivacana*) is used here in the sense of being a part of a dual.

Just as in the rule *liṅsicau* (A 3.4.103), the term "ātmanepada" is applied to a part of the ātmanepada—namely, the suffix *sīyuṭ* according to *liṅaḥ sīyuṭ* (A 3.4.102)—there is a purpose for such a designation. [What is that purpose? It is in the case of *khaṭve*. Although this is not a primary dual number, nevertheless, by virtue of the principle of "treating the whole as the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*), it receives the designation of a dual. However, in cases such as *trapuṇī* and *jatunī*, because the augment *num* is a portion belonging to the preceding element, it is a primary dual; therefore, it was not cited [as an example].

If it is argued that [the rule] "ending in *ī*, *ū*, etc. applies to a single element, as in *khaṭve* (Vārttika 2), then since such forms can only occur when *ī* and *ū* stand alone, that interpretation is not accepted. But why is the paribhāṣā "as if having an initial and a final" (*ādyantavat*)—which is formulated for no other purpose—not resorted to? It is said in reply: heaviness does not necessarily consist only in the bulk of the text; rather, it may also consist in the heaviness of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*) or the heaviness of the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-gaurava*).

Therefore, in this alternative, this very same fault is taken up: that one must accept an excessive complexity of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-gaurava*). However, if there were another faultless method, such excessive complexity could be avoided; but since no other method exists here, he resorts to that [solution], stating: "Or rather, not so, because it possesses both beginning and end" (Vārttika 3).

But thinking, "I shall not rely on this either," he says: "Or rather, I will state it thus: 'That which ends in īda and so forth, provided it ends in a dual suffix. Now, one might object: "In a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no extension of the designation to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). True; in a rule prescribing a technical name, when a suffix is mentioned, the extension to what ends in it is indeed prohibited.

But here, the term "dual" (dvivacana) is not resorted to as a name (*saṃjñin*); what then? It is that which ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *as*, and the dual is its qualifier: "that which ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *as* becomes *pragṛhya*-marked, provided it ends in a dual. But how can there be a rule regarding that which ends in *ī* and so on (*tadantavidhi*) by means of direct statement (*śruti*) or context (*prakaraṇa*) without the proximity of the subject (*kāryin*)? [It does not occur anywhere]. In that case, the former position—that "the dual is *ī* and so on"—is untenable.

Some say: "For technical designations (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) operate either at the time of their application (*kāryakāla*) or according to their enunciation (*yathoddeśa*). In that regard, since the designation *pragṛhya* functions within the domain of words (*padādhikāra*) at the time of application, the word is present as the object of the operation (*kāryin*). Just as in the rule ‘ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam’ (A 6.1.13), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*)—whose co-occurrence is obtained through syntactic expectancy (*sāmarthya*)—is relied upon as the object of the operation; likewise, there is a *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) for the word which is the object of the operation, by means of [the vowels] *ī*, *ū*, etc."

Likewise, in the *yathoddeśa* view, when operations (*kārya*) involving pragṛhya vowels are not yet required, the principal word (*pradhāna-pada*) is not relied upon as the locus of the operation (*kāryitva*). Thus, due to the absence of a word as the locus of the operation, there would be a conceptualization [of pragṛhya status] based solely on what is heard in the text. Alternatively, even if it were the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view, because words such as *sat* and *idam* are primary, there would be an absence of the rule for "that which ends in" (*tadanta-vidhi*); however, this is not tenable, for it has been accepted that "the designation (*saṃjñā*) and its application (*bhāṣa*) follow the *yathoddeśa* method."

In that case, first there is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) by means of the dual ending, according to the principle: "When a suffix is mentioned, [the operation applies to] that from which it is prescribed. For here, the presence of the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*) is not necessarily required. Therefore, there is an application of *tadantavidhi* for the name-bearer (*saṃjñin*) ending in a dual suffix, by means of the vowels *ī*, *u*, and so on. It is not the order of utterance—namely, that "that which ends in a dual suffix also ends in *ī* etc."—that is the governing factor; rather, this [word] becomes one that both ends in a dual suffix and ends in *ī* etc.

This being the case, since the basis for the designation (*saṃjñin*) is by way of its suffixal form, the rule of "application to that which ends in this" (*tadantavidhi*) is also established merely through observation; even so, the application of *tadantavidhi* is indeed seen in the case of the technical name "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), as in the rule: “*kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compounds [are nominal stems]” (A 1.2.46). It was stated that the application of *tadantavidhi* is untenable in the fourth alternative alone; that same point should be understood here as well. Alternatively, because it has been established by another fault, this particular fault has not been mentioned. [The rule applies to] that which ends in *ī*, etc. . . .

If [it is argued that] there is a prohibition regarding elision (*luk*), how then can there be a compound of a word ending in a dual suffix, given that the specific features produced by *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) have been described as follows: “The specification of number, the denotation of an individual (*vyakti*), the qualification of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and conjunction [are the results]”? Furthermore, it has been stated that “there is no compound of words ending in dual or plural suffixes. Regarding this, some say: “This elided case-ending is intended as a formal restatement (*anvākhyāta*) of the suffix; however, there is no such thing as a formal restatement by means of elision (*luk*) of an existing word-form.”

In that case, because the specific number [duality] seen in the sentence is abandoned when the word enters into its derivative form (*vṛtti*), that very natural disappearance (*nivṛtti*) is described as the operation of *luk*. And thus it has been said: “The statement regarding the *luk* elision of the suffix *āp* after an indeclinable is purposeless, because there is no gender. But what is the reason that you do not tolerate the *luk* elision of *āp*, yet tolerate the elision of the case-ending? There is a distinction here.

It has been stated: "The Teacher, seeking the characteristic of a condition (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), begins [the rule for] the elision (*luk*) of case-endings. For both [the presence and absence of a suffix] naturally cease; however, the cessation of that which serves a purpose in being expressed is what is declared. But that is not correct, because there is no occasion [for such an expression]. Indeed, the technical term *lopa* (elision) applies to the non-observation of that which was expected to appear.

However, regarding those sentences in common usage that express the meaning of a compound but have not been observed in actual application as compounds—sentences which serve to explain the compound—in that context of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning), where subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) are useful only for their own respective meanings and do not seek distinction through their own individuality, when unity is resorted to as a non-distinct [number] for the sake of designation, there would be no occurrence of words whose scope is dual or plural number. This is so that the subordinate words, which fall within the scope of *ekārthībhāva*, do not resort to distinct numbers but assist only in the expression of their own word-meanings.

[They] are understood. However, in the case of subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) conjoined with other words, even though they do not override the meaning of the principal element, their capacity to manifest a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*) has not ceased; for this reason, in expressions such as *dviśaurpika*, the word "two" (*dvi*) is employed to determine the measure of the price, which would not occur if there were no basis for a specific number. Nor is it logical to set aside the occasion for its usage. In the same way, in the expression *māsajāta*, there is a comprehension of a specific usage.

In the case of *goṣucara*, the employment of the nominal suffix (*vibhakti*) is for the purpose of expressing conjunction with a substance that lacks constituent parts (*anavayavadravya*). According to the view of rejection (*pratyākhyānapakṣa*), the singular number is applied by A 1.2.58, *ajātyākhyāyām*. For indeed, in the case of *goviṣṭhira*, the singular alone is observed due to a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). In *varṣāsuja*, there is an understanding of it as a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*). In *dviputra* and *ubhayabhārya*, this is due to the force of employing the preceding word; for in such cases, the suffix itself has its own primary meaning (*svārtha*).

Likewise, the capacity of the term *nimitta* (cause/condition) to be applied to [grammatical] causes such as *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) and so forth should be understood according to the possibility of each case. Similarly, it is observed that even when a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) has an unmanifested specific quality due to its connection with another word, there is the capacity to employ a specific number. For example: the manifestation of distinction in the family names *gārgya* and others through the presence or absence of the secondary suffix (*pratyaya*); the observation of a derivative form (*vikāra*) subject to transfer (*atideśa*) in the cases of *godau* and *varaṇāḥ*; and the form of the substitute (*ādeśa*) in *tyauṣmākaḥ*, *tāvakaḥ*, and *yuṣmatputraḥ*.

In that case, even in the case of *kumāry-agāra* ("the girl's house"), the dual number operation would have to be based on the manifestation of a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*) as the cause, despite the fact that the state of being a base form (*prakṛtibhāva*) remains. Under this hypothesis, in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, no distinction would be perceived because of the absence of a word expressing a specific [number]. Furthermore, in cases such as *dāsyāḥ putraḥ*, it would follow that singularity is understood merely due to the proximity of the singular suffix. Consequently, it would be untenable to claim that this specific number is produced by the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

And as for what was said: “But surely it cannot be thus; for a name should not exist by virtue of being caused by a word, but rather a word should exist by virtue of being caused by an object. Therefore, let it be seen that this very nature of the object is of such a kind that no distinction is perceived therein. And this must necessarily be understood in this way.

For one who thinks, "Since that word which expresses a specific quality is not present here, the specific quality is not understood," [we reply: in this case, its specific quality would indeed be understood—as in *apsucaraḥ*, *gahucaraḥ*, or *varṣāsujaḥ*. That [objection] is contradicted. Therefore, the rejection or inclusion of the number is not caused by a specific word; rather, this distinction is caused solely by the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This very point will be determined in the *Samartha-vārttika* itself. The mention of the word *artha* ("meaning") in the rule regarding the locative case (*saptamyām*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)...

When the seventh case ending is explicitly heard, or even when it is elided by *luk*, the desired result is already established by the rule of "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Nevertheless, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of excluding the application of the "characteristic of an affix" within the section on *pragṛhya* vowels. This mention of "meaning" must therefore be made for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, this position—that the *paribhāṣā* "as if having an initial and a final" (*ādyantavat*) exists for other purposes and should not be relied upon here—is adopted; for in that case, it would be improper to assume an unnecessary grammatical operation (*prakriyā*).

In that case, we shall qualify the dual number by means of *īd* and so forth. In the third alternative, since there is no mutual connection between *īd* and so forth and the dual number, they are brought together with respect to the aggregate (*samudāya*). Here, however, before the connection with the aggregate, the dual number is qualified by *īd* and so forth. Then, once the rule of "having that as its final element" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained, the aggregate is connected with the dual number as qualified by having *īd* and so forth as its final elements.

And the second [term], *pratyayagrahaṇa* (the mention of a suffix), is a rule for [applying an operation to] that which ends in such [a suffix]. If this is so, since the elements beginning with *ī* (*īdādi*) lack a direct connection with the aggregate [of the suffix and its stem], it would not be logical to show the connection of the aggregate with the elements beginning with *ī* by means of the phrase "ending in *ī* etc. (*īdādyanta*). This is not a fault. Because the term *īdādi* implies the rule for [applying an operation to] that which ends in such [a suffix], it refers precisely to the state of ending in *ī* etc. In that context, as much as is expressed by "beginning with *ī*" (*īdādi*), so much is meant by "ending in *ī* etc. (*īdādyanta*).

Even so, in the case of *evam apy aśukle vastre śukle samapadyetāṃ śuklyāstāṃ vastre*, [the suffix] *cvi* would apply here [to *vastre*]. For in the phrase *kumāryagāre*, the dual ending *os* does not end in *ī* or *ā*; however, here, from the word *śukla* ending in a *sup* suffix, there is the addition of *cvi*, followed by the elision of the *sup* suffix, then the elision of *cvi*, then the substitution of *ī* by A 7.4.32 (*asya cvau*), then the singular case-ending after the *taddhita* derivative which is an indeclinable, and of that [ending], [there is the substitution of *ām*] by A 7.1.37 (*avyayāt...*).

By the rule *A 2.4.82*, there is elision (*luk*); in that case, the substitute for the case-ending is the vowel *ī*. Therefore, this entire aggregate ending in a dual suffix beginning with *ī* exists by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the technical designation of a suffix). However, this *ī* which is actually heard [in the recitation] is cited for the purpose of demonstrating the application of the *yaṇ* substitution.

Regarding this, those for whom the text reads, "For in that case, there is a dual suffix beginning with *ī* and ending in *ī*, and it is so by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*," they should be understood as meaning that what ends in *ī* etc. is denoted by the term *īd-ādi*. The meaning is: "ending in a dual suffix beginning with *ī*."

As for those for whom the text states, "For here [in the sūtra] that which begins with *ī* and so on is heard, and it is a dual ending by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule," even though at present no such form beginning with *ī* and so on is actually heard, there is nevertheless no fault, because it is supported by the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). The meaning is that in the sūtra "īdādi dvivacanam" (the dual ending beginning with *ī*), the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*) is not intended for the dual ending in relation to the items beginning with *ī*.

Whatever meaning is found in the Sūtra is thus grasped; by means of this text, he demonstrates its consistency with the illustrative example: "And [the word] becomes dual-terminating by virtue of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*. Others, however, state that this summary of defects applies to two of the three positions: "For indeed, this [word] ending in *ī*, etc., is heard [as such]. In the third position, the defect is precisely in the case of *kurmāry-agāram*: "And [the word] becomes dual-terminating by virtue of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*."

Regarding the fourth position: having here proposed the specific fault that "the *śuklīyām*" [would result], yet failing to state the justification for it, he says—"This must be considered here"—on the grounds that since *śībhāva* has not been applied, the status of ending in *ī* has not yet arisen, and thus the elision (*luk*) of the preceding [suffix] will occur. ...Even when *śībhāva* is applied, the elision (*luk*) would apply; and even when it is not applied, it would apply. However, once the elision (*luk*) has occurred, there is no possibility for *śībhāva* to apply, because the original element (*sthānin*) no longer exists. For the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not operate in such cases.

Although the majority of examples of *sthānivadbhāva* concern cases of elision (*lopa*), nevertheless, *sthānivadbhāva* applies where there is an operation of another [element] caused by that [elision], but not when it is an operation of the elision itself. Furthermore, the status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) was not invoked for the substitution of *śī*, on the grounds that "an external (*bahiraṅga*) elision (*luk*) subverts even an internal rule. Even so, the elision might still be considered obligatory (*nitya*) in some way.

If this position is held—that the definition is sublated when its object (or specific feature) is disregarded—or if, with regard to the sublation of the effect, the operation of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) applies to the class-form (*ākṛti*) while abandoning the individual instances (*bheda*), then even so, since the genus *sup* remains undifferentiated despite the difference between the original base (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), the elision (*luk*) would be prescribed for that very genus, resulting in its permanence. Even in this case, there is a fault. He will state this later. Now, was it not said that one must rely on the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) as ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*) or a secondary suffix (*taddhita*)? True.

This is so; however, the following position is maintained: because the term *arthavat* (meaningful) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], this very purpose is adopted—that the proximity to worldly meaning (*laukika-artha*) should be relied upon. Furthermore, the position that "the dual ending begins with *ī* and so on" was abandoned for fear of the excessive complexity (*prakriyā-gaurava*) of the grammatical derivation, lest it should resort to the treatment of the beginning as if it were the end (*ādyantavad-bhāva*). Even here, in cases such as *agnī* and *vāyū*, this treatment of the beginning as the end must be desired for the sake of the intended meaning. And thus, [this] is unavoidable in common usage.

That itself is the middle position (*madhyama-pakṣa*). The fourth is a variant of the third position; thus, the second is the middle, and for all four [positions], the second is indeed the middle. Now, in this position, why does the designation *pragṛhya* not apply to the phrase "aśuklyāstām"? Because there is an absence of a grammatical element that undergoes the operation (*kāryin*). Here, the dual number is the element undergoing the operation, and it is not possible to rely on a non-existent element even by means of a rule.

Thus, there are these four positions: (a) *īd* and so forth [are the dual endings]; (b) a dual ending that begins with *īd* and so forth; (c) a whole form ending in *īd* and so forth which ends in a dual suffix; (d) a dual ending that ends in *īd* and so forth.
[The rule] *adaso māt* [1.1.12] [applies].

[1] Regarding the phrase "māt pragṛhyasaṃjñāyām" (before the designation *pragṛhya*): this is either an indication of the scope (*viṣayopalakṣaṇa*) or a statement of the exception (*nyāsanirdeśa*). If it were treated as an exception (*nyāsa*), then the designation *pragṛhya* would be stated by excluding that domain where the relatives of the pronoun *adas-* are not accepted, even if they are not explicitly mentioned; in that case, this fault would not arise. However, under this present formulation (*nyāsa*), because both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*) are unestablished (*asiddha*), the operation (*kriyā*) dependent upon them is also unestablished.

The word *tasya* refers to the entire collection of cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*nimitin*) without distinction; that is, of *ītva*, *ūtva*, and—by virtue of the word *ca*—"of *matva*" is understood. Since these three are not established (*asiddha*), there arises the contingency of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ay*. It is indeed logical that, because *ītva* and the others are not established, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply.

Since the *sthānin*s (original elements) such as *ay* and so on have already been replaced [by their substitutes], how could there be any possibility for them to occur? Furthermore, just as the *īt* and other vowels are treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to the designation of *pragṛhya*, so too in the case of the established *ay-ādi* substitutions, the designation of *pragṛhya* merely seeks to prevent the application of the *yaṇ*-substitution and the like; thus, let there be no *pragṛhya* designation. This is not the case. What is relied upon here is the non-existence of the rule (*śāstrāsiddhatva*). And the transformation of cognition regarding words is caused by the grammatical rules (*śāstra*).

In the absence of a treatise that establishes [the existence of] *buddhi*, the substituend (*sthānin*) remains in its very original form (*prakṛta-rūpa*). Since the cessation of the substituend has not been established there, the substitutions *ay* and so forth would apply: in *amī āsate*, the substitution *ay*; in *amū āsāte*, the substitution *āv*; and in *amī atra*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule "eṅaḥ padāntāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.101). But surely, because they depend on two words, the substitutions *ay* and so forth are "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the forms beginning with *ī* (such as *amī*) depend on a single word and are thus "intrinsic" (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, the extrinsic substitutions are non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to those intrinsic forms; for in that case, the preceding element itself does not exist, such that non-existence could be understood through the paribhāṣā "what is extrinsic is non-existent with respect to what precedes it" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*).

[1] Since the *śruti* (the literal form of the word) is not distinguished [from others], and because there is no specific selection [of one over another], the rule would apply here as well in the case of *kāśe*. Therefore, an exception must be stated for that. For example, when an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs due to the mention of *da*, the prohibition "not *adāp*" is stated.

Because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*), even without the apprehension of the form (*rūpa*), when the exclusion of the object is established through the apprehension of [the suffix] itself, the mention of the "apprehension of the form" alone is for the purpose of accepting the external object as being like the form. Therefore, just as there is no comprehension of synonymous forms when they are connected with other forms, likewise there is none for meaningless [forms] even when their form is identical.

In that case, when the meaningless word *śa*, joined with a meaningful one, undergoes a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) with the singular ending, a deficiency arises; since no distinct meaning whatsoever has emerged from the combination of the meaningful and the meaningless, this word *śa* remains meaningless.

[2] Likewise in cases such as *hariśe* and *babhruśe*. For there, since the two suffixes—the *ṅi* and the possessive (*matvarthīya*)—are meaningful by virtue of their own referents, when these two meaningful elements come together, the whole follows the properties of its parts; thus, because it possesses meaning through the meaning of its parts, this whole is meaningful. However, in the case of a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, because the base (*prakṛti*) abandons its own meaning, only the meaning of the suffix is connected with the meaning of the case-ending. Consequently, the base is meaningless.

But when there is a subsequent statement for the purpose of excluding mere formal application, it follows by the force of the sense that the stem remains [only] for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); thus, there is no fault, because it is stated in the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

[3] Or rather: even though the two constituent parts possess meaning, the aggregate—the word *śeṣa*—has no other meaning [of its own], and thus it is meaningless. Therefore, how is it that here number, object, and so forth are expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as belonging to the referent denoted by the word *hari*, or how is it that the five [objects] already expressed by the word *hari* are manifested by the case-ending? For by what means could there be a connection of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), as qualified by that [referent], with number, object, and so forth? In this regard, according to the view that [the compound] abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*):

Alternatively, if the *vṛtti* (the formation of a compound) is one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), then according to the principle that “the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together,” the aggregate including the base expresses an object that serves as the substratum for number, the accusative case, and so forth. Consequently, because there would be no connection between the meaning expressed by the word *śe* alone and the meaning of the case-ending, the entire aggregate *śe* would be rendered meaningless.
In that case, just as the meaning of the base alone, even though present, is not connected with the meaning of the case-ending, so too the meaning of the suffix alone would not be connected.
*Nipāta ekāj anāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14).

[1] When the term *nipāta* is used as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for *ac*, the fault of over-extension (*tadantavidhi*) does not arise; however, if the relationship were reversed and *ac* were the qualified (*viśeṣya*), that fault would indeed arise. [Why is *nipāta* mentioned? Because a collection [of sounds] is employed for the sake of meaning, and because there is no restriction regarding the inclusion of suffixes (*pratyaya*) in their formal shape, it is only the particle (*nipāta*) that can possess meaning. A suffix has two forms: [one] when it is motivated by meaning, and [the other] when it is meaningless, like individual phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus, suffixes are devoid of meaning.

And sometimes, a certain limit is accepted for that which has the nature of a substitution (ādeśa). For example, in the word *viṃśati*, there is the word *śati* or *ti*; or in the word *aikāgārika*, there is *ika* or *āgārika*. Likewise, for some [grammarians], the *vikaraṇas* arise before the agentive suffix (*kartari*); from that which ends in a *vikaraṇa*, the *sārvadhātuka* suffix *ityati* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). To this it is replied: True.

In the case of adopting worldly meaning, because words are eternal, the parts of words whose preceding portions have identical forms, as well as the constituent parts of word-groups that resemble the words which are parts of sentences, are as devoid of meaning as individual phonemes. However, when those [parts] are adopted in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as having identical forms, they possess meaning through a sense that is understood by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); this meaningfulness is accepted for the sake of grammatical operation (*kārya*).

If, then, the meaningfulness of suffixes (*pratyaya*) is accepted, there arises a contradiction with what is stated in Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*): “Indeed, that which ends in a primary derivative (*kṛt*) or secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is meaningful, but not the primary or secondary suffixes alone. This is not a fault. Because a suffix is eternally connected with a meaning, the term “meaningful” (*arthavat*) is understood by implication; thus, the repetition [of the word "meaningful" in the rule] is so that it may not be rendered purposeless. Therefore, even if some meaning exists [for the suffix], it is set aside because there is no deviation [from its function].

Furthermore, only a meaning established by grammatical rule (*śāstrīya*) is accepted as the basis for the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Otherwise, even a form ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*) or secondary suffix (*taddhita*) that lacks an inflection would be devoid of meaning (*ānarthakya*), just like a suffix; consequently, because it would possess meaning through the meaning of the suffix, the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply to the *ṇal* suffix in the case of *cakārātra*. Similarly, in the case of *atater ḍaḥ aḥ*, [the form] *a āgaccha* would result.

[2] If this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and if it were understood as an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to include that which ends in a particle (*nipāta*), then even a solitary [particle] would be perceived [as such] due to the principle of "treating the beginning as the end" (*ādyantavadbhāva*). And in this case, since the operation of the designation *pragṛhya* would be possible for particles ending in vowels (*ajanta*), the mention of the vowel (*ac*) would result in being purposeless. Therefore, by virtue of the mention of the vowel (*acgrahaṇa*), some specific [interpretation] must be adopted, while another must be abandoned.

In that case, if [the term *ac*] were to be applied only at the end [of the compound], then the suffix *āṅ* would be discarded as a whole; for since the designation *pragṛhya* would be impossible for *āṅ*, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would be meaningless. Therefore, by virtue of its specific gender, the mention of *ac* excludes only the vowel (*ac*) itself and sets aside that which ends in it. This would indeed be so if, when the mention of *ac* were not made, consonant-final elements (*halanta*) were connected with the designation *pragṛhya*.

If there were a connection with the technical term *saṃjñā* [regarding vowels], then the mention of *ac* would be for the purpose of excluding those ending in consonants (*halanta*). Indeed, a fault does not arise merely from a connection with a technical name. Furthermore, when specific operations (*kārya*) are absent, a technical name serves no other purpose; lest the application of the grammatical treatise be rendered useless, even when a general designation is employed, it does not apply to such a domain [of consonant-final elements]. In that case, for one who accepts the *pragṛhya* designation for the sake of an operation, there is no purpose whatsoever [for the mention of *ac*].

Alternatively, for one who employs a qualifier (*viśeṣa*) for the purpose of excluding faults, there is no fault whatsoever for which a qualifier would have to be employed as its negation. For it is within the section on *saṃhitā* that the rule for *prakṛtibhāva* (non-modification) is introduced; and therein, no operation is prescribed for consonants (*hal*) for the sake of which *prakṛtibhāva* would serve as a negation. [Objection: But surely, in cases such as *adho ’gamat* and *namo ’kārṣīt*, where the *ru* substitution has occurred, *prakṛtibhāva* would apply.

In this context, for those who maintain the traditional teaching, the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) is intended to prevent the application of a grammatical substitute (*ādeśa*). However, in this case, the *ru* [substitution] does not occur because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (A 8.2.1). If it does not exist, then the substitution of *u* (*utva*) would also not apply. [Response: The status of being established (*siddhatva*) is granted to the *utva* on account of its basis. But here, since *prakṛtibhāva* applies to that which undergoes modification (*vikārin*), there is no such modified element for which *prakṛtibhāva* could be performed. Furthermore, as for the *sakāra* that does exist, no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for it.

But surely, because the whole (*samudāya*) is subject to *prakṛtibhāva*, the substitution (*ādeśa*) of its part would be prevented? Even if the whole is subject to *prakṛtibhāva*, there is no such thing as a "substitution" for that which does not exist; so whose substitution would be prevented? Furthermore, since the letter *s* that actually exists is not said to undergo the change to *ū*, then—given the dependence on *prakṛtibhāva* of the *r*, the non-existence of the *r*, the fact that the basis (*āśraya*) for the change to *ū* is unestablished, and the fact that no operation is prescribed for the *s*—it is impossible here to prevent the change to *ū*. Therefore, regarding words ending in consonants (*halanta*), there is neither any fault nor any purpose [for this rule].

[3] Even so, since neither term is explicitly mentioned, when the exclusion of one or the other is being effected, the status of "as if being the beginning or the end" depends on rules based on the final element (*antāśrayavidhi*). Because of this relationship between cause and effect (*nimittanimittabhāva*), the operations [governed by] *tadantavidhi* would be unestablished in one case; thus, both paribhāṣās would have their scope. Since it is impossible for that which has no scope to be sublated, the scope of the paribhāṣā *yena vidhis tadantasya* is [found in examples like] *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*.

The scope of the introductory and concluding paribhāṣās is where there is an explicit mention of the word *anta* (end), such as in the rules: “of a root” (*dhātoḥ*), “the end” (*antaḥ*), “after the last vowel among consonants” (*midaco ’ntyāt*), and “the *ṭi* is that which begins with the last vowel” (*aco ’ntyādi ṭi*). Regarding the phrase *samavasthitayoḥ*: it means "when both have arrived" here; or, because they remain together within their own respective domains, they are called *samavasthitau*. Even though this [paribhāṣā] functions as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) in the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*, it is introduced here by means of a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*). For example:

Regarding the statement "the term *adhikāra* is of three kinds," we shall not here investigate which sequence of cognition is appropriate or which [of these] is the correct basis for inclusion. First, since the initial and final technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) serve as the cause for the rule of "application to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*), it is impossible for them to include [a term] when their cause is not present. Therefore, this technical name *ac* causes one to understand the named entities (*saṃjñin*) as those ending in *ac*.

By the force of the non-mention of *āc*, once either [of the two] has been excluded, it is improper to abandon the application of the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) which had already been reached. True; by sequence, the rule of "ending-in" alone would be adopted. However, since a formal indicator (*liṅga*) is stronger than sequence, when the application of the rule of "ending-in"—which is opposed to that indicator—is set aside by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *āṅ*, the determination occurs solely through the paribhāṣā regarding "beginning and end. This determination would indeed occur if the operation of those things possessing a cause could be obtained without a cause.

If, however, the rule regarding "that which ends in it" (tadantavidhi) were not applied, then because there would be no [element] possessing a beginning or an end caused by that [suffix], the determination [of the designation] would not follow from it. If this is so, then by this [rule], even when the two paribhāṣās have their common scope excluded, the vowels being grasped will obtain the designation *pragṛhya*. For that much is the thing to be enjoined; and that is established when this is the case. It might indeed be established, but this statement [of yours]—"this paribhāṣā will apply here: 'as if having a beginning and an end in one'"—is not tenable.

Since technical rules (paribhāṣā) exist for the sake of others, when their application ceases, they are connected with the designation *pragṛhya* of those [sounds] being grasped; because this rule has a result, its existence is justified by the presence of that result. For example: "If it is one, then the markers *ṅ* and *k* [are applied]."

Now, when there is the mention of *vāj* (the suffix *vat*), upon the abandonment of one or the other [of the two meanings], and because the cause for the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) exists, the paribhāṣā "as if beginning and ending" (*ādyantavat*) does not apply. Consequently, the rule of *tadantavidhi*, having fulfilled its purpose merely by providing access to the paribhāṣā "as if beginning and ending," withdraws. For example:

Because the gender is explicitly mentioned as a condition (*liṅgopādānāt*), the application of the rule for "that which ends in [something]" (*tadantavidhi*) with respect to its own meaning is not possible; and when that is absent, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which begins and ends in" (*ādyantavat*)—which serves to qualify the gender—does not apply. Therefore, the application of the *tadantavidhi* here is for the sake of another (*parārtha*). Since its purpose is fulfilled by that much, it does not effect its own meaning due to a conflict with the gender. Alternatively, whether there is an operation (*kārya*) for the consonants (*hal*) or not is considered precisely within those very places where the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) are prescribed.

In the same way, when both paribhāṣās are present due to their being internal (antaraṅga), the determination will occur through the paribhāṣā regarding the beginning and end (ādyanta-paribhāṣā) by virtue of the sign (liṅga) [of the mention of *aj*], since one or the other is excluded by the mention of *aj*.

[4] In that case, the mention of "single" (*eka*) is made for the purpose of excluding a collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*). And by this mention of "single," it is indicated that in other instances where there is a mention of vowels (*varṇagrahaṇa*) in which a specific number is already included as subordinate members (*parāṅgabhūta*), the number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Furthermore, since the designation *pragṛhya* is being prescribed here, the mention of vowels (*ajgrahaṇa*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the designation. And when elements are subordinate, the number is not intended to be significant. For example:

"One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). Now, since a name (*saṃjñā*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*), primacy belongs to the named objects (*saṃjñin*) with which it has a conventional connection; in that case, the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding number is indeed appropriate. True, there is primacy of the named objects in a mere reference (*pradeśa*), but because the name is being enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*), the name itself possesses primacy—as in "Make a white cloth" (*śuklaṃ paṭaṃ kuru*) or "One should immolate a white [animal] dedicated to Vāyu" (*śvetaṃ vāyavyam ālabheta*).

In that case, if the number [of phonemes] were not intended to be significant, then the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply to the collection of vowels in the phrase "a i u apehi," which is a collection of particles (*nipāta*). But how could a collection of particles be grasped by the term "particle" (*nipāta*)? It would be so understood because of the requirement for the vowel (*ac*), since a collection of vowels cannot constitute a single particle; thus, the designation of "particle" would apply to the collection as a whole. Let it be so; since the reference is to the genus (*jāti*), it will apply to each individual member as well. If this were possible, then the purpose would be achieved.

But when the designation applies to the aggregate as a whole, since the purpose of the individual parts is already fulfilled by that very designation, there is no further application of it to the parts. For example, when reduplication is performed on a single vowel belonging to an aggregate, because the purpose of the aggregate is fulfilled, there is no further reduplication of the individual parts; likewise, when the designation "consonant cluster" (saṃyoga) is applied without distinction to the aggregate, there is no further [application] to each of the two [sounds].
