If, then, the parts have their purpose fulfilled by the effect [of the rule] based on the whole, and because they possess the status of *pragṛhya*, there would be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for each individual part; however, there is no further preservation of the original form for the parts, because the preservation of the original form has already served its purpose in the whole. Consequently, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not apply to the final [vowel], and the substitutions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* (beginning with *ā*) would apply to the two preceding [vowels].

How then, when the designation of *prātipadika* applies to a meaningful aggregate, and while some phonemes are meaningful and others are meaningless—given that the designation of *prātipadika* is not being applied solely on the basis of the "meaningful" (*arthavat*) criterion—is the objection raised regarding the undesirable consequence of *nalopa* (the elision of the final *n*) due to the production of case-endings for every individual phoneme in words such as *vanaṃ* and *dhanaṃ*? Regarding meaningfulness first: since they possess distinct meanings, the meanings of the individual phonemes are each capable of serving as the cause for the designation of *prātipadika*, according to their respective functions.

Even though [the mention of] "singularity" (ekatva) might be redundant in some cases because the whole is not grasped [as a single unit], this operation regarding the whole is understood to apply to those instances. In that context, since the number is dependent [on the whole], the mention of "one" (*eka*) is made as a qualifier for the mention of *aj* (the vowel *a*), which has become subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to what is to be designated. This serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "in other instances where phonemes (*varṇa*) are mentioned as subordinate and possess specific numbers, the genus (*jāti*) does not have its number dependent [on the individual]."

What is the purpose of making this known? It is so that when the term *hal* is employed in the rule *halantāc ca* (A 1.2.10), even though the *hal* is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), the designation of *kit* for the suffix *san* does not involve an intention to specify a particular number. But was it not said that "there is no priority based on general [application]"? This is not a statement [of a settled fact].

For in the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, since it is impossible for multiple suffixes with distinct meanings to simultaneously function as *aṅga*s of a single base (*prakṛti*), and because the purpose of suffixes with identical meanings has already been fulfilled [by one], and because the subsequent position (*paradeśa*) is already occupied, there is no relation of posteriority (*paratva*) for multiple suffixes; therefore, it is said that in general there is no sequential order (*paurvāparya*). Where, however, the suffix is of identical form, there the posteriority belongs to the genus (*jāti*). For example: [the rule] *āto ṅitaḥ*... [etc.]
"One *prakṛti* and many *yaṅ*s. Because the mention of the *hal* in the rule for *dambh-* intends to refer to the class (*jāti*), there is no contradiction in [the suffix] following an *ik*.

[5] Why is it that this does not occur here? ... It is indeed thus: because, upon the cessation of the *anubandha*, there is an absence of any specific auditory perception (*śruti*). If, at the time of the *anubandha*, some particular form of meaning were ascertained as being connected, then even after the *anubandha* has ceased, the state of having an *anubandha* would be inferred by means of that meaning which co-occurred with the *anubandha*. In that regard, the connection of a word with an *anubandha* is observed in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣat*), as in the case of the prefix *ā-* in the sense of "slightness."

Because the prefix is taught with its *anubandha*, its connection with an action is also understood to belong to that which possesses the *anubandha*. Furthermore, in the rule *“āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ”* (A 2.1.13), it is precisely the form with the *anubandha* that is referred back as having the designation of a *karmapravacanīya*. Therefore, even when the *anubandha* has been removed here, the meaning of the *anubandha* is inferred through its concomitants. Regarding the two cases of sentence and recollection, [the term] is *aṅit*; in the context of a sentence, for example: *“ā evaṃ nu manyase”*.

A certain sentence-meaning, established as either the object of a preceding injunction or the object of a prohibition, is modified; in that case, this particle is employed: *ā evaṃ nu manyase* ("Is it that you now think thus?"). This form *ā* is used here with reference to the subject matter of the preceding statement, in the sense: "You did not think so before, but now you think thus. Others, however, say that what is intended here is a specific syntactical constituent (*vākyāvayava*) within the context of the sentence.

In this context, since it is prescribed that the augment *aṅ* (the letter *a*) is replaced by an anusvāra only when it is meaningless (*anarthaka*), its meaningfulness as a pure vowel is logically established. First, the vowel *ā* is employed with reference to an object to be remembered, as in “*ā evaṃ kila tat*” (“Ah, indeed, it was thus”). Subsequently, after the act of recollection, the etymological explanation “*ā evaṃ kila tat*” is made.

[1] [This is a collection of particles (nipātasamāhāra): Since there is a multiplicity of meanings, this must necessarily be a collection of particles. Alternatively, if there is no distinction in meaning, it is clearly a single particle. In that case, how can these two contradictory things coexist in one place? It is said:

One may consider it possible to maintain that because expressions such as *iṃ kam sīm* are meaningless—since no meaning ever actually emerges when there is either unity or a collective aggregate—the delimitation of a boundary, which depends on the distinction or non-distinction of meaning, is impossible. For instance, in the case of *o ṣu yātaṃ marutaḥ* (where it is read as *ā u su yātam*), the designation *pragṛhya* would apply by the rule *nipāta ekāc*, but this is prohibited by the rule *anāṅ*.

In this case, because prohibitions are stronger due to their posteriority, the prohibition "not after *āṅ*" (*anāṅ*) ought to apply. But surely, a rule other than *āṅ* is being resorted to? Indeed, there is an *o*-vowel here that is other than *āṅ*. However, due to the treatment of the end as the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*), when [the preceding element] is constantly present in its designation, it is impossible to designate it as "this is other than *āṅ*."

How then, in the case of "the field is mown" (*lūyate kedāreṇa*), does the verbal root receive the designation "intransitive" because the agent itself functions as the object? In this instance, even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being an object, the agent's own inherent state of being non-objective (*akarmatva*) is not removed. Furthermore, nothing here is said that would depend upon an [external] object; rather, the agent's non-objectivity is innate. Therefore, since no dependence on an external object is being assumed for the meaning of the verbal root connected with that agent, the designation [of "intransitive"] is appropriate. For example:

Since the innate status of being a *kṣatriya* has not ceased [in the case of one who acts like a *brāhmaṇa*], the expression "give to a non-*brāhmaṇa*" (*abrāhmaṇāya dehi*) remains connected with specific actions based on that very status.

And just as in the command "Let a *brāhmaṇaka* village be brought," even though a *kṣatriya* is present there, because the act of bringing is enjoined as having the *brāhmaṇa* as its locus, what is brought is the village possessing that [status]; so too here, due to the proximity of the designation through the principle of "behaving like" (*ādivadbhāva*), the repeated exclusion (*paryudāsa*) can be understood.

Even so, in cases such as *agauḥ gauḥ samapadyata* ("the non-cow became a cow") or *go 'bhavat* ("it became a cow"), [the rule would] apply [undesirably]. If that is the case, then since the understanding of the form itself is already established by the mention of *sva-* in the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* (A 1.1.68), the explicit mention of *rūpa-* (form) is for the purpose of ensuring that the form is understood even when the external factor—the meaning—is present. In that context, once meanings are excluded and meanings are accepted, there is an understanding of the primary sense over both the primary and the secondary senses.

That which comes from a quality (*guṇa*) is *gauṇa* (secondary); that which is like the face (*mukha*) is *mukhya* (primary). In this context, this statement does not apply; rather, this worldly principle is adopted here. In this case, the word "cow" (*go*), having functioned with respect to genus, substance, gender, number, action, and so forth, becomes connected with external [factors] such as commands or reproaches, and it assumes the status of either a qualifier or a qualified relative to the meanings denoted by other words.

In that case, when the internal meaning connected to the word itself is not present, it is improper to expect an external meaning residing in another word. In the expression "The ox is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), the meaning such as "a person from Vāhīka" is denoted by another word; since that other word has not been employed, its meaning has not yet appeared. Thus, due to its absence, it is impossible to perform an expectation (*apekṣā*) for it.

Indeed, because the presence of permanent and impermanent objects is not invariably concomitant, the comprehension of the permanent object is the logical one. For the connection of the word "cow" with the Bāhīkas and others is inconstant; since for some people, the nature of being a cow exists among the Bāhīkas even when it is not intended [to be expressed]. Likewise, even those actions and qualities that have an established relationship [with the word], such as stupidity, impurity, and the like—which are the opposites [of the qualities of a cow]—may at times be intended to be expressed in the case of a Bāhīka, such as sharpness, cleverness, and so forth.

In that case, when there is an intention to express a contradictory quality, the word "cow" (go) does not apply at all. Furthermore, between a common and a specific meaning, it is logical that the word "cow" conveys that which is its specific referent.

In the case of the Vāhīkas, however, because of the convergence of many qualities, whatever object has a well-established connection with certain actions or qualities, the word denoting that [object] applies there as well. Thus, whichever quality of a Vāhīka one intends to express, one employs a term for that quality in reference to him. Consequently, since words such as "ox," "horse," "elephant," and "bird" are applied [to him], it cannot be said, "This is an ox alone."

Therefore, when "cow" (gaur) is uttered, there arises a cognition of that meaning which is internal, non-deviating, and specifically restricted to that very [referent]. Consequently, the Vāhīka is not [directly] associated [with the word]. How then do the operations of *vṛddhi* and *ātva* occur with respect to the Vāhīka in such cases as "the cow stands" (*gauḥ tiṣṭhati*) or "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*)? This occurs in this way by virtue of the [intended] meaning.

When both a secondary (gauṇa) and a primary (mukhya) meaning are possible for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) based on its general application, this distinction cannot be prevented—namely, whether the meaning here is secondary or primary. Even if there exists a basis for the secondary meaning here, it cannot be excluded because its cause has not yet manifested.

Why? Because when a word accompanied by its case-ending is connected with another word for the purpose of determining the distinction between their meanings, it then serves to delimit the secondary meaning (gauṇa) which is differentiated by the other word; and in the absence of the employment of another word, only the primary meaning (mukhya) is understood.

Therefore, although the meaning of a nominal stem (prātipadika) may potentially contain the seeds of multiple meanings, since it lacks the capacity to express a specific distinction [among them], grammatical operations based on the nominal stem proceed by relying solely upon what is directly heard (śrutimātra). Alternatively, first of all, the nominal stem is connected with its primary meaning—which is internal, unique, non-deviating, and principal—and the case-ending (vibhakti) is produced precisely from that which functions as the primary meaning.

And because no other meaning has appeared [in place of the original], grammatical operations are performed upon the word that still functions in its primary sense within the inflectional ending (*vibhakti*). Once the word, functioning in its primary sense, has been produced with its inflectional ending and has performed its own function, then—given the presence of another word such as *vāhīka*—that very word functioning in its primary sense undergoes a transformation into a different meaning. In that case, when there is a connection with a different meaning, the contradictory meanings are withdrawn.

However, because the established connection with the qualities of action is not contradictory, its persistence occurs. Therefore, at the time of the prescription of *vṛddhi* and *ātva*, since the secondary (gauṇa) meaning—which is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)—has not yet arisen, this maxim regarding "the secondary and the primary" does not apply here, as its cause has not been reached; thus, it does not enter into this domain.

Therefore, because there is no encounter with an object that lacks a corresponding counter-entity (*pratidvandvin*), if it is thus an indicator (*jñāpaka*), then due to the absence of a contradictory cause, the object does not receive its primary designation (*mukhyavyapadeśa*). For, being a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), it receives its primary designation only when a secondary one exists. Consequently, due to the absence of a primary designation, an operation based on the word is prescribed for the mere word itself.
And because of the absence of a contradictory object, when the expectation of a secondary or primary [object] is non-existent, the status of being based on the word applies to *vṛddhi* and *ātva*.
ūṃ is substituted for uñaḥ. // 1.1.17–18 //

[1] Regarding the single rule *uña* [ūṃ], since the Vedic tradition of Śākalya (*śākalyaśruti*) serves its purpose within the optional substitution (*ādeśavikalpa*), the designation of *pragṛhya*—by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*—is understood to apply in those cases where no substitution occurs. However, when there is a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), because even the substitution is not required, the optional application of the designation is understood through the Vedic tradition of Śākalya.

Even when the optional designation *pragṛhya* is understood, if the substitution of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) were prescribed independently of the particle *vā*, the complete disappearance of the original element (*sthānin*) would be understood; as in the rule "for *as*, *bhū*" (A 2.4.52). However, because of the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), once the optional *pragṛhya* designation is determined, two forms result from the preceding rule: namely, "u" and "v".

And in the subsequent rule, although a substitution would have been obligatory, by means of the expression "optionally" (*vā*) joined with the statement of the substitute, two forms arise—namely *ūṃ* and *u*—due to the connection with the explicit mention of the option; thus, three forms are established across the two rules.

However, for those who hold the view that the purpose of the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is to prevent the application of the *Śākalya-vibhāṣā*, there would be no designation as *pragṛhya* because the nasalized form (*niranunāsika*) has already been excluded; consequently, there would be no audible pronunciation of the form ‘u iti’ once the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) has taken effect. Furthermore, when there is a dependence on a substitute (*ādeśa*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*), although subordinate, does not enter into a relationship with the named element (*saṃjñin*)—which already possesses an established connection—because it would result in a deficiency; rather, it functions solely as a term whose referent is its own form alone.
And the vowels *ī* and *ū*, when they stand in the sense of the locative case, [are called *pragṛhya*].

[1] Here, because "when a suffix is mentioned in a rule for designating a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the inclusion of that which ends with it is prohibited," the word *saptamī* here denotes the suffix alone. In that regard, when the vowels *ī* and *ū* are primary and the locative case (*saptamī*) functions as a qualifier, it is understood as follows: the designation *pragṛhya* applies to that locative suffix which consists of the vowels *ī* and *ū*.

When the locative case (*saptamī*) is primary and the vowels *ī* and *u* function as its qualifiers, then—since there exists no locative case ending that actually terminates in *ī* or *u*—the rule of "ending-inclusion" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply here. In that context, were it not for the explicit mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*), the designation of *pragṛhya* would apply only where the locative case is explicitly heard, such as in the word *sarasī*. However, when the locative case has been elided, the designation cannot take effect at all because the thing to be designated (*saṃjñin*) is absent, leaving the designation without a domain of application.

Furthermore, if one were to assume that the designation *pragṛhya* applies based on the mere conceptualization of a connection [between sounds], then there would be no comprehension [of the designation] even for that which occurs in a sense associated with the locative case (*saptamī*), because such a word lacks the necessary semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). However, by including the term "meaning" (*artha*) in the rule, the designation *pragṛhya* is established even for a word like *gaurī* in the verse "somo gaurī adhi śritaḥ" (RV 9.12.3), which—though its suffix has been elided—occurs in the sense of the locative case.

[2] Here, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is not elided; rather, having set aside both the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) and its lengthening (*dīrghatva*), the substitution of *āṭ* and the substitution of *ām* would apply. If that is so, then the elision (*luk*) applies everywhere. In that case, since the primary [application of the rule] is impossible, we shall understand the mention of the word-form ending in *ī* or *ū* as being intended for the sake of shifting the meaning to the locative (*saptamyartha*). We shall understand it as such. This cannot be obtained from the explicit statement (*vacana*). In a matter concerning the determination of the primary [meaning], one cannot assume a secondary [meaning] on the basis of the explicit statement.

How so? Here, since the word *sarasī* is derived from a stem ending in a consonant with the locative case suffix (*saptamī*) applied, and since the rule "the addition of *ī*, *yā*, *īya*, *īk*, and *īkā*" prescribes the substitution of *ī* for that locative suffix, it is possible to maintain the primary interpretation that the *ī* in *sarasī* is indeed the locative case-ending. And when that [primary interpretation] is possible, the designation of *pragṛhya* does not apply to forms where the case-ending has been elided, as in *somo gaurī adhi śritaḥ*.

[3] Furthermore, if it were *sarasī*, there would be no purpose in mentioning the word "artha" (meaning). For when the locative case ending (*saptamī*) produced after the word *sarasī* has undergone elision (*luk*), since the primary referent for the conceptualization is absent, the form ending in *ī* is considered a locative by virtue of the rule for the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, because an affix is absolutely impossible in that context, this is not a mention of an affix. And if it is not a mention of an affix, then by means of the vowels *ī* and *ū*, the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) will apply to those words that function in the sense of the locative.

Or, by means of the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [the rule] applies when the vowels *ī*, *ū*, and *e* follow a locative case ending (*saptamī*), provided they are accompanied by that locative ending. This would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the status of being "ending in that" (*tadanta*). In the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, whether one does or does not rely on the principle that "in the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the mention of a suffix refers to the suffix itself," when the mention of "ending in *os*" is made—given that the status of "ending in that" exists—this serves as an indicator for the absence of the characteristic of being a suffix.

This is an illustration made with reference to the rule "it would be so if [the suffix] ends in that. If, then, the application of suffix-characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not occur in the designation of *pragṛhya* due to an indicator (*jñāpaka*), what is the scope for this sūtra? Or, if the application of suffix-characteristics does occur in the designation of *pragṛhya*, what is the purpose of its formulation? Therefore, this rule must be formulated; it fulfills its purpose by indicating the cessation of the application of suffix-characteristics elsewhere. Thus, the designation of *pragṛhya* will indeed be established within its own domain, whether the application of suffix-characteristics is present or not.

[4] Or let it not be so for the preceding member. . . . as in *aśvo nadyām ātiḥ* . . .; by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (A 2.1.44), when there is a compound, the short *ī*-ending word functioning in the sense of the locative would obtain the designation *pragṛhya*, but because of the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*), it does not occur.

Now, even though the term "meaning" (artha) is included [in the definition], why does this [undesired consequence] not occur here? It is because, in both types of *vṛtti*—first, in the case of *ajahatsvārthā*—the assistance (*upakāra*) consisting of the power (*śakti*) of actions inherent in the agent or object, which are themselves inherent in other substances, is relied upon; and since that [power] has not ceased, [the rule applies].

Even in a compound where the primary meaning is abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*), although there are qualifiers that have become subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*) to that primary meaning, because the relationship of the meaning being connected has become obscured, if the subordinate member did not function for the sake of the principal meaning, then—since there would be no mutual assistance between the principal and the subordinate—the inclusion of the quality (*guṇopādāna*) would be purposeless.

Therefore, qualifiers whose own meanings have become subordinate and which merely take up the meaning of the principal [word] become redundant. In that case, because the clay lump—like dust and water—is not prevented from being mixed with its own essence, there occurs a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) through the merging of its distinct parts; and since its prior distinction was perceived, it is designated as a "whole" (*samudāya*) when it is inferred as such. In this context, by the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the rule *saptamyarthe*, the meaning of the whole is not what is denoted.

Alternatively, when the case endings (vibhaktis) express the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha)—whether as a pentad (*pañcaka*) for those meanings that are doubtful or unmanifested, or as a triad (*trika*) for those expressing number, objecthood (*karman*), and so forth—they denote a collection of meanings characterized by a specific number, because they express that group of meanings upon which a particular number has been based; thus, by the mention of the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*), a mass of meanings associated with a specific number is denoted.

In a compound, however, when the specific number has ceased to function, that meaning remains unestablished; since it then functions with a diminished sense, there is no comprehension of the locative meaning [that was previously present]. Therefore, the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of conveying the conventional, conceptual, and technical meaning adopted within the treatise.

If, then, the meaning of the locative case were not understood here as having its specific number set aside, then even when elision (*luk*) has occurred, because the specific number would not be conveyed, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply in the case of "somo gaurī adhi śritaḥ. Therefore, it cannot be said that the mention of the word *artha* (meaning) is for the purpose of expressing a specific gender and number; for in this way, in the example "vāpy aśvo nadyātir . . . ," the meaning of the collective whole is expressed.

In that case, because the substance—which is the substratum for the quality that serves as the cause for the designation "locus"—has its power subordinated and possesses a specific thing to be contained (*ādheya*), it is not grasped by the quality which is inherent in that particular substance and which causes the manifestation of a specific name; furthermore, even when the thing to be contained exists, the construction [of the locative] is understood through another meaning, and the sense of the locative case is inferred as following after the nature of that specific thing to be contained.

And when a primary sense exists that is not confused with another meaning, it is not appropriate to postulate such a sense of the locative case. In this regard, just as in the rule *jātyākhyāyām*, the mention of the word *ākhyā* (name/designation) is understood to refer to a genus abstracted from its substance, so too here, by the mention of the word *artha* (meaning), the sense of the locative case is taken as residing in itself alone, without any further substrate being supplied.

[Ī] Alternatively, because of the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) in the phrase “in the sense of the locative case,” the worldly meaning (*laukiko ’rthaḥ*) is what is intended. Why is this so? For those meanings of a composite (*samudāyārthāḥ*) which, according to the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), are to be inferred through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*) and are adopted as the causes for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*)—namely, the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), the prior member (*pūrvapada*), and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—these are not [considered] composites [in that context]. In the world (*loke*), however, these constituent parts are devoid of meaning (*ānarthakya*), just like individual phonemes (*varṇa*).
But the fully established composite (*pariniṣpannaḥ samudāyaḥ*), not deviating from its own meaning, conveys its own indivisible self.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the meaning of the aggregate" (*samudāyārtha*): the aggregate, which is the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of the aggregate, is designated as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) when it has attained a state of being a real entity (*sattvabhūta*), having ceased its distinctness from that [meaning]. In that case, because the locative sense (*saptamyartha*) is included, there is a grasping of the thing exactly as it is. But here, since it does not become [an aggregate] in that manner, no fault arises.
*dādhā dhvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20).

[1] Here, the designation *ghu* is applied to those forms that have been accepted as such; furthermore, these forms consist of two parts, namely those containing the letter *d* and those containing the letter *dh*.

And because that [ā-deletion] does not depend upon their pronunciation (*tad-āśraya*), even though the substitution of ā has occurred for the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *jñā*, *mā*, and *sthā*, there is no designation of *ghu* because of the absence of the sounds *d* and *dh*. Just as in the case of *dīṅ* and *dṛṅ*, and *dhīṅ* and *dhṛṅ*, even though the sounds *d* and *dh* are present, the designation of *ghu* does not apply because of the lack of the pure form and because the forms have become different from *dā* and *dhā*; likewise, since *deṅ* and *dheṭ* do not undergo the substitution of ā before a *śit* suffix, they would also lack the designation of *ghu* due to their differing from the forms *dā* and *dhā*. Therefore, he recites [the following rule] regarding the designation of *ghu*:

"The mention of *prakṛti* (the base form) is for the sake of [rules concerning] *śit* [affixes]. He does not read "for the sake of modified forms" (*vikṛta*). He thinks thus because the maxim regarding "that which is taught by its technical definition versus that which is taught by its actual wording" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*) is defective. For this is its defect: "there is no distinction in the case of mentions of *ā* following *gā*."

The followers of Bhāradvāja, however, considering that the designation *ghu* would apply even to these two [roots] when they have undergone the substitution of *āt*, because their status as being taught (*aupadeśika*) has been superseded by other forms such as *dādhā* which possess that status through instruction, recite the rule: "The term *śit* is for the sake of the modified form. Their intention is this: since the original forms (*prakṛti*) do not possess the form of *adādhā*, and since the modified forms (*vikāra*) are not directly taught (*anaupadeśika*), they incur neither the fault of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) nor any other defect.

This introduction is for the purpose of demonstrating that this very [term] possesses meaning (*arthavattva*). However, if the base form (*prakṛti*) were included, then by the rule "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*, A 1.1.56), the designation *ghu* would apply to the derivatives as well. The other [Vārttikakāra] asks: "What is the purpose? His intention is as follows: since the imitations of the verbs *praṇidadāti*, *yacchati*, *dayati*, *dadhati*, and *dadhāti*—by means of words that imitate them—possess meaning through the sense of the action being imitated, they would fall under the prohibition "that which has meaning" (*arthavat*) regarding the designation of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and so forth.

Since the substitution of *āt* occurs even before the production of case-endings—as it is not dependent on any specific condition—and since there is a prohibition when a suffix marked with *ś* follows, [the author] raises the objection that the mention of the "original form" (*prakṛti*) must be performed here by means of those [words] for which the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation has been prescribed: "How can the designation *ghu* apply to the original forms? [The purpose is: so that once the original forms have acquired the designation *ghu*, the designation may likewise apply to their modifications, either through the connection with the original form or by virtue of the rule regarding the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

However, for the *prakṛtis* that are themselves modifications (*vikāra*), [the designation] would not apply by virtue of the property of being a modification, because the *prakṛtis* do not possess the nature of a modification. In that case, since their own essential form (*svarūpa*) is grasped even without the mention of "prakṛti," the designation *ghu* is established; thus, the injunction of the term "prakṛti" would be redundant.

However, regarding forms such as *ayaṃ tu dātā* ("this one is a giver"), [the author] considers that the actual forms of those roots which have acquired the letter *t* before ārdhadhātuka suffixes are explained by the imitative word *dā-dhā*. Thinking that they possess the status of *kārita* (causative) even in their *kṛt* (primary derivative) forms, and desiring to establish the capacity of the word to determine its own designation (*ghu-saṃjñā*) through the rule of that name, he raises the objection that the mention of the "original form" (*prakṛti-grahaṇa*) must be made. Furthermore, it is not understood that the phrase "and there is no mention of the original form" means that only the word *prakṛti* itself should be mentioned.

What then? The meaning is that the very forms of those bases (*prakṛti*) which have undergone the substitution of *āt* must be understood in their own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), preceded by the removal of their modifications (*vikāra*). However, the author of the *Cūrṇi*, considering that the mention of the bases through the removal of the mention of the modifications was intended, and [furthermore] thinking that it is impossible to grasp the bases in their own essential nature by removing the modifications—lest the distinction between base and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bheda*) be lost—he postulated that the very form of the word "base" (*prakṛti-śabda-svarūpa*) itself is what is enjoined as the thing to be performed.

He explains: the other, intending to state that if one relies on the instruction of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of similar items), the injunction regarding the base (*prakṛti*) and its further base would be purposeless, asks—"What is the purpose? The other replies—"Of those that have become *āt*," because when there is a reference to a modification (*vikāra*), the mention of the base is not obtained; [he says this] because in the case of a reference to removal (*apakarṣa*), it is so designated. "Those that have become *āt*" means those which have attained the state of *āt*. Now, since the root *bhū* is intransitive, the expression "those that have become *āt*" is not tenable.

Nor does this [root] *bhū* incur the status of being transitive (*sakarmaka*), because it signifies attainment (*prāpti*). But is there not some instance where this *bhū* signifies attainment? Yes, he says there is. For example: “By means of this, Bharadvāja equipped Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa. He became the sovereign (*rāṣṭra*). Whomever one desires to become a ruler, thinking ‘May this man be the sovereign,’ one should equip him with this; he indeed becomes the sovereign” (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 3.3.7).

Likewise, in the expression “the moon is a great being” (*mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*), it is said that it has attained greatness (*mahattva*). Alternatively, they are "become through *āt*-ness," meaning they have attained *āt*-ness. Now, one might object: the majority of operations designated as *ghu* are taught to occur in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, and therein these [roots] are seen to have become *āt*. Since their functional utility (*kāryatuṣa*) is minimal outside the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, it is not proper to assume the inclusion of the root-form (*prakṛtigrahaṇa*) on the basis of such scant utility.

Indeed, it is not appropriate to assume a different meaning for the genitive case—which, among the seventeen types of grammatical relations (*ādeśa*), functions to express the relation of "substitution" (*sthāneyoga*)—for the sake of [the suffix] *iṭ*. Furthermore, as for that "grain of chaff" regarding the grammatical operation, it is established by the fact that the mention of the "base" (*prakṛti*) must necessarily be repeated in the rule for *ṇatva* (nasalization), even though it has already been brought down from its previous context; thus, he indicates that the mention of the base is otherwise redundant.

Or rather, when another meaning is postulated, there is an obstruction for the majority [of forms], whereas this is not the case when *prakṛti* (the verbal root) is accepted; therefore, he says that this is not a valid solution: "For the sake of the suffix *śit*, the status of being a *ghu* is prohibited. Since the roots *deṅ* and *dheṭ* do not possess the form *dā* when they are *prakṛtis* of the *ghu* class, if they were not *ghu*, the operation of *ghu* would not apply, and thus in the forms *praṇidayate* and *praṇidhayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after the prefix *ni* would not be obtained.

The followers of Bhāradvāja recite the word *vikṛtārtham*; for them, this is an addition. *Praṇidātā* and *praṇidhātā* are forms derived from the roots *dāṅ* (to give) and *dheṭ* (to suck). He says "between that which is taught by a rule and that which is taught by its specific wording" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktayor*) because the specific wording (*pratipadokta*) ending in long *ā* does not apply here. However, Kātyāyana did not state this, as it is already established by the principle: "In the case of the mention of *gam*, *āda*, and others, there is no distinction."

[3] Now, regarding the phrase "even when it is being performed": he thinks as follows—when *dā* and *dhā* are in proximity, the mention of the *prakṛti* (root) should not apply to those that have become *vikṛti* (modified forms), nor should the designation *ghu* be applied to such *dā* and *dhā* forms; thus, the designation *ghu*, which would otherwise apply to all domains, becomes restricted to a specific domain when it is being formulated, and is thereby obstructed. Therefore, it cannot be understood in this way. How, then, is the dual nature [of the designation] to be explained? It is said:

[a] In the assumption of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is favor shown to the root *dā-dhā* because it is not for the sake of another; however, there is obstruction of the mention of the *prakṛti* because it is for the sake of another.

However, regarding the sense of the genitive case, there is a conflict because the direct mention of *dā* and *dhā* serves another purpose, whereas the direct mention of the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) receives support; thus, a deliberation arises due to their equal strength. Now, one might object that in this rule, "The roots *dā* and *dhā*," the plural number should not have been used, since the plurality of the roots is already understood by the term *dādhām* itself—just as in the cases: "May the eye go to the sun" (*Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* 4.13.4) and "The chest was struck by the feet" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 3.1.4.3).

Nor is there a difference in the base (*prakṛti*) despite the difference in the substitutes (*vādeśa*); rather, the use of the plural number here is solely because of their generic nature (*jātitva*), for the purpose of indicating that the base differs with each individual substitute. "It is not understood in this way"—herein lies the intention: in this case, the injunction (*codanā*) becomes highly effective; otherwise, however, there would be an internal contradiction. But even so, would it not apply to the base alone? No; because the base has a requirement (*sākāṅkṣatva*) and no other modification (*vikāra*) is specified, it is understood that the base is precisely *dādhā*.

[5] Next, I shall explain the statement "dā-dhā-dhu-adā-barthaḥ. [Objection: Since *dā* and *dhā* possess meaning, and because there is an absence of meaningless elements, the qualification [by "meaning"] is redundant. [Response: By the force of the recurrence [of the term from the previous rule], it will be understood that the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is intended as a reference to the first [element, i.e., *ghu*]. [Objection: If "that which has meaning becomes designated as *ghu*," then the designation *ghu* would undesirably apply to every single thing that has meaning. [Response: Because they are specified as *dā* and *dhā* alone, the connection will be with the meaning belonging to those [two roots].

And because they are impossible in the sense [of "meaning"], the relationship will be understood as being with those words that convey that sense. Furthermore, since this [relationship] pertains to the base and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*), it will apply to everything. Alternatively, the word "in the sense" (*arthe*) mentioned in the locative case is carried over [from the previous rule]; thus, whatever occurs in the sense [of "giving" and so on] is designated *ghu*. There is no risk of the designation applying to everything that exists in the sense [of "meaning"]. The terms *dā* and *dhā* are connected because they were mentioned immediately prior. The other [proponent] says: "The desired [result] is established, but an undesired one also follows; therefore, it cannot be done in this way."

[6] First of all, there is no purpose for the mention of the *prakṛti* (the base form). To this he says: "It must necessarily be stated. Let it be; even if the *prakṛti* is mentioned here, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) must be performed again. That very mention will serve both purposes. Otherwise, the substitution of *ṇ* prescribed for the word *me* when it occurs as *mā* would not apply. Therefore, the mention of the *prakṛti* must be made there. That [mention] will be moved forward [to the rule] "in the case of a verbal root beginning with *dh*" (*dhuprakṛtau*). And that very [mention] will then be connected with the word *mā*.

The other [Vārttikakāra] states the fault when the term *prakṛti* (root) is included in the rule regarding the substitution of *ṇatva* for *naṭvaśāsta*: "In *praniminoti* and *pranimīnāti*, the [substitution] would also apply here. This is because these two roots also possess the form *mā* as their base (*prakṛti*), due to the prescription of the vowel *ā* by the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (A 6.1.50). The other [Patañjali], wishing to explain this by his own reasoning, says: "Now, even if the inclusion of the term *prakṛti* were not made..."

He states the solution: "That very same [solution] which he will state here regarding the absence of *ṇatva*—namely, that 'pranimātā' and 'pranimātum' occur even when there is the inclusion of the root-form (*prakṛti*)—is what applies here. He says: "The inclusion of a root ending in long *ā* that has a *ṅit* marker shall be understood. The other, explaining by his own direct statement, says: "In that case, just as when it is not being done..."

[7] A prohibition regarding words that are identical in form must be stated. The thought is as follows: when the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied to the roots *dṛś* and *dhṛś*, the forms *dā* and *dhā* are produced by means of the vowel *ā*. Furthermore, this *ṛ*—which is an augment (*āgama*) prescribed as *rapara* in place of the *ṛ* of the root—does not destroy the meaningfulness of the base (*aṅga*), because even augments are included under the term "the base" (*āgamigrahaṇena*). Therefore, since the meaningfulness of the base remains intact, this prohibition of identical words is stated specifically in reference to the inclusion of meaningful elements.

Because there is no distinction in terms of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) between *abhakta* and *parādita* due to the presence of the letter *r*, or alternatively, because the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) implies the inclusion of "meaningful" (*arthavat*), this pair of forms—*pranidārayati* and *pranidhārayati*—is presented in the treatise in order to demonstrate that the inclusion of meaningful items occurs in many ways.

[a] There is no prohibition against identical words. This has already been stated: because of the mention of "its own form" (*svarūpa*) in the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* (A 1.1.68), a word functions in the grammatical treatise as having a dual nature—both consisting of its formal shape (*rūpātmaka*) and consisting of its meaning (*arthātmaka*). Therefore, the designation *ghu* applies only to those forms of *dā* and *dhā* that possess meaning. Furthermore, the word-forms *dā* and *dhā* [in the context of the roots] are meaningless; this is because the word-forms *dār* and *dhār* (the augmented forms) possess meaning. But surely, by the mention of those [roots], their augments (*āgama*) are also included?

This would indeed be so if this *repha* were an augment (*āgama*) of the word *dā*; but of what is it [an augment] then? It is that the *aṇ* following the vowel *ṛ* becomes followed by *ra*. As for the two positions—that [the *repha*] is not part of the preceding [vowel] or that it belongs to the beginning of the following [vowel]—they do not exist at all, and thus no refutation is offered there.

Regarding the rule *ā anupasargād vā*, the author now offers a rebuttal by relying on the designation *ghu* even for the word *dā-* when it is meaningless: "Let this [word *dā-*] have the designation *ghu*; however, since the operation prescribed for that [specific form] occurs, there is no fault. For a mere designation does not constitute a fault. Indeed, in the rules for *ghu*, *mā*, and so forth, the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed by the rules *naḥ* and *upasargāt* (A 8.4.16, 14). Furthermore, the designation 'preverb' (*upasarga*) applies only in connection with a verbal action (A 1.4.59), and here the word *dā-* does not denote a verbal action."

That which is designated as a *gati* or *upasarga* [by A 1.4.59–60] does not receive the designation *ghu*. And since that which possesses such a designation lacks the capacity to denote an action (*kriyā*), it cannot be an *upasarga* with respect to that [action]; thus, there is an absence of *ṇatva* [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*].

If you think that [the designation *ghu*] is permanently excluded because of its meaninglessness or because it lacks a prefix, then even in your desired case, the *ghu*-designation would not apply; thus he says: "In this case as well, then, it would not apply. For here too, the word *dāp* possesses meaning, and its connection with action is precisely with respect to that [meaning]; whereas the word *dā* does not possess meaning, nor is there a connection with action with respect to it. Thus, by means of a single solution, he effects the exclusion of both.

He effects a distinction from that [base], yet when there is an increase or decrease in it, there is no cessation of its designation. Just as in the world one who has acquired the designation "Devadatta" does not lose that designation, so too, when the *tṛc* and *san* suffixes have acquired the designation of *ardhadhātuka*, another element such as the vowel *i* arises due to the influence of the suffix; or, when the *a* of the *san* has disappeared, there is no cessation of the designation *ardhadhātuka*. For if that were the case, [the forms] *lavitā* and *pipaṭhiṣitā* [would be impossible].

(When a quality [guṇa] is present, that which is caused by an ārdhadhātuka suffix would not occur); likewise here too, although the letter *p*—which, due to the suffix, produces non-distinction between the two parts just as in common usage or in the treatises—is produced or disappears once the designation "dhruva" has been obtained for the roots *dā* and *ghu*, there is no loss of the designation "ghu."

This being the case, when the letter *p* is added to the two elements *dā* and *ghu*—which have acquired the designation *ghu* and do not differ [from their prior state]—and while they still retain the designation *ghu*, the rule "after a preposition" (*upasargasthāt*) is stated with reference to them as being meaningful (*arthavat*). However, even for that which has acquired a designation but is itself meaningless, there is no loss of its designation when another element is added that does not cause it to differ [from its prior state].

For instance, when it is said, "There is *guṇa*, there is *vṛddhi*," caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the letters *a* and *ā* become headed by the letter *r*. Likewise, this is introduced by way of the verb *dāpayati*; thus it is said, "An augment (*āgama*) belongs to that which possesses meaning. Even when there is an increase (or decrease) in that which has already acquired its designation, there is no loss of its own designation. For likewise, even for words consisting of initial, middle, or final parts, there is no loss of their own designations.
[Pāṇini 1.1.22: *taraptamapau ghaḥ*.

[1] Here, because they are marked with an *anubandha*, the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* refer specifically to the objects of the memory of the father (*pitṛ*). The form *taraptamapau* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). This [expression] is an imitation of an imitation (*anukaraṇānukaraṇa*). Furthermore, there are two views regarding *anubandhas*: an *anubandha* is treated as nothing other than an imitation; it merely undergoes the grammatical operation (*kārya*) while being imitated. Others, however, think that this [operation] is performed by the imitations themselves, which possess those very properties (*taddharma*).

In every respect, since "anubandha" (suffixal marker) has never before been understood as "gati" (a particle), it can be remembered here [in the rule *nady-uttara-pada*] that it is not a *gati*. Therefore, the designation *gha* would apply. In this regard, two solutions are possible: either the principle of "between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ*), or the association (*sāhacarya*) based on the expression "this cow has need of a second. Since the word *tarap*, which expresses excellence, is properly applied to the suffix *tamap* when there is no observed deviation from its primary sense, the association is not relied upon here.

However, being taught by its specific technical definition (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktatva*) is not possible here; for the definition does not teach the form ‘tarap’, but rather the word ‘tara’. And this word is indeed taught by its specific definition. Therefore, this is neither a form [taught] in the treatise nor a form used in actual linguistic practice; it is simply another way of presenting the matter.

He offers another solution: "In the case of the technical term *ghasaṃjñā*, there is no prohibition regarding the crossing of rivers (*nadītara*). That is to say, a prohibition need not be formulated. Furthermore, the word "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*)—derived from the verbal root *sidh* with the prefix *pra*- and the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "the act of prohibiting"—is connected with the negative particle *nañ* by virtue of its nature as an action. However, the author of the Bhāṣya, relying on the sense of a substance (*dravyabhūya*), explains it thus: "A prohibition that is purposeless is a non-prohibition (*apratiṣedha*)."

This negation, too, is designated as "negation" because it consists in the non-performance of an action, since it is established even without a formal negation. For the inclusion of the suffix *tarap* is *aupadeśika*: it is employed in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), or it exists within the instruction; thus, that word *tarap* which occurs in the grammatical treatise is understood here in its constituent sense—this is what he explains. He states: "The word [is used] for the sake of connecting with the accompanying *anubandha* (indicatory letter)."

And that suffix (*anubandha*) indicates another meaning or some other certain cause where there is identity of form; however, where there is no identity of form, it indicates the word-form itself. When this [suffix] takes on such a form as being accompanied by a suffix (*sānubandhaka*), and since the concealment of the meaning-form occurs upon connection with the audible word (*śruti*), the actual usage is carefully considered.

In this regard, he says that one which is non-deviant, eternal, and employed in its primary sense should be adopted: "And the apprehension of the form of a word does not occur without worldly usage. This is the logical conclusion. When there is a connection [to meaning], they should proceed with worldly usage. In that case, worldly usages need not be performed because the worldly practice involving the connection has ceased; therefore, this suffix *tarap* is not used.

What then? We rely on the word *tarap* as it appears in common usage, setting aside its secondary, non-eternal application. And what is that? It is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). In instruction, the word is *ap* and not *atarap*; this form does not exist in common usage nor in the technical treatise (*śāstra*). Since there is no occurrence of such a conceptual form, the designation *ghu* does not apply.

[2] Or rather, regarding "vāstvasya": it is the action (*kārya*) that leads to a fault, not the designation (*saṃjñā*). This refers to the case of *ghā* and *ḍi* suffixes in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). First of all, this example "nadyās taraḥ" (the crossing of the river) is one of non-coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the two suffixes expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*) and those which are self-referential (*svārthika*) function in coreferentiality when they denote excellence of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). When, then, that very river is itself the crossing? [One might object: "Should it not rather be 'tīrṇiḥ'? This is not a fault.

When it is said that "tara" means "that which is crossed," the general term "tara" alone is primarily relied upon. However, when subsequently the qualifier "river" is added—such as in the expression "the river is crossed"—then there is no abandonment of the gender of the primary element, just as one says "the nose has speech as its companion" (*mukhadvitīyā nāsikā*) and not "speechful" (*vacanī*). Alternatively, it is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); the word "tara" is qualified by "river," for words function with respect to aggregates.

The terms *strīliṅgeṣu* (in the case of feminine bases) and *ghādiṣu* (beginning with *gha*) [from A 6.3.43] and *striyām* (in the feminine) [from A 6.3.3] are understood [to carry over]. For when a collection [of phonemes] is associated with a gender, it is designated as "feminine" even if it is a term used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*). Examples include *brāhmaṇīrūpam*—meaning "this form is like a Brāhmaṇī woman"—and *brāhmaṇīveyam ākṛtiḥ*, which is called *brāhmaṇīrūpam*. Some cite *sāmataraḥ* from *sāmnas taraḥ*; since this would require the augment *nuṭ* by A 8.2.17 (*nādūghasya*), it is countered by the argument that it will not occur because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, [the term *saṃkhyā*] is defined by A 1.1.23: *bahuguṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* ("*bahu*, *guṇa*, *vat*, and *uḍati* are numerals").

Regarding the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) in the rule for the technical designation of number: it is a locative of reference (*adhikaraṇasaptamī*), meaning that the mention of "number" occurs within the sūtra that defines the technical term "number. Alternatively, it means that the mention of "number" applies whether the designation of number is being prescribed, about to be prescribed, or has already been prescribed. Furthermore, regarding this specific grammatical operation (*yoga*), the rule should be read as: "The words *bahu*, *guṇa*, *vatu*, *ḍati*, and numbers are designated as 'number'. This is demonstrated by stating: "It must be stated that a number also receives the technical designation of 'number'."

Alternatively, the reading should be formulated as follows: first "bahuguṇavatuḍati," and then "saṃkhyā ca. What is the purpose [of this]? This is the intended meaning: just as in the technical usage of the treatise (śāstra), worldly terms such as "animal" (*paśu*), "offspring" (*apatya*), "deity" (*devatā*), "of the Easterners" (*prācām*), and "of the Northerners" (*udīcām*) are employed—even though there is no formal definition (*paribhāṣaṇa*) for these in other treatises—so too these [words] beginning with "one" (*eka*) are merely worldly, being undefined by other treatises. And it is precisely with worldly terms that such linguistic usage is conducted.

Alternatively, what is the purpose? Is it for the sake of understanding an additional meaning? Here, this mention of *saṃkhyā* (number) is for the sake of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for these very words beginning with *bahu* when they denote number; so that it does not apply to the word *bahu* in the sense of "abundance," as in *bahurodanaḥ* ("much rice") or *bahuḥ sūpaḥ* ("much soup"). Nor should it apply to words denoting a multitude (*pūga*), a collection (*saṃgha*), or a quality (*guṇa*).

"The thirsty herd of deer drank the water here"—this is how it is described. When *saṃkhyā* (number) refers to "bahu" and so forth, he shows that this is for the purpose of determining that "saṃkhyā" is a technical term (*saṃjñā*). Regarding the phrase "of numbers beginning with one in the rules concerning number": since a technical term exists for the sake of its function (*kārya*), he takes up the rule (*pradeśa*) itself. For the purpose of acquiring a name is not for the sake of the named things themselves; rather, it is for the sake of understanding their function.

"Just as there is a conventional understanding that 'paśu' (animal) means 'apatyam' (offspring), so it will be here as well," he says: "But surely, in common usage, numbers such as one and so forth are recognized as being 'number' (*saṃkhyā*). For otherwise, there would be no conventional understanding because of its artificiality, just as in the world. Why? Because between the artificial and the non-artificial, the conventional understanding of the operation applies to the artificial; for you have understood this precisely from common usage. What is this principle by which such a conventional understanding exists in the world? It is said in reply:

In this context, the word *gopālaka* (cowherd), when employed on the basis of a specific cause for its meaning, would require a corresponding justification (*pratividhāna*), such as "he plows with five ploughs" [where the number is justified by the tools]; or it would require agency, as in "he protects these [cows]"; or it would require a genus (*jāti*). Alternatively, a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) being adopted on the basis of one cause excludes another cause, just as an action excludes genus and the like. A restriction applies only to objects of the same class; so it is here as well. Thus, since only words beginning with *bahu* are the subject under discussion here, the suffix *bhav* [is applied]. . . .
The sixth Āhnika in the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā:
[Pāṇini 1.1.27] "The words beginning with *sarva* are pronouns (*sarvanāman*)."

1.1. Regarding the expression *sarvādīni*, what kind of compound is this? [Response: The question is inappropriate because there is no doubt [regarding its nature]. Doubt arises only where, despite the same phonetic form being heard, there is no basis for determining a specific meaning. For example, in the case of *sthūlapṛṣatīm*, because the accent is not determined, it is not known whether the word under discussion is a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*. But here, it is not so. If one were to assume that it means "that which is both *sarva* and *ādi*," then the word *ādi* would be redundant.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the gender and number of the word *ādi* to be abandoned on account of its predominance; otherwise, the inclusion of *viśva* and the others as subordinate members would be purposeless. If it is instead conceived that "it is called *ādi* because things are taken from it (*asmād ādīyate*)," such that "everything is taken from this," then such a conception is untenable, because the word *ādi* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*).

1.3 Furthermore, even if one were to say "the beginning of everything," this is not so; since there is nothing else that could be its beginning, the doubt that "this is indeed a *bahuvrīhi* compound" is untenable. Likewise, when it has been taught that "it is a *bahuvrīhi*," it should not be asked: "What is its analysis (*vigraha*) here?"

1.4 This is not a fault. Here, in the process of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), when "the two Gārgyas" (*gārgyau*) is intended, sometimes the speaker intends to express the specific quality of having a living father, and sometimes the general quality of being a descendant of Garga. This comprehension depends on what is intended to be expressed. Just as in the rule *tadādyācikhyāsāyām* (Pāṇini 1.1.27), although it could have been stated simply as *tadākhyāyām*, the inclusion of the term *ācikhyāsā* (desire to express) is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule applies even when the speaker intends to express [the first member] as being the beginning (*āditvena*). Otherwise, how would it apply in such a case? Thus is the meaning.

1.5 And here, he asks this: is this a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the *ekaśeṣa* has already been performed, or does it function as a single primary referent (*prāthamaikārthavṛtti*)? [The answer is: "It is both *sarva* and the beginning (*ādi*"), thus *sarvādi*. These are the *sarvādi* [words] because the word *sarva* is their first. This is formed either by the rule *napuṃsakam anapuṃsakena* (A 1.2.68), or by the option [stated in] *svarabhinnānāṃ yasyottaraḥ svaravidhiḥ* (A 1.2.64, Vārttika 24). Furthermore, the expression "it is both *sarva* and the beginning" is employed for the sake of conveying a uniform form.

Thus, it is possible to postulate *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from a group of identical items). And even without the mechanism of *ekaśeṣa*, it is possible to rely on the fact that what is denoted by words such as *sarva* and others is called a "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). (1.6) The other [opponent], having taken the principle about to be stated into his mind, demonstrates that this *bahuvrīhi* functions in its primary sense and does not involve the internalization of another word-meaning; thus he says, "It is a *bahuvrīhi*. What is its analysis (*vigraha*)? From the analysis, this meaning can be understood as being close at hand: "Either it is a simple *bahuvrīhi*, or it is one in which *ekaśeṣa* has been performed."
Just as from the analysis [of the compound] *sthūlapṛṣatīm* one understands that the compound is for the sake of a specific meaning, he asks: "What is its analysis?"

1.7 Now, for what purpose is it said, "these very ones" (*tānīmāni*)? It is said: because without this [expression], there would be no status as an external referent (*anyapadārthatā*). For the compound *citragavaḥ asya* does not constitute a *bahuvrīhi* merely by these two words, because the cows are merely being characterized (*upalakṣyamāṇatvāt*). And where the possessive (*tadvat*) is qualified by "having variegated cows," there the *bahuvrīhi* occurs; thus, a difference in form arises regarding the relationship between the subordinate and the principal. Furthermore, the external referent is pointed out by the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in such expressions as "one who possesses cows," "one born in the month of Māsa," or "the one with variegated cows."

1.8 If this is so regarding the word *sarva*: if this *bahuvrīhi* compound functions according to its primary meaning, because a *bahuvrīhi* has as its referent the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). For it is the meaning of another word that is the determining factor for a *bahuvrīhi*. This is because the meaning of another word is predominant in a *bahuvrīhi*.

Just as in the compound *rājapuruṣam ānaya* ("bring the king's man"), according to the theory that a compound abandons its own literal meaning (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), the meaning of "king" is not expressed by a word; it serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and, having entered into a state of being subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) to the man, does not attain the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*). Thus, the action [of bringing] is not understood as being for the sake of the king. In the same way, even though the "variegated cows" are heard as a defining characteristic, they do not function as the principal. What then? It is said: although not expressed by a word, they are understood as having attained the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatā*) when they are in proximity to the action.

1.9 Alternatively, that which exists together with qualities (*guṇa*) is "possessing those qualities" (*tadguṇa*). The meaning is that in the expression *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*, the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—which is qualified by the term *saṃnihita* ("proximate")—is understood as being associated with the action. But why is this so? For it has been stated: "Or [it is so] because the former [term] is prescribed in the sense of possession" (*matvarthe vā pūrvasya vidhānāt*; A 2.2.25, Vārttika 5). Furthermore, some possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) have as their sole domain the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), as in the word *gomān* ("possessor of cows").

One [type of *bahuvrīhi*] has as its object a direct contact (*saṃsarga*), such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Another has as its object an indirect contact (*ayuta-saṃsarga*), such as "the horned one" (*viṣāṇin*). For a bull that has a horn attached to its neck does not become "horned" merely by the presence of the horn; likewise, one is not called "wearing the sacred thread" (*yajñopavītī*) simply because the thread exists, nor is one called "wearing it around the neck" (*nivītī*). In this way, the *bahuvrīhi* compound "white-clad and red-turbaned" refers to a specific contact, just like the word "horned."

The statement "This is Citragu" has as its object merely the relationship of owner and owned; it should be understood that this very nature of the word functions with respect to objects through such differentiation. Furthermore, this is not the view in Grammar—that without which [something] does not exist—such as [the view that] "without the reality of the object... there is no eating," or likewise, "without two garments. Therefore, even the two garments are a part of the act of eating; such is the meaning of the word. In Grammar, however, the determination of meaning is based on the state of being that and being produced by that (*tadbhāva-tadbhāvitatvena*).

1.11 This also is not accepted, nor is it the case here that, as elsewhere, there is a "co-ordination of the primary and the subordinate" (*guṇopaguṇasaṃvijñāna*) regarding what is taught. For instance, when one says, "Bring him who was seen wearing white clothes," the two garments are certainly not the defining characteristic [of the person]. And when it is commanded, "Feed those Devadatta and the others who were seen," then even a Devadatta who was not previously mentioned is understood as a recipient of the meal. Therefore, the very form of the word itself must be accepted [as the basis].

1.12 But surely, even in a *kriyāsaṃvijñāna* compound, the word *sarva* should not function as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Rather, it should be a name for those words beginning with *viśva* that are intended therein and are accompanied by the word *sarva*. Just as when one says, "Let the one wearing a snake-sacrifice-thread be fed," only the one actually present who wears the snake-sacrifice-thread eats, and not the snake separately; in exactly the same way, when one says, "Feed the son in the aggregates," it is that son who eats.

1.13 This is not a fault. Just as in the case of the command "feed [him] together with his son" (*saha-putram bhojaya*), the verb *bhuj* (to eat) applies to the son—even though he is subordinate—when the word *saha* is employed; for it is not the case that one has eaten "with his son" if the son does not eat. Thus, this is merely a verbal distinction (*viśeṣa*), but we do not say that the comprehension arises from the word itself. Just as someone might eat with two people, so too when it is said "this man eats well with his son," the son is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as he participates in the action; yet this is not a property of the word.

1.14 Here too, the designation of *sarva* and the others as *viśva* and so forth is directly perceived. Furthermore, the word *sarva* is also understood through inference and other means; thus, the status of *sarva* and the others as [belonging to] the *sarvādi* group is established. For the application of words occurs in many ways: in some cases there is merely the state of being an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), not actual proximity, as in the case of "the owner of brindled cows" (*citragu*). In some cases, one is proximate to an action but not actually engaged in that action, as in "feed the white-clad one" or "let the one wearing a serpent as a sacred thread be fed. In some cases, one who is performing an action is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, the word *ādi* (beginning) is employed here in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*). And since that proximity qualifies the aggregate itself rather than the individual parts such as *viśva* and so forth, [the designation] is applied to the parts because it cannot be connected to the name of the aggregate. Since those parts are being inferred, just as *viśva* and the others are connected when they are being inferred, why should the word *sarva* not also be understood in the same way?

1.16 But when the word *ādi* signifies "type" (*prakāra*), then it is also established. For example, in the expression "the nights with the fifth being auspicious" (*kalyāṇapañcamā rātrayaḥ*), although it is said "the fifth is auspicious," from this one does not derive the status of primacy for that [fifth]; what then? It is [the status of primacy] for "these" (the nights). Just as in the case of the command, "Let the Brahmins be brought from Devadatta’s house," Devadatta is also brought because he is a Brahmin, or because of his connection to the house; so too the word *sarva* occurs in the sense of another referent (*anyapadārtha*) as in "of these" (*eṣām*).

1.17 However, regarding the rule of established usage (*vyavasthā*), the objection raised by relying on the word "beginning" (*ādi*) and the sense of "proximity" (*samīpa*) has already been answered; moreover, those two are indeed distinct. It has also been demonstrated in the *Bhāṣya* that for a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [compound], the meaning of the compound is the collection (*samudāya*).

As for the expression "here, the pronouns" (*iha sarvanāmāni*): surely there is no application of the terms "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) to technical names (*saṃjñā*). Even if it were so, this would still not apply to technical terms used in the science of grammar (*śāstra*). What then? It would apply to worldly [names]; yet even this is not tenable.

2.2 Furthermore, since the relationship between a name and the named is being established, this must be stated in every case: "How does the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* operate? For it has been stated [by Patañjali]: "The relationship between word and meaning is already established" (MBh Paspaśā Vārttika 1). Moreover, it must be stated whether the name is formed with the *ṇ* substitution already applied, or whether it is formed without the *ṇ* substitution and subsequently acquires the *ṇ* substitution.

If, first of all, the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) has already been performed, by what means would that *ṇatva* occur prior to the existence of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)? Or, if *ṇatva* occurs in a word where it has not yet been performed, even so, because the word undergoes modification, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being non-eternal (*anitya*). Furthermore, since the speaker has freedom of choice regarding the essential form (*svarūpa*), this usage as a single word might occur only occasionally. Why is this so? Because in the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-darśana*), this distinction does not exist at all.

2.4 In the technical usage of the treatise (*śāstra*), however, the analysis [of compounds] sometimes follows the literal meaning of the words, as in the case of the word *rājapuruṣa*, where there is a correspondence with the literal meanings of the words as they occur in a sentence. Sometimes, however, there is an explanatory derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of a group of words whose actual function pertains to a different meaning from the individual components, as in *gaurakhara*, *lohitaśāli*, and *kṛṣṇasarpa*. For in the compound as a whole, the properties of being a "cow" (*gotva*) and so forth, or the properties of being a "donkey" (*kharatva*) and so forth, do not exist at all.

When a composite whole (*samudāya*) that functions solely in its own essential form (*svarūpamātra*) is grammatically explained (*anvākhyāna*) through two [words] functioning as distinct classes (*jātyantara*), the conventional distinction between "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) does not cease.

(2.5) Furthermore, technical designations (*śāstrasaṃjñā*) do not differ from worldly designations (*laukikī saṃjñā*). Since that very same property (*dharma*) which belongs to the former also belongs to these [latter], it follows that here too there must be the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*].

(2.6) Nor is eternality (*nityatva*) contradicted in the case of a connection with a designation. Why? Because the restriction of capacity (*śaktiniyama*) is a human convention (*pauruṣeya*). This is because a person’s activity consists in the adoption of a limitation of capacity, whether based on the observation of a single capacity or the observation of multiple capacities.

2.7 The view of others: Those very word-meaning relations which are perceived directly—such as "cow," "horse," "fire," and "water"—are eternal. However, that which causes understanding through inference is non-eternal, namely that which is preceded by convention (*samaya*). Just as worldly people, having established [the relation], convey the object through inference arising from the conjunction of the sense organs, whereas *śruti* conveys it directly.

2.8 But another says: even in that case, the group of words consisting of technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*) is indeed eternal; the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) effects the substitution of *ṇ* for that which has already had *ṇ* substituted. Thus, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs within the name, and the word becomes correct once the substitution of *ṇ* has been made. It does not create a different form. A name should not be formulated without the substitution of *ṇ* having been made. For the rule concerning the substitution of *ṇ* is precisely what effects the removal [of the original sound]. And having established this, it was said: "In the case of names and the like, there is a conceptualization based on what is logically appropriate (*nyāyyabhāvāt*)."

2.9 Regarding the designation *sarvanāman*, there is an absence of *ṇatva* due to specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*). Now, it might be objected that by this very principle, the rule for *ṇatva* would indeed apply. This is not a fault; rather, it demonstrates the following: in common usage (*loka*), this word does not have *ṇatva* applied to it. In the scientific treatise (*śāstra*), however, the Teacher has employed it in its form without *ṇatva*. For if that were the case, it would indeed be incorrect (*asādhu*). But even in common usage, wherever it serves as a designation for whatever [referent], it is remembered here by the Teacher precisely in its form without *ṇatva*; and thus it is so.

2.10 Alternatively, this objection is raised by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*): "When the substitution of *ṇ* has been established by a prescriptive rule (*vidhi-vākya*) accompanied by an explanatory supplement (*upaskāra*), [the rule] 'Aṅga-final *ṇ* is not substituted after a word other than the first member when it is a name' (A 8.4.3) applies. How can this *śruti* (direct statement), while operating for another purpose, be occupied with the relationship between a name and the named, and thus become a sublater? 2.11 But the other [respondent] says: "[This is] a traditional rule (*smṛti*) belonging to the position of inference. Therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* is inferred, and from this [rule], the absence of *ṇ* (*aṇatva*) is also [inferred]. Thus, the substitution of *ṇ* is established by its own nature (*svabhāva-siddha*), while the absence of *ṇ* is merely remembered (*smaryate*).

2.12 What is this so-called *nipātana*? You establish the prohibition by means of *nipātana*, stating that "the prohibition of *ṇatva* must be stated. And if *nipātana* is equivalent to a prohibition, then this is appropriate. In what way is *nipātana* equivalent? If it sets aside a rule (*vidhi*), then the cessation [of the rule] is unqualified; for that very reason, it becomes equivalent to a prohibition.

2.13 Whatever is the property of negation is the very same as that of nipātana (the setting aside of a rule). For negation is, by its very nature, an inference regarding what has not occurred; it does not function according to the logic of a stake and its counter-stake. Since the setting aside (nipātana) is likewise so, he introduces this [question]: "Now, what is called negation?"

2.14 Having stated something without qualification—namely, *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (A 4.1.5)—and then stating it with a qualification—namely, *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* (A 4.1.10)—the teacher’s intention is clearly understood there: that this [suffix] does not apply. It is understood that the teacher’s intention is that he did not intend to include, nor did he actually employ, that particular word [in his formulation].

2.15 But what is the reason that, between the injunctions of prescription and prohibition, the prescriptive sentence does not become weakened, whereas the prohibitive sentence alone becomes weakened—as in "The Brahmins are to be fed" and "Kauṇḍinya is not to be fed"? It is said in reply:

2.16 [a] Neither a conjunction nor a disjunction can be established; nor does an alternative (vikalpa) obtain. Cessation would be utterly contradicted. Because of contradiction, a conjunction cannot be conceived or established; nor does an alternative obtain, since cessation has been admitted. For how could there be cessation at the very outset? If it is argued that "one prevents what has arisen," then everything must cease entirely.
Furthermore, for one who has accomplished his purpose, there is no further injunction to eat elsewhere.

2.16 [a] Alternatively, words are indeed distinct in every sentence; yet, because they have an identical phonetic form, they serve as means of communication for a cognizer who perceives them similarly. One thinks that when the word *kauṇḍinya* is uttered, it is the undifferentiated word *brāhmaṇa* itself that is expressed. 2.16 [i] This is the view of others: [No. It is not that the *śakalakaṇṭaka* fruit is intended to be grasped, but rather its inclusion is necessary as a concomitant. Likewise here, it is not that *kauṇḍinya* is intended to be expressed, but it is included due to its necessary concomitance; thus, *kauṇḍinya* is excluded from the positive injunction (*vidhi*).

2.16 [Ī] Another view: Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stronger than inference (*anumāna*). Thus, in the case of the Vedic revelation regarding Brahmins, there is doubt as to whether [the injunction] applies; however, in the case of a prohibition, there is no doubt. Furthermore, it is improper for two ritual actions enjoined by both direct perception and inference to be performed alternatively.
