But surely, the injunction applies to Kauṇḍinya by virtue of his being a Brāhmaṇa, not by virtue of his being a Kauṇḍinya; for when the word "Brāhmaṇa" is heard, [the application] is directly perceived. This is not so. Since a universal is that which has its distinctions unmanifested due to a particularity, one should not apply [the injunction] optionally. Furthermore, since the universal is a distinct entity, Kauṇḍinya is connected with "Brāhmaṇahood"; therefore, one who understands [the injunction] in accordance with that [universal] becomes connected with the act of eating precisely through inference. However, in the case of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), because it is directly enjoined, an option is likewise not tenable.

2.16 [u] The view of others: This restriction applies only when [the primary application] is impossible; for there is no such thing as an impossibility that cannot be conceived. Because Kauṇḍinya was fed on account of his being a Brāhmaṇa, it would follow that he was not fed; since this is impossible, the exclusion occurs by the very force of the meaning. 2.16 [ū] Others think: This very verb *bhuj* (to eat) is prescribed in the form of both engagement and withdrawal, just as in the case of the "optionally fixed" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) rule.

2.16 [e] Another view is as follows: this statement occurs within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) and serves as a subordinate means (*upāyabhūta*) to some primary sentence (*pradhānavākya*). It is not logical that the meaning established in a subordinate sentence should be applied to the primary sentence, because it constitutes a different verbal expression, just as the words "cow" (*go*) and "donkey" (*khara*) are meaningless when used together.

2.17 But this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Feed the Brahmins. Now, while they are being fed, no transgression (*pratyavāya*) occurs, for the purpose of the caste (*jāti*) has been fulfilled without deficiency.

2.18 But here, when someone is addressed after specifying certain individuals with the words "A Brahmin must not be killed," a transgression necessarily occurs if he is killed; for in that case, the act of killing has been carried out. Here, however, non-killing is what is enjoined. In that context, performing the opposite action leads to fault.

"In this way, when it is said 'the Brahmins are to be fed,' once some have been fed, they are indeed considered fed; however, when one Kauṇḍinya has been fed, another Kauṇḍinya need not be fed. This refers to the prohibition of the act of eating (*bhujeḥ pratiṣedhe*). And having established this, it is said: "Prescriptive injunctions (*vidhi*) are not set aside by non-performance [of the action], but a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) brings the action to a halt."

2.19 Furthermore, as for what is postulated—that Kauṇḍinya, who was included by the word "brāhmaṇa," is excluded—it is not that a person acts in accordance with one word and not the other. Just as when one says "Do it" and another says "Do not do it," one accepts one of the two as authoritative; yet the matter has not been left unexpressed by either one, so it is here as well. However, it must be explained why he does not act in both ways; and this has been demonstrated in detail.

In the world as well, having said "Go thus," one says again "Do not go"; one understands that this person acts with some purpose in mind. 2.20 Alternatively, speakers in the world may be at fault; however, one who has *darbha* grass and a *pavitra* in hand, who is observant in speech, whose conduct is virtuous, who is like a mother and father, and who does not contradict what is heard in the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*—in such a case, it is inferred that there is simply no [contradictory] attainment [of the opposite].

2.21 But as for that which is prohibited when it has already become applicable, such as "the village cock is not to be eaten," in this case there is no inference of what was previously unobtained. For when activity proceeds according to the indication of the purpose (*arthalakṣaṇā*), one perceives the visible purpose and, understanding even the afterlife result [of abstaining] from killing and so forth, does not come to grief.
2.22 This entire principle applies to the case of irregular forms (*nipātana*); thus he says: "An irregular form (*nipātana*) is also of this very same kind."

2.23 But surely, by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there would be the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, just as there is the substitution of *ṇ* in *prāpaṃ*. This is what [the author] intends: a prohibition is essentially a form of cessation. In that case, the cessation of that [substitution] is appropriate. However, since an irregular derivation consists of a linguistic form, its own nature must be understood; thus, it is precisely the substitution of *ṇ* prescribed by another rule that is ceased. Since this is a distinct linguistic item (*śabdāntara*) which is declared to be correct, the restriction of its technical name (*saṃjñāniyama*) is logically consistent.

2.24 Are there other instances of this kind? For example, the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (A 6.1.77). Here too, there is no relationship between a modifier and a modified entity (*vikārivikārabhāva*), because [the letters] are accepted as being eternal. Thus, in the absence of the "ashes and khadira-wood" maxim (*bhasmakhadiranyāya*), this is merely the occurrence of another word; consequently, the word *dadhy-*—being understood as correct only within a *saṃhitā*—would not sublate the word *dadhi-*.

2.25 "The genitive case is employed here"—this is the intended meaning. When the term *sthāna* (substitute) is applied to a *yaṇ* that has not yet been previously modified, then there is an absolute non-application [of the rule], because [the previous form] has ceased according to the principle "in *saṃhitā*, an *ik* is replaced. When the cognition of the *yaṇ* enters into the word as its phonetic form, even there, that cognition is either displaced by another cognition or arises [as a new one]. Therefore, in both views, the cessation [of the original form] is logical. Here too, where the genitive does not occur... [text fragment]...

Regarding the rule "in *saṃjñā*... (A 8.4.3), there is an absolute absence of the letter *n* there; however, in this case, because the genitive case is absent, an option (*vikalpa*) arises. Why? Because that [genitive] is either not expressed or is merely indicated, an option consequently follows. 2.27 The substitutes for *śap*, such as *śyan* and others, will be treated as such. If it were so, then in the form *karoti*, there would be an extension (*atideśa*) of the *pit*-status [of the affix]. The *nit*-status of *śyan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this does not occur. Thus, in *vidhyati*, [the *nit*-status] does not apply. But in another case, the *śit*-status exists, and by that, the *ṅit*-status does not occur.

2.28 Furthermore, in the case of *kurvīti*, the augment *num* would apply according to the rule *śapśyanor nityam* (A 7.1.81). This is not a fault, because of the inclusion of *śyan*. As for *dhinute*, how is it that the elision of *a* applies by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (A 6.4.48)? Here too, there is an indicator (*liṅga*) regarding its being a non-sārvadhātuka suffix: namely, that [Pāṇini] recites the letter *ś* in the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ* (A 3.1.77).

2.29 Even so, since the suffix *śap* is applicable in its proper place, it would follow that *śnam* occurs after it, because *śnam* is an exception (*apavāda*) to that very place. First, this must be asked: why does the augment *iṭ* not occur at the beginning? If you think [it does not] "because it is superseded by more numerous [suffixes]," then here too there is supersession by *śyan* and the others.

2.30 It might be argued: "The genitive case [ending] is one, namely 'of the *la* affix' (A 3.4.77). But that is not so; because there is a distinction between each individual substitute (*pratyādeśa*), the genitive is manifold. However, in this case—namely, in the rule "for *phali*, *pāṭi*, *nabhi*, *mani*, and *jan*, there is *guk*, and *paṭi*, *na*, *aki*, *dha*, and *ta*" (Uṇādi 1.18)—because the general relation is what is introduced, the constituent syntactic statements (*vibhāgavākya*) are indeed distinct expressers. Thus, the genitive has distinct referents with respect to the operations of the expressers.

2.31. If this is so, then [the augment] should occur by that very designation (*ādeśa*) as *sup* (or *num*). No; because of its status as a *mit* [augment], why does this [augment] come after what is proximate? As in the rule “*bhrasjo ropadhayoḥ...*” (A 6.4.47). Why is it not the same in the case of *payāṃsi*? This has been examined under the rule “*midaco ’ntyāt paraḥ*” (A 1.1.47).

2.32 “That indeed is what was indicated first. Now, it might be argued that there would be an option (*vikalpa*) due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) [of the term]; however, this is incorrect. Even without the recurrence [of the term], one accepts the relationship between the sublated (*bādhyam*) and the sublator (*bādhakam*) when there is the abandonment of what follows from the thesis (*pratijñā*). An option arises precisely in that case. Furthermore, if an option were to exist even when there is such a recurrence, there would result a contradiction with what follows from the thesis and the consequence of [the argument becoming a mere] restatement (*anuvāda*); this is how it stands.

2.33 In that case, regarding the rule "avyayasarvanāmnām... (A 5.3.71), there is no restriction of location here. What then? Because it has already been stated, it raises the objection that there should indeed be an option; thus, one would obtain the forms *uccakaiḥ* and *uccaiska*.

2.34 This demonstrates that nothing is commenced [or applied] unless [the conditions] have been reached. Even more so when Pāṇini’s rule is accepted, there is neither a prescription nor a cessation of anything; rather, there is absolute non-application. . . . This is what is appropriate here. If this is so, then regarding the application of *akac*, no specific distinction has been indicated, as it is enjoined in a general sense. Thus one understands . . .

And wherever either an alternative (vikalpa) or a conjunction (samuccaya) is possible, one should understand that in every such case, having perceived the relationship between the general and the particular, the specific [meaning] is not enjoined here by means of a general term.

2.35. An irregular formation (*nipātana*) is also of this same kind. If, then, these are indeed irregular formations, it was with reference to this very case that the following was questioned: "Why is it stated [in A 6.1.144] that 'for the sake of the continuity of the action' (*kriyāsātasya*)"? Even when an irregular formation exists, an option (*vikalpa*) is observed—as in the forms *satatam* and *saṃtatam*. Therefore, how is it to be understood that there is only an exclusion (*nivṛtti*) and not an option? And if this were the case, two genitive cases would result.

Effort must be exerted here, for there are indeed exceptions (*nipātana*) that cause obstruction, according to the principle stated previously. This [rule] must be formulated for the sake of the meaning of the word *hita*, in order to establish the forms *saṃhita* and *sahita*. In that very context, this [usage] should be added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyeya*). Furthermore, there is no continuity (*sāṃtatyam*), because of the rule regarding sheep (*avyika-nyāya*). Regarding the prohibition concerning technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and secondary members (*upasarjana*): the author of the Vārttika indicates their distinctness on the grounds that they are different words. The author of the Bhāṣya, however, says "of those that have become technical terms or secondary members," maintaining that it is the same word that has reached this particular state.

3.2 “Give to *sarva*. But surely, by the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*), this will not occur—just as in the case of “the two boys are Agni and Soma”? This is not so. This principle applies to word-operations (*padakārya*); however, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to nominal bases (*prātipadika*). And in that context, this [principle] does not apply; thus it has been stated: “[The rules for] *vṛddhi* and *āt* [substitution] depend on the word-form (*śabda*).”

3.3 Even so, according to the rule "a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is applied to that which resides in a single substance" (A 1.4.1 Vārttika 44), the technical name for a name (*saṃjñā-saṃjñā*) is a sublater of the preceding [technical name]. Just as the technical name *saṃjñā-saṃjñā*—stated in "a genus (*jāti*) is a compound, a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a pronominal (*sarvanāman*), and that which has all genders" (A 1.4.1 Vārttika 41)—sublates the technical name *guṇavacana*, such that [the word] *daivadattya* does not occur [as a *guṇavacana*], this [present case] must likewise be sublated. This statement is made without relying upon that [sublation].

3.4 “*atisarvāya dehi*” (give to one who surpasses all). This is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound). For if it were a *bahuvrīhi*, the prohibition [of the designation *sarvanāman*] would already have been established. How then is there the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with such a term)? Its purpose lies in the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables (*avyaya*). Alternatively, in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), the member of the compound (*aṅga*) is qualified by the words beginning with *sarva*; and this must necessarily be accepted for the sake of establishing forms such as *paramasarvasmai dehi*. 3.5 How should that [list of *sarvādi* words] be formulated? Is it in the form of a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), or in the recitation (*pāṭha*), or in the list (*gaṇa*), or in the sūtra, or in both places?

3.6 Exclusion by virtue of being listed in the recitation (*pāṭha*). For if a prohibition were made regarding the technical name (*saṃjñā*), the internal operations of the group (*antargaṇakārya*) would not be avoided. Since the prohibition is applied to the entire list (*gaṇa*), there is no possibility of its application to the first case endings (*prathamādiṣu*); thus, it is precisely here that the reading is specified. The purpose of assigning the technical name is only for those items actually listed here. Therefore, "all" (*sarva*) and the others are [treated as such] provided they are not technical names (*asaṃjñā*) or subordinate members (*upasarjana*), whereas other [items] are not included in the list at all.

And those which are of such a nature are designated as "all names" (*sarvanāman*); yet, because they are not established as being similar [to the others], one does not recognize them as having that designation. Just as in the rule for contempt and repetition (*kutsanāhīkṣṇyayoḥ*), the words *gotra* and so forth [are used] in those two senses, but the words *gotra* and so forth are not used elsewhere.

3.7 Is it without distinction? Does the prohibition apply to that which is the operation for all [words] by virtue of the term "sarvanāmnaḥ"? The meaning is: both with distinction and without distinction. That operation characterized by the arrangement in the *gaṇapāṭha* belongs to specific [words], as in “from those ending in -ṅatara, etc. (A 7.1.25) and “of *tyad* and so forth” (A 7.2.102). However, that which is stated as “from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*” (A 7.1.27) applies without distinction.
Although this sequence applies to these two within a group (*gaṇa*), it is not adopted here; rather, this is simply a different arrangement.

(3.8) The purpose [of the mention of] *ḍatara* and so on is for the occurrence of *adbhāva*. *Adbhāva* does not occur after *atikatarat* because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). However, it is understood that it must occur here, as in *paramakatarat*. (3.9) A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made later. Because of the formulation "not when it is a technical term" (*asaṃjñāyām*), the items beginning with *sarva* are disregarded. And in that case, the specific arrangement already mentioned is expected, not the technical term itself.

3.10 The rule *anupasarjanāt* (A 4.1.14) is rejected. But surely this rule must be formulated for the sake of the *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) by means of the principal [element], so that forms such as *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* and *soka(? kauru)careyaḥ* may be obtained? This is not a reference to a *kṛt*-suffix; for there is also an *aṇ* suffix that is a *taddhita*.

3.11 This purpose does not exist. For it has already been stated: "In the case of the mention of a suffix, [the rule applies] when it is not a feminine suffix. Thus, there is no need to refer to the specific prescription "from feminine [stems], the suffix *ḍhak*" (A 4.1.120). If this is so, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding secondary members (*upasarjana*). To this, too, a remedy has been provided: "not when it is a secondary member" (*upasarjane na*).

3.12 Being thus rejected, the technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is understood as having the letter *a* and the letter *kā* as its indicators. Wherever one says "after an *a*" and "the two letters *kā*," the term "non-derivative" (*anupasarjana*) applies there, meaning "the non-derivative sense. Alternatively, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of case-endings, *suluk*... (A 7.1.39). Or else, it is a reference to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, the construction of case endings occurs according to the specific requirement.

3.13 If this were so, forms such as *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad* would not be established. In the case of *atiyuṣmad ānaya* ("bring those who have surpassed you") or *atiyuṣmadānaya*, the substitution of *at* [for *ad*] prescribed by the rule *pañcamyā at* (Pāṇini 7.1.31) would not apply. This is a composite (praśliṣṭa) formulation: wherever *a* and *kāra* (the letter *a*) are prescribed after an *a*, there the term *ad* refers to that which is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*). For them, the substitution of *tyadādi-atva* (the replacement of *tyad* etc. with *a*) is not included, because it is not prescribed after a stem ending in *a*.

Now, how should the form *priyau dvau asya* be analyzed? For the letter *a* here is not [the *a*] following the [first] *a*. Furthermore, the presence (*satvam*) [of the *a*] is indeed not prohibited, as in the case of *atitad*. And this [form] *atisarvāya* has likewise not been resolved.

3.14 Alternatively, regarding the section on *aṅga* (the base), that which is stated applies when [the base] is being grasped with its case-ending. In a specific rule (*pradeśa*), whether the case-ending is different or the same, when a relationship of qualifier and qualified is conceived between words having the forms of those being grasped, if the term *aṅgasya* is introduced as the primary element, then *ḍatara* and so forth are the qualifiers; thus, while *paramakatara* is established, here [the form] *atikatara* would result.

3.15 Now, if *ḍatara* and so forth are the primary element (*pradhāna*), then because there is no rule for [substitution] of that which ends in them (*tadanta-vidhi*), forms such as *atikataram* are established; however, *paramakatarad* is not established, nor are *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad*. 3.16 Now, if the understanding is that "of the *aṅga*" is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) and "of *tyad*-etc. is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then—meaning "the *akāra* replaces those *tyad*-etc. elements which are parts of the *aṅga* when a following case-ending (*vibhakti*) intervenes"—the form *paramasa* is established. But here too, it would undesirably apply to *atitad*.

3.17 However, if it can be assumed here that the rule regarding "that which ends with [an element]" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies to the context of "all names" (*sarvanāmāni*), such that "all names" means "names of all," then this section [beginning with] "the words beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādīni*) serves as a qualifier. Consequently, the meaning here results in: "That which has something beginning with *sarva* at its end is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Furthermore, a pronoun does not include that which ends in a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Therefore, there is no application of the *tadanta-vidhi* in those cases; thus, forms such as *paramasarvasmāt* will be valid, but *atisarvāya* will not.

However, the grammatical operation beginning with *ḍatara* cannot be avoided, because it is not extraneous to the context (*aprākaraṇika*). But regarding that rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadanta-vidhi*) which is extraneous to the context, there is both application and non-application, based on the statement: "The purpose [of this rule] lies in the technical designations of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables" (Vārttika 8 on A 1.1.72). Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya resorts to another method: "That [designation] applies to the case-ending belonging to the words being taken. This means the case-ending is related to the words being taken—that is, those being uttered—and the relationship is not understood as being characterized by the act of prescription.

What then? It is for the purpose of indicating meaning; that is, when the case-ending indicates the meaning of words such as *tyad* and so on, [the substitution applies] to the base (*aṅga*). And likewise, it applies to those two [suffixes] which indicate the meanings of "self" and "one's own" belonging to *ḍatara* and so on; similarly, it applies to *ḍasi* and *ṅi* belonging to a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). But in this case, the forms *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad* are desired.

3.19 If it is thus, the intention is that "the supreme fivefold" refers to the relationship of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) characterized by its rule of application (*vidhāna*). Alternatively, since the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) of words such as *tyad* and so forth is relied upon [in the rule], it means the case-ending associated with the meaning of that which has the form of *tyad* and so forth; and this [case-ending] is not a case-ending belonging to the intrinsic form itself.

3.20 This is not a fault. This compound has six as its primary element. The relationship exists for the purpose of illuminating the meaning; it is not the formal appearance (*rūpa*) of the words *tyad* and so forth that is relied upon. A word is merely an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the meaning. [The rule means: "in a case-ending (*vibhakti*) connected with that which is seen to be the meaning of *tyad* and so forth. Or rather, because the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is understood to apply to the primary element, that [compound] is designated by the meaning of that [primary element]. Just as when horses are walking, one says, "the king is walking."

3.21 Here, however, this objection arises: in the case of *pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ* ("groups of five birds"), since the suffix *kan* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by A 7.1.22, *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, would apply. 3.22 In that case, consider *priyasakthnā* ("by one who has dear thighs"). For here, there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) connected with the meaning of *sakthi*. If the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) were not in force, this form would not be established. 3.23 It is stated [in the Vārttika] that what is taught regarding a term specified in the locative case applies when the original case-ending (*prakṛtavibhakti*) is present. In the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau* (A 7.1.73), the suffix *anaṅ* is taught; this is an indication of the meaning, namely, "when the original case-ending is present."

3.24 There are three [interpretations]: first, that the rule applies to *asthi* and so on when they follow immediately after whatever case-ending (*vibhakti*) belongs to the stem (*aṅga*). Alternatively, by means of the term *asthi* and so on, there is an application of the rule to that which ends in those stems (*tadanta-vidhi*). Or else, "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is the qualifier and *asthi* and so on are the qualified.

3.25 If this is the case, then [the rule] would apply excessively (*ati-prasaṅga*). This [word *ati*] is also stated in the locative case; therefore, there is the undesirable consequence of the rule applying just as it does to *asthi* and so on. 3.26 And that must also be stated: [the rule does not apply] "when the case-ending of the item being cited (*gṛhyamāṇa*) is [the one in question]. What then? It is said: "that which is prescribed when [an element] is indicated in the locative."

3.27 Here, in the rule “*itarādibhyaḥ...*” (Pāṇini 5.3.16), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used. But is it not the case that [the word *bhis*] is governed by the rule “*ato bhisa ais*” (Pāṇini 7.1.9)? [Response: There is equality of case endings due to the transformation of the case ending (*vibhaktipariṇāmāt*). Alternatively, there exists the interpretation that [the rule applies] to the *bhis* that belongs to the base (*aṅga*), meaning “of that which follows the *bhis* belonging to a base ending in *at*. Thus, the connection with another case ending is possible either in the sense of the suffix *vat*—where the case ending belonging to the base of words such as *katara* and so on is [taken as the referent]—or [directly] as the case ending of the base itself.

How can this be said, "other than the prescribed suffix"? For if [the word] *vihita* (prescribed) were a qualifier, then forms such as *paramakatara* would not be established; nor would this form *paramaṣaṭ* [in the compound] *atiyuṣmad* be established.

3.28 Herein is the intended meaning: if, when an interpretation is constructed according to the literal text (*yathāśruti*), the desired result is not achieved, then there must be either a modification (*pariṇāma*) or another construction (*kalpanā*). In this case, however, this very [literal] reading is adopted. Therefore, it is accepted exactly as stated in the scripture. Furthermore, it is demonstrated by means of the fifth [case-ending] that in this scriptural statement there is no rule for eliding the final vowel (*tadantavidhi*). How then is *paramakatarat* formed? Since it is not cited in the Bhāṣya, this remains indeed doubtful. How should it be? According to this construction, it should be *paramakataram*.

How is it that there is "suppression" (*luk*) of the two case-endings *jaś* and *śas* when they follow the six [pronominal bases] (*ṣaḍbhyaḥ*)? This [term] *ṣaḍbhyaḥ* is not in the ablative case; what then? It is in the dative case, as in the rule: “The suffix *cha* occurs after words meaning ‘those who live by weapons’ when [the word] *parvata* follows” (A 4.3.91). Thus, there is suppression of those two case-endings, *jaś* and *śas*, which have the sense of the six cases. How is it that there is suppression in the form *atiyuṣmad*? Just as in the rule “*ais* replaces *bhisi* after *at*” (A 7.1.9), where it refers to the stem (*aṅga*), or by means of the principle of extension (*tadantavidhi*)—namely, that [the rule applies] to that which follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—or by means of the principle of mutual exclusion (*vyavasthāvibhāva*).

3.29 However, for those who hold that the view must be "the other [alternative] is better," they think as follows: Just as in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadika...* (A 4.1.1), suffixes such as *sva-* and others are prescribed for meanings such as singularity (*ekatva*), it has been demonstrated there that even though the term *prātipadika* is not explicitly mentioned, these technical designations (*saṃjñā*)—namely, *aṅga*, *pada*, and *bha*—will apply to the word functioning in that way, because they are prescribed for what expresses that [meaning]. In the same way, here too, regarding the meaning of *-ḍatara-* and so on...

They consider that when [the suffixes] are prescribed, the prescription is based on the meaning (*arthāśraya*) alone, not on the word-form (*śabdāśraya*); thus, it ought to be *paramakatarat*. For here too, the two [suffixes] *svam* and *smau* are prescribed only in the sense of the *ḍatara*-class and so forth.

If this is so, then in *atisaḥ*, the substitution of *a* (for the final vowel) would not apply, just as in *atitad*. This compound has *tyadādi* (the pronouns beginning with *tyad*) as its predominant element; "he is excellent" is *atisaḥ*. And even when it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) where the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant, then it should likewise be *asaḥ*, *aṣaṭ*, or *akatarat*.

3.31 Alternatively, this is not the creation of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). "Sarvanāmāni" is not a designation for the words beginning with *sarva*. What then? It is a qualifier of the recitation; it is a qualifier of the arrangement. Those which are the names of all [words] are those arranged in the list (*gaṇa*), and no others. Therefore, since these two [terms, *sarva* and *nāman*,] are established as qualifiers, there will be no [application of the term *sarvanāman*] to a name (*saṃjñā*) or a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, their status as *sarvanāman* is restricted to their own specific domain, just as a genus (*jāti*) is said to be "all-pervading" because it pervades its own entire domain.

This being the case, for all those names which have as their basis a specific arrangement (*saṃniveśa*) that constitutes an effect, there would apply [the rules] *adṅḍatarādibhyaḥ...* (A 7.1.25) and *tyadādīnām...* (A 7.2.102). However, in cases such as *atikataram* and *atitad*, these do not apply; for here, it is that which transcends (*aty-akrāmat*) which is denoted.

3.32 If this were so, [the suffixes] would not apply based on the name (*saṃjñā*), because no naming has been performed; for the word "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) is exhausted as a qualifier of the specific recitation [of the list]. And this being the case, it would follow that what is stated is: “The arrangement of *sarva*, *viśva*, *bhaya*, and so forth, is meaningless. In that context, it should be understood that the term is taken according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*): namely, that which is the name of all things. Therefore, the suffixes *smāy* and so forth should occur after such a member (*aṅga*).

3.33 And the word *sarva* signifies "entirety" (*kṛtsna*), yet it pertains to three domains: the domain of number, the domain of type, and the domain of portion. In the domain of number: "All the men have arrived," meaning as many as were listed, whether sixteen or seventeen. It is in this sense that speakers say, "all the food has been eaten, without remainder. In the domain of type: "He eats all the food" means he eats every kind of food.
And in the domain of portion: "All the rice has been eaten" refers to whatever rice was served in the dish.

3.34 If this is so, then [the designation *sarvanāman*] would also apply here in the case of "the entire (*sakalam*) whole (*kṛtsnam*) world," because [the rule] states that *smāy* and so forth occur after a word ending in *a*, while *akac* and so forth occur elsewhere. Furthermore, since these too are *sarvanāmans* within their own domain, whatever word occurs within that domain—such as in "all rice (*sarva odana*)" or "one rice (*eka odana*)"—the grammatical operation dependent on being a *sarvanāman* would apply in that domain. Consequently, one would obtain forms such as *odanasmin* in the sense of "in all rice" (*sarvasmin odane*) or "in one rice" (*ekasmin odane*).

3.35 This appears to be an inconsistency on the part of the author of the Bhāṣya, who is an expert in logic (*nyāyavid*). How so? The word *sarva* (all) expresses a universal and refers to both rice and non-rice; likewise, the word *odana* (rice) also refers to both the whole and its parts. That which constitutes the specific determination [of meaning] is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), not the meaning of the two individual words. It is with this in mind that it was stated: "That which is the surplus here is the sentence-meaning. How, then, is it determined that the word *odana* has a universal scope?

3.36 Furthermore, even if they have the same object, it may still be the case that one word relies upon a certain portion of the meaning, just as the word "blue" [relies on] the blue portion [of the object] in relation to the lotus, and the word "lotus" [relies on] the lotus portion. Thus, the object of these two would be either devoid of both [aspects] or possessed of both forms. Likewise, the word "all" is fixed upon the portion of totality, while the other [word, "rice"] relies upon the portion of being rice. Even so, their having that [same] object is untenable.

3.37 Herein is the view: whenever one perceives a blue quality (*nīlaguṇa*) as conjoined with all [other] objects through [its association with] substances and universals (*dravyajāti*), then the application of a word occurs according to that cognition. Thus, the word "blue" (*nīla*), conforming to its own cognition, is employed to denote all objects. Just as the word "blue" denotes a substance possessing the blue quality, so too the word "lotus" (*utpala*) has an object conjoined with all [other] objects. Both are equally attached to that [object]. Why is it, then, that one of them undergoes the grammatical operations of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*), while the other does not?

3.38 In that case, both [functions] are performed by this [sūtra]: the words beginning with *sarva* are delimited as being pronominal (*sarvanāman*), and it is precisely those that receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun."

But how can both [meanings] be obtained by a single effort? For words are dependent on their own referents; they rely on a single mode of operation, and because there is no other mode of operation apart from that, they are incapable of grasping another meaning. In that case, neither the individual parts nor the whole can logically possess both meanings. Just as a single impelling effort is not capable of both [impelling and] restraining, a separate effort must be initiated for the latter.

3.39 This is an indication by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one). But how can there be *ekaśeṣa*, given that it is undertaken when there is a plurality of things (*vastu*) such that multiple [instances] would otherwise follow? For example: "tree, śvattha, and plakṣa" (or "tree, and tree, and tree, and trees"). But here, in the case of "sarva" and "viśva," there is no plurality among these [words themselves], nor is there plurality in the referent denoted by words such as "sarva."

The second [interpretation] of the word *sarvādi* (beginning with "all") functions as follows: those which begin with "all" (*sarva*) are the names of all things; thus they are called *sarvādi* (or *sarvanāman*, "all-name"), while others are not *sarvanāman*. Furthermore, by means of words formed through *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the essence of the meaning is designated as having a single time and a single commencement; however, here the related meaning has different times and different commencements.

The meaning that "those which are all nouns are the *sarva*-class, and those which are of such a nature are designated as *sarvanāman*," cannot be understood [as intended] when the *ekaśeṣa* (the single remainder) is uttered.

3.40 This should not be regarded as a case of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one from among several identical items). Rather, it is presented as "ekaśeṘa" because it is similar to *ekaśeṣa*. What, then, is this? It is called *tantra*, a method by which a single word, through the influence of various speakers, is perceived as having both a single and multiple forms. Or, for example, when a single sound is produced by a reed on a musical instrument, multiple sounds of echoes are perceived due to specific locations; yet its multiplicity is not real in the world.

And for this reason, there is no multiplicity; they say that when one employs a single word such as "ghaṭa" while conforming to its various aspects, it is precisely through the means (*upāya*) that a single thing is understood to possess multiple forms. Why, then, is it not accepted that the multiple is of a single form? Therefore, the Teacher has employed the word "tantra" as a means, and thus uttered it in a single form despite its manifold nature.

3.41 There are only two means for the utterance of words: succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*). By way of succession, their individual forms (*rūpa*) differ, but not the aggregate (*samudāya*). Alternatively, it is taught by means of a *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions) that "the *sarvādi* group [beginning with] *sarva* are the pronouns" (*sarvanāmāni*), referring precisely to the aggregate. And even if they were [treated as] parts, it would be possible to comprehend [the rule] through a hundred sentences.

3.42 Alternatively, there exists a property of the self belonging to the word called "occurrence" (*vṛtti*), just as [there is occurrence] for actions. In the expression "he eats five times," the number five does not belong to the act of eating; for those five are not acts of eating themselves. What then? The word *bhuji* ("to eat") occurs in reference to a recurring action.

But when its occurrence (*vṛtti*) is counted—namely, how many times it has occurred—at that time, the word *pañca*, being applied to an occurrence related to an action (*kriyā*), produces a suffix. Just as there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) for what occurs in the sense of "intensive repetition" (*samabhihāra*), so too the master [Patañjali] has accepted that even a word whose form is complete (*savrāmaśabda*) undergoes repetition.

3.43 Even if [a word or mantra] is uttered only once, the applicator (*viniyoktṛ*) applies it with distinction. For example, among the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, although the first and last *ṛc*s are recited only once in the sacred text (*āmnāya*), the applicator applies them with distinction, saying: "He recites the first three times; he recites the last three times.

3.44 Or rather, we may assume that even a single [word or mantra] possesses two capacities (*śakti*), just as one who wishes to heal and one who wishes to see a wound in the darkness employs a lamp by relying on its twofold capacity.

The Teacher, too, has employed the word *sarvanāman* (pronoun) by assuming two powers (*śakti*), just as in the passage "Viṣṇu strode across this," where the single word *viṣṇu*, possessing multiple powers, functions through those respective powers with respect to the deity of proximity, the inner self (*adhyātma*), the sacrificial ritual (*adhiyajña*), the Self (*ātman*), Nārāyaṇa, and the *caṣāla* (the wooden ring on the sacrificial post). And having done so, in the case of "the wolf, the month-maker" (*vṛko māsakṛt*), there is also a distinction of referents (*graha-bheda*). When it refers to the moon, the word *māsa* is separated (*avagṛhyate*) [as *māsa-kṛt*]. Thus, "the wolf, the month-maker" is seen as a repetition (*āvṛtti*).

3.45 ... [they] abide in a specific [meaning]. Likewise, the word *sarva* (all), though seen in a sentence, occurs in reference to a specific [instance]. For now, their status as *sarvanāman* (pronouns) should not be accepted in this way. If it were imagined that each one individually denotes all [things], then none of them would possess the status of a pronoun. For the word *idam* (this) refers to what is perceptible, not to what is imperceptible; likewise, the word *tad* (that) refers to what is imperceptible, not to what is perceptible.

Therefore, it must be admitted that these [words] possess the nature of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) with respect to their own objects; for, like generalities and particulars, they pervade all that constitutes their own domain. (3.46) Furthermore, by taking as its basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the totality (*kārtsnya*)—which has number, substance, and category as its object—a word such as "rice" (*odana*), while remaining established in the generality, does not exclude particular instances such as *odana* and so forth. However, when used in connection with "rice" and the like, because a specific instance is understood, this is grasped as the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

When a word is applied to rice (*odana*), it does not abandon its own ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); because words denote their objects by falling upon specific portions [of that ground], even when speaking of rice, it expresses it precisely in its entirety. Thus, the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) is not lost for any of them.

3.47 But when the word *sarva* is employed as the name of something, then, having abandoned its own basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it functions merely as its own form and undergoes the state of being a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, this is the abandonment of its own basis of application; this is the state of abiding in this particularity. And having done so, it is said that in the phrase "of whom" (*kasyed*), in the context of making known [the name], it should be *kāya* in both ways [as masculine and neuter]. However, when the designation is based on a quality (*guṇanimittā*), it should be *kasmā*.

3.48 Thus, even a subordinate word (*upasarjanapada*), whether it has abandoned its own meaning or not, once it has passed beyond [its primary referent] and attained the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), functions with respect to the object that has been surpassed (*atikrāntārthavṛtti*). And since that which has been surpassed does not exist by means of its own ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), there is no persistence as a qualified entity (*viśeṣya*). However, in a sentence (*vākya*), it does not abandon its own ground; therefore, it is designated [by its original name].

3.49 [And since a name is not lighter than a conventional expression: verbal usage is lighter and more subtle; therefore, even more so than that, a name (saṃjñā) should be made lighter. For it is thus that the world conducts its affairs. The greatness in a name is based on an inferential cause (anumāna), being employed by means of a cause (nimitta); just as the word *kṛṣṇa* is applied to Vāsudeva by means of a cause, and that is a proper name (*nāmadheya*), so too the name *sahasrabāhu* is applied by means of a thousand arms. Likewise, the proper names of the words beginning with *sarva* are applied by means of their status as pronominals (*sarvanāmatva*).

3.50 Here an objection is raised: Even so, an operation that depends on a technical name (*saṃjñā*), such as *smāy* and the like, would not apply to those [words] that have become subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*) to that name, as in *sarvāyā* and *atisarvāyā*. Why? Because the technical name “pronominal” (*sarvanāman*) applies to the [entire] class of pronouns. However, as for the operations within the sub-group (*antargaṇa*), such as *adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ* (A 7.1.25) and *tyadādīnām* (A 7.2.102), they would apply without distinction. An answer is provided to this objection: Let it be so. But regarding the substitution of *akāra* and *kāra*, the solution is exactly the same as that given previously.

Now, however, they say: it is not understood in this way—that "all names" (*sarvanāmāni*) refers to whatever the names of all things are, and nothing else. What then? The connection is made in this manner. For what purpose is this great designation (*saṃjñā*)—*viśva*, *ubha*, *ubhaya*, and so on—applied to these? For what purpose are these the instigators of this great designation? This is inferred: since these possess the status of being "all-name" (*sarvanāmatva*), therefore they employ this great designation.

Just as when there is blackness and there is thousand-armedness, these two are the motivators for the designations [of "black" and "thousand-armed"], so it is with these [words] as well. This being the case, those things endowed with that property are grasped, while those not endowed with that property are not grasped. Since words such as *katarādi* and *tyadādi* are established as possessing their own inherent properties, it has been demonstrated that every grammatical operation (*kārya*) depends upon the designation and depends upon the arrangement [of sounds], even in the case of those [words] where the designation is subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*).

4.1 Now, what is the purpose of *ubha* being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)? "The purpose is [the application of] the suffix *akac*"—this is the completed meaning of the sentence. However, the author of the Bhāṣya does not explain the meaning of the sentence in this way; he merely sets forth the purposes for its recitation. Otherwise, there would be a change of form, because it falls under the scope of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. This word *ubha* falls under the scope of the dual number and *ṭāp*; for the word *ubha* is employed by resorting to a distinction that pertains to the primary object, as in the expression "both hands are facing forward."

Just as the word *dvi* denotes mere duality, this [term] is therefore the domain of the dual number (*dvivacana*) and the domain of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. It is not the case that whenever it is the domain of *ṭāp*, it is so in every instance. He considers that, other than in the dual, it is the domain of *ṭāp*, meaning the domain of the various types of *ṭāp*. What, then, are these various types of *ṭāp*? They are the *svārthika* (suffixes added in their own sense).

4.2 Here, other grammarians recite: “In place of *ubha*, when followed by a suffix or a subsequent member of a compound, there is the substitution of *ubhaya* except in the dual and before the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. According to others, the reading is: “In place of *ubha*, there is the dual, as well as the elision of *tap* and the suffix *ṭāp*. For them, by the mention of *ṭāp*, the suffixes beginning with *ṭāp* are indicated, just as in the rule “*ardharca* and so forth may also be masculine” (*A* 2.4.31). According to others, the reading is “except in the dual and before *ṭāp*” (*advivacana-ṭāpau*). Still others, however, read it thus: “In place of *ubha*, there is *ubhaya* except in the dual. That is to say, *ubhaya* occurs in place of *ubha* except in the dual.

4.3 This is established by logic (*nyāya*) in this treatise. How so? First, in this context, regarding the word *ubha*—which expresses duality—as in the examples "a pair of jewels" (*ubhayo maṇī*) and "both gods and humans" (*ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*), the word *ubha* does not apply to a single jewel which, though composed of distinct parts, is a single whole; nor does it apply to the collection "gods and humans," because that collection is understood as having a plurality of constituent parts. Furthermore, even when [the word *ubha*] functions as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound, it operates having abandoned its specific number, since the subordinate member denotes the individual entities. Thus, [the word *ubha*] does not apply to the aforementioned cases. Therefore, it is established that the word *ubha* applies only to two things that are mutually exclusive. Consequently, the rule "of *ubha*" (*ubhayataḥ*) is stated. However, in the case of "on both sides of the river" (*ubhayato nadīm*), the word *ubha* does not denote two distinct banks, but rather expresses a single bank characterized by two sides. Therefore, the suffix *tasi* is applied here according to the rule "in the sense of *ubha*, the suffix *tasi* is used" (*ubhād udātto nityam*). Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is: "The suffix *tasi* is applied after the word *ubha* in the sense of 'on both sides' (*ubhayataḥ*). This is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the word *ubha* may be interpreted as denoting a single entity that possesses two sides. In that case, the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case, the suffix *tasi* is used" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*); the locative case ending is elided by the rule "the case endings are elided after a stem ending in *a* when followed by a suffix beginning with *t* or *d*" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the forest" (*ubhayato vanam*), however, the word *ubha* denotes two forests, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the village" (*ubhayato grāmam*), the word *ubha* denotes two villages, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the ablative case" (*ubhayād apañcamyāḥ*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the mountain" (*ubhayato girim*), the word *ubha* denotes two mountains, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the road" (*ubhayato rathyām*), the word *ubha* denotes two roads, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the field" (*ubhayato kṣetram*), the word *ubha* denotes two fields, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the tree" (*ubhayato vṛkṣam*), the word *ubha* denotes two trees, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the house" (*ubhayato gṛham*), the word *ubha* denotes two houses, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the wall" (*ubhayato bhittim*), the word *ubha* denotes two walls, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the pillar" (*ubhayato stambham*), the word *ubha* denotes two pillars, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the post" (*ubhayato yaṣṭim*), the word *ubha* denotes two posts, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the rope" (*ubhayato rajjum*), the word *ubha* denotes two ropes, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the mat" (*ubhayato kaṭam*), the word *ubha* denotes two mats, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the cloth" (*ubhayato vastram*), the word *ubha* denotes two cloths, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the garment" (*ubhayato vastram*), the word *ubha* denotes two garments, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the blanket" (*ubhayato kambalam*), the word *ubha* denotes two blankets, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the bed" (*ubhayato śayyām*), the word *ubha* denotes two beds, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the seat" (*ubhayato āsanam*), the word *ubha* denotes two seats, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the chariot" (*ubhayato ratham*), the word *ubha* denotes two chariots, and thus the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *tasi* is optionally applied after the word *ubha* ending in the locative case" (*ubhayo 'nyatarasyām*). This is the meaning. In the case of "on both sides of the horse" (*ubhayato aśvam

And once the distinction has ceased, the word *ubha* must also cease; for words such as *eka* and so forth are not synonyms of this [word *ubha*]. A word should function only by means of that specific phonetic form with which it is identical, or by means of whatever object it denotes; thus, the word *ubhaya* alone functions [in place of *ubha*]. For the verbal origin (*śabdopakrama*) of these two words, *ubhau* and *ubhaya*, is distinct in its nature as a linguistic form, yet their objective referent (*arthātman*) is the same. Indeed, when one says, "Bring both" (*ubhāv ubhayam ānaya*), those very two are brought.

4.4 If this is so, then even the word *dvi* (two) would result in being incorrect (*asādhu*) because its distinction (*bheda*) has been abandoned in the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*). Even though the distinction is abandoned, the word *dvi* still functions because its own ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not abandoned. Therefore, in the context of a compound, there exists a connection between the part and the whole expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*). However, the word *dvaya* (pair/dual) does not apply in such cases as "these two [parts] constitute this aggregate" (*saṃgha*).

4.5 If it is asked why [the word] *ubha* [is mentioned], it is for this very purpose that the Teacher makes the mention of "always" (*nityam*) in the rule *ubhād udātto nityam* (A 5.2.44). It is established that this [word *ubha*] always denotes the whole (*avayavin*) in this form [i.e., as *ubhaya*], and not in the form of the word *ubha*. In this treatise, the word *ubha*, having become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) and abandoned its distinctness, is unable to denote the whole; therefore, the word *ubhaya* is employed.

4.6 Furthermore, when this word *ubha* has the dual suffix *ṭāp* as its scope—whether by its inherent verbal nature (*śābdasvabhāvataḥ*), by explicit statement (*vacanāt*), or by logical necessity (*nyāyāt*)—what else could it possibly have? It has nothing else; elsewhere it is simply *ubhaya*. It has already been demonstrated that this word *ubha* has the dual suffix *ṭāp* as its scope. Now, he questions the statement that the reading [of the sūtra] is for the sake of the suffix *akac*: "What would happen if *akac* were not present here? What [form] would result? [The answer is: the form *au* would result, because of the absence of *akac*.

Not perceiving any difference in form or sound, he asks: "What then is the distinction between *kāka* and *cau*? There is no regard for the *avagraha*; for it is said: "The authors of the *pada-pāṭha* are not to be followed by means of grammatical rules."

4.7 It has been stated that this word *ubha* is the domain of the dual number (*dvivacana*) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. By saying "the absence of others [is due to] its being the domain of the dual and *ṭāp*," it is demonstrated that this word *ubha* is the domain of the dual and the domain of *ṭāp*. Therefore, the word *ubha*, when heard as occurring after the dual number, must be correct (*sādhunā bhavitavya*) when it is present, not when it is elided (*lupte*), nor when it is separated (*vyavahite*). This [word *ubha*] is understood as having a domain characterized by its position [of occurrence].

If, however, there were a word [expressing plurality], then this [word] *aka*, by virtue of its gender, being included within that [group], would not be the cause for a difference in the Vedic text (*śruti*); thus, when this is established, its status as the object of a dual number is not contradicted.

4.8 Furthermore, if *ke* follows, why would this [word *ubha*] not be followed by a dual ending? Since the former [element] has been elided and the other is separated [by the suffix], the word *ubha* would result in being ungrammatical; thus, either its non-usage would follow, or else the usage of the word *ubhaya* would be required. In that case, its status as being followed by a dual ending must be stated. Either an extended application (*atideśa*) must be made—stating that it behaves like the domain of the dual in certain contexts—or it must be stated that the word *ubha* is grammatical when followed by a dual ending.

4.9 If that is so, then [the objection] that "even when *āp* is present, it is not followed by a dual ending" is untenable; for *āp* is dependent [on something else]. Since it has been established by stating "because it is the domain of the dual ending and the suffix *ṭāp*," this claim that "even when *āp* is present, it would not be followed by a dual ending" is inconsistent with the correctness of the domain of *āp*.

4.10 Regarding this, they explain: “In the rule ‘*ubhaya* is the dual form for both *ubha* and *ubhau*’ (*ubhayo 'dvivacanam*), there is no inclusion of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; therefore, this objection is raised with respect to that rule. However, the venerable ones here say: “You have shown that the word *ubha* is correct when the dual ending follows immediately after it, yet you did not include the suffix *ṭāp*. But you cannot rest content with this much alone.”

This also must be stated: "And that *ṭāp* occurs only when followed by a dual ending, not when followed by a singular or plural ending. Thus, the fact that even an *āp*-ending [suffix] must be followed by a dual ending is the point proposed by the author of the Bhāṣya, just as [it was said]: "When *ke* exists, so too when an *āp*-ending [suffix] exists."

4.11 Even though it is not explicitly stated, that statement [is understood] to refer to that [cognition directed toward another]. It is not on the basis of the literal presence of the dual suffix that something is considered "having the dual suffix as its subsequent element" (*dvivacanapara*), such that it would be the object of the dual; rather, being "subsequent to the dual" is defined by the sense. Where there is an expression for the sake of another, once the distinction [between self and other] has ceased, [the use of the suffix] is ungrammatical. Since suffixes such as *ṭāp* are used in their own primary sense (*svārthika*), even when the suffix *kap* follows [a word] where the subordinate and the principal have been inverted, it remains grammatical provided that the distinction has not been abandoned.

4.12 If this is so, how is it that [the forms] *ubhābhyām* and *ubhayoḥ* are used here? These two also do not refer to an external object; thus, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word *ubha* would follow [only in those cases], and consequently, forms such as *ubhataḥ* and *ubhatra* would result. Now, if you think that the suffix *tral* occurs only when there is an external capacity—as in *adhistrī*, where the compound refers to an external locus in the feminine—then even in the case of *ubhābhyām* and *ubhayoḥ*, grammatical correctness would not be obtained.

Therefore, this is the resolution: because *tasil* and the other suffixes are indeclinables (*avyaya*), it is said that "they are alike in all three genders and in all case-endings. Since all distinction is abandoned in the case of *tasil* and the others when they express merely the sense of a case-ending, there is a lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*) in this particular context. Thus, the word *ubhaya* is employed in the expression *ubhayo 'nyatra*.

4.13 If this is so, then in the case of *ubhayo maṇiḥ* ("two jewels") as well, since [the word] exists for the sake of another (*parārtha*) in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*), it would abandon its distinction [as a dual], and thus it would incur the fault of being ungrammatical (*asādhutva*). This is not a fault. This very thing is its primary form of origination. Having acquired its form here, it proceeds elsewhere even when the word *ubha* has ceased [to be used as a dual]; and if it proceeds in the expression of the meaning of another, this word *ubha* is then entirely [treated as] a [general] word.

4.14 By means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), an option is established for *dvivaṇḍy* and other such forms: *ubhāñjaliḥ* or *ubhayāñjaliḥ*, *ubhāpāṇiḥ* or *ubhayapāṇiḥ*. All of this has been explained as establishing the correctness or incorrectness of the word *ubha* within its scope by way of the *kākac* dilemma. However, the purpose of the suffix *akac* need not be applied; rather, the recitation [of the rule] must be for another purpose: namely, so that the rule “*sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*” (Pāṇini 2.3.27) may apply, as in the examples: "this was obtained from both causes" (*ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām*) and "from both causes" (*ubhayor hetvoḥ*).

4.15 Now, as for [the forms] *bhavataḥ*: for what purpose is this arrangement? The question is: "Why do not [the suffixes] *smāt* and so on occur after stems ending in a consonant? [The answer is: for *bhavat*, there is the addition of *akac*, the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel, and the substitution of *ātvam*. The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not have the definition of a pronominal (*sarvanāman*). What then? It is based on the specific arrangement [of letters], namely the rule "tyadādīni... (Pāṇini 1.1.74). This is merely an illustration...; the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is also desired. For the author of the Bhāṣya as well, it is merely an illustration; there exist other grammatical operations based on the same arrangement [of letters]. [Thus, one must ensure that] the form *bhāvatyam* does not occur.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when it is a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*), the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies. Pāṇini 2.2.26.

1.1 For what purpose is the mention of "direction" (*dig*)? This is the intention of one who wishes to state here that which was mentioned in the rule concerning the *bahuvrīhi* compound; [he does this] so that the style of the text is not broken, and thus he introduces every sūtra from the commentary (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, there is a reason for this inquiry. He thinks as follows: just as there may be a state of both affirmation and negation, and an option (*vikalpa*) regarding another individual instance.

Otherwise, because [the formation] would have been accomplished by alternative analysis (*vikalpa*), the statement of the prohibition would be purposeless. Furthermore, the opposite view is not accepted because of the instruction regarding what is beneficial for man; thus, he will state the prohibition in the rule *na bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.29). For ignorance is not removed without a definitive determination of this specific scope. In this regard, one should not harbor resentment toward the fact that the scripture itself is the instructor; this is what he expresses with this passage.

2.1 Now, for what purpose is the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*)? He thinks as follows: just as when there is the mention of a compound (specifically a *bahuvrīhi*), the elision of the case-ending (*sublopa*) and the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) are obtained, why should this option (*vibhāṣā*) not also be obtained here? [The rule applies] only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Just as [the term] "agent" (*kartṛ*) refers only to one who is an agent, so too [it applies] only to that which is a compound, namely a *bahuvrīhi* compound; it should apply therein, but not where it is not a compound. Alternatively, the word "compound" (*samāsa*) is intended to be accented (*svaryate*). Having taken "compound" as the base, [the meaning is]: "that which is a *bahuvrīhi* [occurring] within a compound."

2.2 Now, what is this mode of expression: "that which is a *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of being treated as a *bahuvrīhi*"? For, insofar as it is merely an extended (*atideśika*) *bahuvrīhi*, it does not actually become a *bahuvrīhi*, but rather merely undergoes its grammatical operation. This is not a fault. Just as there is this designation "This is Brahmadatta" even without the suffix *-vat* for extension, so too is this designation. Or else, within the theory of extended designation, the position that the designation itself is extended exists even without a formal cause; therefore, this statement is also logical.

3.1 Now, for what purpose is the mention of *bahuvrīhi*? That which is about to be stated resides in the mind. However, at this point, he thinks as follows: those members which occur in a *dvandva* are listed among the *sarvādi* group. When the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied to them in every type of compound formation (*vṛtti*), that very same member denotes the whole from the aggregate. . . . [therefore] there is no absence of the augment *suṭ*.

3.2 Let there not be [the application of] *dvandva* [compounds]. Regarding [the compound] *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*: in the case of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in any grammatical formation (*vṛtti*), there is a difference in the analytical process (*prakriyā*). Some apply the masculine treatment to all [members of the compound], while others apply it only to the prior member (*pūrvapada*) when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Among these, those who apply it to the prior member when followed by a subsequent member do not do so in all cases; because it contradicts common worldly understanding (*lokavijñā*), the masculine treatment should not occur here in the form "aparādakṣiṇottarāṇām."

3.3 But surely, if the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were applied to all [elements], there would be an impossibility in cases such as the designation of gender according to the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*). This is not a fault. In the state of the sentence (*vākya*), the gender of the subsequent member is observed; that [gender] is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the compound. Alternatively, by the application of the masculine form, only the word-form (*śabdamātra*) is replaced. Since the meaning (*artha*) is not removed, the gender of the subsequent member is extended. In that case, either when what precedes the aggregate has been removed, the suffix *ṭāp* arises, or from a stem ending in *ṭāp*, a second *ṭāp* arises.

Because of the treatment as being like the beginning and the end (*antādivadbhāva*), there exists the state of ending in *ā* (*ābantatā*), and there is also the rule regarding what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*), according to the statement: "The purpose [of this] is for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables" (Vārttika 8 on A 1.1.72). Now, if there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) for the subsequent *ṭāp*, and a second *ṭāp* does not arise, then how can the base (*aṅga*) have the state of ending in *ā*—given the rule "when a suffix is mentioned, [the operation applies] to that from which it is prescribed..."? To this it has been said: "by means of a suffix that is not feminine."

3.4 Regarding the phrase *yena nāprāpta* etc.: But surely this statement is incorrect because of the difference in the objects [of the rules], for there is no prohibition in the case of a *dvandva* by the rule *na bahuvrīhau* (A 1.1.29), nor is there one in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* by the rule *dvandve ca* (A 1.1.31).

3.5 It is said: this has been introduced in another manner by the rule "yena nāprāpta... and so forth. How? By that [rule] which, through a prohibition, applies where [the suffix] is not unobtained—that is, not non-pervasive—with respect to its own domain, this optional alternative (vibhāṣā) would apply. In that case, that prohibition must be set aside by this optional alternative. Why is this so? Because, in the context of a bahuvrīhi compound, this [optional rule], having already achieved its purpose by applying prior to the occurrence of the subsequent [prohibition], is overridden by another prohibition due to the principle of "the later [prevailing] in the case of a conflict" (vipratiṣedha). Thus, since this [optional rule] does not apply to that [specific case] where the subsequent [prohibition] occurs, it is superseded by the other prohibition.

Alternatively, exceptions stated earlier are sublated by another treatise, and treatises are expected to differ from one another; thus, a treatise that has already fulfilled its purpose competes with the other.

Regarding the rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ*: But surely this compound is formed by A 2.2.26, *diṅnāmāny antarāle*. And this principle is stated in cases where a word is employed in its defined form, such as in A 2.1.59, *śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ*. It is replied: here, the status of being "stated in the rule" (*pratipadoktatā*) is understood in terms of designation (*vyapadeśa*). Who could possibly understand the designation “compound of directions” (*diksamāsa*) except where there is the actual verbal expression “direction” (*dig*)? Is it where the term “direction” exists, or not? It is logical that it applies where the verbal expression “direction” exists.

3.8 But was it not said that every *bahuvrīhi* is a "specifically prescribed" (*pratipadokta*) compound because of its specific formulation, as in the example *mahābāhuḥ*? That was said with reference to its dependence on other compounds; however, within its own category, it possesses the status of being "specifically prescribed," just as in the rule "the most effective means is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*, A 1.4.42).

3.9 This solution is applicable when the rule *diṅnāmāny antarāle* (A 2.2.26) is being formulated; however, when that rule is rejected on the grounds of the Vārttika *dig-samāsa-sahayogayoś cāntarāla-pradhānābhidhānāt* (A 2.2.28 vā. 1), then this solution is no longer possible.

3.10 Then this is the purpose: the mention of *bahuvrīhi* remains for the sake of what follows, as well as for the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana*). For even though it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the locative plural (*jasi*) is overridden by the intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) prohibition. Otherwise, the recurrence of the second mention of *bahuvrīhi* would indeed be purposeless.

3.11 But how, then, is there the application of the rule *vibhāṣā jasi* here? For the two words that form the dvandva compound—namely the words *vastrāntara* and *vasanāntara*—are not themselves listed among the *sarvādi* group. One might argue that [the designation] would apply by means of the rule for suffixation to a word ending in [a member of that group] (*tadantavidhi*), but that is not possible because the word *antara* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) and because technical names (*saṃjñā*) are established according to their literal meaning. Neither a technical name nor a subordinate member possesses the status of being a *sarvādi*, as in the case of *atisarvāya*. Thus, the purpose of including the mention of the *bahuvrīhi* compound [in the rule] is not observed. [The sūtra: *na bahuvrīhau* // 1.1.29 // [is stated.]

1.1 What is the example? The intended meaning [is as follows]: because of the rule regarding the prior placement of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is no such thing as being "ending in that" (*tadanta*). Furthermore, wherever another word is to be placed first, that [compound] will not be employed, such as *priyaviśvāya*. Why? Because since there exists another word with the sense of "lineage" (*kulya*), one would instead employ [the form] *viśvapriyāya*.

1.2 As for this [sūtra] "dvyanyāya": since a numeral, which is necessarily dependent upon that which is to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), must necessarily be placed first by virtue of its status as a qualifier, there is indeed the application of the rule regarding the inclusion of what ends in such a term. But is it not the case here too that [the rule applies] only to pronouns (*sarvanāman*)? It is for this purpose that the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) was made: "In the case of the conjunction of a pronoun and a numeral, how should that [term] be placed first which would otherwise not obtain the position of being first? And for which [term] does it not obtain it? For the pronoun.

1.3 This is not a fault. [The author] will say "this will be explained. By this it is explained: "This is not the meaning of the sentence that has been imagined by you. And this is also an example; he demonstrates this. Furthermore, this word is seen in common usage in the sense of "in order to inspire confidence" (*pratiyaviśvāsāya*). And the evidence for its being seen is precisely the mention of the option (*vā*), as in the rule *vā priyasya* (A 2.2.35 vā. 2).

1.4 What is the purpose? It is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*). [The rule] "the substitution of *āt* occurs in the third case ending, in *smāt* and so on" is an operation pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*). And this is not possible in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. First, regarding the initial [point], it is prescribed for words ending in *dṛk*, *dṛś*, and *vat*. Then, pointing out another grammatical operation—the non-hearing of the third case ending and of *smāt* and so on—he says, "lest *akac* [be applied]," meaning that *akac* should not occur. Not seeing any difference between *kak* and *akac* in the case of stems ending in vowels, he asks: "What, then, is the difference between *kak* and *akac*? [The answer is: There is a difference in the case of stems ending in consonants.

This is intended to demonstrate a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*): even among those ending in non-consonants (*avyañjana*), there is a distinction, as in *dvikaputra* versus *dvakiputra*. But how can this be so, even for one who desires it? For while the compound meaning (*anyapadārtha*)—which is the cause for the formation of a *bahuvrīhi*—has not yet arisen, the cause for the prohibition [of *sarvanāma-saṃjñā*] is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Furthermore, since the technical name *sarvanāman* is based on the single word [itself], and *akac* is its cause, the *akac* suffix must occur within the domain of the *bahuvrīhi*.

1.6 As in the example *gomatpriya*. The observation of a grammatical marker (*liṅga*) found in the treatise—namely, the rule *pratyayottarapadayoś ca* (A 7.2.98)—is justified in this way: either "an external formation (*bahiraṅga*) subverts an internal one (*antaraṅga*)," or "a rule conditioned by a compound subverts an internal one. This general principle is adopted as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Effort is made in that regard; such is the intention. The indicator applies only to the domain of elision (*luk*), not to all domains, so that there may be no subversion of the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*.

1.7 There exists [an instance] in this statement where both a positive injunction (*vidhi*) and a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) share the same locus, as in *priyaviśvāya*. This is also established by the prohibition regarding the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). All the modes mentioned in the *sarvādi* sūtra—such as the assignment of technical names based on their literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) and so forth—are to be understood here as well.
1.8 Now, he demonstrates that this is indeed the meaning of the word itself: there is the application of a term to something because it is for its sake (*tādarthyāt tācchabdyam*).

1.9 If this is so, then in the case of *ahakaṃ pitā* as well, a prohibition of *akac* would apply because it serves that purpose (*tādarthyāt*). This is not a fault. Because this word is qualified by its distinctness (*bhedaviśiṣṭatvāt*), this introduction [of the suffix] does not have that as its purpose. For only those non-worldly forms (*alaukika*) which are unfit for actual usage attain the status of serving that purpose.

1.10 But Gonardīya says: What is this teacher’s view? Some explain that the mention of *bahuvrīhi* should be recited for the sake of [excluding] "those between whose garments there is another garment" (*vastrāntara-vasanāntarāḥ*). In that case, since there is a purpose, it would be impossible for an internal rule (*antaraṅga*) to be set aside by the *bahuvrīhi*, or for its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) to be understood. This is not so; for it was just stated that "this is also established by the prohibition regarding the subordinate member (*upasarjana*)."

Furthermore, the word *antara* is also a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya explains this as a [supplementary] rule (*sūtra-vyākhyāna*). [Example: *āḍhyapūrvāya dehi* ("Give to one who was previously wealthy"). Since this is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] does not apply; thus, a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is stated. It is said [in the rule] "when there is a restriction" (*vyavasthāyām*). However, no such restriction is understood here. The meaning is "by way of predominance. For in the compound, the word *pūrva* has entered into a state of subordination (*guṇatā*) with respect to the previous wealth that has passed away. Because it is not predominant, it possesses the status of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and consequently, it does not belong to the class beginning with *sarva* (the *sarvādi* group), just as in the case of *atisarvāya*.

2.2 Others describe it thus: "In this case, no fixed status (*vyavasthā*) is understood. Just as in the expression *dakṣiṇā gāthakāḥ* (southern singers), the quality of being from the South (*dākṣiṇya*) is removed while the term *gāthaka* remains; so too, in [the case of] *āḍhyapūrva*, the quality of being wealthy (*āḍhyatva*) is removed while the word remains. But this is not possible. Why? Even if the quality of being wealthy is removed, the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) remains fixed.
