Furthermore, the fixed status belongs to the qualifiers such as "prior," and not to the quality of wealth. 2.3 Others describe it thus: "In a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, there is no sense of fixed status," specifically regarding a *tṛtīyā-samāsa* (instrumental compound). [Pāṇini 2.1.30]

1.1. While the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the following is considered: even without the explicit mention of "compound," when the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.30) is prescribed, another sentence is supplied—either through direct statement (*śruta*) or by implication (*anumiti*)—to the effect that "words beginning with *sarva* followed by a word ending in the third case are not designated as pronouns (*sarvanāman*). In the preceding rule, because the term is used figuratively to denote that which is for the sake of that [compound], *akac* is not heard [as applied to the compound]. Here, however, the operation of being a pronoun (*sarvādikārya*) is precluded specifically within the sentence itself.

Because it is possible to bring about such an operation by following some similar property, its purpose (tādarthya) is determined; however, there is no prohibition in the case of a sentence that is entirely devoid of meaning, such as "not by Devadatta in the past time."

1.2 Alternatively, while the term *samāsa* (compound) is already understood [from the previous rule], why is *samāsa* mentioned again? Is this not already an exclusion of compounds (*asamāsagrahaṇa*)? It is said in reply: even though that is so, nevertheless, when there is a reference to homogeneous vowels (*savarṇanirdeśa*) in the form of *kṛt*, this [mention of] *samāsa* applies directly to the literal hearing of the word (*śruti*), whereas the other does not; thus he says "the mention of *samāsa*. Furthermore, by the maxim of the exclusion of what is connected with *nañ* and *iva* (*nañivayuktanyāya*), the prohibition applies to that which resembles a compound (*samāsasadṛśe*) when it is not a compound (*asamāse*), but not to an expression such as "by Devadatta at a former time" (*devadattena pūrvasmin kāle*). *vibhāṣā jasi* // 1.1.32 // [The substitution of the long vowel *ā* for the final *i* or *u* of a stem ending in *i* or *u* is optional before the nominative-accusative plural suffix *jas*.]

1.1 Regarding the operation of *jas*, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). This means that *akac* does not occur after *jhi*. Here, both operations depend on a pronoun (*sarvanāman*): the operation of *jas* and the suffix *akac*. When *akac* is prohibited and [the suffix] *ka* is present, because of the intervention [of *ka*], the substitution of *śī* does not take place, as in *kataraka-tamaka-āḥ*. Some explain that this [substitution of *śī*] should be added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyeya*). Others say that *jasi* refers to the case ending *jas* itself. Still others maintain that since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for each individual application, the designation is prescribed specifically for this rule "the *śī* of *jas*" (A 7.1.17); therefore, the option applies only to the operation of *jas*, while elsewhere there is a prohibition.

The words *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* [are optionally termed *sarvanāman*] when they denote relative position (*vyavasthā*) and not as proper names (*asaṃjñā*). Pāṇini 1.1.34.

Furthermore, the inclusion of *avara* and the others in the recitation of the Sūtra would be purposeless, as they are already listed in the group [of *sarvādi*]. That there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the nominative plural (*jas*) is already known from the examples provided by the author of the Vṛtti. Moreover, it is also understood that the designation "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) applies invariably everywhere to the *sarvādi* group; thus, *pūrva* and the others are listed as being characterized by specific meanings. Therefore, here the author of the Vākya does not challenge the composition of the Sūtra itself.
He introduces the following point with this sentence: "For what purpose is the recitation of the nature of all [these] performed word by word by means of three sūtras?"

1.2 Regarding *avara* and the others—those belonging to the lowest category whose essential nature is dependent [on their context]—the author of the *Vārttika* has already rejected the reading of *avara* and so forth in every instance within the three rules (*trisūtrī*), on the grounds that they will be recognized as having been specified in the *Gaṇapāṭha*. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, explaining the intention of the author of the *Sūtras*, offers a rebuttal: "But how is it known that 'that' was the previous reading and 'this' is the current reading?"

1.3 Here, regarding this arrangement of distinct textual sections, what constitutes the sequence? By means of such a sequence, the burden of relying on the [original] recitation order is avoided. In this regard, other commentators support the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya as follows: This word *ādi* is observed to be employed for certain groups whose arrangement is fixed and well-known, such as the *śreṇī* (guilds) and so forth; it is used there precisely for the purpose of establishing that fixed order.

In some cases, however, groups (*gaṇas*) are recited in the sūtras as if they were instances of new collective formations (*apūrvasamudāyavṛtti*), serving as examples for the purpose of illustrating a specific type; these resemble worldly applications that are endowed with similarity in certain respects. For instance, the group beginning with *kṛta*. And so he will state: "The groups beginning with *śreṇi* are recited; the group beginning with *kṛta* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form)."

1.4 Furthermore, in those cases where the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of restriction (*vyavasthā*), the Sūtra is commenced with respect to those items whose arrangement was previously established and whose sequence was already determined. However, in those cases where the word "etcetera" is used in the sense of a category (*prakāra*), the meanings are recited at a later time for the purpose of illustrating the lists, following the recitation of the Sūtra—just like examples in a commentary (*vṛtti*)—based solely on their similarity to the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). And in those Bhāṣya-sūtras, no effort is made regarding the weightiness or lightness [of the phonemes].

And thus it is said: "The teachers do not now compose sūtras and then set them aside. For the sūtras of the Bhāṣya are intent upon demonstrating and supporting [the doctrine] through both definitions and detailed elaborations.

And likewise, regarding the specific arrangements of case-endings (*vibhakti*) in those [lists], some are modified while others are left unmodified and are recited exactly as they are; similarly, in other grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*), there are specific arrangements of *gaṇa*-sūtras with an uninterrupted traditional sequence, where some are modified while others are left unmodified and are recited exactly as they are. For instance, usage is observed primarily through the recitation of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) by means of the designations and instructions of former teachers, such as:
"that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix, the letter *m*, or a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*), as well as an *avyayībhāva* compound," and so forth.

1.5 In that context, when words such as *vyavasthāpya* (or *vyākhyā*) are understood, that is the earlier reading, uttered by the Teacher previously; the recitation of the Sūtras, however, belongs to a later time. Accordingly, the repeated recitation of *avara* and so forth—intended so that the Sūtra might be made concise (*laghu*)—was rejected word-for-word in the three Sūtras.

If, however, the word *ādi* has the sense of "and so forth," and subsequently some [words] have been collected—either because they are recited among the *gaṇas* by the Teacher like the *grahaṇaka*, or because they were composed for the sake of the tradition (*smṛti*) by skillful authors—then there is no regard for their relative weight or lightness (*gurulaghubhāva*). Furthermore, even what has already been recited is recited again, and supplementary additions (*upasaṃkhyāna*) are also inserted, such as: *upāddvyajajinamagaurādayaḥ* (A 6.2.194), and *nirajinodajinopājināḥ*.

‘The lengthening of the vowel in *śvan* [occurs] in *prasāraṇa*. / ‘[The suffix *ḍa* occurs] after a word ending in the second case, provided no preposition precedes it. / ‘In the group beginning with *pravṛddha*, [the form] *khaṭvārūḍha* [is included]. / Regarding the rule for the udātta accent on the first syllable of words ending in feminine suffixes like *nadī* and *ajā*, there is a supplementary statement (*vārttika*): “An addition should be made for *bṛhat* and *mahat*” (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.173). Thus, in the *gaurādi* group, one finds *bṛhatyaḥ* and *mahatyaḥ saudharmyaḥ*. As for the *bidādi* group, the reading of *gopavana* and others follows exactly as in the second chapter [of the *Gana-pāṭha*]. The *kaṇva*s and others are already listed in the *gargādi* group, yet they are listed again in the rule “*kaṇvādibhyaḥ . . .*” (Pāṇini 4.2.111).

In the rule *‘haritādibhyo ’ñaḥ’* (A 4.1.100), the words beginning with *aharita-* are not recited; nor are they [recited] in the rule *‘sarvatra lohitādikatantebhyaḥ’* (A 4.1.18). Regarding this, it is stated: “But in the case of *kaṇva*, *śakala* is desired before [the suffix], and after *kata*. Furthermore, in the case of *cheda* it is one way, and in *saṃhitā* it is another; it is recited differently with the *mindas* and differently with the *āhāryas*. For example: *sthūlabāhu* and *sthūlabāhu*; *triveṇī* and *trivaṇam*.

In the case of *paśau lūnaviyāte*, *paśau lūnavihīne*, and *paśau lūnavighāte*, the forms *kapigaviyudhayaḥ* are recited at their initial occurrence. The forms *jārabharā* and *śvapacāḥ* are likewise [recited] word by word. Furthermore, as in the case of *codanapāce ubhayam*, the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) has been explained. And in the list beginning with *nyaṅku*, the rule for the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) is initiated for the word *śvapāla*. All of this, whatever it may be, that is recorded in some way, is authoritative (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the word *ādi* ("etcetera") is recited in the Sūtra in the sense of "of this kind."
Subsequently, having determined the meaning within the *Gaṇapāṭha*, the inclusion [of the word] with elaboration (*prapañca*) would not be faulty. This is by way of an alternative explanation.

How, then, is it known that this word "ādi" (etcetera) is for the purpose of restriction (*vyavasthā*) and not for the purpose of indicating a type (*prakāra*)? It is established as such. Why, then, might there be a suspicion of it being a type? Because the scripture functions in both ways, as seen in usage: "O Indra and Agni, you are present on the highest earth, on the middle, and even on the lowest" (*Ṛgveda* 1.108.10); and "Standing in the same place, he offers the oblation" (*Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* 1.4.12).

1.7 These are "eastern" (pūrva) and so forth; these are "lower" (avara) and so forth. Having established the fixed order based on the grammatical indicator (*liṅga*) in the rule "from the nine beginning with pūrva," he speaks. But the other thinks as follows: "By this, the utterance pertaining to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) has been presented. How, then, is it known that that is the prior recitation? The sequence of recitation refers to the designation of the arrangement of the text. That is how it remains established.

For example: when the question "How is it known that this one is the elder and that one is the younger? is asked, the determination is stated as "because of being born at an earlier time" and "because of being born at a later time. Thus, the intention here is that sequential utterance is resorted to for the sake of such determination. These are the words beginning with *pūrva* (prior). By the mention of *pūrva*, the word *pūrva* as situated in the list of the *gaṇa* is indicated. These also include the words beginning with *avara* (subsequent); however, in the sūtras, only the word *pūrva* as situated [in the sūtra itself] is indicated.

1.8 However, some consider that the word *pūrva* (prior) is indicated by the mention of *avara* (subsequent). In that regard, just as "prior existence" (*pūrvabhāva*) is simply being (*sattā*) itself, which—relative to all other operations—is designated as "subsequent existence" (*avarabhāva*) with respect to destruction; and just as destruction is designated as an "end" because it is the disappearance of specific existence (*viśeṣasattā*), so too here, due to the distinction between two recitations having a fixed sequence, the designation "prior" and "subsequent" is understood to apply to the word *pūrva* alone. By the word *ādi* (beginning), the commencement of an arrangement is indicated.

1.9 For those [terms] beginning with *pūrva*—the word *pūrva* refers to a specific established state of priority (*prāptavyavasthāviśeṣa*), and it is the first among them; that which is characterized by it is the commencement of the others. These are the [terms] beginning with *avara*. Since they are known to belong to a later time than the sūtras situated within the section on pronouns (*sarvanāma*), that which is first placed and characterized by it is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*); the remainder is the commencement. Alternatively, by the word *pūrva*, the sūtras beginning with *avara* are referred back to.

1.10 Thus, considering that the determination of the fixed order [of the suffixes] cannot be established on the basis of indicative marks (*liṅga*), he says: "Even these [terms], beginning with *pūrva* and so forth, cannot be explained by mere assertion alone. Since the treatise functions in both ways and because we observe its usage, it is possible to justify this word *ādi* as denoting a type (*prakāra*)."

1.11 Thereupon, the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅgadarśana*) previously mentioned is now made manifest as the reason for establishing the rule regarding the restriction of sequence: namely, that [Pāṇini] employs the mention of "nine" in the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo* (or *navabhyo vā*). For in the recitation of the lists (*gaṇapāṭha*), the mention of "nine" is purposeful only for the sake of excluding words such as *tyad* and so forth. And if the recitation of the lists were established according to conventional usage, possessing a fixed sequence and a well-defined specific nature, then the mention of "nine" could be meaningfully connected [to those nine items].
For example: “of the eight [roots] beginning with śam” (A 7.3.74), “and of the seven [roots] beginning with phaṇ” (A 6.4.125), and “and of the five [roots] beginning with kir” (A 7.2.75).

Thus, since the comprehension [of the rules] is established by a concise means through the arrangement of exactly nine [categories], beginning with *pūrva* and so on, in the Sūtras, the mention of the number "nine" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that: "There exists a recitation (*pāṭha*) external to the Sūtras which was previously handed down by the Teacher and has an unbroken tradition from other grammatical systems, and it was certainly not invented [by him]. Furthermore, he employs [the terminology] even according to the arrangement of the Sūtras in certain instances; for example: "In the case of *ca* and so on... (A 8.1.58).

Thus, this word "ādi" (beginning with) serves to establish a specific restriction based on such indicative marks (*liṅga*). Furthermore, because it pertains to the domain of Vedic meter (*chandas*), the observation of usage is not a definitive mark for its denoting a class (*prakāra*).

Another [teacher] says: those words beginning with *pūrva* are recited in the *sarvādi* group. Their association (*sāhacarya*) within that group with respect to specific meanings has been established. Therefore, even when only a portion is mentioned in the rules (*sūtra*), the recognition of the whole is established. For example, as it is said, “*ktena ca pūjāyām*” (Pāṇini 2.2.12), by which the definition characterized by the meanings of "thought," "perception," and "reverence" is understood.

Furthermore, having observed that the words *pūrva* and *avara* are recited in the *gaṇa*, those who consider them to be indicative (*lakṣaṇa*) based on their association (*sāhacarya*) within the sūtras, record a portion of *avara* and so forth in the sūtras. These [words] beginning with *pūrva* are also [included]. Here, the recitation in the *gaṇa* is relied upon; therefore, when any single word is taken as an indicator, a collective group is formed from it, and thus there is a sequence of priority and posteriority according to the order in which they are perceived.

1.13 If this is so, then since the words *pūrva* and others are listed in the *gaṇapāṭha* as being characterized by specific meanings, when an option (*vibhāṣā*) is introduced in the rules (*sūtra*), how can it be ensured that only those meanings [of the specific types] are invariably included? To address this, the *pratipadapāṭha* (word-for-word recitation) is again resorted to through the division of three rules. For in other contexts, whatever indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) are initially employed, their function is restricted to the presence [of the operation] within their specific domains.

For example: "Bring one who is white-robed," or "one who has matted hair and a head-ornament. However, when something characterized by some particular mark is taught for one purpose and is then taken up again in another context for a different object, the operation of the word through those marks is not assumed to be present there. Therefore, in the *Vibhāṣā*, the repetition is for the sake of the operation regarding the non-difference of words through the proximity of the meanings. And this he will do at the end.

1.14 Just as in the case of [the rule] "from the nine beginning with *pūrva*... (A 7.1.16), where only those *pūrva* and so on that function as designators of spatial relations (*vyavasthā*) are understood, so too will it be here. And meanings serve as differentiators. For instance, even in the case of a word for a portion of something existent (*sadeśa*), if it is not situated in a specific relation, it is not grasped [as such], as in the expressions *tailamātrā* ("a measure of oil") or *ghṛtamātrā* ("a measure of ghee"). In that regard, just as a meaning is indicated by an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), so too, when there is an actual hearing of the word, the differentiator of meaning is recognized.

Thinking that "in the same way, [grammatical] designations (vyavasthā) and so forth will also serve as causes for the exclusion of specific meanings," he says: "These very [words] are recited in the list (gaṇa) as being thus qualified."

1.15 The repetition is intended so that there might not be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by way of excluding "two" and so forth. Here, according to Āpiśali, the words beginning with *tyad* and ending with *asmat* are included; then follow the three rules beginning with *pūrvaparāvara*; then the words beginning with *svara*. By that arrangement of the recitation, an exclusion of "two" and so forth would apply to *pūrva* and the others. In this regard, just as in the case of the statement, "The designation of *karmapravacanīya* is redundant when used with *anu* because it is already established by the general rule," as in the example *vidyud anu vanam* ("lightning [is] along the forest"), [the specific rule is unnecessary].

The third [rule], by its re-initiation, sublates that [second rule]; for the second case-ending, characterized as a *karmapravacanīya* because it has reached another position, sublates it. Likewise, in the case of suffixes such as *tasil*, the designation *sarvanāman*—which is being enjoined through the repeated utterance of each individual word (*pratipadam*)—sublates the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) which was an exception (*apavāda*) to those suffixes; this designation, by postulating a transition to another position for *tasil* and the others, sublates them. In that regard, the permanent designation of "eastern" (*pūrva*) and the others is enjoined again by three rules.

Furthermore, because the svarita accent is applied through a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) in each sūtra, it is inferred that the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies to the suffix *jas*. And this [optionality] is not possible if there were a single unified sentence (*ekavākyabhāva*). The explicit mention of each term is for the purpose of establishing the proximity of the optionality through a syntactic split. However, when there is no requirement for such a split, it is logical that they form a single sentence.

1.16 As for those who accept the former recension of the sūtras, none of them adopt a fixed sequence as a restrictive indicator (*liṅga*). For example, the statement that the [final vowels] of *deva* and *brahman* are unaccented (*anudātta*) serves as an indicator that, even if there were a different recension, another arrangement would be established by virtue of the underlying capacity (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, the addition of the rule for *kim* following the prohibition of [the suffix] *dvi* and so forth serves as an indicator that the former recension of the sūtras is not accepted here in this context.

1.17 Regarding the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (A 8.2.1), in order to exclude that [rule] from applying to the case of a grammatical marker (*liṅga*), the Vārttika introduces another marker pertaining to a different word: *jaśbhāvād iti ced uttaratra* (Vā. on A 8.3.13.2).

1.18. Since the designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) is already established for those beginning with *pūrva*, the statement "I shall state an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the suffix *jas*" is a restatement made through three distinct rules (*yoga*). Furthermore, because the meanings associated with these rules are distinct, they cannot be included in a single rule without causing confusion. Therefore, even if a different recension were postulated, the division of rules—namely that there are seven items beginning with *pūrva*—would not be eliminated.

And so, just as those very [factors] are the apprehensions and thus there is no disparity caused by weightiness or lightness, likewise those very three are the yogas, and thus there is no distinction whatsoever caused by lightness.

1.19 But what is the reason that when meanings are not apprehended by each individual word alone, an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that has been reached does not apply? In the case of an optional rule, its operation is preceded by a restatement (*anuvāda*); and because of the difference in the mode of operation, the established application of the word in a restatement of what has already been stated is obstructed. Furthermore, even in the case of a difference in operation, prolixity (*gaurava*) follows. And it has been said: "By means of little effort, one should grasp great matters. Therefore, let there be a previously unestablished injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), or let there be a restrictive rule (*niyama*); [in this context] it will be a previously unestablished injunction, not a restrictive rule.

1.20 But what is the reason that the non-differentiating nature of those meanings seen in the *gaṇapāṭha* which are included within the *sūtras* is not recognized? It is because, when a conflict with a general rule (*nyāya*) is possible, an operation [of a specific rule] cannot occur due to the proximity of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that has already fulfilled its purpose elsewhere; thus, there is a proximity of that conflict with the general rule.

For example: "Let this goat that is tied be brought quickly; let him who is standing in the water performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) be fed; let him who is silent, motionless, and steady be appointed as a witness. But in the case of non-contradiction, [the application occurs] without the operation of the word itself. For instance, in the statement, "Let him who was seen wearing white clothes be fed," the indication (lakṣaṇa) presents itself indifferently through both proximity and non-proximity. Consequently, no distinction in application is recognized because the subject matter lacks any specific emphasis.

1.21 But surely here too, the scope for the technical designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) has already been determined by the rule "pūrvādīni sarvādīni," and this is merely being reiterated; or else, the word *sarvanāma* is understood as a qualifier of the named items (*saṃjñin*), just as the word *saṃkhyā* functions in the definition of the term *ṣat*. It is not possible here to carry forward (*anuvṛtti*) the phrase "beginning with *sarva*" [from the previous rule]. If that were carried forward here, it would be understood as an optional application (*prāptavibhāṣā*).

Nor is the word *sarvanāman* (pronoun) one whose referent is its own form; for even in subsequent grammatical operations where there is an option regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*), it functions by way of the property of being a name, and thus it can be understood as specifying a named object (*saṃjñin*) through that very same undifferentiated form. In the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyaḥ*, the word *sarvanāman*—which has an established connection [to the term] "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ smai*)—will be understood as having the named objects as its referent and serving as the cause for delimiting the nine beginning with *pūrva*.

However, in those sub-groups where the defining characteristics have already fulfilled their purpose, one must devise an effort regarding the proximity or non-proximity of these characteristics so that there is no contradiction among them. [Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.35: "The word *sva* [denotes] one's own property when it does not refer to kinsmen."

1.1 This word *sva* is a synonym for *ātman* (self), *ātmīya* (one's own), *jñāti* (kinsman), and *dhana* (wealth). It also denotes mastery (*īśvara*) or conduct (*carya*) within the scope of the suffix *āminij*. For example: “He places them turned away in his own dug-out place” (*MS* 3.2.4); “For one does not harm what is one’s own” (*TS* 5.1.7.1). Likewise, it refers to that which belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*), as in “his own house,” “his own man. It occurs in the sense of wealth (*dhana*), as in: “As many as are his possessions (*svāḥ*), he makes them compliant and non-disputing for him” (*MS* 4.3.7).

1.2 Why is the term "denotation" (ākhyā) mentioned? The intention [is as follows]: the meaning of a sentence is a relation (saṃsarga). For example, in the expression "the animal, the goat" (*paśuṃ chāgam*), the denotation of the word *paśu* is either "animality" (*paśutva*) or the substance characterized by it; likewise, when the word *chāga* is employed, its denotation is merely the state of being fit for sacrifice (*medhyāvāpamātra*), and not "animality"—neither less nor more. Thus, there is the exclusion of donkeys, mules, and the like.

For it is not possible that "cowness" (paśutva), which inheres in the same object as a goat, could simultaneously possess either a deficiency or a surplus when inhering in the same object as a donkey. Likewise, the proponent of the view of relation (saṃsargadarśin) rejects the inclusion of the term "ākhyā" [in the definition], arguing that while the word *sva* itself denotes "one's own," the "surplus" (ādhikya) constitutes the meaning of the sentence.

1.3 [The purpose of the rule is] so that there may be the inclusion of the word *sva* (own) when it functions as a synonym for "kinsman" (*jñāti*) or "wealth" (*dhana*). The remainder of the sentence is "there is a prohibition. For others, the text reads "not a synonym for kinsman or wealth. They justify this by saying "it is indeed *avidhavā* (not a widow). However, according to this view, the distinction lies in the meaning of the sentence itself. There are many words for *sva* that function according to their respective meanings.

In that regard, because the general form is heard, words whose specific meanings are not manifested are designated as "these" by virtue of their function toward a distinct meaning through another word. Therefore, under the view that the meaning of the word *sva* is "kinsman"—as in the expression *svaputrāḥ* (one's own sons)—a prohibition would apply; however, by the inclusion of the term *ākhyā* ("name"), this is accomplished: how could there be a prohibition in a case where the cognition of "kinsman" or "wealth" arises from the very form of the word itself, without the employment of another word?

1.4 Alternatively, by the inclusion of the word "naming" (ākhyā), it is established that the prohibition does not apply in cases where, through either the context or the meaning, it is clearly understood that the term refers to kinsmen or wealth.
The term *antara* [denotes] that which is between the upper garment (*yoga*) and the lower garment (*upasaṃvyāna*). // 1.1.36 //

1.1 Here there is a difference of opinion. Some think that *bāhiṣā* means "connection with the outside. For them, *antare gṛhāḥ* ("houses within") and *antarā gṛhāḥ* ("houses between") refer to the dwellings of Caṇḍālas and outcasts which are outside the enclosure wall. But for those who hold that the meaning is "connection with the exterior" (*bāhyena yogaḥ*), *antare gṛhāḥ* refers to houses inside [the wall], and they are called *antarā gṛhāḥ*. Just as there is a disagreement here, so it is also regarding *upasaṃvyāna*, because it is a word denoting both an object and an instrument. That by which one wraps oneself is *upasaṃvyāna*.

1.2 [Objection: "The inclusion of the term *upasaṃvyāna* (lower garment) is redundant. [Response: In that case, it must be stated for the sake of including things such as a pair of garments (*śāṭakayuga*). This is the intention: when objects are joined externally, even if they are of equal measurement and not worn, it is difficult to discern specific characteristics and so forth. However, even when not worn, items such as a *puṣpaṭa* or a loincloth (*kaupīna*) are recognized as either an upper garment (*uttarīya*) or an inner garment (*antarvāsas*). But this is not the case with a pair of garments. Therefore, it is not established by the mere fact of being joined externally.

1.3. Here too, regarding this person who is a "man": this is the intended meaning. Some commentators explain that even when the term *upasaṃvyāna* (lower garment) is employed, the expression "a pair of cloths" (*śāṭakayuga*) is not established; they hold that the designation will be applied by taking the future lower garment into account within the mind. Others, however, think that the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) was made in the sentence for this purpose: namely, for the sake of three cloths or four cloths.

In that regard, concerning the meaning of the sūtra "when three garments have been put on, there is connection with the outer one," [the definition] would not apply to the first garment. If, on the other hand, it were "connection with what is outside," even so, it would not apply to the first or the middle garment. Yet, it is intended for both to be called "inner garments" (*antarāḥ śāṭakāḥ*). Therefore, the sense of "pairing" (*yuga*) has been rejected; rather, the meaning should be stated as follows:

2.1 It should be stated that [the word] *apūrī* [is used]. Since the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, it includes its gender-distinct form" would otherwise apply, this prohibition is therefore stated. Furthermore, a city (*pūḥ*) is constructed in some places only within the enclosure wall, while in others it is outside the enclosure wall; thus, there exists both types of cities characterized by external connection.
The sixth lesson in the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā: For the sake of what follows, [the rule states that] "svarādi" (beginning with *svara*) and "nipāta" (particles) are "avyaya" (indeclinables). 1.1.37.

[1] There are four possibilities here: either the recitation of *svarādi* (particles beginning with *svara*) within the *cādi* group, or the recitation of *cādi* (conjunctions) within the *svarādi* group; or the designation *nipāta* (particle) alone should be applied, or the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) alone; and in the case of a single recitation, only one designation should be applied—either the designation *nipāta* or the designation *avyaya*. Regarding the *avyaya*, however, this is certain: "In this context, some indeclinables have action as their primary meaning, while others have the meaning of a case-ending as their primary meaning."

"Nor does this meaning have a connection with gender or number. Particles such as *svar* and so forth are also exclusively non-substantive (*asattvavacana*) because their primary function is to express case-meanings (*vibhaktyartha*). Indeed, this is the distinction: particles like *svar* are denoters (*vācaka*), whereas particles like *ca* are indicators (*dyotaka*). Since particles such as *svar* are in every respect non-substantive, one might question why they are recited separately [from the list of particles]. However, the response seen—namely, "or [the rule applies] to particles like *ca* which are non-substantive"—is found to be inadequate.

[2.1] He asks why one or the other designation was not employed: "Now, for what purpose are both designations used? Having recited *prāgrīśvarān nipātāḥ* (A 1.4.56), this should have been recited after it: *svarādi* (A 1.1.37), *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (A 1.1.38), and then *cādayo 'sattve* (A 1.4.57). He states the full purpose: that the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply even to the items beginning with *svara*.

Where here—in the case of *kim* + *at* (A 5.3.12)—would there be the status of a *taddhita* suffix for the vowel *e*, such that its *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) would depend on being a *pragṛhya*? [2.2] As in the case of *ca* and so forth, according to the rule “optionally when *ca* and others are elided” (A 8.1.63). But that is not so; the statement of the prohibition “not *āṅ*” (*anāṅ*) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and it does not mean that four [particles] are being included. [2.3] If that is the case, then let it be the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Even here, the aforementioned fault persists. And if the designation of an indeclinable applies only to this single [vowel], then that sūtra should be read as follows: “An indeclinable consisting of a single vowel, except for *āṅ*. The particles beginning with *svar* are then understood by implication (*anuṣakta*).

[2.4] As for the objection raised—that it would be better to state "by way of inclusion" (*nyāsa*) out of a desire for brevity—this can be countered as follows: one will read the rule as *avyaye naÑ-kuc-ādīnām*. In this way, the understanding applies only to the four cases. Furthermore, because there is a prohibition regarding the suffix *-ktvā* and because of specific technical derivations (*nipātana*), there is no over-extension to forms such as *snātvākālaka*; thus, there is no need for an exhaustive enumeration.
*Taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* // Pāṇini 1.1.38 // [The *taddhita* suffixes that do not represent all case-relations are also indeclinables.]

[1.1] Is this designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) for that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix, or for the *taddhita* suffix alone? It is understood to apply to the whole complex. Why? Because of the rule: "When a suffix is mentioned, it refers to what begins with that [suffix] from which it is prescribed.

[1.2] But is it not the case that in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix is mentioned, the rule of "referring to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited? If so, then this is a case of the extension of the rule of "referring to what ends in that" based on the context (*prākaraṇika*), as an additional provision (*aupasaṃkhyānika*), according to the statement: "The purpose is for the designations of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinable (*avyaya*). For example: *paramoccais* and *paramanīcais*.

[1.3] But what is the distinction between the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) for the whole (*samudāya*) or for the constituent part (*avayava*)? If the designation of *avyaya* were applied to the constituent part, then in the rule *tatra yatra* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), the elision (*luk*) would not occur; for there, the case-ending (*sup*) is prescribed after a suffix (*pratyaya*), and not after an *avyaya*. [1.4] It is said in reply: By the authority of the explicit statement [of the rule], the elision will be effected here by relying merely on the principle of "priority" (*paratva*). The statement would otherwise serve the purpose of excluding *aka*. Therefore, when the designation of *avyaya* applies only to the whole, and the elision of the case-ending (*sup*) prescribed after an *avyaya* occurs, there is no fault in the application of other rules.

[1.5] Now, if the collective whole (*samudāya*) is being relied upon, how is this connected with the phrase "not having all case-endings" (*asarvavibhakti*)? For a case-ending is not the cause for the production of a collective whole, since wholes are to be inferred; rather, it is only suffixes (*pratyaya*) that are prescribed. [1.6] Even in this case, because [the property of "not having all case-endings"] is impossible in the collective whole, the designation proceeds by relying on its parts: "A word ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) if it has as a part a suffix that does not have all case-endings. There is no difference whether the designation applies to the suffix itself or to the word ending in it.

[2.1] Regarding the term *asarvavibhakti*: commentators have understood the distinction based on different analyses (*vigraha*). For some, the analysis is: "Not all case-endings (*vibhakti*) are the cause for its production. However, this is a demonstration of the meaning that for such words with non-co-referential members (*asamānādhikaraṇapada*), there is no *bahuvrīhi* compound; it refers to the meaning that "case-endings" (*vibhaktayaḥ*) are the cause and "suffixes" (*pratyaya*) are the effect. But in the constituent member of the compound (*vartipada*), it means "its case-endings are not all [present]."

Others offer this analysis: "asarvā vibhaktir asmāt" (from which [word] there is a non-universal case-ending). According to their view as well, because the previous rule is prescribed for the sense of possession (*matvartha*), there is an absence of a *pañcamī*-based *bahuvrīhi*; thus, the suffix (*taddhita*) functions as the cause and the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as the effect. This is merely a demonstration by means of the *pañcamī*, but the actual conceptualization is simply this: "asarvā vibhaktir asya" (of which there is a non-universal case-ending).

[2.2] In this regard, those who maintain that not all case endings (*vibhakti*) serve as the cause for the production of this [suffix] offer the following counter-example: for what purpose is the term *taddhita* mentioned? [Consider the examples: *upasarajaḥ* and *mandurajaḥ*. Both the suffix that follows immediately after a case ending and that which is separated by other elements function as the cause for the production of every [suffix]. Furthermore, this suffix *ḍa-* is prescribed based on the locative case ending in the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.97); however, it is not a *taddhita* suffix.

[2.3] The counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the inclusion of "not all case-endings" (*asarvavibhakti*) is *aupagavaḥ* and *kāpaṭavaḥ*. How is this a counter-example? For even if the inclusion of "not all case-endings" were made, the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya-saṃjñā*) would still apply. How so? If it is first assumed that this is based on the case-ending belonging to the word-form itself—as in “*tasi* after the fifth case when used with *prati*” (A 5.4.44)—or...

Regarding the rule *akartari tṛtīyāyāḥ* (A 5.4.46), this [suffix] is one that does not occur with all case endings (*asarvavibhakti*). Furthermore, in the rule *aṇaś ca tasyāpatyam* (A 4.1.92), the genitive case is resorted to in its meaning-form (*artharūpa*), not in its word-form (*śabdarūpa*). Herein lies the fault regarding the rule *prakāravacane thāl* (A 5.3.23); for in this case, there is no case ending whatsoever that possesses a verbal form.

[2.4] Furthermore, suppose it is argued that this suffix is prescribed by depending on all case endings—namely, in the senses of "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), "existing therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), and "come from there" (*tata āgataḥ*). Even so, this is not possible, because the fourth case ending is not included. Yet, that [fourth case] does exist, as in *bhākta* ("given for food"), derived from the rule *bhaktād aṇ anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.4.68), meaning "that to which food is given. However, in the case of *dākṣi*, since the suffix *iñ* is prescribed only in the sense of "offspring," its status as not being applicable to all case endings remains unaltered.

[2.5] In this regard, the view of the author of the *Vṛtti* is observed: "A *taddhita* suffix is produced after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, that word which constitutes the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) and pertains to differentiation does not belong to the domain of the compound (*vṛtti*). Thus, at the time of grammatical derivation when the production of a suffix is intended, both that which ends in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*) and that which is a nominal stem are equally unfit for usage. Consequently, it is possible for the base (*prakṛti*) to be either that which ends in a case-ending or a nominal stem; hence, it possesses the character of all case-endings.
It is determined thus: however, the fault in this regard has already been shown in the Vārttika itself with the words "without *nānā*" (vinā nāneti) [at 2.6].

Regarding the term *asarvavibhakti*: if this *bahuvrīhi* compound is accepted in the sense that "that which does not possess all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*) is the cause (*nimitta*)," then the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "not having a case-ending" (*avibhakti*) must be formulated. In that case, how is the phrase "having a cause that is not a case-ending" (*avibhaktinimitta*) to be understood? If, first of all, it is described as "a word for which a case-ending does not exist is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that serves as the cause," then there is a fault in the case of forms such as *aupagava*.

Furthermore, if "avibhakti" is interpreted as that for which no case-ending is heard (*aśrūyamāṇavibhakti*), then the fault remains that [the suffix] would be *nitya* (obligatory). For this suffix *tyap* is prescribed after the word *niṣ* when no case-ending is heard. If "avibhakti" is taken to mean that which does not depend on a specific case-ending (*anāśritavibhaktiviśeṣa*), even so there is a fault in the case of words such as *viśaṅkaṭa*. Therefore, this reading is not correct. What then? This is merely an illustration. Of what? Of the list in the *gaṇa* (grouping). Those which are enumerated in the *gaṇa* deserve to be included (*upasaṃkhyāna*) in this meaning of the rule; however, they need not be included in other meanings of the rule.

[2.7] But surely it is stated that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is expressed by means of a verbal statement (*vācā*). This is not a fault; for he uses the word "addition" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to refer even to the recitation of the text (*pāṭha*). For example: "Since there is a prohibition regarding 'two' and so forth, what is the addition? (cf. Pāṇini 5.3.2, Vārttika 2). [2.8] In this regard, one might ask: if the list of words (*gaṇapāṭha*) exists, what is the purpose of the rule (*sūtra*)? [The answer is: It is so that they may be indicated through both grammatical markers (*lakṣaṇa*) and detailed explanations (*prapañca*).

Alternatively, it proceeds thus even when the previous cause exists: "of that which has no case-ending as its cause. For those who hold that this definition does not apply to cases where there is no case-ending as the cause, yet such forms are desired, they must provide an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Without relying on the recitation of the word-list (*gaṇapāṭha*), it is stated: "except for *nānā*. Since no specific case-ending is mentioned in the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is established that [the suffixes] arise without distinction, and once arisen, they are restricted; thus, their status as having all case-endings is determined. Consequently, words such as *viśaṃkaṭa* would also follow by this same logic. However, the non-application of that [rule] to them has already been explained according to the previous sequence.
[2.10] But what is the reason that it is not established? Because its establishment depends on a different meaning of the Sūtra.

[2.11] For this [word] occurs with all case-endings (*sarvavibhakti*). What is the reason? Because there is no distinction. Who else could there be who does not possess all case-endings? Or, he for whom all case-endings are the cause of their arising, or he for whom none at all are—both of these are indeed distinct from that. Alternatively, it is because it is prescribed without distinction.

They describe it thus: because it is prescribed without depending on a specific case-ending (*vibhakti*), or rather, because the case-endings (*sup*) are prescribed without distinction, there is the production [of the suffixes] from an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that ends in any case-ending.

[Regarding the rule 5.4.58: "The addition of *tral* and so forth is to be enumerated. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be understood as indicating a class or type; this is because *tasil* is also included in the Bhāṣya.

"But surely these [words] are distinguished [by their specific application]"—this is the intended meaning. [The objection is: "In connection with *abhavat* and similar forms, only the fifth (ablative) and seventh (locative) case endings are the cause [of the suffix -vat]. In contrast, since the use of all case endings is permitted in connection with *bhavat* and similar forms, there is the status of all case endings in this context; therefore, [the rule for -vat] does not apply. To this, he says: "He will explain this."

[2.14] Furthermore, if it is argued that "the word is without case-ending" (avibhakti), meaning "one whose case-ending is not heard"—if this were so, then in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, the word *rāja* would be an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it lacks a case-ending; why then does it not undergo the accentuation of the original form of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*)? [Answer: In the case of compounds where the case-ending is not elided (*aluk-samāsa*), such as *dāsyāḥ putra* and the like, the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) will apply. This is also established by the enumeration of categories [in Pāṇini’s grammar]: "In the case of indeclinables, the negative particle *nañ*, and particles (*nipāta*)."

[2.15] In that case, regarding the forms *dadhi* and *madhu*, the suffix *akac*—which is characterized by being indeclinable (*avyaya*)—would apply, resulting in *dadhakī*. However, the form *dadhikam* is what is intended. If this is so, then the word-form (*śabdākṛti*) must be relied upon; yet this word-form is not devoid of inflection (*avibhakti*), for in other numbers it appears with inflections as well, such as *dadhinī* and *dadhīnī*. Furthermore, when the word-form is grasped, the meaning-form (*arthākṛti*) is also necessarily relied upon, since in other numbers it likewise appears with inflections as *dadhinī* and *dadhīnī*. Thus, in the apprehension of the word-form, the meaning-form is also taken into account.
Because there is a difference between the form of the meaning and the form of the word *iti* which is similar to it, it will not be an indeclinable, just as in the case of "the cart is *iti*.

But how will this fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) not occur? He thinks as follows: the status of being an indeclinable is based on the absence of case-endings by relying upon worldly understanding; and in actual usage, these [words] are entirely devoid of case-endings. Therefore, we shall proceed without relying upon the technical understanding of the grammatical treatise.

[2.17] Because they are mutually dependent when undivided, there is no establishment [of the forms]. An objection is raised by relying on the understanding of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). For in the treatise, suffixes such as *sva-* (the nominative case-ending) are taught after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) without distinction. Just as there is incorrectness (*asādhutva*) regarding the offspring of those who are not signifiers—such as *Babhru-maṇḍula-maka*—so too is there incorrectness for these various *vinā* and so forth. In that regard, a rule that excludes [the suffixes] must be commenced to establish the correctness of the undivided form: "After an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the feminine suffix *āp* and the case-endings (*sup*) are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*).

Seeking the purpose of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, [the author] explains by means of *luk* (elision) this meaning: that from indeclinables (*avyaya*), the suffixes beginning with *su* are neither produced nor uttered. This is for the purpose of ensuring that those properties such as the designation of a "word" (*pada*) which are observed when a suffix is present, occur here even though a suffix is absolutely impossible. And this being so, the learner understands from the treatise that these [indeclinables] lack case-endings (*avibhaktitva*).

Since the absence of case-endings occurs when there is *luk*, and since this *luk* is dependent upon a specific effort [of the grammarian], such a characteristic is not capable of performing any functional operation (*arthakriyā*).

[2.18] Or, [it may be said that they are] "without gender" (*aliṅga*) or "without number" (*asaṃkhya*). Because the former [position] is unstable, the alternative is untenable. There is no fault, however, because of the connection of one sentence with another. This very [point] is brought forward as a connection: "'Unestablished' because of mutual dependence when undivided; or 'without gender' and 'without number' because of mutual dependence. Thus, it is simply that there is no establishment due to mutual dependence. And when this is accepted, the state of mutual dependence is not avoided.

Alternatively, the connection may be made as follows: regarding what was stated, "the word is *avibhakti*," the term *vibhakti* is taken either as referring to the suffixes beginning with *sva*, or else as a synonym for "division" (*vibhāga*), meaning "distinction. And the divisions of a noun (*nāman*) are precisely these: gender, number, object (*karman*), and so forth. Among these, by the non-mention of gender and number, the categories such as the object (*karman*) are to be understood as excluded. Therefore, this establishes the following: either *avibhakti* means that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has been elided; or else, that which has not reached any distinction is *avibhakti*.

[2.20] Furthermore, seeing that no instruction whatsoever is given regarding the meaning [of the term], and thus avoiding the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he presents this alternative: "Alternatively, [the word *avyaya* means] that which has no gender (*aliṅga*), no number (*asaṃkhya*), and is indeclinable (*avyaya*)."

[2.21] Even so, this results in a mutual dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). A learner understands that a certain meaning belongs to a word from the treatise itself; for instance, he understands that the fruit of an action may belong to the agent when it is possible for the verbal root (*dhātu*), and that it does not belong to it when it is impossible—based on the fact that the root is marked with a *svarita* accent or has the suffix *ñi*. However, the learned person understands even in the absence of such a mark, just as the mention of *svarita* and *ñi* was rejected [in the case of the rule *kartṛ-sthe ce...*, etc.].

And having established this, those very [words] were recited by the Teacher as being possessed of both [gender and number]. Therefore, one who understands from the treatise that these [words] possess gender and number also incurs the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), since he would have to understand even the possession of gender and number from the treatise itself.

[2.22] This is not something based on explicit statement (*vācanika*), nor is it a mark of being "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyatā*). What then? It is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Everything is indeed intrinsic; however, some things are seen to deviate [from their literal meaning], such as: "My eyes are beautiful to behold," or "My feet are more delicate" (MBh 1.322.5, 6). That for which an effort is relied upon to exclude deviation is called "based on explicit statement. But that which is seen not to deviate—since no undesirable [literal sense] is observed there—no effort is made [to exclude it].

And so it has been said: "Or rather, [it is] not [so], because we do not observe [such usage]" (*Vārttika* 2.2.30,2). For there is no usage such as *puruṣarāja* when *rājapuruṣa* is intended; nor is *pacatipra* used when *prapacati* ought to be used. Since this situation applies even to words where deviation is observed, how much more so in the case of meanings? Therefore, because it is merely a formal proposition, this [reasoning]—whether regarding number or non-number—is devoid of logical mark (*aliṅga*), as its deviation is both seen and unseen. This being the case, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) does not exist.

[2.23] "But it is established by the reading. To the extent that the fault of mutual dependence remains for the author of the *Vākyapadīya*, there is the presentation of the reading. Others, however, explain the word *tu* in the sense of *vā*—that is, "or it is established by the reading. For them as well, this is not possible, because everything has been rejected.

[2.24] The suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc* are included [in this section]. This is also recited thus in the list (*gaṇa*): "The secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) beginning with *tasil* and ending with the suffix *edhāc*. The suffixes beginning with *śas* and ending with the compound-terminating suffixes (*samāsānta*) are included from the rule “*śas* after words meaning ‘much’ or ‘few’” (*bahvalpārthāc chas*) up to “*ḍāc* after *madra-* in the sense of ‘shaving’” (*madrāt parivāpaṇe*). The suffix *thāl* is included by the rule “*thāl* after *viśva-* and *anya-*” (*viśvemāt thāl*). This is not subsumed under the *vārttika*, yet an effort is made [to include it].

Since the suffix *thāl* occurs in the sense of "in this manner" (*prakāra*) according to A 5.3.23, it is used in the Vedic language (*chandas*) with words such as *pratna* in its own sense (*svārtha*) according to A 5.3.111. [The suffixes] ending in *m* are *am*, *ām*, and *ām*. However, in the *Vārttika*, because *taddhita* suffixes are the subject under discussion, *ābhi* is not mentioned there. The suffixes expressing the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*) are *kṛtvasuc*, *suc*, and *dhā*. [The suffixes] *tas* and *vat* are included. So too are *nānā* and *añ*; *tenaikadik* and *tasi*; and *vati*, as in the rule "when the action is equal, *vati* is used after the word denoting that with which it is compared" (A 5.1.115). It is stated in the list (*gaṇapāṭha*) that these many [suffixes] are to be recited.

[2.25] Or rather, let it be so. Having resolved the circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) regarding the basis of meaning, he now resolves it regarding the basis of linguistic usage (*śābdāśraya*). For whatever meaning is understood from the treatise (*śāstra*), that is also understood from common worldly usage. If the usage of uninflected forms were restricted solely by the treatise, then those who do not know the treatise—unlike those who possess specialized knowledge—would not employ such uninflected forms; yet they do employ them.

Therefore, the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) will proceed by relying solely on worldly understanding (*laukikī pratipatti*), and not on the understanding derived from the technical treatise (*śāstra*). That very same understanding is now made clearly known [by the statement]: "And the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are also worldly. By this, he refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which is the basis for the determination of meaning. For it is through worldly means that people determine objects possessing singularity, duality, or plurality without doubt. This is cited for the sake of illustration: "one cow" by means of another object [i.e., a price].

However, this [distinction] is not useful for the application of words; for even a fool, when engaged in buying and selling, proceeds in exactly this same way. Therefore, this [treatise] is intended solely to establish the determination of meaning. Just as meanings are determined in linguistic practice (*arthavyavahāra*), so too are they in the employment of words. Thus, regarding the objects that serve as the basis for those words, the meanings are determined exclusively with respect to objects that possess oneness and so forth.

Why is this so? Because even when pronouncing them incorrectly, people do not interchange the singular and plural endings in words such as *vṛkṣa* (tree); they employ number-words (*saṃkhyāśabda*) that are in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with those [nouns]; and they generally do not employ words such as *nānā* (various). Furthermore, it is not the case that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) function as numbers for meanings such as "one" and so forth. Therefore, since it has been stated that "a word without case-endings (*avibhakti*) is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," it is logical that those things in which unity and so forth do not exist are taught as being "nouns without case-endings" (*nāmāvibhaktika*).

[2.26] And let it be seen that this too is to be understood through inference. Now he states the logical justification (*upapatti*): "This matter is also known through reasoning. Even if a grammatical case-division (*vibhāga*) were possible, it should be understood that this is merely a conventional expression (*prāyokti*). Some indeclinable (*avyaya*) has the meaning of a case-ending as its primary sense; for the property of indeclinables is said to be twofold. In that regard, however, this must be understood."

Nothing indeclinable (avyaya) has the meaning of a case-ending as its primary sense, nor does it have action as its primary sense; thus, by this [definition], the attainment of some property is concealed. This arrangement—that a property which is to be brought forth and not abandoned—this he expresses by the term "akathita" (unspoken/unstated).

Regarding the statement "high" (*uccaiḥ*) and "low" (*nīcaiḥ*), the *Bhāṣya* establishes the conclusion that these two primarily express the meaning of the locative case. For it has been stated: "The creator of high mats" (*uccaiḥ kaṭānāṃ sraṣṭā*). An indeclinable (*avyaya*) is merely a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and its case-meaning is "capacity" (*śakti*); furthermore, that capacity is non-substantial (*asattva*). Indeed, it is because of this that there is an absence of connection with gender and number.

[2.28] Regarding the statement that *hiruk* and *pṛthak* are primarily expressive of action (*kriyāpradhāna*): just as particles such as *pra-* and others are primarily expressive of action because they manifest a specific quality inherent in the action, so too *hiruk* and others are said to be primarily expressive of action. If this is the case, their usage would be untenable without a verbal expression, as in *pṛthag devadattaḥ*; for there is no such usage as *pradevadattaḥ*. Their usage will occur through the implication (*ākṣepa*) of a grammatical factor (*sādhana*), just as in the case of *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*.

If it is argued that [the usage] is appropriate only in a compound, [we reply that] an elliptical expression (*ākṣepa*) is also seen in non-compounds: for instance, in the *Mahābhāṣya* there is the usage "he measures out a span after a span" (*prādeśaṃ prādeśaṃ viparilikhati*) even without the employment of another verb; [the sense being] "having measured with a span, he draws. If this were so, then the employment of the instrument as a separate word (*pṛthagbhūta*) would be untenable. This is not a fault. Just as the expression *praparṇaḥ* ("one from whom leaves have fallen") is employed, so too will it be employed here.

Furthermore, because another indicator (nimitta) is prescribed, [the suffix] always functions without abandoning its status as a verbal action (kriyādharma); thus, the rule "there is no connection with gender and number" (Pāṇini 1.4.22) has been rejected, as has the rule "a taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings" (Pāṇini 1.1.38).

[2.29] Here an objection is raised: How is it with the *svar-ādi* group? If they express existence (*sattva*) as their meaning, then this contradicts the statement that "some indeclinables (*avyaya*) here [are not so]. Furthermore, since the connection with gender and number does not cease when expressing existence, the definition "an indeclinable is that which lacks case-endings" would fail to include the *svar-ādi* items. Likewise, in the case of *pīlumūlītaḥ*, if the final word-meaning is fixed as expressing existence; or if its meaning is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), then it occurs in the non-existence (*asattva*) of that [meaning].

[2.30] Here, however, that which was established in the Bhāṣya regarding the separate recitation of *svarādi* and the others from the beginning is now examined. In this case as well, in the expression *pīlumūlataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* occurs in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) as characterized by the meaning of another word (*anyapadārthopalakṣite*). They explain it thus: *pīlamūlī* [is used] when the meaning of another word is characterized by the meaning of a case-ending. Just as the injunction *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) applies to both the primary and the subordinate agent, as in *pacati* ("he cooks") and *pācayati* ("he causes to cook").

[2.31] And this too is done far too much nowadays. By "nowadays," the present time characterized by the commencement of the Sūtras is intended. If this rule (*yoga*) were not formulated, far too much would be done: if only "the singular is prescribed for the agent" (*kartari*) were stated, then the mention of "singular" (*eka-grahaṇa*) alone would suffice; the rules "the dual is for two" and "the plural is for many" would be sublated by that single term. Consequently, it would apply both to things that are non-numerical and to those that possess the number one.

[2.32] But surely, this restriction applies without distinction to those [suffixes] produced from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In that case, if there is a restriction on the number (*vacana*) within the fivefold meaning of the nominal stem, there would be no restriction on the meaning; and if there is a restriction on the meaning, there would be no restriction on the number. How, then, can sublation (*bādha*) be established? Alternatively, if the nominal stem has a threefold meaning and the singular number is not employed for an external object, how could it express that meaning? Or, if the meaning is grasped even though it is not explicitly employed, it would follow that both [singular and plural] apply.

Therefore, relying on the position that this is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), it was stated: "The singular number shall be established as the general rule (*utsarga*). Where one says 'the dual,' there it should be understood that the term 'of two' is present. This is because even at the time of the prescription for those [suffixes] designated as dual, the term "of two" is present; thus the prescription proceeds in this manner: "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a *prātipadika*, the suffixes *au* and *os* occur when two [objects] are to be expressed," and likewise, "the suffixes *jas* and so forth occur when many are to be expressed. And according to this interpretation, since the singular number would not otherwise apply, this [rule] is commenced as an exception (*bādhaka*) to it.
And because specific rules are prescribed for those two, there is no application [of the general rule] to one of them.

Nor should the analysis (*vigraha*) be made thus: "not all" means "not every [suffix]. Furthermore, my friend, in this analysis, is the fault you pointed out—that "not all case-endings arise from this"—applicable? No, he says. What then? It is: "not all case-endings are the cause for its arising. It is said: when this analysis is performed, the fault that exists in the Sūtra has already been stated.

Now he introduces the opinion of another commentator (*vṛttikāra*), according to which no fault arises in the sūtra when that particular view is adopted. By what perspective is this maintained? [The view that] "not all case-endings" (*asarvā vibhakti*) applies. Setting aside that [previous] position, he relies on this: "this is *asarvā vibhakti* because of this."

[2.35] Here it is said: regarding the production of case endings (*vibhakti*) in indeclinables (*avyaya*), there are four ways. According to the view that they are produced without distinction and that there is a restriction (*niyama*) for those already produced, [the case endings] are produced merely for the sake of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), without being dependent on a connection to a meaning. In that regard, although this analysis (*vigraha*) is "not all case endings," there is nevertheless no harm, because every non-case ending has been produced.

And the indicator for the production of all [these cases] is as follows: “Not after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *a*, except for the fifth case” (A 2.4.83), and “The third and seventh cases [are optionally retained] diversely” (A 2.4.84). When there is an activity directed toward a single referent, it follows from the sense that it is so after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), just as it is after an *avyayībhāva*.

[2.36] Furthermore, even if it were imagined that it could be formed by some specific grammatical rule, from what [source] would the suffixes *su* and so forth, as well as those dependent upon them, proceed? Moreover, there is no purpose in deviating from the established rule (*am*). Therefore, the singular number belongs exclusively to the nominative case (*prathamā*) alone. Even so, the analysis (*vigraha*) is constructed in such a way that the desired form is achieved.

[2.37] Now, however, the purpose of mentioning the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has been stated. [The question is: how is the first case (*prathamā*) derived from indeclinables (*avyaya*), given that the rule "optionally [the first case is applied] when the first case is preceded by something else" (*sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyāvibhāṣā*) would establish this only in the analysis "this [first case] is not all the case endings (*vibhakti*) from this"? In this [analysis], however, it is not established that "not all case endings [are produced] from this. For indeed, it is determined that all case endings have already been produced.

[2.38] In this context, that which was presented immediately prior is the position (pakṣa) adopted. And this singular number (ekavacana) is used immediately following because, according to this view, all singular numbers proceed from indeclinables (avyaya). Furthermore, the word *sarva* also functions to denote the totality of types (*prakārakārtsnya*), as in the examples: "all kinds of food have been eaten" and "all kinds of behaviors have been seen."

Even when only one part [of the word] is present—whether it be the word *su* or the word *vā*—there would be the designation "all case-endings have arisen. Therefore, for the sake of conveying the sense of totality, the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is resorted to: "not all case-endings" (*asarva-vibhakti*).

Furthermore, the fact that the neuter gender (*liṅga*) arises in all case-endings (*sarvavibhakti*) serves to demonstrate that the *avyayībhāva* compound itself possesses differentiation (*bhedavattva*). This is just as, in the section on compounds (*samāsakāṇḍa*) and the section on singular treatment (*ekavadbhāvakāṇḍa*), there are statements concerning the application of collective formation (*samāhāra*) to the principle of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*). Thus, the rule “*sapūrvāyā . . . vibhāṣā*” should be understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Even when the sequence [of rules] is bypassed in the grammar, the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) remains the prior one rather than the first; thus, even in actual usage, the sequential order is maintained.

[2.41] This being the case, this [rule] applies equally even to *kṛt* suffixes. Since the analysis (*vigraha*) remains thus, one need only recite: "not all [are called *asarvanāman*], therefore it is not an *asarva*-case-ending. Consequently, this quality of not being an *asarva*-case-ending applies equally even to *kṛt* suffixes; thus, the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39) need not be recited. The point is that the mention of the suffix ending in *m* is for the sake of its specific grammatical operation (*kārya*), and not for the sake of that [designation of *asarvanāman*]. The three meanings of *kṛt* suffixes refer to the enumeration of *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun*.

These words whose meanings are already established by their inclusion in the recitation (*pāṭha*) need not be treated [as *nipātana*]; therefore, the *yoga*s are to be applied—the *yoga*s such as “the *nipātana*s beginning with *svara*” (A 1.1.37), and so forth.

[2.42] Now, others explain it thus: "By that [rule], others should not be formed. In this case, however, because it does not express a fixed state (*avyavasthāvācitvāt*), the feminine suffix *śī* is difficult to obtain. Some explain it as follows: "The forms *iyāṭ*, *iyāc*, and *īkāra* [are included]. Regarding the statement, "There are three rules for the non-inclusion of *kṛt* meanings": the term *kṛdarthāgrahaṇa* means that in which there is a non-inclusion of *kṛt* meanings; that is, when which cause is relied upon is the non-inclusion of *kṛt* meanings initiated? And what is that cause? The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "not every case-ending" (*na sarvā vibhaktiḥ*).

And there is no mention of the term *taddhita*. In that regard, just as the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39) is not recited [in the *Uṇādi-sūtras*], so too these three rules derived from it—namely, *svarādinipātam avyayam* (A 1.1.37), *ktvātosunkasunaḥ* (A 1.1.40), and *avyayībhāvaś ca* (A 1.1.41)—need not be formulated either.

[2.43] Now, this being the case, for those who rely on the specific rule regarding number—such as *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, and *bahavaḥ*—the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) would follow because they do not possess all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*). Therefore, in order to exclude these, the mention of *taddhita* must also be made by Pāṇini. Even if the mention of *taddhita* were made, there would still be no application of the rule to *ṇamul* and other suffixes; thus, the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* must be stated. Furthermore, words such as *svarādi* are neither *kṛt* nor *taddhita*.

Now he says: "Therefore, the inclusion of *svara* and so forth must be made. Even so, there is a fault in the case of *viṃśati* and others; for the word *viṃśati* ends in the singular and is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Others explain: even so, there is a fault in the case of *varaṇa* and others; for the word *varaṇa* also ends in the plural and is a secondary derivative. Likewise, the word *ubhaya* sometimes does not have the dual as its scope, and thus the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would apply [undesirably].

Therefore, by this [statement], he demonstrates that even for this very commentator (*vṛttikāra*), the *gaṇapāṭha* alone is superior. [The inclusion of] *kṛt* and *taddhita* [suffixes occurs] only in the *gaṇapāṭha*. That is to say, both *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes must be recited within the *gaṇa* itself. And that being the case, this indicative statement—that the author of the *sūtras* and the author of the *vṛtti* proceed by way of a mutual relationship of defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)—is established.

[3.1] It was stated that "one should recite this entire [section] as having the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) according to its recitation"—that is, "this designation *avyaya* is effected by means of the recitation. Consequently, [the designation] does not apply here in cases such as *paramoccaiḥ* and *paramanīcaiḥ*. Since there is an absence of direct hearing (*śruti*), context (*prakaraṇa*), or syntactic capacity (*sāmarthya*) in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), there is no application of the designation to that which ends in [the listed items]. Therefore, the designation must belong only to those whose extent has been specified; thus, it will occur through the rule of extension to what ends in [the listed items] (*tadantavidhi*).

Furthermore, there is a need for the extension to what ends in [the listed items] by means of the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) regarding the designations of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables (*avyaya*).

[3.2] In that case, would it not follow here as well that one could say *atyuccaiḥ*, *atyuccaisau*, or *atyuccaisaḥ*? How can there be a compound in this instance, given that the word *uccaiḥ* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti-pradhāna*), and yet there is no connection with the act of exceeding (*atikramaṇa*) that locus? Just as in the expression “look there,” the verb *dṛś* (to see) has no connection with the locus itself. With what, then, is it connected? It is connected with that which is situated therein (*tatrasthasya*). Or, if it is conceived in this way: because it is associated with the locus "high" (*ucca-adhikaraṇa-sahacaritatvāt*), it receives the designation "highly" (*uccaiḥ*).

Even so, the status of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is difficult to establish. Just as a grammatical operation (*vidhāna*) devoid of meaning is postulated even without the word *nānā*, so too here there would be an absence of a second [word]. And this has been stated: "Words beginning with *ati* are compounded with a word in the second case when they have the sense of 'surpassing' (*krānta*), etc. Therefore, it is postulated in this way: "Indeed, for someone, that which is expected from the sense or from the context is already known," as in the example "the Brāhmaṇas' white [clothes]. Nor is the view of the followers of Śākalya (*saunāga*) being relied upon.
What then? It is established by the rules: "Because of the mention of *kva-aṅ-svati* as having a low state" and "The words beginning with *pra* [are used] in the sense of a *kta*-suffix."

[3.3] It will be argued that there will be a prohibition by the rule "not for a subordinate element" (*upasarjana*). Since the aggregate (*samudāya*) is not a subordinate element, how could there be a prohibition? It is replied: because it is a constituent part of a subordinate element, it will receive the designation "subordinate element. For that which is a constituent part of a subordinate element, the technical name "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) does not apply; thus, the prohibition occurs within the context of the technical name "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*), where it is recited. And in that case, the mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*) should be applied. However, that [mark] is indeed rejected there. If it were not pronounced, the application of the circumflex accent would be impossible or unnecessary.

[3.4] This is so that the name may be understood as being "in accordance with its meaning" (*anvartha*). Now, if a name is conceived as being in accordance with its meaning, it would entail dependence upon an external object; thus, not being grounded in its own form (*svarūpa*), its status as a "name" would be difficult to maintain. Alternatively, if it were independent of the object and based solely on its own form, then the inclusion of the object would be unattainable. It is said in reply: In the world, names are of two kinds. One occurs when a cause (*nimitta*) exists and is attached to that cause, yet it functions without directly denoting the cause itself.

Or, for example, although the name *Śrīkṛṣṇa* was given to this very deity because of his dark (*kṛṣṇa*) qualities, the word *kṛṣṇa* does not function by conveying the quality of blackness; sometimes even a fair-skinned person is given the designation "Kṛṣṇa. In the same way, this designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya-saṃjñā*), being applied on account of the non-occurrence of elision (*anānāgamana*), functions without denoting that non-occurrence of elision. The inference for this is that its purpose is to effect greatness: "this is the designation for that which possesses the non-occurrence of elision."

But for that which has no repetition (*nānāgamanam*), there is none; and because the word "very loud" (*atyuccaiḥśabdaḥ*) goes to various [cases], it is not an indeclinable (*anavyayatvam*). Alternatively, just as in the technical term *prasāraṇa* a specific case-ending is the mark of its recurrence (*āvṛttiḥ*), so too here this explanatory sentence (*nibandhanavākyam*) is presented. But this [sentence] "this [word] is repeated" is the application-sentence (*viniyogavākyam*) for the inclusion (*upagraham*); or rather, its mark is its greatness (*mahattvam*), by which it is determined that the form of the word is an indeclinable (*avyayam*) because it recurs. Or else, its mark is its greatness in the sense that two words have been uttered through a single action (*ekakriyayā*) by way of a *tantra* (simultaneous operation).

[3.6] "It does not pass away" means it is "immutable" (*avyaya*). Where, then, does it not pass away? Since the locative case is used in the verse, it is likewise indicated here by the locative. Feminine, masculine, and neuter genders; the qualities of being (*sattva*); singularity, duality, and plurality; and the states of persistence, manifestation, and disappearance that occur for the sake of the functioning of qualities such as form and so forth—these are understood as its immutability (*luṅgatva*).

Furthermore, because there is no capacity to denote a specific [quality], there is only the denotation of the general capacity, as in the case of "in the five. Or, because its purpose has been fulfilled by the suffix expressing the action, the singularity is already expressed; thus, a word denoting that [singularity] does not function, just as in the case of "agnicit" (one who has piled the fire-altar).

[3.7] Alternatively, it means that where there is neither the capacity to denote a universal (*sāmānya*) nor the capacity to denote a particular (*viśeṣa*). He explains this very point with a verse: "It is similar in the three genders.
