For similarity arises either from the inclusion of a universal, from absolute non-existence, or from the abandonment of distinction, due to a similarity of form. "In all case-endings" (*sarvāsu vibhaktiṣu*) refers to the inclusion of the objects of action (*karman*) and so forth. "And in all numbers" (*vacaneṣu sarveṣu*) refers to the inclusion of number (*saṃkhyā*).

In all these nominal portions (*nāmabhāga*), that which does not pass away (*na vyeti*) should be understood as the indeclinable (*avyaya*). How is this so regarding those [words] beginning with *svar* that denote existence (*sattvavacana*)? Even there, they denote a substance (*dravyavacanatva*). However, such things as "what gender" or "what number" do not exist for them; rather, they are said to possess whatever number is obtained by general rule. This is merely the case of possessing a number characterized by non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*); it is not the case that they have [specific numbers like] one, two, or many. [The rule] *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39) [applies].

[1.1] When both causes are present, and there is a statement showing the defect in adopting either one while the other is absent, a question arises therein: "How is this to be understood? [1.2] This alternative—that a *kṛt* suffix ending in *m* [is the subject]—is established in this way: if this technical name (*saṃjñā*) applies to those named things (*saṃjñin*) when they have not yet attained their technical names, then those named things, having not yet attained their dependence on others and being fit for connection with qualifiers, are connected with the rule *kṛnmej*. Such is the operation of this alternative.

[1.3] However, if they were first grasped by their own designations (*saṃjñā*) and then employed for the purpose of conveying another designation—whereby those subordinate elements, which have entered into that [larger unit], have attained the status of being designators themselves, yet possess specific distinctions as the doors of their designations—then there is the rule of "application to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*). This is the position: that the suffix *me* (the genitive case ending) qualifies a *kṛt*-formed word, namely, that which ends in *m* and is not itself a *kṛt* formation.

[1.4] Nor is the rule of "specification of the end" (tadantavidhi) impossible here, because of the statement: "In the case of technical designations (*saṃjñā*) involving the mention of an affix (*pratyaya*). Why? Because the rule is initiated with the purpose: "for the sake of the technical designations of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinable (*avyaya*). Alternatively, it follows from the etymological definition: "it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it does not go away" (*na vyeti*). For neither a manifold going nor a non-going exists for an affix alone; thus, even without the explicit mention of "the end," this twofold distinction is observed.

[1.5] However, those who—disregarding the rule of extension (*atideśa*) that applies to what ends in such an element, as well as the etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) resulting from the mention of the word "end" (*anta*)—imagine the possibility of this alternative view, they should be questioned as follows: What is obtained? Is it a connection with the rule of extension, whereby the designation is applied to a *kṛt*-affix ending in a *meṅ* (the causative suffix *ṇic*), or is *meṅ* the primary element here and *kṛt* its qualifier?

If the connection with the rule of extension is obtained, then that very purpose for which this alternative was proposed is not established, namely in the case of *kārayāṃcakāra*; for in this instance, it does not end in a *kṛt* affix.

[1.6] Now, if it is conceived in this way—that because of the statement "if that is a *kṛt* suffix," the mere letter *m* does not exist [as such], and thus only that which ends in *m* would have the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), while the pure vowel *eC* exists [as such] in the word ‘dṛśa’, then for that which ends in *eC*, [the status of an indeclinable] would not apply in the case of ‘kartave’. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) appears to be purposeless. [1.7] However, in the *Nyāsa*, the purpose of including the term "end" is stated to be for the sake of understanding those [words] ending in *aiC* by their own nature, so that [the rule] does not apply here in the case of *kumbhakārebhyaḥ*.

[1.8] Alternatively, based on the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), that which is established by logic is here indicated by the statement: "In this case, the *kṛt*-suffix is the primary element (*pradhāna*) and the *mej* is the qualifier.

[1.9] Or else, this is a mnemonic verse (*grahaṇakavākya*). However, that which is connected with the refinement of usage (*prayogasamskāra*) based on this [rule] should be understood as being of such a nature: "A word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix followed by *mej* is indeclinable (*avyaya*)."

[2.1] If it is understood that "a *kṛt* suffix ending in *m*" [is meant], as in *kārayāṃcakāra*, then since the letter *l* here does not end in *m*, the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) would not apply. However, if one relies on the interpretation "that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and ends in *m*," then this [designation] applies because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix by virtue of its suffixal characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and it ends in *m* by direct hearing (*śruti*). But if this were the understanding, then [the designation] would also apply to *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ*. This too is a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix and ending in *m* by direct hearing through the *kvip* suffix; thus, by the rule "after an indeclinable" (*avyayāt*, A 2.4.82), there is elision (*luk*).

[2.2] But surely, since the singular ending *ām* is already eliminated by the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc., what is the purpose of *luk*? This is the intended meaning: just as in the case of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), dual and plural endings occur due to the difference in the number of agents (*sādhana*), so too they occur in the base form (*prakṛti*) of *ām*. The suffix *liṭ* arises when there are two or many agents or objects; therefore, dual and plural endings also occur after a form ending in *ām*, as in *kārayāṃcakratuḥ* and *kārayāṃcakruḥ*. However, *akac* is not cited as an example because, since its meaning is incomplete, there is no connection with words such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*).

[2.3] "It is indeed accepted that [the suffixes] exist merely as conditions (*pratyaya-mātra*). This is what he demonstrates: for there is no such thing as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix which is elided by *ām*. How so? First, if the suffixes expressing contempt, praise, or intensity remain unmanifested by means of *ām*, then they ought to undergo elision (*luk*), because their non-manifestation would be unstable. Alternatively, if they arise from the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) and manifest contempt and the rest belonging to *ām*, even then, they should not have arisen from *ām* in the first place.

[2.4] Having established non-occurrence through reasoning, he establishes it by means of scripture as well: "And for this reason it is desired. For thus it says: *kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi* ("the root *kṛ* is also employed after [a verb ending in] the *liṭ* suffix"). Here, the word *ām* is understood from the preceding context; the meaning is that *ām* is employed, immediately following *ām*. And if there were a suffix such as *tarap*, then *kṛñ* and so on would not be employed immediately after it. This being the case, [the rule] is stated as "for the purpose of excluding what is separated" (*avyavahitanivṛttyartham*). Furthermore:

If the *svādi* suffixes were elided, even though the verbal root (*vacana*) would still be manifest, then—just as in the case of [roots] ending in *kṛt* where the agent (*puruṣa*), voice (*upagraha*), and so forth are derived from the other complete word—so too in the case of those ending in *ām*, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) which is relied upon for the manifestation of all meanings would not occur.

[2.5] As for the fact that he recites this word *praśām* among the *svarādi* group: here, indeed, the rule *mo no dhātoḥ* (A 8.2.64) does not apply, because its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by virtue of being already accomplished. Nor is this form possible for the root *śāna* in the sense of "sharpening" (*tejane*), because that root is invariably followed by the suffix *san*. If the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) were not operative here, how could one explain forms such as *kārayāṃcakāra*? It is on the basis of this [example] that it is understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule does not apply to a verbal root ending in *m* when it belongs to the same class [of roots].

However, the status of having a prefix (*sopasargatva*) is not accepted here, lest there be [the undesired form] *pratāma*. But under this view, the rule would apply to *laur* from the root *lāvati*, because this is a *kṛt*-derived form ending in *ej*. This is a rejection of [forms] that have no other base (*ananyaprakṛti*). Alternatively, since this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by means of a metarule (*paribhāṣā*), this fault indeed remains in the case of *laur*.

[2.6] When the natural forms *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* (as well as their long counterparts) are excluded, it is possible for *e*, *o*, and *ai* to have *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* as their natural bases, but not for the *m*-group (*mam*). Regarding the rule *ādhaye*: here this must be considered—once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, should the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) take effect, or should the *ayādi* substitutions? Because they are subsequent, the *ayādi* substitutions apply; because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the designation of "indeclinable" applies. Once the designation of "indeclinable" has been established, there ought to be elision (*luk*). Furthermore, both cases are non-eternal (*anitya*). When elision occurs, there is an absence of the *ayādi* substitutions.

Since the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is prescribed on the basis of the presence of [the suffix] *ayā* and so forth, there would be no elision (*luk*). However, according to the principle that "an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules," the elision would indeed occur. Therefore, this must be stated as an exception here.

[2.7] Regarding the phrase "from the potters" (*kumbhakārebhyaḥ*): it is possible to establish a prohibition there based on the principle that, between a term mentioned by its technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and one mentioned as a ready-made form (*pratipadokta*), the ready-made form is preferred. For it has been stated that the inclusion applies to that which is eternal, of that specific form, perceptible, and internal (*antaraṅga*). However, this [term *kumbhakārebhyaḥ*] is to be inferred, being non-eternal and external (*bahiraṅga*). This point was not explicitly stated [in the rule], as I shall examine the purposes of other metarules (*paribhāṣā*) later.

[3.1] *Saṃnipāta*, *saṃśleṣa*, *samparka*, and *ānantarya* are synonymous. The meaning is: that rule (*vidhi*) which has this as its characteristic. That is "without cause" (*animitta*). Of what? Of its obstruction (*tadvighāta*). "Its obstruction" means that which obstructs it; it is without cause for another obstructing rule. And I shall demonstrate the obstruction only with respect to specific purposes, whichever obstruction occurs.

[3.2] Shortening (*hrasvatva*) is a *saṃnipāta-vidhi* because it is an operation of the augment *tuk*. In the example *grāmaṇikulam*, the shortening—governed by Pāṇini’s rule “*iko hrasvo ’ṅyo gālavasya*” (A 6.3.61)—depends upon both the preceding and the following members of the compound. Such a *saṃnipāta-vidhi* cannot be the cause for the destruction of that very [condition] upon which it depends. But what is destroyed here? First of all, the long vowel *ī* is the element that possesses the *saṃnipāta* [of conditions], and it is prescribed precisely by means of shortening. Here, the augment *tuk* is not the destroyer of the *saṃnipāta*-possessor; rather, it is the destroyer of the *saṃnipāta* itself.

The *tuk* augment serves to destroy the immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*) between the preceding and following members of a compound. This purpose is valid only if this *tuk* is considered a part of a specific member and if a part of a member is not itself grasped by the term "member" (*avayava*). However, if the *tuk* is considered a part of the entire aggregate, or if it is either a part of a member or a member itself, then the contiguity is not destroyed at all; thus, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) would serve no purpose.

[3.3] Shortening (*hrasvatva*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), while the *tuk* augment is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*). Because it depends on two words, shortening is extrinsic; because it depends on a single word, the *tuk* augment is intrinsic. Now, how is it that in forms such as *grāmaṃ nayati* and *kulaṃ grāmaṇi kulaṃ*, where shortening does not apply to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), this distinction holds? Even here, since the shortening—by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47)—depends on the entire compound (*samudāya*), whereas the *tuk* depends on individual phonemes (*varṇa*), its status as extrinsic is established.

However, if the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical cause) were applied, there would be the fault in the form *grāmaṇicchatram*. For in this case, after the shortening [of the vowel] in *grāmaṇyaḥ chatram* has been effected, the *tuk* augment—which is conditioned by the *kvip* suffix—would not apply because it is *antaraṅga* (internal); nor would the [shortening] conditioned by *cha* apply because it is based on a *saṃnipāta* (an immediate combination). Consequently, the form would result in the hearing of the *atuk* [augment], yielding *grāmaṇichatram*. But if the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding external operations) were applied, the [shortening] conditioned by *cha* would indeed take effect, because both rules share the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*).

[3.4] *nalopo vṛtrahabhiḥ*. The elision of the *n* (the *nalopa*) which depends on both the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is characterized by its own grammatical occasion (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it does not serve as a cause for the application of the augment *tuK*. Now, why does the rule "elision of the *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*) not apply when the suffix *kvip* follows? This has already been stated: "that which ends in *a* in the original teaching (*upadeśa*) of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes"—and thus the elision of the *n* is considered unestablished (*asiddha*). Both types of non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) apply here: non-establishment with respect to what precedes (*pūrvatrāsiddhatva*) and non-establishment due to being extrinsic (*bahiraṅgāsiddhatva*).
Because it depends upon the case-ending, the elision of the *n* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

[3.5] Regarding the state of having *ud* as a penultimate (*udupadhatva*) in the case of *nikucita*: the elision of the *n* which occurs by the rule “*aniditām . . .*” (A 6.4.24) is dependent upon the suffix being *kit*. Immediately thereafter, the state of having *ci* as a penultimate (*cidupadhatva*) arises; this destroys the designation of *kit* for the suffix that brought about the *saṃnipāta* (the immediate sequence). By this *paribhāṣā*, it is understood that [the state of having *ci* as a penultimate] is not the cause for the designation of *akittva* (non-*kit*-ness). In this case, even though there is no *kit*-ness, there is no obstruction whatsoever to the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of the *saṃnipātin* [suffix].

[3.6] When *nābhāva* (the substitution of *na*) is to be applied by this rule (*amunā*), the *mubhāva* (substitution of *mu*) is already established. However, the purpose of the statement is formulated by postulating that what would otherwise apply [by another rule] is considered asiddha (non-existent) in relation to that. Relying solely on the letter *u* in this sūtra, the application of *nābhāva*—being characterized by its phonetic combination (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*)—does not serve as a cause for the destruction [of that combination]. What is destroyed here? For how much is the subsequent phonetic combination not destroyed by *nābhāva* itself? There is indeed immediate succession (*ānantarya*). In this regard, the following is postulated.
And that *saṃnipāta* (conjunction), when lengthening is applied, is obstructed by the vowel *ā*. Therefore, it does not become the cause for the destruction of the form of the preceding *saṃnipāta*.

[3.7] It is not the case that "mu" is a substitute; he will state that the compound ends in every case-ending (*sarvavibhaktyanta*). And it will remain precisely because it relies on the general relationship with every case-ending.

[3.8] He has adopted the substitution of *ā* for the property of being *kit*. When *sic* follows in the *luṅ* tense, after the *guṇa* substitution has been made, one subsequently relies on this grammatical process (*prakriyā*)—namely, the substitution of *āt*—and thus the substitution of *āt* possesses the characteristic of being conditioned by its own occurrence (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, that substitution of *āt* is not the cause for the *kit* designation which is dependent upon the technical name *ghu*. In this case as well, the *kit* status is based on a formal designation (*vyapadeśanimitta*). And when this is established, even the form of the subsequent element that was present in the immediate proximity (*saṃnipātinaḥ*)—namely, "after a short vowel of the stem" (*hrasvād aṅgāt*)—is here destroyed.

[3.9] The status of being "three" (*tri*) and "four" (*catur*) is for the purpose of applying the suffix *ṅīp*. Furthermore, the substitution [of *tricatur* for *tisṛ-catasṛ*] depends upon both the nominal stem and the case-ending; thus, it is characterized by its own immediate causal condition (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*). That [substitution] is not a cause for the [application of the] long vowel *ī*. For when the long vowel *ī* is applied, it destroys the contiguity between the two factors that constitute the immediate condition, and it also alters the form of the preceding element through the substitution of a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*).

[3.10] As for this rule, “*na tisṛcatasṛ*,” this is not a marker (*aliṅga*). Why? Because this would be for the purpose of a compound, as in *priyatisṛṣṇāṃ brāhmaṇānām*. However, it is stated that this is taught in the Vedic language (*chandas*), and it is presented there; for these two words, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, are recited in the *svasrādi* group.

[3.11] Hundreds and thousands [of examples exist]. Relying on the fact that *aṅga* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the augment *num* is introduced by the condition of *saṃnipāta*. When the subsequent condition (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting of *saṃnipāta* undergoes elision (*luk*), there is a disruption of the form; consequently, there is also a disruption of immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*). Even here, since there is an explicit statement of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), this [objection] is seen to be without merit, especially because of the mention of "the end" (*anta*) in the rule *ṣṇānta*.

[3.12] In the case of *śakaṭau* and *paddhatau*, by the rule *acca gheḥ* (A 7.3.111), the vowel *au* is substituted. Because of that single substitute (*ekāra*), the altered form of the subsequent element would, by virtue of being an *at* vowel, cause the preceding element to be treated as such; however, the suffix *ṭāp*, which would then be triggered, would destroy the immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*) between the stem (*aṅga*) and the affix (*pratyaya*). And that contiguity cannot be destroyed, because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) behaves like the final element (*antavadbhāva*). Now, if it were to be destroyed in this way, it would be so only with respect to the operation (*kārya*) itself, for the status of behaving like the final element applies to the operation, whereas contiguity is not itself a grammatical operation (*śāstrakārya*).

There might be an intervention [of another element] because this [suffix] is worldly (*laukika*). If the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were present, and once the *yāḍ*-augment and the substitution of *ām* had been applied, the undesirable form *śakaṭāyām* would result. Furthermore, they explain that the very purpose of the marker *t* in the rule *audacca gheḥ* is precisely to prevent this; therefore, [the intervention] must not occur.

In *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa*, when the *guṇa* is to be applied, the suffix *ām* would otherwise be obtained. Here, although *iyaṅ* is prescribed, because the domain of verbal roots (*dhātu*) precedes the domain of *l*-substitutes (*lādeśa*), the *l*-substitute is applied first due to its being *antaraṅga*. Then, because it follows after reduplication, the *guṇa* is applied by A 7.3.86 (*pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*). Once the *guṇa* has been effected, the vowel *e*—which is characterized by its specific phonetic configuration (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*)—no longer serves as the cause for the suffix *ām*. For if *ām* were present, there would be a contradiction and a disruption of the form of the suffix that constitutes that configuration.

How is it introduced as "uvoṣa"? For the suffix *ām* is indeed optional according to A 3.1.38 (*uñ-vid-jāgṛbhyo...*). He thinks this: the optionality [of the suffix] has served its purpose in cases like *ūṣāṃcakratuḥ* and *ūṣāṃcakruḥ*, where the suffix is added after a *kit* ending. But here, since *guṇa* is applied before a *pit* suffix, the suffix *ām* would apply by another rule. Furthermore, the meaning of the possessive suffix *matup* is described here as expressing "constant connection" (*nityayoga*); thus, this *ām* belongs to that which is constantly heavy. Since this [case] is not constant, this too is not a valid justification.

[3.14] Its fault lies in its dependence on phonemes (*varṇa*). How is it established here that the characteristic of "coming together" (*saṃnipāta*) applies, given that the cause is simply the suffix (*pratyaya*) as it exists in its own nature (*prakṛti*)? He thinks as follows: by the rule *atiñ* (A 4.1.95), the technical designation of being a suffix (*pratyayatva-saṃjñā*) is applied to that which exists by virtue of its own essence. Alternatively, the correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs to the entire complex; or rather, the correctness belongs to that very suffix which exists as something subsequent. Or else, the correctness belongs to the technical designation itself, which is characterized by the coming together [of the base and the suffix].

[3.15] The suffix (*pratyaya*) does not have the characteristic of being a combination (*saṃnipāta*). This is the intended meaning: indeed, for some teachers, it functions like an operation (*kāryavat*). By the rule *buddhau kṛtvā* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the suffix is perceived even when it has not yet arisen by virtue of its original form (*prakṛti*). And this position is described in the sūtra *paraś ca* (A 3.1.2): "That very thing is the operation of the subsequent element (*para*), namely that the subsequent element should come into existence. Furthermore, neither grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) nor a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) could be the cause for the displacement of phonemes (*varṇavicāla*).
Perception is the cause only through a continuous succession; it does not become such a cause in its actual state. Thus he explains that the condition is not characterized by a mere conjunction.

[3.16] In that case, the designation of a stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) would be without a cause (*animitta*). For the designation of a stem is characterized by the conjunction of base and suffix; it would thus be without a cause for the displacement of phonemes (*varṇa-vicāla*), since such a conjunction is produced by means of form (*rūpa*). In this regard, the following remains unestablished: that a suffix based on a vowel (*avarṇa-āśraya*) is the cause for the displacement of a vowel. Because the designation of a stem is characterized by conjunction without distinction, all stems whatsoever would result in their operations being finalized.

[3.17] Some introduce this example: *adhukṣat*, *alikṣat*. For this *ksa* suffix, occurring in dependence upon a verbal base ending in a *śal*-letter and a *cli* affix that lacks an *iṭ* augment, becomes characterized by its immediate proximity (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*). This [suffix] is not the cause for the substitution of *gh* for *h*, *ḍh* for *dh*, or *k* for *kh*. Nor is there the status of being "not yet established" (*asiddhatva*) here; for this paribhāṣā does not apply to a substitute (*ādeśa*), as it is a rule concerning the location of an operation (*vidhideśā*). Thus, it cannot be designated as "prior" (*pūrva*). However, the author of the Bhāṣya, relying on this very reading of the sentence—"the suffix depends on the vowel"—adduced the example *dākṣiḥ*.

[3.18] Regarding the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) before the suffix *puK*: in the form *krāpayati*, when the suffix *ṇiC* follows and the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied, the rule for the substitution of *ā* is characterized by its own immediate context (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*); thus, that *ā*-substitution becomes the cause for the insertion of *puK*. For the immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) of the two elements joined by *puK* would otherwise be destroyed. The fault was stated by considering *puK* to belong to a specific part—the *ākāra* of the stem—thinking that *puK* is attached to that particular member.

[3.19] In the case of *adīdapat*, the immediate proximity is destroyed by *puK*; however, since this destroys the immediate proximity of the preceding element (the *ā*), it would not be the cause for the subsequent operation.

[3.20] Since the substitution of *at* for the initial vowel of *tyad*-class stems is prescribed by eight rules, the substitution of *at* for the stem and the case-ending would not be a cause (*nimitta*) for the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, because that substitution is produced by their conjunction (*saṃnipātakṛta*). For when *ṭāp* exists, there is the absence of the subsequent element with which it was conjoined.
[3.21] In the case of *papivān*, the augment *iṭ* would not be a cause for the elision of the preceding conjoined element, as that conjoined element has ceased to exist.

[3.22] In the case of *agnimān*, based on the fact that the suffix *matup* is preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*), the acute nature of *matup* is a result of its own immediate context (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*). That [acute accent] would not serve as the cause when the circumflex (*nihāta*) is to be applied to the preceding [vowel] by the rule “a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]” (A 6.1.158). For if the [preceding vowel] were to become unaccented, the audible presence of the preceding element in its immediate context would be destroyed.

[3.23] Regarding *brāhmaṇī* and *brahmabandhu*: for here, the shortening prescribed in the vocative by the rule *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ* (A 7.3.107)—which is characterized by its own cause (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*)—would not be the cause for the destruction of that which possesses the cause (*saṃnipātinaḥ*). Let it not be so; it will rather be from that which ends in a *ṅī* suffix. For when the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is absent in the rule *halṅyāp* (A 6.1.68), there is no substitution of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*), because of the prohibition. For it has been stated: "In the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, [the reference is to] the long vowel."

And this analysis applies to the word *brāhmaṇī*, but not to the word *brahmabandhu*, because [the former] ends in a feminine suffix (*aṅ*), whereas [the latter does not]. Regarding the rule "the elision of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) is obligatory": it is not the case that the elision occurs only by virtue of being designated as a "vocative. Rather, it is any elision of the vocative by whatever grammatical rule. Since both [the elision of the final vowel and the elision of the vocative ending] are optional, the elision of the vocative ending would not apply once the shortening has taken place due to its subsequent status. If one asks what the scope for such an application is, the examples are *devadatta* and *yajñadatta*.

[3.24] These faults are either equal or greater. This is a worldly mode of expression: when many benefits have been rendered in the world, yet some single obstacle arises, one says, "A great deal of harm has been done. Likewise here, because the technical definition (paribhāṣā) is faulty, it is spoken of in this manner.

[3.25] But surely, since the word *sama* is listed among the *sarvādi* group, it ought to be *sama*. If you argue that this is established by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), then the listing [of *sama*] in rules such as A 1.3.10, "The designation of a corresponding number follows those that are equal" (*yathāsaṃkhyam anudeśaḥ samānām*), would be purposeless. To this, they explain as follows: the word *sama* listed among the *sarvādi* group is a synonym for the word *sarva*, and not one having the meaning of "equal."

Furthermore, is there a word *sama* listed among the *sarvādi* group that is used in the sense of the word *sarva*? He says: "There is. Where? In both common usage (*loka*) and in the Veda. First, in common usage, when a king is not present, speakers say, "This is now a *samarājya*," meaning "the kingdom of all" (*sarveṣāṃ rājyam*). In the Veda, there is the usage: "mā naḥ samasya dūḍhyaḥ" (RV 8.75.9).

The author of the *Nirukta* (5.23) provides this explanation: “May [the word] not [be applied] to us, who are all of evil intellect, that is, of sinful intellect. However, the definition for other [words] is: “*sama-* [is used] in the sense of ‘joined’ (*yukta*)”; the word *sama-* occurs in the sense of being joined, that is, in the sense of being proper (*nyāyya*), and it receives the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). But here, the word *sama-* is not employed in the sense of being joined; thus, there is no fault.

[3.26] Therefore, there is no purpose in this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). What is the intention? If there are many faults and few purposes, then only those [purposes] should be enumerated; a technical rule should not be formulated for that which permits its own faults. For it is not the case that a technical rule should not be formulated simply because faults exist.

This demonstrates the following: every word is subject to error, being accompanied by defects; for instance, in the rule "the substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*), even the prohibition regarding vowel-elision (*alvidhi*) would apply—so why should it not be formulated? Yet, one provides counter-arguments against those defects. Furthermore, as for your thought that the defects are more numerous, that is not so. Why? Because the defects have indeed been enumerated in their entirety, whereas the purposes [of the rules] are merely illustrated by examples.

How so? Here, since the rule "guṇa occurs for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārddhadhātuka*" is qualified by the condition "provided they are not marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*akṅiti*), it is determined that this [rule] does not apply to any other specific case except for that one. Thus, setting aside those defects mentioned here, this is stated: "Therefore, those which belong to this"—meaning that this general grammatical rule (*śāstra*) operates here, encompassing its intended purpose and referring to the general domain.

[3.27] However, all the purposes (*prayojana*) have indeed been stated in the Bhāṣya; there is no fault in not enumerating them exhaustively, because other faults exist. Here, in the rule *aṅer yaḥ*, the substitution of *y* (yatva) is characterized by the immediate sequence (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*); it follows that this becomes a non-cause for the lengthening [of the vowel], because the form of the element in immediate sequence undergoes a change of form, as in *amunā*.

[3.28] “It must be remedied regarding the faults,” it is said; yet no remedy has been stated. To this, the following remedy is offered: if the designation *aṅga* (suffix-base) were without a cause (*animitta*), then the rules prescribing suffixes (*aṅgavidhi*) would become entirely inapplicable. Consequently, even the designation *aṅga* itself would be purposeless. In the case of *krāpayati*, because the form ending in long *ā* is prescribed, the augment (*āgama*)—which is meaningful—is understood as being subordinate to that [base]. Thus, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) maintained in the grammatical treatise is not violated.

From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form *adīdapat*, we understand that there is shortening [of the vowel]. For this very reason, the author teaches the *mit* designation for the root *jñā*—which belongs to the group "māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu jñā" (DhP 9.2)—in the rule *jñājanor jā* (A 7.3.79). Here, because the domain of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is in force, it is determined from the specific instruction that there is no shortening as long as the *puK* augment has not been applied; this is according to the rule *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* (A 7.4.55). This is also evident from the specific mention in the rule *na yāsayoḥ* (A 7.3.45). As for other cases involving the elision of the *ā* vowel and so forth, a counter-argument must be considered. And [the compound] is an *avyayībhāva*. (A 1.1.41)

[1.1] Whether it be the Sūtra or the reading—namely, "The *avyayībhāva* compound ends in a *kṛt* suffix, the letter *m*, or a diphthong"—or even if it is not inherently indeclinable (*anavyaya*), it becomes indeclinable (*avyaya*) and is thus called an *avyayībhāva*; likewise, there is an extension of application (*atideśa*) such as "it does not take all case-endings" (*asarvavibhakti*) or "it lacks gender and number" (*aliṅgasaṃkhya*). In every respect, however, the purposes [of this designation] are elision (*luk*), initial accentuation (*mukhasvara*), and conventional usage (*upacāra*). (Vārttika 1)

[1.2] In expressions such as *upāgni* and *pratyagni*, because they function as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), and because they denote a general property (*sāmānya*) despite being non-substantive in meaning, they indeed possess the quality of lacking gender and number. Even though the word *pañcan* denotes a substance (*sattvavacana*), it lacks the capacity to express a specific gender. However, in cases such as *dāsyāḥ putraḥ*, the case ending is not employed for the sake of expressing number; rather, it serves as a qualifier (*upādhi*) for the purpose of insult. Similarly, in *varṣāsujaḥ* and *foṣucaraḥ*, the case ending is used for the purpose of manifesting a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

But here, by the rule *suluk*, only the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) is effected by the case-ending, not the comprehension of a specific number. [1.3] Otherwise, in *upāgnimukha*, there would be the accent of the first member (*mukhasvara*), and in *upapayaskāra*, there would be the substitution of *s* for *t* (*satva*). Thus it should be stated: "The purpose is the prevention of the application of accent. This is not a fault. He explains that the purpose is such that the general rule (*utsarga*) remains established along with its exceptions (*apavāda*), just as the accent of the first member and the application [of the rule] are established.

[1.4] But is this an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) or merely an illustration (*udāharaṇamātra*)? Now, if it were merely an illustration, the presentation of the statement would not even be employed, since all purposes are desired. This is the intention behind the question: if it were merely an illustration, the statement would be entirely purposeless; if it were an exhaustive enumeration, the Sūtra would be redundant, for these [meanings] can indeed be understood even from the indicative marks (*liṅga*).

[1.5] He says "an enumeration" (*parigaṇanam*). The word *iti* is used either to indicate the teacher or as a particle of emphasis (*lolam*). "Api khalv apy āhuḥ" means "indeed, they also say thus. By this, they support the very fact that it is an enumeration. Since other [purposes] are also excluded, therefore these alone are the purposes. Alternatively, some have explained the purposes according to their own nature, while others exclude those that are undesirable. The author of the Bhāṣya explains that among those [purposes], these are the ones which have not been excluded.

[1.6] Regarding the example *uccair adhīyāna*: because it functions as a vocative (*āmantrita-kāraka*), the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) would apply; this is prohibited by the rule "not for indeclinables" (*avyayānām na*). Consequently, the accent remains that of separate words (*nānāpada-svara*). This same [rule] would apply here as well in the case of *upāgny adhīyāna*. Since the word *upāgni* functions here as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the act of studying near the fire, its status as a vocative (*āmantrita-kāraka*) is not accepted, and thus the prohibition for indeclinables does not apply. Due to the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), there is only a single accent (*aikasvarya*), because the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is included in the rule regarding the suffix *akac*.

Just as the superlative degrees (*prakarṣa*) and so forth of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) are mediated by action (*kriyā*), so too here; thus, there would be a connection with *akac*, and consequently the undesirable form *upāgnakī* would result. [In this context,] "become near the jar" (*upakumbhībhūta*) means "having become situated near the jar."

[1.7] "The activity of the Teacher indicates this. To this, it is objected: if the cessation of *yogavibhāga* is established on the basis of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), then the rule *sārvadhātukārthadhātukayoḥ* (A 7.3.84) should not have been composed at all. For one can understand that the rule exists because of the prohibition concerning *kṅit* suffixes; such is the intended meaning therein.

Even while this *yoga* is being formulated, only specific purposes such as elision (*luk*) and so forth should be kept in mind, and not the prohibition of the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) and the like. If this is the case, those [purposes] can be established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) alone; what is the use of the rule? [The term] "standing before a subsequent word" (*anuttarapadasthasya*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, its recurrence here must necessarily be accepted for the sake of forms such as *paramapayaḥkumbhaḥ* and *gopayaḥkumbhaḥ*. Therefore, because it stands before a subsequent word (*uttarapadasthatvāt*), [the rule] will not apply here in the case of *upapayaḥkāraḥ*.

[1.9] A single purpose does not motivate the undertaking of a yoga—whether it be a *saṃjñā-yoga* or a *paribhāṣā-yoga*. Rather, another purpose motivates it, as in the cases of *jāgurūkaḥ* (A 3.2.165) and *aṇ kuṭilikāyāḥ* (A 4.4.18).

[1.10] If this were the purpose, the intention would be as follows: when the general term is uttered in the Sūtra, there is comprehension through inference of the specific operation; however, when the specific operation itself is thus uttered, there is direct comprehension. In that case, since direct comprehension is superior to comprehension through inference, the rule "not after an indeclinable compound, an indeclinable, a word denoting direction, *go*, or *mahat*" (*nāvyayībhāvāvyayadikśabdagomahat*) should have been recited precisely within the section on accent (*svaraprakaraṇa*). Yet it has not been so recited.
Therefore, this too is not a [valid] purpose; thus all commentators have concluded that, by the very force of the opening tone, it must be "upāgnimukha."

[1.11] Others explain it as follows: this is one purpose, namely the prohibition of the accent of the word *mukha*, yet there is no inclusion of that [word] therein. As for what was stated—that "a single purpose does not motivate the commencement of a grammatical rule"—it is by means of that statement, which establishes that an indeclinable can be determined as non-indeclinable, that this is proven: in that prohibition, by means of that indeclinable directional word (*dikśabda*), there is an extension of the grammatical operations (*kāryātideśa*) of an indeclinable to the *avyayībhāva* compound.

[1.12] Now, it is explained in the Bhāṣya: "In that very context, he might say: 'It has not been stated. And yet this sūtra exists. Therefore, another purpose must also be inferred here. What, then, is that? It is the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), as in *devadattasyopakumbham* [‘Devadatta’s near-the-jar’], by the rule *su-hitārtha-sad-avyayam...* (A 2.2.11).
*Śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*. (Pāṇini 1.1.42)

[1.1] If it is argued that *ś* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* by virtue of the rule "suṭ for what is not neuter," then there would be a prohibition of *ś* in the case of *jas*. If it were recited in this way, then if it were instead recited as "suṭ for the feminine and masculine," this fault would not arise. For in this formulation, the meaning of the term "not neuter" (*anapuṃsakasya*) can be conceived as "it does not apply to the neuter."

[1.2] Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the rule "śi is a sarvanāmasthāna"? It is said: for the purpose of indicating its scope (*viṣaya*). For if it were understood in this way—that *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*—then the application that would otherwise follow from the rule "śi-sarvanāmasthānam" would not occur. Others explain it thus: if, just as "śi-sarvanāmasthānam" were an independent rule (*lakṣaṇa*) regarding technical designation (*saṃjñā*), one were to state by means of a separate sentence that "suṭ is a sarvanāmasthāna," then this fault would arise in the prohibitive rule "tato 'napuṃsakasya."

[1.3] Regarding the prohibition of *śi* when *jas* occurs: in this context, *jas* is presented as the domain (*viṣaya*) by way of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, *śi* is that which falls within the scope of *jas*; or alternatively, *śi* is the substitute for *jas*, hence "the *śi* of *jas*" (*jasi-śi*). The scope (*avakāśa*) for the rule characterized by *śi* is that *śi* which falls within the scope of *śas*, as in the example: *kuṇḍāni paśya*.

[1.4] This compound should be regarded as an *asamartha-samāsa* (an "incoherent" compound). Where an action denoted by a constituent word (*vartipada*)—being constant—is understood even when not explicitly heard because it is inferred, and its own inherent cessation is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*), there the compound is a *samartha-samāsa* due to direct connection. But here, because the word *napuṃsaka* has no connection with the negative particle, this is stated—"this should be regarded as an *asamartha-samāsa*"—on account of the lack of connection with that which effects the designation *sarvanāmasthāna*.

[1.5] And this fault exists when there is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an ungrammatical compound). Why? Because of the prohibition. Although in both cases—whether it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) or a *paryudāsa* (relative negation)—there is an inference of non-attainment, this is the distinction: in *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, the operation begins with the exclusion (*viccheda*), whereas in *paryudāsa*, one who understands the qualified object itself understands the exclusion.

[1.6] And regarding this exposition, it is possible to provide an interpretation. In that case, because it serves our intended purpose, we shall interpret it thus: this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). When there is an exclusion, the non-neuter form is employed for the purpose of indicating something else. For activity proceeds in two ways: by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and by way of the absence of another's characteristic (*paralakṣaṇābhāva*). This is like the expression "feed the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras," or alternatively, "feed those who are not Brāhmaṇas."

If this very injunction is the sole rule and there is nothing else that establishes an absolute exception for a Brahmin, then a Brahmin is not fed. And where there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there too [the action] does not apply.

Here, since the male and female are indicated by the absence of the neuter, and because the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is primary, whether it be a prohibition or a prescription, it pertains to that which is associated with it; thus, it does not touch upon the neuter, but rather indicates that the male and female are indicated by it—this is what is meant by saying there is no operation regarding the neuter.

[1.7] Or, it is because of non-application (*aprāpti*). Even when an incompetent compound (*asamartha-samāsa*) is observed, there is no application of the prohibition. Why? Because of the principle: "A rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding. And here, "immediacy" is both semantic (*arthakṛta*) and phonetic (*śrutikṛta*). How so? If a separate prohibition were resorted to in the form "not for the neuter," then it would be impossible to prohibit [the designation of *śi*] by the rule "śi is a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (P. 1.1.42). Why? Because of the force of its formulation (*ārambha-sāmarthyāt*). For *śi* occurs only in the domain of neuters.

Therefore, for this reason, the subsequent application [of the term] *suṭ* is based on its active form; it is indeed impossible to block it, whether one considers the application of *suṭ* as such or as *śi*. What then? The application as *suṭ* itself is not negated by the rule "it does not apply to the neuter"; thus, the preceding application will take effect.

[1.8] But is it not the case that this later *prāpti* (attainment) sublates the earlier *prāpti*? The intention is that it does so by way of contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*). What, then, is the contradiction here? Since the coexistence of designations (*saṃjñā*) is intended, there is no contradiction between those two. Nor is it possible for two grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) to conflict, because they have the same function. The function of a designation is one and the same. It is said in reply: Contradiction exists either between two rules where one is qualified by a prohibition and the other is not, or between two designations; and from the prohibition, there is indeed opposition.

And those [rules] which have results distinct from their own [application] are contradictory; there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of them. In that regard, the scope (*avakāśa*) of *śi* is [seen in] "kuṇḍāni paśya" (look at the pots); the scope of *suṭ* is [seen in] "rājānau" and "rājānaḥ". Here, both would apply in "kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti" (the pots stand). Because of its priority (*paratva*), it must be by this [rule for] *suṭ*. Priority is an inference based on the non-application of the preceding rule. Furthermore, the prohibition of the subsequent [rule] is an inference from its non-attainment. And when the killer of Devadatta has been killed, Devadatta does not come back to life. Being prohibited, [the subsequent rule] is unable to set aside [the preceding one].
The term *vibhāṣā* means "optionally. (Pāṇini 1.1.44)

[1] Regarding the formation of the term *na-veti-bhāṣā*, this is untenable in either case. Because the referent (*artha*) does not exist and because the referent is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), its connection with a designation (*saṃjñā*) is impossible. Whether the words *na* and *vā* are taken as distinct—as in *na* and *vā*—or whether *na* and *vā* are taken as a single unit, as in *nakir* and *mākir*, in every instance the negation, the alternative, or the exclusion of another word that is to be negated or qualified is illuminated.

Furthermore, in this case, because the words expressing that which is to be negated and that which is subject to option—namely *na* and *vā*—are not employed in the expression *na veti vibhāṣā*, the referent itself does not exist. Of what, then, could a designation (*saṃjñā*) be made? Even if such a referent were present, even so it would not be the case; for [the alternatives] would be "it is," "it is not," or "it might be" or "it might not be. And since such a referent lacks the nature of a real entity (*asattvabhāva*), there can be no connection with a designation. For regarding a designation, either the genitive or the nominative case is operative toward the designatum (*saṃjñin*).

Furthermore, that which has become a non-existent entity cannot undergo the state of being a remainder, nor can it be designated as "this is that. Thus, what was stated—that [the negation applies] because of the absence of an object—is incorrect. Why? Because the word *na* (not), when occurring in a sūtra as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*), functions either in proximity to a substance-word (*dravya-śabda*) or in proximity to an action-word (*kriyā-śabda*). And an action-word is of two kinds: one in which the action is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-kriya*) and one in which the action is primary (*pradhānībhūta-kriya*). In that regard, when there is a connection with a substance-word, the two—negation (*pratiṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*)—do not occur.

Why? Because words denoting substances (dravya-śabda) function by producing a cognition that possesses a fixed form regarding substances; whether that object exists or does not exist, it is precisely the nature of such an object that cannot be denied or conceptualized otherwise. Only that object which has the nature of being predicated (vidheya-rūpa) is either excluded or conceptualized. What, then, is this? It is action (kriyā), existence (sattā), or the nominal stem (prātipadika)—the latter serving as the basis when a word expressing action is employed.

[4] How is it that one is "not a cook" (*apācaka*)? Regarding this, some maintain that the negative particle (*nañ*) is directly connected only with the verbal root *pac* (to cook). Others, however, think as follows: it illuminates a specific state of existence belonging to the agent of the cooking action as being excluded from its own essential nature (*svabhāva*). [5] How about here in the case of "he does not cook" (*na pacati*)? Here too, some maintain that the negative particle is connected to the very root *pac* in its specific state of existence. Others, however, hold that because the relationship of "means and end" (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between "being" (*bhavati*) and "cooks" (*pacati*) is not perceived, the negative particle negates only the connection of the root *pac* with existence.

[6] Regarding the expression "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), where the grammatical perspective differs, some hold the following view: this residual relationship (*śeṣabhāva*) in the case of "remembering the mother" is like "the king's man" or "the tree's branch. Just as these involve an intervention by an action—namely, the act of giving (*dadāti*)—and an abiding (*avasthāna*), so too is this act of remembering. Since remembrance has the mother as its object, it proceeds toward her and abides therein; thus, either the proceeding (*pravṛtti*) or the abiding (*avasthāna*) constitutes the cause for the residual relationship.

In that case, even when memory (*smṛti*) is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), if it is not intended to be expressed in its state as an object to be accomplished but is introduced as a related factor by means of the genitive case, it becomes the cause (*nimitta*). When, however, it is intended to be expressed in its state as an object to be accomplished, then only the accusative case occurs, as in *mātaraṃ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"). This is just like *vṛkṣasya phalam* ("the fruit of the tree") or *vṛkṣāt phalaṃ patati* ("the fruit falls from the tree").

According to the view of some, even in the absence of any other action, the act of remembering itself becomes the cause for the remainder; for an action can be expected by a substance either as something to be accomplished or as a related factor.
[8] There is an absence of mutual assistance among substances; it is logical that their connection arises from action and its cessation. Therefore, the word "new" (nava) is meaningful.

[9] As for what is said—that there is no connection because of the non-existence of the entity—we reply: at the time of assigning a name, since there is a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of that which has become an entity, the connection of the name with the action is logical. Here, when the essence of an object (*arthātmā*), having been relied upon as being serviceable, is brought forward in its form as a real thing (*vasturūpa*), then, being reflected upon by a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it becomes connected with an action. For example: "He who cooks, his offspring" (*yas tasyāpatyam*). Likewise: "This object has become an entity" (*sattvabhūto 'yam arthaḥ*).

Thus, at the time of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the meaning of *vā*—as apprehended by the pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—are real entities (*vastubhūta*). However, when the operation of the word is applied in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), they are indeed non-existent (*asattvabhūta*); therefore, their connection is logical. One should understand that this designation "option" (*vibhāṣā*) applies to whichever meaning is expressed by "it does not exist" or whichever meaning is expressed by "it exists."

[10] Furthermore, how can a single entity be both a sentient being and a non-sentient being? On this point, some have elaborated that the reality (*vastu*) possesses all powers (*sarvaśakti*). They maintain that words, falling upon specific portions of its meaning, delimit those respective powers. Others, however, hold that no such entity exists at all; rather, it is the words themselves, as they function, that conceptualize each respective object.

And that power of conceptual construction is restricted [in its application], as in: "Go, Kaṃsa is being killed. With respect to one and the same entity, one person employs the term *pacati* ("he cooks"); another, having reduced it to the state of a residual factor (*śeṣabhāva*), employs the term *pacateḥ kartā* ("the agent of cooking"); and another uses *pācakaḥ* ("the cooker"). But it does not take the form of an instrument or other kārakas, as in: *dātreṇa lunāti* ("he cuts with a sickle"), *grāmād āgacchati* ("he comes from the village"), or *brāhmaṇāya dadāti* ("he gives to the Brahmin").

[11] Now, what is this statement "in the *naveti-vibhāṣā*"? For it has already been established that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is prohibited for meaningful aggregates. It is replied: here, the status of being a nominal stem applies because it is an imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*). Consequently, this aggregate does not consist of meaningful [parts]; rather, this is a single word that is meaningful by virtue of its own meaning. But would not the prohibition of the nominal stem designation apply here by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "an imitation is like the original" (*prakṛtivad anukaraṇam*)? This is not a fault.

That [designation] which is perceived through the extension (*atideśa*) of a designation based on its *prakṛti* (base) is capable of being negated; however, there is no negation of that which resides in its own locus (*svāśrayā*). Even so, because it does not end in the suffix *āP*, the rules for *yāṬ* and *ām* do not apply, since [the suffix] *āP* is not prescribed after the whole [stem]. This too is not a fault. That in whose final position the sound *ā* is heard is called "ending in *āP*" (*ābanta*). For the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) has been prohibited by the rule "not when a feminine suffix follows" (*astrīpratyayena*). And this is indeed the case. Alternatively, it is explained as follows:

Having uttered "or not" (*na vā*) and relying upon that option (*vibhāṣā*), this is stated regarding that option: "the making of a name for the sake of meaning. What is the purpose? He asks: "What is the purpose intended by you when this is the case? He replies: "for the sake of the comprehension of the word. Alternatively, even by way of the opposite—that is, as something functioning as a negator—it is taught as a purpose, just as in other cases. For in those other instances, two reasons are included within the example; for indeed, in the making of a name elsewhere, there is an absence of hearing the actual meaning.

Just as the hearing of the word *dādhā* is employed to convey its own meaning as an unconditioned object and is thus accepted as a name (*saṃjñā*)—this being for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *dāśati* and so forth—and yet the form *dādhā* is perceived in its specific usage (*pradeśa*), it is not logical that the meaning of a word exists in proximity when the word itself is being perceived, because the meaning is something to be inferred; therefore, at the time of naming, as well as in its usage, there is no contact with the meaning.

Thus, here too, he explains that because the object is not present and because [the form] is inferred in its specific location, the comprehension of the meaning is not logical—this is expressed by the phrase "as in other cases. Therefore, in the rules providing options (*vibhāṣā-pradeśa*), the word *navā* would be a substitute even when indicated in the nominative case, as in the examples *avirāga* and *viraṅgam*.

[13] Therefore, that designation of meaning (*arthasaṃjñākaraṇa*) must be performed. The performance of a specific action is the function of the general act of performing. Alternatively, the treatise (*śāstra*) states that the designation of meaning must be performed. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the meaning. The particle *iti* is employed; "performance" (*karaṇa*) means that which is performed (*kriyate*). Thus, it is both *iti* and a performance, hence *itikaraṇa*. Furthermore, due to the relationship between the general and the particular, there is a connection between the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

[14] Is this [the word *iti*] merely a particle (*itinā*), or does the addition of the word imply an addition of meaning? This is what is being asked: "Should we accept something that is logically untenable simply because the word *iti* has been uttered by you—a state which is like the cawing of a crow? There is another perspective: this is a treatise on traditional authority (*smṛti-śāstra*).

In this regard, just as in the world people remember the measurement [of objects] by means of clods of earth and the like, so here the indeclinable *iti* serves as the cause for such recollection; however, it has been stated that a word may be employed as a "mark" (*liṅga*) when there is an application of a contrary mark, as in the expression "grapes with much molasses."

[15] He says, "It is understood (*gatam*). The meaning is that it is recognized (*pratītam*) or grasped (*upasaṃgṛhītam*). Why? Is it from common usage (*loka*) or from grammar (*vyākaraṇa*)? Some meanings are understood from the treatise (*śāstra*)—for example, the understanding that *vṛddhi* consists of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* comes from the treatise alone. [The meanings of] "animal," "offspring," and "deity" come from common usage. Alternatively, "why" (*kutaḥ*) means "from what cause" (*kuto hetoḥ*) or "from what reason" (*kuto nimittāt*). Because it is not fully established in grammar, one resorts to common usage alone—hence, "from common usage" (*lokataḥ*).

[16] For example, in common usage, when one says, "He said, 'cow' (*gaur*)," the particle *iti* is employed after the word *go*. Because the word *iti* is used following the nominal stem, it is said that the word *go* has the word *go* as its own form (*prakṛti*). [17] But how is this so, given that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal? Even though the word and the meaning are absolutely unconnected to one another, some words have their basis solely in their own form (*svarūpa*), while others have their basis solely in the meaning (*artha*). And in every case, a deviation from one's own meaning is not possible.

[18] In this regard, the principle that "a word, having expressed its own meaning, is independent" was set forth as a practical application for the sake of facilitating comprehension. For it is not tenable to say that a word uttered once functions repeatedly, such that after expressing one thing it then expresses another. There is no expression by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because conjunction has multiple words as its substratum—as in "the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*" or "the tree and the tree. And conjunction is as follows: "the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*" or "the tree and the tree."

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is also not possible, because the meanings of words are not understood through successive synonyms. Therefore, for the proponent of the theory of association (*saṃsargavādin*), a cognition arises in which all objects endowed with their respective qualifiers are integrated. When a word denoting a specific qualifier is uttered, just as when a medicinal drink is tasted one extracts its components such as molasses and so forth, thinking "this is it, this is it," so too, when a cognition proceeds toward a qualified form, one extracts the possible objects that constitute its domain.

And when someone, for the sake of understanding the effect, grasps this form through abstraction (*apoddhāra*), they first comprehend the universals (*jāti*) on the grounds that "there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) being apprehended. However, another person, on the grounds that there is no activity [of cognition] residing without a substratum, first comprehends the substance (*dravya*) itself.

[19] Likewise here too, the word does not exist first and the object later; rather, just as when the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* have been brought to the state of *vṛddhi* and transformed into that very form, they—through the connection "this is that"—become subject to the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) and are designated by the term *vṛddhi* itself according to the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*; even so in common usage, the word "cow" (*gośabda*) designates the physical body (*piṇḍa*) which has been brought to the state of being a cow, such that when the word "cow" is employed, is this [word] [meant] for the object?

"Whether it is cast aside or not, there is no distinction. When the particle *iti* is employed, it manifests the usage of that which remains in its state of non-transformation (*apratyastarūpatā*) regarding the meaning intended. In that context, the non-modification into a verbal form (*śabdabhāva*) of whatever meaning it possesses constitutes its "falling away" (*pracyuti*) here.

[20] If this is so, how is it that the particle *iti* occurs here after the word *navā*? For in this case, since the meaning does not fit, the word cannot function as its own form (*svarūpa*). True; this is indeed so. However, once the relationship between word and meaning is well-established, there may occasionally occur a transformation such that "this meaning is the word *navā*. The particle *iti*, when employed, excludes the absence of distinction between the meaning of the word *navā* and the word itself—it is only for this much that they [the grammarians] provide an explanation. Others, however, describe it differently.

Regarding word and meaning, sometimes the word is primary and the meaning is secondary (upalakṣaṇa), or the meaning is primary and the word is secondary; the particle *iti* causes this reversal of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal—this is "falling away" (*pracyavana*). Alternatively, a single word is endowed with all powers, and by the particle *iti*, its power is cut off—this is "falling away."

Alternatively, words are indeed distinct; however, due to their similarity of form (*sārūpya*), they become the cause for the arising of the cognition of identity, "This is that very same [word]. Thus, others maintain that the word *go* which is employed with respect to the object is one thing, while this [perceived word] is another. In this view, the theory of phonetic modification (*pracyuti*) is not tenable. Or rather, it is possible that, unlike the phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*) are themselves devoid of meaning; and in this very way, the comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence itself, as in: "He said this: *gauh*."

Since a collection possesses meaning, how could the word *go* have "word" as its referent? Thus, there is no deviation [from the rule]. However, in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it is established that in common worldly usage, meanings are well-known; therefore, the words *iti* serve to illuminate this reversal of expectation. This is the conclusion: the particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating a meaning.

[21] Now, what is this manner of expression, namely that "it has the word-meaning as its object"? For it is said that having the word-meaning as its object is a relation (*saṃbandha*). One who falls away from the relation necessarily falls away from the object as well. Furthermore, since this object is apprehended through the relation, it is logical that one should apprehend precisely that which is the cause for the denotation of the object.

[23] The negation of synonymous terms (*samānaśabda*). Those things which have a common expressive word are "synonymous terms" (*samānaśabda*); the negation of their status as designata (*saṃjñitva*) must be stated. For the word *na-vā* has multiple meanings. If the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as being a negation or an alternative (*vikalpa*), were not relied upon, then everything denotable by the word *na-vā* would necessarily become a designatum.

Or, even if a distinction were resorted to, from what source would this distinction arise such that "this is it and not the other"? Thus, there would be either the over-extension of the rule to all cases or doubt; therefore, the prohibition of the word *samāna* (identical) is urged. In the expressions "not new" (*navā*) or "not a small water-pot" (*navā ghaṭikā*), the sense of being "fresh" (*pratyagra*) is indicated. And it is logical that this should belong specifically to the word expressing "freshness. For in those cases, another sentence is inferred from hearing two instances of the word *nava*—which are parts of a single sentence—in the forms of a negation and an option (*vikalpa*).
But here, the expression of "freshness" is direct.

[23] Furthermore, what would be the consequence? For a *saṃjñā* (name/designation) is not itself a *saṃskāra* (grammatical operation). What then? It is the effect produced by that [designation]. This is according to the rule: *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*. How can this be said, given that words such as *sarva* and so on [are the subject], and "newness" and "antiquity" (*navapurāṇatva*) are not properties of words? Nor is there any possibility for the designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) to occur through "newness" and "antiquity. Moreover, in the case of *dakṣiṇapūrva*, it is the direction itself that is being denoted.

Furthermore, its [the word *diś*] absolute impossibility as something new or old is established by the rule in the Sūtra, *avibhāṣā diksamāsa*, which introduces the sense of "recent" (*pratyagra*). In that context, the undesirable consequence (*prasajyate*) arises that the technical designation of pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) would apply to that [word *diś*] when it functions in the sense of "recent. And when direction (*dik*)—in the form of "this from here"—is applied to specific parts, then this very meaning functions as the point of reference (*avadhi*), as in: "The tree is to the east of the village."

In this way, when even the intermediate space (*antarāla*) has its form established as a part, then another hall, being resorted to as an intermediate space, comes to exist through its state of being new or old; thus, the freshness suggested by the *smāya* suffix and others is understood from this grammatical explanation, just as the excellence of a tree's leaf is understood [from the context] in such expressions as "on well-levelled ground" (*susthaṇḍileṣu*).

[24] Or rather, there is no positive injunction because the cognition of a negation is preceded by it, as is seen in the world. When the meaning of a word is delimited by context, purpose, and so forth, its restriction to a specific sense is observed. For instance, when the word *saindhava* is used in the context of a meal with the command "Bring the *saindhava*," its restriction to salt is observed; whereas in the context of hunting, its restriction to a horse is observed.

Thus, because the designation "not new" (*anava*) is prescribed here in these specific rules (*pradeśa*), it is appropriate to understand the meaning of "new" (*nava*) in its true sense as it applies to those rules; for the words of the *Vibhāṣā* in these rules are preceded by a formal injunction. Therefore, since that which is to be enjoined is either being urged forward or is already well-known, this [term] will serve the purpose of negation (*pratiṣedha*), not the purpose of indicating something newly acquired (*pratyagra*).

Even in common worldly usage, when the word "new" is employed in a context under discussion, it is understood to have the sense of negation rather than the sense of something newly acquired; taking this into account, the example has been presented.

[24] The other party refutes the example by stating: "There is a cause by which the world exists. For you are making a statement with a discordant gender (*viliṅga*). "Discordant gender" means that the genders do not agree (*vyadhikaraṇa*). From this very indication of discordant gender, there is an understanding of negation, and not because it is preceded by an injunction. He supports this very point by saying: "Come now, let the statement be made with a concordant gender. And we do not know where in grammar this is ever done.

In grammar, there is never an indication by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Here too, in the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyāśālāniśānām* (A 2.4.25), the indication would be one of identical gender, but not one of identical case-ending (*samānavibhaktika*). Therefore, in the sections concerning optionality (*vibhāṣā*) in grammar, it is not possible to determine from the mere concurrence of the sounds heard whether there is coreferentiality or non-coreferentiality.

But when [the direction] such as "southeast" and so forth is conceived through a human effort, then there may or may not be a cognition arising from the contact with the word expressing negation; however, this is not the case for a word expressing "freshness" (pratyagra). This he explains by the following manner: "Moreover, there is freedom of choice" (kāmacāra).

[26] By this, he refutes what was stated previously, namely, "there is a cause. Even when the indication possesses the same grammatical gender (*liṅga*), because a negative sense is understood from it, it is incorrect to say: "For you are making an indication with a different gender. For even when the word *nava* is employed, if it coincides with that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*), then, due to its absolute lack of connection with the substance (*dravya*), it expresses negation; but when it stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a word denoting a substance, then it expresses "freshness" (*pratyagra*).

It is not possible to say that the very same thing possesses a mark and is yet without a mark. Furthermore, when this is well-known—as in the case of the Taittirīyakas, who state that "he always eats fresh, very hot gruel"—the word *nava* cannot possibly mean "new" (in the sense of recently produced); rather, it is understood as signifying "fresh" (not stale). Thus, it is perceived as expressing a negation [of staleness].

However, for one for whom the eating of gruel is not thus established as a possibility, it is taught first; in that case, since the inclusion of a word expressing a prohibition would be meaningless, it is logical that a sense of "freshness" (pratyagra) is understood. As for the statement "the speaker has freedom of choice," even if there were such freedom of choice in this technical treatise (*śāstra*), there would still be no fault. But since the speaker’s activity is consistently of a single nature, this [notion of "freshness"] does not apply here either. Thus, it is never used in the sense of "fresh."

[27] This is supported by the statement: "And here, not by the mention of *vibhāṣā*. Why? Because the mention of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is primary. In that context, the verb *bhavati* is presented as the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and thus it is primary; the others are its subordinate members (*aṅga*). Leaving aside the primary thing to be enjoined, the heard mention of *vibhāṣā* will not apply to its subordinate members, namely the *sarvādi* group. Thus, the previous reason remains for not including the word *pratyāgrā* [in the list]: "Or rather, because the understanding of a prohibition is preceded by an injunction" (*na vā vidhipūrvakatvāt pratiṣedhasaṃpratyayaḥ*).

[28] The prescription of non-eternality is untenable because it is the designation of a negation (*pratiṣedha*). In the Sūtra, the words *na* and *vā* are a single indeclinable (*nipāta*), just as in the cases of *nakir* and *mākir*. Furthermore, this [word *vā*] has the sense of negation, just as in the immediately preceding sentence where it is employed for negation: “*na vā vidhipūrvakatvād...*”. Therefore, the meaning of the word *navā*—namely, the negation that constitutes the sense of *vibhāṣā*—is designated by the term *vibhāṣā*, as in the rule "*vibhāṣā śveḥ*". This being the case, the forms *śuśāva* and *śuśuvatuḥ* would not be established.

[29] But it is established by the statement of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Even in common worldly usage, absolute negation is observed, as in: "The village is to be gone to by you, or not? For the application of a sentence of negation is not logical without something to be negated. Therefore, from the sentence of negation itself, the sentence of the contingency (*prasaṅga*) is inferred. However, the term *vipratiṣiddham* (contradictory) refers to having made a single object of indication (*lakṣya*) present in the mind, one says: "There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the root *śvi*. This form *śvayati* is a single entity.

In that case, it would follow that for a single form, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" would apply, which is a contradiction; this is what he expresses by asking, "It is not known with what intention [this is said]."

[30] The other [teacher], because he has understood the authority of the Master, understands this rule "vibhāṣā śveḥ" in the following way: many of these forms derived from the root *śvi* are included here in their actual form as they occur in the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). Among them, some form remains established having undergone the substitution (*nivṛtti*) of *saṃprasāraṇa*, while others remain subject to its application (*prasaṅga*). Just as a prohibition might apply to certain cases based on distinct verbal roots, so too should this be viewed.

Why? Because there is an absolute contradiction between injunction and prohibition regarding a single object. Thus, in the rule *ūrṇor vibhāṣā*, this [sūtra] establishes that many instances of the root *ūrṇu*, as well as many suffixes such as *iṭ* and others, or the entire collection [of them], are to be understood. Or rather, by the force of the context, it applies [the option] elsewhere than in the scope of the prohibition.

[31] Where is this established? For in those cases where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what has not been obtained, both the contingency (*prasaṅga*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) remain unfulfilled; thus it is logical that the prohibition should serve the purpose of providing an option, since the cause for its application is equal. However, in the case of an option regarding what has been obtained, the preceding rule—having been promulgated as a general principle—is already fulfilled. Consequently, the inference of non-application regarding a particular instance necessarily constitutes a sublation (*bādha*) of that rule; therefore, there is no option here. To this, an objection is raised:

If an absolute exclusion were to result from the *prāptavibhāṣā* rules, then in the rule *“vibhāṣā diksamāse”* (P. 6.2.103), the mention of *vibhāṣā* would be a statement of the alternative meaning of the word *navā* (or rather, of the negation) and it should simply have been stated as *“bahuvrīhau”* (in a *bahuvrīhi*). Thus, the formulation of the prohibition *“na bahuvrīhau”* (P. 6.2.104) would be redundant; the term *vibhāṣā* itself would simply carry over (*anuvarteta*) there. Similarly, in the case of *“vibhāṣā vipralāpe”* (P. 1.3.50), the rule which has already served its purpose in *“vyaktavācāṃ samuccāraṇe”* (P. 1.3.48) would be superseded by the rule regarding *vipralāpa*.

[33] The term *vibhāṣā* is applied as a designation (*saṃjñā*) for something "great" (*mahat*). Elsewhere, great designations possess an etymological significance (*anvarthatva*); however, here there is no inference of greatness based on its etymology. What then? It is merely an inference of a specific distinction among the things designated (*saṃjñin*). This is not a single indeclinable (*nipāta*); rather, it is a pair of indeclinables. This designation applies to two meanings: negation (*pratiṣedha*) and optionality (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, *vibhāṣā* is not the denoted meaning (*vācya*) of the word, nor is it the duality of the things designated. What then? It is merely the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of the term].

In this case, however, this alone must be investigated: is this designation [of "prohibition" and "option"] applied to each individually, as is the case with the designation *vṛddhi*, or is it applied to the aggregate, as is the case with the designation *saṃyoga*? If it were applied to each individually, then there would be no such rule that "this [operation] should apply to one thing simultaneously by means of both prohibition and option. Consequently, just as in some cases the vowel *ā* is a *vṛddhi* and in others the vowel *au*, so too in some cases there would be a prohibition and in others an option.

Furthermore, the sequence is difficult to establish, namely that cessation occurs first and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) afterwards. If, on the other hand, the collection (*samudāya*) is what possesses the designation (*saṃjñin*), even so, just as the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) belongs only to the collection and not to its two constituent parts, this [designation] would likewise belong only to the collection; thus, this [proposed view] is untenable.
