One might argue that since there is nothing to be negated among the optional rules (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*), the option will be established by the word "or" (*vā*). But if the designation has already fulfilled its purpose with respect to the collection, how could it convey the application [of the rule] to the constituent parts? Moreover, the sequence is utterly impossible.

Because a collection [of atoms] is impossible due to its lack of sequentiality, this [objection] is also untenable. To the claim that "once it has been negated by the word 'not,' there will be an alternative [option] expressed by the word 'or' (vā)," it is replied:

Just as when the aggregate [of dice] is connected with actions such that one says, "Let them be broken," "Let them be eaten," or "Let them be played with," it undergoes those actions through contact with its parts; for by some particular part, something specific must be done—some must be broken, some must be eaten, and some must be played with. Thus, when a part is broken, the aggregate is broken; when a part is eaten, the aggregate is eaten.

Likewise here too, in the case of *aprāpta-vibhāṣā* rules, since there is no purpose in the operation of any individual constituent, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not operate; however, when the particle *vā* operates, it is the entire complex itself that becomes operative.

[33] Even so, a designation (*saṃjñā*) has been made for affirmation and negation; yet that [designation] is not established when they are non-substantial (*avastubhūta*) and inactive (*avyāpṛta*). For it is possible to apply a designation by taking two even contradictory things as its basis, such as the designation "this is *saṃsāra*" applied to birth and death. In the case of specific grammatical rules, however, the term *vibhāṣā*—meaning "optionally"—conveys that meaning through the form of both simultaneous cessation and engagement. And that meaning is an action (*kriyā*).

That single, undifferentiated entity would have its attributes manifested either by the negative particle (*nañ*) or by the word *vā*. Just as in the cases of "he lifts up" (*abhyuddharati*) or "he brings together" (*upasamāharati*), the single agent who lifts is manifested as being qualified by orientation through the employment of prefixes; yet such a nature of an object cannot possibly exist, because of contradiction.

For just as height and facing upward can both pertain to a single object, so too [the notions of] "it becomes" and "it does not become" cannot coexist in a single action because existence and non-existence are absolutely contradictory; thus, an action characterized in such a way is impossible. Now, if you think that these are two separate actions, then because there would be no connection between two actions, and in the absence of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), the word *vibhāṣā* would be unable to bring together both the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the non-*saṃprasāraṇa*.

In that context, regarding the statement "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*," since there is no second application of the word *vibhāṣā* in its conclusion, this [phrase] "it does not occur" (*na bhavati*) is absent. Now, if the verb *bhavati* is supplied as a conceptual construct—meaning "the non-occurrence of the verb *bhavati* which possesses the sense of transformation"—then because it would be utterly incapable of expressing the intended meaning due to the lack of definition for the new sense in those specific rules (*pradeśa*), it is said: "If it is argued that it *is* [the case], then it is not a prohibition."

If it is determined that "the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs," then there is no prohibition. On the other hand, if it is relied upon in the form of non-existence, as in "it does not occur," then there is no injunction. Why is there no injunction? Because injunction and prohibition are absolutely contradictory.

[34] But it is established that the former is sublated by the latter; the subsequent rule sublates the preceding rule. What is meant is this: first, equality is brought about through negation, and only afterwards does the option (vikalpa) operate. For if the option were to operate first and the negation afterwards, the option would be purposeless, because it would be absolutely sublated. How, then, is this sequence obtained? It is said:

This technical designation—*iti*, *veti*, *ca iti*—has been applied by the Teacher to a collection (*samudāya*) because it functions through a sequence of parts that are apprehended without interruption. If this [designation] did not perform its function in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), the very creation of the designation would be purposeless. Furthermore, in common worldly experience, when the parts are perceived, there arises a recollection of the whole; for one who perceives the white part separately and the black part separately remembers the whole: "This whole is brindled."

But was it not said that since a word is unable to express an object of such a nature, this operation (vyāpāra) must be resorted to as something non-verbal? It is replied: This operation is indeed non-verbal; however, the assignment of a technical name (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) serves as a means for the inclusion of such a type of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the operation is of three kinds: either a positive injunction (*vidhi*) characterized by optionality (*anityatā*), such as "optionally after the suffix *ūrṇ*" (*vibhāṣor ṇoḥ*); or a negation (*nivṛtti*) joined with optionality, such as "optionally in the case of idle chatter" (*vibhāṣā vipralāpe*).

Furthermore, the formation of such a technical term (saṃjñā) would not be purposeful in this sense, because [the meaning] is already established through worldly usage (*laukikī pravṛtti*). As for those rules where there is an option in both cases, such as "vibhāṣā śveḥ" and so forth—in these instances, the word *vibhāṣā*, which occurs once in the world, would apply either to the positive injunction (*vidhi*) or to the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

If it were to apply to a prohibition, it could not be applied to an injunction, because it does not exist after the operation [of the injunction] has taken place; or, if it were to apply to an injunction, it would not apply to a prohibition, because it is exhausted by that [injunction]. It is precisely with this in mind that it was asked: "Is this *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) prescribed for *ral* before *ktavatu* and *kvasu*, or is it prohibited?"

For one who proceeds in this manner, by means of the application of designations, he demonstrates—without distress—the sequential operation of the two parts through their division across various locations: "By this sequence, you must understand this meaning regarding the word *vibhāṣā* in these respective locations."

However, for the learned person who understands that the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) operates repeatedly by distinguishing itself according to each thing characterized—just as every root *śvi* is taken in its distinct forms within the scope of the optative (*liṅ*) and the word *vibhāṣā* is distinguished by those distinctions and thus operates repeatedly—for such a person, the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) is indeed useless; as he will state at the end: "Or rather, it need not be taught, because it is already known."

[35] Regarding "in the case of correct instruction" (*sādhvanuśāsane*)... that which is subject to option (*vibhāṣā*) possesses correctness (*sādhutva*). This was stated previously: "Because the negation is preceded by a positive injunction, its comprehension [arises]. And since the treatise (*śāstra*) is for the purpose of understanding correctness, technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and so forth are constituent parts of correctness. Therefore, once it is established that correctness is the context and the primary subject, it follows that the occurrence of correctness is subject to option; this is what is arrived at.

For when the primary [form] is possible, it is not proper for the effect to reside in its subordinate part; thus, by the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ*, this is what is meant: the form of the root *śvi* that has undergone vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is optionally correct (*sādhu*), and the form that has formed a compound is optionally correct. And having established this, it is said here: "that which is the primary element is the subject under discussion; the application of qualities [occurs] by virtue of the context. This being so, correctness (*sādhutva*) would be optional, but not duality.

There is another way [to resolve this]: this is established by the treatise (*śāstra*). It is impossible for a compound (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*), which have different meanings, to assume each other's form. Consequently, the mention of the option (*vā*) would be purposeless. Furthermore, since it is undesirable for a technical term (*saṃjñā*) to both exist and not exist with respect to its own domain, correctness (*sādhutva*) alone is connected with the option. Thus, there is no fault.

[36] It is not the case that the incorrect form will not be employed; for just as when both edible and inedible food are present, only the edible is taken, so too here, when both are present, only the correct form will be employed. Indeed, the incorrectness of this word *rājapuruṣa* is never intended. For the learned never fail to employ this word. Nor is there any cause for apprehending a distinction regarding correctness here, by which it might be known that "this one is correct" and "this one is incorrect."

Even those [forms] characterized by the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound and so forth, their status as "limbs" (aṅga) exists only when they are grammatically correct (*sādhutva*). Thus, that which has undergone the compound-final-accentuation is correct only optionally (*vibhāṣā*). Furthermore, there is a twofold understanding: first, for the sake of the treatise, for the purpose of understanding the optional form; and second, the lack of such understanding. When correctness is being deliberated upon, it follows that the root *śvi* with its semivowel vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is correct only optionally. Consequently, the forms *śiśvāya* and *śiśvayatuḥ* would not be established.

[38] Furthermore, for one for whom words are produced, it is that optionality (*vibhāṣā*) which brings about the compound. But what kind of impermanence belongs to words, or what kind of permanence? If it is because the form (*ākṛti*) is permanent, or if the permanence of individual instances (*vyakti*)—which are manifested by sound—is relied upon, then what connection is there with optionality? For it does not arise from a difference in the activity of the Teacher; nor indeed is there any such inconsistency, since the scripture itself functions in this manner.

Therefore, whether it be Pāṇini’s grammar or another system of grammar, this consideration applies everywhere to the cognizer: one cognizer understands this grammatical explanation through the relationship between a modification and that which is modified; for instance, regarding the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, he understands that in the form *dadyatra*, this is simply a state of the word *dadhi* itself. Another, however, understands it otherwise: "This is a different word altogether, existing in the form of *yaṇ* when in the state of *saṃhitā*; the treatise merely provides an explanatory description."

Therefore, O King, regarding this rule for the formation of technical terms (*śāstrapravṛtti*), two words apply to the base *puruṣa* when it is thus understood: namely, *rājapuruṣaḥ* and *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*. Since the compound is that which is being produced, it is the primary element (*pradhāna*). And since optionality (*vikalpyatva*) applies to the primary element, there is no fault. Even for one who holds that [grammatical correctness] is eternal, this fault does not arise. Even though correctness (*sādhutva*) is primary, optionality cannot be postulated, because correctness is not subject to optionality. And why is it not subject to optionality? Because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeyatvāt*).

In this regard, just as in the expression "eaten by a hundred Brahmins," the number—even when emphasized—is not connected with the act of eating because it is impossible [for a single act to involve a hundred], and thus it functions as a qualifier of the object numbered, meaning "eaten by those numbering one hundred"; likewise here too, since that which is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) is capable of being conceptualized (*vikalpya*), it is the designation itself that is human, and that is what is conceptualized, not its correctness (*sādhutva*). For example: "the sacrificial animal is optionally [so called]."

Since the states of being a sacrificial animal (*paśutva*) and being an ox (*anaḍuttva*) are not products of human authorship, the act of touching (*ālambhana*) prescribed in the context is subject to optionality. However, it is not deliberated upon whether "it is an ox" or "it is not an ox. Furthermore, the intellect of one who deliberates does not function in such a manner; for an object that has not been deliberated upon is not determined by way of existence or non-existence.

[40] But has it not been stated that "neither the existence nor the non-existence of a *saṃjñā* is admitted"? True; this is so. However, this is said by virtue of the mode of comprehension (*pratipatti*). For one who comprehends it thus—that the application occurs both in the compound (*vṛtti*) and in the sentence (*vākya*)—for him alone does the bringing [of the rule] occur. Furthermore, the heard form (*śruti*) is identical, as in "the son of a female slave" (*dāsyāḥ putraḥ*), "the son of a female slave. In such a case, the compound would necessarily result in subverting the sentence. It is just as when [the suffix] occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting the actual meaning.

The *Vibhāṣā* is commenced with the thought that the Sūtra must be absolutely set aside, as in the rule “or [the augment] before the *liṭ* suffix” (A 2.4.55). To that person, this is said: “What then? A technical name (*saṃjñā*) is connected. But for one who understands it as having a different meaning altogether, this is stated: “And neither the existence nor the non-existence of a technical name is intended here. Furthermore, it should not be thought that “this is being said merely according to my own whim.”

For thus it was stated under the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā* (A 4.1.82): "In that case, then, should the option (*vā*) not be mentioned? It must indeed be mentioned. What is the purpose? Words are eternal (*nitya*). In that regard, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the sentence is established by this [option]."

[41] Regarding the operations (*kārya*), there is simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of the two types of *anvācaya* (addition). What is the connection of this statement? You have proposed that for one who perceives [words] as eternal (*nityatā*), optionality (*vibhāṣā*) regarding correctness (*sādhutva*) would result. That has been refuted. However, if correctness is admitted to be something produced (*kāryatva*), there is no fault in its being optional. But this is the fault: "there is simultaneity of the two types of *anvācaya* which are not simultaneous."

Since the word *yaugapadya* is applied when things are produced simultaneously—just as the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied in the case of the term *yaugapadya* itself—and since here the intended meaning is precisely a collective group (*samudāya*), that [group] being inferred from the context of the word, it is referred to by the term *anvācaya* in the rule *“ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt”* (A 4.1.111), following the rule *“tavyat-tavya-anīyar-ah”* (A 3.1.96). What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is thought as follows:

He for whom words are to be produced [as effects] explains those words independently of their usage; having mastered the words from the treatise (*śāstra*), they are put into practice. And the suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* are prescribed as alternatives (*ekaśabda*) when there is a single means of accomplishment (*ekasādhana*). Just as when fire is sought through friction, the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice also necessarily follows as the first [result], so too, when the suffix *tavyat* is employed, there must be the employment of the other two suffixes, *tavya* and *anīyar*.

Just as in their occurrence (*pravṛtti*), there must also be simultaneity in their employment (*prayoga*). Alternatively, just like the words themselves, the meaning (*artha*) is also their effect; thus, for those who have understood the simultaneity, the meaning is prescribed for them as a collective whole. Therefore, the meaning is grasped in whatever state it exists, and the employment must likewise be in that very same state. As for the view that "they are eternal" (*nityā*): he merely explains the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of those words employed in common usage. But since there is no such thing as the employment of something that is [strictly] eternal in this manner, simultaneous expression is not tenable.

[43] Regarding the statement that "the suffix *para* occurs": one might object that since they share a single basis (*ekasādhanatva*), just as there is no duality in the case of *tavya*, so too—because *tavya*, *tavyat*, and *anīyar* have a single basis—there would be only singularity, and thus the possibility of *para* (occurring after) would not arise. Furthermore, the word *para* is employed even with respect to what is separated, as in: "Pāṭaliputra is further than Mathurā. Moreover, the status of being *para* has been stated for more than one thing, as in: "There is one base (*prakṛti*) and many *yañ* suffixes. This is not a fault.

To begin with, multiplicity has already been accepted by him at the very outset; for it is only when there is multiplicity that this [phenomenon of] simultaneity or accumulation is possible. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the grammatical treatise in the rule *sad-avyaya-tvaya-* (Pāṇini 2.2.11). Therefore, for the sake of brevity, the mention of "single means" (*eka-sādhana*) is made in the form "one should not utter separate case-endings. Moreover, the word *para* ("subsequent") has been removed from the rules involving the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), by virtue of the inclusion of the term *nirdiṣṭa* ("specified").

Furthermore, multiple individuals (*vyakti*) are characterized by being posterior; since the individual is accepted as being posterior to the form (*ākṛti*), the form alone is indeed prior, while the individuals are at best separated [from it]. Moreover, since suffixes such as *tavya* cannot possibly be associated with a single form, it is impossible for them to have the form as their primary referent.

Nor do we say that a chain of conditions (*pratyayamālā*) is reached; it is not stated that they arise after a single base (*prakṛti*) or that they are uttered simultaneously. What then? It is this kind of simultaneous utterance that is enjoined—that they are employed at one and the same time after other bases. For such is the application of meaning when there is an injunction.

[45] "The employment of words is for the sake of conveying meaning. And the meaning accepted by the suffixes (*pratyaya*) is prescribed; however, this is not explicitly included here. Or, if the status of the meaning being prescribed exists, the rule *tavyat-tavya-anīyar* [Pāṇini 3.1.96], which prescribes the suffixes for the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), serves merely as a proximate statement that explains the application rules (*viniyoga-vākya*). From those [application rules], one understands both the words and their meanings.

Therefore, these statements are undermined: "The suffix *tavyat* occurs after a verbal root in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); the suffix *tavya* occurs in the sense of the abstract action and the object; the suffix *anīyar* occurs in the sense of the abstract action and the object. Furthermore, the undesirable consequence that is tied to the [grammatical] means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) can be averted. Since the understanding of words that are injunctions (*codanā*) depends upon the speaker, one is able to conceive of a connection according to one's desire.

[46] And regarding the study (*śīlana*) of the region of the Teacher (*ācāryadeśa*), there is the status of being its object (*tadviṣayatā*). Furthermore, that which is the repeated mention of "the Teacher" (*ācārya*) in various places in the *Śāstra* is called this "study. In that context, the study of the region is intended to have that [region] as its object, such as in the rule *aiṅ prācāṃ deśe* (A 1.1.95). However, an objection is raised: "How can the study of the Teachers—whether by their name and lineage or by their directional connection—be understood as having that [Teacher] as its object? Why? Because he thinks as follows:

He who understands the treatise as the authority holds that the application [of grammar] is governed by the treatise, not the treatise by the application; according to this view, an application not established in common worldly usage is established by the treatise. Thus, the rule "iko hrasvo 'ṅyaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.61) is the means of establishing it—namely, that short vowels are to be employed. And since any speaker might have been applicable, there is a restriction on the speaker: "according to Gālava. Having taken up this very point, the example was stated: "Five times Jamadagni indeed... and so forth.

[47] But is this not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? Since an explanatory passage is a supplement to an injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*), an injunction is understood therein. And that injunction is: "They cut four portions" and "For the son of Jamadagni, five times" (*Mānava Śrautasūtra* 1.3.2.5). Because this matter is beyond ordinary experience, it is determined from the scripture (*śāstra*).

In this regard, just as its application regarding all agents is established by the rule "they cut off four times," so too the application "five times" would follow [by analogy]; however, it is restricted to a specific agent, namely the *avadātṛ* (the one who cuts off) who is a descendant of Jamadagni (*jāmadagnya*). It does not apply to one who is not a descendant of Jamadagni. [This is shown by the texts: "Jamadagni indeed [performed] this," and so forth. Some explain that, through the connection "this is he," the descendant himself is designated by the word for the father (*pitṛśabda*). Furthermore, in the expression *avādyat*, the suffix *leṭ* occurs in the sense of the present tense; it is the fifth *lakāra* (the optative), and by way of diversity (*bāhulakāt*), the *śyan* affix is applied.

Others, however, think that just as the son follows the conduct of the father, he too commits faults. But for one for whom words are eternal, since the treatise (śāstra) is dependent upon usage, the authors of the tradition (smārtaḥ) regarding usages well-known in the world are merely recorders and not the original creators; thus, the shortening of the final vowel is presented as optional, and Gālava alone is cited as the authority for this recording. Gālava records the shortening.

Of what nature is it? It is "as it truly is in the world. This refers to Gālava’s authoritative status; whether for the sake of honoring his intelligence or because Gālava himself remembers the short vowel, thus his tradition remains unbroken. Others, however, remember it as long. It is not the case that another does not employ what was remembered by Gālava, nor is it the case that Gālava [rejects] what was remembered as long by another; therefore, there is no lack of scope for that [tradition]. The mention of "in the world" (loke) is for the sake of renown.

Fame (*kīrti*) is renown (*khyāti*) or being celebrated (*saṃśabdana*); and because they are the marks of renown, even palaces and such are designated as "fame" itself. Furthermore, some things that are celebrated result in a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), such as the case of Indradyumna and others. But [one might object]: "Is it not the case that for someone else [the fame] is an effect?"

In that case as well, worship can be conceived—for in the world, worship is indeed seen even through self-aggrandizement; for instance, Gālava’s engagement with Yama [regarding the short vowel] implies that "you too should employ it," which constitutes worship by virtue of its being accepted as authoritative. However, there is no dual apprehension [of the rule]; thus he says: "And in the mention of that, there is dual apprehension. This means that from the treatise (śāstra), one apprehends only the short vowel, not the long one.

[49] Or, it is not a technical term (*saṃjñā*) because it is already known; the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. The meaning is: "or it is a term. A verbal designation (*śabda-saṃjñā*) is based upon its own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*); it is the application of that very form to specific instances within a treatise (*śāstra*), and through it there is linguistic usage (*saṃvyavahāra*), as in the case of *vṛddhi* and so forth. This [term], however, does not exist in such a manner; this is what he explains by saying, "for even those who do not initiate this designation..."

Taking a general example, he introduces a specific instance as an illustration, saying: "Indeed, even the ritualists (*yājñika*s)... Alternatively, while ordinary people might understand [the meaning] by learning it from a treatise (*śāstra*), the ritualists—because they follow a distinct system (*bhinna-tantra*)—would not employ the terminology of one treatise within that [other] treatise.

[50] In this regard, when the application is such that the form of the rule (*śāstrākṛti*) operates upon the form of the characterized element (*lakṣyākṛti*), then the *yoga* must be formulated for the sake of an option (*vibhāṣā*) applicable to both cases. Otherwise, the word *vibhāṣā* in the rule “*vibhāṣā śveḥ*” (A 6.1.30) would either be exhausted by a single supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) or not; since there is no other mode of operation, it would be incapable of effecting both.

But when you consider that the specific instances of the grammatical rules (*śāstravyakti*) reside within the specific instances of the linguistic data (*lakṣyavyakti*), then—on account of this very connection—one understands from the rule "vibhāṣā śveḥ" onwards as many individual rules as are contained therein throughout the entire range of linguistic data. Thus, the rule need not be commenced [as a separate entity]. And it was precisely to demonstrate this point that the Teacher established distinct linguistic usages with different characteristics in various locations [of the grammar]. He demonstrates this by saying: "Indeed, the Teacher, while introducing a technical designation (*saṃjñā*... [and so forth].

How is it said that “Bhāradvāja is displaced from his own mother”? It is said: because he is displaced from what was recorded by him after having remembered it. Regarding the term *aprāpte trisaṃśayāḥ*: the word *aprāpte* is emphasized here. As for *trisaṃśayāḥ*, it does not mean “those optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) in which there are three doubts. Why is this so? Because doubt is a single entity; just as in the case of “Is it a post or a man? there is only one doubt, not two doubts. Therefore, it is called *trisaṃśayāḥ* because it has three bases.

The phrase “*dvandve ca* / *vibhāṣā jasi*” is employed here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the section concerning optional rules (*vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa*). However, a doubt arises regarding the rule “*prathamacaramataye*”: if the term “*sarvādīni*” is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then [the present rule applies] where [the previous rule] would otherwise apply; yet if it has ceased [to apply], then there is a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Likewise, if it has not applied, then there is a subsequent counter-exception (*paravipratiṣedha*). Thus, it applies in both cases. “*Sarvādīni* . . .”

The scope for this [rule] is in cases where *jas* is not applied, and there is an option regarding [the forms] beginning with *dvau*; for instance, since [the word] does not belong to the *sarvādi* group in the dual—as in *dvayau*—here both [rules] would apply in the case of *ubhaye*. The author of the *Dhyāna-graha* stated: "Because of the prior prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) when [the subsequent rule] has not yet been reached, or because of its being *antaraṅga* (internal). Why is it considered *antaraṅga*? Because it relies solely upon the base form (*prakṛti*). However, the *vibhāṣā* (option) is *bahiraṅga* (external), as it relies upon both the base and the suffix (*ubhayaja*).

But this [author], not relying on either of these two [interpretations] and before reaching the *vibhāṣā* (the option), describes it thus: "In the sense of 'not reached' (*aprāpte*), *ayac* is a different suffix. That which is accepted as the substitute *ayac* will be understood as a different suffix from the word *ubhaya*. In that case, the recitation is made as follows: "After *ubha*, when meaning a part, *ayac*"; then "after a numeral, *tayap*"; and "after *dvi* and *tri*, *ayac* is substituted for *tayap*. Alternatively: "After a numeral, in the sense of a part, *tayap*"; "after *ubha*, *ayac*"; and "optionally after *dvi* and *tri*."

[The suffix] *mātra* [would] also apply here in the case of *tailamātra*. But is this not simply ending in the vowel *ā*? This is not a fault. It is not said that [the suffix] applies from the word *tailamātra*; rather, it is intended that there should be the form *tailamātrī*. Regarding the phrase "even of a similar one that is not situated [as a suffix]," how can it be understood that this [suffix] is not situated? It is said: even when the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is absent, the meaning itself is perceived as the cause for recognition.

And thus, in this context, it will be understood by its very meaning that "that which functions with respect to measurement (pramāṇa) is what is 'situated' (saṃniviṣṭa). However, for that which functions with respect to dimension (parimāṇa)—such as "this is its measure" or "this is its dimension"—there is no such situating. This is because the term "situating" applies to what follows a nominal stem when it denotes measurement (pramāṇa), as stated [in the rule]: "Because we see the suffix *sic* and others in the *luṅ* tense."

[51.3] Regarding the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) of the root *ūrṇu*: if this [rule], whose operation is incomplete, were not prescriptive of anything and were instead employed as a mark for an attached *svarita* accent—just as in the rule “*samarthānāṃ prathamād vā*” (P. 2.1.57)—then, in the context of the rule “*asaṃyogāl liṭ kit*” (P. 1.2.5), having acquired its own operation, it would function as a separate sentence (*nānāvākyatva*). Thus: “The *liṭ* affix becomes *kit* after a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant”; and “After the root *ūrṇu*, it is optionally so. And the fact that they constitute separate sentences is inferred precisely from the mention of the term “non-conjunct” (*asaṃyoga*).

For it is only when there is no final consonant cluster (*asaṃyogānta*) that the root *ūrṇu* [takes the augment]; however, in this case, the statement is for the purpose of depending upon the augment *iṭ*. Now, if this were an injunctive rule (*vidhāyaka*), then since it would not apply in the domain of the optative (*liṅ*), these two [rules] would have scope; thus, in the event of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), if it were a "conflict with the subsequent" (*paravipratiṣedha*), then this [augment] would not apply here. If it were a "conflict with the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), then it would apply in both cases. How so? Here, the preceding is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) and the subsequent is a compulsory (*nitya*) rule; whereas in the former case, the subsequent is an optional rule and the preceding is a compulsory rule.

[This applies] when [the condition] has not been reached; for *kittva* is one thing and *ṅittva* is another. *Ṅittva* is optional, whereas *kittva* is a permanent rule (*nityavidhi*). This difference arises from the distinction in their verbal roots (*śrutibheda*), such that the grammatical operations of *saṃprasāraṇa* and *asaṃprasāraṇa*, and so forth, are distinct for these two.

"If there is one [rule], then it concerns both *ṅit* and *kit*. How can there be oneness? He thinks as follows: This is not an extension (*atideśa*) of the [technical] designation itself; rather, it is an extension of the *kārya* (grammatical operation). That which proceeds by virtue of the extension is the *kārya*. And that [operation] is common to both the *ṅit*-ness and the *kit*-ness of the root *ūrṇoti*. The operation here is the prohibition of *guṇa*. But is this prohibition permanent (*nitya*) or optional (*vibhāṣā*)? To address this, he says: "If there is one. Even if they are distinct, such a doubt still arises."

But how does this rule, "vibhāṣorṇoḥ" (A 6.4.51), apply here in reference to "sārvadhātukam apit" (A 1.2.4)? Since the augment *iṭ* is not *apit*, its application is inferred to occur through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). In that case, if the *sārvadhātuka* suffix were *ṅit*, then since the rule "vibhāṣā ūrṇoteḥ" (A 1.2.3) would apply here to the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, [the present rule would be redundant]. Alternatively, if it is not specifically accentuated, then there is scope for "sārvadhātukam apit" in cases such as *cinutaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*, [the forms] *prorṇavitā* and *prorṇuvitā* are obtained; here both [alternatives] would apply—namely, *praurṇuvīti*. Therefore, he says: "When [the rule] has not yet applied. This is a case of *paravipratiṣedha* (a conflict where the subsequent rule prevails).

[51.4] Regarding the option (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of *upayamana*: "But surely, since there is an absolute difference between *gandhana* and *upayamana*, there should be no doubt [regarding their application]. It is thought thus: *upayamana*, which is a subordinate part of *gandhana*, is designated as *gandhana*. Just as when lightning flashes from the womb [of a cloud], one says "it flashes from the cloud" (*balāhaka*). In this case, because of the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the option applies where [the rule] would otherwise not have applied. Alternatively, it is based on *upayamana*, and it is not based on *gandhana*. Why? Because of the latter's lack of predominance (*aprādhānya*). Thus, this is an option where [the rule] would otherwise not have applied.

[51.5] Regarding the rule *anupasargād vā*: either because of the introduction of the rule *upaparābhyām* [which restricts the optionality], the terms *vṛtti* and so forth are not connected at all; or else, *vṛtti* and so forth are simply impossible when preceded by *upa* and *parā*. As for the rule *āṅaḥ udgamane* (A 1.3.40), a different meaning altogether—one that contradicts *vṛtti* and the rest—is adopted. Likewise for *veḥ pādaviharaṇe* (41). And according to *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām* (42), these two [prefixes] share the same meaning in the sense of "beginning" (*prārambha*), but not in the case of *vṛtti* and so forth.

[51.6] There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding trees, animal figures, and so forth. Those living beings here, such as deer and the like, are not governed by the rule *ajātir aprāṇinām* (A 2.4.6). However, trees and the like are indeed insentient (*aprāṇin*). In that context, this option applies to those animal figures made of leather and so on; it does not apply to actual living beings. This is an option where [the previous rule] would otherwise have applied. The rule *ajātir aprāṇinām* is suspended, and there is also a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

Even without the previous counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where there was no prior application; since the understanding applies to the primary (*mukhya*) rather than the secondary (*gauṇa*), the optionality applies to actual animals and not to clay-cows and the like.

[51.7] Regarding *uṣavid*... when *ām* would have been obtained by the rule *pratyayāntāt*, [it is argued that] in the rule *ijādeḥ*, the phrase *pratyayāntāt* is not connected; for since this rule (*vidhi*) is also compulsory (*nitya*), the statement [of the alternative] would result in being purposeless. Now, how do *uṣādi* and the others, which end in suffixes, receive the designation *uṣādi*, given that the option (*vibhāṣā*) is prescribed after taking up those *uṣādi* items whose extent is limited to the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone? It is said in reply:

Regarding the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), there are four possible interpretations: understanding it as referring to a part [of the whole], extension by analogy (*atideśa*), the relationship between a technical name and its bearer (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*), or its outright rejection (*pratyākhyāna*).

First, regarding the cognition of a single part (*ekadeśavijñāna*): for example, by the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in the rule *samāsānta*, the suffixes such as *ḍac* are understood to be parts of a compound because they are included under the term "compound. Similarly, here too, when it is understood that "those which have *san* and so forth as their end" means "those whose beginning is not *an*," and "those whose parts are these" means "these are *sanādyanta*," then the root *uṣ* is understood as a part of *san* by the mention of the root *uṣ*. But if this is postulated, does this not mean that this is not a rule for technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*), and thus there is an application of the principle of "that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) to *san*?

And this being the case, even a form ending in *san* might be understood as a part of something else. This is not a fault. A form ending in *san* may be either a part of that which has the same meaning, or of that which has a different meaning. In that regard, because a form with the same meaning has already been stated, there is no usage such as *pac* or *pipakṣati*. Because a form with a different meaning is contradictory, and since there is no connection [to the original root], there is an absence of usage such as *pipakṣati*. Alternatively, we shall rely on the suffix *san* itself as the primary factor; and there is no rule for "that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*) based on the primary element.

While the phrase "because of the cognition [of the term] in certain instances" is being carried over, since the term *uṣi* is included by means of the mention of *uṣigrahaṇa*, the rule would apply as an option (*vibhāṣā*) when that is already established; this present rule is therefore an option. Alternatively, if [the previous rule] has ceased, then even the simple *uṣi*—even when followed by *sanat*—is [included]. In that case, there is a doubt: is this a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) when [the previous rule] is not otherwise applicable, or is it a subsequent counter-exception (*paravipratiṣedha*) when both [rules] are applicable?

Or rather, this is an extension (*atideśa*) similar to that: just as in the rule "The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vat*, and *u* are numerals" (A 1.1.23), when the word *saṃkhyā* is understood to have meanings such as "one" and so forth, an extension is recognized in the sense that "it behaves like a numeral."

Thus, in this treatise, the term *dhātu* (verbal root) is well-known as referring to the roots beginning with *bhū*; and those [elements] which are the grammatical operations (*kārya*), being included here as a part of the meaning of the word, are stated as "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots," meaning that those ending in *san* and so forth become like verbal roots and thereby obtain the grammatical operations pertaining to verbal roots.

This, however, must be examined: even though there is such an extension (*atideśa*), is it only the general operation extended [to the *san*-affixes] beginning with *uṣ* that is to be obtained—namely, the production of the suffix and the acute accent on the final syllable—or is it also whatever operation applies specifically to *uṣ* and the others? This refers to the general operation under discussion. Why is this so? Because particulars deviate from the general; just as when one says "in this case, like a Brāhmaṇa," what is extended is not necessarily what applies to Māṭhara.

And having established this, it was said: "In the extension of a general rule, there is no extension of specific details. This is true; so it is. But here, when the general is being extended, the extension itself would be purposeless, because this meaning remains the same even through the relationship between a name and the named. Therefore, one should understand it thus: "That which occurs on account of the word's own nature. This employment of a general term is for the sake of brevity; however, this [general rule] is restricted to each specific case and is presented in the form of "bhū" and so forth.

Just as in the case of *bhavati* and *edhati*, so too in the case of *bhavati* [derived from] the root *uṣ* followed by the suffix *san*; because there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the status of *uṣ* to that which ends in *san*, the application of the grammatical operation is optional. However, this is the defect here: the grammatical operation that applies to all roots ending in *san* and the like would [erroneously] apply [to the base as well]. How is it when there is a relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*)? If it is conceived in this way—that the term "roots" (*dhātavaḥ*) refers to the category beginning with *bhū*, and those roots beginning with *bhū* are the names for those ending in *san* and the like—[then the rule holds].

If this were the case, then the rules "after a verbal root denoting an action... (A 3.1.7) and "after a monosyllabic verbal root... (A 3.1.22) would also result in over-extension. Now, if you think that in those cases *bhū* and so forth are understood [as the referents], then here too [in the definition of a root] they are understood: "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots. Therefore, this designation of *dhātu* for both *bhū* and so forth and for those ending in *san* and so forth has the same time [of application] and takes the word-form itself as its meaning.

However, where a specific [suffix] is uttered, that would be a technical name (*saṃjñā*), as for example, by the rule *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* (A 3.1.120), it would be the name for *cikīrṣati*. But this has been rejected: since the suffixes *san* and so on are prescribed in the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the technical name is established there through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). [Objection: Since [the suffixes] do not apply [to the base], those ending in suffixes are different roots.

This has been explained in this manner: that for *san* and the others, there is not a "partial designation" (*naikadeśasaṃvijñāna*), nor is there an extension (*atideśa*) in that way; rather, there is a relationship between the name and the named, or else it is a rejection (*pratyākhyāna*). Consequently, because of the addition [of the term *uṣ-*] and because it is not included by the mention of *uṣ-ādi*, doubt is not justified. Others describe the doubt in this way: that *uṣiḥ* is both a form ending in *kvip* and a form ending in *kvip* used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), and that its sound is heard [in the rule]. They also justify this by saying, "those ending in suffixes are different verbal roots. However, there is no *kvip* in the sense of habitual action derived from this [root *uṣ*].

[51.8] Regarding the option (*vibhāṣā*) for *dīpa* and so forth: it is inferred from here that the rule *dīpajana...* (A 3.1.61) is being cited by its accentuation. It is inferred by means of the whole collection—that the suffix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and that for *dīpa* and so forth there is an option. This is not, however, by way of a relationship between part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgin*). Why is this? Because of their separate recitation. For otherwise, one would have recited it simply as: *bhāvakarmaṇor dīpādibhyo vibhāṣā*.

Now, this is an injunction (*vidhāyaka*); and since the term *kartari* has been excluded, this option (*vibhāṣā*) applies when [the suffix] is not otherwise obtained due to the subsequent prohibition (*paravipratiṣedha*), and when it is obtained in both cases due to the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

[The word] *aprāpte* [is used]; for the term *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is understood to carry over. The intention is that this [sūtra] is prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*). Even so, there remains a doubt as to whether [the rule applies] to a legitimate agent (*nyāyye kartari*) or to a reflexive agent (*karmakartari*). If the term *kartari* is also marked with an accent (*svaryate*), then in that case, lamps and the like, being included under the category of agents, receive the designation of "action" (*kriyāśabda*) here through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Since the suffix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and since the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies to the agent and the object after roots such as *dīp*, this is the option (*vibhāṣā*) that is established.

Now, if it is not specifically restricted to the agent (*kartṛ*), then since "the agent of the object-become-agent (*karmakartṛ*) becomes an agent," when both [rules] apply to the object-become-agent of lamps and the like, a doubt arises due to the conflict between the preceding and succeeding rules: "The agent of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) becomes like the object (*karmavat*). Even though *budh* is transitive, I shall state a single, uniform resolution; thus it was stated without distinction: "And lamps and the like are intransitive (*akarmaka*)," meaning that they become transitive when accompanied by prepositions (*sopasarga*).

For when accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*), it acquires the sense of another meaning, as in *bhavati* (he becomes) or *anubhavati* (he experiences). Regarding "those whose state resides in the object" (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and "those whose action resides in the object" (*karmasthakriyā*): the essence of the meaning is divided into two types—motion and non-motion—and these are taken separately as "state" (*bhāva*) and "action" (*kriyā*). But how is this obtained? It is stated there [in the Mahābhāṣya] as follows: "An action residing in the object is expressed by the word 'object' (*karman*). For example, the root *pac-* ("to cook") has an action residing in the object; for indeed, a distinction produced by the action is perceived in the object.

But this contradicts the rule *acaḥ kartṛyaki* (A 6.1.15). For it is established there [in that rule] with the example *jāyate svayam eva*. In this case, the substitution of *āt* occurs for the root *jan-* even at the stage of its original enunciation (*upadeśe*). Consequently, at the stage of enunciation, this [root] ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). And if this [action] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), how could there be the suffix *yak* after the agent? Thus [the objection].

In the *Vibhāṣā*, regarding the rule for words beginning with *agra* and *pūrva*: the term “in the sense of repetition” (*ābhīkṣṇye*) is no longer operative, and there is also a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). In that context, however, this was stated: “In the case of *agra* and so forth, there is a prohibition of compounding because the rule would otherwise apply without restriction. For when the rule is applied without restriction, *agra* and the others serve as the cause for the production of the suffix. But if this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where the rule already applies, then since *agra* and the others are the cause for the cessation [of the suffix], they lack the status of being a subordinate word (*upapada*).

But if this *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) were applicable, then—given that [the rule] "the cause of cessation (*nivṛtti*) is from *nimitta* onwards"—there would be an absence of the status of being an *upapada*. And a solution has already been stated: namely, that only that which is mentioned together with [the suffix] as an *upapada* is compounded.

Regarding the *vibhāṣā* for *tṛn* and others: in the rules “*tṛn-anna-tīkṣṇa-śuciṣu*” (A 6.2.161), “*ākrośe ca*,” and “*saṃjñāyām*”—if the term “*ackau*” has ceased to apply, then there must be doubt [as to whether the option applies]. But if “*ackau*” continues to apply in the rule “*ākrośe*,” then this is undoubtedly an *aprāpta-vibhāṣā* (an optional rule applied where the formation was not otherwise established).

[51.11] The phrase “in a technical name (*saṃjñā*)” is understood from [Pāṇini 6.3.59] *ekahalādau*. It should not be inferred for [the rule] *aiṣaṃ vāsa...* (58), because of the force of its specific formulation. But is there any possible technical name [applicable] to “when a word beginning with a single consonant is to be completed”? He says: yes, namely *upadāna*. [51.12] Regarding the phrase “in connection with *ca* and so forth”: in connection with what? With *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. For example: *grāmas tava ca svam mama ca svam* (“the village is yours and mine”). However, when there is a connection with the word *sva*, then the substitutions do indeed occur: *grāmaś ca te svam nagaraṃ ca me svam* (“the village is your own and the city is my own”).

Regarding the rule *yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.2.20), which would otherwise apply obligatorily, the phrase *yaṅi* is understood to carry over into the rule *aci vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.2.21). Thus, it means "in the case of *yaṅ*, before a vowel (*aci*). Consequently, this [doubling] should occur only where there is a suffix *yaṅ* following a stem that does not end in a vowel. And where does this occur? It occurs in forms such as *nijegila* when *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*). Others explain it differently: once a portion has been elided within the *yaṅ*, the doubling occurs before that vowel which constitutes one part of the *yaṅ*.

However, for those who explain it as in *nijegilyate*, since the status of being "like the end" or "like the beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) cannot apply due to its dependence on both sides, the condition of being followed by a vowel (*acparatva*) after the *yaṅ* is difficult to establish.

And when [the condition] is met: there is neither a prior prohibition nor a subsequent prohibition; rather, there is an extension (*anuvṛtti*) into these cases. Regarding "optionally in the case of confused speech" (*vibhāṣā vipralāpe*): even for those with indistinct voices, there is confused speech, as in "the birds are quarreling," because they indicate what is desired or undesired. It also occurs for those with distinct voices, as in "the astrologers are disputing. When [the condition] is met, the term "those with distinct voices" (*vyaktavācām*) continues to apply; therefore, it should be "the birds are quarreling" (*vipravadanti śakunayaḥ*).

[51.16] When a meaning is understood through a *vibhāṣā* (optionality) rule accompanied by an *upapada* (governing word), proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is indicated by both the *upapada* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), as in the example *tvaṃ pacasi* ("you cook for yourself"). Having established this, when there is doubt, the *upapada* is the indicator. This is an optionality (*vibhāṣā*) that does not apply otherwise (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*). It applies in both cases. [The rule] is set aside, and there is a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

[51.17] *hṛ-kroḥ anyatarasyām*: For the root *hṛ*, the cause is its meaning of "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*); for the root *kṛ*, it is its meaning of "motion" (*gati*), which results in its being intransitive (*akarmaka*).
This concludes the sixth lesson (*āhnika*) of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first book (*prathama-adhyāya*).
In the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā, the seventh lesson:
*ig yaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (1.1.45).

[1] Is this designation (*saṃjñā*) for a sentence (*vākya*), or rather for a phoneme (*varṇa*)? Because the grounds for both are possible, because they cannot exist simultaneously, because faults are seen in both cases, and because signs (*liṅga*) for both are observed in the treatise (*śāstra*), the question is asked. But has it not been stated that a sentence is a verb (*ākhyāta*) together with its qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*)? A verbal form (*ākhyātapada*) is not heard [in the examples]. If it is thus postulated that "the verb *as* [is understood] when followed by *bhavantī*..."

Even so, a contradiction arises: in the rules concerning *saṃprasāraṇa*, the statement “*saṃprasāraṇa* occurs” is supplemented by the rule “*ig* replaces *yaṇ*. If it exists, then it does not occur; if it occurs, then it does not exist. It is replied:
because the sūtra requires supplementation (*sopaskāratvāt*), we shall justify the word “occurs” as a necessary completion of the sentence—namely, “*ig* replaces *yaṇ* occurs.”

Even so, because this sentence lacks the status of being a single word (*padatva*), its status as a designatum (*saṃjñitva*) is untenable; for a designatum must end either in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) or the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), and a sentence does not end in either the nominative or the genitive. It is replied: the meaning of the sentence is designated by the term "sentence" (*vākya*), just as the sense of possession is expressed by the suffix *matup*, according to the rule: "The suffix *cha* is used after words denoting hymns or *sāmans* when the sense of possession (*matau*) is intended" (A 5.2.59).

But is it not the case that this object (*artha*) is also non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), and thus why is it characterized by the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) of the word "this" (*iti*)? It is said in reply: At the time of establishing the relationship between a name and its referent, the object is reflected upon; it is subsumed under a universal form by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); it becomes fit for designation as "this is that"; and having experienced the state of being named, it presents itself in the various rules (*pradeśa*) through its own operation precisely as something non-substantial.

Regarding the meaning of the rule "igyaṇaḥ bhavati," once that meaning has been designated by the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*, it presents itself in the specific rules (*pradeśa*) as: "igyaṇaḥ bhavati" [the *ig* becomes the *yaṇ*], "igyaṇaḥ jāyate" [the *ig* is born as the *yaṇ*], or "igyaṇaḥ niṣpadyate" [the *ig* is produced as the *yaṇ*].

[3] Or rather, does it refer to the phoneme? Is this the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) that "the *ik* which occurs in place of a *yaṇ* is called *saṃprasāraṇa*"? Now, if it is a designation of a phoneme, it remains undecided whether this designation applies to that *ik* which stands in place of a *yaṇ*, or to the *yaṇ* itself. For in the word *saṃprasāraṇa*, if it denotes its own form as the object of the term, it ought to be the *yaṇ* that serves as the designated (*saṃjñin*); whereas in the case of the mention of the designata (*saṃjñin*) as *manaṇarin*, it ought to be the *ik*. It is replied:

The genitive case here in *yaṇaḥ* is not used because [the substitution] has already been effected by the *saṃprasāraṇa*; what then? It refers to *ik*. Why is this so? Because otherwise there would be a contradiction. For if it were understood in that way—that the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* applies to *yaṇ*—then the mention of *ig* would be redundant.

[4] If the designation *saṃjñā* were applied to the sentence (*vākya*), then the grammatical operation (*vidhi*) concerning the phoneme (*varṇa*)—namely, its becoming prior (*pūrvatva*) and its lengthening (*dīrghatva*)—would not be established. Therefore, the designation must be prescribed for the phoneme. For instance, if the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* were applied to the sentence, it would be a designation for that which arises from the *ik* vowels; however, arising is a matter of meaning (*artha*), and there can be no designation of "prior" or "subsequent" with respect to a meaning, nor can a meaning possess the status of a *sthānin* (original locus).

But for what reason is this pair mentioned—the impossibility of both the designation (*nirdeśa*) and the action (*kārya*)? This is demonstrated as follows: even if a designation is made by means of an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), such as "By whom am I coming?", it would still be a mere designation; however, because the action is impossible within the sentence, it does not proceed at all.

[5] If the production [of the vowel *ī*] were due to the notion of color (*varṇasaṃjñā*), then by the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (A 6.1.13), that very *ik* would first be difficult to obtain. Even if something is not actually found in the world, it is said to be "difficult to obtain. Furthermore, even if it could somehow be obtained, it is stated [only] through a conceptual construction in the commentary: "By what [rule] would this [substitution] take the place of the *yaṇ*?"

They explain it as follows: Alternatively, since that very [condition] is difficult to obtain, what is stated here is merely the non-application of another rule, just as the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) was mentioned regarding the technical term *vṛddhi*. Or again, even if it were somehow possible to obtain it, this is said by relying on the principle: "But it is established because words are eternal" (*siddhaṃ tu nityaśabdatvāt*, A 1.1.1, Vārttika 9). As it has been stated: "The phonemes *a*, *e*, and *o* remain eternally present."

By what means would that *ik* be established in place of the *yaṇ*? It is established by this very [rule]. He demonstrates this: there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) regarding the form of the *ik*. What then? [The fault lies] in the comprehension of the substituend (*sthānin*). For the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* applies to that which is an *ik* in place of a *yaṇ*, and once the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* exists, there is the status of being in place of a *yaṇ*. This conceptualization of the modification and the modified is derived from the technical treatise (*śāstra*), not from common worldly usage; thus it is said that "this becomes a case of mutual dependence."

[6] However, the specific indication by means of case endings serves as an indicator. In grammar, there is an indication by means of the locative case, as in *saṃprasāraṇasya* (A 6.3.139) and *saṃprasāraṇāt* (A 6.1.108). And this [use of the genitive] is not possible when the name-bearer (*saṃjñin*) is the meaning of a sentence. Furthermore, since the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (A 6.1.13) is not possible when applied to a phoneme (*varṇa*), it is inferred that this sūtra recurs; however, it was uttered only once due to parsimony, or else these two rules are [to be understood] through the method of *tantra*.

Just as a single word, when uttered with different referents, is observed to have two forms, so too is a single [phoneme] manifold; thus the Teacher instructed his disciples in both ways—some regarding the sentence, and some regarding the phoneme.

Alternatively, let it be that the sentence itself conveys [the meaning] without repetition (*āvṛtti*) or ellipsis (*tantra*). For example: "A crow is born from a crow. To this, an objection is raised: a crow becomes a crow precisely through its connection with its own species. And having established this, it is said: "By the very same cause that one is a crow, another is also [a crow]. This is indeed so. However, this [example] demonstrates that there are in the world those who bear the designation of "father" among fathers, such as Babhru, Maṇḍu, and Lamaka.

"In the cases of Bābhravya, Māṇḍavya, and Lāmakāyana, those [names] are superimposed [upon the individuals]. Furthermore, even when the secondary characteristics (*upavyañjana*) that mark the nature of a crow are absent, one still says "crow" in that state as well. In this regard, just as there is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) for a genus (*jāti*) such as being perfumed, so too is this birth (*janman*) presented [as a manifestor]. Even a word functions through its connection in the form "this is that" and through the accomplishment of an action.

In the case of "this woman belongs to the leader" (*praṣṭha*), the word *praṣṭha* functions as a feminine term based on a prior distinction [of possession] followed by the connection "this is that. Alternatively, there is an attachment to the position of the leader in the female; when the position is occupied, the word *praṣṭha* applies to the female just as it does to a man, being entirely independent [of gender]. Likewise here, the distinction is "born from a crow," or the connection "this is that" serves as the cause. Alternatively, an association with the state of being inhabited by a crow is established.

In this context, it is established that "birth" (*janman*) is that which manifests the meaning of the genus (*jāti*); for instance, because he was born from a crow, he is called "this crow. Likewise, there is a designation of the action and its possessor as non-different, such as in the expression "born from *saṃprasāraṇa*.

Alternatively, the phoneme associated with the action comes to possess that [action], while the effect (the phoneme) comes to possess the status of a substance; just as in the relationship between a name and the named, the sentence-meaning, having been reflected upon, experiences the state of being the named, yet in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), it remains purely non-substantial.

[8] Alternatively, one observes people employing parts of sentences within full sentences. For instance, in the word *praviśa* ("enter"), there is an action (*kriyā*), and since an action does not proceed without a substratum, it takes up a suitable means of accomplishment; thus, it functions as the object (*karman*). The meaning expressed by the two words in the phrase *praviśa gṛham* ("enter the house") is what is expressed by the word *praviśa*. Regarding that means of accomplishment, some understand it as being explicitly denoted (*abhidheya*), while others understand it as being merely implied (*gamyamāna*).

Because the entry into the *piṇḍī* is impossible, a suitable means (*sādhana*) is either stated or understood. Similarly, the word *piṇḍīm* also expresses the meaning "one should eat the *piṇḍī*. (Regarding the phrase "of the means"? the term *sādhana* implies a suitable action, since there can be no means without an action. Just as in the case of a jar of curds and so forth, actions such as "filling" are supplied, so too the word "from *saṃprasāraṇa*" supplies a suitable action.

And since "nirvṛtti" (result) is appropriate, this [word] expresses the meaning "resulting from a *saṃprasāraṇa*"; or else, the word "from *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*saṃprasāraṇāt*) is used, or rather, the meaning is understood. Why? Because in the context of the sentence-meaning, which is the technical term (*saṃjñin*), the properties of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) and "long" (*dīrghatva*) are impossible [if applied directly to the *saṃjñin*].

[9] And [one uses] parts of words for the words themselves. Now, it might be argued that names based on their own essential forms (*svarūpa*) are incapable of conveying meaning when joined with other forms; therefore, there is no elision of what has been uttered. Furthermore, when a name is bestowed right then by the parents, some maintain this view: "When a part is uttered, the whole is inferred, and from that, the comprehension of the meaning arises. Others think: "The parts also exist within the whole—such as *deva* and *datta*."

And those two [the *drākṣā* and *mṛdvīkā*] are connected with the name as a whole is connected with its designation; thus others think. These other names are produced as secondary consequences (*anuniṣpādīni*). For Pāṇini, who undertakes the elision (*lopa*), the intention is that these forms are correct only as such secondary consequences resulting from the elision of those [original names], but not that the *drākṣā* itself is inherently of such a form. And just as the names are produced as secondary consequences, so too, this being the case, the meanings are not produced as secondary consequences.

In the sentence-meaning, when the term *ika*—which is produced in place of *yaṇ* by the rule "in place of *yaṇ*, [there is] *ik*"—is established as the designatum (*saṃjñin*), it does not follow as a corollary that the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is also established. However, the understanding of *saṃprasāraṇa* arises from the mention of *saṃprasāraṇa* itself, because it is produced from *saṃprasāraṇa*. Alternatively, he says again: "with regard to *āyām*. Here he demonstrates this: just as in the expression "Let a hundred Brahmins be fed," this is a specific instance of the act of eating, and the number is understood only if those who are numbered (the hundred) are the ones being fed; likewise, in expressions such as "Let the tiger be fed" or "Let the elephant be fed," these are indeed specific instances of the act of eating.

Thus, whether it be the lengthening of a *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel or the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), such an operation—either the production of length or the production of a preceding form—is performed upon the phoneme which is the fruit of that action.

Alternatively, let it be that the designation (*saṃjñā*) is yet to be produced (*bhāvinī*). Is this "state of being yet to be produced" (*bhāvitvam*) in relation to the connection between the designation and the designated (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*), or rather in relation to the specific rules (*pradeśeṣu*)? If it were in relation to the connection between the designation and the designated, then for those things already existing, the connection between the designation and the designated would have to be something yet to be produced. If, on the other hand, it were in relation to the specific rules, then since this very [connection] has already been established in the rule for long vowels (*dīrgha-vidhi*) and in the preceding rule, from where could the state of being yet to be produced be conceived? It is said in reply:

Just as the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) was stated regarding the technical name *vṛddhi*—namely, "because the name [vṛddhi] does not exist for that which already possesses the quality of vṛddhi, etc. (A 1.1.1, Vārttika 8)—if, at the time of naming, the named entities (*saṃjñin*) were expected to be either past or future; whereas in cases such as "vṛddhi replaces *mṛj*" (A 7.2.114), where the forms such as *ā* and so on are the basis for that name, there is indeed mutual dependence. Likewise here, at the time of naming, the name *igyaṇaḥ* functions with respect to the named entities (*saṃjñin*) even though they are not present, just as it would function when they are past.

But here, in the rule "There is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *ṣyaṅ*" (A 6.1.13), how can the term *saṃprasāraṇa* apply? For it is not possible for those *ik*-sounds that have already been produced to be made the substitutes here, because they have already been exhausted; nor can it apply to their general forms (*ākṛti*), because there is no distinction between them. Indeed, is there any distinction between the *ik* in words such as *indra* and the *ik* that occurs in place of *yan*? Since there is none, what do we understand [the term to refer to]?

In the relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), that which is yet to be [designated] is understood as already established. In this context, the rule "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *ṣyaṅ*" means this: apply such a substitute for *ṣyaṅ* as acquires the technical designation "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*). This is the method for applying a substitute that is fit for that designation.

Just as in the expression "weave a cloth for this thread," when the verb *vayati* (to weave) is used in reference to a continuous process (*saṃtāna*), the word *śāṭaka* (cloth)—though no cloth yet exists—is understood as having been taken up as a reality by establishing in the mind a future relationship between the designation and the designated object. For even when an object does not exist, the employment of a specific term is intended for the sake of conveying a specific meaning; thus one understands: "Begin such a continuous process that those who shall receive this name will [recognize it]."

[12] Regarding the phrase "the occurrence of *ijādi* and *yajādi*": the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) is merely a transformation of the intellect (*buddhi-vipariṇāma-mātra*), as in the expression "mango trees to the east of the village. For in common usage, there is the occurrence of *ijādi* and *yajādi*, such as in the words *iṣṭam* ("sacrificed") and *yaṣṭavyam* ("should be sacrificed"). However, according to the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the cognition of *ijādi* in the case of *yaja*, *ḍuvapa*, and *vaha* is set aside; rather, by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), it is produced in a specific domain, being correct when followed by a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix.

"Whatever usage is established as twofold in the world, that alone is considered correct; this much is what is explained by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding this, there is the phrase "of that which is intended as correct. They explain it thus: [the meaning is] "of that which is intended as correct among the correct forms," meaning that the form beginning with *ij-* is recognized by the treatise in the presence of both *kit* and *ṅit* suffixes. However, under this view, the form *aduhitarām* remains unexcluded. Likewise, because of the specific mention of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), even when there are two rules, it remains unexcluded.
The augment marked with Ṭ (ṭit) is placed at the beginning [of the element], and the augment marked with K (kit) is placed at the end. Pāṇini 1.1.46.

[1] This is a concise statement (*samāsanirdeśa*). In that regard, it is not understood what is established by this; for in a concise statement, the correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyakatva*) is not known. To such an extent that even in a non-concise expression, as in "the goat, the wealth, and the sheep of Devadatta and Yajñadatta," it is not known whose goat and whose sheep they are.

[2] It is said: He demonstrates this by way of the following—namely, that the correspondence according to order does not exist in the world or in other treatises, but only in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*); and thus the sequence is regulated.

Those learned in the sacred scriptures have declared that the sequence of duties is determined, respectively, by direct scriptural statement, by the purpose, by the order of recitation, by the commencement, by the position, and by the primary sense.

They say that sequence is derived from scripture (*śruti*), as in: "One cuts [the portion] first from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.3.10.4; *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa* 3.8.3.16, 17). Here, the word *atha* is heard as an indicator of immediate succession; thus, the engagement in sequence occurs according to the principle: "Having done this, this must be done. As for sequence by meaning (*arthakrama*)—even when it is said, "Feed Devadatta; bathe, anoint, rub with unguents, and massage him," the sequence is determined by the sense: namely, massage, rubbing with unguents, bathing, anointing, and feeding.

In the case of Vedic sentences which possess a fixed sequence, when multiple purposes are to be served, the order of recitation establishes the relationship between the subject (uddeśin) and the predicate (anudeśin) through their simultaneous requirement [of application], as for example in the Smṛti rule: "Wiping, burning, scraping, and washing [are prescribed] for metallic, earthen, wooden, and woven objects," respectively.

Others think as follows: when multiple [words] are employed for a single referent—as in "Feed Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra"—they understand the act of eating according to the very sequence [in which they were mentioned]. In that case, even though the related object is presented as distinct, comprehension can be achieved according to each [word's own function] by means of this manner: "this belongs to him," "this belongs to him," just as in the cases of *ghna* and *jighna*, or *dhma* and *dhama*.

However, in the case of a designation by name (*saṃjñā*) through a compound (*samāsa*), since the names themselves lack sequence, the named objects (*saṃjñin*) would be understood simultaneously and thus become connected with all the subsequent terms (*anudeśin*). Likewise, even in a compound designation, a single undivided meaning consisting of a collection is expressed by a *dvandva* compound; this is what was stated by the author of the Vārttika: "Because of the designation by name through a compound, there is the undesirable consequence of [the subsequent term] applying to all."

In that context, so that they might proceed according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), *tiP* becomes *ṇal*, and *tas* becomes *atus*; therefore, this compound designation cannot be construed as a possibility. This is what he explains by saying, "this is a compound designation.

Even if this is an example seen in the world, even if there is such a usage in the world—nevertheless, regarding both the example and the observation, it is said that "human effort" (*puruṣārambha*) is something unprecedented and not established in the world, being something to be accomplished through exertion.

[4] "Which two, then, are those that possess the markers *ṭ* and *k*? This is what he asks: for whom are these two, characterized by *ṭ* and *k*, prescribed? What kind of element do they become—is it the beginning (*ādi*) or the end (*anta*)? He says: "They are augments" (*āgamau*). He explains this as follows: when an augment is prescribed subsequently while the verbal root remains established in its form before the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, it attains the status of being a constituent part (*avayava*) without displacing any other existing constituent part.

"But it is logical that [this applies] to eternal things. He says this to show that this is not the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of our treatise. Now, if by some manner of speaking this [word] must indeed exist by its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), what does it matter to us whether it exists? Or, if it is logical that [the word] exists in these words—just as you accept that [the word] "exists" (*asti*) occurs even for an eternal sound after having set aside [the notion of] "becoming" (*bhavati*)—then you should likewise accept the traditional scripture (*āgama*). Thus, it must be understood here through other words.
It is not that existence (*bhavati*) is produced by erasing [the letter]; what then? The meaning is: "in the case of the verb *as*. [Objection:

"In that case, these will be substitutes (*ādeśa*). [Response: This is not a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). This is a relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*): "The letters *ṭ* and *k*, occurring at the beginning and end [of a marker], shall be names. It is a name for the meaning of the beginning and the meaning of the end, because only the meanings (the objects denoted) are taken up. Or rather, the word "iti" is supplied [to the rule]. If this were so, the designation *it* would not apply to the letters *ṭ* and *k*; for in that case, the letters *ṭ* and *k* would no longer be the beginning and the end.

It has been asserted that [the two suffixes] are designated by the term *it*. In this regard, because they occupy the same position as those termed *it*, they are designated by the property of *it*; and because of their commonality of cessation (*nivṛtti-sāmānya*), just as that which is termed *it* ceases, so too do these two. Therefore, by the letter *i* in the word *iṭ*, the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi-artha*) is established; thus, what is meant is that "there is *iṭ*. And since every substitute (*ādeśa*) beginning with the vowel *i* would otherwise be applicable, by virtue of being the closest internal correspondence (*antaratama*) in place, the form *itavya* occurs for *tavya*.

But here, how is it that [the rule] *aḍudāttaḥ* (A 6.4.71) applies? He thinks as follows: since *aṭ* is a bahuvrīhi compound, it means "an affix beginning with the vowel *a*. Since the member (*aṅga*) is indicated here, the heard udātta accent is connected to that member. And this being the case, the member would result in having an indefinite udātta accent. Therefore, this is a three-membered bahuvrīhi; thus, in the sentence itself, the vowel *a* becomes the qualifier of the udātta: "that whose beginning is the udātta vowel *a*."

Therefore, even in the case of a *vṛtti*, that [meaning] can be understood through inference, as in the example "the owner of brindled cows" (*citragu*). In that case, however, where there is no recurrence [of the word], the intention is this: the word is not actually uttered there; rather, it is inferred.

But when this view is held—that another sentence arises from the inference of another word similar to it—then there is no fault. And here, the causal statement is this: "The augment *āṬ* is applied before roots beginning with vowels" (*āḍ ajādīnām*), which results in the sentence: "The augment *āṬ* is udātta for those [roots] beginning with vowels."

[8] Alternatively, he states the solution even from the perspective of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "one should teach only as much as one is able to teach in a general sense": here, some [grammarians], having taught merely the sound *s*, prescribe the augment *aṭ* for those verbal roots ending in *p*; others [prescribe] the elision of the vowel *a* for those verbal forms not ending in *p*.

In this way, having taught the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes such as *tavya* after both high-pitched (*udātta*) and low-pitched (*anudātta*) verbal roots (*prakṛti*), the Teacher, by prescribing the augment *iṭ* after the high-pitched ones, demonstrates this: that the suffix *itavya* follows high-pitched verbal roots. And having done so, he says: "By that specific [augment], one arrives at a different word as a composite whole. The mention of the "composite whole" is for this purpose: that the vowel *i* does not arrive later once the suffix *tavya* and so forth have already been established.

What then? It is the aggregate itself as qualified by the vowel *i*. For example, in the expression "of the *khadira* and *barbara* trees. The genitive case used here—"that which you consider to be the commonality"—is used in relation to this [aggregate]. But what is the commonality between those two? It is that both the *khadira* and the *barbara* have white trunks and fine leaves; thus he explains that they understand the aggregate itself as being so qualified.
