Likewise here, the vowel *i* is neither added nor removed from the end of other *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; rather, for some verbal root (*prakṛti*), the suffix is *itavya*, and for some other root, it is *ta[vya]*.

[9] Or rather, by this sequence... he refutes [the opponent]. Now he presents the total refutation (*sarvāpalava*): this division which you have relied upon—first the base (*prakṛti*), then the suffix (*pratyaya*), and after that the augment *iṭ*—all of this is merely a means of demonstration; for it is not the actual reality (*bhūtārtha*). Not even any of the roots beginning with *bhū* exist as such in the word used in practice, such as *bhavati*; nor do [grammatical rules] such as "when *śap* is present, *laṭ* [is applied]" exist in reality.

What then? These are merely means for the application [of grammar]. Nor is the permanence of the means asserted in the treatise; rather, the permanence of the application is what is asserted. Furthermore, this distinction—namely, that first there is the base (*prakṛti*), then the suffix (*pratyaya*), and then the augment *iṭ*—does not exist within the aggregate (*samudāya*) that arises through the application. It is the preceding aggregate that is being established. This is demonstrated in brief: "Attain the truth by means of the untruth."

[10] Regarding the rule for the designation of *ṭ* and *k* at the beginning and end (*ādyantavidhāna*), there must be a prohibition of the status of being an affix (*pratyaya*). The term "rule for the designation of beginning and end" refers to the grammatical treatise stating, "The *ṭ*-marked and *k*-marked [elements] are designated as the beginning and the end. Alternatively, when the status of being the beginning or the end is prescribed for those marked with *ṭ* or *k*, a prohibition of the affix-status of that which is marked with *ṭ* or *ṭ-ness* must be stated, namely: "The *ṭ*-marked and *k*-marked elements at the beginning and end are not affixes. This is established by the subsequent statement.

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of a subsequent rule" (*paravacanāt*): by this subsequent rule, namely *vipratiṣedhe param* ("in case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]"), the posteriority of the suffix will be established. The scope of the rule *ādyantau* ("the first and the last") is exemplified by *iṭ valādeḥ* (A 7.2.35) and *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (A 7.3.40); likewise, the scope of the posteriority of the suffix is exemplified by *tavyattavyānīyarāḥ* (A 3.1.93). Here, both [rules] would apply simultaneously: *careṣ ṭaḥ* (A 3.2.16) and *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ* (A 3.2.3).

Alternatively, the phrase "on account of the mention of 'para'" (*paravacanāt*) is explained as follows: it refers to that very mention of *para* in the rule *pratyayaḥ paraḥ* (Pāṇini A 3.1.1–2), which is connected with the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

Or else, "on account of the mention of *para*" means that whatever is *para* receives the technical designation *pratyaya*; and when there is the status of being followed by a *pratyaya*, the letters *ṭ* and *k* receive the designation *it*; when the designation *it* exists, there is the application of the terms *ṭit* and *kit*; and when the application of the terms *ṭit* and *kit* exists, the status of being initial (*āditva*) and final (*antavya*) [is determined], so that for the *pratyaya* itself there is neither the status of being initial nor the status of being final.

In this way, however, the status of *bahuj* and others as suffixes (*pratyaya*) would be contradicted. Therefore, a suffix is not dependent on being "subsequent" (*paratva*). That which is subsequent must exist; there is an exception (*apavāda*) to this stated later: [the rule] "before the *ṭi*" and "subsequent to the vowel. Others explain: since the status of being subsequent is already established by the ablative case, the repeated mention of "subsequent" (*para*) is for the purpose of setting aside [other rules]. Thus, the exception to being subsequent—namely, the rule "the *ṭit* and *kit* markers are placed at the beginning and end"—is set aside by the repeated mention of "subsequent."

Therefore, [one might argue that] the subsequent rule will prevail. However, the contradiction has already been stated under the view that "technical terms and paribhāṣās follow the order in which they are enunciated" (yathoddeśam); but under the view that they apply at the time of operation (kāryakāla), since there is a single sentential unity in rules such as "careṣ ṭaḥ," priority and posteriority are simply impossible to establish.

[11] If it is argued that [the rule] is established by another statement, we say no, because it is an exception (*apavāda*). He thinks as follows: [The suffixes *ṭi* and *kita* are introduced] either in the context of the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*) or within the governing heading on suffixes (*pratyayādhikāra*). In the former case, the rule "the genitive [case ending] denotes the element to be replaced" (A 1.1.49) applies; in the other case as well, there is the condition of being followed by a suffix (*pratyayaparatva*). This being so, since this [new rule] is commenced even when the other [rule] would otherwise apply, it sets aside not only the status of being an element to be replaced (*sthāneyogatva*), but likewise the condition of being followed by a suffix (*pratyayaparatva*) as well.

And he provides an illustration: for example, the rule "mid aco 'ntyāt paraḥ" (P. 1.1.47), when applied along with "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ" (A 7.1.72) and "rudhādibhyaḥ śnam" (A 3.1.78), subverts the application of the "in place of" (sthāne) relation and the requirement of being followed by an affix (pratyayaparatva).

[12] This is an unequal comparison. Here, although the *lakṣaṇa* (the general rule) is beyond doubt, as for the *nimitta* (the cause or condition), because there is doubt regarding it, the exception (*apavāda*)—since its application is itself subject to doubt—is inferred to be weak. Thus it has been said: “The introduction of the marker *ṅ* in *tātaṅ* has a specific scope” (cf. Pāṇini 1.1.53, Vārttika 2). For the state of being marked by *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) is indeed an exception to the universal substitution (*sarvādeśa*). However, the *ṅittva* of *tātaṅ* is doubted, because other purposes are possible.

It is doubted whether the *ṅit*-designation is intended for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*—namely, whether this *ṅit*-designation is for the sake of preventing *guṇa* or for the sake of ensuring the substitution of the final letter. When the cause [of an operation] is itself doubtful, a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) whose cause is thus uncertain does not apply, just as in the case of *anaṅ* and other such elements; therefore, it was stated that there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between these two [possibilities] when both are in doubt.

Similarly here as well, regarding the rule *careṣṭaḥ*, if that [the suffix *ṭa*] is the cause for the application of the paribhāṣā concerning the beginning and the end (*ādyantaparibhāṣā*), then there arises a doubt: "Is it for the sake of the vowel *ī*, or for the sake of the beginning? Just as it operates in the case of the augment *iṭ* and others, so too does it operate here. However, in the case of *śrama* and the rest, because their purpose is fixed and there is no other possibility, they are beyond doubt. Since the cause and the definition apply where there is no doubt, it is logical that they constitute an exception (*apavāda*); thus he says: "The comparison is unequal."

[13] That which must necessarily follow from something is called its *prayojana* (purpose). Here, the *nimitta* (cause/condition) is that which operates independently of anything else; for example, in the rule “*kamer ṇiṅ*” (A 3.1.30), the addition of the marker *ṅ* operates independently of other factors for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings, for the sake of prohibiting *vṛddhi*, or for the sake of preventing the obstruction of general reference. The letter *ṇ* serves both for general reference and for the prohibition of *vṛddhi*.

Thus, in this case, the *ṅit*-ness of the suffix *tātaṅ* does not function to prohibit *guṇa* by the mere fact of its being *ṅit*; what then? It functions when there is a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). In the same way, it is possible to state the purpose of its *ṭit*-ness as well: if that [suffix] follows, then the *ṭit*-ness can serve as the cause for the substitution of the vowel *ī*.

Since that very purpose for which the ambiguity of the *ṭit*-designation is accepted is itself dependent upon posteriority (*paratva*), it is therefore the cause of doubt; thus, because there is no longer any doubt, this posteriority must be set aside by this [rule], and so it is said: "Not so, because it is an exception (*apavāda*)."

[14] On what basis is this stated—“established by virtue of being subsequent” (*paravacanāt*)? It is because one perceives the possibility of the purpose for the vowel *ī* in a *ṭit* suffix. This purpose is possible when the *ṭit* suffix remains subsequent; thus, this topic is introduced based on mere possibility, in the sense that “if subsequent status could somehow be obtained. However, in other cases where there is absolute subsequent status, the status of being a *mit* (shortening cause) is precluded.

But when the operation is resorted to for that duration of time—not because of the possibility of a purpose—then the cause for the substitution of *ī* has not yet arisen; for that [substitution] is dependent upon posteriority (*paratva*). Therefore, there is no apprehension of posteriority due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If this very [operation] were not obstructed, why would it not proceed once the cause—the status of being *ṭi*—is present? Thus it was said: "That which is called a 'purpose' must be stated."

Alternatively, it is established by the statement of another: "The vowel *ī* occurs after a suffix marked with the marker *ṭ*"; thus, it remains there that [the rule applies] "after that which ends in a *ṭ*-marked suffix. If the suffix were at the beginning [of the word], then because of the absence of anything ending in a *ṭ*-marker, the vowel *ī* would not occur at all. Therefore, this very fact of the suffix being subsequent would be the subverting factor by way of its opposite. However, he speaks while relying on that which possesses both [characteristics], saying: "That purpose must indeed be stated."

He explains this very point with the following commentary: "Why should it be that, because of the addition of the marker *ṭ*, this [suffix] will be subsequent (*para*) and not initial (*ādi*)? Why is the possibility of a purpose (*prayojana*) relied upon, rather than the mere possibility of its application at that time? When the capacity of the statement of the vowel *ī* for the marker *ṭ* is relied upon exclusively, this resolution—that it belongs to what has the marker *ṭ*—is indeed established; the meaning is "of that which has *ṭ*" (*ṭita eva*). In that case, since being initial (*āditva*) is incompatible with being subsequent (*paratva*), the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is logically justified.

[15] Furthermore, this is not a valid rebuttal: if [the suffix] were produced in the form of a constituent part (*avayava*), there would be the evidence of the prohibition "not before *i*" (A 7.2.4). For if it were used in the sense of proximity, there would be no application [of the rule] due to the very fact of intervention. Moreover, it is impossible to understand that a constituent part is posterior to the whole (*samudāya*).

Now, how do these *samāsānta* suffixes, being parts of a compound, come to have the status of following a suffix (*pratyaya*)? In this case as well, you should understand it thus: having established the verbal root (*dhātu*), consider that this [suffix] follows from it, thinking, "Let this be its final element. In that regard, there is this fault: in the forms *ādhyoḥ* and *pradhyoḥ*, if [the suffix] were considered a part of the root, then by the rule *dhātuyaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.217), the acute accent of the case-ending would be prohibited, just as in the form *khalapvaḥ*. The same applies to *ādhī*. Consequently, the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekācaḥ...* (Pāṇini 6.4.82) would occur.
[16] Furthermore, there is no escape from this: even when a purpose has been conceived and undertaken, as for what might arise from this, one asks, "Where would this be?"

Regarding the rule *gāpoṣ ṭak*: here, because the conditions for both [the suffixes] apply at the beginning and the end, there are the properties of being *ṭit* and *kit*. In that context, the scope for the rule *ṭid-ādiḥ* is provided by *iṅ valādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35); the scope for the rule *kid-antaḥ* is also provided by *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (A 7.3.40). Here, both would apply to *gāpoṣ ṭak*; however, by the principle of "subsequent [application] over preceding" (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*), the property of being *anta* prevails. Consequently, the long vowel *ī* is established from what ends in a *ṭit* suffix.

As for the case of *carer ṭādiṣu*, since there is no subsequent application [of the *kit* property], this argument—"it is established by the statement of the subsequent [rule]"—is not a valid resolution.

[17] But it is established by the statement under the heading of the genitive case (Vārttika 3): "This rule should be stated under the heading of the genitive of location. Where there is a genitive of location, the markers *ṭ* and *k* occur at the beginning and the end respectively. Since the genitive under the heading of suffixes (*pratyaya*) is subject to contradiction due to its status as a subsequent element, even in the rule *gāpoṣṭag*, there is no application of the marker to the end.

[18] "Or because the genitive case-meaning exists at the beginning and the end" (Vārttika 4). Here, the word *artha* does not mean "denotable object," for the meaning of the initial element is certainly not denoted by the genitive. Therefore, the word *artha* signifies "purpose. Since the genitive has a purpose at both the beginning and the end, we understand that in its absence—that is, in the absence of the genitive—the initial and final elements surely lack a motivator (*prayojaka*) by which the genitive, as the motivated (*prayojya*), might be postulated.

The other [opponent] says: "Since there is no sixth case [ending] for that which does not exist, therefore even the meaning of the prefix *ā-* (beginning) does not exist; thus, you have accepted that the object is preceded by the word. He replies: "But it is logical that a name has the word as its cause. The other explains: "The absence of the word is the inference for the absence of the object, whereas the word is indeed preceded by the object"; that is to say, the word has the object as its sole cause. Furthermore, if he had intended to discuss the meaning of the prefix *ā-* (beginning), he would have employed the sixth case ending itself.

Therefore, it must be understood that this excludes the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau* [P. 1.1.46]. Furthermore, when the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is directly perceived, it serves as the basis for understanding the meaning of "beginning"; however, this [genitive] is a case of inference based on the fact that [an element] has the marker *ṭ* or *k*. Therefore, it is rightly said: "In its absence, there is no comprehension" (Vārttika 4). But where the genitive occurs in the formulation of a suffix-rule (*pratyayavidhi*), that too functions in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). Alternatively, it follows the principle that "the substitutes for case-endings (*sup*) may themselves function as case-endings."

Alternatively, [the word "from"] is indeed an ablative case used to indicate the origin of an affix—meaning "from the root *gā-pū*," or "from the nominal stems *kapi* and *jñāti"—and not a genitive case. [Pāṇini 1.1.47:
"The augment *m* follows after the final vowel."

[1] For what purpose is this stated? ... It is a negation of the condition (*pratyaya*) based on its position. "Negation of the condition of another" means a negation of the *dharma* (the property), not a negation of the *dharmī* (the substratum). Or, "another" refers to that very cognition which is the condition; the negation of that [condition] is effected by this [rule] through the expression "after the final vowel. Alternatively, the word *para* expresses a quality (*guṇavacana*) even without a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*). Thus, "the posteriority of the condition" is expressed as *pratyayapara*.

The prior placement [of the word *ava*] is due to its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group. However, the author of the Bhāṣya, disregarding the literal meaning of the letters, explains it according to the sense, stating that this is an exception to the rule regarding the posteriority of an affix (*pratyayaparatva*).

Why, then, was it not stated previously as "the prefixes *ava* and *pra*"? This would have been established in such a way: "the two affixes *ṭit* and *kit* are subsequent," rather than "the beginning and the end. Because the status of being a substitute (*sthāneyoga*) has been set aside, the status of being subsequent to an affix is not affected.

He thinks as follows: What is this logic? When there is an expectancy for a grammatical rule (*śāstra*) and an expectancy for a specific distinction (*bheda*), one should apply [the rule] to that very first [element], because the occurrence of the subsequent one is not yet known. Or, when there is an expectancy for usage (*prayoga*) or an expectancy for a whole (*samudāya*), since there is no priority or posteriority (*paurvāparya*) in the usage itself, and because the whole is immediate (*ānantarya*), it cannot be said of this [first element] that "this is before" or "this is immediate.
Thus, the application of the stage (*kakṣā*) occurs when the preceding—whether already perceived or not—is perceived, but not when the subsequent is unperceived.

[3] If this principle does not apply here, how can it be said that "because of the *mit*-designation of *śnam*"? From what is the *mit*-status of *śnam* known? It is known from usage—as in *ruṇaddhi* and *bhinatti*. For it has been stated: "The teacher, knowing the purpose, attaches the *anubandhas*" (MBh. 1.266.20–21). Likewise: "Even for that which is not *bha*, by the power of the application of the *anubandha*" (MBh. 3.225.15). Alternatively, the treatise (*śāstra*) teaches technical designations (*saṃjñā*) without being restricted [by prior usage].

And the elision preceded by that has been set in motion. When one considers what its purpose is, this is understood: having set aside the "subsequent-ness" (paratva) obtained through the governing rule (*adhikāra*)—namely, the state of being in a specific location—the phrase "the augment *miṭ* follows after the final vowel" (*mid aco 'ntyāt paraḥ*) is connected [to the present rule]. By means of this perspective, this preceding rule is presented as an illustration, as in: "just as this rule, 'the augment *miṭ* follows after the final vowel'."

[4] *kuṇḍāni* and *vanāni*. According to A 7.1.72 (*napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*), if it were stated there that "of a neuter [stem],"—just as in the case of A 7.3.43 (*ruhaḥ paḥ*), where this exception is begun when the general rule of substitution (*sthāneyoga*) would otherwise apply, namely that the *pa* replaces the *ha* of the root *ruh*—then here it is deliberated: is this single genitive in *napuṃsakasya* [intended to mean] "of a neuter"? In that case, if the genitive in *napuṃsakasya* is for the purpose of qualifying the vowel (*aj*), then there is no application of the rule of substitution (*sthāneyoga*).

Now, if [the rule] were based on the principle of *sthāneyoga* (substitution), it would be impossible for the vowel (*ac*) to function as a qualifier. Just as when *mid* is a qualifier of *ig*, there is no *sthāneyoga*. True, this is so. However, when these two [terms, *ajanta* and *acaḥ*] are taken up as they are—meaning "of a neuter [stem] ending in a vowel, [the suffix *na*] comes after the vowel"—and not [as a qualifier] of the *aṅga* itself, nothing is required by this [vowel] that is connected to the *aṅga*. Since there is no verbal mention (*śabdopādāna*) of a *sthāneyoga*, one understands through proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) that the final vowel belonging to that which is connected to the *aṅga* is intended.

[5] This example, "kuṇḍāni," would be appropriate; for in that case, once the vowel (*ac*) has been elided, it is impossible for [the suffix] to follow after the final vowel. But here, in "payāṃsi," such a possibility exists: having elided the *s*, it could indeed follow after the final vowel.

Nor does the Lord issue a command such as this: "In the *Śāstra*, some sublation has been initiated by the rule *'vipratiṣedhe param'* (A 1.4.2); some has not been initiated by the principle *'the non-eternal sublates the eternal'*; and this [principle], *'the internal is stronger when there is an option,'* has also not been initiated in the *Śāstra*. It might be thought that it is initiated in the world, but even in the world it is not initiated. By saying 'nor does the Lord issue a command,' he explains that [the rule] has a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*)."

People carry out the word of the Lord (Īśvara) with respect to visible matters such as killing and the like; however, the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* explain this [word] regarding invisible matters, such as: "this is edible," "this is inedible," and "this is [to be done] by this [means]."

What then? This is a worldly example; this is a worldly illustration. He says that an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a demonstration (*darśana*). Alternatively, it is a reference back to what is about to be stated—just as in the expression: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins. For in the world, even when there is no other context for the matter, if someone says, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," no one would ever give curd to Kauṇḍinya.
Therefore, perception alone is the cause; no further logical justification needs to be stated here, just as the heat of fire is not explained by means of a logical argument.

[8] Furthermore, an instance of such [usage] is indeed produced. Here, however, regarding the expression “curd for the Brahmins,” one must consider whether the word “Brahmin” is applied with primary intent (*tātparya*) toward Kauṇḍinya, or rather by way of necessity (*nāntarīyakatva*), just as in the case of the expression “while going to the village, he crushed the base of the wall. In the case of the offering of buttermilk, however, it is taken with primary intent. And since there is neither a combination nor an option (*vikalpa*) between that which is established by necessity and that which is established by primary intent, neither of those two [alternatives] is tenable.

(2) Alternatively, the word *brāhmaṇa* is ambiguous with respect to Kauṇḍinya. For the word *brāhmaṇa* applies not only to Kauṇḍinya but also to others; thus, it is uncertain which [meaning] is being employed here. And when there is doubt regarding two things—one doubtful and one certain—it is logically untenable to treat them as equivalent in enumeration. (3) Alternatively, Kauṇḍinya is not the referent (*padārtha*) of the word *brāhmaṇa*, though its form (*rūpa*) may occur [therein]; however, for the word *kauṇḍinya*, he is indeed the referent. Furthermore, it is not appropriate for direct perception and inference to be of equal status.

[8.1] On this very point it is said: We do not say that the gift of curd is prompted by Kauṇḍinya. What then? It is prompted by his being a Brāhmaṇa. There is an application [of the term] to Kauṇḍinya because of his connection with the quality of being a Brāhmaṇa, and because of the primary intention regarding the meanings of the words *brāhmaṇa* and *adana* (eating). In that case, just as one obtains buttermilk (*takra*) because of his being Kauṇḍinya, why should one not also obtain curd (*dadhi*) because of his being a Brāhmaṇa? Thus it is argued.

[8.2] (4) Therefore, the Naiyāyikas accept that the definition of sublation (*bādhā*) is precisely "sublation by the inference of non-attainment" (*aprāptyanumāna*). Furthermore, non-attainment is not produced by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is inferred in the case of non-attainment. For example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; it must not be given to Kauṇḍinya. Here, both the act of giving and its cessation are heard through the relationship of general and particular. If the act of giving were to proceed unconditionally from the status of being a Brāhmaṇa, then the scriptural prohibition would be sublated.

Alternatively, if it were by way of an option—such that sometimes it is given and sometimes it is not given—then the exclusion [of the action] in one alternative would be sublated. Furthermore, comprehension through the aggregate [of both alternatives] is impossible due to the contradiction between giving and its cessation; thus, there is an inference of the attainment of a prohibition.

Even though both [examples], "Curd for the Brahmins" and "Buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya," involve both a general rule and a specific exception, nevertheless, just as smoke is established as an inference when smoke is inferred from that which possesses smoke, so too does the relationship between the general and the particular exist in a sentence of exclusion (*nivṛtti*). Therefore, in this case as well, non-attainment is understood through inference, and thus non-attainment is established.

[8.3] (5) Alternatively, one must consider this: when the word "Let curd be given to the Brahmins" is employed while its generic form (*ākṛti*) is neither deficient nor incomplete, it applies even to Kauṇḍinya despite his being impaired; thus, it follows that he too would receive the curd.

In this regard, just as in the case of the statement "the Brahmins are to be fed," where Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya are mentioned by way of serving food, they are not included within the act of eating based on the word [expressing] inference; likewise, Kauṇḍinya, who is the object of the gift of buttermilk (or, in the case of the gift), being mentioned as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), is not included within the gift of curd.

[8.4] Thus far, it has been stated on the basis that "two [actions] give. Others, however, think as follows: this single verb *dadāti* ("to give") possesses distinct objects and distinct recipients. At the very moment when one portion of the act of giving is connected with curd (*dadhi*), another portion is simultaneously connected with buttermilk (*takra*). Since there is no temporal separation at the time the word is employed, it is determined that Kauṇḍinya is the recipient of the gift of curd.

But this is the ultimate truth: this single entity existing in the world, which lacks spatial division, is metaphorically treated as if it were a distinct object. And this is the meaning of the sentence for the world: "Let curd be given to the other Brahmins, excluding Kauṇḍinya; but let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya."

[9] *Antyāt pūrvo maśeḥ* (Vārttika 2). Since it has already been stated that the augment *mit* follows the final vowel, this new rule is commenced. This is stated under the view that the designation *saṃyoga* applies to a group of many consonants. For what purpose are two examples cited, namely *maṅktā* and *magna*? Even if an effort were made regarding the elision of the *anubandha*—namely, by the rule *anupadhāsthasya ca maśeḥ*—then while *magna* would be established, this form *maṅktā* would not be established.

[10] Regarding the rule *bharjim arcyoś ca* (Vārttika 3): [the suffix *cha* is applied after these]. Thus, *ūmīm*. Since the word *marīci-* is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group, it must necessarily be recited here [in the list], as in the formation *mārīciḥ*, meaning "the offspring of Marīci. The word *bharuja-* is also listed among the *aṅguli-ādi* and the *bāhu-ādi* groups, according to the statement: "The river named Bharujā is the Candrabhāgā. By this, one forms *bhārujikaḥ* and *bhāruhiḥ* (or *bharuji*).

[11] He himself establishes the position: "If *anta* (end) is understood [to carry over]," this refines the statement that "the *para* (following) [element] after the final vowel is the *anta*. Is this *anta*, being *para*, a part (*avayava*) or the whole (*samudāya*)? As he will conclude at the end: "This [term] belongs to the aggregate (*saṃghātabhakta*); it does not [apply to the individual parts]," it is therefore determined that this [term] belongs to the aggregate.

Now, the term "beginning" (ādiḥ) is understood from the previous context; therefore, it means "beginning of what follows. For it is not possible that [a single element] could simultaneously be subsequent to the final vowel of one [word] and the beginning of the preceding one. Thus, by the recurrence of the word "beginning," its status as the beginning of the subsequent element is determined.

[11.1] (1) In the case of *abhakte*... "the *kuṇḍas* and *vanas* do not exist as final members of a compound. But has it not been stated that "the mention of *tadādi* is for the sake of *syad* and *num*"? And on this view, that [mention] must be remembered for the sake of *num*, since it is established in the case of a prior final member (*pūrvānta*). Even in the case of a subsequent initial member (*parādau*), the long vowel is established, for he will state [later]: "A long vowel occurs before *yañ*, and also before *sup*" (A 7.3.101–102). However, the form *asthīni* is not established.

(2) *agne trīti*: The final *n* of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not exist here. Since this is Vedic (*chāndasa*), the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) will occur; thus, the substitution of *ś* [for the final *s*] is difficult to obtain. If one assumes the elision of a phoneme (*varṇalopa*), then because that [elision] is established as a fact, the rule "of the penultimate" (*nopadhāyāḥ*) would not apply, and lengthening would not be attained. However, it could be argued that this [form] is seen in the middle of a name; yet this would require remembering too much. (3) *sarvāṇi jyotīṃṣi*: Because of the intervention of the *num* augment between the nominal suffix (*sup*) and the word, there is no immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*). If [the *num*] were treated as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), it would be included by the mention of the word *sarva*; if it were at the beginning of the following element (*parādau*), it would be included by the mention of the nominal suffix (*subgrahaṇa*), and thus there would be contiguity.

(4) "It is performed as a *nyāsa* (an explanatory insertion)" means this: the mention of *num* must necessarily be made for the sake of that which is neither a final *n* of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) nor a case-ending (*vaibhakta*), such as in the form *prāhiṇvat*. (5) They explain that *dviṣantapaḥ* is cited incidentally; for since it falls within the scope of those [rules], it is included by the mention of them. Furthermore, the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established even when there is an *anusvāra*; thus, since this [word] is now at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *anusvāra* is established. However, the actual example is *paraṃtapaḥ*.

(6) Furthermore, the substitution of *śī* is not established. Because [the suffix] is *nitya* and because it is subsequent, once *num* has been applied, the substitution of *śī* for the neuter does not apply due to the intervention. [11.2] (1) Regarding *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, *aut*, etc., at the beginning of what follows... [in the case of] *trapuṇe*. In this view that "that which has *ṅ* as its *it* is *ṅit*," there is a fault; for when [it is interpreted as] "that which is *ṅ* itself is the *it*," then by the rule "whatever occurs before a vowel, one should know that it belongs to the beginning of that," it must occur at the beginning of a *ṅit* element.

(2) Furthermore, the *anusvāra* would not be established. In this case as well, *dvaṣantapaḥ* is not a valid example. For if [the augment] were initial (*parādittve*), the *mum* augment would be a part (*bhakta*) of the letter *t*, and since that [letter *t*] is at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *mum* augment, being its part, would also receive the designation "at the end of a word" (*padāntavyapadeśa*).

(3) Regarding the substitution of *śī*, there is a prohibition of the letter *n*. When the substitution of *śī* occurs, the cessation of the letter *n* must be stated as being prohibited. This is because grammatical substitutes apply only to that which is explicitly mentioned; for example, in the rule *pādaḥ pad* (A 6.4.130), the substitution does not apply to a word ending in *pād*, but rather to the form actually heard as occurring in conjunction with the instrumental case-ending. Likewise here, the substitution does not apply to the word *nau* when it ends in the vowel *au*, but rather only to that very form which is actually heard as *au* in its phonetic realization.

Why, then, does it not apply to that which is specifically pointed out? Because it is separated by the *num* augment. When the form is understood as being in immediate contact with the audible word (*śruti*), it is because of that separation. In this context, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: "the prohibition of the letter *na*" means that its prohibition is caused by the letter *na*.

[11.3] Regarding the rule for the shortening of the neuter in the *pūrvānta* (the preceding member) and the accent of a *dvigu*: since the addition of the augment *num* is possible in the neuter, one might think it should simply state "shortening of the neuter. However, the intended meaning is as follows: in the case of *niṣkauśāmbinī*, the shortening of the *upasarjana* (secondary member) ought to apply because it is a subsequent rule (*paratva*). But once *num* has been applied—because it is a permanent (*nitya*) operation—the status of the *upasarjana* as ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) is destroyed, and its status as ending in a *ik* vowel is also lost; consequently, neither the shortening nor the accent would apply.

[11.3.1] Or rather, it is not so, because it is an external (*bahiraṅga*) characteristic. Shortness (*hrasvatva*) is independent of case endings (*vibhakti*). And regarding accent, it has been stated: “The mention of *pada* is for the sake of delimiting its extent” (A 4.3.140, Vārttika 4). But *num* depends on a case ending that incorporates an external object; therefore, it is external (*bahiraṅga*).

"He is one whose food is a composite" (*saṃghātabhakta*). In a composite whole that possesses a different form [from its parts], the constituent parts do not abandon their own nature. Just as in a variegated whole (*avayavin*), a single part does not receive the designation "white" or the designation "black," so too, why should the word *aratni* lose its status as ending in an *ik* vowel when the member [of the compound] has taken on a different form? Furthermore, since the accent is initiated for the preceding member when there is a subsequent member, the status of ending in an *ik* vowel is not lost; thus the accent is established. *eca igghrasvādeśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.48). [When a short vowel is substituted for *ai*, *au*, or *e*, it is treated as the original.]

[1.1] For what purpose is this stated? In every case where a certain matter is established even without a specific statement, yet fails to be established when that statement is undertaken—or where a logical fallacy (*prasaṅga*) arises—there an inquiry is appropriate. However, in the present instance, the inquiries are prompted by the risk of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), regarding what will be stated later: “It is established because *eṅ* has a place of articulation in common” (Vārttika 3), and “And because *ai* and *au* have a greater number of constituent elements” (Vārttika 4).

[1.2] Furthermore, there are three types of syntactic integration (*prakriyābheda*) here: the unification of various sentences into a single sentence (*nānāvākyānām ekavākyatā*), the exclusion of a portion of what has occurred (*bhūtāṃśanivṛttiḥ*), and the statement of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣavaca*). We shall demonstrate these in the Bhāṣya itself later on.

[1.3] To exclude those of the same phonetic quality (*savarṇa*), [the rule] "in the teachings regarding short vowels" (*eṅo hrasvaśāsaneṣu*) [is stated]. Because they are *praśliṣṭa* (coalesced) *a*-sounds, the half-*e* and half-*o* would be considered *savarṇa* with [the full *e* and *o*]; however, it is said that this does not apply to the *ai* and *au* which have distinct (*viśliṣṭa*) phonemes. Furthermore, phonemes have restricted domains: just as the syllable *oṃ* is not used at all in certain Vedic recensions (*śākhā*), so too these two half-*e* and half-*o* are not employed elsewhere, yet they are employed here.

[1.4] "These two, *ai* and *au*, are called *samāhāravarṇa* (composite sounds). This is because they are designated as *samāhāravarṇa* since they consist of parts (*avayava*) that are produced through a process of combination (*samāhāra*). "*Ai* and *au* have two morae (*mātrā*); the mora belongs to the sound *a*. That which is divided eighteenfold—its *mātrā*, i.e., its single part (*ekadeśa*), is a constituent part (*avayava*) of this [diphthong]. The same should be applied to the sounds *i* and *u* as well. Regarding the phrase "in the rules concerning short vowels," he explains this: "This treatise is an exception (*nivartaka*) for these [two], but it is an injunction (*vidhāyaka*) for others."

But surely, because *ai* and *au* are more open (*vivṛtatara*), *i* and *u* will be [more] open than those, but not closed (*saṃvṛta*) like the vowel *a*. In that case, why is it said, “sometimes there might be the sound *a*”? How, for one thing, can two sounds that are more open become [identical with] the open ones? Moreover, it is established in this treatise that proximity based on place of articulation (*sthāna*) is stronger; thus, in the production of *i* and *u*, only the palate as the place of articulation is accepted, while the throat as the place of articulation is abandoned.

In that regard, because the term "place" (sthāna) is mentioned, it might be thought that [the vowel] could sometimes be unvoiced; therefore it is said: "Alternatively, since it is possible to produce even the letter *v* as more open (*vivṛtatara*), there is this contingency; however, having been restored [to its original state], it will be employed."

[2.1] However, long vowels would also apply; for one who understands that the short vowel (*hrasva-śruti*) forms a single syntactic unit, the *ik* vowels alone would enjoin what has not been previously established, and by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), the long *ī* and *ū* would thus apply, as in *atiri* and *atinu*. But how can there be the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) by means of a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*)? It is enjoined in that case where inclusion is possible. And by what is such inclusion possible? It is possible by means of the letter *u*.

But surely, since it is stated that there is a substitution of short vowels (*hrasvādeśa*), long vowels will not occur; for if a long vowel were to apply, the mention of the substitution of short vowels would be purposeless. Therefore, this was said: "The *ec* vowels undergo a substitution of short *ic* vowels. The other [opponent] says: "If there were no other purpose for this, we might accept it. But there is such a purpose. What is it? This must be for the sake of delimiting the scope (*viṣaya*), lest there be the undesirable application (*prasaṅga*) of short vowels to the *ec* vowels."

In the rule for the substitution of short vowels (*hrasvādeśa*), this [rule] applies: "The *ec* vowels become *ic*. Otherwise, if the term "substitution of short vowels" were not explicitly stated here, the same would apply even in cases such as *devadatta*. Therefore, within the scope of the teaching on short vowels, the rule "a short vowel occurs" applies by way of a distinct syntactical split: "A short vowel occurs for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," and "the *ec* vowels become *ic*"; thus, a short vowel occurs in place of the *ec* vowels, except in other instances.

Then, because there is no connection [to the preceding rule], there would be the undesirable consequence that all [vowels] become short; however, due to proximity (*āntaratamya*), a two-mora vowel would result. But this rule is understood as an exception to the shortening, just as the substitution of *di* for *dvi* is an exception to reduplication (*dvirvacana*); otherwise, the shortening would apply once again.

[2.2] There is no difference in status between the two sentences as separate utterances. But surely, if they form a single sentence (*ekavākyabhāva*), it is a restatement (*anuvāda*); whereas if they are separate sentences (*nānāvākyabhāva*), it is an injunction (*vidhi*)? True, this is so. However, it is improper to satisfy the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of that which already possesses expectancy; furthermore, there is prolixity (*gaurava*) in assuming multiple operations, so only a single operation is required. Moreover, if separate sentences were assumed, then in the rule *eca ig*, the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* would remain uncontradicted, because the former would not touch upon the latter.

Now, if a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is assumed, then in the rule "eCa iK hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya," since the short vowel is heard [in the sūtra], *ac* is taken as the locus (*sthānin*), and *ec* is included therein; furthermore, *ec* is superimposed as the locus. That which is being superimposed becomes the short vowel *ec*, and thus this is what is meant: "the neuter [stem] becomes short, and *ec* becomes the short *iK. For if it is construed in this way, the separate operation of the rule prescribing short vowels is upheld.

[2.3] Others describe it yet again as follows: "Because it causes cessation. By this [rule], *eca* and *ig*, while remaining in their very state, have this much done to them: that *ig* remains and *anig* is caused to cease. Just as in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), one remains and the others cease, they do not at all describe these vowels (*ecām*) and the *ik* sounds as having a relationship of original element (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*). Rather, in whatever state the *ig* remains, in that very same state it remains; thus the portion consisting of *anig* ceases, and the *ig* is established.
And as for that which remains short and not long, therefore it is well said: "But there is no possibility of [the vowel] becoming long, because [the rule] is a negator."

In this regard, however, the following objection is raised: because the *i* and *u* vowels are more open (*vivṛtatara*), there ought to be the hearing of that which is more open, namely *atiri* and *atinu*. Furthermore, since the effort (*prayatna*) here is different, there being no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the rule for lengthening by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would not apply in the case of *atirīn*. Moreover, in the alternative view where the latter [vowel] is predominant, there would result the hearing of only half a mora (*mātrā*). And it would be impossible to perceive the division between two vowels that are fused together (*praśliṣṭa*).

[2.5] This is not a fault. For the state of being more open (*vivṛtatara*) proceeds by depending upon a lack of articulation (*avarṇa*), just as a crystal assumes the color of its substrate due to the influence of that substrate. And when the substrate has been removed, it remains in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Likewise, the state of being more open depends upon a lack of articulation; when that [lack of articulation] is removed, how could it possibly be otherwise? It remains precisely as "more open. Furthermore, the Sūtra has already been refuted in the section concerning the subsequent [sound] being greater.

The Teacher also demonstrates the division even between closely joined phonemes (*praśliṣṭavarṇa*), just as it is said that "the swan separates milk from water. And regarding the statement "because of the greater predominance of the latter" (*aicōścottarabhūyastvāt*): here, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* are a composite (*samudāya*) produced by the throat and the palate. Since there is no short vowel for a composite that occupies both places of articulation, the closest correspondence (*āntaratamya*) residing within the composite cannot be established.

What then? Of those two constituent parts, one is guttural and the other is palatal. In this regard, which constituent part is the basis for designation? And since that [part] would be the subject under discussion as the *sthānin* (the original element) in the rule "syār" (*sya-ar*), it is said in response to this inquiry: "The designations apply to the majority. That constituent part which exists in a state of preponderance is the basis for designation.

Because it exceeds [the other] by half a mora, that phoneme is perceived as being of the same nature as that [other]; however, that which is deficient is understood as if it were adventitious (*āgantuka*). Since the morae of the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels are more numerous, the place of articulation (*sthānin*) receives the designation of palatal (*tālavya*) or labial (*oṣṭhya*), and does not receive the designation of guttural (*kaṇṭhya*), just as one says "a grove of mango trees" (*āmravana*) or "a grove of *śāla* trees. Even when other constituent parts are present, it is due to their numerical preponderance that the mangoes and the *śāla* trees serve as the basis for the designation, and not the other constituent parts.

Thus, because Brāhmaṇas are numerous, they are the basis for the designation [of the village], and not other constituent parts. Furthermore, the word "village" (grāma) is observed to apply to human beings; for in the case of a forest settlement (*sāraṇyaka*) which is denoted by the word "village," the Brāhmaṇas would be designated as its owners—[as in the expression] "this is the religious village (*dharma-grāma*) of the Brāhmaṇas.
This is the rule for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is a connection with a substitute (*sthāna*). (Pāṇini 1.1.49)

[1] What is this "sthāneyoga"? [This is] a question, because a compound and a non-compound cannot exist simultaneously. Since the locative case (*saptamī*) is heard, this would be a non-compound; however, because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is employed in the word "yogā," it would be a compound. Otherwise, the form "yuktiḥ" would result. Therefore, he says: "What is this 'sthāneyoga'? That which has its application (*yoga*) in place (*sthāne*) is "sthāneyogā."

In a compound, there is comprehension of the meaning; however, in a non-compound, there is no comprehension of the meaning even through inference. Therefore, this is a designation by means of a compound. The elision of the locative case ending occurs by virtue of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). This is what is meant: "this word should be employed. In that context, he explains that the connection pertains to the domain of the *sthāni-yoga* (the relationship with the original element), and not to any other domain. Alternatively, there is the substitution of *e* for the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), because its connection is with the *sthāna*. [The rule continues: “... before *āccha*...”

One might think that this *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *ai*) is the result of the *śe*-substitution [prescribed by Pāṇini 7.1.39]; however, because this is Vedic (*chāndasa*), its employment in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is difficult to justify.

[1.1] Furthermore, there are two ways of interpreting the genitive case in rules such as *aster bhūḥ* (A 2.4.52). Some hold the view that the genitive in *asteḥ* does not denote a relationship with the root *bhū*, nor is it related to *bhū* at all. What then? It is employed to indicate position (*sthāna*). However, the root *bhū* is introduced as that which is to be substituted (*ādheya*). For certain words are incapable of producing a distinction from their own form, just as in the expression "Yajñadatta of Devadatta."

The word *yajñadatta* does not produce a distinction in *devadatta* from the form of *yajñadatta* itself. For if it were conceived in such a way, there would be a cognition of a mere collection—as in "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Yajñadatta. Therefore, the distinction [of Devadatta] is from other referents—such as Yajñadatta being Devadatta’s father, son, master, servant, or neighbor. However, some say that the distinction arises from the very nature [of the object] itself, as in the cases of "slave," "son," or "hand."
Others think that the word *bhu* itself, having been grasped, is the reason for exclusion (*vyatirekahetu*) because it possesses its own inherent properties such as proximity and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning is "place" (*sthāna*), in the sense that "the word abides in this. In this view, the verb *bhavati* occurs in the sense of the root *as*. It is said that the purpose of this is to express the cessation of the other [root].

[1.2.1] Now, regarding the substitutes (*ādeśa*) for phonemes (*varṇa*), what is the meaning of "place" (*sthāna*), given that phonemes have no meaning at all? Even in that case, according to the view that "all [phonemes] are substitutes for all words," it is logical that the word *dadhi* is replaced by *dadhy*, and *ruhi* is also replaced by *rupi*.
[1.2.2] Alternatively, the word "place" (*sthāna*) denotes time (*kāla*); that is, the time of the *ik* vowels is occupied by the *yaṇ* consonants.

[1.2.3] Or, just as the word *aster* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of those forms resembling *as-* that are employed for their meaning, and those [original forms] are the substituends (*sthānin*), whose meaning is expressed by the verb *bhavati*; in the same way, here too in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, those *ik*-sounds which are imitated—such as those standing in the place of *dadhi* and so on—their own form (*svarūpa*) is the meaning, namely, the substituend (*sthāna*).

[2] But for what purpose is this stated? If a sūtra were begun [in this manner], the status of being a "locus of application" (*sthāneyogatva*) would apply everywhere; consequently, there would be no establishment of the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. Furthermore, since an explanation is undertaken for the sake of benefiting the various qualifiers that converge upon a single qualificand, whatever meaning can be obtained through such [an explanation] is what is intended.

[2.1] The statement regarding the application of the genitive case is for the purpose of restriction (vārttika 1). This is said with reference to the reading "there are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive," namely: the relationship of possessor and possessed, proximity, and collection; or "as many as there are. That is to say, "as many as exist in common usage. Alternatively, even though there may be the possibility of multiple meanings, the phrase "or as many as" refers to those that are actually possible according to the textual tradition. This [sūtra] is stated for the purpose of restricting the application to that specific number.

In this regard, some have proposed the following: for a cognizer whose intellect has been diverted by a general term and who does not apprehend the specific [meaning], this is the means for apprehending the specific: "The specific intended here by the Teacher is what is called *sthāneyogatva* (the state of being in the place of another). Understand it thus regarding the indications of the genitive case. Others think: "The general form *asteḥ* is unable to take on a specific [referent]; therefore, the word *sthāne* presents itself.
From its presence, this sentence is inferred: 'In the place of *asti*, *bhū* occurs.'"

[2.1.1] However, [the grammatical operations] based on the partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) are not established. They are not established because the speaker intends to express the whole without distinction (*aviśeṣa*). Because the whole without distinction is intended, there is here a superimposition of another statement. Since these two rules—*gohaḥ* and *upadhāyāḥ*—are both genitives of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), [if they were taken as partitive genitives,] the substitution would apply to the final letter of *guh*, where it is modified, and it would not apply in the case of *kṅit* suffixes. Furthermore, it would apply to the mere penultimate (*upadhā*) of other roots such as *pac* and so forth.

[2.1.1.1] Furthermore, there is no application of the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, because the connection is beyond doubt (Vārttika 3). By "non-application," it is not only the non-application of the genitive that is meant; rather, it is the non-application of the restrictive rule (*niyama*). How so? Regarding what you have proposed—that "the statement of the genitive is for the sake of restriction"—a restriction is established by this [rule] only where multiple meanings are possible.

Furthermore, it is not logical to assume that where another meaning has been specified, there the exclusion of that [other] meaning constitutes its status as being "connected by way of substitution" (*sthāneyoga*). For if you were to proceed exactly as I have proposed, then, given that a restriction can apply to multiple meanings, such an interpretation would be appropriate; however, it is not the case that one must exclude a different meaning and then establish the status of "substitution" for what remains.

Now, if you think that meanings are prescribed by grammar alone, even so, how is the abandonment of *goḥ*—which functions in dependence upon the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)—justified? Furthermore, it would be logical to assume a previously non-existent status of "substitution" (*sthāneyoga*), such that when multiple meanings are possible, the status of substitution serves to exclude the others. Moreover, he demonstrates that in common worldly usage, instruction does not proceed in such a manner, stating: "This is a worldly example."

For when there are two paths in the same direction and it is not known on which part of the path the village is situated, instructors point it out by saying, "the right-hand [path]," "the left-hand [path]. Even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the quality is not explicitly named, the final member's placement is correct; "dakṣiṇa" is derived from the roots *dāśati* or *dakṣati*, and does not signify a fixed rule.

Alternatively, since the term *dakṣiṇahasta* is a designator for that which is connected with the hand—specifically, that which is to the right of the hand—it is indeed a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). However, they do not teach the application of the term to the horizontal path (*tiryakpatha*), because that [path] does not function [as a hand]. For it is not the case that one would be confused regarding this [hand]. Thus, the Teacher teaches only that genitive which is itself subject to doubt and is connected with a specific meaning; he does not teach that [genitive] which is already inherently connected with a specific meaning.

[2.1.1.2] Alternatively, "in the absence of application" (*sthāne ayoge*) means: this is said with reference to one who conducts linguistic usage by taking the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) alone as authority, regardless of actual derivation (*upapatti*). Regarding "in the absence of connection" (*avyakta-yoge*): although it has been stated that "the negative particle [is used] in the sense of existence" (*naño 'sty arthānām*, A 2.2.24, vā. 15), even so, since there is no genitive case without a connection (*yoga*), it is postulated that "this [genitive] lacks a specific connection."

Alternatively, "yogavatī" means "possessing a connection. Since everything possesses a connection with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it is designated as "bhūmnī" (abundant). That which is related to multiple meanings is precisely what is "yogavatī" (possessing a connection). However, that whose connection is already fully determined is neither "ayogā" (without connection) nor "yogavatī"; it will exist in its proper place.

[2.2] Or rather, the genitive case is distinguished as being used in the sense of "substitution" (*sthāneyoga*; Vārttika 4). Relying on the *svarita* accent that is produced by a fraction (*kalādhmāta*), I shall explain its status as substitution; and because of its connection with gender (*liṅga*), I shall declare its human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*). With this in mind, he says: "And that gender-sign will not be applied in cases such as the genitive of parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)."

The other [teacher], thinking that this [student] would not understand the connection with the *liṅga* due to a lack of conviction, says: "The rule *śā hau* (A 6.4.35) requires the inclusion of the mention of *śās*. They think as follows: *śis* is inferred here; and since it functions as a qualifier of the *upadhā*, it presents itself here as well, possessing that same form even when its connection [to the specific root] is absent.

As for what was said previously regarding the sense of the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*): how so? It explains that "the heading" (*adhikāra*) is of three kinds. If you think thus—"this is a single word, and it is not logical for a single thing to possess both gender and the absence of gender"—that is not so, because the heading is of three kinds.

For that which is drawn along by [the rules] "and when there is an addition at the end of a word" (A 6.3.79), "and when the second member is indefinable" (A 6.3.10), and "and in an *avyayībhāva* compound, provided it does not denote time" (A 6.3.81)—namely, the rule "of *saha*, *sa-*" (A 6.3.78)—its recurrence occurs without distinction; that is, it applies both here and there. In this way, it can also be understood regarding a *paribhāṣā*: having gathered together the various specific rules (*pradeśa*) that possess the characteristic [of being governed], the term "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) remains established through the principle of *tantra*. However, the distinction that exists in its application (*viniyoga*) arises from the distinction in the application of the person (*puruṣa*).

But when one who is thus attached to the gender indicated by the accentuation establishes himself in each yoga, it is determined therein: "these yogas possess that [property]. Just as one who understands the possessors of those properties through distinct words perceives their form with the intellect, so too in that case... Thus, one word is without a gender-indicator (*aliṅga*), while another word, possessing a gender-indicator (*liṅgavat*), is determined by the intellect in this manner.

This would be a mere matter of conviction. This is what is being demonstrated: from the utterance of the word "śāsaḥ" and because of its connection with the grammatical marker (liṅga), it is understood that the form "śāsaḥ" exists in the rule "śa hau"; however, it is impossible to understand this as having an equal marker without direct audition (śruti). Thus he says: "for one cannot utter a word without..."

[2.2.1] If that is so, then that indicative mark will be applied to the substitute. In the rule *śa hau*, the word *śā* will be treated as either a phonetic modification (*kala*) or a blowing (*dhmāta*). However, this indicative mark does not belong to the substitute; rather, it belongs to the original base (*prakṛti*) itself. Yet, that base is not actually uttered. Since it is impossible to apply an indicative mark to something that lacks a substratum, the application of the indicative mark—namely, the state of being *svarita*—is intended solely for the purpose of indicating the specific form.

[3] Where there is a single genitive case and multiple things to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), some explain that it connects with that which follows immediately as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For if, having understood the connection through gender (*liṅga*) as being in the place of substitution (*sthāneyoga*), one were to say "that" (?). But we say: just as in the case of *rasāmādyau* [the rule] does not apply because of the word *aṅgasya*. If the position is that there is a restriction in case of doubt, then indeed there is a doubt.

Now, [the opponent argues that] non-application (*ayoga*) is the application of the unmanifest (*avyakta-yoga*), and thus application is "possessing application" (*yogavatī*); however, in this regard, the following objection is raised: if the genitive case in *aṅgasya* is taken as referring merely to the word-form itself without relying on its meaning, then because it is devoid of meaning, there is no application at all—how then could there be "application in place" (*sthāneyoga*)? For the comprehension of meaning occurs only when there is a connection with the various applications (*yoga*).

Furthermore, even if one relies solely on the meaning without depending on the operation of the word, it functions in its acquired form in subsequent instances—just as in the *vibhāṣā* rules, the prohibition and the option are operative [only] when they have been applied, and not at the time of the connection with the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, whether there is a connection between these two positions or not, there is no fault in either case.

If, however, the word *āśrita* or the word *āśrita* is understood to have as its referent the object (*artha*) that is dependent, then, because the specific [referent] has been removed, it is possible in both cases—by way of connection—to understand grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *saṃprasāraṇa* through the rule of "that which ends in" (*tadanta-vidhi*), and to understand grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) by treating it as a qualifier of the constituent part (*avayava-viśeṣaṇatvena*).

However, he thinks as follows: even when the sūtra is accepted, this conceptualization is possible—that "of the member" (*aṅgasya*) refers here too to the consonants (*vyañjana*) of the specific meaning. . . . Thus, in this case as well, under the view that "of the member" expresses a specific [element], there is no introduction of other specific sentences; for when a general relation is taken up, the specifics are understood through the sentence.

But was it not said that there are one hundred and sixty meanings of the genitive case? This is not a fault. The intention is as follows: certain relations that are semantically appropriate are expressed by the word. For example, in the expression “Devadatta’s wife of the servant,” the understanding does not arise that “she who is the wife of the servant is his [Devadatta’s] mistress. What then? It is simply a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) involving two qualifiers of the subordinate term (*upasarjana*). Likewise, in the expression “these are the houses of Devadatta’s maidservant,” it is simply a conventional usage.

Thus, here too, just as in the case of "aster bhūḥ," whatever meaning is appropriate must be the one that exists in the words; and since there is no other meaning for it that is appropriate as the sense of the genitive, we shall understand it as "connection by way of substitution" (sthāneyogatva).
The other [opponent], however, takes the genitive sense to be an inherent connection with the word, and says: "For a word, too, there are connections such as proximity (nāntarya) with another word."

This is merely a matter of doubt (*saṃdehamātra*). What is meant is this: just as the Sūtra being composed must be explained, so too should you understand it precisely through that very explanation. Alternatively, its non-existence does not follow from doubt. Just as in deep darkness there is no perception of specific colors, yet form (*rūpa*) exists, so too at all times the "particular" (*viśeṣa*) exists—whether unmixed or mixed. However, one must seek the means for the comprehension of that particular.

Likewise here as well, in the rule "for *as* there is *bhū*" (*aster bhūḥ*), this is the means for the comprehension of the specific [form]: that the form *asteḥ* (of *as*) is its own essential nature, which is eternal and exists in a state of inseparable connection like its own form; thus, the relationship of the substituendum (*sthānin*) is inherent in the word-meaning, whereas words such as *samīpa* ("near") are external to the meaning of the essential form. Alternatively, the use of the verb *bhavati* in the sense of "being near" is not appropriate, because it has already been expressed by *asti*. Or rather, because it has been expressed by *bhavati*, only *asti* is used.

[4] That which ends in the genitive case is to be connected with its *sthāna* (original place); that which is heard ending in the genitive is what is to be connected with its *sthāna*. That which is merely implied is not to be so connected. Since the genitive is uttered, it possesses the capacity for connection with an operation (*kāryayogitva*); this is the meaning obtained from the commencement of the Sūtra. And this is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "Substitutes apply to that which is being specifically indicated (*nirdiśyamāna*)" (Vārttika 12).

Therefore, in the rule *pādaḥ pat* (A 6.4.130), the word *pād* ending in the genitive case is directly heard (*śrutyanupātī*), whereas that which ends in it is merely implied (*pratīyamāna*); thus, that which ends in it cannot be connected with the [substitution] by virtue of its position. Now, one might object: since the word *pādaḥ* is heard as a whole, it causes that which ends in it to be understood, and consequently, there would be the undesired consequence of the substitution applying to that which ends in it. To this, some explain: "The paribhāṣā concerning that which ends in it is set aside by this [rule]. But this is incorrect.

In this case, there would be a fault: the substitution of *pad-* would apply even to the root *pādayati* when it does not end in a suffix. For in that case, it would not apply [as intended] in a form such as *vyāghrapād*. Therefore, by this [rule], the extension of the rule to what ends in that [root] (*tadantavidhi*) which has already been reached is excluded.

Just as you understand from the treatise that "pādaḥ" refers to that which ends in the word *pāda*, so too should you understand this very statement from the treatise to be of such a nature: namely, that for that which ends in *pāda*, the substitution of *pad* occurs for the word *pāc*. Alternatively, it means that when an operation applies to the whole (*samudāya*), the constituent parts (*avayava*) undergo that operation through the medium of the whole, and not directly.

How is it that [the rule] “*yīvarṇayor dīdhīvevyoḥ*” (A 7.4.53) is formulated? There too, because *dīdhī* and *vevī* are being specifically indicated (*nirdiśyamānatva*), the elision (*lopa*) would result as a substitute for the whole. True; this is so. However, by means of the restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*), the rule “*alo ’ntyasya*” (A 1.1.52) will ensure that it applies to the final [phoneme].
“A substitute similar to the original occurs in its place” (A 1.1.50).

[1.1] What is the example? “*iko yaṇ aci*” (A 6.1.77)—as in *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*. Both [types of examples] are cited: that in which this [rule] operates is an example, and that for the sake of which it is cited is also an example. However, the question [of what constitutes an example] is redundant because it is established even by another definition. But he introduces [the topic] seeing only a mere discrepancy, namely: “*iko yaṇ aci*. He thinks as follows: there are many [sounds] called *ik*.

They become the substituends (*sthānin*). Since the vowels *i* and *u* each have eighteen varieties, they constitute thirty-six; together with *ṛ* and *ḷ*, there are thirty. Thus, there are sixty-six varieties. There are also seven varieties of the *yaṇ* [semivowels]. Alternatively, since *ḷ* lacks the status of a substituend due to its impossibility [in this context], there is a disparity between the substituends and the substitutes (*ādeśa*).

This is also established by means of a subsequent reference (*anudeśa*) according to numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). This is indeed an unprecedented type of irregularity (*vaiṣamya*): here, a distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*) is not resorted to; rather, it is the universal class (*jāti*) that is intended—namely, the *ig*-class and the *yaṇ*-class. And for these, there is a fourfold set on both sides. As for what was said—that the phoneme *ḷ* does not exist—that numerical correspondence does not apply to the domain of actual usage (*prayoga*), but rather to the domain of subsequent reference (*anudeśa*).

*tasthasthamipāṃ tāṃtaṃtāmaḥ* (A 3.4.101). The intended meaning is as follows: when one understands the correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) by means of the svarita accent as a marker, then, in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the application of the svarita to the vowel *i* would be purposeless, as it is not co-occurrent (*asamavāyin*). The same applies to the semivowel *y*. Thinking that the svarita is purposeless because there is no *guṇa* substitution for *y* before a vowel, one understands the correspondence according to order.

However, since the assignment of the *svarita* accent for *tām* and the others—which are inherent in the actual usage—would also be for the sake of audible perception (*śruti*), one does not resort to a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). The statement "one meaning [is substituted] for one meaning" is merely illustrative. In this way, being posterior to the suffix *ktvā* and being a limiting condition (*upādhi*) of consciousness are possible meanings; when these are present, there is no confusion among the verbal forms. For indeed, the *s* situated in the place of the substitute *tām* does not function in that position.

But is this not also established by the very mention of the numbered items? This can be understood from the commentary: the application of the *svarita* accent to these is for the sake of establishing a correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), not for the sake of being heard; for the application of the *svarita* to these two is solely for the purpose of governing the subsequent rule (*adhikāra*), not for the purpose of being heard.

[1.2] Regarding the phrase "where there is a multiplicity of *āntarya*": here, because of the employment of the *svarita* accent, another rule (*śabda-antara*) is inferred from another *sūtra*. And this inferred rule, depending upon the term "*antaratama*," operates through a distinction as "in place, in place" (*sthāne sthāne*). By this, the following meaning is obtained: "In place, that which is most similar (*antaratama*) occurs; and that which is most similar in place, that occurs."

Where multiple *antaratama* [substitutes] are possible, and where that [term] has multiple meanings and functions by means of different causes, there the proximity of place (*sthānāntaratamya*) is stronger. Otherwise, when multiple operations converge, the rule "in place of [the original], the most similar [element] occurs" would effectively exclude proximity based on meaning, quality, or quantity. Furthermore, if [the sūtra] were occupied with [specifying] "these two," then the statement "it occurs in place [of the original]" would become redundant.

One person is an insider by means of a single cause, while another is so by means of many. How could one who [is an insider] by means of many [causes] be [an insider]? For example, in the world, there is someone with one father and various mothers, someone with one mother and various fathers, and someone with one father and one mother. And if this [definition] were to adopt a worldly state of affairs, then that non-acceptance would be purposeless; for if it adopts a worldly understanding, the very Sūtra is rejected.

[2] For what purpose, then, is this stated? Has the purpose not already been stated by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (A 6.1.101)? It is replied: he asks this in order to determine what undesirable consequence would follow if this were not stated. This is because the substituend (*sthānin*) is indicated as being singular. How is the substituend indicated as singular? If it were by means of its technical name (*saṃjñā*), then the substitute (*ādeśa*) would also be only one, namely, the long vowel (*dīrgha*).

Now, due to the distinction of their designations (*saṃjñā*), there is multiplicity of the substitute (*ādeśa*), and consequently, there is also multiplicity of the original element (*sthānin*). In that regard, it is said that the original element is indicated as a unity because it has already come into being; thus, it is referred to by the term ‘*akaḥ*’. Since the original element, when indicated in the presence of a homogeneous vowel (*aci savarṇe*) by means of a case-ending denoting what has already occurred (*bhūtavibhakti*), cannot be manifold, it is not expressed by this term ‘*akaḥ*’ in its differentiated form. However, the term ‘*dīrghaḥ*’, because it is something yet to be produced (*bhāvyamānatva*), can exist in many forms; therefore, it is indicated as being manifold.

Just as in the world, when one says, "Make a modification of a lump of clay," one perceives the lump of clay as a single entity, while perceiving the modification as manifold—and since it is perceived as manifold where one thinks, "I am making a modification"—so too here, because [the vowel] is being produced as "long" (*dīrgha*), long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) would consequently apply to each individual *ak* vowel in turn among those of the same class.

Others explain it as follows: Just as in the case of the instruction of technical names (*saṃjñā*) and abbreviations (*samāsa*), since there is no fixed order and no mutual reference, a rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) would apply to everything; so too here, when the name *akaḥ* is mentioned without a specific distinction and no mutual reference is made, and when the name *dīrghaḥ* is mentioned, since all vowels (*ac*) having an *uk* [as their substitute] would be subject to the operation, this meaning—that "this long vowel becomes the substitute for this *aka*"—would be impossible. Why, then, was a mutual reference not made? This is undertaken for the sake of brevity by the rule: "In place [of one thing], that which is most similar [is the substitute]."

[3] Furthermore, regarding this "immediate manifestation" (*antaratama-nirvṛtti*): [the phrase] "furthermore, in what way" (*yathā punar*) means *in which manner*. And as for the "continuous recitation" (*saṃhitā-pāṭha*): in the continuous recitation there is a specific distinction; thus, those students who study by means of the continuous recitation should be questioned. In this regard, the view is as follows: "The continuous recitation is the original form of the word" (*padaprakṛtiḥ saṃhitā*, ṚV 2.1). For the continuous recitation alone is the true original form of words that are otherwise unreal [when isolated].

Then, the words (*pada*) are extracted; for while there is a cutting off of the meaning (*artha*), there is no cutting off of the word-form (*śabda*). And having done this, [one sees that] even with a single word, the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not lost. In this regard, he asks here: "Of what kind of word should [the constituent part] be extracted in the rule *sthāne 'ntaratama uraṇ raparaḥ*? In the expression *sthāne 'ntaratama*, the term "*ṣaṣṭhī*" (genitive case) is understood to carry over.

Therefore, in this context, that very base which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the substitute is indicated by the genitive case, and no other is indicated; thus, this is understood as a restriction regarding the base (*prakṛti-niyama*). However, when there is a choice among several possible substitutes, since there is no restriction on the base, the genitive is used everywhere, while the substitute itself is restricted—[indicating] "this does not occur" and "this occurs. For example, in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*: some *ik* vowels are more distant than others; those consisting of two morae (*dvimātra*) are more distant than those consisting of one mora (*mātrika*). Since the one-mora vowels are slightly closer, the genitive is obtained for the short vowels alone, and not for the long ones.

But was it not stated at the beginning that this is not a valid example? True; this is so. When the position is that proximity (*āntarya*) is determined by the substitute (*ādeśa*), then it is not a valid example because [the desired result] is already established by another rule. However, when proximity is determined by the original element (*prakṛti*), this very case is the primary purpose. How so? Because the genitive case endings (*ṣaṣṭhī*) do not apply to long *ik*-vowels. And as for what was said—that proximity of place (*sthāna-āntarya*) is stronger—that was stated with the understanding that proximity may be due to various causes: some by place, others by measure (*pramāṇa*). And this [substitute *i*] is proximate to the *yaṇ* both by place and by measure.

Thus, regarding the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (A 1.1.3), the long vowels *e* and *ai* are [the substitutes]. Since for these two, only the long vowels are the most similar (*antaratama*), the genitive case [in *iko*] refers to the long vowel. But is it not the case that in *nāyakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*, and so forth, the *vṛddhi* [substitute] is governed by *acaḥ...* (A 7.2.115) and is not characterized by the term *ig*? Here too, because of the word *acaḥ*, one must consider the original base (*prakṛti*) to be the most similar [vowel].

Likewise, regarding the possibility of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the vowel *ṛ*: why, then, is this stated? For by the rule "guṇa and *vṛddhi* [replace] *iK*" alone, this would have been enjoined. This is the distinction: *guṇa* might apply to a one-mora (*mātrika*) vowel, but not to a two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel; *vṛddhi* might apply to a two-mora vowel, but not to a one-mora vowel. However, in this case, both [substitutions] would apply to the long *iK*.

Regarding the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (A 6.1.79), a specification of the substituend (*sthānin*) must be made; otherwise, because every *ec* vowel has been mentioned [in the preceding rules], the substitute *vānta* would apply to all of them. However, on the view that the original form (*prakṛti*) is intended, since the most similar original forms (*antaratama*) for the *vānta* substitutes are the vowels *o* and *au*, there is no need for a specification of the substituend. How is this established in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtra? It should proceed by taking into account what has already occurred [in the preceding rules]. Therefore, the term *ecaḥ* from the previous rule is carried over (*anuvartate*) into this rule *vānto yi*.

However, that which is seen here as the substitute *vānta* when there is an *ac* vowel [following] becomes [the substitute] when the suffix *yi* follows. Only this much is required: for what is it seen to occur when an *ac* vowel follows? It is for the vowels *o* and *au*.
