"In that case, then, 'other than in the sense of what is possible' (śakyārtha)..."—he thinks thus: "If the phrase 'in the sense of what is possible' were abandoned, then forms such as *kṣeyāḥ* could not be produced. He explains that this is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). By the rule "the words *kṣayya-* and *jayya-*," forms such as *kṣeyāḥ* and so on are produced; by the rule "in the sense of what is possible" (*śakyārtha*), there is likewise no application of these two elsewhere.

In that case, even here [in this context], it would not follow because of the restriction. He thinks as follows: if inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, then there is exclusion everywhere; but if it is a particular (*viśeṣa*), then a specific instance is intended. The meaning is that a restriction applies to what is of the same class, and a particular instance—such as *kaṇṭhatālvya* (produced by the throat and palate)—is being taken up. The other [opponent] understands that this concerns a subject matter where the phonemes are fused (*praśliṣṭa*), and says: "Even so... it is *raiyatī*. ... "*Rāyi*" is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

It is demonstrated that in the vernacular (bhāṣā), there is no usage [of a word] followed by the letter *ya*. For it has been stated thus: “after a word ending in a vowel identical to those of *go*. Thus it is studied so that there is no usage in the vernacular.

[3.1] Regarding *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* (A 6.4.89): ...the mention of the term *upadhā* must be made. Here it is objected: "In this case, the entire complex (*samudāya*) itself is indicated by the genitive; there is no possibility of anything else. Therefore, how can this be said? This is the intended meaning: if you understand this as a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) due to the absence of any other [logical] indicator (*liṅga*), then you should understand it as an extension (*anusaṃhāra*) from this very treatise.

And this is the conclusion: that which is most proximate (*antaratama*) cannot possibly exist for the substitute (*ādeśa*); therefore, it is not at all connected with the genitive case. Just as by the *alontya-paribhāṣā* (P. 1.1.52), in the rule *ruhaḥ paḥ* (A 7.3.43), there is the understanding that the *pa* replaces the *ha* of *ruha*, so too in the case of *goha*, there ought to be an understanding that [the substitution applies] to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of *go*.

This is done precisely in the *Nyāsa* commentary; if something were to be done that was not previously established, then a fault would arise. And if the view of the base form (*prakṛti-pakṣa*) were faultless or possessed of few faults, it would be appropriate to state it.

The inclusion of the letter *t* must be made. Now, if the inclusion of the letter *t* is not made, how could [the rule] apply to *carita*? It would not be excluded, for the *niṣṭhā* suffix follows immediately. Furthermore, by the rule “of the substitute of what follows, [the operation applies] to the first element” (A 1.1.54), the substitution would apply to the letter *i*. This is the intended meaning: because of the application [of the rule] to the most proximate base (*prakṛti*) by the phrase "of the *niṣṭhā*," the substitution of *n* will occur only for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Thus, the formal statement (*nyāsa*) itself is established. This is what is being said.

Does this [substitution] sublate another subsequent application (*anusaṃhāra*), or is it itself sublated by another subsequent application? If, first of all, it sublates, then because the subsequent application of "the final letter" (*alontya*) has been sublated by the rule *ruhaḥ paḥ* (A 7.3.43), since the letter *u* is labial, the sixth case ending would apply to the letter *u*. Likewise, in the word *trayam*, it would apply to the letter *y*. If, on the other hand, you think it is sublated, then in the rule *goha ūkāraḥ*, it would apply to the letter *h*.

Since the substitution of *jaś* [i.e., *d* for *t*] is established in the rule *bhinnavadbhyām* even when the letter *t* does not exist, and since the dental *d* is the most similar (*antaratama*) original form (*prakṛti*) for the nasal *n*, for it has been stated: "As are the third [consonants], so are the fifth; their additional property is nasality" (MBh 1.61.18, 19). Now, if you think that by the rule *pūrvasya ca daḥ* the substitution does not apply to the following [letter], this [new rule] would be intended to provide what was previously unobtained. Therefore, the original formulation alone is superior.

[4] But what, then, is this "productive" (*nirvartaka*)? The author of the *Bhāṣya* introduces this by means of a question for the sake of the style of the text. For the author of the *Vārttika*, however, since there would be pointlessness (*anarthakya*) in a rule of non-application (*ayoga*) regarding that which is productive or expressive, it possesses purposefulness (*arthavattā*) when it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*). Just as, according to the method of the sixth [chapter], [the rule] is independent, as in "a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) replaces an *ik* vowel before a vowel" (A 6.1.77), so too does it produce the most similar substitute (*antaratama*) in place [of the original].

Furthermore, since that [substitute] is proximate and exists as the most internal element for everything, it must be applied. But does it belong to the whole alone, or to the parts? Since it is impossible for both the whole and the part to exist simultaneously, at one time there would be a substitute for the whole, and at another time for the part.

Furthermore, regarding these rules—namely, *aster bhūḥ* (A 2.4.52) and *ruhaḥ paḥ* (A 7.3.43)—it must be examined whether by these [rules] that word is optionally replaced by the most similar substitute (*antaratama*), or rather, whether it is superseded (*bādhyate*).

[4.1] “When a substitute (*antaratama*) is produced in place of an original element (*sthānin*), there is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of that original element” (Vārttika 2). What kind of linguistic expression is this—“the cessation of the original elements occurs”—when it is certain that the word *dadhi* must necessarily cease here? This is the intended meaning: when the word *dadhi* is being substituted for the word *dadhi*, what kind of cessation could there be among those of identical form and among those possessing the same accent? A total void (*śūnyatā*) is not possible; otherwise, the very usage of the word would be severed.

If a substitution (*ādeśa*) were to occur in a changed form, then, this being the case, its meaningfulness would not be established; thus, in this conceptualization, its lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) is undertaken [as a premise].

And if this were so, there would be a dual form in some instances. Regarding those whose text reads "dissimilarity" (*vairūpya*), those who cite "dissimilarity" as an example—arguing that because the substitute for *viṣ* contains the letter *s*, the rule for the change to *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) would apply—they should be questioned as follows: "If this were the case, it would not happen."

But when this view is held—that even the individual parts undergo the substitution in turn, and that in this context the whole is not stated to be the recipient of the grammatical operation, as in the rule "for a monosyllable, [the first part] is doubled" (A 6.1.1)—then the substitution of *ṣ* would indeed apply; thus, the two forms are justified. However, when the whole is the recipient of the operation, then [the substitution] should not occur; therefore, the inclusion of the term "substitution" (*ādeśa*) is also justified. In this way, the point regarding the two forms (*dvairūpyam*) is established.

Thus, he says "in some cases" (*kvacid*) for this purpose: in a certain alternative (*pakṣe*), there is either a change of form (*vairūpya*) or a double form (*dvairūpya*). Similarly, even in rules such as *aster bhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52), when the substitution applies to both constituent parts, then [double form] occurs; in some cases, however, there is a triple form (*trairūpya*).

Furthermore, the intended systematic arrangement would not be established. This might be the intention: that since the completion of the action occurs in the aggregate, only those aggregates employed for a specific purpose possess the capacity for that action, and thus there would be no inconsistency. However, the intended systematic arrangement is not possible; one would have to repeatedly apply another most proximate factor as a displacer. But surely its displacement would occur at the very moment of its initial application?

This is precisely what we ask: what is the purpose of the single occurrence [of the word], if the grammatical instruction (*ādeśa*) is of such a nature? Or, if it occurs without a purpose, by what is its subsequent occurrence prevented? In that regard, whatever word arises, every one of them is oriented toward cessation; thus, just as the usage of an incorrect form (*asādhū*) such as *lāva*—which is oriented toward the grammatical substitute—is impossible, so too is the usage of every word impossible once it is non-abiding (*anavasthita*).

In this way, regarding the word *buddhau*, the notion that "this [suffix] is correct" would be subject to infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), and thus the grammatical operation (*prayoga*) itself would be obstructed. Similarly, in the case of *dadhi atra*: since both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) are oriented toward the substitution (*ādeśa*), the cause does not remain as a cause, nor does the effect remain as an effect; consequently, there would be no comprehension of the principle that "this [element] must undergo this specific grammatical operation in this context."

Just as sesame seeds thrown into a heated pan do not remain stable and produce the notion that they are constantly rising and falling due to the uninterrupted succession of their upward and downward movements, so too these [phonemes], being unstable in their status as correct forms (*sādhutva*) through the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*), would not be recognized because of this instability. Therefore, this position is untenable.

Alternatively, let it be the case that [the rule] is expressive (*pratipādaka*). According to the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), all long vowels (*dīrgha*) have been produced, applied, and then ceased for the phoneme *a*.

By means of this [rule], the correct application (*pratipatti*) is established for those forms already produced by other rules. According to the principle *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* ("in place of [the original], that which is most similar is substituted"), that which is made most similar in its place is the correct one; it is that which should be employed. Others, even if they have been produced, should not be employed. For example, someone might say, "Let goats be brought," and once they have been brought, he might say, "Keep the black one; remove the others. This sūtra is for this purpose, and it is not redundant here. Nor does it result in the sublation of the word-form as if it were a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*).

[4.2.1] Regarding the realization [of a word], there is the production [of that word] (Vārttika 3). The intention is that the production of desired words is not established. However, the other [opponent] objects by taking recourse to the generality of production: "What then is meant by saying that production is not established? For what purpose would this [rule] be now? He thinks as follows: [If] all [words] were present everywhere, this Sūtra would become useless; therefore, the undesirable consequence of [all words being used everywhere] will not occur.

[4.2.2] And it is meaningless (vārttika 4). This is what is meant: this is not the operation of the word itself. For in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (A 6.1.77), the substitution of *yaṇ* is merely a factor for the application of usage in *saṃhitā* for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), just as the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* is a factor for its application; likewise, the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (A 6.1.101) is also such a factor.

But now that they have ceased to exist, this [usage] currently occurring cannot establish that "those who are correct are those who are correct by contemporary consensus. For another might say, "Only those are correct. Therefore, just as it is impossible to deny the act of eating for one who has already eaten, so too is the cessation of these [words] once they have come into being impossible. It is just as if someone were to say, after goats have been brought in, "The goats have not been brought in"; such is this case.

Therefore, without entering into a discussion of the word *śabda*, he considers the cessation of that which was introduced in the context of *buddhi*. Precisely when there is the introduction of a single sound—namely, "the *ik* vowel becomes *yaṇ*"—regardless of whether some substitute is applied to the original element (*prakṛta*), such as the letter *v* or any other, this [rule] does not apply because it is the most similar (*antaratama*) prior to its occurrence; for immediately after that [introduction], it (the rule) is absent.

Now, if the form of actual occurrence (*pravṛtti*) is not relied upon, and if the consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies to those possessing distinctions—namely, that there is a consequence for *ik* sounds when *yaṇ* sounds are applicable—then this very position does not exist, because this [rule] would be a mere indicator (*pratipādaka*). Therefore, the aforementioned conceptualization is purposeless.
But the other says: "Or it has already been stated" (*uktaṃ vā*). . . .
*uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51).

[1] Is this statement regarding *uraṇ rapara* intended for the purpose of excluding other [substitutes]? In the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3), the dependent status (*pāratantrya*) of this rule is understood. Nevertheless, despite that dependence, since it merely concerns the domain of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*), wherever there is a genitive, this [rule] establishes itself as a new substitute, overriding other previous substitutes. And having established [the occasion for substitution], it prescribes the *rapara* status for this very [substitute] through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*): "An *aṇ* occurs in place of *u*, and that [aṇ] is followed by *r*."

In that context, when the rules for the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*) accents are being formulated, because the genitive case "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) is present, this [rule] presents itself: "Ṛ is replaced by *u*. Since the substitution of *ṛ*-sounds by something not previously connected to a vowel excludes those substitutes that are not the closest possible (*anantaratama*), the purpose of this rule is fulfilled; thus, elsewhere the maxim regarding the closest substitute (*sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā*) is set aside. Or rather, is it merely the fact of having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*) that is effected by this? The function of this rule is merely to bring about the connection with the *guṇa* [vowel].

Regarding the rule *uraṇ*, however, there is only this much dependence: that whatever *u* exists in the place of *u* which has become an *aṇ* by another rule, that [aṇ] is followed by *r*. Thus, those [sounds] which have become *aṇ*s obtain the status of being followed by *r*.

[... there is a fault regarding the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth. (Vārttika 1)] But are those [substitutes] endowed with qualities such as the acute accent, or not? In either case, there is a fault; for if the form were heard exactly as it is prescribed, would this fault not apply? Even so, the rule *ṛkārasyāṇ raparaḥ* (the substitute *ṛ* is followed by *r*) would apply to the vowel *ṛ*. Therefore, the expression *tṛtīya* must indeed be stated for the sake of excluding [the application of that rule]. However, in the case of specific substitutions (*pratipadādeśa*), this [rule] *uraṇ raparaḥ* is superseded by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (A 7.1.100) and *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (A 7.1.102).

For in that case, the Vedic revelation stating "u" would be contradicted in the prescription of all vowels; however, because this [vowel] is being prescribed by this [rule], it is difficult for the substitution of *ra* (raparatva) to apply as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to this.

There is no realization of the *avarṇa* [vowel] in the case of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions (Vārttika 2). By the rule for the substitution of *ra* (raparatva), it would follow that when there is an injunction for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, the *ṛ*-vowel of the *aṇ* [vowels] would be difficult to find as a substitute for which *raparatva* could be applied. For what is more appropriate than the *ṛ*-vowel in the place of a non-homogeneous vowel (*asavarṇa*)? Is there a reason for the *ṛ*-vowel in the place of a non-homogeneous vowel, or rather, what is the better reason? This same fault applies even to the former position;
namely, the fault already mentioned regarding the position of the exception (*apavāda*), where this defect also occurs: the non-realization of the *avarṇa*.

But it is not the case that *eṅ* and *aic* [are substituted]; rather, since *iṭ* and *ut* would also result [as substitutes], a definitive understanding of the *a*-vowel [substitution] is not possible. Now, if it is thought that [the rule] "in place of *uḥ*, both *aṇ* and *anaṇ*" applies—whereby what was previously proposed, namely that "a new *aṇ* is produced which sublates [others]," is rejected—is that so? No; rather, it is restricted [to specific cases].

Regarding this, some explain as follows: the term *sthāne* (in place of), having undergone elision (*lopa*), is understood here either in the genitive plural or the locative plural. The connection is made thus: "there is a *guṇa*, there is a *vṛddhi*; in place of an *ṛ*-vowel, a *guṇa*—an *aṇ* followed by *r*—occurs; a *vṛddhi*—an *aṇ* followed by *r*—occurs. Since *i* and *u* are not themselves *guṇas* or *vṛddhis*, they will not be subject to these rules.

Alternatively, as for the genitive case *ur* in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, this is not independent (*anapekṣā*). What then? It is dependent on what is applicable (*prasajyamānāpekṣā*). Among those [substitutes] that are applicable in place of *u*, only *aṇ* occurs; no other occurs. And when it does occur, it is followed by *r*. Since the application of substitutes is governed by other rules of the science (*śāstrāntarapratibaddha*), no restrictive rule (*niyama*) is made here; thus, how could there be an application of *i* and *u*? In the former view, the understanding of the vowel *a* is established.

For that very same aforementioned position of exclusion (*apavādapakṣa*) is here adopted in the form of the cessation of another, and not in the form of the production of some previously non-existent new element (*apūrva*). And having established this, in some versions of the earlier text there is no use of the particle *eva*. The text is simply this: "An *aṇ* [substitute] occurs in place of *u*. It does not mean that what is being prescribed here excludes another; for just as there is the exclusion of others in the case of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), so it is here as well.

As for that which was said regarding the fault in the case of the acute (*udātta*) and other accents—does that fault arise here? He begins with a question: "How do you think it is? This is the intention: this [rule] establishes the determination by means of the *sthānentaratama* paribhāṣā; vowels such as the acute and others are the most similar (*antaratama*). Once the most similar ones have been established, there is no possibility of the application of the *aṇ* [substitute].

Now, if this very *paribhāṣā* governs only the first contingency, namely "an *udātta* vowel" (*aca udāttaḥ*), then a fault arises. The other [opponent], considering that the *uraṇ rapara* rule has already established the closest possible substitutes (*anantaratama*) and thus the present rule does not apply to them, says: "The *antarata* rule [is required]; otherwise, that fault arises. How so? Because by the word "acute" (*udātta*), both *aṇ* vowels and non-*aṇ* vowels are indicated.

Even though [substitutes] are specifically indicated, they do not actually apply; rather, "the most similar one (*antaratama*) occurs in its place. The intention is that, because of the *antaratama* paribhāṣā, this other restrictive rule will not operate in the present case once the primary restriction has been established. Why indeed is this so? Between two paribhāṣās... the scope (*avakāśa*) of the *antaratama* paribhāṣā is seen in rules such as *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (A 6.1.101) and *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām* (A 8.4.62).

The scope of the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* is, for example, *kartā*, *hartā*. Here, however, both rules would apply simultaneously in the forms *kṛtiḥ* and *hṛtiḥ*. It is established by the paribhāṣā *sthānentaratamaḥ* (the substitute is the most similar to the original), and not by this rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*. Thus they explain.

Whence is this derived—that there will be a prohibition of the preceding rule (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) and not, on the contrary, a prohibition of the subsequent rule (*paravipratiṣedha*)? Or rather, when the most proximate (*antaraṅga*) application of the rule "the vowel is acute" (*aca udāttaḥ*) has occurred, another restrictive rule (*niyamāntara*) will not apply; but it does not mean that this very rule "uraṇ raparaḥ" restricts the preceding application itself.

And as for the statement, "and those which belong to the vowel *ṛ*": for where there is the application of something else, there this rule (or connection) assumes the nature of a restriction (*niyama*). But here, since the application belongs only to *i* and *u*, there is an absence of such a restriction; consequently, the principal sentence—"an [vowel] occurs in place of *uḥ*"—does not even come into operation. And because that does not operate, the subordinate sentence—"it becomes followed by *r*"—also does not operate.

But [the desired result] is established in the present context because of the substitution of *r* for *ra*. It is kept in mind that two instances of the term "place" (*sthāna*) are being carried over here. Even though the second position—that by this rule only the substitution of *ra* for *r* is effected—is indeed the same position as before, this specific distinction is now adopted: previously, the time was not determined; now, the time is determined. However, in this case, there is attainment (*prāpti*), not restriction (*niyama*), nor completion (*nirvṛtti*).

In that case, having set aside both the restriction (*niyama*) and the occurrence (*nirvṛtti*), the substitution of *r* for *ra* is applied precisely at the time of attainment (*prāpti*). What is meant by this is as follows: that very same time which is fixed for the position (*sthāna*) by means of attainment is itself the time for the substitution of *r* for *ra*.

In that context, at the very moment the intellect functions with the thought "by what [substitute] must it be replaced?", the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* is already obtained; thus, since the *repha* (the sound *r*) is not present at the time of the application of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, the closest internal substitute will occur. This has been established: the rule *uraṇ rapara* arises as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for the cause of the operation of the maxim *sthānentaratama*.

"If the injunction were thus without qualification," he thinks, "one [term] *sthāna* (place/position) would follow; by that, time is determined. But that [element] whose time is thus determined, when it is associated with *rapara* (followed by *r*), would apply either immediately before or in the vicinity of *u*. How so? For where the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed as having already occurred, the rule 'the genitive [denotes] the place' (A 1.1.49) does not apply here. And for this reason it does not apply, because he recites: 'In the place of the *āt* of the northerners... (A 7.3.46)."

The mention of *sthāna* (place/position) from the second [sūtra] is carried over here. Some explain it thus: by virtue of the context, the word ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) here becomes nominative (*prathamānta*), as in "the *aṇ* is the place. We, however, say that this explanation is made in this way: at the very time when *u* is the place—meaning at the time when [the substitute] followed by *r* (*rapara*) is about to be applied—this place has not yet been occupied by the substitute; it is precisely at that time that the quality of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) applies.

There is another interpretation: that by which both the view of an exception (*apavāda*) and the view of a restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*) are possible. [The opponent argues: "It becomes a quality (*guṇa*) of the *aṅga*. For even when there is a mention in the genitive case, such as in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, this very [rule] operates in this manner: "A *guṇa* occurs for the *aṅga*; the *uṭ* is *aṇ*, and that [substitute] has *r* as its subsequent element (*rapara*). Thus, first of all, a previously unestablished *aṇ* is prescribed by this [rule]; therefore, it is the view of an exception.

Then, by being connected with the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, it attains the status of a single sentence: "The *guṇa* of the *aṅga* occurs; but the *guṇa* is *aṇ*, not any other *guṇa*; the *vṛddhi* is *aṇ*, not any other *vṛddhi*. In this way, a restriction (*niyama*) arises. However, in this interpretation, no distinction is observed, since in the previous interpretation a second mention of "place" (*sthāna*) was relied upon, whereby only *aṇ* occurs in place of those [sounds] that were not otherwise applicable.

If this alternative were not accepted, then in the section concerning *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there would arise the contingency of requiring substitutes that are not otherwise obtained by implication; thus, for these [substitutes], it would be as if they were *aṇ*. If this alternative were not accepted, then in the case of the two injunctions regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* forming a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*), the result would be: "the *u* is *guṇa*" and "the *aṇ* is *vṛddhi*. However, all other enumeration [of such consequences] and the failure to remedy the resulting defects [would follow].

[2] What is the purpose of including the mention of *an*? This is an introduction to the subsequent section. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of stating the elision (*lopa*)?", it is for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), or, according to the view that [the substitute] begins with the final letter (*parādipakṣa*), for the sake of the *r*-sound (*rutva*). [Example: *hotāpotārau*. Once the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) has been applied to the *r*, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur; as in the case of *pacann*.

[3] An addition should be made regarding the single substitute (ekādeśa). This is the intended meaning: just as in the case of receiving a bride, it is recited as "to Prajāpati," but not separately for the ornaments as "to Agni," nor for the garment as "to Bṛhaspati," so too here, by the rule *pūrvaparayoḥ* (A 6.1.84), the composite whole is stated to be the locus of substitution (*sthānin*).

However, because that [composite] consists of the prior and posterior parts, it is referred to as "of the prior and posterior" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*), just as the composite whole [in *pra-u-aṇa-ka-*] becomes the phoneme *ṇ*. Thus, there is an absence of the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatva*).

It is established by the mention of the "part" (*avayava*). Since there exists within this aggregate the phoneme *ṛ* as a part, the designation *ur* is based upon that; thus, the rule of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) will apply. For example, when it is said, "Māṣa beans are not to be eaten," even those mixed with them are not eaten. However, this principle is contradicted; for it has been stated: "A grammatical operation concerning a whole does not apply to its part, just as [the term] 'substance' [does not apply to a part of a substance]. (MBh 1.25.3)

"Clarified butter is not for sale; oil is not for sale"—yet cows and mustard seeds are sold. This being the case, no distinct designation is seen for the eight [substances], such as *surā* and the rest. Likewise, the consumption of *māṣa* beans and so forth is not explicitly mentioned; it follows merely from the presence of desire. Furthermore, there is no word in common usage to the effect that "these *māṣa* beans are of such a kind, while those are not. To whatever extent the scent of *māṣa* exists, that entire collection is indeed *māṣa*, because it consists of those very parts.

Since no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for the aggregate as a whole, the operation must reside in its constituent parts (*avayava*). However, when it is conceived in this way—as a substitute (*ādeśa*)—there is a prohibition regarding that which ends in *r* (*rānta*). For even in the case of a substitute, the form of the *aṇ* vowel exists, and the aggregate remains inactive. Just as the designation *ur* is applied because the form of the *ṛ*-vowel exists therein, so too the substitute is designated as *aṇ* because it possesses the *aṇ* as a constituent part; thus, the status of having *r* as its final element (*raparatva*) would follow. But how can logic be abandoned? This is the intended meaning: the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is expressed by the rule "the *aṇ* is followed by *r* (*uraṇ raparaḥ*)."

The vowel *ṛ* is the primary [substitute], and it is also the original element (*sthānin*) by virtue of its status as such. Since the whole is both that which is to be replaced and that which effects the replacement within the aggregate, it is impossible for it to rely on the nature of its individual parts; thus, neither the part to be replaced nor the part effecting the replacement exists. However, if one relies on the operation of the word (*śabdavyāpāra*) and adopts the notion that the form of the whole is what is grasped, then the status of being the original element (*sthānitva*) is established; yet, in the case of the substitute (*ādeśa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *rapara*. Furthermore, if the original element were to consist of the vowel *ṛ* at its end...

Some, however, say that the term *antagrahaṇa* (mention of "end") must be supplied. Others explain it thus: "Wherever there is a genitive case, this [rule] applies," and thus it is a rule concerning the end of that which ends in a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyantatadantavidhi*). And where is the prescription? It is in the rule *aṅgasya guṇaḥ* ("there is guna of the stem"). If here the phrase "of that which ends in *i*" and "of that which ends in an *ṛ*-vowel" were connected as a restatement of what was not previously established, then in the word *kartṛ*, because of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the form *set* exists; therefore he says: "This too [is included] by virtue of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* as ending in an *ṛ*-vowel."

Now, if it is argued that this is a case of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), then a distinction could be postulated based on the acceptance or rejection of its meaning; for a *vyapadeśivadbhāva* is not tied to a single form. Indeed, one does not say "the jar of the jar. And here, a prohibition of the quality of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) would have to be stated—as in "of the mother" (*mātuḥ*) and "of the father" (*pituḥ*). This is what is intended.

If, after applying *uttva* to both the preceding and following sounds by A 6.1.111 (*ṛta ut*) and then applying *raparatva*, the substitution of *ru* for the *s* of the case-ending were made, followed by the elision of *r* by A 8.3.14 (*ro ri*) and the lengthening of the vowel, then the form *mātūḥ karoti* would result.

Neither the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) nor the prohibition (*niṣedha*) should be made; this is what is demonstrated by the statement "here, when two [elements] are indicated by the genitive. In the expression *pūrvaparayoḥ*, the two parts themselves are the substituends (*sthānin*), because the completion of the sentence applies to each one individually. The whole (*samudāya*) is indicated by them, and the singular marker (*ekagrahaṇa*) serves as a sign so that there may not be a distinction [of the substitute] due to the distinction of the substituends. Just as a single son is designated as belonging to both [parents], so too is the substitute.

By the rule *‘rāt sasya’* (A 8.2.24), there is elision of the *s* as in *atsā*; however, by the rule *‘apratyayavisarjanīyasya’* (A 8.3.34), the substitution of *ṣ* would apply. It is thought thus: a designation (*saṃjñā*) that refers to a whole does not extend to its constituent part, the vowel *a*. Therefore, the *repha* (the *r*) is not a suffix (*apratyaya*). Yet, this [visarga] is indeed a suffixal *visarjanīya*. This is the intended meaning: because that vowel *a* is a constituent part of the suffix, it receives the designation "suffix"; consequently, the *repha* is designated as belonging to the suffix.

"In this case, the *visarjanīya* of the suffix is elided. At the stage when the substitution of *u* (*uttva*) is prescribed, the designation "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) has not yet been acquired by the vowel *ā*; it is acquired later by the consonant *s*. Since that [designation] has ceased, it is incorrect to say that the previously unacquired [designation] is now acquired by the vowel *ā*. Therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) would apply. Now, he sets aside this [objection] by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*):

The mention of *bhrātuṣputra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur after a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). That is to say, it does not occur for a following *visarjanīya* that follows an *iṇ* vowel which has that single substitute as its cause.

[4] But what is this "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*)? Furthermore, in the instruction "how is *ra* the subsequent," how is the *repha* (the sound *r*), which has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), connected as either the end or the beginning? It might be thought that since only the mere conjunction with the *repha* is prescribed by this rule, the *repha* possesses primacy. If primacy were based on functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*), then the word does not prompt such a *repha*; therefore, it is connected with the qualifiers.

In this regard, they say as follows: this is what is meant—it should not be necessary to mention "the subsequent" (*para*) when adopting the view that the term refers to the preceding (*pūrvānta*). Let it be simply: *ur aṇ ra*. The word "end" (*anta*) is understood from the previous context. The same applies to the view that it refers to the subsequent (*parādipakṣa*). Even in the case where *ur* is taken as a fifth-case (*pañcamī*) form, once its status as being subsequent is established, there is no need to mention "the subsequent."

Now, if it is applied, the meaning of the sūtra becomes "for the sake of the individual letter" (*vyaktyartha*); thus the sense of the sūtra is established: "In place of *u*, that which is mentioned [as *ṛ*] becomes *ra* following this [vowel], and it becomes the initial [element]. Now, if neither [of these two conditions] is carried over, then it is "unattached" (*abhakta*).

This investigation, however, is appropriate by resorting to the position of restriction (*niyamapakṣa*). And in that position, recourse is made to the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), or there is a connection of one restriction with another restriction. By collecting all the nominative case indications (*sarvān ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśān*) regarding the substitutes for *pratipad* and taking them as a whole, it is accepted that the restriction is established on the grounds that "there exists something to be produced. When a fault occurs, there are three positions.

But when the position is that "in the case of *prasaṅga*, the *r* follows," then just as there is no inquiry regarding the letter *n* in *anaṅ* and the like—namely, whether the *n* of *anaṅ* is non-separable (*abhakta*) or initial (*parādi*)—so too there should be no such inquiry here: namely, whether this [substitute] is initial and non-separable.

However, even in this view, one may infer this by the very force of the recurrence of the word "initial" (*ādi*): at the time of the cessation of the original element (*sthānin*), it is a part of that; but subsequently, in whatever operations [are to be performed], it becomes initial, just like the suffixes beginning with *syat*.

In this context, "beginning" (*pūrvānta*) refers either to the end of the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) or to the [final] vowel (*aṇ*). However, because it is a part of a part, it also applies to the aggregate itself. Likewise, [the term "beginning"] refers to that which is followed by a case-suffix (*vibhakti-pratyaya*) or another collection of suffixes (*pratyaya-samudāya*) whose presence is invariably fixed.

[4.1] *gīḥ* / *pūḥ* / For when there is no division (*abhakta*), an indivisible entity cannot receive a designation as a "part. Thus, it is swallowed (*nijegilyate*). In the case of *giraḥ* with the *repha*, this genitive case—which does not relate to any constituent part—is impossible to justify. It is itself swallowed (*gīryate*). Even if there were an explicit statement of instruction (*upadeśavacana*) regarding the intervention of *yak* by means of the *repha*, it would still not be established, precisely because of that intervention. According to the rule "in the formulation of vowel rules (*svaravidhi*), a consonant is as if non-existent," this *paribhāṣā* must be resorted to in this view.

One must provide a remedy for these faults. Even in the case of the repeated syllable (*abhyasta-svara*), this same solution applies; however, it was not employed because it has already been stated. [Regarding *halādiśeṣa*: Whatever remains as the residue (*śiṣyate*) must be replaced by that very same form. Thus, under the assumption that the reduplicated syllable becomes non-consonantal (*ahal*), the rule would not apply because the letter *r* occupies more than one position. This refers to the prohibition regarding the *visarjanīya*. For, since it is not part of the preceding element (*abhakta*), it becomes a word-final (*padānta*) due to the inclusion of its initial portion.

"Because that which begins with what is subject to the rules for suffixes (*sup* and *tiṅ*) is called a *subanta* or *tiṅanta* word" (Paribhāṣā 23). Furthermore, there would be an instability regarding suffixes, as in the forms *kirataḥ* and *girataḥ*. What is the intention behind the requirement of the dual number? In the case of *kiratī*, both the *aṅga* (the stem) and the *vikaraṇa* (the verbal suffix) would apply. Since the *vikaraṇa* is obligatory, it must occur; whereas the *guṇa* substitution of the *aṅga* is non-obligatory, because it is prohibited once the *vikaraṇa* has been applied.

Therefore, when the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) has been applied, since the correctness of the form is authorized on the condition that the doubling (*cittva*) follows from it, there is no lack of systematic order. But here, in the case of the dual, both are obligatory: the stem-augment (*āṅga*) and the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*). Because the stem-augment applies first due to its higher priority, the suffixal augment follows later; thus, because the *r* is not part of the suffix, it does not belong to the verbal root (*dhātu*), and consequently, the incorrectness of the suffixal augment following that *r* would result.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the *repha* [the sound 'r'] following an affixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) is permissible, yet because it does not follow a vowel (*aṇ*), the desired form is not established, then the non-establishment of the suffixes is illustrated specifically in the case of the dual number.

[4.2] The restriction regarding *ru* must be formulated as "in the case of *sup*" (A 8.3.16) for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is because in forms such as *gīrṣu* and *pūrṣu*, the *ru* is at the end of a word (*padānta*) when followed by *sup*. However, if it were treated as part of the following element (*parādau*), it would be included by the very mention of *sup*; thus, even though it is not a constituent part (*abhaktaḥ*) of the suffix, it would still be affected by the rule due to the principle that "it belongs to what precedes it" (*tadādivacanāt*). Therefore, the restriction regarding *ru* must be made. It must also be made to exclude that which is inherently present even when [the *ru*] occurs at the beginning of the following element, so that it does not apply here in the case of *caturṣu*.

This is for the sake of [the example] *nārkalpi*. This [suffix], being part of the compound word *kalpi*, is not able to obstruct the status of the preceding element as being at the end of a word (*padānta*). When the suffix *iñ* is prescribed after the word *nṛkalpa*, and the *vṛddhi* strengthening is applied, of what does the *repha* (the letter *r*) become the initial? It becomes the initial of the entire complex of the suffix, namely the word *kalpi*. With respect to that complex, the *repha*, which is a constituent part of it, cannot be excluded by the rule "it is preceded by that" (*tasmin pūrve*).

However, that which is the word *kalpa* does not have [the suffix] as its constituent part (*avayava*). A constituent part can be designated as being either prior to or subsequent to another constituent part. Therefore, because the mention of "that beginning with it" (*tadādi*) applies to the *kalpa*-suffix, the letter *r* possesses the status of being a word-final (*padānta*). What kind of expression is this—"it is not capable of being a constituent part"? This is the meaning: because it is included within the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), it is a constituent part of that aggregate.

Regarding that member of a compound which possesses the status of being a word-final (*padānta*) within its own constituent part (*kalpa*), one cannot deny it; thus say others: "This [member] is subordinate to the compound of the word *kalpa*. They explain it as follows: a word that is a constituent part of *kalpa* is designated as a *kalpi-pada*. Therefore, a non-*kalpi* word is not a *kalpi-pada*. Its constituent part, namely *kalpi*, is what is meant.

[4.3] [Regarding *dhunutaḥ*: ] Here too, in the singular form, there is no difference whether the elision of *dhinoti* occurs or not. Whether the *guṇa* substitution is applied by [the rule] *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), or once the *guṇa* has been made, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) is applied by [the rule] *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97)—as in the case of *paca*—therefore the dual form is cited [as an example]. [The phrase] "that which ends in *a* in the *ārdhadhātuka* instruction" means "that which ends in *a* when the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is being introduced."

For at the very time when it acquires the nature of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there is never a moment when the state of having an *a*-vowel ending for these two—taught by way of a fixed grammatical connection (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*)—has not been attained; thus, the elision (*lopa*) is established.

"It is said that substitutes (ādeśa) occur for that which is indicated by the genitive case. But does this not contradict the subsequent summary (anusaṃhāra), namely "as follows" (*yathā*)? This is not a fault. That which is signified by the genitive form *ṇalaḥ*—namely, the domain of usage—is what undergoes substitution. Because there is no distinction between the form itself and its designation, and because they are determined to be one, it is stated: "for that which is indicated by the genitive. Consequently, the diphthong *au* replaces the vowel *a* belonging to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*.

The form *akāra* is directly perceived through hearing; however, that which is devoted to it (*tadbhakta*) will not be considered as being "inferred" (*anumīyamāna*), because of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54). This is because [the substitute] is separated by the letter *repha*. Furthermore, the vowel *akāra* is relied upon in its own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*), and its specific form (*tadrūpa*) is what is separated. If, however, it were stated as *liṭaḥ* or *pratyayasya*, then because there would be no separation, the substitution (*ādeśa*) would indeed occur.

In the case of the suffix *caṅ*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel. [Objection: But surely, by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), this shortening would apply even to a vowel that is not in the penultimate position, since the rule teaches the substitution of *e* in "at smṛdṝtvara... (A 7.4.95). [Response: True, this is so; however, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This [shortening] would also occur here: *acīkṛtat*, *acikīrtat*.

Furthermore, the systematic application (*vyavasthā*) of the augment *iṭ* would not be established, resulting in the form *āstaritā*. This is the thought: [if the rule were applied first,] both the *guṇa* substitution and the *iṭ* augment would apply. Because the *guṇa* is both subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*), it would take precedence. Once the *guṇa* has been applied, the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply by the rule "there is no *iṭ* after a root ending in *r*, nor in the case of roots beginning with *v*," resulting in a lack of systematic application in the form of non-occurrence. If [the *iṭ*] were to occur, there would be the undesirable systematic application of hearing the *iṭ* before the *repha*. However, if the *iṭ* were to occur first and the *guṇa* afterwards, there would be no fault whatsoever; for that which is subsequent in its actual state becomes the initial element of that which has manifested.

Lengthening does not occur in cases such as *gīḥ* and *pūḥ*. If, while the elision (*lopa*) has not yet taken place, the substitution of *u* for *i* or *u* (*idutva*) and the replacement by *r* (*raparatva*) were to apply, then the elision itself would not take place, because the designation *apṛkta* would be absent. Therefore, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *u* for *i* or *u* and the replacement by *r* occur after the elision has taken place. Under the conception that "this [suffix] is the initial element of that which follows when a *sup* suffix has arisen," once the elision [of the *s*] by the rule *rāt sasya* (A 8.2.24) has been performed, lengthening would not apply.
[This is governed by the rule: *alo ’ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

[1] What is this non-specification (*agrahaṇa*)? Because the formulation is identical, it is not known whether this is the nominative plural or the genitive singular. They support two alternatives and explain the subsequent text as follows: "If, however, it were stated that 'it belongs to the final phoneme' (*alantyasya*). If it were explained in this way, one would explain it without doubt by means of an alternative interpretation that this [term *al*] ends in the nominative plural. However, for others, the text remains exactly as it stands.

One might argue that this mention of *al* ought to function solely as a qualifier of the final [element], and thus they determine that *al* is in grammatical apposition with "the final. Even if it were a qualifier of the final, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would remain unspecified; consequently, the form of a substitute consisting of multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) would also be determined by the rule "such a form belongs to the final *al*," which would result in a multiple-phoneme substitute applying to the final element. Therefore, under this view, the sūtra must be formulated as: "That which consists of multiple phonemes or is marked with *ś* replaces the whole" (A 1.1.55).

If, however, it were stated as "of the final" (*antyasya*), or if this were explained in that way, then by resorting to such an interpretation, the form of the substitute would be established as having the nature of the final [element] alone; consequently, elision (*lopa*) would apply to the whole [word], according to the rule "there is elision of *ra*, *ho*, and *rajas*" (A 5.4.51), as in the case of *virajīkaroti*. Furthermore, the entire collection [of letters] would result in being the final [element], because when a letter is mentioned elsewhere, it refers to the genus (*jāti*).

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the mention of *al* here? [the answer is: for the sake of elision (*lopa*). And [this is so] lest the elision apply to the final [sound]. However, it is understood from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that this is not a reference to a genus (*jāti*). What is the indicative mark? It is [the rule] *ṅic ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53). For if there were a reference to a genus, then since an operation marked by *ṅ* would already be established as applying to the final [sound], this [rule] would possess a restricted capacity. It is called a "restriction" (*niyama*) because its result is restriction.

Since [the rule] states that "substitutes (*ādeśa*) occur in place of the final," the mention of *al* is for the purpose of excluding non-vowels (*anala*), because even non-vowels are implied by that [statement].

Even so, the final [element] remains unspecified; that is, it is not specified as being "of such a form. This being the case, whatever final element is possible in a grammatical derivation and is indicated by the genitive case would apply to everything. For instance, in the case of *paramānaḍudbhyām*, because *anaḍuh* is indicated by the genitive case, the letter *d* would have to apply to every occurrence of the word *anaḍuh* since it is its final element. As for the phrase "even of a sentence," the mention of a "sentence" (*vākya*) is made because the fault pertains to it; however, it is not possible for a sentence to be a final element indicated by the genitive case.

Therefore, the position that qualifies the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indeed faulty; thus, only the position that qualifies the final letter (*antya*) is faultless. Even if this were the intended meaning, it establishes the following: this rule (*yoga*) must necessarily be formulated, for [it would otherwise fall under] the prohibition of exceptions (*apavāda-vipratiṣedha*) in a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), resulting in the substitution of the whole. For if the reading did not exist, there would be no sequence, and thus neither the preceding nor the subsequent [substitution] would be possible.
However, if one observes merely brevity (*lāghava*), then even in the case of the position qualifying the final letter, that [rule] need not be composed.

[2] The rule *alo 'ntyasya* is a restatement (*anusaṃhāra*) of what has been understood as a substitute in its place. The entire sūtra *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (A 1.1.49) is here pronounced with its accent (*svaryate*). Therefore, that genitive case which is recognized as being connected to "in the place of" (*sthāneyoga*), which is delimited, distinguished from other domains, and not overridden by exceptions—that [genitive] refers to the final phoneme (*alo 'ntyasya*). Or, it refers to whatever is the substitute (*ādeśa*). This restatement regarding the place does not apply elsewhere; rather, for that which is heard exactly as it is, whether it be the beginning or the end of a word ending in a genitive, or something subsequent, it is applied.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). If only the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) were intended to be emphasized, then whatever genitive occurs in grammar would apply to the [entire] audible form. What then? It applies to the final *al* (phoneme). Just as the rule for the exception to the genitive is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), so too is this rule "of the final *al*" a subordinate element; thus, this genitive in *ārdhadhātukasya* does not refer to the entire complex, but rather to the final *al*.

That [substitution] operates according to its actual purpose: in some cases by way of the relationship between a substituendum (*sthānin*) and a substitute (*ādeśa*), and in other cases by the total elimination of both the substituendum and the substitute. [If it were otherwise,] even those marked with *ṭ*, *k*, or *m* would apply to the final letter; thus, the augment *iṭ* would have to precede the vowel *ṛ*, as in *bhavitā*. Furthermore, in this way, the augment would not belong to the entire base (*samudāya*), but only to the vowel *ā*; however, what was stated—that "an augment belongs to that which possesses meaning, being subordinate to it" (MBh 1.75.5)—would then be untenable.

And likewise, in the case of *praṇidāpayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* is not established. Similarly, as for the question "of what is the *num* [augment]?"—even under the view that it belongs to the final letter (*antyasya*), since there is no *num* for the *aṅga*, neither the elision of the *n* nor the change of *gīḥ* to *gh* would apply.

[2.1] Furthermore, if this were understood as a remainder of a rule (*yogaśeṣa*), it would establish that only the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not supplied. How so? For this sūtra, "of the final [sound] (*alo 'ntyasya*)," [is a remainder]. And in the case of a remainder of a rule, what [would happen]? An undesirable consequence would follow. The form of the sixth case in the phrase "of the *ārdhadhātuka*" (*ārdhadhātukasya*) is established even for the final [element] by a primary (or general) statement.

In this regard, since the rule *ādiṣṭi* is operative, why should it subvert the form of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—namely, that "this [rule] does not apply here because of the final *al*"? Or rather, should it subvert the restriction of scope (*viṣayaniyama*)—namely, that "there is no connection with a substitute" (*sthāneyoga*)? It is logical that it should subvert the scope while not subverting the form of the genitive here; for it is precisely the subsequent application (*upasaṃhāra*) that is subverted accordingly, and not the scope itself.

(Regarding the rules *ādeḥ parasya* and *anekālśit sarvasya*: He states that "in this view, the fault is equal," thus saying: "Therefore it is well said... 'otherwise, there would be the contingency of an undesired result'. And this subsequent application (*anusaṃhāra*) is set aside by another subsequent application, namely by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*; whereas the rule *anekālśit sarvasya*, even though its application is possible, is a sublater (*bādhaka*). And [the substitute] marked with the marker *ḍ* [replaces the whole]. (Pāṇini 1.1.53)

[1] Because the application of the *ṅit* designation for *tātaṅ* has its own scope, even an exception (*apavāda*) is set aside by the fact that another rule applies to the same locus. For instance, in the compound *devadattaputraḥ*, the rule "the final syllable of a compound is udātta" (*samāsāntodāttatva*) supersedes the rule "after a word denoting an agent, the suffixes *datta* and *śruta* [are udātta]" (*A 6.2.148*). Likewise, it is with the rule "and when *ṅit*" (*ṅic ca*). Although this [rule] sets aside the general application [of the accent], nevertheless, since the *ṅit* designation of *tātaṅ* could serve other purposes as well, whether it is motivated by the *ṅit* status remains doubtful.

Because of that doubt, the application (*upasthāna*) of the rule is itself doubtful, just like the general rule (*utsarga*). Since its strength is diminished by being set aside (*apakṛṣyamāṇabala*), it is unable to sublate [the exception]; thus, it is called a "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*).

[2] Regarding the purpose [of the marker]: "that which is mandatory" (*niyogataḥ*). For it is not possible that the *ṅit*-ness of *ṇiṅ* serves the purpose of causing the *ātmanepada* endings and the purpose of not obstructing the general inclusion [of roots], in the same way that the addition of the marker *ṇit* is possible for the purpose of general inclusion; this is because the addition of the marker *ṇit* to *ṇiṅ* would have its own scope [elsewhere]. However, in this case, when the status of being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*) has been obtained, then the addition of the marker *ṅit* would indeed serve the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*.

"But that very thing is difficult to accomplish," he says; for that which is the cause of the doubt regarding its application—that very cause is absent. Therefore, why would this rule *ṅidyo 'ntyasya* ("when a marker *ṅ* is present, the operation applies to the final letter") not apply? In that case, [the author] intends to demonstrate: "Since he makes this marker *ṅ*, this [substitution] must be a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa). How so? This application of the marker *ṅ* by the Teacher is solely for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. And since that prohibition is not possible unless there is a replacement for the whole, the application of the marker *ṅ* is itself the means to ensure it is a replacement for the whole.

If, however, the introduction of the marker *ṅ* is intended for the sake of the final element, then it is possible to understand that it is a substitute for the final letter through another means; thus he says: "Otherwise, he would have stated it right in the section on the substitution of *u* for the *e* of the imperative (*loṭ*). [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.55: "That which consists of more than one phoneme (anekāl) and that which has the marker *ś* (śit) replaces the whole."

This is not so; [the replacement] will be a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa) precisely because of the utterance of the sound *ś*. The meaning is that this occurs because [the substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). But surely, the hearing of the sound *ś* would then follow? This is not a fault. For the elision (*lopa*) of anything other than the purpose [of the marker] is intended here. In this case, the purpose of the sound *ś* is that the entire group [of sounds] should be set aside. And once the group has been set aside, that which was employed for the sake of the grammatical operation will itself be set aside.

In that case, consider the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (A 7.1.21). Previously, it was shown that the principle *alo 'ntyasya* (A 1.1.52) applies; now, the application of *ādeḥ parasya* (A 1.1.54) is being demonstrated. Or rather, its inclusion is for this specific purpose. Alternatively, the possibility of an illustrative example is being established. The letter *ś* is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since there is another purpose for the letter *ś*, it will not be for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Thus, it occurs in place of the final [phoneme].

How can there be the substitution of *śi* or *śī* for the final [element], given that these are both ablative case endings (*pañcamī*)—namely, “of a pronoun” (*sarvanāmnaḥ*) and “from a neuter” (*napuṃsakāt*)? In such a case, the rule “for what follows, the initial [element is affected]” (*ādeḥ parasya*) would have to apply. However, it is thought as follows: the term “of a pronoun” (*sarvanāmnaḥ*) is a genitive of relation (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*), and “from a neuter” (*napuṃsakāt*) is a qualifier of that which is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*).
